stem: An electrician employed by a subcontractor arrives to start work on a new-build site. He assumes the induction is the main contractor's job alone and plans to skim the rules afterwards. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The principal contractor must provide the induction, but responsibility for the rules then rests with the site manager rather than with individual workers
options.B: The principal contractor must ensure a suitable induction is provided, and the electrician must still follow the site rules and report shortcomings
options.C: The electrician's own employer must run the induction, and the principal contractor only has to confirm that the electrician holds a valid CSCS card
options.D: Induction is good practice rather than a legal requirement, so the electrician may decline it if he has worked on similar sites before

explanation: The principal contractor must make sure a suitable induction is given, but each worker also has a legal duty to cooperate, follow the site rules and report dangers.

why_wrong.A: Workers have their own legal duties to follow site rules and to take reasonable care.
why_wrong.C: The principal contractor must ensure a suitable site-specific induction, and a card does not replace it.
why_wrong.D: Site induction is a requirement under CDM, and previous experience elsewhere does not remove it.

common_mistake: Thinking that once the principal contractor has run the induction, the worker has no further duties to follow the rules or speak up. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 1 --- Legal Responsibilities

stem: A groundworks firm starts on a small site on Monday. The client says toilets and washing facilities will arrive on Wednesday, and meanwhile the crew can use a tap by the neighbouring yard, which is marked as not for drinking. What is the correct view?

options.A: The duty to provide welfare belongs to the client, so the firm can start work and leave the delay for the client to resolve
options.B: Two days without them is acceptable for a small crew, provided the crew is told to bring bottled water and use the yard toilets
options.C: Toilets, washing facilities and drinking water must be there from the start, so work should not begin until they are provided
options.D: The tap is fine for washing and for drinking in an emergency, as long as the crew boils the water before they use it

explanation: Welfare facilities, including a supply of wholesome drinking water, have to be in place when work starts, and a tap marked as not for drinking cannot meet that duty.

why_wrong.A: Contractors also have duties for the welfare of their own workers, and the client cannot remove them.
why_wrong.B: There is no grace period, and relying on a neighbour's facilities does not meet the duty to provide welfare.
why_wrong.D: A supply marked as not for drinking is unsuitable for drinking, and boiling does not make an unknown supply wholesome.

common_mistake: Treating welfare as something that can follow the start of work. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 5 --- Occupational Health and Welfare

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the worker is properly protected because he is wearing an FFP3 mask rated for fine dust. What is the main problem with this view?

options.A: The mask is rated too low for plaster dust, so a higher-grade disposable mask with a valve would give the seal and protection that he needs
options.B: A tight-fitting mask can only protect if it seals to bare skin, so a different type of RPE or a change of work method is needed
options.C: The only fault is that the window is closed, since fresh air through the room will carry the remaining dust away from his face and lungs
options.D: The mask needs only a quick check on the day, and tightening the straps will close the gaps and keep dust out of the breathing zone

explanation: Tight-fitting facepieces rely on a seal against the skin, so the rating alone does not guarantee protection and alternative RPE or better dust control is needed.

why_wrong.A: A higher grade does not cure a leaking seal, because every tight-fitting mask depends on contact with skin.
why_wrong.C: Ventilation helps, but it does not replace RPE that actually fits the wearer.
why_wrong.D: Tighter straps cannot make a mask seal over hair, and a fit test is not a strap adjustment.

common_mistake: Judging respiratory protection by the mask's rating without checking that it can seal against the wearer's face. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 6 --- PPE and Signage

stem: Roofers must replace flashings on an old warehouse roof. The rooflights are green with moss and look just like the sheets around them, and the foreman says that anything which is not obviously glass can be walked on. What is the best plan?

options.A: Treat every rooflight and sheet as fragile whatever it looks like, and use edge protection, rooflight covers and staging for any walking
options.B: Walk only on the sheets that look sound and sit next to a purlin line, and mark the rooflights with spray paint so the crew can step around them
options.C: Rely on a harness clipped to a long lanyard anywhere across the roof, since a fall would then be arrested before the worker reached the floor
options.D: Test each rooflight by pressing a boot on it first, and only keep clear of those that flex or crack when they take weight

explanation: Weathered rooflights and old sheets can fail without warning, so they should be treated as fragile and protected with covers, edge protection and load-spreading staging.

why_wrong.B: Appearance is not a reliable guide, and paint marks do not stop a person falling through.
why_wrong.C: Fall arrest at height across a fragile roof is a last resort that was not planned, and clearance is rarely enough.
why_wrong.D: A test of this kind can itself cause a failure and tells the worker nothing about how it will bear a fall.

common_mistake: Judging whether a roof will carry weight by how it looks instead of treating the whole surface as fragile until proved otherwise. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 7 --- Working at Height

stem: On a school refurbishment, all waste goes into one skip and is sorted by the waste firm later. The site manager decides to improve things. Which arrangement best supports both recycling and safe disposal?

options.A: Separate the waste where it arises into clearly signed skips for each type, brief the crews on what goes where, and keep hazardous waste apart
options.B: Provide signed skips only at the main gate, and ask the crews to carry their waste across site to them at the end of each working week
options.C: Label the skips by colour but give no briefing, since workers can identify the right container from the colours without needing to be told
options.D: Keep one mixed skip but add a large sign that lists forbidden items, since the waste firm will sort whatever arrives and carries the legal duty

explanation: Segregating at source into clearly labelled containers keeps materials clean enough to recycle and prevents hazardous items contaminating other loads.

why_wrong.B: Skips need to be close to where waste arises, or crews will dump it in the nearest place instead.
why_wrong.C: Labels work only if the crews know what they mean, so some briefing is needed.
why_wrong.D: Mixed loads cut recycling, and the producer of the waste still has duties for how it is handled.

common_mistake: Assuming a mixed skip is acceptable because someone further down the chain will sort the waste out. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 10 --- Environmental Protection

stem: A slab pour was assessed for a concrete pump, but the pump breaks down and the gang proposes barrowing from a skip beside an unprotected edge. The supervisor says the assessment already covers placing concrete. What is the correct response?

options.A: Carry on with the barrows, then amend the assessment at the next monthly review, as the existing document already names concrete placing as a task
options.B: Pause the pour, review the assessment for the new method, amend controls such as routes and edge protection, and brief the gang first
options.C: Allow the most experienced operative to choose safe barrow routes by judgement on the day, and note any changes on the paperwork after the pour
options.D: Add a handwritten line to the original assessment saying barrows may be used, and have the supervisor initial it before the first load goes out

explanation: A significant change in the work means the assessment must be reviewed and changed before the new method starts, and workers told of the new controls.

why_wrong.A: Waiting for a scheduled review lets the new hazards go uncontrolled, whereas a significant change requires review before work.
why_wrong.C: Leaving controls to individual judgement and writing them up afterwards does not give workers the planned controls before they start.
why_wrong.D: A single line adds no assessment of the new manual handling, edge or route hazards and tells the gang nothing about controls.

common_mistake: Do not assume an assessment covering the task name stays valid when the way of doing it changes. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 2 --- Risk Assessment

stem: Look at the scene. The bricklayer says the scaffold is tied, fully boarded and has a ladder, so it is ready for work. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The scaffold boards cover the lift fully and leave no space for storing bricks and mortar tubs, so materials need a separate tray
options.B: The ladder rises through a hatch in the platform and should be moved to the outside of the scaffold at the end bay
options.C: The ties to the wall are visible and will need to be removed before he can lay the courses near the top of the wall
options.D: He has built himself a higher standing level on the boards, so the guardrails no longer protect him from falling over the edge

explanation: Standing on stacked blocks and bricks raises his position above the guardrail, so the edge protection is no longer effective; the scaffold should be adjusted to the correct working height.

why_wrong.A: Full boarding is correct, and materials can be stored on the platform within its loading limits.
why_wrong.B: A ladder through a protected hatch is an accepted access arrangement and is not the main hazard here.
why_wrong.C: Ties must stay in place while the scaffold is in use and cannot be removed to suit the work.

common_mistake: Checking that scaffold parts are present without checking how people actually stand and work on them. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 7 --- Working at Height

stem: A supervisor reads the safety data sheet for a solvent-based floor primer. Section 8 suggests organic-vapour respirators, so he orders them. A water-based primer, suitable for the substrate, is available at a slightly higher price. What is the best next step?

options.A: Keep the solvent product and add forced ventilation, because extra cost is a valid reason to skip substitution whenever a control already exists
options.B: Switch to the water-based product and drop the assessment, since a less hazardous product removes any need for a record of the risks
options.C: Follow the sheet exactly, because suppliers set the required controls and the employer has met its duty once the recommended respirators are issued
options.D: Use the data sheet as input to the COSHH assessment, and first consider swapping to the water-based product before relying on respirators

explanation: COSHH requires employers to eliminate or substitute a hazardous substance where reasonably practicable before controls such as RPE, and the sheet only informs the assessment.

why_wrong.A: Substitution comes before other controls where reasonably practicable, and a small price difference does not make it impracticable.
why_wrong.B: Even a safer product needs checking through the assessment, and its own data sheet must be read.
why_wrong.C: The sheet is supplier information, and the employer must still assess the risk and consider substitution first.

common_mistake: Treating the PPE section of a data sheet as the finished control plan instead of first asking whether the hazard can be removed. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 4 --- Hazardous Substances, Noise, Vibration and Manual Handling
chapter_to_revise: Chapter 4 — Hazardous Substances, Noise, Vibration and Manual Handling

stem: A delivery lorry must reverse into a tight yard. The storeman acting as banksman keeps stepping away to sign delivery notes, then stands directly behind the lorry to stop it at the wall. What is the most appropriate correction?

options.A: Keep the storeman as banksman, but ask the driver to reverse more slowly and sound the horn, because speed is the main danger in a tight yard
options.B: Let the driver judge the wall using his mirrors and camera, and call the storeman only if he feels unsure, as the driver has final control of the lorry
options.C: Give the signaller no other duties while the lorry moves, agree signals first, and place them in a safe visible spot beside the path
options.D: Let the storeman keep both jobs but stand behind the lorry so the driver can see his hi-vis in the mirrors, as that gives the closest view of the wall

explanation: A banksman needs full attention, agreed signals and a protected position in the driver's view, because standing in the swept path or being distracted defeats the control.

why_wrong.A: Slower speed and a horn do not fix a distracted signaller or an unsafe position, and they replace no proper control.
why_wrong.B: The driver cannot see everything behind the lorry, and relying on him to ask for help removes the supervision the site planned.
why_wrong.D: Standing in the reversing path puts the signaller where he can be crushed, and divided attention leaves the movement unsupervised.

common_mistake: Do not assume that any person in hi-vis who stands behind a reversing vehicle counts as a proper banksman. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 9 --- Plant, Vehicles and Lifting

stem: A 1.8 m supported trench has a ladder with its top level with the ground, and a spoil heap beside the access point. The excavator is parked next to the heap. Which set of changes best provides safe access and edge control?

options.A: Extend the secured ladder about 1 m above the landing, keep the landing clear, set spoil back from the edge and park the machine well away
options.B: Provide a longer ladder resting on the spoil heap, so the climb is shorter, and park the excavator behind it, to prevent anyone being struck by the bucket
options.C: Leave the ladder where it is, but trim the spoil heap flat at the access point so workers can step across it, and keep the excavator engine switched off
options.D: Remove the ladder and rely on the excavator bucket to lift workers out in an emergency, since a bucket can reach the trench floor faster than climbing

explanation: A ladder should stand firmly and rise at least 1 m above the landing, with spoil and plant kept back so they add no load to the sides or into the access.

why_wrong.B: A ladder resting on loose spoil is on an unstable base, and parking the machine close to the edge still adds load to the sides.
why_wrong.C: Spoil left at the edge still loads the sides and can fall in, and a ladder that does not rise above the landing gives no handhold.
why_wrong.D: Lifting people in a bucket is not an approved means of access, and an everyday climb out needs a proper secured route.

common_mistake: Do not treat a ladder that merely reaches ground level as proper access, or plant parked beside the edge as harmless. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 8 --- Excavations, Confined Spaces and Electrical
chapter_to_revise: Chapter 8 — Excavations, Confined Spaces and Electrical

stem: Look at the picture of a precast beam being placed. The crane operator says the beam is well within the load chart and the slings are in date. What is the most significant problem, and the best correction?

options.A: Only one signaller is present, so a second one should stand beneath the beam beside the first to confirm each movement as it is lowered
options.B: The lifted beam has no spreader beam fitted, so the lift should continue until the bricklayers have a spreader beam delivered to the working area
options.C: A person is working under the load, so stop, lower it and keep everyone clear until positioning is arranged from outside its path
options.D: The man's hard hat gives no protection from a beam, so he should wear a higher-grade helmet and stay in place while the beam is lowered

explanation: No one should be beneath or within reach of a suspended load, because a slip or failure would crush them, so positioning must be planned from a safe place.

why_wrong.A: A second person in the same position doubles the number exposed to the load and fixes nothing.
why_wrong.B: Missing lifting accessories are not the main issue in the picture, and continuing the lift leaves the man under the load.
why_wrong.D: No helmet will protect against a precast beam falling, and PPE does not replace keeping people out of the danger zone.

common_mistake: Do not think a load within the chart and good slings makes it safe for someone to stand under it. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 9 --- Plant, Vehicles and Lifting

stem: A trained worker opens a first-floor storeroom with one door and finds a waste bin burning by the far wall, flames at knee height. A water extinguisher hangs beside the door. Which response is correct?

options.A: Close the door on the fire, walk back to the cabin to find the supervisor, and leave the decision about the alarm to him once he has looked
options.B: Tackle it straight away while it is small, because speed matters most, and raise the alarm afterwards only if the extinguisher fails to put the fire out
options.C: Move past the bin to attack it from the far side, keeping a clear view of the whole fire, and shout for help only if flames reach the wall
options.D: Shout and operate the alarm so others leave, then tackle it only while it stays small and the door is behind him, withdrawing at once if it grows

explanation: The alarm must be raised first so everyone can escape, and a trained person should only attempt a small fire while keeping a clear exit behind them.

why_wrong.A: Closing the door is sensible, but walking off to find someone instead of raising the alarm immediately wastes vital minutes for everyone else in the building.
why_wrong.B: Delaying the alarm leaves others unaware and gives no warning if the attempt fails, so raising the alarm must come before any fire-fighting.
why_wrong.C: Standing beyond the fire puts it between him and the only exit, which breaks the rule of always fighting a fire with an escape route behind you.

common_mistake: Assuming that a small fire and a trained person mean you can deal with it first and sort out the alarm and your escape route later. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 3 --- Accidents and Fire

stem: A 65 kg cast-iron roll-top bath must reach a first-floor bathroom up a narrow stair with a turn. A window opening is wide enough, and a telehandler with a suitable lifting attachment is on site. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Have four fit workers carry it up the stair, since their combined strength comfortably exceeds the weight of the bath and the carry is only short
options.B: Brief the team on good lifting posture and agree rest breaks, since training and job rotation are the main controls for heavy awkward loads
options.C: Avoid the stair carry by hoisting the bath through the window, then assess and reduce the short remaining handling with aids and trained people
options.D: Strap it to a stair-climbing sack truck and send two workers up, as a mechanical aid means the route and load need no further assessment

explanation: The regulations require hazardous handling to be avoided where reasonably practicable, and only then assessed and reduced, so a mechanical lift through the window comes before any carrying plan.

why_wrong.A: Adding people does not remove the awkward shape, narrow turn and poor grip, and it skips the duty to avoid the handling when a mechanical option exists.
why_wrong.B: Training and rotation are weak controls that cannot make a 65 kg awkward load safe, and they ignore the higher-order option of avoiding the carry.
why_wrong.D: A truck reduces some effort but is not the first step, and the stair turn, footing and load stability still have to be assessed.

common_mistake: Jumping straight to who is strong enough to lift the load instead of first asking whether it needs to be carried by hand at all. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 4 --- Hazardous Substances, Noise, Vibration and Manual Handling
chapter_to_revise: Chapter 4 — Hazardous Substances, Noise, Vibration and Manual Handling

stem: Look at the scene. The labourer says the lead is heavy-duty and the tool is protected by an RCD, so it is fine to carry on. What is the most significant risk of electric shock?

options.A: A cable coupling sits in standing water at ground level, so water can reach live parts; raise it clear and use a waterproof type
options.B: The lead is much longer than the job needs, so it should be wound tightly onto a drum to cut voltage drop and stop anyone tripping on it
options.C: The lead is yellow, a colour meant for dry indoor work only, so it should be swapped for a blue 230 V lead to cope with the rain
options.D: The lead passes close to the scaffold tubes, which can conduct current into the structure, so it must be rerouted well away from all scaffolding

explanation: Connections left in puddles can let water reach live conductors, so couplings must be kept off the ground and be of a suitably water-resistant rating, not relied on to be saved by an RCD.

why_wrong.B: A cable wound tightly on a drum while in use can overheat, and length and tripping are not the shock hazard the picture shows.
why_wrong.C: Yellow identifies the reduced 110 V supply that is the preferred choice on site, and a 230 V lead would raise the shock risk in wet conditions.
why_wrong.D: Scaffold tubes carry no current from an undamaged lead, and the real concern is the water reaching the connection, not simple proximity to the scaffold.

common_mistake: Believing that an RCD or a heavy-duty lead makes it acceptable to leave electrical connections lying in water. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 8 --- Excavations, Confined Spaces and Electrical
chapter_to_revise: Chapter 8 — Excavations, Confined Spaces and Electrical

stem: At shift start an operator finds a boom MEWP left by the night crew, who say it ran fine. The hire firm's thorough examination report is in date. The route to the work area crosses a bay with overhead pipework. What should he do?

options.A: Do a visual walk-round for leaks and damage, since function tests belong to the hire company, then plan the route while he drives the machine
options.B: Carry out his own pre-use check, including emergency stop and lowering function tests from both control positions, and survey the route and work area first
options.C: Rely on the night crew's word and the in-date examination report, and watch for the overhead pipework as he travels with the basket raised
options.D: Test only the controls he will use from the basket, because ground controls and emergency lowering are covered by the six-monthly examination

explanation: Each operator should check the machine and test its controls before use, as an in-date examination does not replace the daily check, and the route and working area must be surveyed for hazards.

why_wrong.A: Visual checks alone miss failed controls and safety devices, and route planning must be done before the machine moves, not during travel.
why_wrong.C: Another crew's verbal assurance is no substitute for his own checks, and spotting obstructions only while travelling raised comes too late.
why_wrong.D: The ground controls and emergency lowering must be proved before use since they are what a rescuer depends on, and the examination interval cannot cover daily faults.

common_mistake: Treating an in-date examination report or a colleague's say-so as proof that the machine is safe to use today. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 7 --- Working at Height "Every question you missed has a reason behind it. The other 1,000 come with the same: why the right answer works, and why the tempting wrong ones don't." FRONT MATTER

stem: A worker breaks their wrist falling from a stepladder and is off work for five days. The employer doesn't report it under RIDDOR, reasoning that the over-seven-day threshold wasn't reached, and doesn't log it in the accident book either because it 'wasn't a major injury'. What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.A: Both duties were triggered only because the injury followed a fall from height, and falls from height are treated as reportable in every case
options.B: RIDDOR was correctly skipped under the over-seven-day test, but the accident book should have been completed because it uses the same threshold as RIDDOR
options.C: A fracture is a specified injury reportable under RIDDOR whatever the days off, and the accident book is a separate duty that applies at any severity
options.D: The injury should have been reported to the HSE, but the accident book only has to be completed once an injury goes beyond seven days of absence

explanation: A fracture (other than to fingers, thumbs or toes) is a specified injury that must be reported to the HSE whatever the time off work, and recording in the accident book is an independent duty that applies even to minor injuries.

why_wrong.A: The fracture itself makes this a specified injury; the fall is not what triggers the report, and not every fall from height is reportable.
why_wrong.B: Wrongly applies the over-seven-day test to a fracture and also invents a shared threshold; the accident book has no severity threshold at all.
why_wrong.D: Gets RIDDOR right but invents a seven-day threshold for the accident book, which records injuries regardless of severity.

common_mistake: Treating the over-seven-day rule as the only RIDDOR test, and assuming the accident book follows the same threshold.

stem: An HSE inspector finds an unguarded cement mixer in use with its drive belt exposed at hand height. She issues an Improvement Notice giving 21 days to fit a guard, allowing work to continue meanwhile. Which statement best identifies the problem with this enforcement choice?

options.A: An exposed belt in use risks serious personal injury, so a Prohibition Notice stopping the work until it is guarded was needed, not a timed Improvement Notice
options.B: A Prohibition Notice can only be served where members of the public are at risk, so danger to workers on site is properly dealt with by an Improvement Notice with a time limit
options.C: Inspectors have no power to serve notices on site, so only a court can order work to stop or require a guard to be fitted to the mixer, and then only after a prosecution
options.D: The notice was correct, since an Improvement Notice is the normal first step for any contravention and prohibition is held back for repeat offenders or for refusals to comply

explanation: Improvement Notices give time to put right a contravention; where an activity involves a risk of serious personal injury, a Prohibition Notice stops it, immediately or after a deferral, until the risk is controlled.

why_wrong.B: Prohibition Notices apply to risks of serious personal injury to anyone, including the workforce.
why_wrong.C: Inspectors hold their own powers to serve both notice types without going to court.
why_wrong.D: Prohibition notices depend on the level of risk, not on whether the duty holder has offended before.

common_mistake: Assuming the choice of notice depends on the offender's history rather than on how serious and imminent the risk is.

stem: A supervisor sees a worker refuse the fall-arrest harness issued for roof work because it is 'uncomfortable', then continue working at the edge unprotected. The supervisor takes no action, saying PPE is optional once it has been offered. Which duties have been breached together?

options.A: Neither is in breach, because discomfort is a valid reason to decline PPE and the hierarchy of control favours other measures over harnesses at a roof edge
options.B: Only the employer is in breach, because workers carry no personal legal duties under health and safety law once the employer has issued PPE and given instruction on its use
options.C: Only the worker is in breach, because the employer's legal obligation was fully met once suitable PPE had been supplied to him free of charge and shown how to wear it
options.D: The worker failed to cooperate with the safety arrangements, and the employer failed to ensure that issued PPE is actually used, not merely provided

explanation: Employees must cooperate and use equipment as instructed, and employers must take reasonable steps to make sure PPE is used, so both sides of the duty fail here.

why_wrong.A: Discomfort is a reason to find better-fitting PPE or another control, not to work unprotected at an edge.
why_wrong.B: Employees have their own statutory duties, including cooperating and using equipment correctly.
why_wrong.C: Ignores the employer's duty to ensure PPE is used, which includes supervision and enforcement.

common_mistake: Believing that providing PPE discharges the employer's duty, without enforcing its use.

stem: After an injury caused by a worker who ignored a safe system of work, the employer argues it has no liability because it gave the worker full training and the breach was entirely the individual's fault. No supervision checks were ever carried out. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: The employer is not liable, because the negligence of an individual worker who knowingly ignored a trained safe system breaks the chain of responsibility
options.B: Liability rests with the supervisor personally, because employers pass their safety duties to supervisors when they appoint them to the role, even where none were checked
options.C: Training alone does not discharge the duty without supervision and monitoring to check the safe system is followed, so the employer can still be held responsible
options.D: The employer is liable only if the training was delivered within twelve months of the incident, as older training is treated as out of date in law and so does not count

explanation: The employer's duty is to ensure safety so far as is reasonably practicable, which includes supervising and checking that arrangements are followed, so one worker's non-compliance does not automatically remove the employer's responsibility.

why_wrong.A: An employee's fault may be relevant, but it does not erase the employer's duty to supervise and enforce.
why_wrong.B: Employers cannot delegate away their statutory duties by appointing a supervisor.
why_wrong.D: No fixed twelve-month rule decides liability; adequacy of training, supervision and enforcement does.

common_mistake: Assuming that once training is recorded, any later breach by the worker is the worker's problem alone.

stem: A private commercial client plans a build expected to run for 35 working days with up to 25 workers on site at once, using several contractors. The client doesn't notify the HSE or appoint a principal designer or principal contractor, saying CDM notification only applies to public bodies. What is wrong?

options.A: The project is notifiable only if it lasts more than 12 months, so a 35-working-day build with 25 workers on site at once falls below the threshold
options.B: Nothing is wrong, because CDM notification and appointments apply only to public bodies and not to private commercial clients, whatever the size or length of the project
options.C: The project is notifiable (over 30 working days with over 20 workers at once), so the client must notify the HSE and appoint a principal designer and principal contractor
options.D: The client need only notify the HSE; appointing a principal designer is optional on commercial work, even with several contractors on the project, if the client coordinates

explanation: Notification and appointments under CDM 2015 depend on the size and duration of the project and the number of contractors, not on whether the client is public or private.

why_wrong.A: The test is duration over 30 working days with more than 20 workers at once, or over 500 person days, not 12 months.
why_wrong.B: CDM 2015 applies to private commercial clients as well as public bodies; only domestic clients are treated differently, and this project is notifiable on its size and duration.
why_wrong.D: With more than one contractor, both a principal designer and a principal contractor must be appointed.

common_mistake: Thinking CDM duties depend on who the client is rather than on the scale and duration of the project.

stem: A risk assessment for removing old ceiling boards was written by an admin colleague with general safety awareness but no training in asbestos hazards. It has not been looked at for three years, although the work method has since changed. Which combined failing is shown?

options.A: It was not written by someone competent in this specific hazard, and it was not reviewed when the work method changed, which triggers a review whatever the date
options.B: Only the missing review is a failing, since any employee with general safety awareness may write a risk assessment for any hazard on site, asbestos work included
options.C: Only the author is a failing, because the law requires reviews just once every five years, so a three-year-old assessment is not yet due for any review
options.D: Neither is a failing, because the assessment was signed off when it was written and a signature is all the regulations ask of the employer, so no review is needed

explanation: A suitable and sufficient assessment needs someone competent in the hazard, and it must be reviewed when circumstances change, not only on a fixed date.

why_wrong.B: Competence for the specific hazard is part of what makes an assessment suitable and sufficient.
why_wrong.C: There is no fixed five-year rule; changes in method or conditions trigger review.
why_wrong.D: A one-off sign-off does not satisfy the duty to keep an assessment valid and current.

common_mistake: Treating the existence of a signed document as proof of a suitable and sufficient assessment.

stem: Mid-task, heavy rain and fading light create conditions the written RAMS never anticipated. The supervisor says the RAMS is signed off so work continues as planned. What is the correct position?

options.A: Only the site manager may reassess the risk, so workers should carry on under the signed RAMS until he arrives and makes a decision on the work
options.B: A signed RAMS does not replace the ongoing duty to reassess as conditions change, so work should pause or be adjusted until the new risks are assessed
options.C: Work should continue, because a signed RAMS gives the supervisor legal cover for later changes in conditions that the document did not anticipate, such as weather
options.D: Work must stop for the day only if rainfall or light levels pass a fixed national limit set in law, otherwise the plan continues exactly as written

explanation: Dynamic risk assessment means continuing to check conditions against the assumptions in the written document, and stopping to review when reality departs from them.

why_wrong.A: Anyone can and should stop work when conditions are unsafe, and supervisors should reassess promptly.
why_wrong.C: Sign-off does not cover conditions the document never considered.
why_wrong.D: No fixed national rainfall limit exists; the decision comes from assessing the actual risk.

common_mistake: Treating the written RAMS as final, rather than a starting point that must be checked against real conditions.

stem: A firm with three employees has no written risk assessments, its director arguing that recording is only legally required from five employees upward. A client's contract requires RAMS before any site work. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Written risk assessments are required by statute for every firm from one employee upward, so the director is wrong and the contract adds nothing
options.B: The client's contract is irrelevant to the question, because only legislation can require written RAMS and the firm is below the statutory threshold
options.C: The director is right that with fewer than five employees no risk assessment of any kind is needed, so the client's request has no basis in law or guidance
options.D: The five-employee rule only removes the duty to record findings; the assessment must still be suitable and sufficient, and the contract can require it

explanation: Recording is a statutory minimum for five or more employees, but the underlying duty to assess applies to everyone, and clients commonly require written RAMS as a condition of working on their site.

why_wrong.A: Statutory recording applies at five or more employees, though other requirements may still demand it.
why_wrong.B: Contractual and CDM requirements commonly require written RAMS regardless of the statutory minimum.
why_wrong.C: The duty to assess applies regardless of headcount; only recording is tied to five employees.

common_mistake: Mistaking the threshold for recording findings as a threshold for carrying out the assessment at all.

stem: To save money, a supervisor places a hazard warning sign above a physical barrier in his control options, reasoning that signs are cheaper and should be tried first. Which statement best corrects this?

options.A: Cost is the first factor in the hierarchy, so the cheapest reasonable control is applied first and barriers are only considered if signs fail to work
options.B: Signs and barriers sit at the same level of the hierarchy, so either may be chosen at will according to which is easier to install on site
options.C: A physical barrier is a stronger control than a sign, because the hierarchy ranks controls by how well they reduce risk, not by cost
options.D: Signs rank above barriers, because a sign warns everyone approaching the area whereas a barrier only blocks a single route into it, and signs cost less

explanation: Physical measures such as barriers sit above information and signage in the hierarchy of control, so a sign cannot replace a barrier where one is reasonably practicable.

why_wrong.A: The hierarchy is based on effectiveness; cost only matters when judging what is reasonably practicable.
why_wrong.B: They are not equal; physical controls rank above signage and instruction.
why_wrong.D: Warning signs depend on people noticing and obeying them; barriers physically prevent access.

common_mistake: Letting the cost of a control decide its place in the hierarchy instead of its effectiveness.

stem: A site manager with twenty years of general building experience but no scaffold inspection training signs the inspection record for a scaffold because he is 'the most experienced person on site'. Which statement best describes the problem?

options.A: The inspection is valid provided the manager also holds a CSCS card, because the card confirms competence to inspect any structure or equipment on the site
options.B: The inspection is invalid only if a second person has not countersigned the record, as the number of signatures decides its legal validity
options.C: There is no problem, because the most senior and experienced person on site is treated as the competent person for every inspection carried out there by law
options.D: Competence is task-specific: general experience or seniority does not make someone competent to inspect scaffolding without relevant training

explanation: A competent person must have the training, skill and knowledge for the specific inspection, so seniority and years in the industry are not substitutes.

why_wrong.A: A CSCS card shows general competence in a role; it does not by itself qualify someone to inspect scaffolding.
why_wrong.B: The number of signatures is irrelevant; the issue is the inspector's competence.
why_wrong.C: Seniority does not equal task-specific competence.

common_mistake: Equating long general experience with competence for a specialist task.

stem: A fire starts in live electrical distribution equipment. A worker grabs the nearest water extinguisher and prepares to discharge it, without isolating the power. Which statement identifies the problem?

options.A: Water conducts electricity and risks shock on live equipment; isolate the power if safe, then use a CO2 or dry powder extinguisher
options.B: Water is acceptable on electrical fires provided the extinguisher is in test and the operator keeps a safe distance from the equipment
options.C: No extinguisher should be used on live equipment; the worker should raise the alarm, evacuate and leave all fire-fighting to the fire service
options.D: A foam extinguisher is the best choice here because it smothers the flames and forms a barrier that stops current passing through the agent

explanation: Water and foam are unsuitable on live electrical fires; isolating the supply where safe and using CO2 or dry powder reduces both the shock and spread risk.

why_wrong.B: Testing and distance do not change the problem; water conducts electricity and remains unsuitable for live electrics.
why_wrong.C: Fire-fighting is appropriate if it is safe and the person is trained; the error here is the wrong agent and no isolation.
why_wrong.D: Foam is water-based and also unsuitable on live electrical equipment.

common_mistake: Choosing the nearest extinguisher without checking that its agent suits the type of fire.

stem: In a site cabin corridor, a fire door is wedged open 'for airflow' and stored materials partly block the route to the final exit, described as 'temporary'. Which combination of failings does this show?

options.A: The wedged door defeats the compartmentation that slows smoke and fire, and the obstruction compromises the means of escape, which must stay clear
options.B: Neither is a failing provided a suitable extinguisher is positioned close to the door and the cabin has a working smoke detector fitted
options.C: Only the obstruction matters, because fire doors mainly provide security and sound control rather than holding back fire and smoke
options.D: Only the wedge matters, because short-term obstructions are acceptable while a competent person is nearby and ready to move them at once

explanation: Fire doors only work when closed, and escape routes must be kept unobstructed whenever the building is occupied, so both are separate failures.

why_wrong.B: Extinguishers and detectors do not replace compartmentation or clear escape routes.
why_wrong.C: Fire doors are specifically designed to hold back fire and smoke.
why_wrong.D: Escape routes must be clear at all times; staffing a blockage is not an exemption.

common_mistake: Treating a fire door or escape route as a convenience that can be compromised temporarily.

stem: A site with 20 workers, regular work at height and machinery in use appoints only an 'appointed person' with no first-aid qualification, because 'we've had very few injuries'. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: First aid is the client's responsibility alone through the site welfare arrangements, so the contractor has no separate duty to provide any for its own workers
options.B: A trained first aider is only needed once a reportable injury has occurred on site and the accident book shows a pattern of incidents
options.C: A needs assessment of the site's risks should set first-aid provision, and work at height and machinery usually justify a trained first aider
options.D: An appointed person is adequate for any site of this size, because first-aid provision is set by headcount bands rather than by the risks

explanation: A first-aid needs assessment considers the nature of the work, hazards, numbers and remoteness; a low injury history is not a sound basis for reducing provision on a higher-risk site.

why_wrong.A: Employers have their own first-aid duties for their workers.
why_wrong.B: Provision must be planned in advance from the risks, not triggered by a reportable injury.
why_wrong.D: No fixed headcount rule applies; the needs assessment decides.

common_mistake: Basing first-aid provision on past injury numbers instead of the risks actually present.

stem: A manager says the general construction risk assessment already mentions fire hazards, so a separate fire risk assessment is unnecessary. Which statement best describes the position?

options.A: Fire safety law requires a separate suitable and sufficient fire risk assessment, which a passing mention of fire in another assessment does not meet
options.B: A fire risk assessment is only needed after a fire or near miss has occurred, when the cause can be properly investigated, recorded and reviewed
options.C: The manager is correct, because a general construction risk assessment covers every hazard on site, including fire, if it is reviewed regularly and signed off
options.D: A fire risk assessment is only needed for permanent buildings, so temporary site accommodation and the works themselves are exempt from it

explanation: Fire safety law requires a specific fire risk assessment by the responsible person, so a general health and safety assessment that merely mentions fire is not enough.

why_wrong.B: It must be carried out and kept up to date before an incident.
why_wrong.C: Fire has its own statutory assessment duty with specific content.
why_wrong.D: Temporary site accommodation and the works themselves must also be covered.

common_mistake: Assuming a general risk assessment that mentions fire satisfies the separate duty to assess fire risk.

stem: After cutting steel near stored timber, a hot works crew checks that the cutting has stopped and leaves immediately. Forty minutes later smouldering material ignites. Which principles were missed?

options.A: A hot work permit is unnecessary for cutting steel, since steel itself cannot burn and the timber was stored a sensible distance away from the cutting
options.B: Combustibles should have been removed or protected, and a fire watch kept after work stopped, as heated material can smoulder and ignite later
options.C: A fire watch is only needed during the cutting itself, and it can safely end once the tool is switched off and visible sparks have stopped
options.D: Only oxygen needed removing, since the heat source and the fuel around hot work cannot realistically be controlled on a live construction site

explanation: Removing the fuel breaks the fire triangle, and a post-work fire watch covers the delay between hot work finishing and any smouldering material igniting.

why_wrong.A: The hazard is ignition of nearby combustibles, which a permit and fire watch control.
why_wrong.C: The fire watch must continue after work stops to catch delayed ignition.
why_wrong.D: Fuel can and should be removed or protected; oxygen cannot realistically be controlled in open air.

common_mistake: Assuming the fire risk ends the moment the heat source is switched off.

stem: A COSHH assessment relies on local exhaust ventilation (LEV) for a solvent task. The LEV looks fine and works when switched on, but has not had a thorough examination and test for 16 months. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: LEV needs testing only after it has visibly broken down or the operator reports reduced airflow, since a working system is assumed to be capturing contaminants
options.B: A visual check by the operator at least once a year is the only legal requirement for LEV, provided the result is recorded in writing
options.C: LEV must be thoroughly examined and tested at least every 14 months, so it cannot be relied on until checked, however well it appears to work
options.D: Because LEV is in place the COSHH assessment is complete, and nothing further is needed beyond training operators to switch it on

explanation: COSHH requires periodic thorough examination and testing of LEV, because a system can look and sound normal while failing to capture contaminants.

why_wrong.A: Testing is periodic precisely so hidden failures are found before exposure occurs.
why_wrong.B: A thorough examination and test by a competent person is required, not just a visual check.
why_wrong.D: The control must be maintained and proven effective to count as a control.

common_mistake: Judging a ventilation system by whether it looks and sounds like it is working.

stem: A worker with a daily noise exposure of 82 dB(A) is told hearing protection is compulsory on pain of discipline, while a worker at 90 dB(A) is told wearing it is 'his choice'. What has gone wrong?

options.A: Noise law only recommends hearing protection, so neither worker can be required to wear it and discipline for refusing would be unlawful
options.B: The positions are reversed: protection is made available at the lower action value (80 dB), but its use must be enforced at the upper action value (85 dB)
options.C: Both approaches are correct, because wearing protection is compulsory from the lower action value upward and the employer may discipline either worker
options.D: The 90 dB worker is correct to choose, since personal choice applies until exposure passes the exposure limit value of 87 dB, with protection factored in

explanation: Employers must make hearing protection available at 80 dB and make wearing it compulsory at and above 85 dB, so the 90 dB worker must be required to wear it.

why_wrong.A: Above the upper action value its use must be enforced.
why_wrong.C: Compulsory use starts at the upper action value, not the lower.
why_wrong.D: Above the upper action value and the limit value, protection is mandatory, not optional.

common_mistake: Mixing up the lower and upper noise action values and what each requires.

stem: A worker using a breaker says anti-vibration gloves let him safely work beyond the daily exposure limit value for hand-arm vibration. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Anti-vibration gloves give no reliable protection, so exposure must be controlled through trigger time, tool choice and job rotation instead
options.B: Gloves are a cold-weather measure, and a worker wearing them can safely exceed the limit because warm hands tolerate vibration better
options.C: Gloves reduce vibration enough to allow roughly double the usual daily exposure, provided they are certified to the relevant standard
options.D: The exposure limit value applies only to workers not wearing gloves, because gloved hands are treated as a separately protected group by the manufacturer

explanation: Gloves cannot be relied on to reduce vibration to a safe level, so the control is to keep daily exposure under the action and limit values through tool choice, trigger time and job rotation.

why_wrong.B: Warm hands help circulation, but gloves do not permit exposure above the limit values.
why_wrong.C: There is no such allowance; gloves are not a recognised way to exceed the limit.
why_wrong.D: Limits apply to the vibration exposure regardless of gloves.

common_mistake: Believing anti-vibration gloves are a reliable control that allows higher exposure.

stem: A load is within the HSE guideline weight and the lifting task was assessed as acceptable. A worker returning from a shoulder injury is put on the same task without reassessment because 'the load hasn't changed'. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The individual's capability is part of the assessment, so it must be reviewed for someone returning from injury even if the load is unchanged
options.B: The worker should lift smaller amounts at a time on their own judgement, which is enough in place of a formal reassessment by a competent person
options.C: Only the load needs reassessing; the worker's own capacity is not part of a manual handling assessment, which looks at the task alone
options.D: No reassessment is needed, because the HSE guideline weights are legal maximums that apply to every worker once the task is signed off

explanation: The TILE assessment includes the individual's capability; an injury changes the risk for that person even though the task and load stay the same.

why_wrong.B: Informal self-limiting is not a substitute for reassessing the task for that person.
why_wrong.C: The individual is one of the four assessed factors.
why_wrong.D: Guideline figures are not legal limits and do not apply to everyone.

common_mistake: Treating guideline weights as a pass mark that applies equally to every person.

stem: A worker uses three different vibrating tools through one shift. Each tool's use was assessed separately and judged under the action value, but nobody totalled the day's exposure. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The total only needs calculating once a worker reports symptoms such as tingling or numbness, when health surveillance is triggered
options.B: Daily exposure must be calculated across all vibrating tools used in the day, as each can be under the action value alone while the total exceeds it
options.C: Only the tool with the highest vibration level matters for the daily total, as the others contribute little to overall exposure
options.D: Each tool is rightly assessed on its own, because vibration from different tools does not combine in the body, so a combined total is meaningless for a shift

explanation: Hand-arm vibration exposure accumulates through the whole shift, so assessing tools in isolation can hide an overall exposure above the action or limit value.

why_wrong.A: Assessment is preventive and should be done before symptoms develop.
why_wrong.C: All tools and their durations contribute to the daily exposure.
why_wrong.D: Exposure is added across the day from all sources.

common_mistake: Assessing each tool in isolation instead of totalling exposure across the whole day.

stem: A site's welfare facilities suited the first crew of six, but the workforce has grown to twenty and nothing has been added. The manager says welfare is only a temporary-site courtesy. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Welfare is the principal designer's responsibility only, so contractors on site have no need to review the facilities as numbers change
options.B: Welfare duties apply however short the project, and provision must be scaled to the workforce on site and reviewed as numbers change
options.C: Welfare rules only apply to projects lasting more than six months, because shorter jobs are treated as temporary work under a lighter regime
options.D: Welfare provision is fixed at the planning stage for the whole project, so extra workers must make do with what was agreed at the outset

explanation: Temporary sites are not exempt from welfare requirements, and facilities fixed at the start of a project must grow with the workforce.

why_wrong.A: Contractors and the principal contractor have duties to provide and maintain adequate welfare.
why_wrong.C: There is no such minimum duration; the duty applies from the start of work.
why_wrong.D: Provision must be adjusted when the number of workers changes.

common_mistake: Treating welfare as a one-off set-up task rather than something that must keep pace with the workforce.

stem: Several workers report constant high workload, no say over deadlines and frequent last-minute schedule changes. The manager deals with it only through individual appraisals, calling it an attitude issue. Which statement best describes the problem?

options.A: Stress is a personal matter for each worker, and the employer's duty to assess risks does not extend to workload, deadlines or schedule changes set by the business
options.B: Stress only becomes a legal issue once a worker has taken more than seven days of sick leave, as the duty to act is triggered by recorded absence from work
options.C: Individual appraisals are the correct tool here, because stress is best understood as a question of personal resilience that each worker must manage
options.D: Work-related stress from demands and lack of control is a health risk to be assessed, and a pattern across several workers points to a systemic hazard

explanation: Psychosocial risk factors such as demands and control should be assessed like other hazards, and several people reporting the same issue signals an organisational cause, not individual attitude.

why_wrong.A: Employers must assess work-related stress as a health risk.
why_wrong.B: The duty to assess and act applies before absence occurs.
why_wrong.C: A shared pattern indicates a work-design problem that appraisals cannot fix.

common_mistake: Treating a pattern of work-design problems as a series of individual performance issues.

stem: Workers exposed well above the upper noise action value wear ear defenders, and the employer says audiometric health surveillance is therefore unnecessary. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Health surveillance is a separate duty that checks controls are working and detects early hearing damage, so issuing ear defenders does not remove it
options.B: Surveillance is unnecessary once hearing protection has been issued to everyone exposed, because correctly worn defenders remove the risk of hearing damage
options.C: Surveillance is only required once a worker reports hearing loss, because its purpose is to investigate symptoms that have already appeared
options.D: Surveillance applies only to workers exposed to hand-arm vibration, since noise exposure is dealt with through assessment and controls alone

explanation: Surveillance verifies the effectiveness of controls over time; PPE being issued does not show that it is being used properly or that no damage is occurring.

why_wrong.B: Issuing PPE does not replace monitoring for harm.
why_wrong.C: It is preventive and aims to detect damage early.
why_wrong.D: Noise exposure above the relevant level also triggers health surveillance.

common_mistake: Assuming protective equipment makes health monitoring pointless.

stem: Workers handling cement eat lunch at their workstations because the welfare cabin is far away and inconvenient, and rarely wash first. Which two points are most relevant?

options.A: Cement is a hazard mainly when its dust is inhaled, so hand washing before eating adds little protection for workers handling it
options.B: Welfare location does not matter provided a cabin exists somewhere on the site, since the duty is met simply by providing the facility at all
options.C: Eating at the workstation is acceptable if the worker keeps gloves on while eating, since the gloves keep the cement off the food
options.D: Welfare facilities must be reasonably accessible so they are used, and for cement washing before eating is needed to prevent skin harm and ingestion

explanation: Facilities that are technically provided but impractical to use defeat the duty, and hand-to-mouth transfer of contaminants is a real exposure route requiring washing before eating.

why_wrong.A: Cement also harms the skin and can be ingested from contaminated hands.
why_wrong.B: Facilities must be suitably located so people can realistically use them.
why_wrong.C: Eating in contaminated areas should be prevented, and gloves do not make it safe.

common_mistake: Counting welfare as adequate because it exists, without checking whether workers can and do use it.

stem: Look at the scene. The worker is correctly wearing high-visibility clothing as the blue sign requires. What is the most significant problem being missed?

options.A: The only problem is that the mandatory sign should be green rather than blue, as green is the colour used for signs requiring protective equipment
options.B: Nothing is wrong, because high-visibility clothing makes the worker visible enough to drivers to cross the vehicle route wherever he chooses
options.C: The red sign is a warning that vehicles may be present, so the worker is free to cross at this point provided he takes care and watches for traffic
options.D: He is crossing where a prohibition sign bars pedestrians instead of using the marked crossing, so obeying the PPE sign does not excuse ignoring the route restriction

explanation: The two signs require different things: the mandatory sign is about PPE and the red prohibition sign is about where pedestrians may go, so compliance with one does not excuse breaching the other.

why_wrong.A: Blue circles are the correct colour for mandatory signs; green is for safe conditions and emergency information.
why_wrong.B: Hi-vis makes a person more visible but does not make unsegregated crossing safe or permitted.
why_wrong.C: A red circle with a bar is a prohibition, not a warning; warnings are yellow triangles.

common_mistake: Treating compliance with one sign, such as the hi-vis requirement, as permission to ignore another sign about route restrictions.

stem: A supervisor says a yellow triangular 'deep excavation' sign and a blue circular 'hard hats must be worn' sign are both 'just reminders' that workers can judge for themselves. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Both are advisory, because no safety sign creates a legal requirement on its own and workers are expected to judge the risk for themselves on site
options.B: The yellow triangle only warns of a hazard, while the blue circle is a mandatory instruction that must be followed, so they do not carry equal weight
options.C: Both are mandatory, because any safety sign displayed on a site must be obeyed in the same way whatever its shape or colour, with no difference in weight
options.D: The triangle is mandatory and the circle is a warning, because a triangle indicates that a specific action must be taken by the worker concerned

explanation: Sign shape and colour carry meaning: warning signs inform, prohibition signs forbid, and mandatory signs require a specific action which employers must enforce.

why_wrong.A: Mandatory signs indicate required actions that employers must enforce.
why_wrong.C: A warning sign informs about a hazard; it does not itself prescribe an action.
why_wrong.D: The meanings are reversed; triangles warn, blue circles mandate.

common_mistake: Treating all safety signs as the same level of instruction regardless of shape and colour.

stem: A worker in a dusty area wears contact lenses and is told standard safety glasses are unnecessary because 'the lenses already protect the eyes'. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Lens wearers must be moved off all dusty work permanently, because lenses cannot be worn safely in any dust and no PPE can address this
options.B: Contact lenses are not eye protection and can trap dust against the eye, so suitable protection is still needed, with goggles where dust makes glasses inadequate
options.C: Standard safety glasses are adequate for any level of dust, because gaps at the sides are covered by the contact lenses underneath
options.D: Contact lenses form a protective barrier over the eye, so additional eye protection becomes optional for lens wearers working in dusty areas

explanation: Lenses give no barrier against debris or dust and can make dust exposure worse, so the worker still needs PPE matched to the hazard.

why_wrong.A: No blanket ban exists; the answer is suitable protection chosen through assessment.
why_wrong.C: Some dust conditions need sealed goggles because glasses leave gaps.
why_wrong.D: Lenses are a vision aid, not protective equipment.

common_mistake: Assuming a vision aid contributes to eye protection.

stem: Workers cutting concrete in a confined yard wear FFP1 disposable masks because 'any dust mask is better than nothing'. The dust is respirable crystalline silica. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: FFP1 is the highest rating available, so it is the best choice for silica and no higher class is needed for cutting work such as this in a yard
options.B: Any FFP mask is equally suitable for any dust, because the number printed on it measures comfort and fit rather than filtering efficiency or the level of protection
options.C: The mask must be rated for the hazard, and silica needs a higher class than FFP1, so a wrongly rated mask gives false confidence without adequate filtration
options.D: A mask is unnecessary if the cutting is done outdoors, because the dust disperses in open air and exposure stays below any workplace exposure limit

explanation: RPE must match the contaminant and exposure level; FFP1 filters far less than the protection required for silica, so it can leave workers inadequately protected while believing otherwise.

why_wrong.A: FFP1 is the lowest of the three classes.
why_wrong.B: The class indicates filtering efficiency and must match the hazard.
why_wrong.D: Outdoor work still exposes workers to silica, which needs controlling at source and suitable RPE.

common_mistake: Believing that any respiratory protection beats none, without checking its rating against the hazard.

stem: The site requires safety footwear, and a worker wears his own trainers with steel toecaps. The risk assessment also identifies loose nails and uneven ground. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Steel toecaps meet the requirement because toe protection is the standard applied to site footwear, and other features are optional extras
options.B: PPE must match the full hazard profile, and toecaps alone do not give the midsole puncture protection and ankle support the assessment calls for
options.C: Personal footwear is acceptable if it is comfortable and in good condition, since a competent worker can judge for himself what suits the ground conditions
options.D: Midsole protection is needed only on roofing work, because nails and debris are not treated as a puncture risk on other types of site

explanation: Footwear must address every identified hazard, including penetration and uneven ground, not only the most obvious crush risk to the toes.

why_wrong.A: Suitability is judged against all assessed hazards, not only impact to the toes.
why_wrong.C: It must still be suitable for the assessed hazards.
why_wrong.D: Nails and debris on any site can require puncture-resistant footwear.

common_mistake: Choosing PPE to cover only the most obvious hazard rather than all the hazards identified.

stem: A canopy could be assembled at ground level and lifted into place by crane, but the manager decides to build it from a mobile tower because the tower is already on site. Which statement best identifies the issue?

options.A: The tower is acceptable because the hierarchy only requires suitable fall protection to be available, and a mobile tower has collective edge protection with guardrails
options.B: The only problem is that a crane lift is itself riskier, so no alternative could be better and the tower is the safer option here in all cases
options.C: Convenience and cost may override the hierarchy if the manager records the decision in writing and the tower is erected and inspected correctly
options.D: Work at height should be avoided where reasonably practicable, and ground-level assembly was practicable, so choosing height work for convenience skips the first step

explanation: The hierarchy requires avoiding work at height first; having equipment already on site is not a valid reason to bypass an option that removes the need to work at height.

why_wrong.A: The hierarchy starts with avoidance, then prevention, then minimising consequences.
why_wrong.B: The choice must be justified by assessing the risks, and avoiding height work is the priority.
why_wrong.C: Recording a decision does not remove the duty to follow the hierarchy where reasonably practicable.

common_mistake: Letting equipment already being on site decide the method, instead of starting with avoidance.

stem: A worker is rigged with a 2 m shock-absorbing fall-arrest lanyard while working 2.5 m above a concrete floor. Which statement correctly describes the problem?

options.A: Fall arrest needs clearance for lanyard, absorber extension and body length; these exceed 2.5 m here, so restraint or another method is needed
options.B: A longer lanyard would solve it, because extra length gives the system more distance over which to slow and stop the falling worker
options.C: The system is adequate because a 2 m shock-absorbing lanyard stops a fall within its own length, so any working height above 2 m is sufficient for a trained user
options.D: The problem is that the lanyard connector is not matched to the anchor type, so clearance below the work position is a secondary matter for the competent person

explanation: Fall arrest only works if the total fall distance, including lanyard length, absorber extension, body height and a safety margin, is less than the clearance below the work position.

why_wrong.B: A longer lanyard increases the free-fall and total distance, making the clearance problem worse.
why_wrong.C: Stopping distance depends on the total deployment length, which exceeds the clearance here.
why_wrong.D: Compatibility matters, but the decisive issue is that the available clearance is insufficient.

common_mistake: Assuming that wearing a fall-arrest system always prevents hitting the ground, regardless of clearance below.

stem: A scaffold was inspected three days ago, within its seven-day cycle. Overnight a storm struck and that morning another trade removed a board to pass materials through. The supervisor says the inspection is still in date. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Re-inspection is only needed if a worker reports a visible fault, because the duty to inspect arises from a defect being noticed after weather or other work
options.B: The scaffold can stay in use until the next scheduled inspection, because the three-day-old report is still valid and the seven-day cycle has not expired
options.C: The seven-day interval is a maximum; the storm and the removed board each require a fresh inspection before use, whatever stage the cycle has reached
options.D: Only the storm requires re-inspection; alterations by another trade are covered by the original inspection, as the scaffolder already signed it off as safe

explanation: Scaffolds must also be inspected after any event that could affect stability, such as severe weather or alteration, so the routine interval does not excuse use in the meantime.

why_wrong.A: The duty arises from the event, not from someone noticing a defect.
why_wrong.B: Events affecting stability trigger inspection independently of the schedule.
why_wrong.D: Alterations are also a trigger for re-inspection.

common_mistake: Treating the seven-day interval as permission to use a scaffold that has since been affected by weather or alteration.

stem: A worker in a mobile elevating work platform basket is not attached to anything because the basket has guardrails. The only other person on site has never been shown the ground-level emergency lowering controls. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Ground-level training is needed, but a lanyard inside a basket creates a worse hazard by tethering the occupant to a moving structure
options.B: A lanyard is needed, but ground-level staff need no knowledge of the controls because the operator in the basket will be able to lower the platform if needed
options.C: Guardrails make a lanyard unnecessary, and emergency lowering may only be operated by the manufacturer's engineer, so site staff should leave the controls alone
options.D: A restraint lanyard is still needed to stop the occupant being thrown out in a jolt, and a trained person at ground level must be able to lower the platform

explanation: Guardrails do not prevent ejection during a jolt or collision, and a rescue plan relies on a trained person at ground level who can lower the platform.

why_wrong.A: A short restraint lanyard is standard practice to keep the occupant inside the basket.
why_wrong.B: A rescue plan depends on someone being able to operate the emergency controls.
why_wrong.C: Occupants are normally restrained, and site staff must be able to lower the platform in an emergency.

common_mistake: Believing guardrails alone keep an occupant in a MEWP basket and that rescue can be improvised.

stem: Look at the scene. The worker says he will only be on the roof for a minute and will walk carefully. Which statement best describes the hazard?

options.A: Walking carefully along the ridge or valley lines of the sheets, where the support is strongest, makes it safe to cross a short distance without boards
options.B: A short visit of under two minutes is classed as low risk because of the limited exposure, so crawl boards, edge protection and signs are not needed
options.C: Fragile sheets and rooflights can fail under body weight however carefully or briefly someone walks, so crawl boards, edge protection and signs are needed
options.D: The main hazard is the moss and dirt on the rooflights, which should be cleaned off before anyone steps onto the roof surface to start work

explanation: There is no safe way to put weight directly on fragile roofing; care and speed do not change that, and the missing warning sign removes a barrier against unplanned access.

why_wrong.A: Weathered sheets and hidden rooflights can fail anywhere; there is no safe line to walk.
why_wrong.B: Duration does not reduce the chance of a fragile roof failing under weight.
why_wrong.D: The dirt masks the rooflights, but the hazard is the fragility of the roof itself.

common_mistake: Thinking that care and a short duration make walking on a fragile roof acceptable.

stem: Edge protection on a flat roof has a single top rail at 900 mm and no intermediate rail or mesh, and the supervisor says the top rail is the main protection so that is sufficient. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A toe board alone can replace the intermediate rail, because it blocks the same gap beneath the top rail and stops anything falling over the edge
options.B: Only the missing intermediate rail is a problem, since top rails may be any height from 800 mm upwards where the roof is flat and the work is short
options.C: 900 mm meets the requirement for a main guardrail on a flat roof, and a single top rail is sufficient where the edge is some distance from the work area
options.D: The top guardrail should be at least 950 mm, and with no intermediate rail the gap exceeds the 470 mm maximum, so both height and gap are deficient

explanation: Edge protection needs a main guardrail at least 950 mm high, an intermediate guardrail or equivalent so no gap exceeds 470 mm, and a toe board of at least 150 mm.

why_wrong.A: A toe board stops objects rolling off; it does not fill the gap between the top rail and the toe board.
why_wrong.B: The top rail height requirement is 950 mm, so the height is also deficient.
why_wrong.C: The minimum is 950 mm and a gap greater than 470 mm is not allowed.

common_mistake: Checking only that a top rail exists, without verifying its height and the size of the gaps beneath it.

stem: A MEWP operator continues working as the wind gusts increase, judging by feel that it is 'not that bad'. Nobody is measuring wind speed against the machine's rated limit. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: MEWPs have a manufacturer's maximum working wind speed, which should be measured, for example with an anemometer, rather than judged by feel
options.B: Operator experience is enough to judge wind safely on a machine they know well, so formally measuring wind speed is unnecessary
options.C: No wind limit applies while the occupant is inside the guardrailed basket, because the guardrails and any harness protect the occupant against gusts
options.D: A single national wind speed limit set in regulations applies to all MEWPs, so the operator only needs to know that one published figure

explanation: Subjective impressions of wind are unreliable, and the safe limit is set by the manufacturer, so it needs objective measurement and a clear stop point.

why_wrong.B: Experience does not replace measurement against a defined rated limit.
why_wrong.C: Wind limits apply because wind can overturn or destabilise the machine.
why_wrong.D: The limit depends on the specific machine and manufacturer instructions.

common_mistake: Judging wind by feel instead of measuring it against the equipment's rated limit.

stem: Look at the mobile tower in use. Which combination of problems makes the situation most dangerous?

options.A: Only the unlocked castors matter, since outriggers are optional on a tower of this size once the brakes are applied and the base is level
options.B: Unlocked castors, no outriggers at this height and climbing the outside of the frame together make a fall or a tipping tower much more likely
options.C: The tower is acceptably used, because climbing the outside is quicker and so reduces the total time spent at height during the task
options.D: The main problem is the worker carrying a power drill while climbing, since the tower itself is set up correctly and stable for this working height

explanation: Castors must be braked whenever the tower is occupied, towers at height need outriggers or stabilisers per the manufacturer's instructions, and access should be by the internal ladder, so the three faults compound each other.

why_wrong.A: Outriggers or stabilisers are required where the instructions call for them at that height.
why_wrong.C: External climbing is unsafe and destabilises the tower; access should use the internal ladder.
why_wrong.D: Carrying tools is a concern, but it does not account for the instability and access faults shown.

common_mistake: Spotting one fault and treating it as the whole problem when several faults combine.

stem: A trench stands open and unsupported, and has been open for three days without incident while an excavator works close to its edge. The supervisor says it has been fine so far so the ground must be stable. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Only depth matters, and trenches under a fixed depth are legally exempt from support, so the supervisor's decision to leave it unsupported is acceptable
options.B: A trench that has stood open for three days has proved itself stable, so no support or battering is needed while the ground conditions stay the same
options.C: Stability so far is no evidence of safety, as collapse can occur without warning and plant vibration adds risk, so support or battering and stand-off are needed
options.D: Vibration from plant affects buried services but not the stability of the trench sides, so working the excavator close to the edge is acceptable

explanation: Excavation stability depends on ground conditions, loads and vibration, so days without collapse do not show safety, and nearby plant makes a collapse more likely.

why_wrong.A: There is no automatic exemption; the need for support comes from risk assessment.
why_wrong.B: Time open does not prove stability; changing conditions can cause sudden collapse.
why_wrong.D: Vibration and surcharge loads near the edge can trigger collapse.

common_mistake: Treating the absence of a collapse so far as proof that an excavation is safe.

stem: A supervisor plans to send a worker down a below-ground chamber to check a valve position, without first considering whether it can be checked remotely. Gas testing will be arranged once the worker is already inside, 'just to be safe'. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Testing during the entry is acceptable because it gives the most up-to-date reading of the atmosphere the worker is actually breathing at that moment
options.B: Avoiding entry only needs to be considered after gas testing shows a hazardous atmosphere, as that is when the real risk becomes clear to the team
