options.C: Let him drive if he drinks coffee and takes more breaks, as self-monitoring is enough for a worker who says he feels alert and capable
options.D: Let him continue because a legal prescription makes the drug acceptable, and check his fitness only if there is an incident or visible impairment at work

explanation: Prescribed drugs can impair alertness, so safety-critical workers must report them and the employer must manage fitness for the task.

why_wrong.B: Policies on fitness cover legal medicines that affect safe operation as well as illegal drugs and alcohol.
why_wrong.C: Drowsiness can be unnoticed by the person affected, so self-judgement and caffeine are not reliable controls.
why_wrong.D: Legality does not remove the impairment risk, so waiting for an incident is too late.

common_mistake: Believing that a medicine from a doctor needs no mention to the employer, whatever the job.

stem: An operative wants to remove the guard from a petrol cut-off saw to make a deeper cut with an oversized disc. He says safety glasses and gloves will protect him instead. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Remove the guard if he wears a full face shield, since a shield stops flying fragments and makes a fixed guard unnecessary on a hand-held saw
options.B: Keep the guard fitted and use the rated disc size, adding a face shield over eye protection, hearing and respiratory protection, and gloves
options.C: Fit the oversized disc with the guard in place, because a guard rated for the saw protects against any larger blade he chooses to fit
options.D: Wear safety glasses and gloves only, since hearing and respiratory protection are needed just for fixed workshop machines, not hand-held tools

explanation: Guards are an engineering control that PPE cannot replace, and the disc must match the saw, with PPE used in addition for sparks, noise and dust.

why_wrong.A: A face shield cannot stop a disc burst striking the body, and PPE is the last line of defence, not a substitute for the guard.
why_wrong.C: A disc larger than the saw and guard are rated for can overspeed or break, and the guard no longer covers it.
why_wrong.D: Cut-off saws produce high noise and hazardous dust, so those need protection just as much outdoors.

common_mistake: Treating PPE as a replacement for a machine guard instead of an extra layer of protection.

stem: Look at the saw station. The foreman says the sign on the hoarding tells operators what to do in an emergency. Which statement about the stop arrangements is most accurate?

options.A: The red button is compliant as installed, because its colour makes it clearly identifiable and the layout around it is a housekeeping matter only
options.B: A second operator standing by to unplug the saw replaces the need for a clear button, since a person can isolate the power just as quickly
options.C: The emergency stop must stay unobstructed and quickly reachable, and a text sign can supplement a safety sign but cannot replace the control
options.D: The handwritten sign is a sufficient safety sign, as text instructions placed near a machine meet the signage regulations on their own terms

explanation: An emergency stop device must be immediately accessible and identifiable, and a text-only notice is merely supplementary and does not make an obstructed control usable.

why_wrong.A: A stop control that cannot be reached quickly fails its purpose, however clearly it is coloured.
why_wrong.B: Relying on a person to reach the plug is slower and less certain than an accessible stop control.
why_wrong.D: Text alone is not a safety sign, and it can only supplement a proper sign or control.

common_mistake: Assuming that a clearly coloured control or a notice is enough, even when stored materials block access to it.

stem: Bricklayers will work along a three-storey elevation for three weeks, with block stacks and mortar close to hand. The supervisor wants long leaning ladders for speed, with a colleague footing each. Which access choice is most suitable?

options.A: A MEWP hired for the three weeks, since its platform gives guardrails and quick access and the same machine will suit sustained bricklaying
options.B: Leaning ladders with a footer at each, because a second person at the base removes the main risk of slipping during sustained two-handed work
options.C: An independently tied scaffold with guardrails and a loading bay, because the duration and the material handling need a stable platform
options.D: Podium steps moved along the wall each day, because a small platform with handrails and a lower height cannot be misused like a ladder can

explanation: Long-duration work with heavy materials needs a platform with collective edge protection and a rated loading area, which ladders cannot give.

why_wrong.A: A MEWP has limited capacity and space for materials and constant repositioning, so it suits short jobs better than sustained bricklaying.
why_wrong.B: Footing does not suit long, two-handed work or materials handling, and it does not provide edge protection.
why_wrong.D: Podium steps suit light, short tasks and cannot support stacks of blocks across three storeys.

common_mistake: Choosing access equipment for speed of set-up instead of for the duration and the load of the task.

stem: A trench box is to be lowered into a 2.5 m trench by the excavator. The banksman asks a groundworker to climb in and steady it by hand while it hangs. What is the correct way to install it?

options.A: Choose any chain from the cabin to lift it, because the box itself is steel and the lifting accessories cannot be the weak point in the lift
options.B: Keep everyone out of the excavation while the box is suspended, use its rated lifting points and inspected accessories, and enter once seated
options.C: Slide the box in empty and have him enter at once, because boxes need not be fully seated before people go in to check the excavation sides
options.D: Let him steady the box with a tag line from inside the trench, as long as he wears a hard hat and moves clear if it swings toward him

explanation: People must never be in or beneath a suspended box, and a box must be lifted by its designed points with accessories of adequate rating.

why_wrong.A: Accessories must be rated for the load, marked and in-date for thorough examination, and the weak link can be the sling.
why_wrong.C: Nobody should enter until the box is seated and stable, since the unsupported sides may collapse.
why_wrong.D: A suspended box can swing or drop, and a hard hat gives no protection against its mass.

common_mistake: Entering an excavation to help position the support while the load is still moving.

stem: Lorries will enter a site from a 40 mph public road. The contractor plans to place a few cones, a road works sign and a portable traffic light set at the gate himself, without telling the highway authority. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Go ahead himself, since signs placed at a private entrance are the site's own business and not subject to any highway authority involvement
options.B: Agree the temporary traffic management with the highway authority and have trained operatives lay out signs, cones and signals to the national code
options.C: Rely on a marshal in hi-vis to stop traffic by hand, because a person with a flag is more flexible than lights and signs and costs less to run
options.D: Put the signs out only for peak lorry movements, since a lower signing standard is acceptable when delivery traffic is brief and infrequent

explanation: Works affecting a public road need agreed traffic management, laid out by trained people to the Safety at Street Works and Road Works code and Traffic Signs Manual.

why_wrong.A: Signs, cones and signals on or affecting the public carriageway fall under road works rules and need agreement.
why_wrong.C: Stopping public traffic is not for site marshals to improvise, and does not replace properly signed temporary controls.
why_wrong.D: Hazards at the access exist whenever vehicles turn, so signing cannot depend on how busy the road is.

common_mistake: Treating the site gate as private ground and so ignoring the rules for signs and signals that affect the public road.

stem: A joiner who has traded alone for years takes on his first full-time labourer. His policy carries 10 million pounds of public liability cover, and he says this already protects the new employee. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The public liability limit exceeds the legal minimum, so it can stand in for employers' liability cover if the labourer is named on the policy schedule
options.B: Employers' liability cover becomes compulsory once he has five or more staff, which is also when the certificate must be made available to them
options.C: He must hold the cover, but the certificate is a commercial document for his insurer and clients and does not have to be available to employees
options.D: He needs separate employers' liability insurance of at least 5 million pounds from an authorised insurer, with the certificate accessible to his employee

explanation: Employers must hold employers' liability cover from the first employee, at no less than 5 million pounds, and make the certificate accessible to staff and inspectors, whereas public liability protects third parties.

why_wrong.A: Public liability covers members of the public and not employees, so naming the labourer on it does not satisfy the compulsory insurance duty.
why_wrong.B: The duty applies from the first employee, and there is no five-person threshold for the insurance or the certificate.
why_wrong.C: The certificate must be accessible to employees, for example on site or electronically, and shown to inspectors on request.

common_mistake: Assuming that a large public liability policy automatically covers the people who work for you.

stem: To answer noise complaints, a contractor boxes a diesel generator inside a sealed plywood enclosure in a basement car park and records the noise risk as 'controlled'. The assessment is not looked at again. What is the best criticism?

options.A: Fumes from hired plant are the supplier's responsibility, so the contractor's own assessment does not have to address them once the unit is installed
options.B: The enclosure is a sound engineering control, so the noise risk is dealt with and the assessment needs revisiting if an injury or complaint arises later
options.C: Enclosures rank below personal protection, so the contractor should have issued ear defenders to everyone in the basement and removed the box
options.D: The enclosure creates new fume, heat and fire risks, so the assessment must be reviewed to cover them, with exhaust vented outside and the unit ventilated

explanation: A control measure can introduce fresh hazards, and a suitable and sufficient assessment must be revisited so that engine exhaust, heat build-up and fire are addressed alongside noise.

why_wrong.A: The contractor controlling the work must assess risks to people on site, whoever owns the equipment.
why_wrong.B: Waiting for harm before reviewing is reactive, and the change itself should trigger a review of the risks it creates.
why_wrong.C: This reverses the hierarchy of control, because reducing noise at source ranks above relying on personal protective equipment.

common_mistake: Closing a risk assessment as soon as the first hazard is controlled without checking what the control itself might cause.

stem: A bricklayer slumps, unresponsive and not breathing normally. A trained first aider reaches him within seconds, and the site defibrillator is in the office, two minutes' walk away. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Place him in the recovery position and monitor his breathing until the ambulance arrives, because compressions risk injuring someone who may still be breathing
options.B: Send one person to call 999 and fetch the defibrillator while the first aider starts chest compressions, then follow the device's spoken prompts on arrival
options.C: Carry him to the site office on a flat board so treatment happens beside the defibrillator, and call 999 once the first aider has begun treatment there
options.D: Start compressions but leave the defibrillator until paramedics arrive, because shocks given by untrained bystanders can harm the casualty

explanation: Cardiac arrest needs compressions straight away and an early shock, so tasks are shared: an ambulance is called, the defibrillator is fetched and CPR continues without delay.

why_wrong.A: The recovery position is for casualties who are breathing normally, and he is not, so he needs CPR.
why_wrong.C: Moving him delays compressions and the emergency call, and he should only be moved if the area is unsafe.
why_wrong.D: Public-access defibrillators give spoken instructions and will not shock unless it is advised, so early use improves survival.

common_mistake: Waiting for the ambulance or for a more qualified person before starting CPR and fetching the defibrillator.

stem: Workers wearing ear defenders during a concrete-breaking phase tell the supervisor they would not hear the fire bell. He points out the alarm was tested last week and worked. What is the correct response?

options.A: Brief the workers on what the alarm sounds like at induction, which meets the duty because awareness of the signal is what the law requires
options.B: Ban ear defenders during breaking work so the bell can be heard, because a fixed alarm cannot be adapted once the system has been installed
options.C: Make the warning effective for everyone, adding beacons or vibrating pagers where needed, and brief workers on the signal and the assembly point
options.D: Rely on supervisors shouting and using radios when the bell sounds, because a successful test proves the system works and workers must listen out

explanation: The means of warning must reach all people on site whatever their task or protection, so the alarm and fire plan are adjusted when a test shows the bell alone is not enough.

why_wrong.A: Knowing the sound is of no use when it cannot be heard, so the warning itself must be effective at the point of work.
why_wrong.B: Removing hearing protection exposes workers to noise damage, and the warning arrangements can be changed to suit the conditions.
why_wrong.D: A passing test shows the bell functions and not that everyone can hear it, and shouting is not a dependable warning.

common_mistake: Treating a fire alarm as adequate because it works when tested, without checking who may not be able to hear it.

stem: A labourer clearing silt from a rat-infested drainage ditch has a cut on his hand and wears fabric gloves. A week later he has headaches, muscle pain and chills. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Take a tetanus booster before the next ditch job, because vaccination gives full protection against the infections carried in rat urine
options.B: Tell a doctor he works near rats and water, and in future cover cuts with waterproof dressings, use waterproof gloves and wash before eating
options.C: Wear a dust mask to avoid breathing in rat droppings, then rest at home for a few days, since flu-like symptoms after a ditch job are normally just a cold
options.D: Use alcohol gel before lunch instead of washing his hands, because the bacteria die quickly once they leave the rat's body

explanation: These are typical early signs of leptospirosis (Weil's disease), spread by contact with rat urine through broken skin, so he should mention the exposure and use waterproof protection and hygiene.

why_wrong.A: Tetanus is a different disease, and no jab protects against leptospirosis, so protection depends on covering cuts and good hygiene.
why_wrong.C: The main route is through broken skin and the eyes or mouth, and dismissing symptoms delays the diagnosis of a serious illness.
why_wrong.D: The bacteria survive in wet conditions, and hands must be washed with soap and clean water, with breaks taken away from the work area.

common_mistake: Putting flu-like symptoms down to a cold and never mentioning contact with rats or water to the doctor.

stem: Dumper drivers on a rough haul road report back pain at the end of each shift. The manager buys seat cushions and tells them to drive faster to spend less time in the cab. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Seat cushions give adequate protection, and faster journeys cut the time spent in the cab so the daily vibration dose falls overall
options.B: Back pain among drivers is a manual handling matter, so no vibration assessment is needed unless a driver is off work for several days
options.C: Repair the haul road, keep seat suspension serviced, slow down on rough ground and have drivers report back pain for monitoring
options.D: Anti-vibration gloves worn on the steering wheel will protect the drivers adequately, since the vibration reaches the body mainly through the hands and controls

explanation: Whole-body vibration is best reduced at source through better surfaces, suitable maintained seats and slower speeds, with symptoms monitored to catch harm early.

why_wrong.A: Higher speed over rough ground increases the shocks received, and a cushion is not a tested control for vibration.
why_wrong.B: Whole-body vibration is a recognised hazard that must be assessed, and waiting for time off lets damage develop.
why_wrong.D: Whole-body vibration enters through the seat and the feet, so gloves address hand-arm vibration and not this problem.

common_mistake: Fitting a cheap comfort item and ignoring the road, the machine and the driving speed that cause the vibration.

stem: Roof tilers on a terrace strip broken tiles and drop them over the edge into a skip on the pavement. They have placed a cone and a sign beside the skip. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Material must not be thrown or tipped from height, so a chute or hoist should be used, with a fenced drop zone below and edge protection above
options.B: Cones and a warning sign are adequate for a low terrace roof, because the short drop to the skip makes the risk of injury minor
options.C: Hard hats on the tilers cover the risk, because the people most at risk from the activity are the workers on the roof and not those below
options.D: The skip should be moved into the road and a colleague should shout a warning before each tile is thrown, since a spoken warning controls the risk

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations forbid throwing or tipping material from height and require falling objects to be prevented or people protected, which a cone and sign cannot achieve.

why_wrong.B: Signs warn but do not prevent harm, and a thrown tile can seriously injure a passer-by whatever the height.
why_wrong.C: Hard hats protect the wearers only, and the people on the pavement below are the ones struck by falling debris.
why_wrong.D: A shouted warning is not a reliable control, and placing the skip in the road creates a traffic hazard on top of the original one.

common_mistake: Believing that a sign and a cone make it acceptable to drop waste from a roof.

stem: Look at the working platform the bricklayer is using. Which statement best describes the main risk?

options.A: The guardrails are too low, so he could topple forward over the top rail while reaching out to place bricks
options.B: The ladder is not secured to the frame, so the main risk is a fall during climbing before he reaches the platform
options.C: The pallet of bricks overloads the platform, risking collapse of the entire scaffold lift while he is laying
options.D: A fall through the open space beside the wall, and bricks sliding off the unprotected outer edge

explanation: The boards leave a gap a person could fall through, and the outer edge has no toe board to stop materials dropping onto the pavement.

why_wrong.A: The guardrails shown are at a suitable height, and the real weakness lies in the gap and the missing toe board.
why_wrong.B: The ladder appears to be tied in, so access is not the weakness in this picture.
why_wrong.C: The load shown is modest and not the main problem, whereas the gap and the unprotected edge are the visible defects.

common_mistake: Checking only the outer guardrails and forgetting the gap and the edge detail at the other side of a platform.

stem: A tipper reverses to the edge of a 1.8 m supported trench to discharge aggregate, guided by a groundworker standing beside the trench. Spoil is heaped along the same edge. Which assessment is correct?

options.A: Heaped spoil pushes back against the trench sides and steadies them, so the aggregate is best tipped on top of the heap right beside the trench edge
options.B: Vehicles and spoil must be kept back from the edge, with a barrier or stops and the guide standing clear, since the weight can collapse the sides
options.C: Because the trench sides are supported, the tipper can approach the edge, and the only added precaution needed is a harness for the guide
options.D: The tipper may reverse in once the driver is trained and the trench has been inspected that morning, because inspection removes loading risks

explanation: Plant and heaped material at the edge add load that can collapse trench sides or push material in, and edges where people could fall need substantial barriers.

why_wrong.A: Spoil at the edge adds weight and can fall into the excavation, and it should be set back and contained.
why_wrong.C: Support systems are not designed for extra loading from nearby vehicles, and a harness does not prevent collapse or falls into the trench.
why_wrong.D: An inspection does not cancel loading from vehicles, so plant must still be kept back from the edge.

common_mistake: Treating trench support as permission to load or park plant right up to the edge of the excavation.

stem: An operator fits a breaker to an excavator's quick hitch but finds the retaining pin missing. A labourer in the trench says a large bolt will do. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Work should stop until the manufacturer's specified pin is fitted, since the hitch can release the attachment without warning and no one should be beneath it
options.B: The breaker can be used with the boom kept low until a pin arrives, since an attachment falling from a small height cannot cause serious harm
options.C: Work can continue once the labourer climbs out of the trench, because the pin is only a secondary item and a falling attachment would be a rare event in practice
options.D: A bolt of suitable diameter is acceptable if the operator checks it first, because the hitch's hydraulic lock holds the breaker securely during normal use, as it would with the pin

explanation: The retaining pin is the key safeguard on a quick hitch, substitutes are not acceptable, and a missing pin can allow the attachment to fall without warning on anyone below.

why_wrong.B: A heavy breaker dropping from any height can crush or kill, so reducing the height does not make the working method safe.
why_wrong.C: The pin is the primary safeguard, and a hitch without it may release suddenly, so the machine should not be used.
why_wrong.D: Substitutes for the specified pin are not acceptable, and the hydraulic lock alone cannot be relied on to hold the attachment.

common_mistake: Improvising a replacement part to keep the job moving instead of stopping until the correct one is fitted.

stem: An inspector serves a Prohibition Notice stopping all use of a hoist with a damaged brake, with immediate effect. The contractor says he will appeal, so the hoist can stay in use until the tribunal decides. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Because the notice is only formal advice from the inspector, using the hoist during an appeal carries no penalty if the appeal later fails
options.B: The notice only binds him once a 21-day period for compliance has run, so he may keep using the hoist normally until that period has fully ended
options.C: The notice stays in force despite the appeal, so use must stop unless the tribunal directs otherwise, and the appeal must be lodged within 21 days of service
options.D: An appeal automatically suspends every enforcement notice, so the hoist can carry on in use under a banksman's control until the tribunal has decided the matter

explanation: An appeal suspends an Improvement Notice but not a Prohibition Notice, which stays in force unless the tribunal directs suspension, and appeals must be made within 21 days of service.

why_wrong.A: Failing to comply with an enforcement notice is a criminal offence, and the notice is a legal requirement and not advice.
why_wrong.B: A compliance period is a feature of Improvement Notices, while a Prohibition Notice stops the activity immediately or from the stated deadline.
why_wrong.D: Only an Improvement Notice is suspended by an appeal, whereas a Prohibition Notice continues to apply unless the tribunal specifically suspends it.

common_mistake: Assuming that lodging an appeal buys time to carry on with the work that the inspector has stopped.

stem: A site planner spends six hours a day at a laptop in the cabin and gets headaches and blurred vision by mid-afternoon. She asks for an eye test. Her manager says eyesight is a personal matter and glasses are not the firm's concern. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Eye tests apply only to office staff in permanent premises, so a worker in a temporary site cabin is outside the screen equipment rules
options.B: As a habitual screen user she can ask for an employer-paid eye test, and special glasses are paid for if needed for screen distance; her workstation should be assessed too
options.C: The employer need only act if an optician has already diagnosed a condition, and the employee pays for the test and any glasses herself
options.D: The employer must pay for her ordinary prescription glasses in every case, but is not required to look at the workstation or lighting

explanation: DSE users are entitled to an employer-funded eye test on request, with glasses funded only where special screen-distance ones are needed, and the workstation assessment should look at the setup causing symptoms.

why_wrong.A: The duty depends on habitual screen use, not the type of premises, so a temporary cabin does not remove it.
why_wrong.C: The entitlement arises on request from a DSE user and the employer pays for the test, so no prior diagnosis is required.
why_wrong.D: Glasses are funded only where special ones are needed for screen use, and the employer still has to assess the workstation.

common_mistake: Treating headaches and eyestrain from screen work as a personal health matter instead of a workplace duty the employer must assess.

stem: At 07:00 a dumper driver arrives smelling strongly of alcohol after a late night, insisting he feels fine. Short of drivers, the supervisor lets him start, since he is not slurring and will only drive on site. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Move him to banksman duty for the morning, because directing traffic needs no coordination or judgement and is a safer task to give him
options.B: Let him drive, since the road drink-drive limit applies only on public roads and an operator who seems alert and steady is not a real risk on private land
options.C: Keep him off driving and other safety-critical work, as alcohol still impairs judgement, and handle it under the site alcohol and drugs policy with support
options.D: Send him home in his own car and record the day as ordinary absence, avoiding a formal conversation until he is sober and calm

explanation: Residual alcohol can impair reaction and judgement even when someone feels well, so the supervisor must protect others by removing him from safety-critical duties and following the policy supportively.

why_wrong.A: Banksman work is safety-critical and relies on alertness and judgement, so impairment is just as dangerous there.
why_wrong.B: Health and safety law requires employers and workers not to endanger others on site, whatever the road driving limit says.
why_wrong.D: Letting him drive while possibly over the limit endangers the public, and treating it as plain absence ignores the policy and any support he needs.

common_mistake: Judging fitness for safety-critical work by whether someone looks and feels all right rather than by the risk of impairment.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative is wearing the right PPE because he has a helmet, safety glasses and a dust mask. What is the most significant problem with this approach?

options.A: His helmet should have a chin strap, because falling debris could knock it off, and the safety glasses and mask then provide enough protection
options.B: Dust is falling into his eyes and airway, so extraction at the tool comes first, with sealed goggles and a well-fitted mask as backup
options.C: He needs ear defenders fitted over the helmet, because drilling noise is the main risk and the other items already deal with the dust
options.D: He should wear a second disposable mask over the first, since layering masks gives the extra filtration needed for fine concrete dust

explanation: Dust at source should be controlled by on-tool extraction, and the PPE that remains must suit the hazard, meaning sealed eye protection against falling dust and a mask that fits the face.

why_wrong.A: A chin strap does not address dust entering his eyes and lungs, and open-sided glasses and a loose mask are inadequate for overhead dust.
why_wrong.C: Noise may need controlling too, but this ignores the dust cloud, which the glasses and loose mask do not properly protect against.
why_wrong.D: Layering disposable masks does not create a seal and gives no reliable extra protection; a fitted mask and source extraction are needed.

common_mistake: Assuming that wearing a standard set of PPE items means the worker is protected, without checking that each item suits the actual hazard.

stem: Labourers carrying pipes through a low plant room are issued light bump caps to stop knocks on pipework. The same room has a chain hoist lifting loads overhead, yet the supervisor says the bump caps count as head protection for the whole room. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Bump caps are enough if a banksman controls the lifting, because a helmet is only needed for loads that are actually moving overhead
options.B: A bump cap is acceptable for experienced workers if it has a chinstrap, because secure fit is what determines protection from falling objects
options.C: Bump caps protect only against knocks on fixed objects, so where loads or tools may fall an industrial safety helmet to EN 397 is needed
options.D: Bump caps meet the same impact standard as helmets, so they are acceptable whenever the headroom is too low for a helmet to be worn comfortably

explanation: Bump caps are not designed for falling objects, whereas an industrial safety helmet is tested to withstand impact from above, so the overhead lifting hazard needs a helmet.

why_wrong.A: Loads and tools can fall unexpectedly and a banksman cannot make a bump cap protect against an impact from above.
why_wrong.B: A chinstrap helps keep head protection in place but does not change a bump cap's lack of resistance to falling objects.
why_wrong.D: Bump caps are tested for minor knocks only and do not give protection against falling objects, however low the headroom is.

common_mistake: Treating any hard-shelled head covering as equivalent to an industrial safety helmet whatever the overhead risk.

stem: Roofers must replace old fibre-cement sheets on a warehouse roof with rooflights. The foreman suggests they walk on the roof ridge and along the sheet overlaps, since those are the strongest points. Which plan best controls the risk?

options.A: Lay a single scaffold board across the sheets to spread weight, as the board makes the sheets safe to walk on and lets the crew move freely
options.B: Put warning signs at the roof access and brief workers to avoid the rooflights, because trained roofers can judge which sheets will carry them
options.C: Walk only on the overlaps and fixings, wear harnesses on a short lanyard, and check each sheet by tapping it before putting any weight on it
options.D: Treat the roof as fragile, work from a platform below if possible, and otherwise use staging with guardrails and nets beneath

explanation: Old fibre-cement and rooflights should be treated as fragile, with work avoided on the surface where possible and collective protection such as staging, guardrails and nets used otherwise.

why_wrong.A: One board does not make a fragile roof safe; it can slip or tilt, and the crew would still be able to fall through next to it.
why_wrong.B: Signs and briefings are useful but cannot substitute for physical controls, and even experienced workers cannot judge fragility by eye.
why_wrong.C: Overlaps are not reliably strong on aged sheets, and tapping does not prove strength; anchored harnesses alone are not a proper fragile-roof system.

common_mistake: Relying on experience to judge by eye which parts of an old roof will take weight.

stem: A mobile access tower is built beside a warehouse wall. To bring the platform right up to the wall, a worker removes the wall-side outrigger. Which approach correctly deals with stability?

options.A: Leave the outrigger off but lock the brakes and keep the platform under three times the base width, as the wall prevents tipping
options.B: Fit every outrigger the manufacturer specifies, shift the tower or cut its working height if space is tight, and lock all castor brakes
options.C: Leave the outrigger off but allow one worker at a time on the platform, since a lighter load cannot overturn a braked tower
options.D: Leave the outrigger off but tie the tower to a window frame, because a tied tower no longer depends on its own base

explanation: The tower's stability is only proven with the manufacturer's full configuration of outriggers and locked brakes, so any shortfall in space must be solved by repositioning or reducing height.

why_wrong.A: A wall is not a designed restraint and gives no protection against the tower tipping away from it.
why_wrong.C: Limiting occupants does not restore the stability the missing outrigger provides, especially under sideways force from working.
why_wrong.D: Window frames are not designed anchorages, and the tower must still be stable on its own base as the manufacturer intended.

common_mistake: Assuming that a nearby wall, a tie or a lighter load can stand in for an outrigger the manufacturer's instructions require.

stem: A labourer holding only an excavator card is told to take over a telehandler for a quick move, because its keys were left in the cab overnight. The supervisor says he has plenty of plant experience. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He needs training and authorisation for that machine type first, and keys should be removed and secured whenever plant is left unattended
options.B: The telehandler can be used if he reads the operator manual first, as the manufacturer's instructions give him the competence needed
options.C: A card for one category of machine qualifies him to use similar plant on site, provided the supervisor accepts responsibility for giving the instruction
options.D: He may use it for a short, simple move, since the risk is low and keys left in cabs are accepted practice on busy sites with trusted crews

explanation: Operators must be competent and authorised for the specific machine type, and removing keys when the plant is left stops unauthorised use.

why_wrong.B: Reading a manual does not amount to practical training, assessment and authorisation for the machine.
why_wrong.C: Competence is machine-specific, and a supervisor's verbal permission does not replace training and authorisation for the telehandler.
why_wrong.D: Short moves still carry crushing and overturning risks, and leaving keys in machines invites unauthorised use.

common_mistake: Believing that general plant experience or a card for one machine type makes someone safe to drive any other machine.

stem: A mobile crane's thorough examination was done four months ago. Last week it was overloaded and its boom took a heavy shock load. The operator says the report is valid for another eight months. What is the position?

options.A: Keep it in use on lighter lifts until the next due date, because the in-date report shows it was in sound condition
options.B: Arrange an examination only if visible damage to the boom is found afterwards, because hidden damage would have shown in use
options.C: Take it out of use until a competent person has examined it, since exceptional circumstances require an examination regardless of the date due
options.D: Rely on the operator's daily pre-use check and the appointed person's sign-off, since thorough examinations only fall due at set intervals

explanation: LOLER requires a thorough examination whenever exceptional circumstances liable to jeopardise safety occur, so the in-date report no longer covers the crane.

why_wrong.A: The report reflects the crane's state before the overload and cannot show whether the shock load caused damage.
why_wrong.B: Damage from shock loading may be hidden, so the examination is triggered by the event and not by visible signs.
why_wrong.D: Daily checks do not replace a thorough examination, which is also required after exceptional circumstances.

common_mistake: Treating an in-date thorough examination report as proof that lifting equipment is safe after it has been overloaded or damaged.

stem: An excavator is refuelled from a mobile bowser parked on bare ground close to a surface-water drain. A little diesel splashes on the ground, and the operator rakes soil over it, saying no one will see it. What is the best response?

options.A: Wash the splash away with water from a hose, so the diluted diesel soaks away and leaves no visible trace on the ground
options.B: Raking soil over the spill is acceptable for a small splash, because the soil absorbs the diesel and bacteria in the ground break it down
options.C: Refuel away from drains using a drip tray, clean up with a spill kit at once, and dispose of contaminated material as waste
options.D: Refuel next to the drain so any splashes are caught, since a gully trap can hold the fuel before it leaves the site through the pipework

explanation: Fuel should be handled away from drains with drips contained, spills cleaned immediately with absorbent material, and contaminated absorbents dealt with as waste rather than hidden in the ground.

why_wrong.A: Washing spreads the fuel towards drains and watercourses and does not remove it, so a hose is the wrong response.
why_wrong.B: Burying fuel spreads contamination, and it can still reach the drain and groundwater, so it must be cleaned up and disposed of properly.
why_wrong.D: A drain does not trap fuel, which would travel into the sewer or a watercourse and cause pollution.

common_mistake: Treating small fuel spills as trivial and hiding them instead of containing and cleaning them up straight away.

stem: A subcontractor starts a refurbishment by reusing the RAMS from a similar job at another building, changing only the address and date. The new site has an open lift shaft and occupied offices next door. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A reused document becomes valid once the manager signs it as reviewed, because the signature shows the earlier controls were judged adequate anywhere
options.B: The assessment must suit this site's own hazards and people, so adapt it to the shaft and offices and brief the gang before work starts
options.C: A generic assessment is sufficient when the gang has worked together before, since their shared experience covers the site-specific hazards it omits
options.D: A reused assessment is acceptable when the activity is identical, because the hazards come from the task and site layout only affects the permit to work

explanation: A risk assessment must be suitable and sufficient for the actual task, place and people affected, so a document from another site cannot be adopted without review and communication.

why_wrong.A: A signature does not make controls suitable for new hazards, and the assessment still has to reflect this site.
why_wrong.C: Experience does not replace a written assessment of the specific hazards, and others such as office staff are not covered by it.
why_wrong.D: Hazards and who is exposed depend on the location as well as the task, so the layout cannot be left to a permit.

common_mistake: Assuming that a risk assessment from a similar job can be recycled with a new address on the front.

stem: A pan of cooking oil on the hob in the welfare cabin catches fire. One worker grabs a bucket of water to throw over it, while another suggests carrying the pan outside. Which action is correct?

options.A: Open the windows and doors to clear the smoke, then let the oil burn out under supervision while the cabin is ventilated
options.B: Carry the pan outside at arm's length, because removing the fire from the cabin protects the building and the people inside it
options.C: Raise the alarm and, if safe, switch off the heat and use a wet chemical extinguisher or fire blanket; otherwise leave and close the door
options.D: Throw the water from a safe distance, since a large volume will cool the pan quickly and put out the flames before the oil can spread to the cabin

explanation: Fat fires need smothering or cooling with a suitable agent after the heat is removed, and anyone who cannot do that safely should evacuate and raise the alarm.

why_wrong.A: More air feeds the fire, and leaving it to burn out ignores the danger of it spreading to the cabin.
why_wrong.B: Moving a burning pan risks spilling fat onto the carrier and spreading the fire along the route.
why_wrong.D: Water sinks below the burning oil and flashes to steam, throwing flaming fat across the room.

common_mistake: Reaching for water on any fire because it is the nearest and most familiar extinguishing agent.

stem: A paving operative uses a breaker with a vibration magnitude of 7 m/s2 for two hours of trigger time a day. The manager notes that the exposure limit value is 5 m/s2 A(8) and says the job must stop. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: About 3.5 m/s2 A(8), over the action value but below the limit, so controls, training and health surveillance are needed without banning the job
options.B: The exposure is 7 m/s2 because magnitude is what counts, and since this is over the limit value the operator must be taken off the tool immediately
options.C: The figure is about 1.75 m/s2 because two hours out of eight is a quarter, so it falls under the action value and no duties apply to the operator
options.D: The exposure is under the limit of 5, so duties begin only if symptoms are reported and no preventive action is needed until then

explanation: Daily exposure scales with the square root of time, so 7 m/s2 for two hours is about 3.5 m/s2 A(8), above the action value of 2.5 but under the limit of 5.

why_wrong.B: Exposure is worked out over an eight-hour reference period, so the tool's magnitude alone does not give the daily figure.
why_wrong.C: Exposure does not scale in a straight line with time, since it follows the square root of the time ratio.
why_wrong.D: Duties such as controls and health surveillance start at the action value, not at the limit or after symptoms.

common_mistake: Treating the limit value as the point where action starts instead of the action value.

stem: While clearing a derelict flat, a labourer is pricked on the palm by a needle hidden in a bin bag. He wants to finish the job before the weekend and says he feels fine. What is the right response?

options.A: Scrub the wound hard with a nail brush and bleach, then carry on, because disinfecting the skin kills any virus before it can spread
options.B: Put a plaster on it and watch for symptoms, seeing a doctor only if he develops a fever or yellowing skin in the weeks that follow
options.C: Squeeze the puncture hard and suck out the blood, then spit it out, because this removes any infected blood before it can enter the body and cause an infection
options.D: Let it bleed gently, wash under running water with soap, cover it, report it and get prompt medical assessment, as treatment can be time-critical

explanation: Prompt first aid, reporting and urgent medical advice matter because blood-borne infection shows no early symptoms and some preventive treatment must be started quickly.

why_wrong.A: Scrubbing and bleach damage the skin and do not replace medical assessment.
why_wrong.B: Blood-borne infections can be silent at first, so waiting for symptoms can mean missing the window for treatment.
why_wrong.C: Sucking the wound is not recommended and risks exposing the mouth to blood.

common_mistake: Assuming a minor-looking injury needs no reporting or medical follow-up when he feels well.

stem: A facade scaffold was handed over last week with a valid inspection record. Bricklayers now want to fix debris sheeting along its full length to keep dust off the street. What should happen first?

options.A: The bricklayers can fit the sheeting themselves, because the existing record stays valid until the next seven-day inspection is due
options.B: The bricklayers can fit the sheeting if it is a fire-retardant grade, since flammability is the only extra risk it adds
options.C: The bricklayers can fit the sheeting if they leave a gap at the top to let wind through, so no further assessment is needed
options.D: The scaffold contractor should assess the extra wind loading and ties, make any changes, then re-inspect and record it before use

explanation: Sheeting increases wind load on the structure, so the alteration needs competent assessment and a fresh inspection before anyone relies on the scaffold.

why_wrong.A: An alteration to the scaffold requires inspection before further use, so the earlier record no longer covers the changed structure.
why_wrong.B: Fire rating addresses ignition only and ignores the major increase in wind loading on the scaffold and its ties.
why_wrong.C: A gap does not remove the extra wind loading and the scaffold's ties and design were not made for sheeted conditions.

common_mistake: Thinking a scaffold inspection tag stays valid after other trades alter or add to the structure.

stem: Look at the trestle platform in the scene. The plasterer says the boards feel firm when he walks along them. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: Boards are laid across only two trestles, when any platform needs at least three supports to remain stable under a working person
options.B: The boards stick out well past the trestle with nothing under them, so standing on that end could tip the platform and drop him
options.C: No ties join the trestles to the wall, so the whole platform could slide sideways away from the work while he is reaching upward
options.D: He carries plaster in one hand, which leaves him unable to grip anything and makes any slip more likely to cause a fall from the boards

explanation: Boards that overhang their support by more than a small margin can tilt when stood on, which makes an unsupported cantilever the key fault here.

why_wrong.A: Two trestles are normal for a platform of this length, and the fault lies in the unsupported board ends.
why_wrong.C: Low trestle platforms rely on firm support of the boards rather than ties, so this misses the real fault.
why_wrong.D: Carrying tools is a lesser concern compared with the platform that can tip when loaded at its unsupported end.

common_mistake: Judging a platform safe because it feels solid underfoot at the middle without checking the board supports.

stem: The boom of a telehandler touches an overhead power line and the machine stops. The operator is unhurt and nothing is on fire. Which action is correct?

options.A: Stay in the cab, warn everyone to keep well clear, and wait until the line owner confirms the line is dead before moving
options.B: Have a banksman push the boom clear with a dry timber pole, since wood is a poor conductor and the line then goes dead
options.C: Reverse the machine away to break contact and then inspect it, since a tripped line is no longer live and cannot re-energise
options.D: Climb down at once and walk away normally, because the tyres insulate the machine and the line will already have tripped

explanation: A line that is touched must be treated as live, and the cab is the safest place until the owner has isolated it and said it is safe.

why_wrong.B: Touching the machine or its load, even with timber, is dangerous and nobody should approach until the line is confirmed dead.
why_wrong.C: Lines can re-energise automatically after tripping, so the operator must not assume the line is dead without confirmation from the owner.
why_wrong.D: Stepping down onto energised ground can pass current through the body, and tyres do not reliably insulate a machine.

common_mistake: Assuming that a line which has tripped or a rubber-tyred machine means the contact is no longer dangerous.

stem: A yellow-cable 110 V drill in a basement has a cracked plug. A labourer fits a blue 230 V plug from the cabin and uses a 230 V socket outlet protected by an RCD, saying the RCD will protect him. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The RCD makes the mismatch safe because it trips on any fault, so a 230 V supply is acceptable provided the drill is used for short periods only
options.B: The drill is rated for 110 V, so withdraw it until a competent person fits a matching 110 V plug, as the RCD cannot cure a wrong supply
options.C: Any worker may refit a plug if the tool is visually inspected afterwards, since this is a simple task that does not require competence or matching
options.D: Taping the cracked plug case and carrying on is acceptable until the tool is next due for portable appliance testing in the coming weeks

explanation: Equipment must only be connected to the supply it is designed for, and defective equipment must be withdrawn and repaired by someone competent.

why_wrong.A: An RCD does not correct the wrong voltage and the tool is designed to run on a reduced supply.
why_wrong.C: Using any plug that fits ignores the colour-coded system that prevents 110 V tools from being connected to 230 V.
why_wrong.D: A damaged plug is a defect and the tool should be withdrawn at once, rather than waiting for a test date.

common_mistake: Fitting whatever plug is to hand and trusting an RCD to make up for it.

stem: Demolishing a brick outbuilding beside a school, a crew damps the debris to stop dust, and the water runs across the yard into a surface-water drain. A neighbour complains of dust anyway. Which response best deals with both dust and run-off?

options.A: Stop damping and move to dry sweeping at the end of each shift, since dry methods create no run-off for the site to manage in future
options.B: Increase hosing so that the dust washes off the debris, because the water goes to the council's drain and is removed from site
options.C: Erect a tall solid hoarding and let the dust settle by itself, since the hoarding stops dust leaving site without extra damping
options.D: Use controlled misting at the source, divert or trap the run-off so silt settles before it leaves, and keep the drain protected throughout the work

explanation: Suppressing dust at source reduces nuisance, while controlling the water prevents silt and contaminants entering the drain, so both effects are managed together.

why_wrong.A: Dry sweeping makes more airborne dust and does nothing to protect the school from it during the work.
why_wrong.B: Washing silty water into a surface-water drain is a pollution offence, however it is described.
why_wrong.C: A hoarding does not stop dust drifting over it, and it does nothing to control run-off.

common_mistake: Solving one environmental problem, such as dust, by creating another, such as polluted run-off.

stem: A boundary tree is protected by a tree preservation order. To lay a drain, the excavator operator plans to cut through its roots 1 m from the trunk, saying only the branches and trunk are protected. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The order matters only if the tree is felled, so cutting the roots is fine provided the tree is left standing when the work finishes
options.B: Cutting roots is a prohibited activity that needs the planning authority's consent, so re-route the drain or obtain consent first and fence the protection zone
options.C: The site manager can approve the root cutting once an arboricultural contractor has walked the route and agreed the line of the drain
options.D: Roots can be cut freely because the order covers only the visible parts, provided the cut is made cleanly with a saw rather than the bucket

explanation: A tree preservation order covers cutting roots as well as felling and lopping, so consent is needed and the work should be changed or authorised first.

why_wrong.A: Damaging a tree is prohibited as well, and cutting major roots can destroy it.
why_wrong.C: Only the local planning authority can consent, and a contractor's agreement does not substitute for that.
why_wrong.D: The order protects roots too, and a clean cut does not remove the need for consent.

common_mistake: Thinking a tree preservation order protects only the parts of the tree above ground.

stem: A client appoints a principal contractor for a four-month refit involving several trades. The client says her architect will write the construction phase plan, and the contractor intends to start setting up the site while it drafts one. Who should produce the plan, and when?

options.A: The client should draw up the plan from her pre-construction information, and the principal contractor then adds site detail once the site has been set up
options.B: Each contractor should write a plan for its own package, and the principal designer then merges these into one document before handover to the client
options.C: The principal contractor must draw up the plan, with the principal designer's help, before the site is set up, then keep it under review as work changes
options.D: The principal contractor may draft the plan once work has started, provided it is finished before the first higher-risk activity begins on the site

explanation: Regulation 12 of CDM 2015 makes the principal contractor responsible for the construction phase plan, to be in place before setting up the site and reviewed as the work develops.

why_wrong.A: The plan is the principal contractor's duty, and it is needed before the site is set up rather than added to afterwards.
why_wrong.B: This confuses contractors' method statements with the single plan the principal contractor must produce and own.
why_wrong.D: The duty requires the plan before setting up the site, not a draft completed later.

common_mistake: Assuming the construction phase plan is a client or designer document that can be finished after work has started.

stem: A principal designer's appointment ends at structural completion, while the principal contractor's fit-out carries on for five more months. The client asks what must now happen to the health and safety file. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The principal designer must give the file to the principal contractor, who then has to keep it reviewed and updated to reflect the fit-out work and any changes
options.B: The principal designer remains responsible for updating the file until practical completion, even though the appointment has formally ended and no longer covers the project
options.C: The file is closed at structural completion, since later fit-out information is recorded in the construction phase plan and does not belong in the file
options.D: The file passes straight to the client, who takes over updating it, because the principal contractor has no duties in relation to it once the designer leaves

explanation: Under regulation 12 of CDM 2015, if the principal designer's appointment ends before the project does, the file passes to the principal contractor, who must keep it up to date.

why_wrong.B: A principal designer whose appointment has ended no longer holds duties and must hand the file over.
why_wrong.C: The file must reflect changes as work progresses and is not frozen when one duty holder leaves.
why_wrong.D: The principal contractor inherits the duty to maintain the file when the principal designer's role ends early.

common_mistake: Treating the health and safety file as a one-off document that is finished once the structure is complete.

stem: An assessment scores three risks: a loose handrail on a spare office stair at 4, cluttered cable runs at 8, and an open lift shaft with no barrier on a busy floor at 20. The manager wants the cheap, easy fixes done first. What is the best approach?

options.A: Close the shaft at the next weekly review, since a lift shaft is a permanent feature and the score is the same whenever it is dealt with
options.B: Barrier the shaft immediately, then work through the other risks in order of score, recording who will fix each one and by what date
options.C: Fix the handrail and cables first as quick wins, then plan the shaft carefully, since a high score means the work needs more preparation
options.D: Treat all three as equal priority and fix them in the order they were found, because the matrix gives an indication and not a ranking

explanation: Controls should be prioritised by the level of risk, so the most serious risk is dealt with first, and recording owners and dates ensures that remaining actions are completed.

why_wrong.A: A score of 20 means serious harm is likely now, and the risk remains until a control is in place, so waiting does not keep it unchanged.
why_wrong.C: Ease or cost of a fix should not outrank severity, and leaving the highest risk exposed while quick wins are done is poor prioritisation.
why_wrong.D: The purpose of scoring risks is to rank them so that those with the greatest potential for serious harm are controlled first.

common_mistake: Letting cost and convenience decide the order of actions, instead of the severity of harm and the number of people exposed.

stem: A fixer using a cartridge-operated fixing tool in a steel-framed hall has a calculated daily noise exposure of 78 dB(A), so a colleague says no noise duties apply. The sharp bang is measured at a peak of 138 dB(C). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Hearing protection must be provided and its use enforced, because the peak exceeds the upper action value of 137 dB(C) whatever the daily average is
options.B: Only the lower peak value of 135 dB(C) is passed, so information and training are due but protection can be left to personal choice
options.C: Protection is only recommended, because the peak is below the 140 dB(C) limit value, which is the level that makes protection compulsory
options.D: No action is needed, because action values are judged only on the daily average and a brief peak is simply absorbed into that figure

explanation: Peak sound pressure has its own action values, separate from the daily average, and exceeding the upper peak value of 137 dB(C) triggers the upper-level duties.

why_wrong.B: At 138 dB(C) the upper peak action value of 137 dB(C) has been passed, so the lower-level duties alone are not enough.
why_wrong.C: Compulsory use applies from the upper action value, and the limit value is a ceiling that must not be exceeded even with protection.
why_wrong.D: The regulations set separate peak sound pressure values that apply even where the daily average is low.

common_mistake: Judging noise risk only from the daily average and forgetting that sudden loud impacts have their own peak limits.

stem: A floor layer spreads epoxy resin for three hours wearing thin disposable nitrile gloves bought in bulk. The supervisor says nitrile is chemical-proof, so one pair will last the whole task. How should glove suitability be judged?

options.A: Nitrile is suitable for every resin and solvent, provided the gloves are the correct size and the wearer checks them for visible holes at the start
options.B: Gloves become necessary once the skin shows irritation, at which point cotton-lined gloves that soak up the resin are the better choice for the task
options.C: Thickness is the reliable guide, so wearing two thin pairs together gives the same protection as a single glove rated for the resin concerned
options.D: Check the maker's breakthrough data for this specific resin, then set a change interval shorter than that and replace the gloves after any splash

explanation: Chemical resistance varies by glove material, product and substance, so selection should rely on the maker's breakthrough data for the actual chemical, with replacement before that time is reached.

why_wrong.A: Resistance differs between chemicals, and a glove can be permeated without any visible damage.
why_wrong.B: Gloves should prevent contact before irritation appears, and absorbent cotton holds the chemical against the skin.
why_wrong.C: Thickness is not a substitute for tested resistance to the specific chemical, and doubling up can reduce dexterity and mask contamination.

common_mistake: Choosing gloves by the material name or thickness rather than by the maker's breakthrough data for the chemical in use.

stem: A worker on a boom-type MEWP must fix a bracket just beyond the edge of the basket. He proposes standing on the mid-rail. Which harness arrangement is correct?

options.A: Wear a full harness with a short lanyard set so he cannot reach a fall, and reposition the basket so he works from the floor
options.B: Clip a fall-arrest block to the top guardrail so he can lean out safely, because the rail is strong enough to hold him
options.C: Wear a full harness with a 2 m shock-absorbing lanyard on the basket anchor, since arresting a fall is safer than restraining him
options.D: Wear a waist belt with a short lanyard to the basket anchor, as the belt is lighter and gives more freedom to reach

explanation: Work restraint keeps the worker inside the basket so a fall cannot happen, and repositioning the platform removes the need to lean out or climb.

why_wrong.B: A guardrail is not an anchor point, and clipping to it would allow a person to be thrown out of the basket.
why_wrong.C: Fall arrest in a basket risks ejection and heavy loads on an anchor not rated for it, and restraint prevents the fall in the first place.
why_wrong.D: A waist belt is not acceptable fall protection because it can cause injury and does not hold the body securely.

common_mistake: Believing that being clipped on makes it acceptable to climb on or lean over the guardrails of a basket.

stem: An excavator bucket snags a buried cable, causing a flash and a bang. The cable looks intact and the operator is unhurt in the cab. A groundworker asks to walk over and check it, saying the cable has clearly tripped off. What should happen?

options.A: The operator stays in the cab, everyone keeps clear, and the cable is treated as live until its owner has made it safe and been told about the strike
options.B: The groundworker should cut the cable ends and tape them while wearing insulating gloves, so the damaged section is isolated until the owner can attend
options.C: The groundworker can inspect it from a short distance and, if the outer sheath is unbroken, work may resume because the protection has already operated
options.D: The operator should climb out at once and move away, since the machine is the hazard, and phone the owner after the trench has been backfilled

explanation: Guidance is to treat all services as live until proven dead, keep drivers in the cab and people away, and inform the owner, because a damaged cable may re-energise or have hidden damage.

why_wrong.B: Interfering with a possibly live cable is dangerous, and only the owner or a competent authorised person may make it safe.
why_wrong.C: A cable that has tripped may re-energise and can be damaged internally, so nobody should approach it.
why_wrong.D: Leaving the cab risks electrocution, and backfilling would hide the damage before the owner has inspected it.

common_mistake: Assuming a cable that has tripped or looks undamaged after a strike is dead and safe to approach.

stem: Look at the delivery being unloaded at the site entrance. The driver says he has run this lorry-mounted crane for years and the load is well within its rated capacity. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The lorry is parked on a steep gradient with its wheels unchocked, so the vehicle could roll when the boom extends and the load swings out
options.B: A stabiliser foot is bearing on a drain cover with no spreader, and the load is passing over people using the pedestrian route
options.C: The driver is operating the crane controls without a hard hat and hi-vis clothing, which is the main reason the lift is not safe to continue
options.D: The load is slung on a worn chain that should have been rejected, and the driver has not checked the date of its last thorough examination

explanation: A stabiliser on a weak, hollow surface can punch through and overturn the vehicle, and lifting over pedestrians exposes them to a dropped or swinging load.

why_wrong.A: The road is flat and the stabilisers carry the load, so rolling is not the key problem shown.
why_wrong.C: The driver is wearing a hard hat and hi-vis, so this is not what makes the lift unsafe.
why_wrong.D: The sling in the picture is in good condition, and nothing shows an overdue examination.

common_mistake: Judging a lift safe from the load rating alone without checking what is supporting the stabilisers and who is beneath the load path.

stem: A telehandler is rated at 3 tonnes at a 500 mm load centre. To carry long timber bundles the driver fits 2 m fork extensions and lifts 2.5 tonnes, saying that is within the rating. What is wrong?

options.A: Capacity only changes on rough ground, so on level concrete with the boom lowered the 3 tonne figure still applies
options.B: Capacity is unaffected provided the load sits fully on the extensions and the forks are held level throughout the whole lift
options.C: Extensions move the load centre forward and cut capacity, so check the load against the chart for that attachment
options.D: Capacity falls only when the boom is extended, so keeping the boom retracted keeps the 3 tonne rating valid for the lift

explanation: Capacity depends on how far the load's centre of gravity is from the forks, so a longer reach means the nameplate figure no longer applies.

why_wrong.A: Ground conditions are a separate issue, and extensions reduce capacity on any surface.
why_wrong.B: Level forks do not change the load centre distance, which is the factor that reduces the safe capacity.
why_wrong.D: A retracted boom does not offset the longer forks, as the load centre has still moved away from the front axle.

common_mistake: Assuming the rated capacity on the machine plate still applies after the load centre has been changed by an attachment.

stem: A site manager bins the waste transfer notes after each skip leaves. A recent skip also took oil-contaminated soil dug from beside a fuel tank, recorded on an ordinary note with the general rubble. Which statement correctly describes what the duty of care requires?

options.A: Contaminated soil must be kept apart as hazardous waste with its own consignment note, and transfer notes must be kept two years and consignment notes three
options.B: The soil can stay in the general skip if the oil has dried, and a single consignment note kept for twelve months covers all hazardous waste in a year
options.C: Only the waste carrier must keep the paperwork, because the producer's duty ends once the skip has left the site and the carrier has taken responsibility
options.D: Mixing the soil with the rubble is acceptable if the load is described as mixed waste, and notes need only be kept until the skip is accepted at the disposal site

explanation: Waste duty of care requires accurate paperwork for every transfer, hazardous waste needs a consignment note, and copies must be retained for the minimum periods of two years and three years respectively.

why_wrong.B: Dried oil residue is still hazardous contamination, and the note retention periods are not twelve months.
why_wrong.C: The producer keeps its own copies, since the duty of care follows waste from site until its final disposal.
why_wrong.D: Hazardous waste must not be mixed with non-hazardous waste, and notes must be retained well beyond acceptance of the load.

common_mistake: Thinking the waste duty of care ends when the skip leaves site and that paperwork can be thrown away afterwards.

stem: A self-employed welder fixing a gate leaves an unfenced, unlit pit beside a public footpath overnight. He says health and safety law protects employees, and that the principal contractor is responsible for the whole site. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He owes a duty to the public only when a written contract with the principal contractor says so, because contracts define exactly who his work must protect.
options.B: The Act's duties cover employees, so a passer-by falls outside what he owes, and responsibility for the footpath rests with the principal contractor on site.
options.C: His duty ends when he leaves site for the day, because the principal contractor takes over control of his work area and its hazards overnight.
options.D: He has his own duty as a self-employed person to protect others affected by his work, such as passers-by, whatever the principal contractor also owes.

explanation: The Health and Safety at Work Act extends duties to the self-employed for the safety of non-employees, so a pit left open beside a public footpath is his breach whatever the principal contractor also owes.

why_wrong.A: Statutory duties to non-employees exist by law and do not depend on any contract wording.
why_wrong.B: This wrongly limits the Act to employees, when section 3 protects other people affected by a self-employed person's work.
why_wrong.C: The hazard he created remains his responsibility, and leaving it unfenced and unlit is the failing.

common_mistake: Assuming that health and safety duties belong only to employers and only to their own workers.

stem: A firm will not fit fixed guardrails on a low flat roof visited weekly. It argues that a fall is unlikely and that the guardrails cost more than a typical minor injury claim. Which statement best describes the legal test?

options.A: Guardrails can be refused only if their cost is grossly out of proportion to the risk reduction, and a possible fatal fall outweighs low likelihood.
options.B: A low likelihood rating allows the firm to accept the risk, because the law only expects controls that cost less than an average claim would.
options.C: A warning sign and a toolbox talk are a lawful substitute because weekly visits count as occasional access to a low roof like this one.
options.D: Cost has no place in the Work at Height Regulations, so guardrails must be fitted on every roof whatever the frequency of access or the circumstances.

explanation: Reasonably practicable means a measure is required unless its cost, time and trouble are grossly disproportionate to the risk, and severe potential harm raises the cost that can be justified.

why_wrong.B: The test weighs cost against the risk reduction and severity, not against a typical claim for a minor injury.
why_wrong.C: Signs and instruction sit at the bottom of the hierarchy and do not replace collective edge protection that is reasonably practicable.
why_wrong.D: The regulations follow a hierarchy and use reasonably practicable wording, so cost is weighed and other measures may be suitable.

common_mistake: Judging a control by how rarely an accident is expected instead of by how severe the outcome would be.

stem: A labourer falls onto exposed rebar and a 15 cm steel offcut is lodged in his thigh, which is bleeding heavily. A colleague wants to pull it out to stop the blood. What is the correct first aid response?

options.A: Pull the object out quickly, then press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth, since the object is what keeps the blood vessel open and bleeding.
options.B: Press hard directly down onto the object to seal the bleeding, then bandage over it tightly and drive him to hospital in the site van.
options.C: Leave the object in place, press either side of it with padding built up around it, and call 999 immediately while a first aider stays with him.
options.D: Leave the object, fit a tight tourniquet above it straight away, and note the time before waiting to see whether the bleeding slows down.

explanation: Removing an embedded object can increase bleeding, so pressure is applied beside it with padding, and emergency help is summoned immediately.

why_wrong.A: Removing the object can worsen bleeding and tissue damage, and it is left for hospital staff to remove.
why_wrong.B: Pressing on the object can drive it deeper, and a heavily bleeding casualty needs an ambulance, not a van journey.
why_wrong.D: Direct pressure around the object comes first, and a tourniquet is not the initial step for this wound.

common_mistake: Assuming the quickest way to stop bleeding is to remove whatever has caused the wound.

stem: A floor sealer task with a solvent that has both 8-hour and 15-minute workplace exposure limits involves a 12-minute burst of heavy fumes in a small room. The 8-hour average is within its limit, so the manager says no further control is needed. Which view is correct?

options.A: Short intense peaks can harm even when the 8-hour average is low, so the 15-minute exposure must be compared with the short-term limit and controlled
options.B: The short-term limit applies only when a burst lasts longer than an hour, so a 12-minute burst is covered by the long-term limit alone
options.C: The 8-hour average is the only legal test, so bursts lasting less than a quarter of an hour can be ignored while the shift total stays under the limit
options.D: Issuing a respirator for the burst removes any need to compare exposure with the limits, as they apply only to unprotected workers

explanation: Short-term limits protect against effects such as irritation from brief high exposure, and a low shift average does not show that any 15-minute period stays within its limit.

why_wrong.B: A short-term limit is defined over a 15-minute reference period, so much shorter exposure is exactly what it is designed to cover.
why_wrong.C: The 15-minute limit applies to any such period in the shift, and averaging over eight hours can hide harmful peaks.
why_wrong.D: Exposure limits are compared with airborne levels, and a respirator is a last resort used after reasonably practicable controls, not a way to ignore them.

common_mistake: Relying on a shift average to show a task is safe when the harm comes from short, intense bursts of exposure.

stem: A site welfare unit's shower and cold-water tank sat unused for six weeks over a shutdown. The supervisor wants the shower open this morning, saying Legionnaires' disease comes from drinking contaminated water and only affects hospitals. Which response is best?

options.A: Display a notice telling workers not to swallow any shower water, which removes the infection route and so makes extra system checks unnecessary
options.B: Run the hot tap for a minute and then allow use, because the bacteria multiply only in very hot water and a cold storage tank cannot be a source
options.C: Leave the matter to the water company, since legionella duties cover only the mains supply and not tanks or showers installed on site
options.D: Flush the system, disinfect if needed and check water temperatures before use, because infection comes from breathing in fine droplets such as shower spray

explanation: Water left stagnant at 20 to 45 degrees allows Legionella to multiply, and showers create breathable droplets, so the system should be flushed, checked and controlled before reopening.

why_wrong.A: The route of infection is inhaling droplets, so a warning about swallowing water does not control the risk.
why_wrong.B: Legionella thrives in stagnant water between about 20 and 45 degrees, including in warm cold-water tanks, and is killed only by sustained high temperatures.
why_wrong.C: Whoever controls the site water system has duties to assess and control the risk, which covers storage tanks and showers.

common_mistake: Thinking that water systems are safe to use again straight after a period of standing unused.

stem: A worker clamping steel plate on a bench drill wears issued cut-resistant gloves because the swarf is sharp. A colleague says extra PPE can only make a task safer. Which view is correct?

options.A: Wear the gloves with the cuffs rolled and taped tight, because securing the cuffs makes entanglement with the spindle impossible in practice.
options.B: Remove the gloves while the drill runs, because the spindle can catch them, and clear swarf with a brush once it has stopped.
options.C: Gloves are acceptable once the drill guard is lowered, because a guard removes any chance of the glove being drawn into the machine.
options.D: Keep the gloves on because swarf cuts are the likelier injury, and a close-fitting glove cannot be caught by a rotating chuck or spindle.

explanation: PPE must not add a new risk, and HSE advises avoiding gloves on machines such as bench drills where they could be caught, so the swarf is handled safely after the drill stops.

why_wrong.A: Taping cuffs still leaves the glove able to snag, and it replaces the safer step of removing it.
why_wrong.C: A guard reduces contact but does not remove the entanglement risk while the operator's hands are near the spindle.
why_wrong.D: Gloves of any fit can snag on a rotating spindle, and the entanglement injury would be far more severe than a cut.

common_mistake: Assuming that more protective equipment always means a safer worker, even around rotating machinery.

stem: Look at the scene. The groundworker says he is fully protected because he has everything the site rules ask for. Which item of protection is missing?

options.A: A full-face respirator, because cutting green timber releases fine dust that is as harmful as silica and is breathed in deeply by the sawyer.
options.B: Arm guards over the sleeves, because the forearm is the part of the body most often struck during a chainsaw cut on a fallen branch.
options.C: A fall-arrest harness with a lanyard, because a heavy branch could pull him off balance while he is cutting it up on the ground.
options.D: Cut-resistant chainsaw trousers, because a chain that kicks or slips strikes the thighs first and ordinary clothing gives no resistance.

explanation: The picture shows head, face, hearing, hand and foot protection but plain denim jeans, and cut-resistant leg protection is the essential item for chainsaw use.

why_wrong.A: Green timber cutting is not a respirable silica task, and the visible gap in the PPE is leg protection.
why_wrong.B: The thigh is the usual injury site, and arm guards are not the standard missing item here.
why_wrong.C: He is working at ground level beside a trestle, so a harness is not relevant to the hazard shown.

common_mistake: Checking that a worker has a full set of PPE without checking that it matches the part of the body the tool threatens.

stem: A painter finds a stepladder with a bent rung and a cracked stile. For a quick job he plans to climb carrying a full 10-litre paint bucket in one hand. Which approach is correct?
