explanation: Good traffic management removes the blind spot, separates pedestrians from vehicles at a defined crossing, and enforces speed with physical measures instead of relying on a sign alone.

why_wrong.B: A mirror gives a limited view and does not remove the blind corner or separate people from traffic.
why_wrong.C: Horn sounding is a weak warning that depends on drivers and pedestrians hearing it and acting in time.
why_wrong.D: A banksman at the gate cannot control speed or movements at the blind corner further inside the site.

common_mistake: Relying on a speed sign alone to protect pedestrians when the layout still hides them from drivers.

stem: A designer's scheme needs a plant-room roof lantern that will be cleaned and serviced twice a year. She can specify either a fixed internal access platform or leave it to maintenance contractors to rig edge protection later. Which approach best meets her duties?

options.A: Leave access to the maintenance contractors, because a designer's legal duties apply to the construction phase and not to later cleaning or servicing
options.B: Ask the principal contractor to choose the access method on site later, since the designer's role ends once the drawings have been issued
options.C: Specify permanent safe access to the lantern, and record any remaining risk in the pre-construction information so it reaches those who need it
options.D: Note on the drawings that operatives must wear harnesses, which passes the risk to the people who will eventually carry out the cleaning work

explanation: Designers must eliminate foreseeable risks, including those in later maintenance, so far as reasonably practicable, and share what remains so others can plan for it.

why_wrong.A: Designers' duties cover the foreseeable risks of maintaining and using the structure, not just its construction.
why_wrong.B: Design duties are not discharged by deferring to the contractor, and the risk should be dealt with while the design can still change.
why_wrong.D: Relying on PPE is the last resort, and a designer cannot simply hand a risk she could have designed out to others.

common_mistake: Assuming a designer's responsibility stops at construction and that maintenance risks can be left for contractors to sort out later.

stem: A contractor will strip the front of a corner shop on a busy road opposite a primary school. His assessor writes that only employees are at risk, as members of the public are not on his payroll. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The assessment must also cover pedestrians and schoolchildren, with controls such as hoarding, protected walkways and timed deliveries
options.B: Employee-only assessments are acceptable, as the local council is responsible for keeping the pavements and school routes safe near building work
options.C: A single warning sign at the site entrance removes the duty, since people choosing to walk past have accepted the risk themselves
options.D: The public only need covering if an incident occurs, so keeping a record of any near misses involving passers-by is enough for now

explanation: Employers must assess risks to other people affected by their work, and vulnerable groups such as children near a site need specific controls.

why_wrong.B: The contractor creating the risk holds the duty and cannot pass it to the council.
why_wrong.C: A sign alone is a weak control and passers-by, especially children, cannot accept risks they cannot see.
why_wrong.D: Risks to the public must be assessed beforehand, and waiting for harm to occur is not prevention.

common_mistake: Believing that duties to assess risk apply only to your own workforce and not to passers-by or neighbours.

stem: A gang needs somewhere to keep six full and four empty LPG cylinders for roofing torches on a site with a basement car park and a surface-water drain beside the compound. Which storage arrangement best controls the fire and explosion risk?

options.A: Inside a locked, unventilated store room within the main building, because shelter from the weather and from theft is the main concern
options.B: A locked steel container at the lowest point of the car park, with cylinders laid flat so that they cannot fall over and rupture a valve
options.C: A secure, ventilated outdoor cage on level ground with cylinders upright, valves closed, clear of drains and the basement, and full and empty kept apart
options.D: Beside the drain under a tarpaulin, so that any leaking gas drains away from the working areas and out of the site altogether

explanation: LPG vapour is heavier than air and collects in low points and drains, so open-air, upright, secure storage away from ignition sources and below-ground spaces limits the risk.

why_wrong.A: Enclosed storage lets leaking gas build up to explosive concentrations, so ventilation matters more than shelter.
why_wrong.B: Low points collect heavy LPG vapour, and cylinders should be stored upright rather than lying flat.
why_wrong.D: Vapour entering a drain can travel and collect elsewhere, and a tarpaulin traps leaks rather than letting gas disperse.

common_mistake: Choosing a lockable low or enclosed store to prevent theft without thinking about where heavier-than-air gas would collect.

stem: A labourer is struck by a swinging pallet and suffers a bruised shoulder. The supervisor writes the entry in the accident book, leaves it open on the cabin desk, and asks the two witnesses to agree what happened together before writing it down. What is wrong?

options.A: Nothing is wrong, since agreed accounts avoid conflicting versions of events, and the book is a site document that anyone on site may read freely
options.B: Only the supervisor's opinion on blame really matters, so witness accounts are unnecessary once the cause looks obvious from the scene
options.C: A bruise is too minor to record, so the entry should be skipped unless a doctor later confirms that the injury needs time off work
options.D: Witnesses should give separate, prompt, factual statements, and the entry's personal details should stay confidential

explanation: Independent accounts taken promptly are more reliable for the investigation, and accident book details are personal data that should be protected from casual view.

why_wrong.A: Joint accounts distort individual recollection, and personal injury details are not for general viewing.
why_wrong.B: Statements establish facts and underlying causes, and an early opinion on blame can bias the investigation.
why_wrong.C: Work-related injuries should be recorded whatever their severity, without waiting for medical confirmation.

common_mistake: Treating the accident book as a casual site log and letting witnesses compare stories before they give their own account.

stem: A new floor resin arrives with a label showing a pictogram of a human silhouette with a star burst on the chest. A flooring operative says only the skull and crossbones means serious harm. How should the supervisor respond?

options.A: It matters little because the label is for transport rules only, and site controls can rely on the operative's own long experience
options.B: It signals serious long-term effects such as sensitisation, so the safety data sheet should feed into the COSHH assessment
options.C: It marks a flammable product, so the main step is to keep ignition sources away and a separate COSHH assessment can be skipped entirely
options.D: It only warns of short-lived skin irritation, so basic gloves are enough and the safety data sheet is only needed after any exposure occurs

explanation: The health hazard pictogram can indicate carcinogenic, sensitising or organ-damaging effects, and the safety data sheet gives the information needed to assess and control exposure.

why_wrong.A: Labels and data sheets are to inform users about workplace risks, and experience alone cannot detect a long-term effect.
why_wrong.C: Flammability has a different pictogram, and COSHH still applies to this product's health risks.
why_wrong.D: The symbol relates to serious chronic effects, and the data sheet is needed beforehand to plan controls.

common_mistake: Assuming that only the skull and crossbones means a product is seriously harmful to health.

stem: Two joiners must carry 2.4 m by 1.2 m plywood sheets 60 m across an open, exposed site on a gusty day. The sheets weigh 25 kg each, and one joiner suggests simply carrying them flat overhead to be quick. What is the best response?

options.A: Include the wind in the task assessment, and use a sheet trolley or other aid, or wait for the gusts to ease, as the sheet acts like a sail
options.B: Let each joiner carry a sheet alone, which halves the time exposed and so reduces the chance of a gust catching the load
options.C: Go ahead, since 25 kg is within a fit adult's capacity and the weight of a load alone decides whether a carry is acceptable
options.D: Carry each sheet one-handed on the windward side, so the wind pushes it against the body and steadies the person carrying it

explanation: Environment is one of the factors in a manual handling assessment, and large flat sheets catch wind, so avoiding or mechanising the move is better than relying on strength.

why_wrong.B: A single carrier has less control of a large sheet, and spending less time does not remove the wind hazard.
why_wrong.C: Weight is only one factor, and the sheet's size, shape and the wind can make a lighter load hazardous.
why_wrong.D: A one-handed carry gives poor control, and a gust can swing or lift the sheet unpredictably.

common_mistake: Judging a carrying task by weight alone and ignoring the size of the load and the weather.

stem: A bricklayer foreman needs more space at a window reveal and tells his labourer to shift a ledger and a transom on the facade scaffold, saying it is only two tubes and he will refit them tonight. What is the most accurate response?

options.A: A labourer may make minor changes provided the tubes go back by the end of the shift and the foreman checks them by eye afterwards
options.B: Moving tubes within a single bay is allowed if a second person holds them in place, since the only risk is from falling objects
options.C: Only competent scaffolders should alter it, and it must be inspected again before use, as the missing members could weaken the whole scaffold
options.D: Alterations are fine if the bay is closed to workers overnight, because a scaffold is only loaded while people are working on it

explanation: Scaffolds are designed as a whole, so alterations must be done by competent scaffolders and the scaffold inspected before use to confirm it remains stable and safe.

why_wrong.A: Competence for scaffold work is required, and a foreman's visual check is not a formal inspection of the altered structure.
why_wrong.B: Holding tubes is no substitute for competence, and the main risk is the loss of the structure's stability.
why_wrong.D: A weakened scaffold can still fail in wind or under its own weight, even when nobody is on it.

common_mistake: Treating a couple of scaffold tubes as a small thing that anyone can move and put back.

stem: A bricklayer is about to start loading the first lift of this scaffold. Look closely at the scaffold. Which combination of problems is the most serious, and what should happen first?

options.A: The ties are visible at height, so the scaffold is stable overall and the bricks only need packing with extra offcuts under the standards
options.B: Soft ground is the only issue here, so a thin plank laid under the bricks is enough while the bricklayer starts with light loads
options.C: The standards lack proper support and the frame lacks bracing, so loading must stop until a scaffolder corrects it and it is inspected
options.D: The guardrails and boards look complete, so loading can begin once the bricklayer has been shown the bracing at the end return of the scaffold

explanation: Standards need base plates on sole boards to spread the load and bracing to keep the frame rigid, so the scaffold is unfit for loading until corrected and inspected.

why_wrong.A: Ties do not replace proper support under the standards, and packing with offcuts is not a safe fix.
why_wrong.B: Missing bracing is a separate serious defect, and improvised packing is not a scaffolder's rectification.
why_wrong.D: Neat upper lifts do not make up for defective foundations and missing bracing, and bricklayers cannot judge them.

common_mistake: Judging a scaffold by its guardrails and boards while overlooking its foundations and bracing.

stem: A service plan shows a medium-pressure gas main running about 1 m from the line of a new drainage run. The operator proposes using a 360 excavator along the whole line since the plan shows the pipe is clear. What is the best approach?

options.A: Rely on the plan's printed distance, since drawings issued by the gas company are accurate to the centimetre and do not need checking
options.B: Treat the plan as a guide, scan with a locator, then hand-dig trial holes to prove the pipe before the machine digs near it
options.C: Dig with the machine in thin layers and rely on the operator's feel for the bucket touching the pipe before it can be badly damaged
options.D: Use a pick to loosen soil directly above the pipe line so digging is quicker, then switch to the machine for removing the spoil

explanation: Plans are indicative and may be inaccurate, so services are located with a detector and proved by hand digging, with machines kept away from the pipe until its position is known.

why_wrong.A: Service plans are indicative and not drawn to be accurate, so they should not be used to measure safe distances.
why_wrong.C: Mechanical digging is a main cause of strikes, and a plastic pipe can be torn before the operator senses it.
why_wrong.D: Picks risk puncturing the pipe, and digging directly above a service is poor practice.

common_mistake: Trusting a service plan as an exact map and letting a machine dig near the marked line.

stem: A tracked excavator with a rollover-protective cab will work along the edge of a deep trench on made-up ground. The operator wants to leave the seatbelt off to jump out quickly and sees no need for stop blocks. What is the most accurate response?

options.A: A rollover cab alone is enough protection, so the belt is optional when the operator is very experienced and works carefully at slow speed
options.B: Check the ground, keep back with stop blocks at the edge, and wear the belt, as the cab protects only an operator who stays inside
options.C: Jumping clear is the safest escape if the machine tips, so the belt should stay off and the cab door should be left open for a quick exit
options.D: Stop blocks are only needed for dumpers, because a tracked excavator is stable enough on any kind of ground near an excavation edge

explanation: Overturn risks are controlled by ground assessment, safe distances and stop blocks, and the belt keeps the operator within the protected space if the machine does tip.

why_wrong.A: The cab and belt work as a pair, and experience does not stop a ground collapse from tipping the machine.
why_wrong.C: Operators thrown out or jumping are often crushed by the machine, and the protective structure only protects those held inside.
why_wrong.D: Excavators can overturn or slip into trenches, especially on poorly compacted ground at the edge.

common_mistake: Believing an experienced operator is safer jumping clear than staying belted inside the protective cab.

stem: A labourer is told to use a hired trench compactor he has never been trained on, as the usual operator is off sick. The supervisor says it works like the old one. Which statement about duties is most accurate?

options.A: He may start once he has read the hire company's handbook, because an employee's only duty is to follow the manufacturer's written instructions
options.B: Training is required only for self-propelled plant, so he can use the compactor as directed and raise any concern after the shift
options.C: The employer must give training on this machine, and the labourer should tell the supervisor he is untrained instead of just starting it
options.D: Following the supervisor's instruction passes all responsibility to the supervisor, so he meets his own duty by using the machine as carefully as he can

explanation: Employers must provide adequate information and training, and employees must follow the training they have had and raise concerns, so an untrained worker should not operate unfamiliar plant.

why_wrong.A: A handbook does not replace the employer's duty to train, and employee duties are wider than following manufacturer's instructions.
why_wrong.B: Training duties apply to any work equipment that carries a risk, and concerns must be raised before use, not afterwards.
why_wrong.D: Employees keep their own duty to use equipment as trained and to take reasonable care, whatever the instruction given.

common_mistake: Assuming that a supervisor's instruction or a similar-looking machine removes the need for specific training before use.

stem: Two groundworkers eat lunch in a closed van with a petrol-fuelled cab heater running. Afterwards both have a headache and feel drowsy and nauseous. One says it is just a hangover, and the other says they would smell any harmful gas. What should happen?

options.A: Let them rest in the van with the heater on so they warm up, and only seek help if either one collapses or loses consciousness
options.B: Give them water and send them back to work, because headaches after a break are most often caused by dehydration and not by gas
options.C: Open the van door briefly, keep the heater on low, and watch how they feel for the rest of lunch, since any harmful gas would have a smell that they would notice
options.D: Get them into fresh air, stop using the heater and seek medical advice, as carbon monoxide has no smell and mimics flu or tiredness

explanation: Carbon monoxide is odourless and its early symptoms are easily mistaken for other illness, so removing people from the source and obtaining medical advice is essential.

why_wrong.A: Waiting for collapse delays treatment, and staying with the source increases the exposure.
why_wrong.B: Assuming a harmless cause ignores the evidence of a fuel-burning appliance in an enclosed space and leaves the hazard in place.
why_wrong.C: Carbon monoxide cannot be smelt, so the lack of an odour gives no reassurance, and the heater remains a continuing source.

common_mistake: Trusting your nose to warn you about dangerous fumes, or putting headaches and drowsiness down to tiredness when a fuel-burning heater is running.

stem: A labourer who lifts and carries all day has had recurring lower back pain for three weeks. He keeps quiet, fearing he will be taken off the job, and his supervisor says anyone with back pain should stop work completely until it has gone. What is the best approach?

options.A: Treat it as a personal matter outside work, since back pain is common in adults and an employer has no part in dealing with it
options.B: Encourage early reporting, review his tasks and handling aids, and agree adjusted duties so he can stay active rather than resting fully
options.C: Send him home until he is completely pain-free, because any work while he has back pain will make the condition worse and cause lasting damage
options.D: Issue a back support belt and let him carry on as before, because the belt removes the need to review the lifting tasks he does

explanation: Early reporting lets the employer look at the work causes, and staying active with adjusted duties usually aids recovery better than prolonged rest.

why_wrong.A: Work factors can cause or worsen back pain and the employer must assess them.
why_wrong.C: Prolonged rest generally slows recovery, and the work causes still need reviewing.
why_wrong.D: Belts are not a reliable control and do not replace assessing and reducing the handling.

common_mistake: Assuming that workers with back pain either need complete rest or have a problem unrelated to the job.

stem: Look at the operative loading the mixer. Which combination of PPE omissions presents the greatest risk to his health?

options.A: No safety boots and no ear defenders, which leave him exposed to crushed toes and to hearing damage from the mixer drum
options.B: No eye or respiratory protection in the dust, and wet fabric gloves with bare forearms that leave skin in contact with cement
options.C: No hard hat and no hi-vis clothing, which leave him exposed to falling objects and to being struck by passing site vehicles
options.D: No harness and no gloves, which leave him exposed to a fall from height and to bare-handed contact with the wet cement

explanation: The picture shows dust rising without goggles or a mask, and cement soaking through fabric gloves onto bare forearms, risking eye injury, lung harm and cement burns or dermatitis.

why_wrong.A: He is wearing safety boots, and the main health problem in the picture is dust and skin contact rather than noise.
why_wrong.C: He is wearing both a hard hat and a hi-vis vest, so these are not the omissions shown.
why_wrong.D: He is working at ground level with no fall hazard, and he is wearing gloves, though they are unsuitable.

common_mistake: Assuming that wearing a helmet, vest and boots makes someone fully protected when dust and skin contact are the real hazards.

stem: A tiler with a full beard, kept for religious reasons, must dry-cut porcelain tiles that create silica dust. The supervisor suggests wearing a tight-fitting FFP3 half-mask over the beard. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Pass a face-fit test with the beard in place and treat the result as proof, since a passed test shows the seal is good whatever the facial hair
options.B: Wear a second disposable mask over the FFP3 half-mask to close the gaps round the beard, which doubles the protection provided
options.C: Trim the beard along the mask's edge and then wear the half-mask, since only hair under the sealing line affects protection
options.D: Provide loose-fitting RPE such as a powered hood or helmet that does not rely on a face seal, and use water suppression or extraction too

explanation: A beard prevents a tight-fitting mask from sealing, so loose-fitting RPE is the suitable alternative, while controls at source reduce the dust the worker is exposed to.

why_wrong.A: Facial hair in the seal area stops a reliable fit, so a test result cannot make a tight-fitting mask safe over a beard.
why_wrong.B: Stacking masks does not seal the gaps and can make the fit worse, so protection is not doubled.
why_wrong.C: Hair around the seal area, including the beard line and stubble, still lets air leak and trimming does not give a dependable seal.

common_mistake: Believing a tight-fitting mask, a trimmed beard or a double mask can seal over facial hair, rather than choosing RPE that does not need a seal.

stem: Steel fixers on a high working platform keep spanners and offcuts on the deck beside a toe board, and a spanner has just fallen to the ground floor where trades pass beneath. Which combination of controls best deals with falling objects here?

options.A: Place a warning sign at the base and stop work on the platform when anyone walks beneath, relying on the fixers to watch the people below
options.B: Tether tools with lanyards, keep the deck tidy with toe boards or brick guards, and fence off the area below as an exclusion zone, using netting if needed
options.C: Raise the toe boards on the platform and leave the ground floor open, since a taller board stops anything from ever leaving the platform
options.D: Issue hard hats to everyone working below and ask the fixers to take more care with their tools, because head protection removes the danger from anything that falls

explanation: Preventing items from falling comes first, using lanyards and tidy edges, and the area below is then kept clear or protected to limit harm if something still drops.

why_wrong.A: Signs and lookouts depend on constant human attention and do not stop objects from falling or protect people who are not looking.
why_wrong.C: Toe boards help but cannot hold every item, particularly dropped tools, so the area below must still be protected from anything that falls.
why_wrong.D: A hard hat is the last line of defence and cannot stop heavy tools from causing serious injury, so it is not a substitute for prevention.

common_mistake: Relying on hard hats and warning signs below instead of stopping objects falling and keeping people out of the drop zone.

stem: An operator in a boom MEWP must replace a lamp on a column beside a live carriageway. The plan shows a few cones around the base, and the basket will extend towards the traffic lane. What is the best control?

options.A: Fit a harness with a long adjustable lanyard so he stays in the basket if it is struck, which is the main protection from vehicle impact
options.B: Rely on the operator's hi-vis and a beacon to warn drivers, because a visible basket will be avoided by motorists approaching at speed
options.C: Agree traffic management with the highway authority, keep the basket clear of live lanes and have a trained ground person ready to rescue
options.D: Work at night when traffic is lighter and keep the same cones, since fewer vehicles lowers the chance of a collision with the platform

explanation: Vehicles can strike a basket or the chassis, so the road space must be controlled and a competent person must be ready to lower the platform in an emergency.

why_wrong.A: A long lanyard can let him be thrown out, and personal protection does not control the risk of vehicle strikes.
why_wrong.B: Visibility does not stop a distracted or speeding driver, and cones and beacons alone do not give physical protection.
why_wrong.D: Fewer vehicles do not remove the hazard, and darkness lowers visibility so drivers are less likely to see the platform.

common_mistake: Treating cones, beacons or hi-vis as enough protection when a work platform extends into a live traffic lane.

stem: At the start of a shift, a driver finds a telehandler's hydraulic hose weeping oil and its reversing alarm silent. The previous driver's sheet is ticked 'all OK'. The supervisor says to finish the morning deliveries and report the faults at lunch. What is correct?

options.A: Rely on the previous driver's sheet, since a tick entered by a trained operator remains a valid check until the next weekly inspection
options.B: Do not use it: record the check yourself, report both defects, and keep it out of service until a competent person has repaired them
options.C: Use it for the morning deliveries only with a banksman covering the missing alarm, then report both faults to the hire company at lunch
options.D: Wrap the weeping hose with tape and top up the oil, then work normally because the alarm is only a secondary warning aid

explanation: Operators must check plant before use and must not operate a machine with safety-related defects, so the faults are reported and the machine taken out of service rather than relied on until lunch.

why_wrong.A: A pre-use check is done by the person about to use the machine each shift, and an earlier tick cannot show the faults found now.
why_wrong.C: A banksman does not make a leaking hydraulic hose or a defective warning device acceptable, since the faults are present for every movement.
why_wrong.D: Taping a hydraulic hose is not a competent repair and a failure under pressure can eject oil, and the alarm is a required control on a site with pedestrians.

common_mistake: Assuming that a ticked sheet from the last driver means you do not have to check the machine yourself.

stem: At finish, a driver parks a forward-tip dumper facing downhill on a sloping track beside the cabins, handbrake on, engine off, with the skip still raised from the last tip. He says the handbrake alone will hold it. What is wrong?

options.A: Nothing is wrong, because a parking brake is designed to hold a machine on a slope and the raised skip only helps rain drain away
options.B: He should leave the engine running in gear, so the transmission also holds the machine, which is safer than shutting it down
options.C: The skip should be lowered, but chocks are needed only on public roads, because the brake secures plant on private land
options.D: The brake alone is not enough, so the machine should go on level ground away from routes, or be chocked, lowered and keyed off

explanation: A parking brake can fail or be released, so plant is parked on level ground where possible, and on a slope it is chocked with the skip lowered and the key removed so it cannot be moved.

why_wrong.A: A raised skip is an extra hazard, since it raises the centre of gravity and can drop or be struck, and the brake is not a sole control.
why_wrong.B: Leaving a machine running and unattended invites unauthorised use and fuel and noise problems, and creates a hazard rather than a control.
why_wrong.C: Chocking is a precaution for any slope on any site, and the duty to secure plant does not depend on who owns the ground.

common_mistake: Trusting the parking brake alone to hold plant and leaving it on a slope with the body raised.

stem: Lorries leaving a wet site track mud onto a residential road. The foreman plans to hose it into the nearby gully each evening and says the road is the council's responsibility. Which approach is best?

options.A: Put up a mud warning sign at the gate and leave the clean-up to the council, which as highway authority owns any mud on its roads
options.B: Hose the road down after each shift using clean mains water, because diluted mud passes through the surface-water gully without harm
options.C: Stop mud leaving at source with hardstanding, a wheel wash and sweeping, and keep washings out of drains, as mud on roads can be an offence
options.D: Brush the road once a week and warn drivers with signs, since occasional cleaning satisfies the duty once the hazard is flagged

explanation: Preventing mud from reaching the highway is the site's responsibility, and washing it into surface-water drains pollutes watercourses.

why_wrong.A: A sign does not remove the hazard, and the site that causes the mud is expected to prevent and clear it.
why_wrong.B: Silty washings in a surface-water gully can reach a watercourse untreated, and dilution does not make the discharge harmless.
why_wrong.D: Weekly cleaning leaves mud as a skid risk for days and does nothing to stop it being carried out in the first place.

common_mistake: Treating mud on the road as the council's problem and washing it away downstream instead of preventing it leaving the site.

stem: A client is tendering a refurbishment of a 1960s office. It already holds an asbestos survey and a structural report noting a weak floor slab. The principal designer proposes sending bidders only the drawings and programme. What should be passed to the contractors?

options.A: A general statement that hazards exist, with detail on request, because the client's duty ends once a competent contractor accepts the work
options.B: The survey summary once the principal contractor is appointed, because only that firm needs site hazard information to prepare its plan
options.C: Drawings and programme only, since hazards in an existing building are best found by each contractor's own survey once work is under way
options.D: The survey and structural findings, with known service routes, issued before tender so contractors can plan and write their construction phase plans around them

explanation: Pre-construction information must give designers and contractors the relevant existing hazards early enough for them to plan, price and prepare the construction phase plan.

why_wrong.A: The client must proactively provide the relevant information, and competence does not remove that duty.
why_wrong.B: Every contractor bidding or designing needs the relevant information early, not just the eventual principal contractor.
why_wrong.C: Known hazards held by the client must be supplied up front, not rediscovered during the work.

common_mistake: Assuming contractors will find the existing hazards for themselves, so known survey results can be held back until they ask.

stem: A labourer wearing contact lenses is splashed in one eye by a solvent degreaser. A tap with a hose is 3 m away, while the plumbed eyewash station is 40 m away across the site. What is the best first response?

options.A: Flush briefly with the hose, then dab the eye dry and let him resume light duties if the pain settles within the following half hour
options.B: Hold the eyelids apart and flush with clean running water from the nearby tap for at least 10 minutes, then send him to hospital with the product label
options.C: Take out the contact lens first, wait until it is out, then flush for about two minutes before covering the eye with a clean pad
options.D: Walk him to the plumbed eyewash 40 m away and flush there, because tap water is not clean enough to be used on a chemically burned eye

explanation: Immediate, prolonged flushing with clean running water limits damage, and chemical eye injuries need hospital assessment, so the label helps clinicians.

why_wrong.A: Chemical eye injuries need prolonged flushing and hospital assessment even if the pain eases.
why_wrong.C: Lens removal must never delay flushing, and two minutes is far too short for a chemical splash.
why_wrong.D: Delaying irrigation while walking increases damage, and clean running tap water is acceptable straight away.

common_mistake: Thinking that a short rinse is enough once the stinging fades, so the casualty can carry on working.

stem: A concrete-cutting team is regularly exposed above 85 dB(A) and has annual hearing checks. This year one man's results show a clear drop since last time. His manager plans to keep the same schedule and issue stronger ear defenders. What should happen?

options.A: He should be asked to report any further difficulty hearing, with the team's records kept by the manager and checked only if he complains again
options.B: He should keep to the usual check cycle, because stronger ear defenders deal with the cause and remove any need for further action
options.C: He should be moved to quieter work and the matter closed, because the damage is his individual problem and not a sign of a wider fault
options.D: He should be examined by a doctor, checks made more frequent, and the noise risk assessment and controls reviewed for the whole team

explanation: Evidence of hearing damage means the person needs medical examination and the employer must review the risk assessment, since the controls have clearly not protected him.

why_wrong.A: Waiting for a complaint ignores a measured drop, and the result requires medical examination now.
why_wrong.B: Evidence of damage shows the existing controls failed, so the cycle and the assessment both need review.
why_wrong.C: Individual damage is a warning about the team's exposure, so the risk assessment must be reviewed for everyone.

common_mistake: Treating hearing defenders as a complete answer even when the checks show that damage is already happening.

stem: A tarmac gang uses vibrating rammers daily. One man mentions tingling fingers that turn white in the cold and difficulty with buttons. His supervisor says it comes with the job and the annual questionnaire is not due until spring. What is the correct response?

options.A: Refer him promptly to occupational health for assessment and review the gang's vibration controls, since continued exposure can make the damage permanent
options.B: Wait for the annual questionnaire, because routine surveillance is the proper route and out-of-cycle referral is only for confirmed injuries
options.C: Provide thicker gloves and carry on with the same tools and hours, since keeping the hands warm will stop the symptoms progressing
options.D: Shorten his trigger time below the action value and note it down, because reduced exposure makes referral and assessment unnecessary

explanation: These symptoms suggest hand-arm vibration syndrome, which worsens with continued exposure, so early assessment and a review of controls are needed rather than waiting for a routine check.

why_wrong.B: Reported symptoms must be acted on promptly rather than held until the next routine check.
why_wrong.C: Warm gloves may ease discomfort but do not reduce vibration or stop the damage progressing.
why_wrong.D: Reducing exposure helps, but symptoms already present still require medical assessment and a control review.

common_mistake: Assuming numb or white fingers are just part of the job and not worth reporting.

stem: A tiler keeps the day's slates on the top working lift of a facade scaffold. Bundles are stacked along the outer edge, higher than the toe board, while pedestrians use the pavement below. How should the supervisor deal with it?

options.A: Keep the bundles at the edge but cap their individual weight, since the weight on the lift matters for safety and the stack height does not
options.B: Leave the stacks, because the guardrails are fitted and would stop any bundle that slides, provided the weight is spread evenly along the bay
options.C: Leave the stacks and put a cone and sign on the pavement below, since warning the public is enough while the load is within capacity
options.D: Keep only the day's quantity on the lift, stacked below toe-board height and within the rated load, and lower surplus to the ground by hoist

explanation: Stored materials must stay within the scaffold's design loading and be kept below the toe board so they cannot be knocked onto people below.

why_wrong.A: Height above the toe board is what lets materials be kicked off, so weight limits alone do not remove that hazard.
why_wrong.B: Guardrails are not designed to retain stacked materials and leave gaps through which slates can fall.
why_wrong.C: A warning sign does not control the source of falling objects, and the stack stays above the toe board.

common_mistake: Thinking guardrails and a clear walkway make any stacking at the platform edge acceptable.

stem: Look at the first-floor slab in the photograph. A plasterboard delivery must be carried across this level this afternoon. What should the supervisor do before anyone carries boards across it?

options.A: Fit guardrails and toe boards, or a secured and marked cover, to the opening and check them before boards are moved
options.B: Rely on the tape and tell the carriers to keep to the far side, since trained operatives can judge a safe distance from an open edge
options.C: Have the labourers carry sheets two to a board, so that a better view of the floor ahead is kept while moving around the opening
options.D: Issue harnesses to all carriers and clip them to the nearest column, because personal protection is enough for work lasting one afternoon

explanation: Falls through a floor opening must be prevented by robust collective protection such as guardrails and toe boards or a secured, marked cover, checked before work proceeds.

why_wrong.B: Loose tape is not a physical barrier, and a carried board blocks the view of the edge.
why_wrong.C: Two-person carrying changes the manual handling, but does nothing to stop someone stepping into the opening.
why_wrong.D: Personal fall protection ranks below collective measures, and a column clip gives no assured anchor or restraint.

common_mistake: Trusting loose tape or warning to guard an opening instead of fitting a physical barrier or cover.

stem: A 2 m deep drainage trench has a trench box fitted. A ladder stands inside with its top level with the ground, spoil is heaped at the edge, and the excavator is parked alongside. Which set of changes is most appropriate?

options.A: Secure the ladder at least 1 m above the landing, fit guardrails and toe boards at the edge, and move the spoil and excavator back
options.B: Run hazard tape round the trench and use a banksman for the excavator, as the trench box makes extending the ladder or barriers unnecessary
options.C: Tie the ladder at its top but keep the spoil heap as it is, since a raised heap works as a barrier that stops anyone walking in
options.D: Extend the ladder and fit an edge barrier, but leave the spoil and parked machine in place, since the trench box supports the sides

explanation: A ladder should project above the landing and be secured, edges need barriers that also stop falling material, and spoil and plant add load and fall risk if left close.

why_wrong.B: Tape is not a barrier, and a box does not replace safe access or edge protection.
why_wrong.C: A loose heap can slide into the trench and does not serve as a substantial barrier, and the ladder still needs to extend above the landing.
why_wrong.D: A box supports the sides but does nothing about surcharge loads from nearby spoil and plant or material falling in.

common_mistake: Believing that once a trench box is in, the edge, access and spoil need no further attention.

stem: An operative gets a sharp jolt from a damaged mains drill lead, shakes his hand and says he feels fine apart from tingling and a small mark on one finger. He wants to carry on. What is the correct response?

options.A: Swap the lead for a new one so work can carry on, and ask the operative to say if the tingling returns at any time during the shift
options.B: Isolate and tag the drill, get him medically assessed that day as shocks can upset heart rhythm or burn deeper than shows, and investigate
options.C: Cool the mark under running water and send him back to work, reporting the event only if he ends up off work for more than seven days
options.D: Let him rest for ten minutes and resume if the tingling fades, replacing the lead later, because no obvious injury means no need for assessment

explanation: Even a shock with little visible injury can disturb the heart or cause hidden burns, so medical assessment, taking the equipment out of use and investigation are all needed.

why_wrong.A: Replacing the lead ignores the possible internal injury and leaves the incident uninvestigated.
why_wrong.C: First aid for a mark does not replace assessment, and the faulty lead must be taken out of use at once.
why_wrong.D: A lack of obvious injury does not rule out heart effects or deeper burns after an electric shock.

common_mistake: Judging an electric shock by how well the person looks rather than getting them checked.

stem: After heavy rain, the bund around a site diesel tank is nearly full of water with a faint oil sheen. The bund has a drain valve, and a labourer proposes opening it to the surface-water gully to restore capacity. What is correct?

options.A: Do not drain it to the gully; pump the water into containers, treat it as oily waste for a licensed carrier, and check the tank for leaks
options.B: Leave the water in place, because oil floats and the bund is still containing it, with action needed only once it actually overflows
options.C: Open the valve slowly and skim the sheen with absorbent pads as it drains, because the water is mostly rain and the oil is only a trace amount
options.D: Scatter absorbent granules to bind the oil and open the valve once the sheen is gone, since clear water can safely go to the gully

explanation: Oily water must never reach a surface-water drain, so it is removed and disposed of as waste, and the sheen should prompt a check for a leak.

why_wrong.B: Rainwater cuts the bund's spare capacity, so it must be removed before it overflows with oil on top.
why_wrong.C: Even a trace of oil in discharged water can pollute the watercourse, and slow release does not remove that risk.
why_wrong.D: Granules do not guarantee clean water, and the valve should not discharge to a surface-water drain in any case.

common_mistake: Assuming rainwater in a bund is harmless and can simply be let out through a drain valve.

stem: A plasterer drops offcuts of plasterboard into the clean brick and concrete skip, saying both are non-hazardous. The skip would normally be crushed for reuse as hardcore. What should the site manager do?

options.A: Bag the offcuts and put them in the general waste skip, since sulphate-bearing waste can be landfilled together with ordinary refuse
options.B: Leave it in, because plasterboard is non-hazardous like the other contents and the crushing plant will screen out the small amounts of it later
options.C: Remove the plasterboard to its own marked container for recycling or suitable disposal, as gypsum contaminates and devalues the rubble load
options.D: Wet the offcuts down to bind the gypsum dust and leave them in the skip, so the whole load can still be classed as clean rubble

explanation: Gypsum waste has to be kept apart from other waste, partly for its sulphate content, and mixing it into rubble spoils the recycling and raises costs.

why_wrong.A: Gypsum must not be mixed with general waste, as sulphate with biodegradable waste causes problems in landfill.
why_wrong.B: Being non-hazardous does not make gypsum compatible, since it must be kept separate from other waste streams.
why_wrong.D: Wetting controls dust only, and the gypsum remains in the load and still contaminates it.

common_mistake: Assuming that all non-hazardous waste can share a skip.

stem: A client's office fit-out is programmed for 24 working days with a peak of 15 workers, but the contractors' own programmes total 620 person days. The principal contractor says it is under both 30 days and 20 workers, so nothing needs sending. Who must act, and why?

options.A: The client must notify the HSE in writing before the construction phase starts, because exceeding 500 person days alone makes the project notifiable
options.B: The principal designer must notify the HSE, because preparing pre-construction information makes notification a core part of that role under CDM 2015
options.C: The principal contractor must notify the local authority once appointed, because it takes over the notification duty from the client at that point
options.D: The principal contractor is right, because the 30-day and 20-worker limits must both be exceeded together before any project becomes notifiable to the HSE

explanation: Under CDM 2015 a project is notifiable if it lasts over 30 working days with more than 20 workers at once, or if it exceeds 500 person days, and the duty to notify the HSE sits with the client.

why_wrong.B: The principal designer plans and coordinates the pre-construction phase but the notification duty belongs to the client.
why_wrong.C: The duty to notify rests with the client and the notice goes to the HSE, not to the local authority.
why_wrong.D: The 500 person-day figure is a separate, alternative trigger, so passing it makes the project notifiable even when the other limits are not met.

common_mistake: Assuming a project is notifiable only when it breaches both the duration and worker-number limits, and forgetting the separate person-days trigger.

stem: A designer specifies 25 kg concrete lintels for a first-floor opening, although a 12 kg lightweight alternative of similar cost meets the load requirements. She adds a drawing note saying 'handle with care' and moves on. What should she have done?

options.A: Chosen the lighter lintel to reduce the handling risk at source, then passed on information about any remaining risk to the principal designer
options.B: Kept the heavy lintel and listed its weight in the specification, as residual risk information is reserved for major hazards like asbestos or collapse
options.C: Kept the 25 kg lintel, since her note shifts responsibility to the contractor who will be carrying out the lifting on site
options.D: Left the choice of lintel to the principal contractor on site, because designers have no duties over how work is carried out during construction

explanation: Designers must first eliminate or reduce foreseeable risks through their design choices, and only then provide information about the risks that remain so others can plan for them.

why_wrong.B: Designers must share information on significant residual risks of any kind, and here a safer option was available anyway.
why_wrong.C: A note does not transfer the designer's duty to reduce foreseeable risks through the design itself.
why_wrong.D: Designers must consider foreseeable construction risks when they make design decisions and cannot hand that choice to the contractor.

common_mistake: Believing a warning note on a drawing discharges the designer's duty when a safer design choice was available.

stem: On Friday afternoon the client orders extra partition work to start on Monday. The supervisor reuses the RAMS from a similar job last month, adds the new room numbers and tells the gang to 'work the same way'. What is the main weakness?

options.A: There is none, because RAMS from a comparable job remain valid for like-for-like tasks done by the same trade with the same tools
options.B: The missing client signature, because a written variation order becomes the method statement once the client has authorised the extra work
options.C: The RAMS was not reviewed for this job's conditions or briefed to the operatives, so it needs revising and communicating before work begins
options.D: Short notice waives the need for a written RAMS on a variation, and a toolbox talk on Monday morning is enough to cover the added scope

explanation: Changed work needs its risks reassessed and the method statement updated, and the people doing it must understand the revised controls before they start.

why_wrong.A: Site conditions, access, services and neighbouring trades differ between jobs, so a generic copy ignores the real hazards.
why_wrong.B: A variation instruction is a change to scope, not a safe system of work, so it cannot replace a reviewed RAMS.
why_wrong.D: There is no exemption for short notice, and a verbal talk does not replace a suitable and sufficient assessment.

common_mistake: Treating a client's variation or a short deadline as a reason to recycle old paperwork instead of reassessing the new task.

stem: A site painter must spray a two-pack polyurethane coating on steelwork in a bay. He plans to wear a disposable FFP3 mask with the doors open for ventilation, and nobody has arranged any health checks for him. Which approach reflects good practice?

options.A: Keep the FFP3 mask for the fine paint droplets and arrange a health check once he later develops a persistent cough, wheeze or tight chest
options.B: Spray in an extracted enclosure in air-fed breathing apparatus, keep others out, and arrange health surveillance for occupational asthma
options.C: Use a full-face respirator with vapour cartridges and change them when he can smell the paint coming through the filter
options.D: Wear a half-mask with combined filters and apply barrier cream in place of gloves so he keeps full feeling in his hands

explanation: Isocyanate paint is a respiratory sensitiser, so exposure must be controlled with enclosure, extraction and air-fed RPE, and surveillance should look for early signs of asthma and skin problems.

why_wrong.A: An FFP3 mask filters particles but not isocyanate vapour, and surveillance should be arranged before symptoms appear.
why_wrong.C: Isocyanates give no reliable warning by smell, and breakthrough can occur before the user notices it.
why_wrong.D: Barrier creams are not a substitute for gloves and provide no full barrier against skin contact.

common_mistake: Assuming an ordinary dust mask and open doors are enough when spraying paints that contain sensitisers.

stem: On a plant-room refit, one operative grinds steel brackets and another decants a corrosive descaling acid into small containers. The supervisor issues everyone the same clear safety glasses with side shields, saying eye protection is eye protection. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: A face shield alone is the best choice for both people, since it covers the whole face and so replaces any need for glasses or goggles
options.B: Goggles are needed for the grinder but the acid handler can wear glasses, as splashes are slower than flying particles and rarely reach the eyes
options.C: Glasses suit the grinder's flying particles, but the acid handler needs sealed goggles for splash, with a face shield added over them for larger pours
options.D: Side-shielded glasses are enough for both tasks, because the shields stop splashes arriving from the sides and the front lens stops them from the front

explanation: Eye protection must match the hazard, so impact needs impact-rated eyewear while liquid splash needs goggles that seal to the face, with a shield giving extra face cover.

why_wrong.A: A shield is secondary protection with gaps at the top and sides, and it is meant to be worn over primary eye protection.
why_wrong.B: This reverses the hazards, because liquid splash is the risk that needs the sealed fit while glasses can suit particles.
why_wrong.D: Glasses leave gaps around the eyes, so liquid can run or splash behind the lenses, which sealed goggles prevent.

common_mistake: Treating all eye protection as interchangeable instead of matching glasses, goggles and face shields to the particular hazard.

stem: A facade scaffold is to be erected over a busy public footway outside a shop, leaving only a narrow gap beside the road. The scaffolder suggests tying a few cones along the edge and fitting brick guards on the lifts above. What is the best arrangement?

options.A: Let pedestrians use the road beside the scaffold with a flagger on duty, since the footway can then be fully enclosed with hoarding
options.B: Fix the cones and brick guards as suggested, because guards keep items on the scaffold and cones are enough to guide pedestrians past
options.C: Glasses suit the grinder's flying particles, but the acid handler needs sealed goggles, with a face shield over them for large pours
options.D: Erect the scaffold only at night when fewer people pass, then take it down by morning so the footway stays open during the day

explanation: People passing beneath must be protected from falling items and kept from the carriageway, which needs a proper walkway or gantry, lighting and the agreement of the highway authority.

why_wrong.A: Sending pedestrians into the carriageway creates a collision risk that is worse than the one controlled, and a flagger is no substitute for a safe route.
why_wrong.B: Brick guards do not stop everything from falling, and cones do not provide overhead protection or a safe, lit route.
why_wrong.D: Building and dismantling scaffold over a footway still endangers anyone present, and the scaffold would not be stable or checked for ongoing use.

common_mistake: Thinking cones and brick guards are enough to protect the public when a scaffold is built over a footway.

stem: A 110 V floodlight set and a heater run from a 50 m cable reel left fully wound, standing in a puddle on a slab. The casing feels warm, and the supervisor says the reel's thermal trip will protect it. What is the best response?

options.A: Unwind the cable fully, check the rating plate figure for the unwound load, and lift the reel clear of the wet ground
options.B: Keep it wound and rely on the thermal trip, because the cut-out will act before the cable insulation can be damaged by heat
options.C: Leave it wound and switch off the floodlights, because a reel overheats only when its full length is drawn out under a heavy load
options.D: Swap to a 230 V reel on the same circuit, because the higher voltage draws less current and so heats the cable less

explanation: A wound reel traps heat and carries a much lower rated load than an unwound one, and a reel standing in water risks shock, so unwinding, checking the plate and raising it off the ground deals with both.

why_wrong.B: A trip is a last resort that can fail or act late, and relying on it is no substitute for using the reel within its rated load.
why_wrong.C: The reverse is true, since a tightly wound reel cannot lose heat and overheats at loads an unwound cable would carry easily.
why_wrong.D: This gives up the reduced shock risk of 110 V supplies on site and still ignores the wound reel and the wet ground.

common_mistake: Assuming that a built-in thermal trip lets you use a cable reel wound up and sitting on wet ground.

stem: Look at the scene. Which action is most urgent?

options.A: Let him carry on if he stays in sight of the operator through the cab window and his hi-vis jacket is clean and bright
options.B: Ask the operator to slow the slewing speed so the labourer has time to step clear if the machine turns towards him
options.C: Give him ear defenders before he passes, since noise from the engine is the main hazard to a person walking at that distance
options.D: Stop the machine and keep pedestrians outside its swing radius, using barriers or a separate route

explanation: The labourer is inside the area swept by the counterweight while the operator watches the bucket, so the zone must be segregated by physical separation, not by awareness alone.

why_wrong.A: Visibility does not help when the operator is watching the bucket and the tail can strike before anyone reacts.
why_wrong.B: Slower slewing is no substitute for keeping people out of the swing area, and the labourer cannot see the machine behind him.
why_wrong.C: Noise is a lesser matter here and does nothing about the crushing hazard from the swinging tail.

common_mistake: Relying on visibility and the operator's awareness to protect people instead of keeping them physically outside the swing radius.

stem: A pickup is being coupled to a plant trailer carrying a light tower. A labourer stands between the vehicles to guide the tow ball onto the hitch as the driver reverses slowly. Once the handle drops shut, they set off. What is wrong with this procedure?

options.A: Nothing, because slow reversing with a guide standing close is the usual method and the coupling can be trusted once the handle drops shut
options.B: The only fault is the guide being too close; the trailer's brake and lighting connections can wait until the weekly plant inspection
options.C: The guide may stand between the vehicles if the driver keeps the engine running and a foot on the brake, so that the brakes hold if the vehicle moves
options.D: Nobody should stand between the vehicles while reversing; guide from the side, then check lock, chain, lights and jockey wheel

explanation: A person between vehicles can be crushed if the driver misjudges, and a shut handle alone does not prove that the coupling, secondary chain and lights are fit for towing.

why_wrong.A: Standing between vehicles exposes the guide to crushing, and a dropped handle does not confirm a secure and complete connection.
why_wrong.B: Brake and light connections must be checked each time the trailer is coupled, not left to a weekly inspection.
why_wrong.C: Brake pressure cannot protect a person from a sudden movement, and an engine running makes an unintended roll more likely.

common_mistake: Assuming a coupling is safe once it has clicked shut, without checking the chain, lights and brakes or keeping people clear.

stem: A sump pump clears groundwater from a pit and discharges by hose into a nearby stream. An excavator working in the pit leaks hydraulic oil and the pumped water shows a rainbow sheen. The foreman says the stream will dilute it. What is the right action?

options.A: Stop pumping to the stream, stop the leak and contain the oily water, then agree a compliant disposal route with the Environment Agency
options.B: Redirect the hose into the foul sewer instead, since sewers can take oily water from sites without any consent being needed
options.C: Keep pumping but pass the discharge through a silt bag first, since filtering will remove the oil along with the soil particles
options.D: Place an absorbent boom in the stream below the outlet and carry on pumping, since a boom will capture any oil that arrives

explanation: Only clean, uncontaminated water may be discharged to surface water, so pumping stops, the source is dealt with and the contaminated water is contained until an acceptable route is agreed.

why_wrong.B: Discharges to a sewer need the sewerage undertaker's consent, and oily water is the kind of effluent that is restricted.
why_wrong.C: A silt bag traps solids and does not remove oil, so the contaminated water would still reach the stream.
why_wrong.D: Booms are an emergency response to an incident and do not make it acceptable to knowingly discharge oily water into a stream.

common_mistake: Believing that a large volume of stream water will dilute oil in pumped groundwater to a safe level.

stem: A labourer sees a guardrail on a loading platform has been left unclipped, but nobody has fallen. He decides not to mention it, because RIDDOR only covers injuries and dangerous occurrences. What is the correct view of his duty?

options.A: He should wait to see whether the rail is reinstated, because reports are only needed when a hazard persists beyond the end of a shift
options.B: He should write it in the accident book instead, because the book is where unsafe conditions are recorded once no injury has occurred
options.C: He need only report it if the platform is on his own work route, because the duty covers just the task he is personally doing that day
options.D: He should tell his supervisor promptly, as employees must report serious danger and shortcomings in protection, whatever RIDDOR says

explanation: The Management Regulations require employees to report serious and immediate danger and shortcomings in the employer's protection arrangements, a duty that is separate from the RIDDOR reporting thresholds.

why_wrong.A: There is no waiting period, and an unreported gap in edge protection can cause a fall before anyone notices it.
why_wrong.B: The accident book records injuries and incidents, and it does not replace telling the supervisor so the hazard is fixed at once.
why_wrong.C: The duty covers shortcomings in protection that affect health and safety generally, so it is not limited to his own task or route.

common_mistake: Assuming that a hazard only needs reporting if it meets a legal reporting threshold or has already hurt someone.

stem: A night crew takes over a partly dismantled temporary propped wall. The day supervisor says verbally, "All fine, nothing changed since the briefing." Two props were removed this afternoon to clear access. What should the incoming supervisor do?

options.A: Rely on the morning briefing and start work, since a briefing already given covers the whole job until the task is finished and signed off
options.B: Replace the two props and carry on, since restoring the original layout removes the need for any further review or briefing at all
options.C: Take a documented handover of props removed and controls remaining, review the assessment for the changed wall, then brief the crew
options.D: Ask the day supervisor to stay for an hour to watch the crew, since his presence is a sufficient substitute for a written handover

explanation: A changed condition makes the earlier assessment out of date, so the incoming team needs a recorded handover of what changed, which controls remain, and a review before work starts.

why_wrong.A: A briefing describes the state at that time and cannot cover a change made later, such as the removal of two props.
why_wrong.B: Refitting props without checking the design or the wall's condition ignores why they were removed and any movement since.
why_wrong.D: Informal presence leaves no record and does not review the risks, so the night crew still lacks a clear picture of the wall's state.

common_mistake: Treating a verbal "nothing's changed" at shift change as a handover, without checking what has actually been altered.

stem: A cabin fire is put out. A worker pulled from it coughs, has soot around his nose, a hoarse voice and no visible burns. He says he is fine and wants to return to work. What should the first aider do?

options.A: Call 999, keep him in fresh air sitting upright and watch his breathing, as airway swelling can develop later
options.B: Lay him flat on his back and give oxygen from the cabin kit, since any casualty with smoke exposure must lie down first
options.C: Let him return once the cough settles, because no visible burns means that smoke has not caused any internal injury at all
options.D: Let him rest on site with water and a long break, then send him to his GP if the cough lasts into the following day

explanation: Soot around the nose and a hoarse voice suggest hot smoke has reached the airway, which can swell and close later, so he needs emergency medical assessment and monitoring.

why_wrong.B: Lying flat can worsen breathing difficulty, and oxygen should only be given by someone trained to do so.
why_wrong.C: Smoke injury is often internal and a lack of visible burns does not rule out damage to the airway and lungs.
why_wrong.D: Delaying assessment risks missing airway swelling, which can become life-threatening within hours.

common_mistake: Judging smoke exposure by whether the casualty looks and feels fine, instead of by how long and how hot the smoke was.

stem: A crew must lay 90 concrete kerbs, each about 70 kg, along a new access road. The foreman proposes two labourers lifting each one with kerb dogs, saying that with two people the weight is shared. A vacuum lifter fitted to the excavator is available. What is the best decision?

options.A: Continue with two-person kerb dogs but rotate the pairs each hour, because sharing the weight and varying the people brings the task within safe limits
options.B: Have the labourers roll each kerb on its edge along the road to the trench, since dragging avoids the need to lift anything off the ground
options.C: Use the vacuum lifter but let a labourer steady each kerb by hand directly underneath, since the suction would hold even if the load swung
options.D: Use the vacuum lifter, run by a trained operator on clean dry kerbs, with everyone kept out from under the suspended load

explanation: Mechanical handling removes the repeated heavy lifting at source, and the lifter only works safely when the kerb surface is clean, the operator is trained and nobody stands beneath the load.

why_wrong.A: Rotation spreads fatigue but does not remove the repeated heavy lifting, so the task still presents a high risk of back and hand injury.
why_wrong.B: Rolling and dragging heavy kerbs still involves awkward twisting and strain, and ignores the available mechanical aid that removes handling.
why_wrong.C: No one should be under a suspended load, and a swinging kerb or a lost seal could crush a person standing beneath it.

common_mistake: Assuming that two people sharing a heavy load, or taking turns, is an adequate control when a lifting aid is available.

stem: Roofers cleaning hot bitumen off their hands and forearms use rags soaked in white spirit, then eat sandwiches. The supervisor says skin checks are only needed if someone complains of a rash. What should the employer do?

options.A: Keep the white spirit but issue barrier cream, since cream applied before work lets rags be used safely and replaces checks
options.B: Provide skin cleansers with hot and cold water, stop solvent cleaning, and have trained staff check skin regularly
options.C: Change nothing until a worker reports a rash, because health surveillance is only triggered once a problem has been reported by a worker
options.D: Allow the rags but provide a clean eating area in the cabin, because separating eating from cleaning deals with skin exposure

explanation: Solvents strip skin and carry contaminants in, so safe cleansers, proper washing facilities and regular skin checks help catch dermatitis or early skin damage before it becomes serious.

why_wrong.A: Barrier cream does not make solvent cleaning safe and is not a substitute for proper washing facilities or checks.
why_wrong.C: Waiting for symptoms means damage is already done, and the point of checks is to find problems early.
why_wrong.D: Eating separately lowers the chance of swallowing contamination but does nothing about solvent damage to skin.

common_mistake: Waiting for a complaint before looking at workers' skin, instead of checking it regularly where substances are handled.

stem: Look at the scene. The yard supervisor says the labourer is properly protected because he wears everything the site rules list. What is the most significant PPE gap, and what should be done?

options.A: His footwear gives no toe or sole protection for handling steel, so he needs safety boots or wellingtons to the correct standard
options.B: His gloves are leather-palmed, so heavier rubber gauntlets should replace them to give better grip on wet steel
options.C: His hard hat has no chin strap, so one should be fitted because loose helmets fail whenever someone bends over
options.D: He has no hearing protection while handling steel, so ear defenders should be worn for the duration of the loading work

explanation: Plain wellingtons offer no impact or crush protection for the toes when heavy steel is handled, so footwear marked as safety footwear is needed before he continues.

why_wrong.B: The gloves shown are suitable for handling steel, and rubber gauntlets would not address crush hazards to the feet.
why_wrong.C: A chin strap is needed where the hat is likely to fall off, and the shown lifting task does not make that the main concern.
why_wrong.D: Hearing protection depends on measured noise, and no loud machinery or tool is running in the scene.

common_mistake: Ticking off the standard list of PPE items without checking that each one is the right type for the task being done.

stem: A store holds unissued helmets stamped with a manufacture date four years ago. The maker's guidance gives a five-year service life. The foreman says the clock starts when a helmet is issued, and wants crews to write their names on shells with solvent marker. What is correct?

options.A: The helmets are already out of life, because any helmet over three years old must be binned whatever the maker's guidance says on it
options.B: Life runs from the manufacture date, leaving about a year, and no solvents or adhesives should touch shells unless the maker approves
options.C: The clock starts at issue, so the helmets are good for five years from then, and a solvent marker is fine on a thick plastic shell
options.D: The helmets can be used until cracked, because the date stamp is advisory and visible damage is the only reason to replace them

explanation: Helmet life is counted from the date stamped on the shell, as plastics age in storage, and unapproved solvents or adhesives can weaken the shell and hide damage.

why_wrong.A: There is no universal three-year limit, and the maker's stated service life for the model in use is the guide.
why_wrong.C: Ageing begins at manufacture, and solvents can soften or craze plastic shells without any sign that shows.
why_wrong.D: The stated service life is a limit even without visible cracks, as age and unseen damage can reduce protection.

common_mistake: Counting a helmet's life from the day it was handed out instead of the date it was made.

stem: Scaffolders will erect a tube scaffold beside bare overhead lines, about 3 m from the nearest conductor. The foreman says no scaffold will touch the wire, so the work is safe. What should the contractor do before starting?

options.A: Use aluminium tubes instead of steel, because lighter tubes are easier to keep well clear and conduct less than steel tubes do, so contact is harmless
options.B: Keep the scaffold at least 3 m from the wire and carry on, because a visible gap of that size removes any risk of electrical injury to anyone
options.C: Issue scaffolders with insulated gloves and boots, then proceed carefully, since insulation prevents harm from near but non-contact exposure to the wire
options.D: Contact the network operator to have the lines made dead, or agree a written safe system with set clearances and barriers

explanation: Electricity can arc to a conductor without contact, so the network operator must be consulted and the lines isolated or a formal safe system with set clearances and barriers agreed.

why_wrong.A: Aluminium conducts electricity well, so a change of metal does not remove the danger of contact or arcing.
why_wrong.B: A gap seen by eye cannot be trusted, since safe distances depend on the line voltage and the network operator's advice.
why_wrong.C: Ordinary insulating PPE is not designed for high-voltage lines and gives no protection from arcing across a gap.

common_mistake: Believing that as long as nothing touches an overhead line, working close to it is safe.

stem: Groundwater seeps into a 2 m supported trench. A groundworker places a petrol-engined pump on the trench floor to clear it and carries on laying pipe beside it. What is the best assessment?

options.A: Exhaust can fill the trench with carbon monoxide, so site the pump at the surface or use electric, and re-inspect the support after the ingress
options.B: The pump is acceptable because trenches are open to the air, and any fumes will rise out of the top and disperse quickly in normal weather
options.C: Move the pump to the surface but skip further checks, because the support was inspected at the start of the shift this morning and passed
options.D: The pump is acceptable if run with the choke half open, since a rich mixture produces fewer fumes and lowers the poisoning risk in the trench

explanation: Petrol exhaust gas can collect in a trench and cause fatal carbon monoxide poisoning, and water ingress can weaken the sides, so the support needs inspecting again.

why_wrong.B: Exhaust gas can collect in a trench and linger in still air, which is how carbon monoxide poisoning happens.
why_wrong.C: Water ingress is a change in conditions, and a morning inspection does not cover its effect on the sides or support.
why_wrong.D: A rich mixture produces more carbon monoxide, and fuel settings are no substitute for removing the source from the trench.

common_mistake: Treating an open-topped trench as well ventilated even when an engine is running in it.

stem: A front-tip dumper rated at 3 tonnes is heaped with wet sand above the skip rim, hiding the route ahead. The driver says the volume is within the skip's heaped rating and he will sound the horn. What is the main flaw?

options.A: A heaped load is acceptable if a banksman walks ahead, because the banksman then replaces the driver's need to see the route
options.B: The volume rating is the limit, so the skip cannot be overloaded, and the view can be fixed by fitting a camera
options.C: The load is acceptable at below walking pace, because the overload and visibility risks both fall away when the dumper moves slowly
options.D: Rated payload is a weight limit and wet sand is heavy, so the load may be over it, and a load hiding the route must be reduced

explanation: Payload is set by weight rather than volume, so wet sand can overload a skip that looks within its heaped capacity, and a driver must see where he is going instead of relying on a horn.

why_wrong.A: This accepts a possible overload, and a banksman walking in front of a moving machine is placed in the danger zone.
why_wrong.B: Volume does not account for density, so a volume rating cannot show whether the weight limit has been exceeded.
why_wrong.C: Slow speed does not reduce the overload on the axles, brakes and stability, and a driver still cannot see pedestrians in the way.

stem: A man buys a terraced house to let out and pays one builder to refit its kitchen and bathroom before the first tenants arrive. He says he is a domestic client because he owns the house personally, so the builder holds his client duties. Which statement is correct?

options.A: He is a domestic client because the house is in his own name, so the single builder takes on his client duties automatically under CDM 2015
options.B: He is a commercial client but may pass every client duty to the builder verbally, because a single contractor can take on the role
options.C: Work done for a letting business makes him a commercial client, so he keeps the full client duties and cannot hand them to the builder
options.D: He becomes a commercial client only once tenants have moved in, so until then the builder carries the client duties as a default

explanation: A domestic client is someone having work done on their own home or a family member's home, not as part of a business, so a property being refitted to let is a commercial client's project.

why_wrong.A: Personal ownership does not decide the status, because the work is for a letting business and not for his own or a relative's home.
why_wrong.B: Commercial client duties cannot be passed on by a verbal agreement, and they remain with the client who commissions the project.
why_wrong.D: The purpose of the work, not the date a tenant arrives, decides his status, and the work is already being done for a business.

common_mistake: Assuming that owning a property personally makes you a domestic client, whatever the reason the work is being done.

stem: A profoundly deaf labourer joins a yard where reversing loaders and telehandlers work all day. The supervisor decides to keep him on the cabin side of the fence, away from the vehicles, rather than discuss the job with him. Which approach is the soundest?

options.A: Keep him on cabin duties permanently, because excluding him from vehicle areas removes the hazard and is the safest way to meet the law
options.B: Use the standard yard assessment unchanged, because he would carry the same legal duties as everyone else and should rely on spotting vehicles
options.C: Give him a hi-vis jacket and a buddy for the first week, and leave the assessment unchanged if no incident has occurred by then
options.D: Assess the risks for his actual tasks with him, then adjust the work, for example with separated routes, visual alerts and a banksman

explanation: Risk assessment should consider the individual's circumstances, and reasonable adjustments can often allow safe, fair work, which is better than excluding him or leaving him to rely on audible alarms.

why_wrong.A: Excluding him without assessing or consulting him can be unlawful discrimination and ignores adjustments that would make the work safe.
why_wrong.B: A generic assessment misses hazards that are specific to him, such as unheard reversing alarms, so it fails to protect him.
why_wrong.C: A buddy and a jacket are a token gesture, and waiting for an incident to occur is a reactive approach rather than an assessment.

common_mistake: Treating a worker's disability as a reason to exclude him, or as something to ignore, instead of adjusting the work after talking to him.

stem: A site architect who uses a wheelchair will attend weekly meetings in a first-floor cabin reached by a stair. The manager says the standard alarm and assembly point are enough, and that colleagues will carry her down in an emergency. What is the best way to deal with her evacuation?

options.A: Rely on the existing site fire plan, since an alarm and a marked assembly point apply equally to every person on the site
options.B: Agree a personal evacuation plan with her, covering the route, any equipment and trained helpers, and test it before she attends
options.C: Ask her to use the passenger hoist on the cabin block when the alarm sounds, as it is the quickest way to reach the ground
options.D: Let two colleagues carry her down by whatever grip is quickest, because speed matters most and the fire service can take over outside
