explanation: Fire arrangements must account for people who cannot use stairs, and a plan agreed with the person, with suitable equipment and trained helpers, is safer than improvised carrying.

why_wrong.A: A general plan does not provide a way for someone who cannot use the stair to get down, so it leaves her without a means of escape.
why_wrong.C: Lifts and hoists can fail or trap people in a fire, so they are not a dependable escape route unless designed for evacuation.
why_wrong.D: Improvised carrying risks injury to her and the helpers, and it relies on untrained people making decisions during an emergency.

common_mistake: Assuming one general evacuation plan covers everyone, rather than planning in advance for people who cannot use the stairs.

stem: At a weekly check, the supervisor finds a cabin extinguisher with its gauge needle in the red and its seal missing. A new labourer who has never been shown how to use one offers to swap it for a spare and use it if there is a fire. What is the correct response?

options.A: Allow the labourer to use the spare on his own initiative, as the instructions on the label are enough for anyone to use it
options.B: Take the faulty unit out of service for a competent person to deal with, and have anyone expected to use extinguishers shown how first
options.C: Leave it in place until the annual service falls due, because a unit that is still hanging on its bracket gives some cover
options.D: Let the supervisor release a short test burst to check it, then refit the seal himself and hang it back on the bracket

explanation: Defective extinguishers must be removed and attended to by a competent person, and people who may use one need instruction, including that they should only tackle a fire when it is safe to do so.

why_wrong.A: Reading a label in an emergency is no substitute for instruction, and untrained users may fight a fire that they should evacuate from.
why_wrong.C: A unit with a low gauge reading and a broken seal may not work, so leaving it gives false confidence at a fire point.
why_wrong.D: Discharging it weakens its effect for a real fire, and resealing or refilling is work for a competent service provider.

common_mistake: Believing a fire extinguisher on the wall provides cover whatever its condition or whether anyone knows how to use it.

stem: A contractor must buy two compressors for a six-month demolition job. Supplier A offers a cheaper unit with no canopy and a high noise declaration, supplier B a canopied unit with a much lower one. The manager prefers A and plans to fence off the area and issue ear defenders. What is the best view?

options.A: Choose the cheaper unit, as ear defenders are legally acceptable for any machine once the exclusion zone is fenced and signed
options.B: Choose the cheaper unit and fit a plywood screen beside it, which will bring the noise down to a safe level for the whole crew
options.C: Prefer the quieter canopied unit, since cutting noise at source comes before hearing protection, and check its output on delivery
options.D: Choose the cheaper unit, because noise controls are not needed until the daily exposure of the crew is above the upper action value

explanation: The noise regulations require noise to be reduced at source where reasonably practicable, so choosing quieter plant using supplier noise data is better than relying on zones and ear defenders.

why_wrong.A: Hearing protection is the last resort, and a fenced zone does not remove the duty to cut noise at source when it is reasonably practicable.
why_wrong.B: A screen is an add-on control of limited effect, and it does not replace buying a quieter machine in the first place.
why_wrong.D: The duty to reduce risk from noise applies from the lower action value, and plant selection should aim to cut exposure well below the upper value.

common_mistake: Treating ear defenders as a cheap answer to noisy equipment instead of choosing quieter plant first.

stem: Labourers tip 25 kg bags of cement from a pallet onto a mixer, tearing each bag open and shaking out the last of it. Dust hangs around the mixer and two of them have sore backs. Which change deals best with both problems?

options.A: Rotate the labourers every hour so that nobody lifts too many bags, and spray water over the dust cloud around the mixer
options.B: Use pre-mixed material or smaller bags delivered at waist height, and open and empty each bag low and gently into the mixer
options.C: Have two people lift each bag and shake it out vigorously, with both wearing a disposable mask and the pallet left at ground level
options.D: Issue back support belts and basic dust masks to all labourers, then carry on as before, since protection covers both risks

explanation: Removing or reducing the lift cuts the manual handling risk, and handling the material low and gently stops the dust being thrown into the air, which is better than relying on a mask.

why_wrong.A: Rotation spreads the strain without reducing it, and spraying water around the mixer does not stop dust forming at the open bag.
why_wrong.C: Pairs lifting from the floor still strain backs, and vigorous shaking creates more dust than gentle emptying.
why_wrong.D: Belts and masks are personal measures that do not remove the lift or the dust, and a belt does not make a poor technique safe.

common_mistake: Dealing with dust and lifting as separate problems, and reaching for masks and belts rather than changing the way the material is supplied.

stem: A fit-out crew hire a 4 m mobile tower for ceiling work. The foreman, who built towers from another maker's kit years ago, plans to erect this one from memory, fitting the guardrails last. The manual is still in the delivery bag. What is correct?

options.A: Let the foreman build it from memory but fit the guardrails afterwards, since the top guardrails protect the person working at the top
options.B: Let the crew build it and inspect it at the end of the first week, since the hire company has already checked every part before delivery
options.C: Have trained and competent people erect it following this maker's manual, with guardrails fitted as it rises, and inspect it before first use
options.D: Allow the foreman to erect it, since experience with another maker's tower is enough because aluminium towers are generally assembled alike

explanation: Towers must be assembled by trained, competent people following the specific manufacturer's instructions, with edge protection in place for each stage, and then inspected before anyone uses it.

why_wrong.A: Edge protection should be fitted as the tower is built, because people working on lower lifts of the assembly are also exposed to falls.
why_wrong.B: The inspection is needed after assembly and before first use, and a hire company's check does not cover how the crew erects it.
why_wrong.D: Systems differ between makers, so memory of another kit is no substitute for the instructions for this particular tower.

common_mistake: Assuming that building a tower once, with another make, is enough to erect any tower without the maker's manual.

stem: Look at the mobile tower in use. Which problem is the most significant?

options.A: He is not clipped to the tower with a harness, which is needed on a tower platform whatever the guardrails
options.B: The cordless drill is held overhead, which is the real hazard because it makes the tower unstable when the bit bites
options.C: The castors are unbraked and no outriggers are fitted, so the whole tower is free to roll or tip while he works
options.D: The operative has raised himself on crates, so the guardrails no longer protect him and the tower is less stable

explanation: Standing on crates lifts the body above the guardrail height and raises the centre of gravity, so a loss of balance can take him over the rail or topple the tower.

why_wrong.A: A tower platform with complete guardrails and toe boards is itself the fall protection, so a harness is not the fault here.
why_wrong.B: Using a drill is normal work on a tower, and the hazard is the unsafe standing position rather than the tool.
why_wrong.C: The castors are braked and outriggers are fitted, so this describes a fault that is not present in the scene.

common_mistake: Thinking guardrails still protect you after you have stood on something to gain extra height.

stem: Two operatives must lift a heavy cast-iron cover in the nearside lane of a busy road. One has a crowbar, the other proposes dropping a single cone and lifting between passing vehicles while a colleague watches the traffic. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Set up signed and coned traffic management first, then lift with a purpose-made lifting key or mechanical aid
options.B: Lift with the crowbar and two operatives using good posture, since the single cone and a lookout adequately cover the traffic risk
options.C: Time the lift for a gap in the traffic and work quickly, because a short exposure means the road risk is acceptably low
options.D: Pull the cover with a gloved grip at the edge while kneeling beside it, as gloves protect the hands from being crushed

explanation: The lift is a manual handling risk and the road is a traffic risk, so both are controlled by protecting the work area before starting and using a proper lifting device rather than hands or a bar.

why_wrong.B: A single cone and a lookout do not protect operatives kneeling in a live lane, and prying with a bar risks trapped fingers and strained backs.
why_wrong.C: Short exposure does not replace traffic management, and a rushed lift of a heavy cover increases the chance of injury.
why_wrong.D: Gloves do not prevent crush injuries or back strain, and kneeling in the road puts the operatives in the path of traffic.

common_mistake: Dealing with only the weight of the cover, or only the passing traffic, instead of controlling both together.

stem: To reach a high soffit, a contractor wants two operatives to ride in a site-made steel cage fitted to the forks of a telehandler. The driver is experienced and says the machine is well within its capacity. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The lift is acceptable if the operatives wear full harnesses attached to the cage, which then prevents any fall from height
options.B: The lift is acceptable because the combined weight of the cage and operatives is below the rated capacity, and the driver is experienced
options.C: The lift is acceptable for short tasks of under an hour, since the extra risk to the operatives grows with the time spent in the cage
options.D: The machine is built for loads, so lifting people is for exceptional circumstances, and a purpose-designed platform or MEWP is safer

explanation: Equipment not designed to lift people should only be used in exceptional circumstances, so a MEWP or a purpose- designed platform with suitable planning and examination is the proper choice here.

why_wrong.A: Harnesses do not make an unsuitable arrangement safe, and a harness cannot replace equipment designed for lifting people.
why_wrong.B: Capacity is only one factor, and a site-made cage on a machine not designed for lifting people does not meet the extra safety requirements.
why_wrong.C: Risk is not controlled by the length of time, because the cage could detach or the machine tip the moment it leaves the ground.

common_mistake: Judging a person-lift on the telehandler's load rating alone, without asking whether the equipment was made to carry people.

stem: A self-employed builder hires a self-employed electrician for one day to run cables in a loft the builder has worked in all week. The builder knows several boards are rotten but says, "He is his own boss, so his safety is his problem." Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The builder controls the loft, so he must warn the electrician about the rotten boards and coordinate the work, while the electrician remains responsible for his own methods and tools
options.B: The electrician alone is responsible, because a self- employed person hired by the day accepts every risk of the premises as part of his agreed day rate and own look-out
options.C: Duties towards people who are not employees apply only to jobs lasting longer than one day, so a single day of hire leaves the builder with no legal duty to him
options.D: Neither tradesperson has an employer, so no health and safety duty arises between them and any responsibility rests with whoever owns the property being worked on

explanation: Self-employed people must not expose others to risk from their work and must cooperate and coordinate where they share a workplace, so the builder owes information about hazards he controls even though the electrician answers for his own working methods.

why_wrong.B: Self-employed status does not transfer the controller's duty to warn of known hazards, and no price agreement can contract out of health and safety law.
why_wrong.C: The duty not to expose others to risk applies to any work activity, however short, and has no minimum duration.
why_wrong.D: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act places duties on self-employed people as well as employers, so the absence of an employer does not remove the builder's duty.

common_mistake: Assuming that hiring someone who is self- employed, even for a single day, passes all responsibility for the work area onto them.

stem: A roadworker has signed an opt-out from the 48-hour weekly working limit. His supervisor rosters him for six 11-hour night shifts every week for the next two months, saying the opt-out covers it. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The opt-out covers only the weekly limit, and night workers cannot opt out of the 8-hour average in 24 hours, so this roster breaches the night rule
options.B: The opt-out also removes the night limit, provided the employer pays a night premium and confirms the roster in writing at the start of every single week
options.C: The 8-hour night figure is a guideline for workers with special hazards, so an ordinary road crew can be rostered well beyond it by agreement with the employer
options.D: Eleven-hour shifts are lawful as long as each is followed by at least 11 hours of rest, because daily rest is the one limit that really matters for night work

explanation: A night worker's hours must average no more than 8 in each 24-hour period over the reference period, and unlike the weekly limit this cannot be waived by signing an opt-out.

why_wrong.B: The night work limit cannot be opted out of, and extra pay or written confirmation does not change that.
why_wrong.C: The average limit applies to all night workers, and the special-hazards rule makes the cap stricter, not looser.
why_wrong.D: Daily rest and the average night-hours limit are separate rules, and meeting one does not satisfy the other.

common_mistake: Believing that a signed opt-out from the 48-hour week lifts every working time limit, including those protecting night workers.

stem: After four hours digging in cold rain, a labourer is soaked, drowsy, confused and slurring his words. A colleague suggests sending him to the cabin alone for a hot shower. What is the most appropriate action while help is called?

options.A: Add extra layers over his wet clothing and let him carry on digging, since heat from steady exercise will bring his body temperature back up
options.B: Rub his arms and legs briskly to restore circulation and give him a small measure of spirits to warm him from the inside quickly
options.C: Call 999, move him to shelter, remove his wet clothing, wrap him warmly including his head, and stay with him talking until help comes
options.D: Let him take a hot shower to rewarm quickly, then rest unobserved so he can recover in privacy, calling help only if he is no better later

explanation: These are signs of hypothermia, which needs emergency medical care, and the safe interim steps are shelter, removing wet clothes, gentle insulation and continuous observation.

why_wrong.A: Wet clothing keeps drawing heat from his body, and a confused worker needs to stop work and get medical help.
why_wrong.B: Rubbing limbs and giving alcohol are both advised against in hypothermia, as they can make his condition worse.
why_wrong.D: Hot baths or showers are not advised for hypothermia, and someone confused must not be left alone or have emergency help delayed.

common_mistake: Treating confusion and slurred speech in a cold, wet worker as tiredness that he can work off rather than as a medical emergency.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative is properly protected because he has a hard hat, glasses, a mask, ear defenders and gloves. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: A half mask and glasses cannot cope with rebounding grit and fine dust, so he needs a supplied-air blasting helmet.
options.B: Cotton overalls are the weak point, because leather aprons would offer better protection from the rebounding grit and the heat.
options.C: Ear defenders should be replaced with earplugs, because defenders cannot seal properly against the hard hat brim in this noise.
options.D: Leather gauntlets should be fitted with grip-assist coatings so the nozzle hose cannot be dropped during the blasting task.

explanation: Abrasive blasting creates a heavy cloud of grit and dust which rebounds, so the face, eyes and airways need a purpose- made blasting helmet with a clean air supply rather than a half mask under glasses.

why_wrong.B: Clothing matters, but the breathing and face protection is a far greater risk from the dust cloud.
why_wrong.C: Defenders suit this noise level, and the picture does not show a sealing problem that plugs would fix.
why_wrong.D: Grip is a minor point compared with the breathing and eye risk, and gauntlets are a normal choice for this task.

common_mistake: Counting the number of PPE items worn instead of asking whether each one suits the actual hazard.

stem: A banksman works beside a block-cutting saw at about 92 dB(A) among reversing dumpers. He keeps lifting his ear defenders off whenever a vehicle moves, to hear the alarms. What is the best way to resolve this?

options.A: Fit louder alarms on all the dumpers so they cut through the defenders, as the noise regulations cover only the equipment that the banksman himself personally uses
options.B: Choose protectors giving roughly 70 to 85 dB at the ear, have him wear them throughout, and add visual warnings and segregation so alarms are not the only cue
options.C: Issue the lowest-rated plugs available so the alarms stay clear, since once any hearing protection has been handed out the employer's duty to protect is met
options.D: Let him lift them off when a vehicle comes within about ten metres, because such short removals add very little to his exposure and the alarm is the main vehicle warning

explanation: Protection must be worn continuously to work, and selecting an attenuation that avoids both under- and over- protection, with other vehicle controls, keeps him safe from noise and traffic.

why_wrong.A: Louder alarms add to everyone's noise exposure, and the regulations require noise to be controlled for all workers affected.
why_wrong.C: Protection that leaves his ear exposure above 85 dB does not control the noise risk, whatever has been issued.
why_wrong.D: Even brief removal cuts the protection achieved over a shift, and an audible alarm should never be the only control on vehicle movements.

common_mistake: Taking hearing protection off for moments to hear a warning, as though a short removal costs little protection.

stem: A new concrete ramp rises 1.5 m to a first-floor slab and has an open side edge. Barrow loads run up it, and the only protection is red-and-white barrier tape between posts. The supervisor says tape and a sign are enough because the drop is under 2 m. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Tape cannot stop a fall or a barrow, so guardrails with an intermediate rail and toe board are needed, as no minimum fall height applies
options.B: A barrier with two warning signs is acceptable if inspected every day, because inspection is what the Regulations actually require for open edges
options.C: Tape is acceptable under 2 m, but a harness must be worn by anyone pushing a barrow along the open edge of the ramp as extra protection
options.D: A top rail alone at the correct height is adequate, because toe boards are needed only where other people are working beneath the open edge

explanation: Edge protection must physically prevent people and materials from falling, and the Work at Height Regulations apply wherever a fall could cause injury, with no minimum height.

why_wrong.B: Inspection checks that protection is working, and it cannot replace physical edge protection that prevents a fall.
why_wrong.C: There is no 2 m threshold in the Regulations, and personal fall protection is not preferred over collective edge protection.
why_wrong.D: Toe boards also stop barrow wheels and materials from going over the edge, not only protect those below.

common_mistake: Relying on the idea that falls from below two metres are minor, so tape and signs can stand in for proper edge protection.

stem: A roofing gang must climb a 6 m fixed vertical ladder with a cage to a flat roof, each carrying a 15 kg roll of felt on his shoulder. The foreman says the cage will stop anyone falling, so no harness is needed. What is the best approach?

options.A: Allow the cage to be relied on, but limit each climber to one 15 kg roll and require a handhold on every third rung.
options.B: Hoist the rolls separately and climb with a harness on the ladder's fall-arrest system, as a cage gives little protection.
options.C: Climb in pairs so the lower person can catch the upper one, and fit a harness only once both have reached the roof edge.
options.D: Fit a lanyard to a rung at head height and climb carrying the rolls in a rucksack so that both hands stay free for the rungs.

explanation: Cages are not reliable fall protection and carrying a load on a vertical ladder prevents a secure grip, so the load should be hoisted and the climber should use a suitable fall- arrest system.

why_wrong.A: A cage does not stop a fall and a load on the shoulder still prevents a firm grip.
why_wrong.C: A colleague cannot catch a falling person and the climb is where the risk is highest.
why_wrong.D: A rung is not a suitable anchor and a heavy rucksack pulls the climber backwards off the ladder.

common_mistake: Assuming a ladder cage is as good as a fall-arrest system and that a load can be carried up on the shoulder.

stem: A lorry must reverse into a site gate across a busy public footway. The marshal stands directly behind it in the gateway and waves pedestrians through behind him whenever the footway looks clear. What is the main fault in this arrangement?

options.A: He stands in the lorry's path and blind spot, so he should stand clear, stay visible to the driver and keep pedestrians out of the reversing area
options.B: He should carry a radio headset and remain behind the lorry, because radio contact lets him warn pedestrians in good time if the driver starts to reverse
options.C: His position is acceptable if his clothing is high-visibility, because a reversing driver is required to stop for any person who is wearing it
options.D: Pedestrians must be stopped from using the footway altogether for every delivery, because a marshal has no practical means of controlling members of the public

explanation: A signaller must stand in a safe position out of the vehicle's way, be visible to the driver at all times and keep the reversing area clear of pedestrians.

why_wrong.B: A radio does not remove him from the swept path, and a person directly behind a reversing lorry is exposed to being struck.
why_wrong.C: Visibility helps but does not make a blind spot safe, and drivers cannot be relied on to see or stop in time.
why_wrong.D: Closing the footway is not the only control, as a marshal can hold pedestrians clear from a safe position, with barriers or planned routes where needed.

common_mistake: Thinking that a marshal standing behind a reversing vehicle can safely control pedestrians just by watching them and waving.

stem: A tipper driver is told to discharge hardcore under a temporary pipe gantry 5 m up, on soft ground that slopes slightly sideways after rain. He says the raised body will clear the pipes by half a metre. Which assessment is correct?

options.A: Tip as planned because pipework, unlike power cables, cannot electrocute anyone, so only the slope matters and a slow tip deals with that
options.B: Tip as planned but with the driver standing well back from the cab holding the controls, which would protect him if the lorry became unstable
options.C: Do not tip there, as the raised body can foul overhead pipework and tipping needs firm level ground, so move to a clear, level area first
options.D: Tip in stages with a banksman watching the clearance, since he can warn the driver in good time to lower the body before it touches anything

explanation: A tipping site must be clear overhead of pipes and cables and firm and level, as a raised body on a slope can become unstable and swing into obstructions.

why_wrong.A: Overhead pipework is also an obstruction that a raised body can strike, so the area must be clear of it as well as cables.
why_wrong.B: The driver should stay in the cab with the doors closed during tipping, not stand outside where an unstable body could fall on him.
why_wrong.D: A banksman cannot correct soft, sloping ground, and instability can develop faster than any warning can be given.

common_mistake: Judging a tipping position only by whether the raised body is expected to miss obstructions, without checking the ground is firm and level.

stem: A site's steel container holds 25-litre cans of solvent paint and thinners on a bare floor beside a tub of oxidising bleach powder. A heater cable is run inside and the doors are kept shut. The spill kit hangs in the site office. Which change best reduces both fire and pollution risk?

options.A: Leave the layout as it is but move the spill kit inside the container and open the doors during working hours so that vapour can escape
options.B: Swap the cans for a few larger 205-litre drums, since fewer containers mean fewer places to leak and much less to monitor for damage
options.C: Use a ventilated, lockable, bunded flammables store free of heaters, keep the oxidiser elsewhere and hold a spill kit at its door
options.D: Stack the cans on pallets and cover them with a fire- retardant sheet, which contains vapour and prevents any spill from reaching a drain

explanation: Solvents need ventilation and no ignition sources, incompatible oxidisers need segregating, and a bund with a kit at the point of storage contains leaks before they reach drains.

why_wrong.A: This leaves the heater, the oxidiser next to the solvents and the lack of any bund unchanged, so both risks remain.
why_wrong.B: Larger containers increase the volume that can be lost in one failure, and the ignition source and oxidiser problems remain.
why_wrong.D: A sheet does not contain vapour, separate incompatible materials or stop a spill, and pallets give no containment.

common_mistake: Treating a lockable container as proper storage without checking ventilation, ignition sources, segregation and spill containment.

stem: An electrician finishes a task covered by a permit to work on an isolated plant room supply. He tells the site manager it is done, and leaves for another job. The manager wants the supply back on straight away. What should happen before the permit is closed?

options.A: The receiver signs the permit back as complete, then the issuer checks people are clear and equipment is safe, cancels it, and only then reverses the isolation
options.B: The permit lapses automatically at the end of the shift, so the manager can re-energise the supply once the planned finish time has passed
options.C: The manager can cancel it on the electrician's verbal word, since the person who did the work knows best that the plant is safe to energise
options.D: The electrician must stay on site until the supply is back on, because the receiver is the person who authorises the isolation to be removed

explanation: A permit is closed through a defined handback: the receiver declares the work finished and the authorised issuer verifies the area before cancelling it, so nobody is exposed when the supply is restored.

why_wrong.B: A permit stays live until formally cancelled, and the passing of a time does not prove that the work is finished or the area is clear.
why_wrong.C: A verbal report skips the signed handback and the issuer's own check that people and tools are clear of the plant.
why_wrong.D: It is the issuer, not the receiver, who authorises restoration, and the receiver's duty is to hand the permit back.

common_mistake: Treating a permit to work as finished when the job is, rather than when the issuer has formally cancelled it.

stem: On a large site with three gates, a labourer collapses on the fourth floor of a block at the back. The first aider rings 999 from her mobile. The only gate open to vehicles today is Gate C. What should she tell the call handler?

options.A: The head office address and the nearest main road junction, since that is the location recorded in the firm's general emergency plan on file
options.B: Only the site postcode and the casualty's condition, because the sat-nav will take the ambulance straight to the casualty and extra detail would delay the call
options.C: The casualty's condition and the site manager's mobile number, since the crew can phone ahead for directions once they have reached the area of the site
options.D: The site address and postcode, Gate C as the open entrance, the block and floor, and that a person will meet the crew at the gate

explanation: Crews need the address, the access point that is actually open and the exact location, and a guide at the gate saves minutes finding a casualty inside a large site.

why_wrong.A: The head office is not where the casualty is, and a road junction does not identify which gate or block to go to.
why_wrong.B: A postcode usually leads to a main gate or road, which may be closed or far from the casualty.
why_wrong.C: Relying on a callback wastes time, and the call handler needs the location and access details during the call itself.

common_mistake: Assuming that the site postcode alone will get an ambulance to the right gate and the right part of a large site.

stem: Roofers heat a bitumen boiler on a flat roof and ladle hot bitumen to the working area. The boiler runs well above its normal temperature to speed the job, and a bucket of rainwater sits beside it. Which approach controls fume and burn risks best?

options.A: Run the boiler hotter to thin the bitumen so less is handled, and wear a simple dust mask because that filters out the fumes rising from the pot
options.B: Keep the water bucket close to cool any spilt bitumen quickly, and stand upwind of the boiler so the fumes are always blown away from the face
options.C: Wear thick cotton overalls and work only for short bursts, because fabric stops hot splashes and short exposures keep fumes below harmful levels
options.D: Hold the recommended working temperature, keep water and damp materials away from the hot bitumen, and cover skin and eyes against splashes

explanation: Overheating raises fume output, water in hot bitumen causes violent spitting, and covering skin and eyes protects against splashes, so these controls address both risks.

why_wrong.A: Higher temperature increases fume and burn risk, and a simple dust mask does not filter bitumen fume.
why_wrong.B: Water thrown on hot bitumen can cause violent spitting, and standing upwind alone does not control skin contact.
why_wrong.C: Cotton can be soaked through by hot bitumen, and limiting time does not replace temperature control and proper protection.

common_mistake: Raising the heat to save time without thinking that it increases both fume and the severity of any splash.

stem: A gang renewing an old brick sewer is told that the hepatitis A and tetanus vaccinations are up to date for everyone. A worker says the jabs mean he need not bother with washing facilities, and he eats lunch in the chamber's access area. What is the correct view?

options.A: The vaccines cover every illness found in sewage, so hygiene precautions are required only for any workers who have not yet been vaccinated
options.B: Vaccination adds protection but does not replace hygiene, so washing before eating, covering cuts and using clean welfare facilities remain necessary
options.C: Hygiene precautions apply to those working inside the chamber, so colleagues at the surface may eat and drink beside the open cover
options.D: Washing is needed only once the shift ends, because eating in the access area is safe provided gloves were worn throughout the whole job

explanation: Vaccines cover only some infections and are an added layer, so the hygiene controls, clean welfare facilities and covering cuts are still needed to stop other infections.

why_wrong.A: Vaccination covers only specific diseases, and many sewage-borne infections have no vaccine.
why_wrong.C: Contaminated tools, boots and spills reach the surface, so eating next to the open chamber exposes people there too.
why_wrong.D: Gloves can carry contamination to food and the mouth, so hands must be washed before eating in a clean area.

common_mistake: Believing that being vaccinated means normal hygiene rules for dirty work no longer apply.

stem: Two fitters on a scissor lift platform, rated for 250 kg, are installing ductwork under a mezzanine slab, where another gang is laying decking. They carry 120 kg of duct and tools between them. Which arrangement best covers the platform and overhead risks?

options.A: Check the combined weight of people, tools and duct against the rated load, and stop or protect work above, with helmets worn on the platform
options.B: Place the lift under a finished section of slab so nothing can fall, and let both fitters stand on the guardrail midrail for extra reach
options.C: Let the fitters lean on the guardrail to reach the soffit, and ask the decking gang to shout before each drop of material above them
options.D: Count only the weight of materials against the rating since the platform is built for people, and rely on its guardrails to catch falling items

explanation: The rated capacity includes people and materials, and guardrails on the platform do not protect occupants from objects dropping from the work above.

why_wrong.B: Standing on rails is unsafe, and the question of the load rating and the other gang's work above is left unresolved.
why_wrong.C: Leaning on guardrails risks overturning the lift, and shouting is not a reliable control over falling items.
why_wrong.D: People count towards the rated load, and the guardrails and toe boards cannot stop objects falling from above.

common_mistake: Forgetting that the people on the platform count towards its rated load, and that guardrails do not stop objects dropped from above.

stem: Look at the scene. The roofer says that because he is wearing a harness he is protected for the rest of the roof inspection. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The parapet is lower than the guardrail height, so the harness is irrelevant and only a taller wall would meet the requirements for edge work
options.B: The ladder rises about a metre above the hatch opening, which leaves a person little to hold when stepping out and onto the roof
options.C: The hatch lid is propped open on a stay, which makes the opening a risk to people below and is the main fault with the roof access
options.D: The lanyard is clipped to a hatch lid hinge that is not a rated anchor, and its slack length allows him to reach the unprotected edge

explanation: Fall protection depends on a designed anchor point and a lanyard set so that a fall is prevented or arrested safely, but a hinge on a hatch lid is not designed for that load and the slack lets him reach the edge.

why_wrong.A: A low parapet does not meet edge protection standards, but the harness is still relevant and its attachment is the specific fault shown.
why_wrong.B: A ladder rising about a metre above the landing is the correct arrangement and gives a handhold, so this is not the problem.
why_wrong.C: An open lid can be a hazard, but the stay holds it and it is not the main danger shown in the scene.

common_mistake: Assuming that wearing a harness means a person is protected, without checking what it is attached to.

stem: A 2.4 m trench with a trench box is finished and the pipe has been laid. The foreman wants to lift the box out in one go with the excavator while two groundworkers stay in to shovel the last bedding. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Let the two stay in the box until it clears the ground, since their weight stops it swinging and the sides stay supported by the laid pipe and bedding
options.B: Lift the box out first and then backfill the open trench in one pass, since the soil looks stable enough for the short time it is unsupported
options.C: Drag the box along the open trench to the next section with the pair walking beside it, because that avoids lifting and re-setting the box
options.D: Get the groundworkers out first, then backfill and compact in stages as the box is raised, so nobody stands in an unsupported trench

explanation: Support is removed progressively as backfilling proceeds, and nobody should be in the trench while the box is lifted, because the sides can collapse once the support goes.

why_wrong.A: People inside a box being lifted risk crushing and collapse, and the pipe gives no support to the trench sides.
why_wrong.B: Removing support before backfilling leaves the sides unsupported, and soil that looks stable can collapse without warning.
why_wrong.C: Dragging a box along an open trench leaves sections unsupported and puts workers beside moving plant and collapsing sides.

common_mistake: Thinking support can come out all at once and people can stay in the trench for the last small tasks.

stem: A mapped 11 kV cable must be exposed so the network operator can divert it. A groundworker says rubber-handled hand tools and insulated gloves make it safe to dig right beside it before the operator arrives. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Dig with insulated tools and gloves at close range, because the cable's outer sheath and the tool insulation together give full protection against a strike
options.B: Start digging after switching off the nearest site supply, because cutting the site power also disconnects a mapped cable lying in the ground
options.C: Treat the cable as live until its owner proves it dead, hand- dig carefully to expose it, and follow the operator's instructions
options.D: Use the excavator to expose the cable faster, as the cab's rubber tyres will protect the operator if the bucket happens to touch the cable

explanation: Insulation on tools gives no assurance against a damaged live cable, so it must be treated as live until the owner has isolated and proved it dead, with careful hand digging used to expose it.

why_wrong.A: A damaged sheath can expose conductors, and tool insulation does not guard against high-voltage arcing or a strike.
why_wrong.B: The site supply is independent of the buried network cable, which remains live until its owner isolates it.
why_wrong.D: Machine digging near cables can sever or damage them, and tyres give no dependable protection against high voltage.

common_mistake: Believing that insulated tools or gloves make it acceptable to work beside a cable that has not been made dead.

stem: A mature oak with a 0.8 m trunk diameter is to be kept beside a new build. Protective fencing is set 3 m from the trunk, and the manager wants to store sand and park a cement mixer just outside it, and wash out within that gap. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Leave the fence at 3 m, as roots grow only below the branch spread, and allow sand to be stored and mixers washed out within the gap
options.B: Fence the root protection area worked out from trunk diameter, and keep storage, plant, fuel and washout outside it
options.C: Move the fence out to 5 m, and allow the plant to park and washout to drain inside the new line as long as nobody digs
options.D: Keep the fence where it is and lay thin plastic sheet over the ground beyond it, because the sheet stops compaction and contamination reaching roots

explanation: The root protection area is calculated from the trunk diameter, so a 3 m line is too close, and compaction, spillage and washout inside it can kill roots.

why_wrong.A: Roots extend well beyond the trunk and often beyond the canopy, and a fixed 3 m line ignores the tree's actual size.
why_wrong.C: Compaction and washout within the protected area harm roots without any digging.
why_wrong.D: A sheet does not stop compaction, and an inadequate fence line still leaves much of the root area exposed.

common_mistake: Setting tree protection by guesswork rather than from the trunk size, and treating the area just outside as free for storage.

stem: A demolition crew clears a brick warehouse. Some bricks are sound and sorted, the rest is clean concrete and brick rubble, and a few pieces are suspected asbestos cement. The client wants it all sent to one skip. Which plan best follows the waste hierarchy?

options.A: Send the mixed skip to an energy recovery plant, as recovery avoids landfill and the contents then need not be sorted on site
options.B: Isolate the suspected asbestos for specialist handling, reuse sound bricks, crush the clean rubble as aggregate, and landfill only what cannot be recovered
options.C: Landfill the whole lot, since sorting costs more than the tax and a single skip is quicker to clear with fewer lorry movements
options.D: Crush everything together as aggregate, since recycling sits at the top of the hierarchy and mixed rubble can still be recycled

explanation: The hierarchy puts reuse before recycling and disposal last, while segregation at source stops contamination from downgrading clean rubble and hazardous pieces need specialist handling.

why_wrong.A: Recovery ranks below reuse and recycling, and mixed loads containing asbestos cannot go to ordinary facilities.
why_wrong.C: Disposal is the last option and the unsorted loads would waste material that could be reused or recycled.
why_wrong.D: Reuse ranks above recycling, and crushing suspected asbestos cement into aggregate would spread fibres and contaminate the load.

common_mistake: Treating recycling as the best outcome for all waste and skipping the sorting that makes reuse and clean recycling possible.

stem: A roofing subcontractor learns that a crane will lift plant onto the adjoining block's roof while his crew works below. His foreman says coordination is the principal contractor's job alone and he will brief the crew only if they ask. What is the correct position?

options.A: His duty to cooperate ends at the boundary of his own subcontract, so a lift on the adjoining roof is a matter for the crane contractor alone
options.B: He must cooperate with other contractors, but consulting his workers is optional unless a trade union safety representative has been appointed within his firm
options.C: He must cooperate with the other contractors as far as safety needs, follow the principal contractor's directions, and consult his own workers on risks affecting them
options.D: The principal contractor carries the whole duty to coordinate, so a subcontractor need only obey instructions and has no obligation to share or seek information from other trades

explanation: Under CDM 2015 every duty holder must cooperate with others working on the same or an adjoining site, and employers must consult their workers on health and safety matters that affect them.

why_wrong.A: The duty to cooperate expressly extends to those working on an adjoining site or related work.
why_wrong.B: Employers must consult workers directly where there is no recognised union representative.
why_wrong.D: Cooperation is a duty on every contractor, not only the principal contractor.

common_mistake: Assuming that coordination and consultation are the principal contractor's job and a subcontractor only needs to look after his own work.

stem: A manufacturer of petrol cut-off saws learns that the blade guard can crack and detach in service, and two users have been injured. The saws were sold through hire firms months ago. The manufacturer says its liability ended at the point of sale. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Its duty continues: once a serious risk becomes known it must pass on revised safety information to those it supplied, so far as is reasonably practicable
options.B: Liability ended at sale, because section 6 duties cover design and testing only, and the hire firms and users take over all later risk for the equipment
options.C: It needs to act only if the HSE serves a notice, since its duty covers the information supplied at purchase and does not extend to later discoveries
options.D: Informing the owners of the two injured users' saws is enough, because information about other units is required only for defects found in pre-sale testing

explanation: Section 6 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires suppliers and manufacturers to provide revised information when a serious risk to health or safety becomes known.

why_wrong.B: Section 6 includes a continuing duty to give revised information about serious risks that become known.
why_wrong.C: The duty arises when the risk becomes known, not when an enforcing authority intervenes.
why_wrong.D: The duty covers everyone supplied with the article, not just those already harmed.

common_mistake: Believing a manufacturer's safety responsibility stops once the equipment has been sold or hired out.

stem: A yard cuts steel reinforcement bars with an abrasive cut-off saw, giving about 100 dB(A) at the operator's ear. The manager asks which sequence of controls follows the hierarchy for noise. Which is correct?

options.A: Fit a screen and defenders together first, then rotate workers, and treat switching to a shear or pre-cut bars as a final option because it needs a purchase
options.B: Issue ear defenders straight away as the quickest control, then enclose the saw, then reduce the time spent cutting, and consider a quieter method last of all
options.C: Rotate operators first to limit each person's daily dose, then fit defenders, and enclose the saw or change the cutting method only if readings stay high
options.D: Order bars pre-cut off site; if not possible use a quieter shear; then enclose or screen the saw; then limit exposure time, with ear defenders as the last resort

explanation: Noise should be removed at source first, then substituted or engineered down, then managed by working arrangements, with hearing protection used only for the risk that remains.

why_wrong.A: Eliminating or substituting the noise source comes first, and purchase effort does not reorder the hierarchy.
why_wrong.B: This inverts the hierarchy by putting personal protection first and elimination or substitution last.
why_wrong.C: Administrative measures and PPE rank below removing or reducing noise at source.

common_mistake: Reaching for ear defenders first because they are quick and cheap, instead of working down from eliminating the noise.

stem: Four labourers build a temporary flood barrier by lifting 25 kg wet sandbags from a lorry to waist height and stacking them on a slippery slope for four hours. One says 25 kg is the safe limit. Which approach best applies the manual handling hierarchy?

options.A: Provide back support belts and require lifting with bent knees, because the belts allow heavier repeated loads to be handled safely over a long period
options.B: Let each worker set his own pace and rest breaks, since assessment of the task applies only to single lifts that exceed the guideline weights
options.C: Mechanise or avoid the handling where possible, then cut load and repetition with smaller bags, a handling chain with rotation, and firm, dry footing
options.D: Treat 25 kg as a legal limit for men and rely on fitness checks and lifting technique training to cover the repetitive stacking on the slope

explanation: Manual handling controls start with avoiding or mechanising the task, then reduce the load, repetition and poor conditions identified through the task, individual, load and environment factors.

why_wrong.A: Back belts are not a recognised control and do not make repeated heavy lifting safe.
why_wrong.B: Repetitive handling and the environment must be assessed even when individual lifts are below guideline weights.
why_wrong.D: Guideline weights are not legal limits and repetition, twisting and slippery footing change the risk.

common_mistake: Treating a guideline weight as a safe limit and ignoring repetition, posture and ground conditions.

stem: The door to a compressor room shows a yellow triangle for noise and a red circle with a diagonal bar over a walking figure. A visitor asks whether he must wear ear defenders and whether the red sign will keep people out. What is the correct reading?

options.A: The yellow triangle is a mandatory sign for hearing protection and the red circle is a physical barrier, so both controls are already in place.
options.B: The red sign forbids entry without defenders, and the yellow triangle tells visitors where to collect them before they go in.
options.C: The yellow sign only warns, so a blue mandatory sign is needed, and the red sign needs a lock or permit behind it.
options.D: The yellow triangle shows a safe condition for visitors, and the red sign is guidance that employees can follow at their own discretion.

explanation: A warning triangle does not instruct anyone to wear anything, a mandatory blue circle does, and a prohibition sign only states a rule so physical access control is needed to stop people entering.

why_wrong.A: Yellow triangles warn of a hazard and do not instruct wearing PPE, and a sign of any colour is not a physical barrier.
why_wrong.B: A red prohibition sign forbids an action and does not set conditions, and a warning triangle does not direct anyone to equipment.
why_wrong.D: Safe conditions are shown in green and a prohibition sign states a rule that has to be followed.

common_mistake: Treating a warning sign as an instruction to use PPE or a prohibition sign as if it were a barrier.

stem: An electrician must run cable across an unboarded loft to a junction box 6 m from the hatch. The ceiling below is plasterboard between joists. He plans to step from joist to joist carrying the drum, stepping on the board where the gap is wide. What is the best way to do it?

options.A: Lay a line of crawling boards across the joists to the work position, carry the drum separately, and keep every foot and knee on the boards.
options.B: Step only on the joists, spreading the feet wide for balance, and use a torch held in the free hand to see where the next step goes.
options.C: Step on the board only close to the wall edge and near a joist, since ceiling boards are firmly screwed at the perimeter and will take body weight.
options.D: Keep to the joists and ask a colleague below to push up on the ceiling board when a foot strays, so any sagging is spotted in time.

explanation: Plasterboard cannot carry body weight, so a person must be supported by boards spanning several joists, and a clear route with good lighting reduces the chance of a foot slipping off the joist.

why_wrong.B: Balancing on narrow joists leaves no margin for a slip, and holding a torch removes a hand that could be used to steady himself.
why_wrong.C: Screws at the edge do not make plasterboard load-bearing, and it will not take body weight anywhere in the ceiling.
why_wrong.D: Plasterboard can fail with no warning and a colleague pushing from below cannot stop a foot or leg breaking through.

common_mistake: Assuming that a ceiling board next to a joist will take your weight if you step lightly.

stem: A mobile crane will lift ducting beneath bare overhead lines. At 8 am the site engineer measured a comfortable gap to the jib and marked it. By mid-afternoon it is hot and the wind has risen. What should the safe system rely on?

options.A: Insulated slings and rubber gloves for the slinger, because contact with the lines is dangerous only when the load being lifted is made of metal
options.B: Isolation by the network owner where possible, otherwise clearances allowing for worst-case conductor sag and swing, with barriers and a trained banksman
options.C: The morning measurement, since a gap that was clear at the start of the shift stays valid all day provided the crane itself has not been moved
options.D: The banksman's eyesight alone, because an experienced signaller can judge by eye whether the jib and load are staying outside arcing distance of the lines

explanation: Conductors sag in heat and swing in wind, and electricity can arc without contact, so isolation or a fixed clearance planned for worst-case movement is needed.

why_wrong.A: Insulated accessories do not make approaching live lines safe, and the whole crane and rope can become live.
why_wrong.C: Lines sag and sway with temperature and wind, so a one-off measurement does not remain valid.
why_wrong.D: Distance to overhead lines is very hard to judge by eye, so physical controls are needed.

common_mistake: Judging clearance from a single morning measurement or by eye, ignoring heat, wind and arcing.

stem: Look at the lift. The slinger says the chains and pallet are well inside the crane's rated capacity. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: Bricks on a banded wooden pallet cannot be crane-lifted and must be moved in a lifting cage or skip designed for loose building materials
options.B: The hook has no working safety catch, so the sling master link could slip off the hook if the load shifts or the chains go slack
options.C: The slinger is standing too close to the lorry while the chains are tensioned and must move back to at least the full height of the jib
options.D: A worker is holding a tag line, which keeps his hands close to the load and should be replaced by steadying the pallet with a long pole

explanation: Lifting hooks must have a functioning safety catch or equivalent so the load cannot become detached, whatever the rated capacity.

why_wrong.A: Banded, properly packaged pallets can be lifted on suitable slings, so this is not the key defect.
why_wrong.C: The slinger is clear of the load path, and no rule requires standing back by the jib's full height.
why_wrong.D: Tag lines are a standard way to control a load from a safe distance and are not the hazard here.

common_mistake: Judging a lift safe because the load is under the rated capacity, without checking the lifting accessories and hook condition.

stem: An operator is loading a 14-tonne tracked excavator onto a low-loader on a muddy verge with a slight slope. The tracks are caked with clay and the ramps are wet. He plans to drive up fast and slew the cab to turn it on the ramps. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Drive up in a single burst of speed so momentum carries the machine over the ramps, then slew the cab round once it is on the bed.
options.B: Park the low-loader across the slope so the ramps are lower, steer the machine as it climbs, and secure it with a single central strap.
options.C: Load on firm level ground with clean tracks and ramps, drive straight up slowly guided by a signaller, then chain it down.
options.D: Have the driver watch the ramp edges from the cab alone, with the bucket raised for balance, and secure the machine after the journey starts.

explanation: Clean tracks and ramps, level ground and a straight, slow ascent prevent slipping or tipping, and a signaller guides the driver from a safe position before the machine is secured to the trailer.

why_wrong.A: Speed on wet ramps invites a skid, and slewing or steering while on the ramps can unbalance the machine.
why_wrong.B: A sloping surface and steering on ramps risk a tip, and one strap would not hold the machine's weight.
why_wrong.D: A signaller helps with the blind spots and a raised bucket raises the centre of gravity, and securing must be done before departure.

common_mistake: Rushing a machine up ramps with muddy tracks, treating loading as a quick task rather than a controlled lift of a heavy machine.

stem: On a dry, windy week, lorries on an unsurfaced haul road raise dust that drifts over neighbouring homes downwind. The manager suggests handing neighbours masks and sweeping the road dry at the end of each day. Which response best controls the problem?

options.A: Offer neighbours masks and a complaints line and log each report, because dust from a temporary haul road is a nuisance rather than a controlled risk
options.B: Suppress dust at source by damping the road without runoff, cutting vehicle speeds and sheeting loads, and pausing dusty work when winds are strong
options.C: Flood the road with water each morning so the surface stays wet all day, because heavy watering is the only measure needed in dry weather
options.D: Raise the boundary hoarding to full height and keep dry sweeping the road each evening, since a screen stops dust and sweeping removes what remains

explanation: Dust is best prevented at source with damping, speed limits and covered loads, with the work adjusted to weather, rather than leaving neighbours to cope.

why_wrong.A: Dust must be controlled at the site, and relying on neighbours' masks is not a control.
why_wrong.C: Heavy watering can cause mud and polluted runoff to drains, and does not address speed or covered loads.
why_wrong.D: Dry sweeping re-suspends fine dust, and a hoarding alone does not control dust at source.

common_mistake: Treating site dust as a minor nuisance to be tolerated or cleaned up afterwards instead of stopped at source.

stem: An inspector serves an Improvement Notice requiring effective dust extraction on a block saw within 28 days. The extraction unit is on back-order and will arrive after the deadline. The manager has not appealed. What should the contractor do?

options.A: Carry on as normal because placing the order shows intent to comply, and the notice is paused automatically while a purchase is outstanding
options.B: Rig a cheap temporary fan and tell nobody, as the notice only demands some visible improvement and not the inspector's agreement to the method
options.C: Wait until the deadline passes and then explain the supplier delay, since an inspector must accept a late delivery as a valid excuse for non-compliance
options.D: Write to the inspector before the date asking for an extension, and fit interim dust controls, because missing it without one risks prosecution

explanation: A compliance period can be extended by the inspector if asked in good time, whereas simply missing the date without an agreed extension is a failure to comply with the notice.

why_wrong.A: A notice is suspended only by an appeal to a tribunal, not by an order being placed with a supplier.
why_wrong.B: The notice requires the specified contravention to be remedied, so an unagreed makeshift measure may not satisfy it and hides the problem from the inspector.
why_wrong.C: A supplier delay is not an automatic defence, and any extension should be requested before the compliance period has run out.

common_mistake: Assuming that ordering the equipment or having a good reason for delay is enough, instead of asking the inspector for more time before the notice period ends.

stem: A method statement for lifting a chiller onto a plant-room roof lists the hazards and PPE, then says only "lift into place" and "call 999 if needed". Which addition would improve it most?

options.A: The company safety policy and general site rules attached in full, so every operative can see the standards that apply across the whole project and its trades
options.B: A step-by-step sequence naming the crane and accessories, plus task-specific emergency arrangements such as who raises the alarm
options.C: Copies of each operative's CSCS card and the crane brochure, since evidence of competence and capacity makes a stated sequence unnecessary
options.D: A line saying the foreman will decide the order of work and the equipment on the day, as he knows the roof and the crew best

explanation: A method statement should set out how the task is done in order, with the plant needed and the emergency arrangements that apply to this particular job.

why_wrong.A: General policy does not describe how this specific lift will be carried out or how an emergency on the roof would be handled.
why_wrong.C: Evidence of competence and capacity supports the plan but does not replace a clear sequence of work and emergency arrangements.
why_wrong.D: The sequence and plant must be planned in advance so that risks are controlled, and cannot be left to be improvised during the lift.

common_mistake: Treating a method statement as a list of hazards and PPE rather than a practical description of the order of work, the plant used and the emergency plan.

stem: In a site joinery workshop, fine sawdust has settled on beams, light fittings and the top of the dust extractor, and a grinder is used nearby. The supervisor plans a Friday clean-up with a brush and a compressed air line. What is the best advice?

options.A: Leave settled dust undisturbed on high surfaces, because it is harmless until timber offcuts catch fire and only visible flames matter
options.B: Sweep daily with a dry brush and keep the doors shut, since sweeping removes the fuel and closed doors stop draughts lifting dust
options.C: Blow it down as planned but with the grinder switched off first, because dust is only a fire risk while a spark is actually present
options.D: Remove it often with an industrial vacuum suited to fine dust, avoid raising clouds, and keep ignition sources away from dust layers

explanation: Settled dust is fuel and a disturbed cloud can ignite or explode, so regular vacuum removal without dispersal controls the risk at source.

why_wrong.A: Dust layers are themselves combustible fuel and are easily disturbed into a cloud by a draught or impact.
why_wrong.B: Dry brushing throws fine dust into the air, and a closed space lets the airborne concentration build up.
why_wrong.C: Blowing creates a suspended cloud and spreads dust onto new surfaces, and hot surfaces and motors can still ignite it.

common_mistake: Thinking fire needs a visible flame source nearby and overlooking that fine settled dust is a fuel that can be thrown into an explosive cloud.

stem: Air monitoring shows a joiner machining hardwood door frames is exposed at about 70 percent of the workplace exposure limit. The manager says that is under the limit, so safe, and removes the extraction hood to speed up the work. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A limit is not a safe line; COSHH needs exposure kept as low as reasonably practicable, so the working extraction must stay.
options.B: The limit is a legal pass mark, so a result of 70 percent leaves a 30 percent margin that can be used up by removing some of the controls.
options.C: The limit applies only to a full eight-hour average, so a short machining task is covered by no exposure standard and needs no controls.
options.D: The result is below the limit, so adequate control is shown and the hood can go, provided the joiner wears a disposable paper mask.

explanation: A workplace exposure limit is a maximum, not a guarantee of safety, and for a substance that can cause cancer or asthma COSHH expects exposure to be reduced as far as is reasonably practicable, which here means keeping the extraction.

why_wrong.B: The margin is not a spare allowance to be spent, because control measures are judged on reducing exposure rather than on staying just inside the figure.
why_wrong.C: Exposure limits are set for specific averaging periods but short tasks still count towards the exposure and the general COSHH duties still apply to them.
why_wrong.D: Being under the limit does not end the duty to reduce exposure, and a paper mask is a weak substitute for a source control that is already working.

common_mistake: Treating a result just under the exposure limit as proof that the work is safe and the controls can be relaxed.

stem: A young labourer says his foreman shouts at him, hides his tools and gives him the worst tasks, and he now dreads work and sleeps badly. Raising it with the foreman is not realistic. What is the most appropriate route?

options.A: Wait until a doctor formally diagnoses a condition, because an employer has no duty to act until illness has been certified
options.B: Ask for a move to another gang and say nothing more, because a transfer solves it without involving management or leaving any paper trail behind
options.C: Take it straight to the HSE, because it investigates individual bullying complaints and can discipline the foreman directly on site
options.D: Report it in writing, with dates, to senior management or HR under the bullying policy so the employer can investigate

explanation: The employer must deal with bullying and work- related stress, and a dated written report to someone above the foreman starts that process and creates a record.

why_wrong.A: Employers must act on the risk of harm from work-related stress and do not need to wait for a diagnosis.
why_wrong.B: Moving away leaves the conduct unaddressed, so others may suffer and the employer is never put on notice to act.
why_wrong.C: HSE does not investigate bullying and harassment, and it expects concerns to have been raised with the employer first.

common_mistake: Assuming that bullying is only a personal matter, or that you must put up with it until it damages your health.

stem: Look at the scene at the pedestrian gate. The gate marshal says the worker crossing is fully compliant with the mandatory signs on display. Which statement best identifies the problem?

options.A: His helmet should be fastened with a chinstrap here, because falling objects from the reversing lorry are the main hazard at the crossing
options.B: He needs eye protection and gloves too, as anyone walking near vehicles and plant must be equipped like a machine operator
options.C: The hood under his helmet blocks hearing and side vision while he crosses a live vehicle route, and it stops the helmet sitting properly
options.D: Nothing is wrong, because he wears each item shown on the mandatory signs and those items give complete protection at a gate

explanation: Clothing that covers the ears and narrows the field of view reduces awareness of reversing vehicles and can stop the helmet fitting correctly, so ticking the sign items is not enough.

why_wrong.A: A reversing lorry is a struck-by hazard and not a falling-object one, and a chinstrap does nothing about his reduced hearing and vision.
why_wrong.B: Eye protection and gloves are not shown on the signs and do not address crossing a vehicle route.
why_wrong.D: Wearing the listed items does not make the combination safe, since his hood defeats the awareness a vehicle crossing demands.

common_mistake: Judging PPE compliance by counting the items on the sign rather than asking whether what he wears leaves him able to see and hear the hazards.

stem: On a hot plant-room refit, an operative dry-sands dusty plaster for seven hours a day despite on-tool extraction. His fit- tested FFP3 mask gets hot and wet, and he keeps pulling it down for air. Which solution is most suitable?

options.A: Move him to a lower-grade FFP2 mask that breathes more easily, because the protection gap between the two grades is small for plaster dust
options.B: Keep the FFP3 but swap it for a fresh one every hour, since a drier mask removes the discomfort without changing the equipment type
options.C: Let him lower the mask whenever the dust looks thin, as visible dust is a reliable guide to when protection is actually needed
options.D: Provide a powered hood respirator with suitable filters, which eases breathing and needs no face-fit test, checked before each shift

explanation: A powered respirator with a loose-fitting hood lowers breathing effort and heat over long tasks and does not need fit testing, though it needs its airflow and battery checked.

why_wrong.A: Choosing a lower grade for comfort cuts protection, and RPE must be selected for the exposure and not for ease of wear.
why_wrong.B: A fresh mask does not fix the heat and breathing effort over seven hours, so he will still be tempted to remove it.
why_wrong.C: The finest and most harmful particles cannot be seen, so the respirator must be worn throughout the exposure.

common_mistake: Choosing respirators by habit or comfort rather than matching the type to the task length, heat and the protection the dust requires.

stem: On a two-storey house extension with a 40-degree pitched roof, a scaffold with guardrails runs along the eaves only. Roofers must fix barge boards along the gable verge. The foreman says the eaves protection covers the whole roof. What is the correct view?

options.A: The verge is a separate fall edge needing its own edge protection, such as a gable scaffold lift, with harnesses only as a fallback
options.B: Harnesses clipped to the ridge are enough for the verge, as collective protection is needed only where roofers work alone on the slope
options.C: Keeping a metre back from the verge in dry weather is enough, since careful, experienced roofers reduce the need for any edge protection at all
options.D: The eaves guardrails count for every edge of the roof, because a person falling at the verge would be stopped by the same top rail

explanation: Edge protection protects only where it is fitted, and collective measures take priority over personal fall protection at every edge from which a person could fall.

why_wrong.B: Collective protection should come before personal protection, which depends on correct use, a sound anchor and a rescue plan.
why_wrong.C: Reliance on behaviour and weather is not a control, and a fall of this height can seriously injure whoever slips.
why_wrong.D: A guardrail protects only the edge it runs along, and the gable verge lies beyond it.

common_mistake: Assuming edge protection at the eaves covers every other edge of a roof, such as verges and gable ends.

stem: A temporary distribution board feeding site tools is screwed to the hoarding at the gate, 300 mm above ground, beside a low spot that floods and the lorry turning area. Its door is wedged open for easy access. Which correction is most suitable?

options.A: Move it to a raised, lockable weatherproof enclosure clear of flooding and vehicles, with cables protected where they cross routes
options.B: Put it in an unlocked indoor-rated cabinet beside the gate, since a roof overhead gives enough protection from weather and damage
options.C: Leave it in position but cover it with a plastic sheet at night, because the sheet keeps rain off while access stays quick for everyone
options.D: Keep the position but add bollards and a higher-rated RCD, since impact protection and tripping devices make a damp low site acceptable

explanation: Distribution equipment must be kept dry, out of the way of vehicle damage and secure against unauthorised access, with cables protected along their route.

why_wrong.B: An indoor-rated enclosure is not designed for outdoor exposure and an unlocked cabinet still allows unauthorised access.
why_wrong.C: A sheet does not stop flooding or vehicle impact and leaves live parts open to anyone who walks up to the board.
why_wrong.D: Bollards and RCDs do not stop water entering a board standing in a flood-prone spot, and devices do not replace a suitable position.

common_mistake: Treating a temporary board as low-risk because it is temporary, and siting it wherever is convenient rather than where it stays dry, protected and locked.

stem: Four people are named on a lift plan for placing a plant unit by mobile crane: appointed person, crane supervisor, slinger and operator. Which description of their roles is correct?

options.A: The appointed person attaches the load and signals, while the slinger plans the lift and selects the accessories that the crew will use
options.B: The supervisor plans the lift and then leaves, the appointed person works the crane controls, and the slinger decides when to stop for safety
options.C: The operator is in overall charge and plans the lift from the capacity chart, the supervisor is the site manager, and the slinger only hooks on the load as told
options.D: The appointed person plans the lift and picks the equipment, the supervisor checks it follows the plan and can stop it, and the slinger attaches the load

explanation: The appointed person plans and organises the lift, the crane supervisor oversees that it is carried out to plan with authority to stop it, and the slinger attaches the load and signals.

why_wrong.A: These duties are reversed, as planning and selecting equipment belong to the appointed person and attaching the load belongs to the slinger.
why_wrong.B: Planning is the appointed person's job, the supervisor must stay to oversee the lift, and the trained operator, not the appointed person, controls the crane.
why_wrong.C: The operator controls the crane within the plan but does not own planning, and supervision must be by a trained person appointed for the lift.

common_mistake: Believing the crane operator or the person nearest the load is responsible for the whole lift, instead of a clear split between planning, supervising, slinging and operating PRACTICE TEST 9

stem: A principal contractor locks the welfare cabin and takes the site rules off the gate on Saturdays, saying none of its own staff work then. A subcontracted electrician works alone one Saturday with its agreement. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Site rules matter only when several trades overlap, so a lone worker needs just a portable toilet and a mobile phone for emergencies
options.B: Welfare must be available throughout the construction phase to everyone working there, and the electrician must still follow the site rules
options.C: The electrician's own employer must arrange toilets and washing, because the contractor's duty covers only its own staff on its planned working days
options.D: A lone worker needs no welfare provision for one day, because facilities become mandatory only once a minimum headcount is on site

explanation: The principal contractor must provide suitable welfare facilities for the whole construction phase and keep site rules in force, so a lone subcontractor on a quiet day is covered by both.

why_wrong.A: Site rules are part of controlling risk throughout the project and apply to every worker, however few are present.
why_wrong.C: The principal contractor's welfare duty extends to all workers on the site, not just its own people or its normal days.
why_wrong.D: The duty to provide facilities does not depend on a headcount threshold being reached on a particular day.

common_mistake: Assuming welfare and site rules only matter on days when the main workforce is present.

stem: Four agency labourers with little English join a site on Monday. The agency says its generic assessment covers them, and the site supervisor plans to hand out the English risk assessment and have one fluent crew member interpret. Which approach best meets the duties?

options.A: Relying on the fluent crew member is fine, as informal interpreting by a colleague is the quickest way to cover every hazard on site
options.B: The agency's assessment is enough, as the agency is the employer and the site only needs to provide the paperwork if anyone asks for it
options.C: Pass on site risks and controls in a form the workers understand, such as translation or a trained interpreter, and check understanding
options.D: Handing over the English document is sufficient, since the workers accept responsibility once they have been given it and have signed for it

explanation: Information on risks and control measures must be comprehensible, and the site where they work knows its own hazards, so understanding must be confirmed rather than assumed.

why_wrong.A: An untrained colleague may omit or misstate risks and nobody checks the other workers understood the controls.
why_wrong.B: A generic assessment cannot cover site-specific hazards, and the site controlling the work must supply that information.
why_wrong.D: Information must be comprehensible to the people receiving it, and a signature does not show it was understood.

common_mistake: Believing that giving someone a document, or an agency's generic paperwork, shows they have been properly informed about site risks.

stem: While stripping plaster in a ground-floor flat, a joiner smells gas strongly. Two colleagues are working upstairs and the lights are off. He is about to switch them on to look for the cause. What is the correct action?

options.A: Turn the lights on to find the source, then tighten any visible joints before the smell spreads, because the fault is probably small
options.B: Avoid switches and flames, open doors and windows on the way out, evacuate everyone and report the leak from outside
options.C: Switch off the power at the consumer unit to remove ignition sources, then continue working in the other rooms while the gas disperses
options.D: Wait for the site plumber to arrive and check it, as the workers are better placed to judge whether the leak is serious enough

explanation: Any switch can spark and ignite a gas build-up, so ignition sources are avoided, ventilation is helped, people are evacuated and the leak is reported from a safe place.

why_wrong.A: Operating a switch may ignite the gas, and untrained repairs inside a gas-filled space add to the danger.
why_wrong.C: Operating the consumer unit can itself spark, and staying inside leaves workers exposed to an explosion.
why_wrong.D: Nobody should stay in the building to investigate, and a plumber is not the emergency service for a suspected leak.

common_mistake: Assuming that switching off electrics or investigating the source yourself is safer than getting out first.

stem: In a site cabin, wet jackets are draped over an electric heater to dry. A four-way adaptor in an extension lead feeds the kettle, microwave and a second heater, and the plug is warm. Which action best controls the fire risk?

options.A: Keep the jackets on the heater but fit a plug-in timer to cut the power, because heat for a limited time cannot ignite fabric
options.B: Place a fire extinguisher by the door and a smoke alarm in the cabin, since detection means the existing set-up is acceptable
options.C: Replace the warm plug and extension lead with a heavier lead, then keep the same appliances running through the adaptor
options.D: Provide a ventilated drying area away from heaters, and spread the loads over separate sockets so no adaptor is overloaded

explanation: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen, so keeping clothing off heaters and keeping circuits within their rating removes both the fuel near the heat and the overheating cable.

why_wrong.A: A timer does not stop fabric on a heater igniting, and it leaves the overloaded adaptor untouched.
why_wrong.B: Alarms and extinguishers are response measures and do nothing to prevent the overheating that starts the fire.
