why_wrong.A: Clearing the building protects others but leaves the person applying the stripper exposed.
why_wrong.C: Reducing duration and diluting vapour are lower in the hierarchy and do not replace consideration of a safer product.
why_wrong.D: PPE is the last line of defence, and a change of finish does not justify skipping substitution.

common_mistake: Starting the control search at the mask or the window instead of asking whether the hazardous product is needed at all.

stem: A flatbed arrives with packs of roof tiles stacked 2 m high. The driver plans to climb the stack to release the top straps, as he has on every site. Which approach best follows the working at height hierarchy?

options.A: Avoid going on the load using ground-based methods or a fixed gantry with edge protection, with other protection only if avoidance is impossible
options.B: Let him climb but require a hard hat and gloves, since he is experienced and 2 m is below the height at which fall controls are needed on a lorry
options.C: Have a labourer hold the corner of the stack while he climbs, as a second person on the ground counts as proper fall protection
options.D: Let him climb using a stepladder set on the lorry bed, because a ladder provides a safe route to work on top of the stacked load of tiles

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations require work at height to be avoided where reasonably practicable, then collective protection such as a gantry, with personal protection used last.

why_wrong.B: There is no minimum height for work at height, and PPE of this kind does not stop a fall.
why_wrong.C: A person holding a stack cannot arrest a fall and is exposed to the load if it moves.
why_wrong.D: A ladder on a vehicle bed is unstable, and it does not avoid the climb or provide edge protection.

common_mistake: Judging a low height or an experienced worker as justification for skipping a safer way of doing the job.

stem: Look at the scene. The operative says his harness is clipped on, the MEWP is on firm level ground and he only needs a few more centimetres of reach. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The basket is set too near the roof deck, so a second worker should hold the bucket steady for him as he reaches
options.B: Standing on the bucket lifts his body above the guardrail, so a lean or slip could throw him out of the basket
options.C: His lanyard should be anchored to the ceiling pipework above him instead of the basket, so that it holds him closer to the work
options.D: The bucket has no slip-resistant top, so a rubber-topped step would make standing on it acceptable in the basket

explanation: The guardrail only protects a person standing on the basket floor, and an improvised step raises the body above it and makes overbalancing and ejection more likely.

why_wrong.A: A colleague cannot make an unsafe standing position safe; the platform should be repositioned instead.
why_wrong.C: The lanyard must be attached to the basket's designated anchor point, never to structure or services.
why_wrong.D: No improvised raising of the standing position is acceptable, whatever its grip.

common_mistake: Adding height with a bucket or box inside a platform to gain reach instead of repositioning the machine.

stem: In a house, an electrician switches off the socket circuit's breaker, plugs a socket tester into another socket on it, sees no lights, and starts replacing a socket. What is wrong with this practice?

options.A: The tester is acceptable, but a non-contact voltage detector held against the cable should be added as stronger evidence of isolation
options.B: Nothing is wrong, because a tester showing no lights proves the circuit is dead and lock-off is needed only on industrial installations
options.C: A plug-in tester does not prove dead; he should lock off, then test with an approved voltage indicator proved on a known source before and after
options.D: He should have switched off the whole installation at the main switch, as isolating a single breaker cannot make a socket circuit safe

explanation: Safe isolation needs the supply locked off and the circuit proved dead with an approved two-pole voltage indicator, checked on a known live source before and after use.

why_wrong.A: A non-contact detector is not a reliable way to prove a circuit dead and is not an approved proving device.
why_wrong.B: A plug-in tester gives no reliable proof of dead, and lock-off applies to domestic circuits too.
why_wrong.D: Isolating the circuit correctly, locked off and proved dead, is a valid method.

common_mistake: Trusting a quick plug-in tester or a switched-off breaker as proof that a circuit is dead.

stem: A contractor wants to crane a 4-tonne mini excavator onto a first-floor suspended slab to break out a screed. The slab is cured and looks sound. What must be established before the machine goes on it?

options.A: That the machine runs on rubber tracks, which spread its weight enough that no check of the slab structure is then needed at all
options.B: That the concrete is over 28 days old, because slabs reach full design capacity then, whatever the load placed on them
options.C: That the machine's weight is below the crane's rated capacity, since a satisfactory crane check also proves the slab can bear it afterwards
options.D: The slab's permitted loading, including track point loads, confirmed by a competent person such as the structural designer

explanation: A suspended slab has a limited design capacity, so a competent person must confirm it can carry the machine, its point loads and other loads on that floor.

why_wrong.A: Rubber tracks lower ground pressure but the total and point loads still need checking against the slab design.
why_wrong.B: Age shows strength gain but does not confirm the slab was designed for this machine's loading.
why_wrong.C: The crane's rating relates to the lift and says nothing about what the slab can carry afterwards.

common_mistake: Judging a floor by how solid it looks instead of checking what the structure was designed to carry.

stem: A groundworks subcontractor sends an 18-year-old, in his second week, to lay kerbs on a principal contractor's site. His gangleader spends the day on another plot, and the site manager says the principal contractor will keep an eye on him. Who must provide the supervision, and how much?

options.A: The principal contractor, because it controls the site, so the subcontractor's own duty to supervise ends once the young worker has attended the site induction
options.B: Nobody specifically, because at 18 he is legally an adult and a signed training record shows he can work without close checking
options.C: The subcontractor, as his employer, must arrange competent supervision matched to his inexperience and the risk, frequent enough to check and correct his work
options.D: The subcontractor, but a weekly visit from the gangleader meets the duty provided he has been given written instructions for each task

explanation: Employers must provide information, instruction, training and supervision for their own employees, and the level rises with inexperience and risk, so the principal contractor's general oversight cannot replace it.

why_wrong.A: A site induction does not transfer the employer's own supervision duty to the principal contractor.
why_wrong.B: Being an adult and holding a training record do not remove the need for supervision matched to inexperience.
why_wrong.D: Written instructions and an occasional visit are not supervision proportionate to a new starter doing risky work.

common_mistake: Assuming the principal contractor's presence on site means a subcontractor no longer has to supervise its own inexperienced workers.

stem: Operatives remediating contaminated made ground rinse their hands under a bowser tap without soap, then eat sandwiches at their break. At day's end they drive home in the same muddy overalls and wash them with the family laundry. Which arrangement best controls the exposure?

options.A: Use alcohol wipes before eating, then wear the overalls home once they have been brushed down, because dried mud carries very little contamination
options.B: Keep rinsing under the tap before breaks and wash the overalls at home on a hot cycle, since heat destroys the contaminants in them
options.C: Wear disposable gloves during the break and fasten the overalls tightly for the drive home, since covering skin matters more than removing soiled clothing
options.D: Wash hands and face with soap before eating, and change out of the contaminated overalls on site, with the employer arranging for them to be cleaned

explanation: Washing before eating stops contaminants being swallowed, and leaving soiled work clothing on site, cleaned by the employer, stops it carrying contamination into vehicles and homes.

why_wrong.A: Wipes do not remove contamination like soap and water, and brushing leaves residues and releases dust.
why_wrong.B: Hot washing does not destroy many contaminants and spreads them through the household machine and laundry.
why_wrong.C: Gloves worn at a meal become contaminated themselves, and soiled clothing still transfers contamination to the car and home.

common_mistake: Treating a quick rinse and taking dirty work clothes home as normal practice when the ground is contaminated.

stem: A two-day fencing job in open farmland is a 25-minute drive from the nearest public toilet. The contractor plans to ask the farmer if the crew can use the farmhouse bathroom, and to bring bottled water for hands. The farmer is often out. Which approach best meets the welfare duty?

options.A: Supply hand gel and a spade for the two days, since the full welfare duty applies to sites that last longer than a week
options.B: Rely on the farmer's verbal permission, because an agreement to use the house counts as provision even when nobody is home to open it up
options.C: Provide welfare before starting, such as a mobile unit, with a toilet, soap, clean water and towels that the crew can reach quickly
options.D: Let workers drive to the town toilets when needed, because travel time to a public facility is accepted as reasonable access on remote jobs

explanation: Workers in remote locations still need toilets and washing facilities within easy reach, and a short job or a hoped- for favour does not remove that duty.

why_wrong.A: Welfare duties apply to any construction site regardless of how short the job is, and gel does not replace washing facilities.
why_wrong.B: Facilities that may be locked or unavailable are not reliably accessible when the crew needs them.
why_wrong.D: A 25-minute drive each way is not reasonable access and wastes working time.

common_mistake: Assuming a very short or remote job does not need proper toilets and washing provided for the crew.

stem: Look at the operative drilling anchor holes into a concrete soffit. The supervisor says he is wearing the PPE the task assessment requires. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The dust extraction fitted to the drill is unnecessary, because a respirator is the correct way to control dust from drilling concrete
options.B: His safety glasses are pushed up on his forehead, so they give no protection from falling dust and chips where the drilling creates the risk
options.C: His helmet-mounted ear defenders cannot give adequate protection from hammer-drill noise, so earplugs must replace them for any overhead drilling
options.D: His work gloves reduce grip on the drill handle, so hammer drilling should be done bare-handed to keep full control of the tool

explanation: PPE only protects when worn correctly at the point of risk, and eye protection resting on the forehead gives no protection against debris falling from an overhead drilling task.

why_wrong.A: Capturing dust at source is preferred, and a respirator does not replace extraction.
why_wrong.C: Properly worn and suitably rated defenders can control hammer-drill noise, and this is not the failing shown.
why_wrong.D: Gloves are normally worn on hammer drills to protect against vibration, cold and abrasion, and they are not the main problem here.

common_mistake: Counting PPE as being in place because it is on the worker somewhere, rather than being worn properly over the part of the body at risk.

stem: Before a roof-edge job, a roofer takes a harness that fitted a taller colleague. The dorsal D-ring sits at the nape of his neck and the leg straps hang loose, though the webbing is undamaged. He says he will clip on and sort the straps later. What should happen?

options.A: Tighten only the leg straps and ignore the ring position, since the lanyard's energy absorber takes the strain wherever it is attached
options.B: Leave the ring high, as that keeps the lanyard clear of the legs, and tighten the leg straps once he has reached the roof edge
options.C: Use it as it is, because the chest strap carries the load in a fall and loose leg straps only affect comfort rather than safety, or injury
options.D: Adjust it on the ground so the D-ring sits between the shoulder blades and the leg straps are snug, with a colleague checking it

explanation: A harness only works in a fall if it is adjusted to the wearer, with the ring centred high on the back and snug leg straps, and a buddy check confirms this before exposure.

why_wrong.A: The energy absorber does not compensate for a poor ring position, which can leave the wearer hanging badly or head-down.
why_wrong.B: Adjustment must be completed before going near the edge, and ring position affects body position after a fall.
why_wrong.C: Loose leg straps can let the wearer slip or be injured in a fall, and a poorly placed ring changes how the body hangs.

common_mistake: Assuming an undamaged harness is ready to wear straight from the van, without adjusting it to fit the wearer first.

stem: On the fifth floor of a concrete frame, a plasterer will work beside an unprotected lift-shaft door opening. The planner proposes orange mesh fencing on freestanding feet plus a sign, saying only lift installers will need the gap. Which control is required before plastering starts?

options.A: Let the plasterer work if he wears a harness clipped to a mobile anchor, with the barrier deferred until the lift installers arrive
options.B: Post a colleague to watch the opening during plastering, because a lookout can warn the plasterer before he gets too close to the edge
options.C: Keep the freestanding mesh and add a taped line two metres back, since keeping distance from the opening is as good as a fixed guardrail does
options.D: Fit a rigid barrier fixed to the structure, with top rail, intermediate rail and toe board, able to take a falling person

explanation: Openings need robust, fixed collective protection that can resist a person's weight, which freestanding mesh and signs cannot do.

why_wrong.A: Personal protection with a mobile anchor is lower in the hierarchy than a fixed barrier and leaves others exposed to the opening.
why_wrong.B: A lookout is an administrative control that fails when attention lapses and does not physically stop a fall.
why_wrong.C: Tape and distance only warn, and a person stumbling or pushing a trolley can still reach the opening.

common_mistake: Believing a sign, tape or freestanding mesh counts as edge protection simply because it is visible.

stem: A re-roofing firm builds a temporary weather roof of beams and corrugated sheeting, carried on tube supports, over a terrace. The foreman wants to stack pallets of new tiles on the beams to save hoisting, saying the frame looks sturdy. What is the correct decision?

options.A: Sheet over the stacks to guard against wind uplift so the tiles can stay on the roof overnight, with the frame checked each morning
options.B: Limit stacks to two pallets high, since the frame was checked as sound by the erector and a visual look suffices for such modest loads
options.C: Stack nothing there unless the designer has set an allowable storage load, otherwise keep tiles on the ground or a purpose-designed platform
options.D: Spread the pallets evenly across the beams above the supports, because even spreading keeps the total load within what any frame can carry safely

explanation: A temporary roof is designed for particular loads such as wind and self-weight, so added stored materials need the designer's agreement or the structure may be overloaded and collapse.

why_wrong.A: Covering the stacks adds wind load and does not address the overloading of the structure.
why_wrong.B: A visual check of soundness gives no figure for capacity, and stacking limits chosen by eye are guesswork.
why_wrong.D: Even spreading does not make an undesigned load safe, since the structure's capacity is not known.

common_mistake: Judging a temporary structure's strength by how sturdy it looks instead of by what it was designed to carry.

stem: An operator compacts hardcore in a narrow yard with a walk- behind vibrating roller. His planned passes finish with the roller reversing towards a brick wall while he walks behind it, and he says the operator-presence handle will stop it. What is the best response?

options.A: Keep the plan but reverse slowly, because the operator- presence control stops the machine and removes any chance of being trapped against the wall
options.B: Station a banksman at the wall to shout when the roller is within a metre, as an operator walking behind cannot judge the gap himself
options.C: Re-plan the passes so he never reverses towards the wall or another fixed object, and keep the operator-presence control as a back-up only
options.D: Let him walk beside the roller on the final reverse pass, steering it with one hand while keeping clear of the gap to the wall

explanation: A safe system of work avoids the crush risk by design, and a protective control is a back-up that must not be relied on as the only safeguard.

why_wrong.A: Relying on one control alone is unsafe, since it may fail or be defeated and leaves the crush risk in place.
why_wrong.B: A shouted warning relies on a person reacting in time and leaves the crush risk in place.
why_wrong.D: Steering at arm's length from beside the machine is not a planned method and still leaves him close to the crush point.

common_mistake: Trusting a machine's safety device to protect an operator whose planned working method already places him in a crush zone.

stem: A forklift has a slab-clamp fitted. The truck's original plate shows 3,000 kg, the clamp is marked 2,000 kg, and a newer plate for the truck with the clamp shows 1,800 kg. The driver wants to carry 1,900 kg of paving slabs, below the first two figures. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The plate for the truck with the clamp fitted governs, so 1,900 kg is too heavy and the slabs must be carried in smaller loads
options.B: Any of the three figures may be used if the driver keeps the mast tilted back and the clamp low, because careful driving offsets the extra weight
options.C: The original 3,000 kg plate governs, because it is the manufacturer's figure for the truck, and the later plate is only advisory guidance
options.D: The clamp's own marking governs, since attachments are rated separately, so 1,900 kg is acceptable when it stays under the 2,000 kg stamped on the clamp

explanation: Fitting an attachment derates the truck, and HSE guidance says a plate relating to the attachment must be applied, so the combined figure is the one that limits the load.

why_wrong.B: Careful driving does not change the rated capacity, and the lowest applicable plated figure must not be exceeded.
why_wrong.C: The original figure applies to the truck as plated with forks, not with a heavy attachment fitted in front.
why_wrong.D: The clamp's rating does not allow for the reduced stability of the truck with it fitted.

common_mistake: Picking whichever rating on the truck or attachment is highest or most convenient instead of the one for the combination actually in use.

stem: Groundworks 20 m from a pond holding great crested newts are covered by a licence method statement requiring an exclusion fence. A dumper flattens 6 m of fence, and an open pipe trench is left overnight beside the gap. What is the best response?

options.A: Cover the trench each evening and continue working, because the licence applies only when a newt has actually been seen on site
options.B: Repair the fence at the start of next shift and continue, since newts are active at night and the gap was not open while work was under way
options.C: Carry on and ask the dumper driver to watch for newts as he works, because a sighting would then trigger a stop under the method statement
options.D: Stop work in the affected area, have the ecologist check and reinstate the fence, and fit ramps or covers to the trench first

explanation: Newts may already be inside the working area or trapped in the trench, so work stops until the licensed ecologist checks and the barrier and trench are made safe for wildlife.

why_wrong.A: The licence conditions apply to the whole works area, whether or not an animal has been seen.
why_wrong.B: Newts may already be inside the area, and continuing without a check risks killing or injuring them.
why_wrong.C: Spotting animals by chance is not a control, and the damaged fence must be dealt with first.

common_mistake: Treating wildlife protection measures as paperwork that only matters once an animal has actually been seen.

stem: A manager's weekly audit sheets show every control ticked as in place for eight weeks, yet an inspector finds a gang working beside an unprotected edge. The sheets are filled in at the cabin desk, copied from the week before. What should change?

options.A: Ask the safety adviser to audit once a year and report, since frequent checking on site only duplicates what the RAMS already covers
options.B: Add more tick-box items to the sheet and make every supervisor sign each page each week, so that responsibility for the answers is much clearer
options.C: Rely on the accident book, because a low injury count over eight weeks shows the controls in the RAMS are doing their job
options.D: Have competent people watch real work, compare it with the RAMS on the ground, record what they see and fix gaps before anyone is hurt

explanation: Active monitoring means observing whether controls actually work in practice, so failures are found and corrected before they cause harm, rather than assuming the paperwork reflects reality.

why_wrong.A: An annual audit is too infrequent to catch changing site conditions, and the RAMS describes intended controls and does not prove they are used.
why_wrong.B: More boxes and signatures still record opinion from the cabin and do not test whether controls work at the work face.
why_wrong.C: Injury figures are a lagging indicator, and an absence of injuries can hide controls that are failing and have simply not yet caused harm.

common_mistake: Believing that a completed checklist proves a control is working, when only watching the work itself shows whether it is.

stem: A plumber starts cutting into old pipework in an occupied flat while electricians test circuits nearby. Nobody has checked where the stopcock, gas valve or consumer unit is, and the stopcock is thought to be under stored furniture. What should have been done before work began?

options.A: Find and test each isolation point, keep access to it clear, and tell everyone on the job where it is and who may operate it
options.B: Nominate one person to know the locations and keep others away from the valves, so nobody operates the wrong one by mistake
options.C: Leave the occupier to know where the valves are, since they live in the flat and will be there if anything goes wrong
options.D: Rely on the utility's emergency line, as the supplier can cut the water, gas or power remotely faster than anyone can find a valve

explanation: Emergency shut-offs only help if they are known, reachable and proven to work before the job starts, since searching for them during a burst or gas leak wastes critical time.

why_wrong.B: If that one person is absent or cut off, nobody else can act, so everyone working must know where the isolation points are.
why_wrong.C: The contractor must plan the emergency arrangements, and an occupier may not be present, may not know, or may not be able to reach the valves.
why_wrong.D: Emergency lines cannot isolate an individual property instantly, and a burst or leak needs shutting off within seconds by people on site.

common_mistake: Assuming someone else, such as the occupier or the utility, will know how to shut things off in an emergency.

stem: Two fitters must swap a 30 kg pump motor in a plant room with 1.4 m headroom and pipework across the route. The job needs pulling it across the floor, bending under pipes and twisting to a bench. The supervisor offers a short lifting-technique refresher. What is the best response?

options.A: Assess the task, load, individuals and environment, then remove the awkward postures with a small hoist or skates and a cleared route
options.B: Let the stronger fitter do the pulling and twisting while the other guides, since a fit individual can tolerate cramped postures without harm
options.C: Issue back-support belts to both fitters, which let them hold awkward postures safely while the motor is dragged and turned into place
options.D: Give the refresher and add a third person to steady the motor, because good technique cancels out the strain of the cramped posture

explanation: The manual handling assessment should avoid or reduce the hazardous movements, and in cramped spaces the environment is the main driver, so changing the task beats relying on technique.

why_wrong.B: Individual strength does not remove the strain from awkward postures, and putting more risk onto one person only concentrates the harm.
why_wrong.C: There is no good evidence that belts make awkward handling safe, and they do nothing to remove the hazardous movements.
why_wrong.D: Technique and extra hands do not remove the pulling, stooping and twisting that the cramped environment forces on the body.

common_mistake: Thinking that training in lifting technique is enough when the real problem is a cramped space and an awkward task.

stem: A crew ties reinforcement mats all day. After lunch their output and attention fall, two have wrist pain, and one nearly stepped into a gap. The foreman proposes a piece-rate bonus to keep them going. Which approach best addresses both the wrist symptoms and the attention lapses?

options.A: Move only the two with wrist pain to lighter duties and treat the lapses in the others as a matter of personal discipline and attitude
options.B: Pay the piece-rate bonus so a faster pace keeps interest high, and give the two with sore wrists elastic wrist supports to wear
options.C: Allow earphones and music so boredom is relieved, as a stimulated mind will keep concentrating through a long repetitive task
options.D: Rotate people between tasks with different movements and mental demands, plan regular breaks and ask the crew about any symptoms

explanation: Varying the work and building in rest reduces repetitive strain and the fatigue and monotony that cause lapses, and asking about symptoms allows early action.

why_wrong.A: Moving the symptomatic workers leaves the cause in place for the rest, and lapses from fatigue are a work-design problem and not a discipline issue.
why_wrong.B: A bonus pushes pace and repetition up, which raises the strain and the chance of mistakes, and supports do not remove the repetitive movement.
why_wrong.C: Earphones mask warnings from plant and colleagues and do nothing for the physical strain on the wrists.

common_mistake: Treating tiredness and lapses on repetitive work as a motivation problem rather than a problem with how the work is organised.

stem: Scaffolders plan to hang a working platform from steel beams across a stairwell void, copying a layout from a guide for standard freestanding scaffolds. The decorators want it tomorrow. Which requirement applies to this scaffold?

options.A: The guide layout is enough provided the tube and fitting quantities match and a trained scaffolder erects it, with no separate design needed
options.B: A competent person must produce a specific design and plan, including whether the beams can carry the load, and it must be inspected before first use
options.C: The building owner's verbal agreement that the beams are sound is enough, with any design check made once the platform is up and in use
options.D: Design is needed only if the load exceeds general-purpose loading, and the first inspection can then wait until seven days after use begins

explanation: A hung scaffold is outside standard configurations, so it needs bespoke design and a plan, and a competent person must inspect it after erection and before it is used.

why_wrong.A: A guide for freestanding scaffolds does not cover a platform hung from the structure, so a specific design is needed.
why_wrong.C: The supporting structure must be checked by a competent person as part of the design before the scaffold is used, not after.
why_wrong.D: A non-standard scaffold needs design whatever the load, and inspection is required after erection and before first use.

common_mistake: Assuming a scaffold can be built from a standard guide when it hangs from the structure instead of standing on the ground.

stem: A roofing gang is about to continue sheeting the roof shown. Looking at the picture, which problem most needs correcting before anyone works further along the roof?

options.A: The eaves guardrail is too low and needs a second top rail fitted, because the roofers could otherwise tip over it when they lean out for sheets
options.B: The newest sheets at the working edge are unfixed and nothing protects the gap beyond them, so a slip or tilting sheet could drop someone
options.C: A strapped bundle of sheets rests on the purlins, and any load placed on the structure before the sheets are fixed is unacceptable here
options.D: The roofers have no harness lanyards clipped to the eaves guardrail, which is a legal requirement whenever anyone is working on a roof

explanation: The progressing leading edge needs collective protection, such as nets or edge protection, and sheets must be fixed as laid so the working edge cannot give way or leave an open fall.

why_wrong.A: The eaves protection in the picture is continuous and at a suitable height, so it is not where the fall risk lies.
why_wrong.C: A secured bundle supported on purlins is normal practice and is not the main fall hazard shown.
why_wrong.D: A guardrail is not an anchor point, and a harness is a lesser measure than collective protection at the leading edge.

common_mistake: Judging roof edge safety by the completed eaves protection and overlooking the moving leading edge where the work is actually taking place.

stem: In a 3 m deep basement excavation a submersible pump stops and water starts to rise. A labourer standing in shallow water reaches for the pump's electrical cable to pull it up and check the intake. What is the correct action?

options.A: Keep the supply on so the pump restarts when it cools, and station one worker beside the sump to watch the water level
options.B: Switch off at the pump's own switch, then lift by the cable, as the pump is then dead and the rope is only meant for lowering it
options.C: Get everyone clear of the rising water, isolate the supply at source, then lift the pump by its handle or rope and not its cable
options.D: Pull it up by the cable quickly, since the RCD on the supply will cut the power if anything is wrong and delay lets the basement flood

explanation: Standing in water with a live supply risks shock, and pulling on the cable can damage it, while a rising level in a deep basement also needs people to leave and be accounted for.

why_wrong.A: Leaving the supply live and a worker in rising water exposes him to both shock and drowning while the fault stays unfixed.
why_wrong.B: A local switch does not prove isolation at source, and the cable is not designed to carry the pump's weight.
why_wrong.D: An RCD is a secondary protection and not a licence to handle live equipment in water, and pulling the cable can expose conductors.

common_mistake: Trusting an RCD or the pump's own switch enough to handle electrical equipment while standing in water.

stem: On a wet plot, a generator-fed saw runs through a 30 mA RCD adaptor, which the electrician tested with its button once on Monday. On Wednesday it trips every time the saw starts, and the operator wants to plug straight into the generator's unprotected socket. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Stop using that saw, treat the tripping as a fault for a competent person to find, and press the RCD test button before every future use
options.B: Use the unprotected socket for this cut only, as Monday's test showed the RCD works and the tripping is just nuisance from start-up surge
options.C: Swap to a 100 mA RCD that ignores the start-up surge, because it still protects people from shock while giving fewer unwanted trips
options.D: Reset it after the saw cools and test the RCD weekly, since the periodic combined test already covers the day-to-day checks

explanation: An RCD that trips is a warning of a fault, it must never be bypassed, and the test button should be used before each use rather than once a week.

why_wrong.B: A trip is a sign of a fault, a test earlier in the week proves nothing about today, and bypassing the RCD removes the protection.
why_wrong.C: Higher-rated RCDs protect against fire and do not protect people from shock, and the underlying fault would remain.
why_wrong.D: Repeatedly resetting hides a fault, and the user test button check is needed before each use as well as periodic testing.

common_mistake: Treating a tripping RCD as a nuisance to be bypassed or swapped and not as a sign of a real electrical fault.

stem: A topsoil stockpile stands 15 m from a surface-water gully on a sloping site. In dry weather it blows dust, and heavy rain is forecast. The drainage plan shows a silt trap downstream, and the foreman says the trap alone will cope. Which action best follows the plan?

options.A: Hose the heap before the rain to bind the surface, since wetted soil cannot wash away and the dust is controlled at the same time
options.B: Keep the heap small and sited away from drains, cover it or bund it, put a silt barrier below it, and check controls after rain
options.C: Leave the heap as it is and empty the trap after the rain, because silt reaching the gully is acceptable where a trap is shown
options.D: Pile sandbags round the gully cover only, so no water enters the drain and the heap can stay in its current position

explanation: Controlling silt and dust at source with a smaller, covered, bunded stockpile and a barrier stops pollution reaching the drain, with checks keeping the measures working.

why_wrong.A: Wetting does nothing to stop rainfall washing soil away and can add to run-off, so it is not a substitute for covering or bunding.
why_wrong.C: Silt must be kept out of drains and watercourses, and a trap is a last line of defence that can be overwhelmed in heavy rain.
why_wrong.D: Blocking the gully risks flooding and sends silty water elsewhere, and it does nothing to control the soil at its source.

common_mistake: Relying on a silt trap at the end of the drain instead of stopping soil from leaving the stockpile in the first place.

stem: A site labels separate skips for timber, metal and clean rubble to support recycling. A subcontractor throws conduit and cable offcuts into the timber skip, saying it all goes to the same tip anyway. Which statement best explains why this matters?

options.A: The subcontractor alone is liable here, since the site's duty ends once the skips are labelled and the crews have been told
options.B: Only the transfer note changes, as different waste types can share a skip if the note lists every type that has been placed in it
options.C: A contaminated load is usually downgraded to mixed waste, losing recycling value and raising cost, so labels need briefing and checking at the skip
options.D: It does not matter because carriers sort every load at the tip, so skip labels are only a courtesy and the paperwork is unaffected

explanation: Segregation at source keeps materials recyclable, in line with the waste hierarchy, and only briefing and checking where waste is deposited keeps the streams clean.

why_wrong.A: The site must manage its waste and cannot discharge that duty by labelling alone, so checking and supervision still apply.
why_wrong.B: Listing the types on the note does not restore the recyclability of the load, and segregating at source is preferred by the waste hierarchy.
why_wrong.D: Carriers and receiving sites do not routinely resort contaminated loads, and the labels exist to keep streams recyclable.

common_mistake: Assuming it makes no difference where waste goes because it all ends up at the same disposal site.

stem: A subcontract electrician's foreman tells the principal contractor that a temporary distribution board in its control has a cracked, open enclosure. The principal contractor replies that it runs the site, so work will continue. Which statement about responsibility is most accurate?

options.A: The subcontractor becomes liable if its workers are hurt, since a concern raised out loud is a request and does not create a duty until someone is injured
options.B: Only the principal contractor is liable, because CDM 2015 gives it control of the site, so the subcontractor's duty ends once the concern has been reported verbally
options.C: Both hold duties, the principal contractor for the board and the subcontractor for its own team, so the foreman should keep them clear and escalate in writing
options.D: The foreman may isolate the whole site supply himself, because reporting a concern gives him authority to stop the other trades' work at once

explanation: A principal contractor's coordinating role does not remove the subcontractor's own duty under CDM 2015 regulation 15 to plan, manage and monitor its work, so each is answerable for its part.

why_wrong.A: Duties arise from the risk and exist before harm occurs, so waiting for an injury is a breach already.
why_wrong.B: A subcontractor keeps its own legal duties to its workers and cannot hand them to the principal contractor by reporting a concern.
why_wrong.D: Raising a concern does not give one subcontractor authority over other trades or the site supply, and an uncontrolled shutdown can create new hazards.

common_mistake: Assuming that because the principal contractor controls the site, a subcontractor's own legal duty to its workers is somebody else's problem.

stem: A contractor planning a cheaper method for work covered by an Approved Code of Practice says ACoPs and HSE guidance are only advice, so ignoring them carries no legal risk. After an injury he is prosecuted. How will the ACoP be treated?

options.A: It has the same standing as ordinary HSE guidance, which a court may set aside where a competent person judged the cheaper method adequate
options.B: Having not followed its relevant provisions, he must prove he complied with the law in another equally effective way, or the court will find him at fault
options.C: It carries no weight in court because only the Act and its regulations count, so the prosecution cannot refer to the code when trying to prove a breach against him
options.D: It is treated as the law itself, so any departure from its wording is an automatic offence, however effective his alternative measures were

explanation: An ACoP has a special legal status: failure to follow it is not an offence in itself, but in a prosecution the burden falls on the defendant to prove compliance by other means.

why_wrong.A: Ordinary guidance is optional, but an ACoP has a stronger status that a competent person's opinion alone does not displace.
why_wrong.C: Courts can and do refer to an ACoP, and its special status shifts the burden onto a defendant who did not follow it.
why_wrong.D: An ACoP is not law, and a defendant who shows equally effective alternative measures can still demonstrate compliance.

common_mistake: Treating every HSE publication as optional advice and overlooking that an Approved Code of Practice has special weight in court.

stem: A contractor boasts 300 days without a RIDDOR-reportable injury and trims site inspections to save time. A review finds weekly inspection actions overdue, lapsed training records and very few supervisor observations. What is the soundest conclusion about measuring performance?

options.A: A low injury count is a lagging measure; overdue actions and lapsed training are leading indicators of weakening controls, so both kinds need monitoring
options.B: The overdue actions matter if the HSE asks for them, because RIDDOR data is the measure the law uses to judge whether a site is managed well
options.C: The injury record proves the controls are working, so inspections can be reduced further until an injury occurs and shows a problem needs attention
options.D: The injury record is the most reliable measure, because inspections and training records describe paperwork and cannot show whether controls are actually working in practice

explanation: Lagging measures such as injuries only record failures after the event, while leading indicators show whether controls are being maintained, so relying on either alone gives a misleading picture.

why_wrong.B: The law requires risks to be managed, and RIDDOR reporting is not a test of performance, so ignoring open actions is a management failure.
why_wrong.C: Waiting for an injury to signal failure defeats the purpose of prevention and ignores the evidence of weakening controls.
why_wrong.D: Active checks reveal control failures before harm occurs, and a short injury record can reflect luck rather than good management.

common_mistake: Reading a run of injury-free days as proof that the safety management system is working.

stem: Two labourers must move a full 205-litre steel drum of lubricant, roughly 180 kg, about 30 m across a compacted yard to a store. They plan to tip it onto its rim and roll it between them, sharing the weight. What is the best control?

options.A: Push the forks of a telehandler straight under the rim, because a trained driver can then carry the drum without anyone touching it
options.B: Roll it as planned but add a third labourer to steady it, since splitting the weight three ways brings each person's share under the guideline figure
options.C: Use a purpose-made drum trolley or handler with the drum strapped on, along a cleared level route, so equipment takes the load instead of people
options.D: Stand it on a pallet and drag it with a rope, as the pallet cuts friction and means nobody has to take any of the weight

explanation: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations expect the load to be avoided or moved by a mechanical aid, and a drum on a strapped trolley is stable and less likely to tip or spill.

why_wrong.A: Bare forks under a rim do not hold a drum securely, and the drum can slip off and burst.
why_wrong.B: Rolling a tipped drum still involves uncontrolled forces and crush and spill risks, and dividing the weight does not remove them.
why_wrong.D: Dragging a loaded pallet involves heavy pulling and an unstable drum that can topple and spill.

common_mistake: Believing a load is acceptable to handle by hand so long as enough people share its weight.

stem: A roofer on a bright summer day buys fashion sunglasses to cut glare and plans to wear them under his helmet while cutting tiles with a disc saw. A colleague says a UV 400 label makes them suitable. What is the best advice?

options.A: Keep the sunglasses, as UV 400 lenses meet the standard for outdoor eye protection and the helmet peak shields the eyes from saw fragments
options.B: Rely on sun cream and the helmet peak, because glare is a comfort issue and eye protection rules apply to dust, sparks and splashes
options.C: Wear safety spectacles marked to EN 166 with an EN 172 sun-glare filter, as fashion lenses are not impact rated and a UV label ignores fragments
options.D: Choose darker wraparound sunglasses, since a closer fit stops fragments reaching the eye and a darker tint gives better UV protection

explanation: Eyewear for outdoor cutting must give impact protection from fragments as well as glare reduction, which industrial sun-glare safety spectacles are designed and marked to provide.

why_wrong.A: A UV label says nothing about impact resistance, and a helmet peak does not stop fragments from the disc saw.
why_wrong.B: Bright light and UV are recognised eye hazards, and the cutting task still needs impact protection.
why_wrong.D: Fit and tint do not make a lens impact rated, and a shattering fashion lens can add to the injury.

common_mistake: Assuming that any dark glasses with a UV label count as eye protection for site work.

stem: A boom MEWP basket is raised beside a flat roof edge. To finish some flashing, the operator proposes unclipping his lanyard and stepping across the small gap onto the roof, saying it is only a short step. What is the correct position?

options.A: Exiting at height is not normal practice; it needs an assessment showing it is safest, plus the manufacturer's transfer procedure with protection still connected
options.B: Stepping across is allowed for operators whose card covers boom MEWPs, since the category includes transfer onto structures as routine work
options.C: It is acceptable for a short step if the basket gate is closed behind him and a second person watches him closely from the ground below
options.D: Unclipping is the right sequence, as a lanyard left on the basket could drag the machine or pull him backwards as he steps across onto the roof

explanation: Operators should not leave a platform while elevated unless a detailed risk assessment shows it is the safest way to reach the work, and the transfer follows the manufacturer's procedure.

why_wrong.B: A card shows training on the machine and does not authorise exiting at height without an assessed plan.
why_wrong.C: A watcher and a closed gate do not control a fall from the gap or the unprotected roof edge.
why_wrong.D: Disconnecting leaves him with no fall protection during the riskiest moment, and the transfer needs a planned anchor arrangement.

common_mistake: Treating a short step from a MEWP onto a structure as trivial because the gap looks small.

stem: Workers heading to the cabins after dark must pass a 1.8 m deep, supported excavation across the walkway, marked by a single strand of tape on stakes and one cone. The foreman says the sides are shored, so nobody can be buried. What is the best assessment?

options.A: Shoring makes the excavation compliant, because a properly supported excavation cannot injure anybody who accidentally steps or falls into it from the walkway
options.B: A banksman is needed during working hours, since an excavation left overnight is not covered by the excavation rules until work starts again
options.C: Support covers collapse only; people must also be stopped from falling in, so it needs a solid barrier, lighting and a protected route
options.D: Tape and a cone are enough because the excavation is under 2 m deep, the depth at which fall protection becomes a legal requirement for pedestrians

explanation: CDM 2015 regulation 22 requires steps to stop people falling into an excavation as well as protection against collapse, which tape and a cone do not give, especially in the dark.

why_wrong.A: A person can still be injured by falling into a supported excavation, and support does not prevent that.
why_wrong.B: Duties continue while the excavation is open, and the risk to people walking past is greater when it is dark and unattended.
why_wrong.D: No such depth threshold exists, and the duty to prevent falls into an excavation applies at any depth where a person could be injured.

common_mistake: Thinking that supporting the sides of an excavation is all that is required to make it safe.

stem: Look at the van moving in the yard. The driver says he has checked both mirrors, they are clean, and he is only reversing a few metres. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The second worker is walking too close to the van's route and should be moved away before anything else is done
options.B: A worker crouched low behind the van lies in a blind zone that mirrors cannot cover, and no signaller is controlling the manoeuvre
options.C: The wing mirrors are poorly aligned, so cleaning and adjusting them before the van reverses would remove the main risk
options.D: The pallet of blocks beside the container is stacked too high and should be lowered before the van moves

explanation: Mirrors do not show a person kneeling directly behind a van, so without a signaller, camera or exclusion of the area the driver cannot know he is safe to reverse.

why_wrong.A: He is well clear of the van and visible, so he is not the hazard that makes the manoeuvre dangerous.
why_wrong.C: The mirrors are clean, and even perfectly adjusted mirrors cannot show someone low down directly behind the vehicle.
why_wrong.D: The pallet is at a normal height and is not what puts anybody at risk from the reversing van.

common_mistake: Assuming that a driver who has checked his mirrors can see everyone behind a reversing vehicle.

stem: A tower crane will lift cladding panels onto the rear of a building, where the operator cannot see the slinger. The plan uses hand signals passed through a second person, and the operator will use the radio channel shared with deliveries. What is the best arrangement?

options.A: Keep the relay of hand signals, since standard signals are clearer than voice and need no equipment that could lose power or signal
options.B: Use the shared channel with clear speech, as any radio will do and the operator can ask other users to confirm an unclear instruction
options.C: Radios on a dedicated channel with call signs and a single signaller, repeating commands during fine movements so a break in them means stop
options.D: Keep a mobile phone call open between the slinger and the operator, since a call cannot be interrupted by other users and needs no call signs or agreed command procedure

explanation: When the signaller is out of sight, standard hand signals cannot be used, so a dedicated radio link with call signs lets the operator know who is speaking and stop if the link fails.

why_wrong.A: Hand signals only work in direct view, and a relay adds delay and the chance of a mistake between people.
why_wrong.B: A shared channel allows interference and unrelated chatter, and an instruction cannot be reliably confirmed by unrelated users.
why_wrong.D: A phone is not a purpose- designed lifting system, can lose signal, and occupies the operator's hands without agreed commands.

common_mistake: Assuming any form of communication will do for a lift as long as the people involved can hear each other most of the time.

stem: To save skip costs, labourers burn timber offcuts, plastic wrapping and plasterboard scraps in a steel drum at the site boundary beside homes. The foreman says one small fire a day is harmless and the waste is only wood and packaging. What is the correct view?

options.A: The fire is lawful if it is kept away from the boundary fence, since only smoke that crosses onto a neighbour's land counts as nuisance
options.B: Burning is acceptable for timber and packaging, but plasterboard must go in a skip, because only gypsum products are unsuitable for a fire
options.C: A small drum fire is acceptable if it is attended and put out each evening, because the quantity burned each day is too small to matter
options.D: Burning mixed site waste can pollute air and cause nuisance and is generally not allowed, so segregate it and send it for lawful recovery or disposal

explanation: Site waste should be segregated and dealt with by lawful means, because burning mixed waste emits harmful smoke and can be an offence.

why_wrong.A: The offence is not limited to smoke crossing a boundary, and the burning itself is generally not permitted.
why_wrong.B: Plastic wrapping and treated timber also give off harmful emissions when burned.
why_wrong.C: Quantity does not make burning mixed waste lawful, and the smoke still affects neighbours.

common_mistake: Treating a small bonfire of site waste as a cheap, harmless way to get rid of it.

stem: Short of trained staff, a small roofing employer asks an apprentice with no work-at-height training to plan and supervise gutter repairs from a ladder. He argues that finding a competent person was not reasonably practicable that week. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Competence has no practicability defence, so the shortage is no excuse, although choosing the access equipment is judged by that test
options.B: Every work-at-height duty is qualified by practicability, so a genuine staffing shortage excuses him if the apprentice was told to take care on the ladder
options.C: A trainee may plan and supervise a job if he is being trained, because the Regulations do not require any trainee to be supervised
options.D: Competence is needed just for work above two metres, so a short ladder job low on the building falls outside the duty

explanation: Regulation 5 of the Work at Height Regulations is an absolute duty with no 'reasonably practicable' qualifier, whereas other duties, such as how the work is carried out safely, are qualified.

why_wrong.B: Several duties, including competence, are absolute, and telling someone to take care does not replace competence.
why_wrong.C: A person who is still being trained may work only while supervised by a competent person.
why_wrong.D: The Regulations apply to any place where a person could fall and be injured, with no minimum height.

common_mistake: Assuming that every legal duty can be softened by arguing that compliance was not reasonably practicable.

stem: Two proposals each look adequate for controlling noise from a bench cut-off saw: a hired acoustic enclosure around it (dearer), or a shift rotation for operators with issued ear defenders (cheaper). Applying the principles of prevention, which should be preferred?

options.A: Whichever the site manager prefers, since the hierarchy of control is guidance and no order of preference is set out in law
options.B: The rotation, because when two controls look equally adequate the cheaper one satisfies the law and the saving can pay for extra training
options.C: Both together, because the law requires every available control to be used whatever it costs, with defenders worn even inside any enclosure fitted
options.D: The enclosure, because collective measures take priority over individual ones, unless the cost is grossly out of proportion to the benefit

explanation: The principles of prevention give collective protective measures priority over individual ones, and extra cost justifies a lesser control only where it is grossly disproportionate to the risk reduction.

why_wrong.A: The principles of prevention in the Management Regulations set a preference for collective over individual measures.
why_wrong.B: The controls are not equal, since the rotation depends on people complying and protects only the operators who wear the defenders.
why_wrong.C: The duty is qualified by reasonable practicability, so not every available control must be used regardless of cost.

common_mistake: Treating the cheaper of two controls as equal in value when it relies on individuals behaving correctly.

stem: During a care-home refurbishment, an electrician cuts a 150 mm hole through a fire-resisting corridor wall to pass cables, then packs the gap with ordinary expanding foam. He says the wall is sealed. What is the correct view?

options.A: Ordinary foam is not fire stopping, so the gap needs a tested product suited to the wall's fire resistance, fitted by a competent person
options.B: The gap can stay unsealed until handover because the corridor has smoke detectors, which give warning and make sealing unnecessary
options.C: Foam is acceptable because it fills the gap and blocks smoke, and only fire doors need rated protection to keep a compartment intact
options.D: Foam is acceptable if it is painted with intumescent paint at practical completion, since the paint restores the fire rating

explanation: Penetrations must be sealed with products tested for the wall's fire-resistance period, otherwise fire and smoke pass through and the compartment no longer protects the building.

why_wrong.B: Detection gives warning but does not stop fire spreading through an occupied building in the meantime.
why_wrong.C: Walls and every opening through them must keep their fire resistance, not just the doors.
why_wrong.D: Paint over untested foam does not create a tested seal, and the gap is unprotected until then.

common_mistake: Believing that any filler that plugs a hole counts as fire stopping.

stem: Labourers hand-sort timber from a soft strip, with protruding nails and broken glass in the waste. The supervisor issues standard cut-resistant fabric gloves and says that deals with it. What is the best improvement?

options.A: Keep the gloves because their cut rating also covers nail punctures, and ask everyone to confirm their tetanus vaccination is current
options.B: Remove nails and bag glass at source using pickers, then add puncture-resistant gloves and penetration-resistant footwear
options.C: Have one labourer sort at a time on rotation, so that only one person is exposed to the sharps at any moment
options.D: Change to thick leather gloves and ask workers to sort slowly, as extra care gives the same protection as removing the sharps

explanation: Reducing the sharps at source comes first, and PPE for what remains must be rated for puncture as well as cut, which are separate performance ratings.

why_wrong.A: Cut and puncture resistance are tested separately, and a vaccination does not prevent injury.
why_wrong.C: Rotating people reduces numbers exposed but leaves each sorter with the same cut and puncture hazard.
why_wrong.D: Care and gloves alone leave the hazard in place, and leather can be punctured by nails.

common_mistake: Assuming a glove marked as cut-resistant is also resistant to punctures from nails.

stem: A groundworker saw a colleague fall from an excavator step and die on site last week. Since then he sleeps badly, jumps at loud noises and avoids the area. His supervisor says he should toughen up and get back on the machine this morning. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Leave him alone and say nothing, because how a worker copes with an event outside his own work tasks is a private matter for him
options.B: Talk to him privately, offer access to occupational health or counselling, allow time off if needed, and review his return to work with him
options.C: Insist that he returns to the machine at once, because keeping to the normal routine is the best way to help someone get over a shock
options.D: Move him to a remote task without telling anyone why, so that nobody sees he is struggling and he is left to recover without any fuss

explanation: Employers should support workers after a traumatic event, and early help and a planned return are better than pressuring someone back to the same task.

why_wrong.A: A serious workplace event is the employer's concern, and silence withholds support.
why_wrong.C: Forcing an immediate return to the scene can worsen distress and risks his safety and others.
why_wrong.D: Isolation without support or a plan does not address his symptoms.

common_mistake: Assuming that people are best left to toughen up after witnessing a serious accident.

stem: Ear defenders hang in a van, crushed under tools. Many have hardened, cracked cushions and loose headbands, and the stores log records only each pair's issue date. What must the employer do?

options.A: Nothing yet, because defenders stay effective until a muff splits and the issue date shows they are within a normal two- year life
options.B: Swap everyone to disposable foam plugs, since plugs cannot wear out and so need no storage, checking or replacement
options.C: Make each worker responsible for storing and replacing their own pair, since personal issue passes the maintenance duty to the wearer
options.D: Provide suitable storage, check condition regularly, and clean or replace worn parts or whole defenders at the maker's intervals

explanation: PPE regulations require employers to maintain, clean or replace PPE and to provide accommodation for it when not in use, because worn cushions and bands lose protection.

why_wrong.A: Hardened cushions and slack bands reduce attenuation before any visible split, and there is no fixed two-year rule.
why_wrong.B: Plugs still need correct fitting and hygienic storage, and the choice must match the noise level.
why_wrong.C: The employer remains responsible for maintaining and replacing PPE it provides.

common_mistake: Thinking PPE is only the employer's concern on the day it is issued.

stem: Look at the scene. The site manager says everyone is correctly dressed and the crane is properly set up, so the area is controlled. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The marked safe route runs beneath the path of the suspended load, so people are directed under it
options.B: The banksman stands at the far end of the walkway and so cannot give clear signals to a crane operator working on the other side
options.C: Red-and-white barrier tape surrounds the crane base, which is a warning colour meant for exclusion areas and should not be used here
options.D: The outriggers rest on timber mats instead of steel plates, so the crane could sink and swing the load into the walkway

explanation: A pedestrian route and its sign must keep people clear of the lifting zone, and the safe-condition sign here sends workers beneath a suspended load, which no PPE can protect against.

why_wrong.B: The banksman's position is not the failing, since the real fault is that people are walking under the load.
why_wrong.C: Barrier tape around a crane base is a normal way to mark the area where the counterweight swings.
why_wrong.D: Timber mats are an accepted way to spread outrigger load, and the crane in the picture is stable.

common_mistake: Assuming a fully dressed workforce is protected when the layout itself puts people under a suspended load.

stem: A plasterer on a mobile tower platform 4 m up leans out over the top guardrail to finish a corner just beyond reach. A colleague suggests clipping his harness to the guardrail to make that safe. What is the right response?

options.A: Allow it on a platform over 2 m if the stabilisers are fully extended and two colleagues hold the base firmly while he leans out
options.B: Place ballast weights on the platform on the opposite side to his lean, to balance the tower and restore stability
options.C: Allow short leans only, because brief movements cannot overturn a tower braced at four corners and are not a risk worth stopping work for
options.D: Stop, and move the tower so the work is within reach inside the rails, since leaning out shifts the centre of gravity and the rail is no anchor

explanation: Leaning beyond the rails adds overturning force that grows with platform height, and a guardrail is not designed as an anchor point for a harness.

why_wrong.A: Stabilisers and people holding the base do not make a lean-out safe, and the tower should be moved instead.
why_wrong.B: Weight on the platform raises the centre of gravity, and any ballast belongs at the base as the maker instructs.
why_wrong.C: A sudden lean or push can start an overturn, and the work should be repositioned regardless of duration.

common_mistake: Stretching beyond the platform guardrail to avoid the effort of moving the tower.

stem: Two operatives repoint a canal wall from the towpath, half a metre from deep, cold water. The rescue plan is that the stronger swimmer will jump in if the other falls, and one buoyancy aid hangs in the cabin. Which change matters most?

options.A: Issue the stronger swimmer a wetsuit, since a strong swimmer in suitable clothing can safely rescue a colleague from the water
options.B: Keep a second buoyancy aid in the cabin, and ask the pair to stay within shouting distance so help can be called quickly
options.C: Stop bankside work in winter only, because cold water shock is a risk in cold months and not in the warmer ones
options.D: Issue worn lifejackets and keep throw lines and a ring buoy to hand, with rescuers reaching or throwing from the bank

explanation: Lifejackets reduce drowning risk, and cold water shock can disable even strong swimmers within moments, so rescue should use throw lines and reach from the bank.

why_wrong.A: A rescuer entering the water risks cold water shock and becoming a second casualty, whatever they wear.
why_wrong.B: Equipment in a cabin cannot help a casualty in seconds, and shouting is not a rescue plan.
why_wrong.C: Cold water shock can occur in any water below roughly 15 degrees, including in summer.

common_mistake: Assuming a good swimmer can safely rescue someone from cold water.

stem: A slinger plans to lift a 1.5 t steel beam with sharp, unrounded edges using a polyester web sling marked 3 t. He says the load is half the marked limit, so the lift is safe. What is the right response?

options.A: Wrap the sling twice round the beam so the extra layers share any cutting, which keeps the marked working load limit unchanged
options.B: Fit edge protection such as sleeves or radius pieces, or use a sling suited to sharp edges, because cuts reduce capacity despite the marking
options.C: Lift as planned, because the two-to-one margin already allows for edge damage, and inspect the sling carefully once the lift is finished
options.D: Pull the sling into a tight choke hitch so the webbing beds into the edges and cannot slide over the steel

explanation: Sharp edges can cut webbing at loads well below its marked limit, so the sling must be protected or a more suitable accessory chosen.

why_wrong.A: Extra turns do not protect the outer layer from the edge and change the rated configuration.
why_wrong.C: A margin does not allow for cutting, and inspection after the lift comes too late to prevent a failure.
why_wrong.D: A tight choke presses the webbing into the sharp edges, increasing the risk of cutting.

common_mistake: Judging a sling only by the weight on its tag without considering what the load can do to it. PRACTICE TEST 11

stem: A company is convicted after a worker loses fingers in an unguarded machine. The managing director had twice been told of the missing guard and deferred the repair to save money, then argued that the company is a separate legal person and the site manager was responsible. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He can be prosecuted only if he personally operated or adjusted the machine, since a director is liable for nothing beyond his own direct acts
options.B: He can also be prosecuted personally, because an offence involving an officer's consent, connivance or neglect makes that officer guilty too
options.C: He faces action only through the company, because directors are personally liable for corporate manslaughter but not for health and safety offences
options.D: He is protected, because handing the repair to the site manager moves all personal criminal liability for the offence onto that manager alone

explanation: Section 37 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 makes a director personally guilty where the company's offence was committed with his consent or connivance, or is attributable to his neglect.

why_wrong.A: Liability under section 37 arises from consent, connivance or neglect and does not require hands-on involvement with the machine.
why_wrong.C: Directors can be convicted of health and safety offences personally, and the corporate manslaughter offence is a separate matter.
why_wrong.D: Delegation does not remove an officer's own liability when he knew of the defect and failed to act.

common_mistake: Assuming a company's separate legal identity shields its directors and managers from personal prosecution.

stem: A 1960s office block with no surviving drawings is to be stripped out and then demolished. The foreman proposes to start at once by removing partitions and edge columns on the top floor, and to have material tested as it turns up. How should the work be planned?

options.A: Remove the edge columns and heavy walls first to open up access, because a structure will always stay stable while its floors remain intact above
options.B: Start stripping now but stop and test whenever suspect material turns up, as a full survey is only needed before the final demolition stage begins
options.C: Rely on the original design intent for blocks of that age, as an unrecorded building from the 1960s will have followed standard practice throughout
options.D: Get asbestos and structural surveys first, then set a sequence that keeps the frame stable, removing non-critical parts before the stiff ones

explanation: Surveys must come before work starts, and the sequence must prevent uncontrolled collapse by keeping stabilising elements until last.

why_wrong.A: Taking out structural members early can cause an uncontrolled collapse, since the stability of a frame depends on its remaining members.
why_wrong.B: Testing as suspect material appears risks disturbing asbestos before anyone knows where it is, and the survey must come before any work starts.
why_wrong.C: Old buildings are often altered or built differently from the standard, so assumptions cannot replace a survey of the actual structure.

common_mistake: Starting strip-out on the assumption that surprises can be dealt with as they appear.

stem: Smoke and a smell of burning hydraulic oil come from the engine bay of a working excavator. The operator can see no flames yet. What should he do?

options.A: Drive the machine clear of the stockpiles and the fuel store first and then stop the engine, because a burning machine is safest in open ground
options.B: Open the engine cover fully to locate the source, then discharge an extinguisher straight into the bay to put out the first flames quickly
options.C: Ground the attachment, stop the engine, get out, move clear and raise the alarm, tackling it only if trained and never by opening the cover
options.D: Leave the engine idling so the cooling fan keeps the bay cool, and fetch a colleague to help fight the fire from the cab step

explanation: Stopping and leaving removes the ignition and fuel feed and protects the operator, while opening the cover would feed the fire with air.

why_wrong.A: Driving on with a fire spreads it, risks the operator's life and keeps pumping fuel and oil to the source.
why_wrong.B: Opening the cover lets in air, which can turn a smouldering fire into a fireball in the operator's face.
why_wrong.D: A running engine keeps feeding fuel and oil to the fire, and remaining on the step puts people in the path of flames.

common_mistake: Trying to find and fight an engine fire by opening the cover instead of stopping the machine and getting clear.

stem: During a refurbishment of the second floor of a working office, the contractor's team removes ceiling tiles that carry emergency lights and bags over the exit signs to keep dust out. Staff remain on the floor above. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Remove the fittings, since the work area is under the contractor's control, and warn the staff on the floor above by email about the changes
options.B: Keep escape routes lit and signed, using temporary emergency lighting and signs where fittings come out, agreed with the responsible person
options.C: Remove them for the duration, since emergency lighting is only needed when the building is dark and this work runs only in daylight hours
options.D: Cover the signs but keep torches in the work area, because torches are accepted as an equal substitute for fixed escape lighting on stairs

explanation: Occupied premises need escape routes that can be found and used if the power fails, so any removal must be covered by an agreed temporary equivalent.

why_wrong.A: An email does not give people a lit, signed escape route, and the staff above still need to use the same stairs.
why_wrong.C: Emergency lighting works when the mains fails, which can happen at any hour, and also in areas where windows give little light.
why_wrong.D: Torches are not a reliable standard for lighting routes used by the public or staff, and covered signs hide the way out.

common_mistake: Treating the building's escape lighting and signs as part of the finishes to be removed or covered during the works.

stem: A new block has stood empty for eight months with its water system filled but unused. Before handover, a plumber flushes only the kitchen taps and says that cold water cannot grow harmful bacteria. What is the best view?

options.A: Risk-assess the whole system, flush all outlets, control temperatures and remove dead legs, because stagnant water can grow legionella
options.B: Add the check to the first annual service, since legionella is a risk only to residents after they have used the system for months
options.C: Flushing the kitchen taps is enough, as the other outlets contain the same water and will be clean once the first taps run clear
options.D: Cold water is safe at any temperature, so only the hot system matters, and bacteria cannot grow in a sealed new installation

explanation: Water left standing in warm pipework, tanks and dead legs can grow legionella, which is breathed in as a fine spray, so the system needs assessment, flushing and temperature control.

why_wrong.B: The risk builds up during the empty period, so action is needed before occupation, not after a year of use.
why_wrong.C: Each outlet and dead leg holds its own stagnant water, so flushing one point does not clear the rest.
why_wrong.D: Cold supplies that warm up above about 20 degrees while standing can also grow legionella, and new pipework is not sterile.

common_mistake: Believing legionella is only a hot-water problem in old buildings, when stagnant water in any new or unused system can grow it.

stem: After cutting concrete blocks, a labourer blows the fine dust off his overalls and the bench using the compressor air line, wearing goggles and a mask. A colleague objects. Why is the labourer's method a poor control?

options.A: It wastes compressed air and wears the line, since dust that has settled is harmless provided that the person doing the cleaning wears a mask
options.B: It puts fine dust back into the air for everyone nearby to breathe, and air at pressure can force particles or even air into the skin
options.C: It is fine with goggles and a mask, but the overalls should be washed at home, since dust on work clothes is a household risk only
options.D: It is acceptable outdoors at low pressure, because the wind carries the dust away and the airflow is too gentle to injure the skin or eyes

explanation: Compressed air re-suspends settled dust and can cause injection injuries, so vacuuming or damp cleaning is preferred.

why_wrong.A: Settled dust is not harmless, and a mask protects only the wearer while everyone else nearby breathes the cloud.
why_wrong.C: Dust must be controlled on site, and the problem lies in the cleaning method rather than in what the clothes later pass through.
why_wrong.D: Low pressure still raises a cloud, and wind does not guarantee dust leaves the work area or avoids other people.

common_mistake: Thinking that blowing dust away with an air line removes it, when it only moves it somewhere else.

stem: A roof worker's fall is arrested and he hangs by his harness at the eaves, conscious but pale and unable to pull himself up. No rescue plan was prepared. The supervisor wants to wait for the ambulance. What should happen?

options.A: Rescue him, have him walk around to restore circulation, and return him to light duties if he says he feels fine after a few minutes
options.B: Delay rescue until a platform can be built, because a properly fitted harness supports the body safely for an hour or more with no harm
options.C: Rescue him promptly with the rescue kit, help him take weight off his legs, and get him medically checked afterwards even if he seems well
options.D: Leave him hanging until the emergency services arrive, since only their specialists should move a casualty, and he should stay as still as possible

explanation: Hanging motionless in a harness can quickly become life- threatening, so rescue must be fast and the casualty needs medical assessment afterwards.

why_wrong.A: A casualty who has been suspended needs a medical check whatever he says, because serious effects can develop later.
why_wrong.B: A harness does not make suspension safe for long, and a hanging casualty can deteriorate in minutes.
why_wrong.D: Waiting leaves him suspended and at risk of losing consciousness, and prompt rescue by trained site staff is needed.

common_mistake: Believing that a worker hanging safely in a harness can wait for the emergency services without coming to harm.

stem: Look at the image. A worker is leaving a parked machine at the end of a task. What is the most serious risk of injury shown?

options.A: He steps down facing outward with a tool in one hand, so he cannot keep three points of contact and may slip and fall
options.B: The bucket is raised clear of the ground, so a hydraulic fault could drop it onto him as he steps away from the cab steps
options.C: The engine appears to be running with the tracks free to move, so the machine could lurch off while he is still half-way out of it
options.D: He is not wearing a hard hat or hi-vis, so he cannot be seen by others or protected from falling objects as he leaves the cab

explanation: Climbing down facing the machine and holding on with two hands and one foot, or the reverse, prevents slips on the steps from becoming a fall.

why_wrong.B: The bucket is shown lowered flat on the ground, so this hazard is not present in the picture.
why_wrong.C: The machine in the picture is stopped with the bucket grounded, so uncontrolled movement is not the main hazard shown.
why_wrong.D: He is wearing both a hard hat and hi-vis clothing, so the main risk lies elsewhere in the picture.

common_mistake: Assuming that a few steps down from a cab are too low to need the same care as a ladder.

stem: A faulty socket circuit in a busy plant room is to be repaired. The manager says that shutting it off would halt production for an afternoon, and that the competent electrician can work live if he wears insulating gloves. What do the Electricity at Work Regulations say?

options.A: Live work needs dead working to be unreasonable, live working reasonable and suitable precautions taken, so lost production alone is not enough
options.B: Live work is allowed on circuits below 400 volts, since the regulation applies only to high-voltage conductors that can arc over at distance
options.C: Live work is allowed if the manager signs a written instruction accepting the risk, as this makes the decision a managerial one to take
options.D: Live work is allowed where the electrician is competent and wears insulating gloves, because suitable precautions alone satisfy the regulation in full
