explanation: Regulation 14 requires all three conditions to be met, and inconvenience or cost of isolating does not alone make it unreasonable to work dead.

why_wrong.B: The regulation applies to any live conductor where danger may arise, including ordinary mains voltage which can kill.
why_wrong.C: A signature does not meet the legal conditions, and the duty for safe working remains with the person doing the work as well.
why_wrong.D: Precautions are only the third condition, and the other two must also be met before any live work can start.

common_mistake: Treating live working as acceptable whenever isolation is inconvenient and the electrician is skilled.

stem: Fitters hang a one-tonne lever hoist from a beam to raise a 400 kg pipe spool. The lever is stiff, so one slides a scaffold tube over the handle, and the apprentice offers to ride the spool upwards to steady it. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The apprentice may ride it if he is clipped to the hook, but the tube must come off since only the lever should operate the hoist
options.B: Both are acceptable provided the beam has been checked, because the spool is well below the hoist's rated load, and the apprentice holds the chain
options.C: Neither is acceptable: a stiff lever signals an overload or fault to check, and nobody may ride a load on equipment not designed to lift people
options.D: The tube is acceptable since the spool is well below the one-tonne rating, but the apprentice must stay clear and use a tag line

explanation: An extended lever can overload the hoist and hide a fault, and lifting equipment not marked for people must never carry anyone.

why_wrong.A: Clipping a person to a hoist hook does not make it a safe means of lifting people, as the equipment is not designed or examined for that.
why_wrong.B: Extending the lever can overload the hoist whatever the weight, and riding a load is never safe with equipment not designed for people.
why_wrong.D: Extending the lever defeats the hoist's design and can mask a fault or overload, even with the load well within its rating.

common_mistake: Assuming that a load well below the rated capacity allows any improvised leverage or a person to ride along.

stem: A contractor is fitting out a retail unit over twelve weeks with forty workers. The shop owner says council environmental health officers police shops, so an HSE inspector's visit is a mistake. Who enforces here, and what may the inspector do on entry?

options.A: The enforcing body depends on who employs the workers, so the inspector may question managers only and needs the contractor's permission to take samples
options.B: HSE enforces only after an accident, so before then the inspector may observe and advise but needs a warrant to examine site documents or question workers
options.C: HSE enforces as this is notifiable construction work, and the inspector may enter at a reasonable time, take photographs and samples, and require documents
options.D: The council enforces because the premises is a shop, and the HSE inspector may only advise, needing the owner's written consent to take photographs or samples

explanation: Construction work is reserved to HSE, and a project lasting over thirty days is notifiable, so the shop's usual council regime does not apply; inspectors hold statutory powers of entry, sampling and questioning.

why_wrong.A: Enforcement follows the type of work and premises, not the employer, and inspectors may question any person and take samples without permission.
why_wrong.B: Inspectors can enter and inspect without waiting for an accident, and can require documents without a warrant.
why_wrong.D: Construction work stays with HSE whatever the type of premises, and inspectors need no owner consent to photograph or sample.

common_mistake: Assuming the type of building decides who enforces, when construction work is usually enforced by HSE wherever it takes place.

stem: A decorator who strips old paintwork in powdered latex gloves develops itchy red hands. Days later he wheezes and his eyes stream when a colleague opens a new box of the same gloves nearby. Which response best fits the risk?

options.A: Issue cotton liners under the latex gloves and a barrier cream, because the rash comes from sweat and the wheeze is probably just hay fever
options.B: Give him powder-free latex gloves only, as the allergy is to the powder rather than the latex, and let colleagues keep using powdered ones
options.C: Have him wash his hands after each glove change and carry on, since symptoms that ease overnight show irritation rather than a true allergy
options.D: Remove him from latex exposure, switch the team to powder-free nitrile gloves, and refer him to occupational health, as airborne glove powder can trigger asthma

explanation: Latex allergy can affect skin and breathing, and powder carries the allergen into the air, so the source must be substituted and the worker medically assessed.

why_wrong.A: Liners and cream leave latex exposure in place and wrongly dismiss two linked symptoms that point to an allergy.
why_wrong.B: The allergen is the latex protein itself, and colleagues' powdered gloves would still spread it through the air.
why_wrong.C: Symptoms that ease away from work often indicate a work-related allergy, so continued exposure risks lasting sensitisation.

common_mistake: Treating a work-related rash or wheeze as a minor irritation instead of reporting it and removing the cause.

stem: A fourteen-person site, including two women, has one toilet cabin with three cubicles opening off a shared room. The doors cannot be secured from inside and no cubicle has a bin. The manager says separate cubicles satisfy the rules. What is required?

options.A: Separate rooms are needed only once six or more women work on site, and until then a notice asking men to knock first meets the duty on privacy
options.B: A single shared room is lawful if the women may use the first-aid room, since the rules count toilets per worker and not who uses them
options.C: Partitions inside one shared room are enough on sites under twenty people, provided women get set times by rota and used items are flushed away safely
options.D: Separate rooms for men and women, or one-person rooms locking from inside, kept clean and lit, with a suitable means to dispose of sanitary dressings

explanation: Construction welfare rules require separate rooms for men and women unless each room is for one person with a door secured from inside, and women need hygienic disposal.

why_wrong.A: The duty to provide separate or lockable rooms is not triggered by a headcount of women, and a notice does not give privacy.
why_wrong.B: The first-aid room must stay available for treatment, and the regulations address separation and privacy as well as numbers.
why_wrong.C: A rota does not create separate rooms, and flushing sanitary items blocks drainage and is no proper disposal.

common_mistake: Counting toilets per head and forgetting that privacy, separation and sanitary disposal are part of the welfare duty.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operator is fully protected for jet cleaning because his head, face, hands and hearing are all covered. What is the most significant gap?

options.A: His rubber gauntlets should be replaced with leather work gloves, which grip a wet lance better and resist a stray jet more reliably
options.B: His canvas trainers give no toe or foot-bone protection, so a stray jet or dropped lance risks crush injury or water injection
options.C: His ear defenders should be swapped for disposable foam plugs, which seal better against the engine noise of a petrol pressure washer
options.D: A full-face visor is a weaker eye guard than safety glasses for jetting, so glasses should replace it to give a tighter seal

explanation: Jetting teams need protective boots with foot-bone protection, because a lance jet can cut skin and force water and slurry into the foot.

why_wrong.A: Waterproof gauntlets are the recommended hand protection for jetting, whereas leather soaks through and loses protection.
why_wrong.C: Ear defenders are suitable for this noise when worn correctly, and plugs offer no extra protection.
why_wrong.D: A visor is the correct guard against spray and splashback, and glasses leave the face and neck exposed.

common_mistake: Checking head, eyes and hands on a PPE inspection and forgetting to look down at the feet.

stem: A plasterer finishes a dusty shift and hangs his half-mask on a van hook with the facepiece coated in dust. He knocks the P3 filters on the wheel arch and plans to reuse them tomorrow, saying he will change them when they "feel blocked". What is the correct approach?

options.A: Blow the dust off the facepiece and filters with compressed air at the end of each shift, then hang the mask on the van hook to dry in the open air
options.B: Clean and dry the facepiece as the manufacturer advises, store it in a sealed clean container, and replace filters that are damaged, dirty, expired or hard to breathe through
options.C: Wash the filters under a tap each week to restore them, then refit them once fully dry, because a washed filter regains its original efficiency
options.D: Keep the same filters until the facepiece seal fails its fit check, as filters only wear out once the rubber seal on the face has worn away

explanation: Reusable masks must be cleaned and stored clean to prevent contamination and deterioration, and clogged or damaged filters cause breathing resistance and face-seal leaks.

why_wrong.A: Compressed air drives dust into the filter media and leaves the mask exposed to fresh contamination on an open hook.
why_wrong.C: Particle filters must never be washed, as water destroys the filter material and its efficiency.
why_wrong.D: Filter life is independent of the facepiece seal, and a blocked or damaged filter can leak long before the seal fails.

common_mistake: Judging a respirator by whether it still feels wearable instead of cleaning, storing and changing it by a routine.

stem: A 4.8 m high flat-roof edge is reached by a ladder whose foot is 0.6 m from the wall and sits on a slumped mound of spoil. Its top is level with the coping. Which set of corrections makes it safe to climb?

options.A: Move the foot about 1.2 m out onto firm level ground and use a longer ladder rising at least 1 m or three rungs above the coping
options.B: Move the foot about 1.2 m out, lay a plank on the spoil to spread the load, and keep the top level with the coping so it cannot snag
options.C: Keep the 0.6 m setting but footing the ladder with a colleague, and extend it by one rung above the coping to give a place to grip
options.D: Move the foot about 2.4 m out to lower the risk of tipping backwards, and pack the spoil flat with bricks, keeping the ladder top level with the coping

explanation: A ladder should sit at about 75 degrees on stable level ground and extend roughly a metre above the landing to give a handhold when stepping off.

why_wrong.B: A plank on loose spoil is still unstable ground, and a top level with the coping gives nothing to hold when stepping off.
why_wrong.C: A foot only 0.6 m out is too steep and may tip backwards, and one rung gives too little handhold.
why_wrong.D: A base that far out makes the ladder slide and leaves no handhold above the landing.

common_mistake: Fixing the ladder angle while ignoring the ground beneath the feet and the handhold at the top.

stem: A bricklayer's scaffold bay carries a notice marked "Loading Class 2". The foreman wants three pallets of bricks placed on the working platform and says the class number only shows how many people may stand on it. How should the class be understood?

options.A: It gives the distributed and point loads the platform was designed for, so workers and materials together must stay within it, or a higher class is needed
options.B: It states the weight of people only, because materials are carried by the ties and standards rather than by the boards of the platform
options.C: It states the scaffolder's competence grade, so a Class 2 notice shows skilled erectors built it and heavy stacking is then permitted
options.D: It states how many boarded lifts the scaffold may have, so three pallets are acceptable if only one lift is occupied at any one time

explanation: Loading classes set the design load per square metre and point load for a working platform, so a task needing heavier stacking requires a platform designed and handed over for that duty.

why_wrong.B: Materials load the boards directly, and the class covers workers, tools and materials together.
why_wrong.C: Loading class is a design capacity, not a measure of the erectors' skill, and does not authorise heavy stacking.
why_wrong.D: The class describes load capacity per platform and has nothing to do with how many lifts are in use.

common_mistake: Reading a scaffold notice as a pass for the structure instead of as the limit on what the platform carries.

stem: Pedestrians cross a haul road used by loaded dumpers where it bends past a stockpile that hides each party from the other. The planner proposes mirrors and a signaller there. What is the better control for the crossing?

options.A: Keep the crossing at the bend as it is the shortest route to the cabins, and add a speed hump and a warning sign facing approaching drivers
options.B: Cut the stockpile height to knee level and keep the crossing in place, relying on drivers sounding their horns as they round the bend
options.C: Move the crossing to a straight length giving clear view both ways within stopping distance, and mark, light and fence the approach
options.D: Leave the crossing where it is, paint it clearly across the road, and brief all drivers that pedestrians always have priority on it

explanation: Siting crossings where drivers and pedestrians can see each other in time, with a clearly marked and lit crossing, removes the hazard at source instead of compensating for it.

why_wrong.A: A speed hump and sign do not restore the missing sight lines, and a short walking route does not justify a blind crossing.
why_wrong.B: A horn only warns people who are already in view, and relying on drivers rather than layout leaves the cause of the blind spot unmanaged.
why_wrong.D: Paint and a priority rule cannot help a driver who cannot see the pedestrian until it is too late to stop.

common_mistake: Adding warning devices to a bad crossing position instead of moving the crossing to where people can see each other.

stem: A rear-tip dumper driver must reverse the length of a yard to the tipping point, where pedestrians sometimes cross. The alarm and beacon work, and he says everyone is therefore warned. Which approach is best?

options.A: Remove reversing with a one-way route or turning area, keep people out of the reversing zone, and check behind before and during any reversal
options.B: Have the driver reverse slowly in short bursts with the window open, because lower speed means anyone behind has time to move out of the way
options.C: Rely on the alarm and beacon and ask pedestrians to listen for them, as audible and visual warnings let anyone behind clear the path in time
options.D: Let pedestrians use the yard freely but wear high-visibility clothing, since being seen by the driver is the main protection near a reversing vehicle

explanation: An alarm only warns others and cannot detect anyone, so the main control is to design reversing out and exclude pedestrians, with the driver checking the way behind.

why_wrong.B: Low speed reduces severity but leaves the driver unaware of anyone behind, and open windows do not give a view.
why_wrong.C: Warnings depend on people noticing and reacting, and they do nothing to show the driver who is behind.
why_wrong.D: Hi-vis helps only if the driver can see the wearer, and it does not separate people from reversing traffic.

common_mistake: Believing that a working alarm lets the driver reverse with no need to look or to remove pedestrians from the area.

stem: A strip-out produces fluorescent tubes, emergency-light batteries and part-used aerosol cans. The labourers plan to crush the tubes to save space and tip everything into a general waste skip. What is the correct handling?

options.A: Crush the tubes in a bag to contain the glass, and put the batteries and cans in the general skip as only large quantities count as hazardous
options.B: Treat them as hazardous waste, keep them intact in separate marked containers, and pass them to a registered carrier with a consignment note
options.C: Send them with the skip operator's ordinary transfer note, as the operator takes responsibility for classifying waste once it leaves the site
options.D: Place the tubes, batteries and cans together in one lidded skip marked hazardous, since mixing hazardous items does no harm once they are labelled

explanation: Tubes, batteries and aerosols with contents are hazardous, so they must be kept separate and unbroken and sent under a consignment note using an authorised carrier.

why_wrong.A: Crushing releases mercury vapour and dust, and hazardous status does not depend on a minimum quantity.
why_wrong.C: Hazardous waste needs a consignment note, and the producer keeps the duty of care for classifying and describing it.
why_wrong.D: Different hazardous wastes can react or contaminate each other, and mixing them without authorisation is not permitted.

common_mistake: Assuming small items from a strip-out can go in the general skip because there are not many of them.

stem: A firm will replace bathroom fittings in a sheltered housing block while residents, some with dementia, stay in their flats. A colleague says the assessment need only cover the operatives, as residents are not employees. What is the best response?

options.A: Limit the assessment to operatives, since residents are the building owner's responsibility and signs on the doors will warn them off
options.B: Residents are people affected by the work, so assess their risks too, then agree work areas, access times and tool security with the building manager
options.C: Assess the residents only if a complaint or incident occurs, because the assessment is meant to track hazards that have actually caused harm
options.D: Brief the residents on the hazards at a start-of-job meeting, because informed adults can then keep clear of the work area themselves

explanation: Employers must protect non-employees affected by their work, and vulnerable residents need specific controls such as secured tools, closed-off work areas and agreed access arrangements.

why_wrong.A: Duties to non-employees affected by the work remain with the contractor, and signs cannot protect people who may not understand them.
why_wrong.C: Assessment is a prior, suitable and sufficient exercise that must anticipate foreseeable harm, not wait for an incident.
why_wrong.D: Briefing cannot be relied on for residents with dementia, so physical controls and supervision are still needed.

common_mistake: Assuming a risk assessment only has to protect the workers doing the job and not the people who live or work around it.

stem: A six-storey timber-frame block is under construction beside a narrow lane. The principal contractor has a written site fire plan but has never spoken to the local fire and rescue service. A subcontractor says contact is only needed after a fire starts. What is the best view?

options.A: Share the plan early, covering appliance access, water supplies and hazards, and update the service when site layouts change
options.B: Send the plan once at the start of the job, because the site layout stays the same and later updates would only confuse the service
options.C: Wait until a fire happens, as the service will then take control and the site plan is for site staff rather than attending crews
options.D: Rely on building control approval of the finished design, since it covers fire access for both the completed building and the building site

explanation: Early contact lets the fire and rescue service plan its response to the real site layout, hazards and access, which is far harder to arrange once a fire is already burning.

why_wrong.B: Site layouts, gates and hazards change as the building rises, so out-of-date information can mislead crews.
why_wrong.C: Crews arriving without knowledge of access, water supplies or hazards respond more slowly and with more risk.
why_wrong.D: Building control approval relates to the completed building and does not address construction-phase access, hazards or water supplies.

common_mistake: Treating the site fire plan as an internal document and leaving the fire and rescue service to find out the layout when they arrive.

stem: Before loft insulation goes in, two labourers must clear years of pigeon droppings from a roof void. The foreman suggests sweeping the dry material into sacks and using a plain nuisance- dust mask. What is the best approach to the biological hazard?

options.A: Dampen the droppings, scoop them into sealed bags, and wear disposable coveralls and an FFP3 respirator, washing before eating
options.B: Do the work in the cooler evening and keep the hatch open, because ventilation alone dilutes any airborne spores to a safe level
options.C: Brush the dry droppings briskly into sacks to shorten exposure time, and wear a nuisance-dust mask for the short job
options.D: Leave the droppings in place and treat the void only with a disinfectant spray, as the spray kills any organisms present

explanation: Dried droppings can carry organisms that cause lung infections such as histoplasmosis, so dust must be suppressed and suitable respiratory protection, clothing and hygiene used under COSHH.

why_wrong.B: General ventilation does not control a dust and spore release in a confined void, so source controls and respirators are still needed.
why_wrong.C: Dry sweeping throws fine infectious dust into the air, and a nuisance- dust mask is not suitable respiratory protection for a biological agent.
why_wrong.D: Spraying alone does not remove the material, and disturbing it later still releases dust and organisms.

common_mistake: Thinking old dry droppings are harmless dust that a basic mask and a quick sweep can deal with.

stem: A kerb layer returns after seven months off with a lower-back injury. He says he feels fine and wants his old full duties from day one. The site manager must decide how to bring him back. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Keep him away until he is completely free of any restriction, because an employer cannot support any adjustments to a worker's duties
options.B: Give him light duties with no end date and no review, since a lighter workload removes the need for any further follow-up
options.C: Accept his own judgement and return him to full duties, because a competent adult knows his body better than his employer does
options.D: Hold a return conversation, agree phased lifting adjustments, review his manual handling assessment, and check progress regularly

explanation: A planned, reviewed return with agreed adjustments protects against relapse, and the employer should review risk assessments for the individual rather than rely on the worker's own opinion.

why_wrong.A: Reasonable adjustments are encouraged, and waiting for full recovery with no support can prolong absence needlessly.
why_wrong.B: Open- ended light duties without review fail to support recovery and ignore changes in his condition or ability.
why_wrong.C: Employers still owe a duty of care, so the worker's confidence does not replace a planned return and review of the risks.

common_mistake: Assuming a worker who says he is fine can go straight back to full duties without a planned, reviewed return.

stem: A scaffolder rigs a gin wheel to raise buckets of mortar to a first-floor lift. The supervisor wants speed and says the wheel is light kit that needs no planning. What must be in place before bricklayers use it?

options.A: A single annual rope inspection by the supplier, on the basis that the scaffold itself needs no assessment for added lifting loads
options.B: A single coupler clipped to a guardrail so the wheel can swing out, plus a rope the team judges strong enough by feel
options.C: Correct fixings to the scaffold, a scaffold able to bear the load, and a rope in good order with a known safe working load
options.D: No formal checks while buckets stay light, with the receiver leaning out to catch each load as it swings in

explanation: A gin wheel is lifting equipment, so it must be properly fixed to a scaffold designed to bear the extra load and used with a sound rope of known capacity.

why_wrong.A: The scaffold must be checked for the additional loads, and the equipment needs inspection before use as well as periodic examination.
why_wrong.B: A guardrail is not designed to carry lifting loads, and rope capacity must be known rather than judged by feel.
why_wrong.D: Light loads still need a sound fixing and rope, and leaning out to catch a swinging load creates a fall risk.

common_mistake: Treating small lifting kit such as a gin wheel as too minor to need a proper fixing, a known rope capacity and a check of the scaffold.

stem: A painter is about to repaint the fascia at this house using the ladder shown. Which combination of faults in the ladder's positioning most increases the chance of a fall?

options.A: The paint tin hangs from a hook, which makes the ladder unstable, and a second person must hold the tin at ground level
options.B: It is an extension ladder, which cannot be used for painting, and a trestle platform should be set up on the soil instead
options.C: Its top bears on plastic guttering that can crack or buckle, and its base sits on soft ground unsecured so a foot could sink or slip
options.D: Its angle is too shallow for the height, and the stiles extend too far above the gutter so the climber has no handhold on the way off

explanation: A ladder must rest against a strong surface or use a stand-off, and stand on firm level ground and be secured against slipping.

why_wrong.A: A light tin hung from a hook is a minor issue compared with the unstable top and base, and holding the tin does nothing to secure the ladder.
why_wrong.B: Extension ladders may be used for short, light work where the risk assessment justifies it, and a trestle platform would be worse on soft soil.
why_wrong.D: The ladder in the picture is at a sensible angle, and extending above the landing point is correct practice.

common_mistake: Checking only the ladder's angle and condition and ignoring what its top rests on and what its feet stand on.

stem: A joiner wants to run his 230 V Class I router on a two-core extension lead because his Class II drill uses one. The supervisor asks what difference the equipment class makes. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both classes are built the same way internally, so a two- core lead suits either tool, provided the extension lead plug fits the socket
options.B: A Class I tool is made safe by an RCD alone, so the earth conductor can be dropped from the lead if the RCD is tested monthly
options.C: Class II tools must be earthed through their metal casing for site use, so the drill needs a three-core lead with its earth wire connected
options.D: Class I tools rely on a sound earth so need a three-core lead, while Class II tools are protected by reinforced insulation

explanation: Class I equipment depends on its earth connection as well as basic insulation, so the lead must carry an earth, whereas Class II equipment has no earth and relies on double or reinforced insulation.

why_wrong.A: Class I tools have an earth conductor that a two-core lead cannot supply, so the protection would be lost.
why_wrong.B: An RCD adds protection but does not replace the earth that a Class I tool depends on.
why_wrong.C: Class II tools have no earth connection, and an earth wire should not be connected to them.

common_mistake: Assuming all power tools need the same lead and that an RCD makes up for a missing earth on equipment that relies on it.

stem: A new 1.8 m deep drainage chamber has its cover removed ready for pipe connections, and a plywood sheet and one cone sit on top. A dumper route passes about 2 m away. What is the best way to protect people and plant from falling in?

options.A: Place the plywood over the opening and park the dumper on it overnight to stop anyone from lifting the board off the chamber
options.B: Leave the chamber open and let the dumper drivers know about it at the morning briefing, since all site plant operators will remember it
options.C: Keep the plywood and add a second cone and a strip of hazard tape, since visible marking is enough to alert drivers and walkers
options.D: Fit a purpose-made cover rated for the loads and fixed against displacement, and route plant away behind a barrier with a stand-off

explanation: A strong, fixed cover removes the fall hazard itself, and a barrier with stand-off keeps vehicles from tracking too close to the opening.

why_wrong.A: Plant must never be parked on an unrated cover, which could collapse under the weight and drop the machine into the chamber.
why_wrong.B: Relying on memory is a weak administrative control, and pedestrians and visitors would still be exposed to the open hole.
why_wrong.C: Marking does not prevent a fall, and plywood that is not rated or fixed can slip or break under load.

common_mistake: Believing a cone and a plywood sheet make an open chamber safe near moving plant.

stem: Dumpers must cross a drainage ditch daily to haul spoil to a stockpile. The foreman proposes driving through at the shallowest point and tipping hardcore into the bed to firm it up. What is the best advice?

options.A: Tip the hardcore in to form a causeway, as inert stone does no harm and the water can pass between the pieces
options.B: Drive through at the shallow point but use a banksman, since slow vehicles stir up little silt and a ditch is not a protected watercourse
options.C: Install a temporary bridge or culvert built for the loads, check whether consent is needed, and keep silt and fuel out
options.D: Cross at the shallow point and wash the wheels in the ditch afterwards, so soil stays out of the haul road and off the public highway

explanation: A purpose-built crossing keeps vehicles out of the water and avoids silt and fuel pollution, and works in or near a watercourse may need consent from the Environment Agency or local authority.

why_wrong.A: Hardcore can block flow, add fines to the water and may need consent, so it is not a harmless fix.
why_wrong.B: Fording stirs silt and drops oil into the water, and a ditch can still be a watercourse that must be protected.
why_wrong.D: Washing wheels in the ditch puts mud and any oil straight into the watercourse.

common_mistake: Treating a small ditch as a drain rather than a watercourse that must be protected from silt and oil.

stem: On a city site, a large diesel generator runs all night at low load for security lights, and excavators idle through breaks. Neighbours complain about fumes. Which action best reduces emissions and fuel use?

options.A: Size the generator to its real load or use a mains or battery supply, switch off idling plant, and keep engines serviced
options.B: Run the generator at light load to keep it reliable, because an oversized set is better for the engine than a matched one
options.C: Leave the excavators idling so restarts are avoided, because frequent starting wears engines and creates more exhaust than idling does
options.D: Fit a taller exhaust on the generator to disperse the fumes, since emissions released higher up no longer count as pollution

explanation: A lightly loaded oversized engine burns fuel inefficiently and smokes, and switching off idling plant and servicing engines cut emissions at source.

why_wrong.B: Running a diesel engine at light load causes poor combustion, wet stacking and extra smoke.
why_wrong.C: Idling burns fuel and emits exhaust for no work done, and normal restarts use far less than long idling.
why_wrong.D: Raising the exhaust only moves the emissions, so the quantity of pollutants and fuel burned is unchanged.

common_mistake: Assuming idling plant and a big generator on low load are harmless or save fuel.

stem: A self-employed plasterer with no employees skims ceilings alone in a client's occupied house, using his own mixer and a hired tower. He says health and safety law only covers people who employ others. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He is exempt because working alone creates no risk to anyone else, though he would have to comply once he took on a labourer
options.B: Construction is a prescribed activity, so he must protect others affected by his work and himself meet the work at height and work equipment rules
options.C: He is covered only for the tower, because hired equipment carries the hire firm's duties while his own mixer falls outside the law
options.D: He owes duties to the occupants but none towards himself, since the rules on his own safety belong to the client who engaged him

explanation: Self-employed people in construction owe general duties to others under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act, and the Work at Height and work equipment regulations apply to them for matters they control.

why_wrong.A: Construction work is prescribed, so the duties apply to a lone self- employed worker, and the occupants and passers-by can be affected by his work.
why_wrong.C: Work equipment rules apply to a self-employed person for equipment he uses or controls, including his own mixer, not just hired items.
why_wrong.D: A self-employed contractor in construction must meet the work at height and equipment rules for his own work, and the client's duties do not replace his.

common_mistake: Assuming that having no employees means health and safety law has little to say about your own work.

stem: A 14-employee groundworks firm has no recognised trade union. Staff elect a colleague as their representative of employee safety, but the owner says he need only consult union-appointed representatives, and any training would be in the colleague's own time. Which statement is correct?

options.A: He may consult only the foreman, who then passes decisions on, as long as the firm keeps a signed record that staff were told
options.B: He must consult, though elected representatives have no right to paid time for their role and the owner alone decides what is discussed
options.C: Consultation applies only where a union is recognised, but an elected colleague may attend training at his own expense if the firm gives approval first
options.D: Staff must still be consulted, directly or through elected representatives, who get paid time off and training at the employer's cost

explanation: Where there is no union safety representative the employer must consult employees directly or through elected representatives of employee safety, who get reasonable training and paid time off to carry out the role.

why_wrong.A: Passing on decisions is information, not consultation, which means listening to employees' views before decisions are made.
why_wrong.B: Elected representatives are entitled to paid time off, and consultation must cover set matters such as new equipment, training and competent persons.
why_wrong.C: The duty to consult covers employees not represented by a union, and the employer must bear the cost of reasonable training.

common_mistake: Thinking consultation on safety is a union matter that a non-union firm can skip or leave to one trusted supervisor.

stem: A painter will spray a two-pack polyurethane coating on steel in a small plant room. The data sheet names isocyanates. He says he will smell it if the level is harmful, so a dust mask and an open door will do. Which statement is correct?

options.A: An open door gives enough dilution in a small room, provided the painter takes regular breaks in fresh air and wears cotton overalls
options.B: Isocyanates matter only to the skin, so gloves and a barrier cream are the full control and no breathing protection is required
options.C: Isocyanates can cause asthma and cannot be judged by smell, so use suitable air-fed or approved respirators with controlled ventilation and health surveillance
options.D: A dust mask is enough for short jobs, because the smell gives early warning and sensitisation only develops after years of heavy use

explanation: Isocyanates are respiratory sensitisers, harmful levels are not reliably detected by smell, and a dust mask does not stop vapour, so proper respiratory protection and surveillance are needed.

why_wrong.A: A small room with one opening does not control vapour, and breaks do not prevent sensitisation.
why_wrong.B: Skin contact is a risk, but the main danger is respiratory sensitisation, which gloves do not prevent.
why_wrong.D: A dust mask does not filter vapour, smell is not a safe warning, and sensitisation can occur after short exposure.

common_mistake: Trusting smell or a basic dust mask to warn of and stop a sensitising vapour such as isocyanate.

stem: After chasing brickwork in a small plant room, fine grey dust lies over the floor and pipework. A labourer proposes sweeping it with a dry brush while wearing a basic paper mask, saying the dust is plainly visible so it is easy to control. What is the best way to clean it?

options.A: Sweep dry with a soft broom after the other trades have left so nobody else breathes the cloud, and prop the door open to ventilate the room
options.B: Sweep dry but wear a half-mask respirator, since correctly fitted respiratory protection removes any need to change the cleaning method used
options.C: Use a standard household vacuum cleaner, which collects the dust without lifting it and so needs no specialist filter
options.D: Vacuum it with an industrial cleaner fitted with a high- efficiency filter, since the finest dust is invisible and sweeping lifts it again

explanation: The most harmful respirable fraction cannot be seen, and dry sweeping lifts it into the breathing zone, whereas a suitably filtered industrial vacuum captures it.

why_wrong.A: This only moves the exposure to the sweeper and leaves airborne dust to settle again, so the method is still wrong.
why_wrong.B: Respirators are a last resort after controlling the source, and they do not stop dust spreading to other workers.
why_wrong.C: Ordinary vacuum filters pass the finest particles straight back out through the exhaust, so a suitable filter is needed.

common_mistake: Judging a dust problem by what can be seen and relying on a mask when a better cleaning method exists.

stem: A labourer rolls a foam earplug, pushes it in without touching his ear, and leaves it sitting half out. He says the plug is comfortable and the breaker sounds only slightly quieter, so it must be working. What should he do?

options.A: Push it in as deep as possible with a fingertip, since the seal gets better the nearer the plug sits to the eardrum itself
options.B: Keep it as fitted, because comfort shows the plug is sitting correctly and a little noise will always get past any earplug in a loud area
options.C: Roll it thin, pull the ear up and back, insert it fully and hold until it expands, then refit it if sound is not clearly muffled
options.D: Swap to a larger plug and leave it uncompressed, as soft foam fills the canal by itself without rolling or holding

explanation: A foam plug gives protection only when it is fitted fully into the canal and allowed to expand to seal, and a poor seal shows as little drop in noise.

why_wrong.A: Pushing plugs deep risks injury to the ear and is not how the seal is achieved.
why_wrong.B: Comfort does not show a seal, and a plug left half out gives much less protection than its rating suggests.
why_wrong.D: Foam plugs must be rolled so they fit the canal and held while they expand, or they will not seal properly.

common_mistake: Assuming any earplug that is in the ear gives its full rated protection without checking how it fits.

stem: A precast concrete stair has been craned into a new stairwell but the balustrades and landing edge protection are not yet fitted. Trades will use it for a fortnight, and the supervisor says firm treads make it a safe route. What is needed before use?

options.A: Handrails on the wall side only, because the stair is a route rather than a work platform and open sides need no rails
options.B: Painted edge markings on the treads and a notice, as fixed guards would obstruct materials being carried up the stair
options.C: A warning sign at the foot limiting use to trained operatives, since edge protection is needed only once a task is being carried out on the stair
options.D: Temporary handrails and guardrails at open sides and landings, treads kept clear of debris, and lighting so the route is visible

explanation: A stair in use needs edge protection wherever a person could fall, plus a clear, lit route, because a firm tread does not stop a fall from an open side.

why_wrong.A: Open sides and landing edges are where falls occur, and the type of use does not remove the need to guard them.
why_wrong.B: Markings and notices only warn, and materials handling is planned around the protection rather than by leaving edges open.
why_wrong.C: A stair used as a route is still a place from which a person could fall, so a sign does not replace physical protection.

common_mistake: Treating a stair as safe just because it is solid, and forgetting the open sides, landings and housekeeping.

stem: A hire company delivers a trench shield and hydraulic props, with a delivery check sheet signed as ready for use. The foreman says this satisfies the inspection rules, so the gang can enter once the shield is placed. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A competent person must inspect the excavation and supports at the start of each shift and after any event affecting stability
options.B: The delivery sheet covers the equipment, so only the ground needs checking, and only before the first entry to the trench by the gang
options.C: A competent person need inspect only when the shield is first placed, then again if the foreman changes the arrangement
options.D: The hire firm's signature passes the inspection duty to them for as long as the shield remains on hire to the contractor

explanation: The excavation rules require inspection by a competent person at the start of each shift and after events likely to affect strength, whatever the hire firm checked before delivery.

why_wrong.B: Support equipment is part of the shift inspection, and the ground and supports need re-checking at each shift and after events.
why_wrong.C: Inspection is required at the start of every shift in which people work in the trench, and also after events affecting stability.
why_wrong.D: The contractor controlling the work keeps the duty to have the excavation inspected, and hiring does not transfer it.

common_mistake: Treating a supplier's delivery check as a substitute for the inspection of the trench on site each shift.

stem: The picture shows a site pickup and plant trailer at the gate before joining a public road. The driver says the trip is only two miles and the machine's own parking brake will hold it. What must be done before he leaves?

options.A: Apply the parking brake and chock the tracks on the deck, because chocks are enough to hold plant on a trailer
options.B: Leave the machine as loaded but keep to low speed and send a banksman on foot behind the trailer to warn the following drivers on the road
options.C: Isolate the hydraulics and remove the key, since an immobilised machine cannot move off the trailer during a short trip
options.D: Secure the machine to the trailer with chains or straps at its anchor points, lower the bucket, and check the towing limit is not exceeded

explanation: Plant must be restrained to the trailer so it cannot shift or fall on the road, and the combined load must be within the towing vehicle's limits, however short the journey.

why_wrong.A: Brakes and chocks resist movement but are not a recognised means of load restraint, and they can fail under braking forces.
why_wrong.B: Slow speed and a banksman do nothing to stop an unrestrained machine moving or falling when braking or turning.
why_wrong.C: Isolating the machine does not restrain it, because the whole machine can still slide or tip on the trailer deck.

common_mistake: Believing a short journey, or the machine's own brake, makes proper load restraint unnecessary.

stem: A hired lifting beam is to carry a 3-tonne precast lintel on a mobile crane. The beam's plate is badly faded, and the lift supervisor says that as the crane chart allows 4 tonnes at that radius, the lintel weight is the only figure to check. What is the best response?

options.A: Check the beam's working load limit and examination certificate but ignore its weight, since accessories are included within the crane's rated figure
options.B: Accept the faded plate if the hire firm says verbally that it suits 3 tonnes, then count only the lintel against the crane chart figure
options.C: The crane's rated capacity covers whatever it lifts, so accessories need no marking provided the lintel is within the chart
options.D: Confirm the beam's working load limit is clearly marked and its examination is current, then add its weight to the load checked against the crane

explanation: Lifting accessories must be clearly marked with their safe working load and be examined, and their own weight and that of slings count towards the load the crane carries.

why_wrong.A: Crane charts give capacity for the load on the hook, so the beam, slings and any hook block weight must be added by the planner.
why_wrong.B: Marking must be clear on the equipment itself, and the beam's weight is part of the load the crane carries.
why_wrong.C: Accessories have their own working load limits and marking duties, and the crane chart does not cover them.

common_mistake: Checking only the weight of the item being lifted and forgetting the lifting accessories and their markings.

stem: A recycling wheel wash feeds a settlement tank, and the site manager wants the tank's excess water piped to the nearest surface-water drain, saying settling leaves it clear. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Recirculate the water, desilt the tank regularly, and send excess to foul sewer with the water company's written consent or by licensed carrier
options.B: Add flocculant, test the pH, and discharge to the surface drain if the reading is in range, keeping a written record of every result
options.C: Run the excess onto soft ground at the site edge, where the soil will filter it more effectively than any drain
options.D: Discharge it to the drain once it looks clear, since settlement removes the silt and oil and the flow in the drain dilutes any cement

explanation: Recirculation cuts water use, and wash water may carry silt, oil and alkaline contamination that surface drains must not receive, so it goes to sewer with consent or off site as waste.

why_wrong.B: A pH reading does not show oil, chemicals or other pollutants are absent, and treated wash water is still unsuitable for surface drains.
why_wrong.C: Pollutants soak into soil and groundwater and can reach nearby watercourses, so it is not a safe disposal route.
why_wrong.D: Clear-looking water can still carry oil and high alkalinity, and surface-water drains lead untreated to watercourses.

common_mistake: Judging wash water by how clear it looks rather than by what it contains and where the drain leads.

stem: A firm introduces a battery stud driver with a new safety procedure. It offers an unpaid Saturday course that staff must pay for, and tells a carpenter with twenty years' experience to skip it. Which statement about the employer's duty to provide training is most accurate?

options.A: Everyone exposed to the new risk needs training, given in working hours at no cost to them, however experienced
options.B: Only employees without a recognised trade qualification need training, though it should still be given in working hours at the employer's cost
options.C: Twenty years' experience is enough, so the employer need only hand over the leaflet and may charge staff for any course they want
options.D: Weekend sessions are fine if attendance is voluntary, because the cost of safety training is normally shared between employer and employee

explanation: The employer must provide the training needed for safety, adapt it to new risks, give it during working hours and bear its cost, and experience does not remove that duty.

why_wrong.B: A trade qualification does not teach a new tool's procedure, so the duty covers everyone affected by the changed risk.
why_wrong.C: Experience does not cover a new procedure, and the employer cannot pass the cost of required training to employees.
why_wrong.D: Required training must take place in working hours and the employer must not charge employees for it.

common_mistake: Assuming that long experience or a voluntary Saturday session satisfies the employer's duty to train people on a changed risk.

stem: At completion of a refurbished office, a principal designer compiles the health and safety file. A colleague suggests adding the construction phase plan, all method statements and the accident log. Which approach to the file's content and keeping is correct?

options.A: Include contract documents and insurance certificates as a record of procurement; the local authority building control office then holds it
options.B: Include information for future work, such as as-built drawings, service locations and residual hazards like asbestos; the client then keeps it
options.C: Include the construction phase plan and every method statement so later contractors see how work was done; the principal contractor then keeps it
options.D: Include the project accident log and inspection results so future owners can judge contractor performance; the principal designer then keeps it

explanation: The file records what later builders and maintainers need to know about the structure, and it passes to the client, who keeps it and makes it available to those who need it.

why_wrong.A: Commercial paperwork is irrelevant to future safety, and no authority is responsible for holding the file.
why_wrong.C: These documents describe the completed construction work rather than hazards for future work, and the client, not the contractor, keeps the file.
why_wrong.D: Construction-phase accident records are not information needed for future work, and the file is not held by the designer afterwards.

common_mistake: Treating the health and safety file as a general project archive instead of a short record of what future workers need to know about the building.

stem: A fire alarm sounds on a four-storey fit-out. A fire marshal sweeps the third floor, sees smoke from a store room, and at the assembly point finds one joiner unaccounted for. The fire service is on its way. What should the marshal do?

options.A: Re-enter wearing a dust mask to search the third floor, because he knows the layout better than the arriving fire crew does
options.B: Wait for the joiner to appear and then finish the roll-call, since the fire service only needs a final headcount once the building is empty
options.C: Send two trained colleagues in with extinguishers to check the store and the floor, as early action is part of a marshal's role
options.D: Tell the fire service the joiner's last known location and what the store holds, and keep everyone out of the building

explanation: Marshals get people out and pass vital information to the fire service, who have the equipment and training for any search, so nobody should re-enter.

why_wrong.A: A marshal has no breathing apparatus or search training, and a dust mask gives no protection from smoke.
why_wrong.B: Delay wastes time, because the fire service needs the missing person's likely position and hazards as soon as it arrives.
why_wrong.C: Marshals are not expected to fight fires or send others back in once an alarm has sounded and a person is missing.

common_mistake: Believing that a fire marshal's job continues inside the building once everyone else has been evacuated.

stem: An electrician makes about 600 terminations a shift with straight-handled side cutters, bending his wrist sharply to reach panel terminals. By week three his forearm aches constantly. Which change best deals with the cause?

options.A: Swap to a heavier, thicker-handled tool for a firmer hold, since a firm grip needs fewer repeated squeezes
options.B: Supply cutters with an angled head so the wrist stays straight, and rotate the task with other work
options.C: Issue padded gloves and a wrist support so the same bent grip can continue, since the wrist then takes less strain
options.D: Let him work longer on termination days so he has fully free weekends to recover from the aching

explanation: Choosing a tool that suits the task keeps the wrist in a neutral position, and varying the work reduces the repetition that causes forearm strain.

why_wrong.A: A heavier tool adds load to the forearm, and a handle that does not suit the task keeps the wrist bent.
why_wrong.C: Padding and supports leave the awkward wrist posture and repetition in place, so they do not remove the cause.
why_wrong.D: Longer exposure on the same movement raises the strain, and recovery at weekends does not fix the tool or task design.

common_mistake: Treating hand-tool aches as a personal fitness issue instead of choosing a tool whose shape suits the task.

stem: A 60-person site has two first aiders whose First Aid at Work certificates expire next month. The manager plans to wait for a spring annual refresher, saying refreshers are a legal requirement. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Expired certificates still count while the first aiders keep practising their skills, until the needs assessment is next reviewed
options.B: Requalify them before the certificates expire to keep cover; annual refreshers are strongly recommended but not a legal duty
options.C: Annual refreshers are a legal requirement, so a spring session keeps the expired certificates valid and fully satisfies the first aid regulations
options.D: A refresher replaces requalification, so a short half-day course lets the certificates run on without any full course

explanation: A first aider whose certificate has lapsed no longer counts as qualified, and HSE strongly recommends but does not require annual refresher training.

why_wrong.A: Practice does not extend a certificate, so the site would lack qualified cover once the certificates lapse.
why_wrong.C: Refresher courses are recommended rather than mandatory, and they do not revive an expired certificate.
why_wrong.D: A short refresher is not a substitute for requalification when a certificate expires.

common_mistake: Confusing an optional annual refresher with the renewal of a certificate that lets someone count as a qualified first aider.

stem: An electrician will work close to exposed live low-voltage busbars in a switch room. He is issued a vented helmet with metal rivets through the shell, rated for impact only. The supervisor says helmets are all equivalent. What is the best response?

options.A: Allow the helmet, since it only protects against falling objects and rubber gloves deal with the electrical risk instead
options.B: Keep the vented helmet but cover the rivets with insulating tape, since tape restores the shell's insulation against accidental contact with conductors
options.C: Supply an electrically insulating helmet, such as to EN 50365, with no conductive fittings, and still isolate the busbars first
options.D: Choose a heavier industrial helmet, since a thicker shell has more electrical resistance and so suits the live work

explanation: An impact-only helmet with metal parts can conduct, so an electrically rated helmet is chosen for the hazard, and isolation remains the primary control.

why_wrong.A: Gloves do not protect the head from contact, and head protection must suit all the hazards present.
why_wrong.B: Tape on the rivets does not make a vented, impact-only shell electrically rated.
why_wrong.D: Shell thickness does not give a tested electrical rating, and live conductors should be isolated rather than approached.

common_mistake: Assuming any hard hat marked to the impact standard also protects against contact with live conductors.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative has all the PPE a petrol disc cutter needs. What is the most significant problem, and what should be done?

options.A: His ear defenders cannot cope with a petrol cutter, so he should add foam earplugs under them and then restart the cut
options.B: The water feed makes eye protection unnecessary, so the dust mask alone is enough and the cut can continue as it is
options.C: His visor is raised, leaving eyes and face open to fragments, so he should stop and lower it before resuming
options.D: His gloves are a risk near a spinning disc, so he should remove them and hold the slab with bare hands instead

explanation: A disc cutter throws fragments and spray at the face, so eye and face protection must be in place and worn correctly, not parked on the helmet.

why_wrong.A: The ear defenders are worn correctly, and the real gap is the unprotected face and eyes.
why_wrong.B: Spray does not stop fragments or chips flying from the disc, so face protection is still required.
why_wrong.D: Close- fitting gloves are acceptable here, and removing them would increase hand injuries without addressing the face.

common_mistake: Thinking that wearing a visor on the helmet counts as eye protection even when it is not lowered over the face.

stem: A maintenance crew will clear gutters beside four old rooflights set in a sound flat roof. The supervisor proposes yellow warning signs and cones around each one. Which arrangement best controls the risk of falling through?

options.A: Post a lookout to warn anyone who drifts near a rooflight, since a trained person watching acts as a dependable barrier
options.B: Fit securely fixed covers or guardrails strong enough to bear a person around each rooflight, kept in place while working
options.C: Rely on the signs and cones plus a briefing, since visible warnings let trained roofers keep clear of each rooflight
options.D: Lay loose scaffold boards over each rooflight, since boards spread weight and remove any need to secure them in place

explanation: Rooflights can fail under a person's weight, so a physical barrier or fixed load-bearing cover is needed, and signs or cones cannot stop a fall.

why_wrong.A: A lookout cannot physically stop a fall and can be distracted or too far away to react in time.
why_wrong.C: Signs and cones only warn, and a lapse or a trip can still put someone through the glazing.
why_wrong.D: Loose boards can slide or tip, and unsecured covers give a false sense of safety.

common_mistake: Relying on signs, cones or a lookout to protect people from rooflights when a physical barrier or fixed cover is needed.

stem: A surveyor must inspect an unlit basement store reached by a steep ladder-stair. Fuel cans were once kept there and it smells of petrol. He plans to carry an ordinary torch in one hand. What is the best control?

options.A: Ventilate and test the air first, light the stair, and use hands-free lighting certified for flammable atmospheres so both hands stay on the stair
options.B: Use the ordinary torch but switch it on before entering and leave it on, since sparks only come from the switch being operated
options.C: Wear a brighter ordinary head torch with spare batteries, since hands-free light solves the stair problem and the smell will fade
options.D: Open the hatch for ten minutes then enter with the ordinary torch, since the petrol smell proves vapour has dispersed

explanation: Ordinary torches can spark in flammable vapour, and carrying one prevents a safe hold on the stair, so atmosphere control and certified hands-free lighting are needed.

why_wrong.B: Ordinary torches are not certified for flammable atmospheres, and leaving one on does not make vapour safe.
why_wrong.C: A non-certified head torch can still ignite vapour, and a fading smell does not prove the air is safe.
why_wrong.D: A weaker smell is not a measurement of vapour, and an ordinary torch remains an ignition risk.

common_mistake: Assuming any torch is safe to take into a basement that may contain flammable vapour as long as the smell seems to have faded.

stem: A three-person crew will close the nearside lane of a 40 mph single carriageway for pipe repairs. The foreman plans to place cones at the works first, then the signs, and says any operative with a CSCS card may lay them. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Signs can go out in any order, but removal should begin with the advance sign so drivers see the lane reopening as early as possible
options.B: Advance warning signs go out first, then cones from the road edge out to the works, with removal in reverse; those laying must be trained and competent
options.C: Cones go out at the works first to protect the crew, and then the signs follow, as a general CSCS card is enough proof of competence
options.D: Put the signs out last and take them down first, since drivers need warning only once the cones are visible; training matters for signals only

explanation: Following the traffic signs guidance, drivers need warning before they reach the cones, and only people trained in signing, lighting and guarding should set them out.

why_wrong.A: Removal should reverse the setting out, taking the advance sign last so warnings remain until the works are cleared.
why_wrong.C: Drivers approach the cones with no warning in the meantime, and a general card does not prove traffic management competence.
why_wrong.D: Signs must warn drivers ahead of the cones, and all signing, lighting and guarding needs trained, competent people.

common_mistake: Setting out cones to protect the crew before the advance warning signs, and treating a general site card as enough for road signing. PRACTICE TEST 12

stem: A groundworker sees the props removed from a deep excavation beside his work area and walks to the cabin to report it. The foreman threatens discipline for leaving without permission and orders him straight back. What is the correct position?

options.A: Procedures must let workers leave serious and imminent danger without waiting for instruction, keep them out, and protect those acting on a reasonable belief
options.B: He should have waited for the foreman's permission first, because leaving a work area without authority breaks site rules whatever danger he believed he was in
options.C: His protection applies once someone has actually been hurt, because the right to leave covers the aftermath of an accident rather than a danger not yet realised
options.D: He may leave, but the foreman's own assessment decides when he returns, because a supervisor's judgement of the risk overrides the worker's belief about it

explanation: Regulation 8 of the Management Regulations requires procedures for serious and imminent danger, and workers who leave in a reasonable belief of such danger are protected from detriment under employment law.

why_wrong.B: Procedures for serious and imminent danger must allow workers to leave without waiting for instruction.
why_wrong.C: The right applies to serious and imminent danger before harm occurs, which is the whole purpose of leaving.
why_wrong.D: Workers must be kept from resuming work while serious and imminent danger continues, whatever a supervisor claims.

common_mistake: Assuming a supervisor's instruction to carry on outranks a worker's reasonable belief that danger is serious and imminent.

stem: Overnight rain turns a pipe-laying task on a flat slab into one on a wet sloping ramp, and the planned two-person team is now one short. The operative says dynamic risk assessment lets him adapt as he goes. What should happen?

options.A: Carry on at a slower pace with extra care, because a cautious approach offsets both the wet slope and the missing second person on the lift
options.B: Stop and make the area safe, tell the supervisor, and restart once the method statement is revised and the team briefed, because the changes are significant
options.C: Carry on using a quick mental assessment and write it up afterwards, because dynamic assessment replaces the written plan whenever conditions change on the day
options.D: Ask the remaining operative to sign the original method statement again, because a fresh signature shows he accepts the changed conditions on site

explanation: Dynamic risk assessment suits small, unforeseen changes, but when conditions and resources change significantly the planned controls no longer fit and the plan must be formally reviewed.

why_wrong.A: Care and speed are not controls and do not replace the second person or the grip the original plan relied on.
why_wrong.C: On-the-spot judgement supplements a plan and cannot replace review when the task and team have changed significantly.
why_wrong.D: Signing a plan that no longer matches the work records acceptance without making the task any safer.

common_mistake: Treating dynamic risk assessment as a licence to keep working on the spot after a major change in conditions or resources.

stem: During dusty cutting on one floor of an occupied office, a contractor bags every smoke detector in the building to stop false alarms. Staff are working on the floors above. Which arrangement best controls the fire risk?

options.A: Cover them while the saws run and uncover them at breaks, because occupants would smell smoke and raise the alarm among themselves
options.B: Bag all detectors but record it in the site diary, because a written note shows the risk was considered and call points will still sound the alarm
options.C: Cover just the detectors in the dusty zone, for the shortest time, with the responsible person's agreement and interim cover, then uncover and test them
options.D: Leave the detectors live and silence the sounders whenever they activate, because dust alarms are known nuisance signals and occupants would see a real fire

explanation: Detection should be disabled only where and when essential, with agreed alternative arrangements, and then reinstated and tested, so occupants elsewhere still get an early warning.

why_wrong.A: Relying on people to smell smoke is not a managed substitute and nobody checks that the covers are removed.
why_wrong.B: Disabling detection across occupied floors removes early warning, and a diary note provides no alternative cover.
why_wrong.D: Silencing sounders defeats the warning for everyone, including people who cannot see the affected area.

common_mistake: Blanking off fire detection across a whole building to avoid nuisance alarms from a localised dusty task.

stem: A joiner's hand is cut on a bench saw whose guard had been off for months. The manager's report says 'operator error'. Further enquiry shows a rushed programme, no supervisor checks and no replacement guard on site. What should the investigation do?

options.A: Order a stronger replacement guard and close the report, because a hardware fix removes any need to look at pressure or supervision on this job
options.B: Interview just the joiner and his gang, because managers and planners were away from the saw and could not have contributed to the injury here
options.C: Look past the joiner to why removal was possible and tolerated, including pressure, supervision and supplies, and fix those causes too
options.D: Accept the finding, because the joiner chose to work without the guard and that decision is the real cause, so retraining him closes the matter

explanation: A sound investigation seeks underlying and root causes in the management system, not only the immediate act, so that the failure cannot simply recur with another worker.

why_wrong.A: A new guard alone leaves the programme pressure and missing checks that let the old one stay off.
why_wrong.B: Managers set the programme, supervision and supplies, so leaving them out hides the underlying causes.
why_wrong.D: Stopping at the immediate act ignores the system failures that made the unsafe act likely and easy.

common_mistake: Closing an investigation at the first person who did something unsafe instead of asking why the system allowed it.

stem: A client's survey of a 1970s office lists no asbestos, but notes that the ceiling void and riser cupboards were 'not accessed'. A contractor plans to strip out both next week. How should he proceed?

options.A: Presume those areas contain asbestos until a refurbishment survey covering them shows otherwise, and keep work out of them until the results are known
options.B: Rely on the client's word that the risk is low, because the other areas were clear and voids in the same building will be similar
options.C: Strip both areas using wet methods and sample any suspect material afterwards, because test results will then show what the contractor should do next
options.D: Proceed because a survey that lists no asbestos shows the building is clear, with the unvisited notes being routine caveats from the surveyor

explanation: Areas not inspected must be presumed to contain asbestos, and refurbishment work needs a survey that reaches the areas to be disturbed before it begins.

why_wrong.B: Different materials are used in voids and risers, and a client's assumption is not a survey result.
why_wrong.C: Sampling after disturbance has already released any fibres, which defeats the purpose of identifying material first.
why_wrong.D: The absence of listed asbestos says nothing about areas that were not inspected.

common_mistake: Reading a survey that lists no asbestos as proof that every part of the building is clear.

stem: Two labourers must move a half-full 45-litre sealed plastic drum of thick liquid across site by hand. The load shifts with each step. A colleague says a coordinated two-person lift deals with the weight. What is the best approach?

options.A: Top the drum up until it is full and then lift as a pair, because a full drum cannot slosh and so is more predictable to carry across uneven ground
options.B: Fit both labourers with back-support belts and carry it low and close, because the belts take the strain from the spine for the whole shift ahead
options.C: Lift as a pair with one person calling each movement, because agreed signals remove the risk from contents that move during the long carry across site
options.D: Avoid hand carrying by decanting into smaller containers or using a mechanical aid, as a shifting load is unpredictable even with two people

explanation: Under the manual handling hierarchy, an unstable load that moves is a hazard in itself, so avoiding hand carrying or reducing the load is better than relying on a coordinated team lift.

why_wrong.A: Filling it adds weight and makes the task heavier, and does not address carrying by hand over distance.
why_wrong.B: Belts are not a recognised control for unstable loads and do not replace avoiding or reducing the hazard.
why_wrong.C: Coordination helps with timing but cannot control a load whose centre of gravity keeps shifting underfoot.

common_mistake: Assuming that two people sharing a lift removes the hazard from a load that is awkward, unstable or shifting.

stem: A hire company delivers a boom MEWP with a service sticker, and the operator completes his daily checks. The thorough examination report in the cab is dated seven months ago. The supervisor says the sticker and checks cover it. What is correct?

options.A: The machine is fine, because a service sticker shows a competent engineer has checked it and the operator's daily check then confirms it is fit for use today
options.B: The report is needed when a MEWP goes over eight metres, because lower machines are classed as access equipment rather than lifting equipment at work
options.C: The report is out of date, as a MEWP needs thorough examination at least every six months and neither servicing nor daily checks replace it
options.D: The report is in date, because the twelve-month interval for general lifting equipment applies to a hired MEWP in just the same way as to other plant

explanation: Equipment used to lift people needs a thorough examination by a competent person at least every six months under LOLER, and servicing and operator checks are separate duties.

why_wrong.A: A service is not a thorough examination, and daily checks cannot substitute for the examination interval.
why_wrong.B: Thorough examination is required whatever the working height, because the platform lifts people.
why_wrong.D: Equipment that lifts people has the shorter six-month interval, not the twelve months for other lifting equipment.

common_mistake: Treating a recent service or the operator's daily check as proof that the thorough examination is up to date.

stem: Look at the scene. The crew say the tower is safe because the castors are braked, the outriggers are fitted and the platform has full guardrails. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The base is levelled with loose bricks and timber under the castors, not adjustable legs on firm level ground, so the tower may shift
options.B: The operative should be wearing a harness clipped to the guardrail, because a worker on a tower platform needs fall arrest while he is working
options.C: The tower should be tied to the wall at every lift, because a tower standing next to a building has to be fixed back to it for stability
options.D: The platform is too narrow for a roller, because a mobile tower used for painting needs a platform wide enough to hold a second person too

explanation: A tower must stand plumb on firm level ground using its adjustable legs, since packing under the castors can slip or collapse and defeats the stability that brakes and outriggers are meant to provide.

why_wrong.B: Complete guardrails are the collective protection, and clipping onto a tower is not required and can add load.
why_wrong.C: Mobile towers are normally free-standing and are kept stable by base ratio and outriggers, not by tying to walls.
why_wrong.D: Platform width is not the issue shown and a single worker on a standard narrow tower is acceptable.

common_mistake: Judging a tower safe from its brakes, outriggers and guardrails without checking that its base is firm, level and set on its own adjustable legs.

stem: A haul route for excavators and dumpers must cross beneath an 11 kV overhead line. The planner proposes leaving the route open, trusting operators to keep their booms low and a banksman to watch the gap. What is the better control?

options.A: Rely on the line being insulated, because covered conductors can be passed at any height by plant without any exclusion zone being set
options.B: Keep the banksman's watch and ask drivers to go slowly, because a trained person on the spot can stop a vehicle that gets too close to the wires
options.C: Mark the line with red and white bunting along the full route, since a visible warning lets experienced operators judge a safe gap for themselves
options.D: Consult the line owner, fence off the zone, and allow one goalposted crossing with a clearance-height notice, so plant passes with booms lowered

explanation: HSE guidance says to keep plant out of the zone with ground-level barriers, to create a minimum number of marked passageways with non-conducting goalposts, and to consult the line owner.

why_wrong.A: Insulation on overhead lines cannot be relied on to protect against contact, so exclusion zones still apply.
why_wrong.B: A banksman cannot reliably judge clearance to a high line, and people are not a physical barrier.
why_wrong.C: Warning flags alone do not physically restrain plant, and judging distances by eye risks arcing.

common_mistake: Relying on operator judgement or a spotter to keep plant clear of overhead lines instead of physical barriers and a controlled crossing.

stem: A mobile crane lifts precast steps from the ground to a first- floor slab. The slinger signals while the load is at ground level, and a second person at the slab edge will receive it. The operator will respond to whoever signals. What is the best plan?

options.A: Leave the operator to judge the landing alone from the cab, because the person who controls the crane is the best placed to put the load down safely
options.B: Name one signaller at a time, hand over with a clear stop and confirm, keep the landing zone clear, and have the operator stop on an unclear signal
options.C: Have the slinger keep signalling after the load rises out of sight, since the slinger knows the load best and can judge the landing from below the slab
options.D: Let both signal together so the operator has two views, because duplicated signals give the operator a double check on each movement of the load

explanation: Only one signaller should direct the operator at any time, handovers must be unambiguous, and the operator should stop on any signal that is unclear or lost.

why_wrong.A: The operator may not see the landing, which is why a signaller is used and the plan must name one.
why_wrong.C: A signaller who cannot see the load or landing cannot direct it safely, so control must pass to someone who can.
why_wrong.D: Competing signals confuse the operator, who needs a single clear source of instruction.

common_mistake: Assuming several people can signal a crane at once, rather than naming one signaller who hands over clearly.

stem: An HSE inspector finds an unsupported trench beside a footpath and sends a written notification of contravention, with no formal notice, because the contractor supports it the same day. The contractor refuses to pay, saying fees follow only enforcement notices. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: A fee can still be charged, as a written notification of material breach triggers it and covers the inspector's time
options.B: The fee covers only the inspector's time on the contractor's site, so office work and later calls with workers cannot be charged for
options.C: A fee applies only if the case is prosecuted and the contractor is convicted, when the court orders the costs to be paid to HSE
options.D: No fee arises because the breach was put right on the day, and fees apply only once an Improvement or Prohibition Notice is served

explanation: Fee for intervention is triggered by a notification of contravention for a material breach, not by an enforcement notice, and it covers the time HSE spends identifying the breach and helping put it right.

why_wrong.B: Chargeable time includes report writing, specialist advice and later discussions as well as time at the workplace.
why_wrong.C: Fee for intervention is separate from prosecution and is invoiced on the strength of the notification of contravention.
why_wrong.D: Fixing the problem quickly does not cancel the fee, and the trigger is the written notification, not a formal notice.

common_mistake: Assuming that putting a breach right quickly, or avoiding a formal notice, means the enforcing authority cannot recover its costs.

stem: Tile-cutters and drain-layers wear waterproof gloves for most of each shift and wash their hands often. One reports itchy, sore skin between his fingers and says the gloves are keeping his hands safe. What is the best advice?

options.A: Use a strong solvent hand cleaner during the shift, because it removes the irritant faster and more thoroughly than ordinary soap
