options.B: He wears no dust mask, so airborne soil dust from drilling in damp ground is the greatest threat to his health on this job
options.C: Loose items such as the dangling scarf end and flapping open jacket can snag on the rotating auger and drag him into it
options.D: His thick leather gloves reduce his feel and grip on the handles, so the machine could twist out of his hands when it snags

explanation: Clothing, scarves and anything loose near rotating parts can be caught and wound in, so close-fitting, fastened clothing with nothing dangling is needed.

why_wrong.A: Thrown soil is a minor concern and the helmet fits properly, whereas entanglement could cause severe or fatal injury.
why_wrong.B: Damp ground in a short task produces little hazardous dust, and long-term dust exposure is a smaller risk than being pulled into a rotating tool.
why_wrong.D: Gloves help with grip, vibration and abrasion on this task, and the picture shows no reason they cause the main danger.

common_mistake: Checking only that the listed PPE is worn and overlooking loose clothing, scarves and drawstrings near rotating machinery.

stem: A traffic crew will work at night beside a 50 mph single carriageway behind a cone taper. The manager issues the cheapest Class 1 hi-vis waistcoats, saying the cones already give protection. What is the best response?

options.A: Keep the Class 1 waistcoats, as their retroreflective bands show up in headlights, provided the cones are positioned accurately by trained staff
options.B: Use Class 3 only for daytime work, since at night the vehicle headlights make the garment class less important than the cone spacing
options.C: Supply the highest class, with the largest fluorescent and retroreflective areas, for fast night traffic, and treat it as an extra layer beside the cones
options.D: Choose Class 2 garments because the class number only describes fabric strength, and any fluorescent colour is equally visible at night

explanation: Higher classes carry more fluorescent and retroreflective material, which suits high-speed roads and night work, and hi-vis clothing supports rather than replaces physical traffic control.

why_wrong.A: Class 1 has the smallest areas of material and is meant for low- risk settings, not fast traffic at night.
why_wrong.B: Retroreflective material works with headlights at night, so the highest class matters most for night work beside fast traffic.
why_wrong.D: The class is set by minimum areas of fluorescent and reflective material, not strength, and fluorescent colour alone adds little in darkness.

common_mistake: Assuming any hi-vis garment is as good as another, or that cones alone make the choice of garment unimportant.

stem: A joiner collects a leaning ladder from the site store on Monday. A tag shows a recorded detailed inspection last month, and he says it needs nothing further until the next one. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He need only check the feet, since the monthly inspection already covers the stiles and rungs and the ladder will be tied
options.B: He must have it inspected and recorded every seven days like all site ladders, so the monthly tag does not meet the requirement
options.C: The tag is enough, as pre-use checks are only needed for ladders that have been left outdoors overnight or stored in poor conditions
options.D: He should still check it before use each working day, because a recorded periodic inspection does not replace a look at feet, stiles and rungs

explanation: Ladders need a pre-use check before each day's use as well as a recorded periodic detailed inspection, because damage can occur at any time between inspections.

why_wrong.A: Stiles, rungs and locks can be damaged between inspections, and tying the top does not make a damaged ladder safe.
why_wrong.B: The seven- day inspection applies to ladders forming part of a scaffold and is not a rule for every ladder on site.
why_wrong.C: Pre-use checks apply to every ladder before use, wherever and however it was stored.

common_mistake: Relying on a periodic inspection tag instead of checking the ladder yourself before each day's use.

stem: Gusts are rising as two roofers carry 3 m profiled steel sheets along a flat roof with guardrails fitted, both clipped to a line. A sheet lifts and swings one man off balance. The supervisor says the harnesses make it safe. What is the best response?

options.A: Stop carrying sheets until the wind eases, since weather must not endanger safety at height, and plan handling to limit exposed sheets
options.B: Keep carrying along the centre of the roof, away from the edge, because wind affects only people working close to the roof edge
options.C: Carry on until an anemometer reads a set speed, since weather limits apply only above a figure that the law fixes for every roof
options.D: Carry on but add a third person to steady each sheet, since the harnesses and guardrails already control the fall risk adequately for everyone

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations require work to proceed only when weather does not jeopardise safety, and a large sheet acts like a sail whatever protects the worker from a fall.

why_wrong.B: Wind acts on a sheet wherever it is carried, and a loss of balance can still cause injury or a fall through the system.
why_wrong.C: No single legal wind speed applies to all roofs, so the duty is to judge whether conditions endanger the task.
why_wrong.D: Fall protection does not stop a sail- like sheet from knocking people over, and more people increase exposure to the same problem.

common_mistake: Believing that harnesses and edge protection make it acceptable to keep handling large sheets in worsening wind.

stem: A 14-tonne excavator is to lift a 1.2-tonne concrete pipe with a chain hooked over the bucket teeth. The operator says the pipe is well inside the cab load chart at that reach and, as it is a one- off, needs no special arrangements. What should happen?

options.A: Proceed because a thorough examination is needed only for machines lifting regularly, and the earthmoving maintenance regime covers a one-off lift
options.B: Use a rated lifting point, count the bucket and hitch weight in the load on the chart, and have the machine thoroughly examined for lifting
options.C: Let the slinger hook on while the operator keeps the boom moving to save time, as long as the load is under the chart value
options.D: Hook the chain on the teeth if the pipe weight is under the chart figure, because only the pipe counts and the bucket is part of the machine

explanation: Attachments count towards the load on the chart, the load must hang from a proper lifting point rather than the teeth, and even occasional lifting needs a thorough examination under LOLER.

why_wrong.A: Even occasional lifting by an excavator needs a thorough examination by a competent person.
why_wrong.C: The operator must not move the machine or load until the slinger is in a safe position, whatever the weight.
why_wrong.D: The bucket and hitch weight must be included in the load, and teeth are not a rated lifting point.

common_mistake: Comparing only the weight of the load with the chart and forgetting the bucket, hitch and lifting-point requirements.

stem: Workers park private cars along the haul road beside the gate, and a single 10 mph sign at the entrance is the only speed control. Loaded dumpers brake hard to avoid the parked cars. What is the best improvement?

options.A: Lower the limit to 5 mph at the gate and tell drivers at induction, since induction is a stronger control than anything built into the site
options.B: Provide a marked parking area clear of plant routes, and back the limit with repeated signs and physical measures like chicanes
options.C: Keep the parking where it is but paint lines to mark the car spaces, since the 10 mph sign already controls dumper speeds sufficiently
options.D: Ask the dumper drivers to sound their horns on approach, so that parked car owners know to keep clear of the moving machines

explanation: Parking areas should be provided wherever practical, and limits are best supported by repeated signs and physical features that drivers cannot easily ignore.

why_wrong.A: Very low limits tend to be ignored, and instruction alone is weaker than physical features that make speeding difficult.
why_wrong.C: A painted line does not move people or cars away from plant routes, and a single sign is a weak speed control.
why_wrong.D: Horns warn people but leave the cars and the speed problem in place, so the hazard is not removed.

common_mistake: Relying on a single speed sign and driver instructions rather than layout and physical speed control.

stem: Clearing scrub for a new access road, an operator finds large holes with fresh spoil, flattened bedding and worn paths on a bank, which look like a badger sett. The manager proposes starting near it at dawn, when the animals should be asleep. What should happen?

options.A: Tell the local planning authority and then carry on, because that notification alone gives the contractor permission to work close to the sett
options.B: Block the holes in the evening once the badgers have gone out to feed, since a sett with no animals inside has no legal protection
options.C: Stop work near the bank, get an ecologist to assess it, and obtain a Natural England licence before work that could disturb the sett
options.D: Proceed as long as no badger is seen or harmed, because the offences cover only injuring or killing the animals themselves

explanation: Badgers and their setts are protected, so interfering with a sett without a licence is an offence even if no animal is hurt, and an ecologist must advise first.

why_wrong.A: Telling the council is not a licence, and work that could affect the sett needs a licence from Natural England.
why_wrong.B: Setts are protected whether or not animals are inside, and blocking holes without a licence is itself an offence.
why_wrong.D: Disturbing, damaging or obstructing a sett is also an offence, even when no animal is injured.

common_mistake: Assuming that wildlife law only applies when an animal is actually seen or harmed.

stem: A contractor seals a room in polythene sheeting to stop dust reaching a live corridor, leaving one taped flap as the exit. The task's risk assessment was written before the enclosure was planned and is unchanged. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Review the assessment, as the enclosure may add risks such as restricted escape, poor light and heat build-up, then amend the controls and brief the gang
options.B: Leave the assessment as written, because sheeting is a control measure in its own right and cannot raise the level of risk for the gang inside the room
options.C: Ask the gang to report any problems at the end of each shift, since they know the task best and can judge the new risks for themselves
options.D: Record the enclosure as a note on the method statement and review the assessment after an incident, since reviews are only triggered by harm

explanation: A control measure can create new hazards, so the assessment must be reviewed when the way a task is set up changes, and the revised controls must reach the people doing the work.

why_wrong.B: Controls can introduce new hazards, and here the enclosure restricts escape, light and ventilation, so assuming it only reduces risk skips the review.
why_wrong.C: Waiting for end-of-shift feedback leaves people exposed meanwhile, and the employer, not the workforce, must assess and control the new risks beforehand.
why_wrong.D: Assessments must be reviewed when circumstances change, not only after someone has been hurt, and a method statement note does not reassess the new risks.

common_mistake: Treating a control measure as automatically safe and forgetting to check what new hazards it brings into the task.

stem: Cordless tool batteries charge overnight on a foam mattress in a cabin beside the stair. At 05:30 one pack is swelling, hissing and smoking as the gang arrive. A labourer offers to carry it outside by hand. What is the best response?

options.A: Raise the alarm, evacuate and call 999 without touching the pack, then charge packs supervised, on hard surfaces and clear of escape routes
options.B: Unplug the charger, cover the pack with a fire blanket and let it cool in the cabin while work starts, as removing power ends the danger
options.C: Carry it outside wearing heavy gloves and drop it on bare ground well away from the cabin, because moving a hot pack removes the fire risk
options.D: Move the other charging packs to a different room and carry on, because only the one swollen pack is faulty and the rest can charge overnight

explanation: A venting lithium-ion pack can burst into flame with no warning, so people should leave and call the fire service rather than handle it, and the cause is addressed by changing how charging is arranged.

why_wrong.B: A damaged cell can overheat and ignite without any external power, and leaving it in an occupied cabin keeps people at risk.
why_wrong.C: Handling a venting pack puts the carrier within reach of a sudden flare or toxic smoke, and it does nothing about how charging was arranged.
why_wrong.D: This ignores the immediate hazard from the smoking pack and leaves the unsafe charging arrangement that allowed the problem unchanged.

common_mistake: Assuming a smoking battery pack is safe to pick up and move, or that disconnecting the charger stops it.

stem: To boost cleaning power, an operative pours a bleach-based mould remover into a bucket of acidic brick cleaner in a small tiled WC. Within a minute he is coughing, with stinging eyes. What is the best action?

options.A: Tip the mixture down the WC and flush it repeatedly, then return to the task once the smell has gone, as the drain removes the hazard
options.B: Finish the rinse quickly with the door open, because the irritation is mild and the gas will clear within a few minutes of ventilation in the room
options.C: Open the window, pour in plenty of water to dilute the mixture and carry on once the coughing has eased, wearing a paper dust mask for the rinse
options.D: Get out into fresh air at once, keep others away, and have the products and COSHH assessment checked before anyone uses them again

explanation: Mixing hypochlorite bleach with an acid releases chlorine gas, so the priority is to get away from the fumes and then fix the cause, which is the product use and the assessment.

why_wrong.A: Disposing of the mixture does not remove the gas already released, and flushing in the same room keeps him breathing the fumes.
why_wrong.B: Chlorine irritation can worsen without warning in a small space, and continuing the task keeps the operative exposed to the hazard.
why_wrong.C: A dust mask gives no protection against chlorine gas, and stirring or diluting the mixture in a small room keeps releasing fumes.

common_mistake: Believing that two cleaning products will work better when combined, rather than checking labels and safety data sheets before mixing.

stem: For several weeks an electrician has soldered with rosin-cored solder in a small plant room. He now wheezes and coughs at night, but thinks it is a cold. He borrows a colleague's inhaler and keeps working as before. What should happen?

options.A: He should tell his employer and see a doctor, mentioning the soldering, so the fume exposure is reviewed and the controls are improved
options.B: He should wait a few weeks to see whether the cough clears, as reporting is only worthwhile once a doctor has confirmed a diagnosis
options.C: He should keep using the inhaler and monitor the cough himself, since symptoms that begin at night cannot be caused by the work done by day
options.D: He should change to a stronger disposable mask and carry on, because a better mask removes the need to report symptoms to anyone else

explanation: Rosin flux fume can cause occupational asthma, which may show hours after exposure, so early reporting lets the employer reassess controls under COSHH before permanent lung damage develops.

why_wrong.B: Early reporting is what allows exposure to be reduced, and waiting for a confirmed diagnosis risks him becoming permanently sensitised.
why_wrong.C: Asthma symptoms from a workplace sensitiser can appear several hours after exposure, including at night, and masking them delays action.
why_wrong.D: A mask is not a substitute for assessing exposure, and once sensitised he may react to very low levels that a mask does not stop.

common_mistake: Writing off a work-related cough or wheeze as a cold because it appears at night instead of during the shift.

stem: Five stock handlers will carry boxes up a leaning ladder to a new mezzanine deck all day for three weeks. The supervisor says ladders are lawful for access and that tying the top makes the arrangement acceptable. Which view is correct?

options.A: Carrying loads in a rucksack with three points of contact makes the ladder acceptable, so a toolbox talk is all the change that is needed here
options.B: Constant loaded climbing is not low-risk, short-duration use, so a temporary stair with handrails is needed and materials should be hoisted
options.C: Swapping the leaning ladder for a large stepladder pushed against the deck edge is the answer, as stepladders suit heavy daily traffic
options.D: A ladder suits any access once it is tied at the top and footed at the base, because securing it makes it suitable whatever the volume or loads

explanation: A ladder is justified only where the assessment shows low risk and short use, or unalterable site features, so frequent loaded access to a deck calls for a stair with materials lifted separately.

why_wrong.A: Good technique helps, but frequent loaded climbing remains a higher risk than a stair, and training does not replace more suitable equipment.
why_wrong.C: Stepladders are for short, light tasks and are not intended as access to another level, so this is a less suitable choice, not a safer one.
why_wrong.D: Securing a ladder does not make it suitable for sustained use or for people carrying loads, and the assessment must justify the choice of equipment.

common_mistake: Treating a ladder as acceptable access for any job once it is tied, however many people use it or what they carry.

stem: Look at the scene. The joiner says the platform is wide, level and standing on a clean floor, so it is as safe as anything he has used. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The trestles are too far apart, so the boards will bend, and spacing them closer would make the arrangement fully safe for this kind of work
options.B: The stepladder is not tied to anything, so lashing its stiles to a trestle leg would be enough to make the set-up acceptable for the work
options.C: The platform has no guardrails, so fitting a top rail and toe boards would fix the problem, whatever else is standing on the boards
options.D: A stepladder stands on the trestle platform for extra height, making an unstable stack with a longer fall, so use a platform of the right height

explanation: Placing a ladder on a working platform adds height and instability to a set-up designed for a fixed level, so the platform should be built or chosen to reach the work.

why_wrong.A: The boards are supported at a sensible spacing and the main fault is the ladder stacked on top, which closer trestles would not correct.
why_wrong.B: Tying a ladder to a trestle does not stabilise the stack, since the base itself can still move and the extra height remains.
why_wrong.C: At about one metre high guardrails are not the main control here, and rails would not stop a fall from the ladder standing above the platform.

common_mistake: Stacking one piece of access equipment on another to reach a bit higher instead of choosing equipment of the correct height.

stem: A mini-excavator bucket splits a yellow polyethylene gas main in a footpath trench and gas hisses loudly. Two groundworkers stand 2 m away and a van with its engine running is at the kerb. What should the supervisor do first?

options.A: Get everyone clear and upwind, keep ignition sources away, then ring the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 and keep the public out
options.B: Backfill the trench over the split with spoil to smother the leak, then ring the gas emergency number once the hissing has stopped altogether
options.C: Try to squeeze the split pipe shut with the bucket or a clamp to stop the flow, and phone the gas emergency number once that is done properly
options.D: Ring the gas emergency number but keep the crew by the trench so they can tell the engineers exactly how and where the pipe was damaged

explanation: Escaping gas can ignite from any spark, so people are moved away and ignition sources kept out of the area while the gas emergency service is called to make the pipe safe.

why_wrong.B: Burying the leak allows gas to travel through the ground into nearby buildings and drains, and it leaves people at the scene.
why_wrong.C: Working at a leaking pipe leaves people close to the gas and risks sparks or further damage, and only the gas emergency engineers should attempt to stop the flow.
why_wrong.D: Keeping people next to an escape puts them at risk of fire or explosion, and details can be given from a safe distance.

common_mistake: Staying near a gas leak to try to stop it, instead of moving everyone away and calling the gas emergency service.

stem: A 2.2 m deep drainage trench will be dug on a former landfill site whose ground investigation notes ground gas. The supervisor plans normal trench support and a no-smoking rule, with a petrol pump available for water. Which plan is best?

options.A: Treat the trench as a possible confined space, monitor its bottom for flammable gas and oxygen during entry, and keep out ignition sources
options.B: Rely on the open air to disperse any gas, because a trench that is open at the top cannot become a confined space whatever the ground contains
options.C: Issue disposable dust masks to everyone entering, as a mask protects against ground gas and no atmospheric monitoring is then required
options.D: Test the air once at the start of the shift and allow the petrol pump if the reading is clear, since gas conditions do not change during the day

explanation: Gases such as methane and carbon dioxide collect in deep excavations on landfill, so monitoring, entry controls and exclusion of ignition sources are needed alongside normal trench support.

why_wrong.B: Heavier gases can pool at the bottom of a trench even though it is open to the sky, so being open at the top does not prevent a dangerous atmosphere.
why_wrong.C: A dust mask does not filter gas or replace oxygen, so it gives no protection against methane or carbon dioxide.
why_wrong.D: Ground gas can vary with weather and pressure and may appear later, so a single start-of-shift reading does not protect people for the whole shift.

common_mistake: Assuming an open-topped trench cannot hold a harmful atmosphere because the sky is above it.

stem: A bulk diesel delivery is due at a site's 2,000-litre bunded tank, which is close to a surface-water gully. The driver will fill it while the labourer who ordered it is away, and the tank gauge is known to stick. What is the best arrangement?

options.A: Let the driver fill it alone, because the bund will hold any overflow and a bunded tank means no checks on the delivery are required at all
options.B: Place a drip tray under the nozzle and let the driver fill the tank unattended, as the tray will contain any drips from the nozzle
options.C: Trust the gauge and have the driver stop when it reads full, then record the volume afterwards, since the paperwork shows what was delivered to site
options.D: Check the tank's spare capacity, have a trained person present throughout, and cover the gully with a spill kit to hand before filling

explanation: Overfilling and hose leaks are common causes of pollution, so the delivery should be matched to the capacity, supervised, and protected by drain covers and a spill kit.

why_wrong.A: A bund is a last line of defence, and overfilling or hose spills can still run over its edge or reach the gully before anyone responds.
why_wrong.B: A drip tray catches only small drips and does not deal with overfilling, and nobody is present to raise the alarm quickly.
why_wrong.C: The gauge is known to stick, so it cannot be relied on, and a record made afterwards will not prevent an overfill.

common_mistake: Assuming a bunded tank makes oil deliveries safe without anyone checking capacity or watching the filling.

stem: A contractor's consent for demolition near homes sets working hours and a noise trigger level at the nearest facade. A boundary monitor now reads above the trigger at 11:00, well inside the permitted hours. What is the correct response?

options.A: Move the monitor to a quieter position on the site boundary, as a lower reading will show that the work is meeting the limits set
options.B: Wait for a neighbour to complain before acting, since the monitor is only an advisory tool and does not bind the contractor to the conditions
options.C: Investigate the cause, cut the noise with quieter methods, screening or relocated plant, and inform the local authority as the consent requires
options.D: Carry on unchanged, because the work is inside the permitted hours and the hours are the only condition that affects whether noise is acceptable

explanation: Consent conditions usually cover noise levels as well as hours, so a reading above the trigger needs prompt investigation, control measures and notification, even within permitted times.

why_wrong.A: Relocating the monitor to get a better reading misrepresents the impact on neighbours and does nothing to reduce the actual noise.
why_wrong.B: Monitoring against agreed triggers exists so that problems are found early, and the conditions bind the contractor without a complaint.
why_wrong.D: Hours are only one condition, and a level above the agreed trigger signals that the noise controls have failed whatever time it is.

common_mistake: Believing that working within permitted hours means the noise is acceptable, regardless of the measured level.

stem: An inspector serves an Improvement Notice on a Monday, giving 28 days to repair a faulty guard. On day 24 the contractor says he will now appeal, and that the notice will pause while the appeal is heard. Which statement is correct?

options.A: An appeal can be lodged at any point but never suspends an Improvement Notice, so the guard must be repaired by the original deadline either way
options.B: The appeal period is 21 days from service, so he is outside it, the notice is not suspended and the 28-day deadline stands
options.C: Appeals go to the magistrates' court within 28 days of service, and the notice stays suspended until the court has reached a final decision on it
options.D: The appeal period runs for the whole 28 days of the notice, so he can still appeal today and the notice will pause once the appeal has been lodged

explanation: An appeal against an Improvement Notice must be lodged with the employment tribunal within 21 days of service, and only a valid appeal suspends the notice, so the compliance date stands.

why_wrong.A: A valid and timely appeal does suspend an Improvement Notice until it is heard or withdrawn, unlike a Prohibition Notice.
why_wrong.C: Appeals against notices go to the employment tribunal, and the time limit is 21 days rather than 28.
why_wrong.D: The appeal window is 21 days from service and is shorter than the compliance period, so day 24 is too late.

common_mistake: Assuming the appeal window is the same length as the time given to put the problem right.

stem: A labourer is injured by an unguarded saw. HSE tells him it will take no enforcement action. His employer says that without enforcement there was no breach, so no compensation claim can succeed. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A claim can proceed only after HSE has prosecuted or served a notice, because courts award compensation just where a regulator has found a breach of the law
options.B: A claim is possible, but the labourer must prove the breach beyond reasonable doubt, which is the standard HSE would have needed in any prosecution of the firm
options.C: A claim can succeed only if HSE releases its investigation file, since a court cannot properly assess the employer's duties without the regulator's findings
options.D: A civil claim is separate from enforcement, is decided on the balance of probabilities, and is not barred by HSE choosing not to act

explanation: Enforcement and civil compensation are independent routes, and a claimant only has to show negligence or breach of duty is more likely than not, whatever HSE decided.

why_wrong.A: A civil court makes its own findings, and no prosecution or notice is needed before a compensation claim.
why_wrong.B: Beyond reasonable doubt is the criminal standard, whereas civil claims are decided on the balance of probabilities.
why_wrong.C: The court decides the case on the evidence presented, and a claimant does not depend on an HSE file to bring a claim.

common_mistake: Believing that if the regulator takes no action then the employer cannot be held responsible to the injured person.

stem: A risk assessment rates a rare but severe hazard, a pallet fork load falling from height, as 'low' because it has never happened on this firm's sites. The manager signs it off on that basis. Which comment is most accurate?

options.A: The rating is sound because severity matters only when an accident has already taken place on the site in question
options.B: The rating should reflect both likelihood and severity, so a potentially fatal hazard needs controls even where it is rare
options.C: The rating should be raised only if the pallet is heavier than a tonne, since weight alone decides the level of risk
options.D: The rating is sound because risk depends on past events only, and an event that has never occurred cannot be a significant risk

explanation: Risk combines how likely harm is with how severe it could be, and a lack of past incidents does not make a potentially fatal outcome low risk.

why_wrong.A: Severity must be considered in advance, not after harm has occurred.
why_wrong.C: Many factors, not one weight, decide the risk.
why_wrong.D: Absence of past accidents does not remove the possibility of a serious one.

common_mistake: Rating a severe hazard as low simply because nothing has gone wrong so far.

stem: An operative uses a disc cutter measured at 100 dB(A) for 30 minutes a day, and works in quiet conditions the rest of the shift. His supervisor says half an hour is too short to matter. Which view is correct?

options.A: The daily exposure is about 88 dB(A), but protectors become necessary only once it passes the exposure limit value of 87 dB(A) for the whole day
options.B: Only peak sound counts for brief tasks, so one 100 dB(A) reading that is well below the 135 dB peak action value leaves nothing to be done
options.C: Averaged over the shift the half hour falls below 80 dB(A), the lower action value, so no assessment or protection is needed for this short task
options.D: That half hour alone averages about 88 dB(A) over the day, above the upper action value of 85, so noise must be reduced and protectors worn

explanation: Every 3 dB doubles the noise energy, so 30 minutes at 100 dB(A) equals roughly 88 dB(A) for a full day, which is over the upper action value of 85 dB(A).

why_wrong.A: Protectors must be provided at the upper action value of 85 dB(A), and the 87 dB(A) limit already assumes the protectors are being worn.
why_wrong.B: Daily or weekly average exposure and peak sound pressure are separate tests, and passing the peak value does not clear the average.
why_wrong.C: Daily exposure is energy-weighted, so a short burst of very loud noise raises the average far more than the simple arithmetic suggests.

common_mistake: Assuming a short noisy task is harmless because most of the day is quiet.

stem: Labourers on a wet, polished concrete floor wear safety boots with steel toecaps and penetration-resistant midsoles, yet two slip in one week. The supervisor says the toecaps and midsoles make the boots suitable. Which statement is correct?

options.A: An SRA or SRB marking proves grip on every surface, so once the boots carry it the wet floor needs no cleaning, mats or other controls
options.B: Slips come from carelessness rather than footwear, because any boot meeting the toecap and midsole standard has been tested for grip on all common floors
options.C: Toecaps and midsoles protect against impact and sharp objects, not slipping, so the boots need a slip-resistance marking such as SRC
options.D: A stiffer steel midsole increases the contact area with the floor, so it improves grip on smooth wet surfaces and the boots are therefore suitable

explanation: Slip resistance depends on sole compound and tread, tested separately with SRA, SRB or SRC markings, so toe and midsole protection says nothing about grip on wet polished concrete.

why_wrong.A: The test surfaces do not represent every floor, so footwear choice supports but does not replace floor management.
why_wrong.B: Safety footwear standards test toe and sole protection, while slip resistance is tested and marked separately and floor conditions differ.
why_wrong.D: A midsole stops sharp objects penetrating the sole and does nothing for friction between sole and floor.

common_mistake: Choosing boots by their toe and sole protection alone without checking grip for the floor they will be used on.

stem: A scaffold lift has bricks stacked in three tall piles on the boards beside the toe board, and a labourer works on the pavement below. The bricklayer says the toe board holds everything in. What is the best response?

options.A: Cover the piles with sheeting so they cannot be knocked, while the labourer carries on working on the pavement below
options.B: Move the piles to the outside edge so they are easy to reach, and warn people below with a sign on the scaffold
options.C: Leave the stacks as they are, because a toe board is designed to hold any material stored at the edge of the platform
options.D: Keep the stacks below the toe board height, use brick guards or netting where higher, and keep people out of the area below

explanation: Toe boards stop only low items from rolling off, so materials need to be limited in height, guarded where higher and the area beneath controlled.

why_wrong.A: Sheeting does not stop bricks falling and leaves people exposed below.
why_wrong.B: Stacking at the edge increases the chance of bricks falling and a sign does not prevent harm.
why_wrong.C: A toe board only stops low items, not tall stacks.

common_mistake: Believing a toe board makes it safe to stack tall piles of material at a platform edge.

stem: An electrician has isolated and locked off a circuit and must replace a socket. He holds a non-contact voltage stick near the cable, hears no beep and starts work. Which statement is correct?

options.A: A stick is acceptable when its battery light is on, and a plug-in socket tester used afterwards on the same circuit is enough to confirm that it is dead
options.B: Absence of voltage must be proved with an approved voltage indicator, itself checked on a known live source or proving unit before and after
options.C: A multimeter on its bare probes is better than any voltage indicator, because a numeric reading proves the conductors are dead without further checks
options.D: Locking off the isolator proves the circuit dead, so testing is needed only where the isolation was not locked or was done by someone else

explanation: A tester can fail without warning, so it must be shown to work immediately before and after use, and non-contact sticks are not suitable for proving a circuit dead.

why_wrong.A: A lit battery indicator does not show the stick can detect voltage, and a socket tester is not a means of proving a circuit dead.
why_wrong.C: An unproved multimeter with unshrouded probes can fail or give a false zero and is itself a shock and short-circuit hazard.
why_wrong.D: Isolation and proving dead are separate steps, and the test is still needed after a lock is applied.

common_mistake: Trusting a silent tester or a lock-off without proving the tester itself works.

stem: Look at the scene in the yard. The driver says he is only travelling a short distance to the stack. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The forks are carried high while the truck moves, which affects stability and view, and a pedestrian is walking close behind it on the vehicle route
options.B: The pedestrian is on foot in a vehicle yard without safety glasses, which is the only significant issue, as the truck is being driven correctly
options.C: The truck has no flashing beacon to warn the pedestrian that it is moving, which is the main failing, as forks and positions are acceptable
options.D: The truck is travelling unloaded, which makes it less stable than carrying a load, so it should always carry a pallet while moving

explanation: Forks should travel low, as raising them lifts the centre of gravity and blocks the driver's view, and a pedestrian sharing the route directly behind a moving truck is at risk of being struck.

why_wrong.B: Eye protection is not the main danger shown, as the forks are raised and the pedestrian is in the truck's path.
why_wrong.C: The truck does have a beacon, and a beacon would not remove the pedestrian from the route or lower the forks.
why_wrong.D: An empty truck is not made safer by adding a load, and the real issue is the raised forks.

common_mistake: Believing a short trip does not need forks lowered or pedestrians separated from the truck.

stem: A housing site backs onto a play area. At finish, a telehandler is left beside the hoarding with its engine off and brake on, but the forks are raised and the key stays in the cab to save time at 7 am. What is wrong?

options.A: Nothing, because the brake being on and the engine being off make it safe, and leaving the key in lets the early crew move it quickly in an emergency
options.B: The forks need lowering, but the key may stay in the cab if the site gate is locked, since a locked gate keeps all unauthorised people out
options.C: The forks should be lowered and the key removed and secured, so that unauthorised people, including children, cannot start or climb on it
options.D: The key must be removed, but the forks may stay raised, since raised forks are harder for a trespasser or a child to climb onto from the ground

explanation: Unattended plant should be left with brakes on, engine off, equipment lowered and keys removed and secured, which stops unauthorised use and removes a fall and crush hazard.

why_wrong.A: Leaving the key in and the forks raised allows unauthorised use and climbing, and an early start is not a reason to relax security.
why_wrong.B: Gates and hoardings can be climbed or breached, so the key still needs to be secured as a second barrier.
why_wrong.D: Raised forks can fall or be climbed, and attachments should be lowered to the ground to remove stored energy and access.

common_mistake: Assuming that a locked gate, a brake and an off engine are enough to secure plant overnight.

stem: For culvert works, an excavator and a diesel generator stand on a stream bank. The foreman plans to refuel both from a bowser on the bank to save carrying, with the generator sitting on bare ground. Which approach best prevents pollution?

options.A: Fill both machines to the brim each morning so that refuelling is not needed during the day, and keep the spill kit in the site office
options.B: Refuel on an impermeable area well back from the stream, stand the generator on a drip tray, and keep a spill kit close by
options.C: Refuel on the bank but lay a plastic sheet beneath the nozzle only, since small drips cannot reach the water once that ground is covered
options.D: Place a floating boom across the stream before work starts and refuel on the bank, because a boom will contain any fuel that is spilled

explanation: Spills are best prevented by keeping fuel handling away from water, putting secondary containment under static plant and having a spill kit ready, rather than relying on cleaning up afterwards.

why_wrong.A: Overfilling increases spill risk and a spill kit kept far from the work cannot be used quickly enough.
why_wrong.C: A sheet under the nozzle does not contain larger spills or leaks from the generator, and the bank is too close to the stream.
why_wrong.D: A boom is a last line of defence that does not catch all fuel, so it cannot replace preventing spills near the water.

common_mistake: Treating fuel handling beside a watercourse as acceptable provided that a clean-up can follow any spill.

stem: At a 60-person contractor, two trade-union-appointed safety representatives send the director a signed letter asking for a safety committee. He says he will consider it at the year-end review, and that a committee is compulsory only when the HSE orders one. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A written request from at least two safety representatives obliges him to set one up, and it must be in place within three months of the request
options.B: A committee becomes compulsory only when three representatives ask, so he may defer to the annual review and consult the representatives informally until then
options.C: The duty arises only when the trade union itself asks in writing, and the committee must then be established within twelve months of that request
options.D: He may decline if he consults the representatives and records his reasons, because the regulations leave the decision on a committee to his judgement

explanation: Under the Safety Representatives and Safety Committees Regulations 1977, a written request from two or more safety representatives requires the employer to establish a committee no later than three months after the request.

why_wrong.B: The trigger is a written request from two representatives, and the law sets a three-month limit that a review date cannot override.
why_wrong.C: The request comes from at least two safety representatives rather than the union, and the time limit is three months, not twelve.
why_wrong.D: Once two safety representatives request one in writing, establishing the committee is a duty and not a matter of employer discretion.

common_mistake: Assuming a safety committee is a favour the employer can schedule or refuse, rather than a duty triggered by a written request from two representatives.

stem: Roofers torch-on bitumen felt to a flat roof while joiners fit foam insulation boards on the deck below in the same bay. Each subcontractor's assessment rates its own work as low risk. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Let the roofers sign a hot work permit and keep an extinguisher on the roof, since the permit also covers the joiners working beneath them
options.B: Treat the overlap as a combined risk, with the principal contractor coordinating through the construction phase plan so the tasks are separated or sequenced
options.C: Raise the score on both assessments by one level and let the work continue, because a higher rating shows that the overlap has been properly considered
options.D: Accept both assessments, since each employer answers only for its own workers and the combined effect lies outside what either firm must consider here

explanation: Two activities that are low risk alone can create a serious fire risk together, so the principal contractor must coordinate the trades and the assessments must reflect the interaction.

why_wrong.A: A permit and extinguisher respond to a fire but do not separate hot work from flammable insulation and the people below it.
why_wrong.C: Changing a score is not a control measure, and nothing in the work method or sequence has altered.
why_wrong.D: Contractors must cooperate and coordinate because one trade's work creates risks for others, so the interaction cannot be ignored.

common_mistake: Assuming that if every subcontractor's own assessment looks acceptable, the combined activity on the same part of the building must be acceptable too.

stem: A fire alarm sounds on a site with five contractors and several visitors. At the assembly point the marshal finds the visitor sign-in book is in the locked gatehouse, and each firm has only its own list. What is the best arrangement for next time?

options.A: Keep a single up-to-date register of everyone on site, including visitors, that the marshal can carry to the assembly point
options.B: Keep the sign-in book in the gatehouse and let the fire service ask around when they arrive, as they are trained to search
options.C: Rely on the marshals' memory of who arrived that day, because a written register goes out of date within hours
options.D: Leave each firm to count its own people, since the visitors will leave with their hosts and need no separate record

explanation: A roll call is only reliable if there is one current record of everyone present, kept where it can be taken to the assembly point, so nobody is wrongly assumed to be out.

why_wrong.B: The service needs to know quickly who may be missing, and the book is out of reach.
why_wrong.C: Memory is unreliable and a register can be kept current.
why_wrong.D: Separate counts miss visitors and anyone whose firm has not recorded them.

common_mistake: Assuming each contractor's own list is enough to account for everyone on a shared site.

stem: A painter pours solvent-based primer from a labelled 5-litre can into an empty water bottle to carry less up the ladder, then leaves the bottle on the cabin table. He says he is the only person using it. What is the main problem?

options.A: The bottle is acceptable while it stays in his sight all day, since an accident needs someone else to find it and he is the only user
options.B: A screw-top drink bottle is acceptable if it is kept in a locked cabin drawer overnight, because secure storage replaces the need for any label
options.C: A drink bottle could be swallowed by mistake and hides the hazard information, so he should use a sturdy container made for it and labelled
options.D: Writing the product name on the bottle with a marker is enough, because the hazard details are in the safety data sheet in the site office

explanation: Hazardous substances must stay in suitable containers that identify the contents and hazards, because food or drink containers invite accidental swallowing and mislead anyone who finds them.

why_wrong.A: Containers get left, moved and found by others, and one person's watchfulness is not a control.
why_wrong.B: Locked storage does not replace labelling, which matters at the point of use as well as when the substance is stored.
why_wrong.D: The container itself must show the hazards so people and emergency responders can see them without finding another document.

common_mistake: Decanting a hazardous product into a handy drink bottle because only one person will use it.

stem: A labourer who breaks out slabs most days notices ringing in his ears each evening and has started turning the television up. He says it always fades by morning, so it is nothing to worry about. What is the best response?

options.A: Ignore it because the ringing fades overnight, which shows the ears have recovered fully and no lasting harm is being done
options.B: Report it, as ringing after noise is an early warning of damage, and ask for the noise controls and his hearing checks to be reviewed
options.C: Keep working but avoid loud music at home, because noise away from work is the usual cause of ringing in the ears
options.D: Wear thicker ear defenders only on the days it happens, since the hearing loss only builds up on the loudest days of work

explanation: Temporary ringing and muffled hearing after noise show the ears are being harmed, and repeated exposure can cause permanent loss, so the symptoms should trigger a review of controls and health surveillance.

why_wrong.A: Symptoms that fade can still mean cumulative damage that becomes permanent.
why_wrong.C: Work noise is the likely cause here and it should be controlled at source.
why_wrong.D: Protection is needed whenever exposure is high, not just after symptoms appear.

common_mistake: Treating ringing ears that clear overnight as a sign of recovery instead of an early warning.

stem: A fitter cuts out a corroded pipe with an oxy-propane torch that throws molten globules and hot spatter near his face. He is given clear spectacles marked '3 F' and told they are rated for splashes. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Field-of-use numbers rank the protection, so a '9' lens resists everything and the '3' is a weaker version suitable only for lighter spatter
options.B: The '3' covers every liquid hazard including molten metal, and the 'F' shows the lenses are heat resistant, so the spectacles suit the task
options.C: The '3' covers liquid droplets and splashes, not molten metal, so he needs eye protection marked '9' for molten metals and hot solids
options.D: Any eyewear with an impact rating is adequate for hot work, provided the lenses are tinted dark enough to cut the glare from the torch flame

explanation: In EN 166 the field-of-use symbol 3 means liquid droplets or splashes, while 9 means molten metals and hot solids, and the F only shows resistance to low-energy impact.

why_wrong.A: The numbers identify different fields of use and are not a scale, so a higher number is not a stronger version.
why_wrong.B: The F marks low-energy impact resistance only and says nothing about heat, and the 3 does not cover molten metal.
why_wrong.D: Impact resistance and tint do not give protection from molten metal, which needs the field-of-use symbol 9.

common_mistake: Reading a lens marking as a general quality rating instead of checking that the symbol matches the actual hazard.

stem: Look at the welder fixing the steel stair stringer. Which change to what he is wearing would most reduce the risk of injury from this task?

options.A: Soak the trouser turn-ups with water before each weld so that falling sparks are put out the moment they land on the cloth
options.B: Add a disposable plastic apron over the trousers so that spatter slides off the surface and away from the welder's legs
options.C: Change the leather safety boots for rubber wellingtons, which shed sparks and spatter more easily than leather and are quicker to take off
options.D: Swap the turned-up trousers for flame-resistant ones with no cuffs, worn over the boot tops, so sparks and spatter have nowhere to collect

explanation: Turn-ups and open pockets trap sparks and molten spatter against the skin, so welders should wear cuffless flame- resistant trousers that cover the tops of the boots.

why_wrong.A: Wetting clothing is not a control, and damp fabric can cause steam burns and increase the risk of electric shock.
why_wrong.B: Plastic melts and sticks to skin when spatter lands on it, and it does nothing about the turn-ups that trap sparks.
why_wrong.C: Rubber melts and sticks to the skin when hit by spatter, whereas leather resists it, so wellingtons would make injury worse.

common_mistake: Checking that a welder has a helmet and gauntlets while overlooking turn-ups, pockets and gaps that collect sparks.

stem: A roofer works from a low platform 3 m above a concrete yard. His 2 m lanyard with energy absorber is clipped to an anchor at foot level, and the supervisor says the harness makes the job safe. What is the main weakness?

options.A: A 2 m lanyard is too short for fall arrest, so a longer lanyard on the same anchor would let the system stop him before he reached the ground
options.B: The foot-level anchor is satisfactory, but a second lanyard should be fitted because two connections would halve the distance he could fall in a slip
options.C: The harness stops a fall before he reaches the ground once the absorber is fitted, so the only gap is the plan to rescue him afterwards
options.D: The clear space below may be too small, since lanyard, absorber and harness stretch could let him hit the ground, so edge protection is preferable

explanation: A fall-arrest system needs enough clearance below for the lanyard, the absorber to extend and the harness to stretch, and collective edge protection prevents the fall altogether.

why_wrong.A: A longer lanyard lengthens the fall, which makes it more likely he hits the ground before the system stops him.
why_wrong.B: Adding a second lanyard does not shorten the fall distance, which depends on lanyard length, absorber extension and anchor position.
why_wrong.C: Rescue planning matters, but the absorber lengthens the fall, so he may hit the ground before the system stops him.

common_mistake: Believing that wearing a harness and lanyard means a fall will always be stopped, without checking the clearance beneath the worker.

stem: Inside a ventilated, gas-tested tank, a fitter cuts out a corroded pipe with oxy-fuel kit, its cylinders on a trolley beside him. At lunch he shuts the cylinder valves and leaves the torch and hoses coiled inside. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The cylinders may stay inside if they are chained upright to the trolley, since securing them prevents falls and so removes any leak risk
options.B: Closing the cylinder valves is enough, because gas can no longer reach the hose or torch once the supply has been shut off at the source
options.C: Cylinders should stay outside with gas fed in by hose, and the hoses must be removed or disconnected at the cylinder whenever work stops
options.D: The set-up is fine while the gas test is still in date, since a valid test shows that the atmosphere is safe for hot work throughout the whole day

explanation: Leaking hoses or torches can enrich the air with oxygen or fill the space with fuel gas, so cylinders stay outside and hoses are taken out or disconnected whenever work is suspended.

why_wrong.A: Chaining prevents toppling but does nothing about leaks, and cylinders should not be taken into the confined space.
why_wrong.B: Gas remains in the hoses and fittings after the valves close, and a leak there can still escape into the confined space.
why_wrong.D: A test records conditions only at the moment it was taken, so it cannot protect against a leak that begins afterwards.

common_mistake: Assuming that a clean gas test at the start of the shift covers hot work equipment left in the space during breaks.

stem: An agency driver trained only on a different make of tail lift rides the platform with a loaded roll cage, pulling it back from the vehicle floor toward himself. He says his licence and a manual handling course are enough. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He needs training on that type of tail lift, and loads should be pushed off the vehicle with him clear of the open platform edge
options.B: His licence and manual handling course cover it, since all tail lifts work in much the same way and extra familiarisation is only a company preference
options.C: Pulling the cage toward himself keeps it under better control, and a platform resting at ground level makes training and edge awareness unnecessary
options.D: Standing on the ground and steadying the cage beneath the lowering platform is safer, because it keeps him off the platform edge altogether and away from the vehicle

explanation: Operators need training on the specific tail lift they use, and pulling a load back toward oneself on the platform risks the load toppling or the operator stepping off the open edge.

why_wrong.B: Controls and residual hazards differ between tail-lift types, so training specific to the lift in use is expected.
why_wrong.C: Pulling a load toward the operator makes it more likely to topple onto him, and a platform edge remains a fall hazard.
why_wrong.D: Standing under or beside a moving platform creates a crushing risk, and steadying a load by hand does not control it.

common_mistake: Assuming a driving licence and general manual handling training qualify someone to use any tail lift. PRACTICE TEST 14

stem: A groundworks contractor on a multi-contractor project wants to sublet its drainage package to a firm it has never used. The site manager says the principal contractor's own vetting covers everyone. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Once the package is sublet, the duty to plan and manage that work passes to the new firm, which becomes solely answerable for its own workers
options.B: The principal contractor's induction is sufficient, so the contractor need not give the firm any information about hazards in the drainage package
options.C: Only the client may check competence on a project, so the contractor need only ask the sublet firm for its insurance certificate before it starts work
options.D: The contractor must itself take reasonable steps to confirm the firm's skills, knowledge, experience and capability, and then pass on the information it needs

explanation: Anyone who appoints a contractor under CDM 2015 must take reasonable steps to check it meets the competence condition, and must provide the information the firm needs, regardless of the principal contractor's own checks.

why_wrong.A: The contractor keeps its duty to plan, manage and monitor work under its control, and cannot hand it off by subletting.
why_wrong.B: An induction covers general site matters, whereas the appointing contractor must still give the firm the information it needs for its own work.
why_wrong.C: The duty to check falls on every person who appoints a contractor, not only the client, and insurance says nothing about competence.

common_mistake: Assuming that a principal contractor's checks or an induction replace your own duty to be satisfied about a firm you bring in.

stem: A client invites three contractors to tender for refurbishing a 1960s warehouse. One asks for existing drawings and past survey reports. The client replies that the winner will find any hazards when it arrives, so nothing will be issued before the contract. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The client must give the relevant pre-construction information as soon as practicable to every contractor being considered, so each can price and plan the risks
options.B: The contractor is responsible for discovering hazards on arrival, because a client with no construction experience cannot be expected to hold such information at all
options.C: The client need only issue it to the winning contractor, since unsuccessful tenderers have no part in the project and are owed no duty of care at all
options.D: A short verbal briefing at the start of the work is enough, provided the principal contractor writes down any hazards found in the first week

explanation: CDM 2015 requires the client to provide pre- construction information as soon as practicable to every designer and contractor appointed or being considered for appointment.

why_wrong.B: The client must give what it has or can reasonably obtain, and a lack of experience does not remove the duty.
why_wrong.C: The duty extends to contractors being considered for appointment, so tenderers must receive it to plan and price safely.
why_wrong.D: Information must be provided early enough to influence pricing and planning, not discovered after work starts, and verbal briefings leave gaps.

common_mistake: Treating hazard information as something the winning contractor finds out for itself rather than something the client must supply early.

stem: A site beside a river receives an Environment Agency flood warning, meaning flooding is expected, with the river rising and perhaps an hour before the access road floods. A crane is parked and a concrete pour is half finished. What is the best response?

options.A: Keep everyone on site above the ground floor of the cabins, since the cabins are raised and the river level will drop again within hours
options.B: Stop work, make safe what can be done quickly, and take everyone by the agreed route to higher ground, leaving plant behind if time runs short
options.C: Finish the pour to avoid wasting concrete, then move the crew out, because a severe flood warning is the point at which sites should properly stop work
options.D: Send the whole crew to move fuel, plant and chemicals to high ground first, then evacuate people once the site has been fully secured

explanation: A flood warning means act now, so the emergency plan is triggered and the priority is getting people out before the access road floods, with property secondary to life.

why_wrong.A: Sheltering in place risks being trapped, and the agreed plan is to leave by a safe route before access floods.
why_wrong.C: A flood warning already means flooding is expected, so waiting for a severe warning risks losing the only access route.
why_wrong.D: Protecting property before people puts workers at risk of being cut off, and life must come before equipment.

common_mistake: Waiting for flood water to arrive, or for the worst warning level, before moving people out of a site.

stem: A rubbish bin of paper and wrapping smoulders in an open- fronted store. The alarm has been raised and a trained worker takes a suitable extinguisher. The fire is waist height, with a clear exit behind him. How should he use it?

options.A: Stand a few metres back with the exit behind him, sweep the jet across the base of the flames, and withdraw if the fire is not quickly controlled
options.B: Carry on discharging even if the fire grows, because the alarm has been raised and the fire service will arrive to take over from him shortly
options.C: Stand between the fire and the only exit so that it cannot spread, and aim at the flames from above while crouching low to avoid the smoke
options.D: Move in until the flames are within arm's reach so the jet is accurate, aim at the top of the flames, and keep discharging until the extinguisher is empty

explanation: Keeping an escape route at his back, aiming at the base of the fire and retreating if it grows keeps a small fire fight safe, with the alarm already raised.

why_wrong.B: Fighting an uncontrolled fire puts him at serious risk, since extinguishers are only for small fires and he must be ready to leave.
why_wrong.C: Standing between a fire and the exit removes his escape route and traps him if the fire grows.
why_wrong.D: Standing too close risks burns, flame tips are not the fuel, and he should retreat if the fire is not controlled.

common_mistake: Staying to fight a fire for longer than is safe because an extinguisher is in your hands.

stem: A flooring crew applies fast-curing methyl methacrylate resin in a below-ground plant room. They shut the doors to keep it warm, run a halogen work lamp and plan to wear dust masks. The vapour smells strongly. What is the best advice?

options.A: Remove ignition sources such as the halogen lamp, ventilate with extraction low down, and use suitable respiratory protection if vapour remains
options.B: Swap the dust masks for FFP3 disposable masks, since a higher-grade particle filter will also remove the resin vapour from the air breathed in
options.C: Add a fan heater to speed the cure and shorten exposure, provided it is switched on before the crew begin and left running until the floor sets
options.D: Keep the doors shut and rely on the smell as a warning, because a strong odour tells the crew when the vapour has risen to a harmful level in the room

explanation: The resin vapour is flammable and heavier than air, so ignition sources must go and ventilation must clear low points, with correct respiratory protection if exposure remains.

why_wrong.B: Particle filters do not remove organic vapour, which needs a suitable gas or organic vapour filter or fresh-air supply.
why_wrong.C: A heater adds an ignition source in a space where flammable vapour collects, and warming also increases evaporation.
why_wrong.D: Smell is not a reliable measure of exposure or of flammable concentration, and closing the doors lets vapour build up.

common_mistake: Judging whether vapour is safe by how strongly it smells and not by the product's hazards.

stem: Two plasterers of very different heights carry a 2.4 m board along a corridor, one walking backwards, with no word spoken and a pallet jack parked in the route. The board bends and they nearly drop it. What is the best way to improve the lift?

options.A: Let the taller person take the heavier end and the shorter one steer, because the two will adjust to each other as they walk along the corridor together
options.B: Clear the route, pair similar heights, carry the board on edge facing forward, and have one person give commands to lift, move and lower
options.C: Use the same method but each wear gloves and back support belts, so that any slip is less likely to cause an injury to either of them during the carry
options.D: Lift the board flat at waist height between them with both facing inwards, since this keeps the load close to the body and supports the whole sheet

explanation: Team lifting works when the route is planned, partners suit each other, the load is held steadily, and one person coordinates every movement.

why_wrong.A: Unplanned adjustment causes sudden load shifts, and uneven height makes the load tilt and unbalances both people.
why_wrong.C: Gloves and belts do not fix the planning, route or coordination faults, and back belts are not proven to prevent injury.
why_wrong.D: A long flat board sags, cannot be gripped well and makes walking backwards or sideways likely, which raises the risk of a trip.

common_mistake: Assuming two people automatically make a heavy or awkward load safe without agreeing who leads and how it will move.

stem: A materials hoist platform carries a notice showing a 500 kg safe working load. A labourer loads two pallets of blocks of 320 kg each, then lays 6 m tubes across the top with one metre sticking out beyond the platform. What is wrong?

options.A: Nothing, as each pallet is under 500 kg and the hoist motor will cope, provided the tubes are laid on top of a pallet and the landing gates are shut
options.B: The 640 kg is acceptable for a short trip with nobody at the landing, as the limit only applies when people are standing below the hoist
options.C: The 640 kg total exceeds the safe working load, and loose tubes projecting past the platform can snag on landings or fall out
options.D: Only the tubes are the issue, since pallets can exceed the notice by a margin if the hoist is serviced regularly and its cable is checked daily by the operator

explanation: The safe working load applies to everything on the platform together, and loads must be contained and secured within the platform so they cannot catch or fall.

why_wrong.A: The rating covers the combined load, and closed gates cannot hold tubes projecting past the platform.
why_wrong.B: The rated load is a structural and braking limit for every journey, not a guide that depends on whether people are nearby.
why_wrong.D: The posted safe working load is a limit that must not be exceeded, whatever the hoist's condition.

common_mistake: Checking each item against the load limit instead of adding up everything that goes on the platform.

stem: Look at the scene. A painter needs to reach a high soffit. Which feature of the set-up most increases the chance of a serious fall?

options.A: The tower stands on a smooth concrete floor, which cannot hold castors in position even when every brake is firmly applied
options.B: A paint tray and bucket on the platform floor will slide off the edge unless every item is tied to the guardrail with rope
options.C: A second worker stands at the base looking up, so he is likely to be struck by falling tools from the platform above him
options.D: A stepladder is opened on the tower platform, so he works above the guardrails on an unsteady, extended footing

explanation: Adding a stepladder to a tower platform lifts him above the guardrail protection and adds instability, so the correct fix is to build the tower higher or use a suitable platform.

why_wrong.A: Braked castors on a level concrete floor are acceptable, and the floor is not the main problem shown.
why_wrong.B: Tools and containers can be managed with toe boards, so this is a lesser matter than standing above the guardrails.
why_wrong.C: The colleague at the base is a minor risk compared with the painter's own exposure to a fall from a ladder on a platform.

common_mistake: Believing a tower's guardrails still protect you when you stand on something to gain extra height.

stem: A mechanical contractor will replace a pipe section directly beneath the runway of a live overhead travelling crane in a client's factory bay. The crane's power runs along conductor bars on the runway. The client suggests hazard tape and a radio call to the crane driver. Which arrangement is best?

options.A: Rely on a radio call to the driver before each lift and post a banksman in the bay, since the crane can then keep working elsewhere in the bay
options.B: Switch the crane off at its pendant and keep the key with the driver, so that nobody else can start it while the pipe is being replaced
options.C: Agree a permit with the client so the crane is isolated and locked off, parked clear of the work area, with the contractor's own lock on the isolator
options.D: Fence the zone with hazard tape and a sign and have the crane driver promise not to travel over it, as the tape marks a clear exclusion area

explanation: Isolating and locking off the crane removes both the moving load and the live conductors, and the contractor's own lock gives personal control over reinstating power.

why_wrong.A: Radio and a banksman still leave a live crane able to travel over the work, and they depend on communication that can fail.
why_wrong.B: A pendant stop does not isolate the supply, and the key held by the driver gives the contractor no control over reinstating it.
why_wrong.D: Tape and a promise are administrative, and do not physically prevent travel or remove the live conductors above the work.

common_mistake: Accepting warnings and promises in place of a physical isolation that the person at risk controls.

stem: A public footpath crosses a housing site between the compound and the dig area, and a dumper must cross it about every ten minutes. The manager plans a "plant crossing" sign, a flashing beacon and a banksman who waves pedestrians through. Which option best follows good practice?

options.A: Rely on the sign and stop the dumper only when the driver spots someone, because members of the public have a duty to watch for site traffic
options.B: Leave the path open but fit the dumper with a reversing alarm and an audible horn that sounds whenever it nears the crossing point
options.C: Divert the public along a fenced alternative route agreed with the highway authority, so plant and pedestrians never share a crossing
options.D: Keep the footpath open and add speed limits, a second beacon and a trained banksman who stops the public whenever plant needs to cross

explanation: Separating pedestrians from vehicles removes the conflict altogether, which is stronger than any warning, signal or person trying to control a shared crossing.

why_wrong.A: The public owe no such duty on a site, and the contractor must protect people affected by its work.
why_wrong.B: Alarms and horns only warn, and they depend on pedestrians noticing and reacting in time.
why_wrong.D: A shared crossing still relies on people obeying a banksman, which is weaker than removing the conflict by separation.

common_mistake: Controlling a shared crossing with signs and beacons when the public could be kept out of the plant's path altogether.

stem: A school asks a groundworks firm to host a 15-year-old for a week of work experience. The manager plans to use the site's general risk assessment, place him with the crew breaking out a slab, and tell his teacher the details afterwards. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The school stays responsible for him throughout the placement, so the firm need only give the normal site induction and rules, since he is not on its payroll
options.B: Briefing his teacher at the end of the week is enough, with a parent told only if he is kept on afterwards, because the information duty protects long-term staff
options.C: A competent supervisor may keep him beside the slab- breaking crew, because close supervision lifts the legal limits on work for anyone under school-leaving age
options.D: A specific assessment for a child must be made before he starts, he must be kept off tasks whose risks he cannot recognise, and his parent must be told the risks beforehand

explanation: The Management Regulations require an assessment that considers a young person's inexperience before employment, bar a child from work with unrecognisable accident risks, and require risk information to reach a parent before a child starts.

why_wrong.A: The host controls the site and its hazards, so it carries its own duties to assess risks and protect the pupil while he is there.
why_wrong.B: The duty is to give a parent comprehensible risk information before a child starts work, whether or not the placement continues.
why_wrong.C: The supervised-training exception applies only to a young person who is no longer a child, not to a 15-year-old pupil.

common_mistake: Assuming that supervision, or the school's involvement, replaces the host firm's own assessment and the duty to inform a child's parent.

stem: Two operatives strip loft insulation in July wearing disposable coveralls and respirators. After 90 minutes one is dizzy and nauseous with a headache, pale and clammy with heavy sweating, but he answers questions clearly. What is the best response?

options.A: Let him rest in the shaded van for ten minutes with the coveralls still on, then put him back to work since a short break should reset him
options.B: Give him an energy drink and a salt tablet, then let him resume lighter loft work once the nausea settles, keeping the pair on the same schedule
options.C: Wrap him in a blanket in the cabin so that he sweats it out, and ring 999 only if he vomits, changing nothing else if he recovers
options.D: Move him somewhere cool, take off the coveralls, give water and cool his skin, call 999 if he is no better in 30 minutes, then revise work-rest times

explanation: These are signs of heat exhaustion, which is treated by cooling, removing clothing and fluids, with 999 if there is no improvement in 30 minutes, and the work pattern must change to stop a repeat.

why_wrong.A: Keeping the coveralls on stops body heat escaping, and ten minutes without active cooling or fluids is not adequate recovery.
why_wrong.B: Stimulant drinks and salt tablets do not cool him, and returning him to the same hot conditions invites a worse heat illness.
why_wrong.C: Wrapping him up traps heat when he needs cooling, and waiting for vomiting delays the emergency call.

common_mistake: Treating dizziness and heavy sweating in a hot space as tiredness that a short break and a sugary drink will cure.

stem: A first aid box on a 25-person site holds plasters, dressings, a bottle of paracetamol tablets and some out-of-date eyewash. A worker gets dust in his eye. The manager says the tablets are a kindness and the box is checked once a year. What is the better approach?

options.A: Keep tablets out of the kit, check contents regularly and replace anything used or out of date, with sterile eyewash available
options.B: Empty the box and rely on the nearest pharmacy, as a site below 50 people does not need any first aid kit
options.C: Keep the box as it is because dust in the eye needs only tap water, so expired eyewash is irrelevant to the site

explanation: First aid kits should hold items first aiders are trained to use, be checked and restocked regularly, and have in-date sterile eyewash where eye injury is possible.

why_wrong.B: Every workplace needs first aid provision based on its assessed needs.
why_wrong.C: Where eye hazards exist, sterile in-date eyewash should be on hand.
why_wrong.D: Medication is not recommended in a kit and yearly checks are too infrequent.

common_mistake: Leaving a first aid box unchecked and stocking it with medicines that first aiders are not trained to give.

stem: Look at the labourer in the foreground, working beneath an overhead hoist on a cold morning. The foreman says he is wearing everything the site rules require. What is the most significant problem, and the right fix?

options.A: His hi-vis vest is worn over a padded coat, so it should go under the coat to stop the coat from covering its reflective bands
options.B: His helmet colour is wrong for his trade, so it should be swapped for the issued colour so that other workers can identify his role
options.C: His gloves look too thin for handling pallets of blocks, so he should swap them for cut-resistant gloves before moving any more material today
options.D: His helmet sits on a woolly hat with the strap loose, so swap the hat for a helmet liner and refit the helmet snugly

explanation: A helmet perched on a bulky hat can fall off or shift on impact and loses its protection, so thermal comfort should come from a liner designed for the helmet.

why_wrong.A: A vest worn on the outside is what keeps the reflective bands visible, so this is correct, not a fault.
why_wrong.B: Helmet colour is a site convention and has no bearing on how well the helmet protects him.
why_wrong.C: Glove choice is a lesser concern than a helmet that is unlikely to stay in place beneath a load, and cut resistance is not the issue shown.

common_mistake: Assuming that wearing a hard hat in any fashion satisfies the rule, even when it is perched on other headwear with its strap loose.

stem: A fitter must steady a pipe flange at about 250 degrees C while a colleague fits a clip, taking roughly 20 seconds. The store holds nitrile gloves, knitted cut-resistant EN 388 gloves, and EN 407 gloves rated contact heat level 2 and level 4. What is the best control?

options.A: Use tongs or a clamp to keep hands clear, and if gloves are needed choose contact heat level 3 or higher, as ratings prove just 15 seconds
options.B: Wear the level 2 heat gloves, because 250 degrees C is exactly their rated temperature and the clip fitting is short enough to stay within that limit
options.C: Wear two pairs of thin nitrile gloves, because layers give the same insulation as one thermal glove and keep enough feel to fit the clip
options.D: Wear the knitted gloves with the highest cut level, because a top EN 388 score shows strong resistance to heat as well as to sharp edges and abrasion

explanation: Removing hand contact comes first, and a contact heat level is tested only for a threshold time of 15 seconds at its temperature, so a 20-second hold needs a higher level and a margin.

why_wrong.B: Level 2 is tested only to a 15-second threshold at that temperature, so a 20-second hold leaves no margin and exceeds what the rating proves.
why_wrong.C: Thin nitrile melts and sticks to skin at that temperature and offers no tested heat insulation, however many layers are worn.
why_wrong.D: EN 388 rates mechanical hazards such as cuts and abrasion and gives no contact heat protection.

common_mistake: Picking a glove because it matches the temperature number on the label, without allowing for contact time or removing the need to touch the hot item.
