stem: A scaffolder hands over the lower two lifts of a facade scaffold with a green tag at the base, then leaves for the weekend. The top lift has boards laid but no guardrails or toe boards. Bricklayers want to start on it on Saturday. What is correct?

options.A: They may fit the missing guardrails and toe boards themselves, because the scaffolder's job is done once the boards are laid and a bricklayer can finish it
options.B: The top lift is not handed over, so it must be barred off with a barrier and prohibition sign and used only once the scaffolder completes it and it is inspected
options.C: The green tag at the base covers the whole scaffold, so they may use the top lift if they clip their lanyards to the standards while the rails are missing
options.D: A supervisor can accept the whole scaffold by signing the handover form for the lower lifts, since that signature transfers responsibility for the rest to the user

explanation: A tag covers only what was completed and inspected, work equipment must be inspected in position before use, and falling-risk areas must be closed to anyone not authorised.

why_wrong.A: Completing or altering a scaffold is work for competent scaffolders, and the result still needs inspection before anyone uses it.
why_wrong.C: The tag certifies only the completed lifts, and standards are not designed or checked as personal fall protection anchors.
why_wrong.D: A signature for the lower lifts cannot make the unfinished lift safe, and the user cannot take over a scaffold that has not been inspected.

common_mistake: Reading a tag at the foot of a scaffold as proof that every lift above it is safe to use.

stem: Two operatives will dismantle a brick chimney stack on a pitched roof with eaves 7 m up. The foreman proposes harnesses clipped to the stack itself, with crawling boards underfoot, saying solid brick makes a good anchor. What is the best view?

options.A: Accept the plan once the stack is checked for loose mortar, because sound brickwork is a reliable anchor and a harness is enough for a job lasting only two days
options.B: Rig a safety net below the eaves instead of harnesses, since a net removes the need for any platform or edge protection at the stack
options.C: Add a second anchor by looping a line round the ridge tiles, since two attachment points share the load if the stack gives way during the work itself
options.D: Provide a scaffold platform with edge protection around the stack, because collective protection comes first and a stack being dismantled cannot be trusted as an anchor

explanation: The work at height hierarchy puts collective measures such as a platform with edge protection ahead of personal systems, and a structure being taken apart cannot be a reliable anchor.

why_wrong.A: A stack being dismantled loses strength as it comes down, so it cannot serve as an anchor however sound it looks at the start.
why_wrong.B: A net at the eaves does not protect someone working at the stack, and it still sits below a working platform with edge protection in the hierarchy.
why_wrong.C: Ridge tiles are not designed to take fall loads, and a personal system is still being used where collective protection is practicable.

common_mistake: Choosing the harness first and then hunting for something solid to clip to, instead of designing out the fall with a platform.

stem: A high-lift skip dumper must tip into a feed hopper. The driver, standing on a gentle cross-fall, raises the skip and edges forward the last metre to line up, saying speed saves time. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Raise the skip only halfway while moving, because stability falls only once the skip is fully vertical, so a half-raised skip stays within the safe limits
options.B: Creep forward in low gear with the skip raised on the cross-fall, because the danger comes from speed and walking pace removes the risk of overturning
options.C: Raise the skip only on level ground with the brake on, then lower it fully before repositioning, since a raised skip greatly reduces stability
options.D: Tip from the cross-fall if the downhill wheels sit on firmer ground, since firm contact on the low side stops the dumper from rolling over

explanation: A high-lift skip must be raised only on substantially level ground and never driven while raised, because stability falls sharply once the skip is elevated.

why_wrong.A: Stability reduces as soon as the skip is lifted, so moving with it partly raised is also unsafe.
why_wrong.B: A raised skip on a cross-fall can overturn at any speed, and low gear does not restore stability.
why_wrong.D: Firmer ground on one side does not make a cross-fall safe, because raising the skip shifts weight and can still tip the machine.

common_mistake: Believing that slow speed, or only part- raising the skip, makes it safe to move or work on uneven ground with the skip up.

stem: A flatbed lorry carries a bundle of 6 m reinforcing bars placed 300 mm behind the headboard and held by two ratchet straps pulled tight. The driver says tight straps are all that is needed for the short trip. Which action best secures the load?

options.A: Leave the bundle where it is, since the headboard catches forward movement and the straps resist sideways movement, so the gap is harmless
options.B: Slide the bundle tight against the headboard, strap it to stop movement in every direction, and recheck the tension soon after setting off
options.C: Add a third strap pulled hard at the rear, since extra tension grips the bundle by friction and the gap to the headboard matters very little
options.D: Swap the straps for chains at both ends, since chains are stronger than straps and the gap to the headboard then needs no attention

explanation: A load should be blocked against the headboard to remove the gap it could accelerate across, restrained in all directions, and rechecked early because loads settle and straps loosen.

why_wrong.A: A bundle sliding across a gap hits the headboard with a damaging shock load, so the gap is not harmless.
why_wrong.C: Friction from strap tension cannot be relied on in emergency braking, and the gap lets the bundle build up momentum before it hits the headboard.
why_wrong.D: Stronger restraint does not remove the need to block the load forward, and chains are no substitute for correct positioning.

common_mistake: Relying on how tight the straps feel rather than on blocking the load and restraining it in every direction.

stem: Japanese knotweed grows on the bank of a drainage ditch on a housing site. The contractor plans to spray garden-centre weedkiller along the bank, then strip the topsoil and reuse it as fill on a second site. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Obtain Environment Agency agreement before using any herbicide near water, use a competent applicator, and handle the soil as controlled waste for authorised management or disposal
options.B: Hire a contractor holding a pesticide certificate to spray, then send the topsoil to the second site, since a treated plant is no longer invasive
options.C: Strip the bank and spread the soil as fill on the second site under a layer of hardcore, because covering it means the soil is no longer waste
options.D: Spray a standard glyphosate product kept a metre back from the water, then reuse the soil elsewhere once visible stems are cut, as rhizome fragments rarely regrow

explanation: Herbicide use in or near water needs Environment Agency agreement, and soil containing knotweed rhizome is controlled waste that must not be spread where it could grow.

why_wrong.B: A certificate does not replace agreement for work near water, and treated soil can still hold living rhizome.
why_wrong.C: Covering does not change the soil's status, and moving knotweed soil to another site without controls can cause spread and offences.
why_wrong.D: Herbicide near water needs agreement whatever the offset, and small rhizome fragments in soil can regrow.

common_mistake: Treating knotweed as a gardening problem solved by weedkiller, instead of a controlled-waste and watercourse issue.

stem: A firm's method statement for roof sheeting sets out sound controls, but nobody checks that the gangs follow them. After a near miss, the director says the paperwork proves the risk is managed. What is the best view?

options.A: The gang leaders should sign a statement each month that they followed the plan, and no supervision is then needed
options.B: The paperwork is enough because the law requires the plan to exist, and gangs are assumed to follow what is written
options.C: Checks are needed only after an injury, so the near miss changes nothing until somebody is actually harmed
options.D: Controls must be monitored on site by supervision and checks, then reviewed, because a written plan alone does not show it is working

explanation: Risk assessment does not end with writing controls down: supervisors must check they are in place and effective, and findings should feed a review.

why_wrong.A: A signed statement without observation does not check that controls are working.
why_wrong.B: Having a plan does not show it is followed, and the duty is to manage the risk in practice.
why_wrong.C: Monitoring should be continuing and a near miss is a prompt to review.

common_mistake: Treating a written method statement as proof that the risk is controlled without checking the work.

stem: A self-employed delivery driver crossing a site is hit by a falling board and taken straight from the site to hospital, where his wrist is put in plaster. The manager has told the insurer and logged the incident, and considers it closed. What is missing?

options.A: A RIDDOR report once the driver's own firm confirms he was off work for more than seven days, because that threshold decides when reporting is needed.
options.B: A RIDDOR report, because a non-worker taken directly from the scene to hospital for treatment is reportable; telling the insurer does not discharge that duty.
options.C: A signed accident book entry from the driver, which satisfies the reporting duty if the injury is also covered by the site's public liability policy.
options.D: Nothing further, since RIDDOR covers the site's own employees and an injured visitor's claim is a civil matter that the insurer handles through its normal process.

explanation: Accidents to people not at work are reportable under RIDDOR where they are taken directly from the scene to hospital for treatment of the injury, and an insurance notification is a separate matter.

why_wrong.A: The seven-day test applies to injured workers, whereas for non- workers the test is direct removal from the scene to hospital for treatment.
why_wrong.C: An accident book entry is an internal record, and neither it nor the existence of insurance cover satisfies the duty to report to the authorities.
why_wrong.D: RIDDOR also covers people not at work, and an insurance claim does not replace the duty to notify the enforcing authority.

common_mistake: Treating notification to the insurer as if it were the same as the legal duty to report to the enforcing authority.

stem: Carpenters spray mould release oil onto steel wall formwork in an unventilated basement and wipe it off with bare hands. The safety data sheet lists mist inhalation and skin irritation. Which control should be considered first under COSHH?

options.A: Spray from the basement doorway and leave the area for ten minutes afterwards, as natural airing clears the mist and removes the need to change the product.
options.B: Check whether a lower-hazard release agent, such as a water-based or vegetable-oil type, can be used and applied by brush or roller, so no mist is created.
options.C: Provide barrier cream and a wash station and carry on spraying, because skin contact is the main route of harm and a mist at this level is a nuisance.
options.D: Keep the current product and issue FFP3 masks and nitrile gloves, since suitable PPE gives equivalent protection to changing the product or the application method.

explanation: COSHH expects elimination or substitution of the hazardous substance, and changing the method to avoid mist, before relying on PPE or personal hygiene measures.

why_wrong.A: Brief airing of an unventilated basement does not reliably clear mist, and it leaves skin contact and the hazardous product itself unaddressed.
why_wrong.C: Barrier cream is a weak control, and treating the mist as a nuisance ignores the inhalation hazard identified on the data sheet.
why_wrong.D: PPE is the last line of defence in the control hierarchy and cannot be treated as equivalent to eliminating or substituting the hazard.

common_mistake: Reaching for gloves and masks before asking whether a less hazardous product or a mist-free method could be used.

stem: On a small refurbishment, workers fill bottles from a hose tap on the bowser beside the mixer wash-down area. The manager says water is water and that no sign or cups are needed. Which statement best reflects the CDM welfare requirement?

options.A: Drinking water must be provided when the work is hot or dusty, and in that case a labelled tap on the wash-down hose is acceptable for the crew.
options.B: Any mains-fed tap meets the duty if workers can reach it, since marking and cups appear in guidance but are not required on short refurbishment jobs.
options.C: Wholesome drinking water must be readily accessible at a suitable place, marked where necessary, with cups provided unless the supply is a drinking jet.
options.D: Bottled water bought by each worker satisfies the duty, because the contractor's obligation ends once workers have the chance to buy drinks during their breaks.

explanation: CDM 2015 Schedule 2 requires an adequate supply of wholesome drinking water at suitable places, conspicuously marked where necessary, with sufficient cups unless people can drink easily from a jet.

why_wrong.A: The duty applies on every site regardless of conditions, and a tap beside a wash-down area risks contamination.
why_wrong.B: The marking and cup provisions are part of the regulations, with no exemption for short jobs, and the location must also be suitable.
why_wrong.D: The duty is to provide or make available the supply, and leaving workers to buy their own does not meet it.

common_mistake: Assuming any tap on site counts as drinking water, regardless of where it is or what the water is used for.

stem: Joiners finish a timber-frame first floor containing a stair void. Barrier tape and a "Danger - void" sign are fixed round it, and materials are stacked beside it. The supervisor says everyone has been told. What protection is needed at the void?

options.A: Barrier tape on posts with a banksman posted at the void during working hours, since supervision is as effective as physical edge protection while someone is watching.
options.B: Two tensioned ropes at about 1 m and 500 mm with hazard flags, because rope barriers are accepted for short-term protection of internal voids.
options.C: A single rigid top rail at about 1 m with a hazard sign, because a solid rail and a clear warning together stop anyone walking into the void.
options.D: Rigid edge protection with a top rail at least 950 mm high, an intermediate rail leaving gaps of no more than 470 mm, and a toe board to stop materials falling.

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations require guard-rails of sufficient strength and rigidity, with a top rail of at least 950 mm and no gap above 470 mm, plus toe-boards to prevent persons or materials falling.

why_wrong.A: Tape and supervision are not collective physical protection and give nothing when the banksman is absent or distracted.
why_wrong.B: Ropes lack the strength and rigidity needed to stop a person falling and give no protection against falling materials.
why_wrong.C: A single rail leaves a gap greater than 470 mm below it and gives no toe board to stop materials being kicked into the void.

common_mistake: Relying on tape, signs and a briefing where a rigid guard-rail and toe board are needed.

stem: Look at the scene. The scaffolder says it is ready for handover because the platforms, rails, ties and ladder all look complete. Which problem must be corrected before anyone uses it?

options.A: The outer face has no debris netting, which must be fitted before the next shift because falling material cannot otherwise be controlled.
options.B: The working platform is too narrow for materials and must be widened with extra boards before any bricklaying starts on the upper lift of the scaffold.
options.C: The standards bear on loose bricks and a cracked slab, not base plates on firm sole boards, so the base could slip or settle.
options.D: The access ladder should stop level with the platform edge so that workers can step across the guardrail without a gap at the top.

explanation: A scaffold's loads pass down through its standards, so each needs a base plate on a sound sole board or firm base, as loose bricks and cracked slabs can shift or crush.

why_wrong.A: Netting is a separate control that depends on the work and does not address the visible instability of the supports.
why_wrong.B: The deck is boarded at a suitable width, so this is not the significant fault in the scene.
why_wrong.D: A ladder should project well above the platform to give a handhold, so stopping it level would introduce a fault.

common_mistake: Judging a scaffold safe from its platforms and rails without checking what the standards stand on.

stem: A 2.5 m deep service trench will be dug 1.5 m from the edge of a live road used by buses and lorries. The foreman plans to use the support supplier's standard strut table for firm ground. What should be done before digging starts?

options.A: Have the support designed for the actual ground, groundwater and traffic loading by a competent person, with inspection at the start of each shift.
options.B: Wait until cracks or water appear in the sides before fitting support, as made-up road base stands unsupported while it remains compacted.
options.C: Use the standard table and add one extra strut level for safety, since traffic adds a small load that the table's margin already absorbs.
options.D: Use the standard table and rely on a weekly inspection to catch any movement, because the road structure carries traffic loads away from the trench.

explanation: Support must suit the real ground, water and loads from adjacent vehicles, and HSE guidance expects a competent person to inspect it at the start of each shift.

why_wrong.B: Support must be decided and in place before people enter, since collapse can happen without warning.
why_wrong.C: A table for firm ground does not account for traffic loading or groundwater, and an extra strut level does not replace a design for the real conditions.
why_wrong.D: Traffic loads can reach the trench sides through the ground, and inspections are needed at the start of every shift, not weekly.

common_mistake: Trusting a generic support table without checking whether traffic loading and groundwater are covered.

stem: A 110 V reel feeds a mixer, with the cable passing through the gap of a hinged temporary site door that is closed against it each evening, then looped over a scaffold coupler. The sheath looks intact. What is the best action?

options.A: Leave it in place, because an intact sheath shows the insulation is sound and the 110 V supply keeps any shock risk to a harmless level.
options.B: Coil the surplus cable on the reel to shorten the exposed run, since a fully wound reel limits the length at risk of damage.
options.C: Re-route the cable clear of the closing door and sharp fittings, using a hook or protector, and include its routing in routine checks.
options.D: Tape the cable to the door frame and over the coupler so it cannot move, because a fixed cable suffers less wear than one that slides.

explanation: Cables must be protected from mechanical damage such as crushing and abrasion, and an intact sheath today does not show the insulation survives repeated trapping and rubbing.

why_wrong.A: A 110 V supply reduces but does not remove the risk, and repeated crushing damages cables in ways not visible from the sheath.
why_wrong.B: A reel left wound under load can overheat, and a shorter run still passes through the same pinch point and over the same edge.
why_wrong.D: Taping holds the cable against the pinch point and sharp edge, so it does not remove the cause of damage.

common_mistake: Judging a cable safe because its outer sheath looks intact, while ignoring where it is routed.

stem: A vibratory roller compacts hardcore for a car park 8 m from a terrace of old houses. Residents report rattling windows and one shows a new hairline plaster crack. The contractor says the roller is within its operator exposure rating. What is the best response?

options.A: Fit damping pads to the operator seat and reassess the operator's exposure, since reducing vibration at the machine reduces it at the houses too.
options.B: Give residents a notice of rolling times and keep to normal working hours, since vibration complaints are handled in the same way as noise, through hours alone.
options.C: Take no action unless a surveyor proves the roller caused the crack, because hairline plaster cracks in old houses usually come from age and settlement over many years.
options.D: Treat it as a separate off-site effect: monitor vibration at the nearest house, review roller settings and method, and record nearby property condition.

explanation: Operator exposure limits do not protect neighbours, and vibration affecting nearby premises can be a statutory nuisance, so monitoring and changes to the method are needed.

why_wrong.A: Seat damping protects the driver but has little effect on the ground-borne vibration transmitted to neighbouring properties.
why_wrong.B: Limiting hours may help but does not measure or reduce the vibration reaching the houses.
why_wrong.C: Waiting for proof of damage ignores the nuisance already reported, and ageing buildings are more sensitive to vibration.

common_mistake: Assuming that meeting the operator's exposure limits means neighbours are protected from the same vibration.

stem: A bowser dosed with a salt-based dust suppressant is sprayed along a sloping haul road. The data sheet lists a hazard to aquatic life, and the road falls towards a surface-water gully. What is the best control?

options.A: Spray more heavily so the surface stays damp all day, since rain dilutes the product before it can reach any watercourse.
options.B: Use the lowest effective rate, keep it off areas draining to the gully, and consider whether plain water spraying achieves the same dust control.
options.C: Carry on as planned, because chemicals used for dust control fall under health and safety rules, and site drains are the council's concern.
options.D: Cover the gully with a plastic sheet and spray as planned, since a covered drain cannot receive the product from the sloping road.

explanation: Substances hazardous to aquatic life must not reach surface-water drains, so the quantity, the application area and the choice of product all need controlling.

why_wrong.A: Heavier application increases the pollutant load and run-off, and dilution does not make a harmful discharge to a surface-water drain acceptable.
why_wrong.C: Polluting a surface-water drain is an environmental matter for the contractor, regardless of whose drain it is.
why_wrong.D: A sheet does not stop the product running off, and it may pool or flow elsewhere, so the source still needs controlling.

common_mistake: Treating dust suppression water and additives as harmless because they are applied to stop a nuisance.

stem: A contractor's engineer prepares the propping scheme for a heavy precast beam lift and says CDM designer duties belong only to the architect and the permanent-works engineer. A principal designer is appointed. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The engineer must design every risk out before issue, which leaves no residual-risk information to pass to the principal designer or anyone else on the project
options.B: The engineer should give notes on remaining risks to the lifting crew on the day, since only the people doing the work need them, not the principal designer
options.C: The engineer is a designer of this temporary structure, so must reduce foreseeable risks in the scheme and pass information on remaining risks to the principal designer
options.D: Designer duties attach to the permanent works alone, so the propping scheme becomes a site matter and the engineer need only issue drawings for the lifting crew to follow

explanation: CDM 2015 treats falsework and other temporary supports as structures, so anyone preparing their design is a designer who must pass information on residual risks to the principal designer for the health and safety file.

why_wrong.A: The duty is to eliminate foreseeable risks so far as reasonably practicable and to give information about those that remain.
why_wrong.B: Information on remaining risks must go to the principal designer and into the health and safety file, not just to people present.
why_wrong.D: The CDM definition of a structure includes falsework and temporary supports, so temporary designs carry designer duties.

common_mistake: Assuming CDM designer duties apply only to architects and engineers working on the permanent structure.

stem: After a gang member is seriously injured, HSE investigates a site supervisor who knowingly ignored the agreed method. A colleague says magistrates can fine no more than 20,000 pounds and only the company can be prosecuted. Which statement is correct in England and Wales?

options.A: The cap applies in magistrates' courts, and the supervisor is protected as an employee, since personal prosecution is restricted to directors who control company decisions
options.B: A cap of 20,000 pounds applies in magistrates' courts, though the supervisor can be prosecuted and the case can be sent to the Crown Court for greater penalties
options.C: Fines are unlimited in either court, and an individual such as the supervisor can be prosecuted personally, facing a fine and up to two years' imprisonment
options.D: Fines are unlimited but fall on the company, while the supervisor risks only dismissal or a civil claim and imprisonment is reserved for manslaughter cases

explanation: Duty holders, both individuals and organisations, can be prosecuted, and in England and Wales fines are unlimited with imprisonment of up to two years available against individuals.

why_wrong.A: The 20,000 pound cap is not the rule in England and Wales, and individuals at any level can be prosecuted for their own breaches.
why_wrong.B: The cap is wrong for England and Wales, where magistrates' fines are also unlimited.
why_wrong.D: Individuals can be prosecuted under health and safety law itself and imprisonment is available beyond manslaughter.

common_mistake: Assuming health and safety prosecution is something that happens only to the company and that magistrates' fines are small and capped.

stem: Midway through a ceiling-board job, the access route and lifting method change. The supervisor tells only the day gang by word of mouth. The night crew and a neighbouring trade are unaware, and the old method statement stays pinned in the cabin. What should happen?

options.A: Revise and re-issue the method statement, brief everyone affected, including the night crew and neighbouring trade, before the new method starts, and remove the superseded copies
options.B: Leave the old statement displayed for reference and add a handwritten note beside it, since removing it would leave the cabin without any statement
options.C: Update the method statement at the end of the week and rely on the day gang to pass the new method on to anyone affected as they happen to meet them on site
options.D: Brief the night crew because they work for the same firm, since the neighbouring trade has its own method statement and is responsible for its own safety

explanation: When the work changes, the arrangements must be reviewed and the new method communicated to everyone it affects before it starts, with old versions withdrawn so nobody follows them.

why_wrong.B: A superseded document left in circulation invites people to follow the old method and should be withdrawn.
why_wrong.C: Changes must reach affected people before the new method begins, not by chance conversation after the event.
why_wrong.D: The neighbouring trade is affected by the change, so coordination and information must reach it as well.

common_mistake: Assuming that briefing whoever attends the morning meeting is enough when a method changes part way through a job.

stem: An operative seals pipe gaps behind a boiler in a small cupboard using cans of expanding gun foam. The door is shut to stop draughts, the boiler's pilot light is lit, and he wears only thin cotton gloves. Which change deals best with the hazards?

options.A: Leave the pilot light burning for warmth, because cured foam is not flammable, and swap to nitrile gloves to guard against any skin contact with the wet foam
options.B: Use a larger can to cut the number of applications, work quickly with the door slightly ajar, and rely on the small quantity of foam to keep any vapour harmless
options.C: Keep the door shut to stop vapour spreading into the house, switch the pilot light off only when the job ends, and wear a basic dust mask against the fumes
options.D: Isolate the boiler and other ignition sources, ventilate well, and wear suitable gloves and eye protection, as the foam holds flammable gas and a sensitiser

explanation: Cans of gun foam contain flammable propellant gases and isocyanate, a sensitiser, so ignition sources must be removed, fresh air provided and skin and eyes properly protected.

why_wrong.A: The propellant is flammable while the foam is being applied, so a lit pilot light is an ignition source.
why_wrong.B: A sensitiser can affect a person after repeated small exposures, so ventilation and control of ignition sources cannot be skipped.
why_wrong.C: A shut cupboard traps flammable gas beside the ignition source, and a dust mask gives no protection against vapour.

common_mistake: Treating a can of expanding foam as an ordinary household product instead of reading its safety data sheet for flammable and sensitising ingredients.

stem: A 'Danger: overhead crane operations' sign is cable-tied to the entrance gate, 80 m from the lifting area. It is faded and half hidden behind a poster. The manager says it covers the hazard, so no new sign is needed. What is the right response?

options.A: Add a second gate sign and rely on induction to cover the lifting area, because more signs inside the site would clutter it and distract the crane crew
options.B: Replace it with a clean, legible sign where people approach the lifting area, and keep it maintained as a supplement to barriers and a signaller
options.C: Keep the gate sign but enlarge it, since a sign read on entry will be remembered by everyone when they later pass near the lifting area on their rounds
options.D: Leave the faded sign until the next monthly inspection, as a displayed warning sign gives legal cover provided it was in place when lifting began

explanation: Safety signs must be clear and legible and provided and maintained where a significant risk remains, so they need to be seen in time at the hazard and supplement other controls.

why_wrong.A: Induction does not replace a legible sign where the risk exists, and the problem here is placement and condition, not volume.
why_wrong.C: Size does not fix its position, and a warning must be seen at the point of risk, not recalled from 80 m away.
why_wrong.D: Signs have to be maintained so they remain legible, and a faded, half-hidden sign cannot warn anyone.

common_mistake: Assuming a sign has done its job once it is fixed to the site gate, wherever the hazard is and however faded the sign becomes.

stem: Maintenance staff reach a flat roof by a fixed ladder inside a plant room, then climb out through a hinged hatch. The roof has no parapet, the hatch is propped open between trips, and the edge is 3 m away. Which control best prevents falls?

options.A: Provide harnesses and lanyards clipped to an anchor at the hatch, since the users are trained and the opening is only open while someone is actually climbing through it
options.B: Fit permanent guardrails round the hatch opening and the roof edge, with a self-closing gate where people step out, rather than personal gear
options.C: Add a handhold at the ladder's top and a non-slip step by the hatch, since falls are most likely on the ladder rather than at the opening
options.D: Mark a painted line on the roof 2 m from the edge and brief users to keep inside it, closing the hatch whenever anyone is up there

explanation: Collective protection such as fixed guardrails guards both the opening and the edge for everyone, and ranks above personal fall protection in the hierarchy for work at height.

why_wrong.A: Personal equipment ranks below collective guardrails, and it leaves the open hatch hole unguarded for everyone else.
why_wrong.C: A better handhold does nothing about the open hatch or the unprotected edge, which are the fall hazards described.
why_wrong.D: A painted line and a briefing depend on behaviour and do not physically stop anyone falling from the edge.

common_mistake: Relying on harnesses, painted lines or briefings where a fixed guardrail around the opening and edge would remove the risk.

stem: In the site workshop, a joiner is about to use a 230 V bench saw when he notices coloured wires showing where the lead enters the plug and a brown scorch mark on the plug cover. The saw runs normally. What should he do?

options.A: Disconnect it and take it out of use for repair by a competent person, since visible wires mean the cord grip has failed and scorching suggests overheating
options.B: Push the cable back into the plug, tighten the cord grip screws and carry on, because the saw runs normally and the scorch mark is only cosmetic
options.C: Keep using it on the RCD-protected socket for the day and report it at finish, as the RCD would trip if the fault were dangerous
options.D: Swap in a plug from stores without a continuity check, then carry on, because the fault appears to be limited to the plug itself

explanation: Coloured wires at the plug show the cord grip is not holding the cable, and burn marks point to a loose connection or overheating, so the item is removed from use until a competent person repairs it.

why_wrong.B: A scorch mark signals overheating at the connections, and a quick push-back leaves a possibly damaged plug in service.
why_wrong.C: An RCD detects earth leakage and does not protect against overheating or loose connections.
why_wrong.D: A replacement plug fitted without checks may be wired wrongly, and the damage to the lead and terminations has not been assessed.

common_mistake: Judging a power tool by whether it still runs rather than by what its plug, lead and cord grip show.

stem: Look at the scene. The mixer driver is reversing towards the pump hopper and says his mirrors are set and the beacon is on. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The access is surfaced with hardcore, which risks the pump legs sinking and the boom moving while concrete is placed
options.B: The drum is turning while the lorry moves, which risks the load shifting and unbalancing the vehicle during the reversing manoeuvre
options.C: A person stands in the gap behind the lorry, outside the driver's view, with no signaller controlling the reverse
options.D: The second worker stands beside the pump, which risks him being struck by the boom when the pour starts

explanation: A pedestrian between the tail of a reversing vehicle and a fixed object can be crushed, and mirrors and a beacon cannot protect someone in a blind area.

why_wrong.A: Ground bearing is not what the picture highlights, and it does not outweigh a person in a vehicle's path.
why_wrong.B: A turning drum is normal for delivery and is not the hazard the scene shows.
why_wrong.D: His position at the far side is not the most significant danger shown.

common_mistake: Assuming that a driver who has set the mirrors and switched on the beacon has covered the danger to anyone behind the vehicle.

stem: A 30-tonne wheel loader reverses all day on a site beside houses, and neighbours complain about its high-pitched beeper. The manager wants the alarm switched off, saying a rear camera gives the driver full sight. What is the best response?

options.A: Keep an audible alarm but change to a broadband type that is less intrusive off site, and keep the banksman and exclusion zone because cameras leave blind spots
options.B: Switch the alarm off during early hours only, since the camera covers the rear, and ask the driver to reverse at a slower speed with extra care and patience
options.C: Fit a louder alarm and add sound baffles round the loader, so that the warning is still heard by workers wearing ear defenders on site
options.D: Replace the alarm with a flashing beacon, since pedestrians in hi-vis can easily see lights, and the beacon causes no noise nuisance to the neighbours at all

explanation: A camera covers only part of the area around large plant, so the audible warning and banksman remain necessary, and a broadband alarm reduces the nuisance without removing the warning.

why_wrong.B: Cameras leave blind areas, and an alarm warns people the driver cannot see on any shift.
why_wrong.C: A louder alarm worsens the nuisance and does nothing about blind spots or the lack of segregation.
why_wrong.D: A beacon warns only people who happen to look at it, so it is not a full substitute.

common_mistake: Assuming a rear camera makes the other warning measures redundant, even though it leaves areas around large plant unseen.

stem: A site keeps torn bags of cement and part-used tins of emulsion paint on pallets in a yard sloping to a surface-water gully. A labourer says emulsion is water-based and cement is only dust, so no cover is needed. What is the better approach?

options.A: Treat only the paint as a pollutant by bunding the tins, while the bags stay on pallets since cement is harmless once it has gone off
options.B: Keep them where they are but lay a plastic sheet underneath, because the sheet will catch any liquid and keep any runoff well away from the gully
options.C: Place a rubber mat over the gully and keep a spill kit beside the pallets, since a covered gully cannot receive any runoff from the yard
options.D: Store both under cover on a hard base away from the gully, in a bunded or tray area with lids on, as runoff from either can pollute drains

explanation: Rain on cement and spilt emulsion paint can carry alkaline or polluting liquid into drains, so both need cover, containment and distance from the gully.

why_wrong.A: Rain-washed cement is strongly alkaline and polluting, so the bags also need cover.
why_wrong.B: A loose sheet on a slope does not contain liquid and leaves rain and spills free to flow downhill.
why_wrong.C: Covering a gully and using a spill kit is a response to releases, and storage should prevent them in the first place.

common_mistake: Believing water-based paint and cement are too harmless to need cover or bunding because they are not oils or solvents.

stem: A site needs an agency slinger-signaller for a three-week lifting package. The manager gives the agency only the start date and pay rate, saying the agency has vetted the worker and the site induction will cover everything else. Which statement about the site's duties is most accurate?

options.A: The agency alone must judge suitability because it employs him, so the site only has to cover its own hazards, welfare and emergency arrangements in the induction
options.B: The site must give the agency the skills, qualifications and health surveillance details the job needs, and the worker still needs a site induction first
options.C: Giving the worker the required skills and health details on arrival at induction satisfies the duty, because he will then know them before lifting starts
options.D: Only workers on fixed-term contracts are covered by the information duty, so agency workers fall under the agency's own arrangements for the whole placement

explanation: Regulation 15 of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 requires the user of agency workers to give the agency this information so it can pass it on, and induction on site hazards is a separate duty.

why_wrong.A: The site using the worker must supply the required skills, qualifications and health surveillance details to the agency, so the duty is not left with the agency alone.
why_wrong.C: The information must reach the agency so it can match and brief the worker beforehand, and handing it over at the gate comes too late to do that.
why_wrong.D: Regulation 15 deals separately with agency workers and with those supplying them, so being supplied by an agency does not remove the user's duty.

common_mistake: Assuming an agency worker's suitability and health needs are the agency's problem once the site has run its own induction.

stem: A groundworker must dig a pit in a factory yard owned by the client. The electricity company's plan shows nothing there, but the client supplies its own old cable layout. He proposes machine- digging to the depth marked on that layout. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Treat both plans as a rough guide because private cables may be unrecorded, then trace routes with a trained locator user and confirm by hand-dug trial holes
options.B: Follow the client's layout to its marked depth, because the owner's own record is more reliable than a locator and needs no further checking before digging
options.C: Rely on the electricity company's plan showing nothing, because statutory undertakers must record every cable in the area including those owned privately by the client
options.D: Dig by machine to half the marked depth and then change to hand tools, because the drawn depth gives a safe margin above the buried cable

explanation: Plans only indicate location and number of services, and private cables may not appear on a utility plan, so locating by a competent person and confirming with hand-dug trial holes comes before mechanical digging.

why_wrong.B: An old layout shows only an approximate position and depth, and it can be wrong or out of date, so it still has to be checked on the ground.
why_wrong.C: A utility plan covers that company's own apparatus and not necessarily the client's private cables, so a blank plan does not prove the ground is clear.
why_wrong.D: Cables are not always at the drawn depth or position, so mechanical digging before locating and trial holes can still strike a cable.

common_mistake: Treating a drawing or a blank utility plan as proof about what lies underground, rather than as a rough guide to be checked.

stem: A city site has one vehicle gate, often blocked by delivery vans and padlocked at night with the key held off site. The manager says an ambulance can simply meet a casualty at the front hoarding. Which arrangement best provides for emergency access?

options.A: Arrange for the keyholder to attend within an hour of any call, since crews can wait at the gate while the casualty is carried out to them
options.B: Rely on the 999 caller giving the postcode, since ambulance crews carry cutting tools and can open the padlock when they arrive on site
options.C: Keep a route to each work area clear at all times, with the entry quickly openable, and name someone to meet and guide responders
options.D: Put a no-parking sign at the gate and leave night security to arrange access, because the vehicle gate is needed only for planned deliveries

explanation: Emergency routes and access must stay clear and usable at all times, and someone must meet and guide the ambulance, so a padlocked or blocked gate defeats the plan.

why_wrong.A: An hour's delay for access is far too long in an emergency, and moving a casualty to the hoarding is not a substitute for a clear and openable entry.
why_wrong.B: Responders should not be expected to force entry, and a locked gate delays treatment when the plan should have ensured quick, clear access.
why_wrong.D: A sign does not keep the route clear, and emergency access is needed at any hour regardless of the delivery programme.

common_mistake: Planning for emergency vehicles by assuming they can work around locked gates and blocked routes when the time comes.

stem: A caulker applies a solvent-based sealant for six hours in thin disposable gloves that show no tears. He rinses them at lunch and wears them again in the afternoon. Which approach to glove selection and use is most appropriate?

options.A: Match the glove material and breakthrough time to the solvent in the safety data sheet, change before that time passes, and never reuse
options.B: Wear two pairs of the same thin gloves and rinse theouter pair at lunch, because the doubled layer will block the solvent for the full shift
options.C: Switch to thick general-purpose work gloves, because thickness is what resists solvents and any heavy glove will cover him safely through a whole working shift
options.D: Keep the thin gloves because an absence of tears shows no solvent has passed through, and replace them only when visible damage appears during the shift

explanation: Solvents can pass through a glove that looks intact, so the material must be matched to the substance, replaced within its breakthrough time, and not reused after rinsing.

why_wrong.B: Two layers of the same unsuitable material only slow permeation slightly, and rinsing does not restore a glove that has already been affected.
why_wrong.C: Resistance depends on the glove material against the specific solvent and not on thickness, and some heavy gloves absorb solvents and hold them against the skin.
why_wrong.D: Permeation happens through intact material, so the lack of visible damage does not show that the glove is still protecting the skin.

common_mistake: Judging whether a glove is protecting you by how it looks and feels rather than by its material and breakthrough time.

stem: A 40-person site buys a defibrillator. The manager now plans to cut the number of first aiders from two to none, because the device covers the heart risk, and to keep it locked in his office. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Provision is voluntary, so it can stay locked in the manager's office with no routine checks, because first aiders will fetch it whenever needed
options.B: The law requires one on sites above 25 workers, which meets the first-aid duty, so first-aider numbers may fall once the device is installed
options.C: Once bought it counts as medical equipment outside PUWER, so the supplier handles upkeep and no written instructions are needed for would-be users
options.D: The needs assessment sets first-aider numbers, and a provided defibrillator is work equipment, so it needs accessible siting, upkeep and written user instructions

explanation: HSE states that no law requires a defibrillator and that first aider numbers come from the needs assessment, while one that is provided falls under PUWER, including instructions and maintenance.

why_wrong.A: Equipment meant for an emergency has to be readily accessible and in working order, which a locked office and an absence of checks cannot ensure.
why_wrong.B: Health and safety law does not require a defibrillator at any workforce size, and it does not replace the first- aid arrangements the needs assessment calls for.
why_wrong.C: HSE says PUWER applies to a defibrillator that is provided, so the employer must ensure maintenance and give users information and instructions.

common_mistake: Believing that buying a defibrillator reduces the need for trained first aiders and other first-aid provision.

stem: A fencer sprays a solvent-based timber preservative in a garage workshop, creating both vapour and fine mist. He wears a half-mask with brown gas filters only, and a colleague says white filters are better. Which advice is correct?

options.A: Stay with the brown gas filters alone, because white only denotes dust and the carbon in a brown filter also traps liquid mist as well as vapour in the air
options.B: Use combination filters such as A2P3, where brown handles organic vapour and white stops the mist particles, with a suitable face fit
options.C: Choose grey B filters, because grey is the standard colour for chemical vapours and is the correct choice for any solvent- based liquid
options.D: Swap to white P3 filters alone, because P3 is the highest class and its pleated medium will also absorb the solvent vapours in the air

explanation: Type A (brown) filters deal with organic vapours of higher boiling point and P (white) filters deal with particles and mist, so spray work with both hazards needs both functions.

why_wrong.A: A gas filter does not capture airborne droplets, so the mist needs the white particle filter in addition to the brown vapour filter.
why_wrong.C: Grey type B is for certain inorganic gases and vapours, whereas organic solvent vapour needs brown type A.
why_wrong.D: A particle filter does nothing against vapours, and so he would breathe the solvent unprotected through a filter that looks high-grade.

common_mistake: Choosing a respirator filter by its class number or familiarity without matching its type and colour to both the vapour and particle hazards.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operator is well protected because he wears head, face, hearing and hand protection. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: His high-visibility jacket is the main fault, because reflective strips are a snagging risk and a plain close-fitting jacket must be worn for tree cutting
options.B: Helmet-mounted ear defenders cannot protect hearing while a visor is down, so earplugs must replace them for any chainsaw work in the open
options.C: His legs have no cut-resistant protection, so a kickback or slip of the running chain could cause a severe injury that his other PPE cannot prevent
options.D: His gloves should be removed because they can snag the chain, so bare hands on the handles are the safer arrangement for controlled cutting

explanation: Chainsaw work needs leg protection designed to stop or clog the chain, and the operator's ordinary trousers and boots leave the most exposed part of the body unprotected.

why_wrong.A: The jacket is the lesser concern, and the real danger is the unprotected legs next to the running chain, so this does not address the greatest risk.
why_wrong.B: Helmet-mounted ear defenders and visors are a standard combination for this work, and the visor does not stop the defenders attenuating noise.
why_wrong.D: Gloves suited to chainsaw use are recommended for protection, and removing them would leave the hands exposed without reducing the chain hazard.

common_mistake: Counting the number of PPE items worn instead of asking whether the part of the body most at risk from the task is actually protected.

stem: A rubble chute is fixed from a second-floor opening into a skip. It is loosely tied at the top, has a gap at one joint and the skip stands uncovered in a pedestrian route. A labourer says the chute is just a way to tip waste safely. What is needed?

options.A: Leave the arrangement as it is, since any chute is accepted as proof that debris is being safely lowered to the skip
options.B: Have someone watch the pedestrian route and shout when waste is tipped, instead of fixing the chute and fencing the skip
options.C: Secure and join the chute properly, enclose the skip area with a barrier and control the loading, so debris cannot fall on people
options.D: Put a sign beside the skip warning pedestrians, because a sign is enough to keep people out of a drop zone

explanation: A chute reduces falling debris only if it is secure, free of gaps and discharges into a controlled area, so the zone beneath needs to be fenced and managed.

why_wrong.A: A poorly fixed chute with gaps can still drop debris onto a route used by people.
why_wrong.B: A watcher cannot stop debris leaving through a gap and shouting is unreliable.
why_wrong.D: A sign does not physically prevent people being struck.

common_mistake: Assuming that fitting a chute is enough without checking its joints, fixings and the area where it discharges.

stem: Scaffolders working beside a fenced 11 kV substation drop a hand tool that lands inside the locked compound near equipment. The foreman proposes climbing the fence to grab it because the unit is silent. What is the correct action?

options.A: Push a scaffold tube through the fence to drag the tool clear, because the tube never enters the equipment area and nobody has to climb in
options.B: Keep everyone out and report it to the operator via the notice contact, so an authorised person retrieves the tool once the area is safe
options.C: Send the site electrician in to fetch it, because a qualified electrician is competent to work safely around any high-voltage equipment on any premises
options.D: Climb in and retrieve it only while the equipment is silent, since the absence of any humming shows the apparatus is dead and the whole compound is safe

explanation: Only persons authorised by the operator may enter a substation, and silence does not show equipment is dead, so the operator must be told and must arrange safe recovery.

why_wrong.A: A long metal tube close to high-voltage apparatus can cause flashover or contact, and it still amounts to unauthorised work inside the operator's compound.
why_wrong.C: Competence on the site's own installation does not give authority to enter the operator's substation, which only the operator can grant.
why_wrong.D: Silence proves nothing about whether equipment is live, and entering without the operator's authority is the danger itself.

common_mistake: Assuming that quiet equipment behind a fence is safe to enter for a quick job.

stem: A storm warning forecasts gusts above a tower crane's in- service wind limit tonight. The operator plans to apply the slew brake to keep the jib over the site and lower the empty hook to the ground for security. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Release the slew brake so the jib can weathervane freely into the wind, leaving the crane as the manufacturer's out-of- service instructions state
options.B: Carry on lifting through the evening with light loads until a gust actually passes the limit, since a forecast alone gives no reason to stop work
options.C: Lower the hook onto a heavy kentledge block and tie it off, because anchoring the hook to the ground holds the jib steady against wind loading
options.D: Keep the brake applied so the jib cannot swing into neighbouring property, because a jib held in one position resists wind better than one free to turn with it

explanation: A tower crane out of service must be free to weathervane so the jib aligns with the wind, and a brake left on can cause structural damage as HSE found in incident investigations.

why_wrong.B: Work should stop and the crane be put out of service before the forecast conditions arrive, rather than waiting for the limit to be exceeded.
why_wrong.C: Tying the hook to the ground restrains the structure in a way it was not designed for and can overload the crane when it is hit by the wind.
why_wrong.D: A held jib faces wind from any side and can be overloaded, which is why out-of-service cranes must be left free to turn into the wind.

common_mistake: Trying to lock a tower crane in place against a storm instead of leaving it free to weathervane as instructed. PRACTICE TEST 15

stem: After a fall from a mobile tower, an HSE inspector asks the bricklayer who witnessed it to answer questions in private and sign a declaration of truth. He refuses, saying his answers could be used against him if his employer is prosecuted. Which statement is correct?

options.A: He may stay silent as he would under a police caution, because an inspector's questions are voluntary until a formal notice has been served on his employer
options.B: He must answer, but anything he says can be used against him in court, so his best protection is to give short answers and decline to sign
options.C: He must answer only if his employer's solicitor is present, because an inspector cannot question a worker without the agreement of the company
options.D: He must answer and sign, because an answer given under this inspector's power cannot be used as evidence against him or his spouse or civil partner

explanation: Section 20 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act lets an inspector require answers and a signed declaration, but section 20(7) bars those answers from being used in evidence against that person or their spouse or civil partner.

why_wrong.A: An inspector's power to require answers is statutory and does not depend on a notice, so the police right to silence does not apply here.
why_wrong.B: The statute prevents these answers being used against him, and refusing to sign the declaration is itself a failure to comply with the requirement.
why_wrong.C: He may nominate a person to be present, but the inspector does not need the employer's agreement and a solicitor is not a condition of answering.

common_mistake: Assuming that talking to an HSE inspector carries the same risk of self-incrimination as being interviewed under police caution.

stem: A client's investors, none with construction experience, will tour a live frame site for an hour. The site manager says the risk assessments cover only the workforce, so visitors need only hi-vis jackets and must stay close to their escort. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Risks to visitors must be assessed too, giving a planned route clear of plant and overhead work, with suitable PPE, a safety briefing and a competent escort
options.B: Visitors are a client matter, so the client's insurer assesses the tour while the contractor's assessments cover people it employs on site
options.C: A formal assessment is needed only if the visit lasts more than a day, because short visits to a site fall below the usual threshold for any assessment
options.D: A signed waiver accepts the risks on the visitors' own behalf, which relieves the site of its duty to assess the hazards they might meet on the tour

explanation: Employers must assess risks to other people affected by their undertaking, so a tour needs its own controls, including route, PPE, briefing and escort, rather than relying on a jacket alone.

why_wrong.B: An insurer does not carry the legal duty, which stays with the contractor controlling the site and extends beyond its own employees.
why_wrong.C: There is no time threshold, and a short visit by untrained people to a live site can expose them to serious hazards.
why_wrong.D: A duty to people not in your employment cannot be signed away, so a waiver does not replace assessment and control of the risks.

common_mistake: Believing that risk assessments only need to cover your own workers and that visitors can be managed with a hi-vis jacket and an escort.

stem: A joiner drilling a ceiling in a 1970s school hits a hidden grey board and fine dust falls; it could be asbestos insulating board. A colleague fetches a brush and an ordinary vacuum to tidy up at once. What should happen first?

options.A: Stop work, move everyone out and keep others from entering, then report to the supervisor so the area is assessed and cleaned under the emergency procedure
options.B: Open the windows and switch on the portable extractor fans to clear the air, then carry on drilling elsewhere in the room once the visible dust has settled
options.C: Sweep the dust gently into a bag with a damp brush while wearing a paper mask, because a quick clean-up stops any fibres from reaching other rooms nearby
options.D: Remove the dusty overalls and shake them outside before resuming work, because fibres cling to clothing and cannot be released in the room

explanation: Preventing further exposure comes first, so stopping, evacuating and restricting access stops fibres spreading before competent people assess and clean up using proper methods.

why_wrong.B: Moving air carries fibres to other areas, and staying in the room keeps people exposed to possible contamination.
why_wrong.C: Brushing and a paper mask disturb and fail to filter fibres, so untrained clean-up spreads contamination and exposes the cleaner.
why_wrong.D: Shaking out clothing releases fibres into the air and onto other people, and work must not resume until the area is assessed.

common_mistake: Rushing to clean up suspected asbestos dust yourself rather than stopping, clearing the area and reporting it.

stem: On a fit-out, the alarm sounds. After two minutes the panel operator silences it because nobody has seen smoke or flames, and workers who gathered at the assembly point start drifting back inside. What is the correct response?

options.A: Workers may return to ground-floor areas after ten minutes, since a fire that has not grown by then is very unlikely to threaten the lower floors of the building
options.B: Workers may return once the bell stops, because a silenced alarm with no visible smoke indicates a false alarm and carrying on saves a good deal of lost time
options.C: Everyone stays at the assembly point until the person in charge has checked the cause and gives a clear all-clear, with the fire service called if none is found
options.D: Each firm's supervisor decides for his own gang, because contractors know their own areas best and can judge whether it is safe to go back

explanation: An alarm must be treated as a real fire until the cause is confirmed, so re-entry waits for an authorised all-clear, and silencing the sounder does not remove the possible danger.

why_wrong.A: A fixed waiting time is not a safety check, and smoke and fire can spread to any level without being seen.
why_wrong.B: Silencing a sounder says nothing about the cause, and a fire can be developing out of sight in a void or store.
why_wrong.D: Re-entry needs one coordinated decision by the person in charge, not separate judgements made by several firms without checking the cause.

common_mistake: Treating a silenced fire alarm as proof that there is no fire.

stem: A conservation mason switches from cement to hydrated lime mortar and tells the crew that, as a natural, traditional material, lime needs no gloves or eye protection. The safety data sheet says it irritates skin and causes serious eye damage. What is the best response?

options.A: Issue protection only after a crew member shows symptoms of burns or dermatitis, then record the first case in the accident book before reviewing the controls
options.B: Provide goggles but allow bare forearms, since lime damages only the eyes and wet lime on the skin washes off harmlessly at the end of the shift
options.C: Treat it as hazardous, following the data sheet with dust control at the mixer, eye protection, waterproof gloves and skin washing facilities
options.D: Accept the claim, because lime is milder than cement and a dust mask alone is enough to keep the crew safe while they are mixing and laying it

explanation: Under COSHH a natural or traditional material can still be harmful, and lime is alkaline, so the assessment follows the data sheet and sets controls for dust, skin and eyes.

why_wrong.A: Controls must be in place before exposure, and waiting for harm to appear reverses the purpose of the COSHH assessment.
why_wrong.B: Wet lime can burn or irritate skin and should be removed promptly, so leaving it on exposed arms for a shift is not acceptable.
why_wrong.D: Lime is strongly alkaline and can damage eyes and skin, so a dust mask does nothing for the splash and contact risks.

common_mistake: Assuming that a natural or traditional building material must be safer than a modern one.

stem: Tilers carry 20 kg tubs of adhesive up four flights because the permanent lift is not yet working. The manager's only measure is a manual handling training session for the gang. Which statement best describes the position?

options.A: The task is acceptable if each worker is limited to one tub per trip, since that keeps every single lift under the 25 kg guideline figure
options.B: Only the supplier can change the load, so the site can do nothing about tub size until the next order is placed, apart from rotating the carriers between floors
options.C: Training is a sufficient control on its own, because a trained worker can lift any commonly supplied tub weight safely if he uses the correct technique each time he lifts
options.D: Avoiding the carry should be considered first, for example by a hoist or delivery to each floor, then smaller tubs and aids, with training supporting those measures

explanation: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations require hazardous handling to be avoided where reasonably practicable, then assessed and reduced, so training alone is the weakest control.

why_wrong.A: Guideline figures are not safe limits, and repeated carrying up four flights adds fatigue and a fall risk that a single-trip rule ignores.
why_wrong.B: The site can order smaller tubs, change delivery points or use a hoist, and rotation does not reduce the risk in the task itself.
why_wrong.C: Technique does not remove the load, the stairs or the repetition, and training sits below avoidance and reduction in the order of controls.

common_mistake: Thinking that training in lifting technique is enough, instead of first trying to remove or reduce the load.

stem: A scissor-type MEWP will be used to repair a ceiling 8 m up in a public atrium, while staff continue to walk beneath it to reach the lifts. The supervisor plans cones, a shouted warning and a sign. Which arrangement best controls the risks?

options.A: Restrict walkers to the far side of the atrium with cones, because the operator can see people below and will stop work at once if anyone approaches the area
options.B: Permit walking beneath the platform while the operator keeps all tools in a bag, since small items cannot injure anyone from eight metres up
options.C: Close off the area beneath with physical barriers sized for the work zone and any falling items, and station a trained ground person to manage the MEWP
options.D: Leave the area open but work only in the quiet early morning, because fewer people use the atrium and the risk becomes acceptable

explanation: Controlling people below by physical segregation protects against falling objects and MEWP movement, while a ground person provides supervision and rescue backup that cones and shouting cannot.

why_wrong.A: Cones are easily crossed or moved, and an operator concentrating on the task above cannot reliably watch the whole area below.
why_wrong.B: Even small items gain energy in an 8 m drop and can seriously injure someone, so bagging tools alone does not remove the risk to those below.
why_wrong.D: Fewer people lowers the chance of harm but does not control it, and anyone arriving early could still walk under the work.

common_mistake: Relying on cones, signs or warnings to keep the public out from beneath overhead work.

stem: Look at the scene. Which feature creates the most serious risk of a fatal injury to the operator?

options.A: His body is trapped between the beam and the controls if he is pushed forward, and nobody at ground level is placed to lower the basket
options.B: The cordless drill is held above head height, which could cause an overreaching strain and a risk of the drill or its battery being dropped
options.C: The harness is clipped to the basket anchor point, which will drag the operator out of the basket if the boom suddenly moves
options.D: The boom is not set on outriggers, so the whole machine will overturn when the operator moves around inside the raised basket

explanation: Operators have been crushed between an overhead obstruction and the basket controls, and a trained person at the base controls can lower the platform quickly in an emergency.

why_wrong.B: Overhead drilling carries ergonomic and dropped-object risks, but these are minor compared with entrapment against the structure.
why_wrong.C: Clipping to the basket anchor is normal practice for a boom MEWP and is not the most serious hazard in the scene.
why_wrong.D: A boom MEWP of this type on firm level concrete does not need outriggers to be used safely, and the operator's movement within the basket is not the main danger.

common_mistake: Assuming that a harness and intact guardrails make a MEWP basket safe, when the structure overhead can crush the operator.

stem: A trench is being dug to the side of a disused underground oil tank, and the groundworker proposes bracing the trench side by wedging struts against the tank shell, saying it is solid steel. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The ground must be supported by designed supports that do not depend on the tank, and the tank treated as a possible source of flammable vapour
options.B: Bracing off the tank is fine once it has been drained, because an empty tank no longer holds any vapour or flammable residue inside it
options.C: No support is needed beside the tank, since the tank shields that side and only the opposite trench wall has to be timbered
options.D: A solid steel tank is strong enough to take the thrust, provided the foreman checks the shell for visible corrosion before any struts are fitted

explanation: A buried tank is not designed to take trench thrust and may hold residues, so independent supports are needed and ignition sources must be controlled until its contents are known.

why_wrong.B: A drained tank can still hold residue and vapour, and draining does not make the shell suitable as a support.
why_wrong.C: A tank gives no guaranteed shielding, and the soil above and beside it can still collapse onto people working in the trench.
why_wrong.D: A tank is not designed to carry trench loads, and corrosion not visible from the outside can still allow it to buckle or leak.

common_mistake: Using a nearby buried object as a convenient trench support, or treating an empty tank as automatically safe.

stem: A hire firm delivers an 8-tonne excavator, and its driver gives a five-minute talk and leaves. The site's operator is experienced but has only used machines with the other joystick control pattern. The foreman wants digging to begin straight away. What should happen?

options.A: Let the operator start, because his years of experience prove competence on any excavator and only a quick demonstration of the bucket is needed
options.B: Check the control pattern and give documented familiarisation using the manual, with a supervised trial away from people, before any work begins
options.C: Have a labourer stand beside the machine to shout corrections during the first shift, while the operator digs normally in the working area of the site
options.D: Rely on the hire driver's short talk, because the duty to instruct passes to the hire firm and the hirer has no further duty after handover of the machine

explanation: The user of work equipment must make sure operators have the information, instruction and training they need, which includes the machine's actual control layout, not just general experience.

why_wrong.A: Experience on a different control pattern can lead to wrong movements, which is a serious danger when working near people.
why_wrong.C: Placing a person beside a working machine exposes him to danger and does not replace proper familiarisation.
why_wrong.D: The hirer remains responsible for making sure its own operator is competent on the specific machine in use.

common_mistake: Assuming that a short handover from the hire firm or general experience means an operator is ready to use a particular machine.

stem: A 12-person groundworks firm has an office manager who holds a recognised health and safety qualification and knows the work well. The owner instead pays an outside consultancy to take care of safety, saying that transfers his legal duties to it. What is the correct position?

options.A: The office manager can assist only if the owner first gains a chartered safety qualification himself, since the employer must hold one personally
options.B: Paying a competent external consultancy passes the legal duty to it, because an accepted specialist takes over the employer's responsibilities for the work
options.C: Both can be used, but the consultancy must be chosen first, because an independent outsider is more objective than anyone employed by the firm
options.D: The owner stays responsible, and should appoint the trained office manager as competent person in preference to an outsider, who can only assist

explanation: Under the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations, an employer must appoint competent persons to assist him, choosing a suitable employee in preference to someone from outside, and appointing an adviser never transfers the employer's own duties.

why_wrong.A: No personal qualification is required of the owner, and competence is judged on training, experience, knowledge and other qualities.
why_wrong.B: An adviser only assists the employer, who keeps the legal responsibility for health and safety however capable the consultancy is.
why_wrong.C: The regulations require a suitable employee to be appointed in preference to an outsider, not the other way round.

common_mistake: Believing that hiring a safety consultant hands the employer's legal responsibility over to the consultant.

stem: After a wet fortnight, a drainage labourer working in a flooded trench in leaking wellingtons reports cold, numb, swollen and painful feet by evening. The foreman says it is just tiredness and the crew can carry on. Which response is best?

options.A: Rub the feet briskly with a towel and apply a hot pad, because strong warming restores circulation and prevents lasting tissue damage in the toes
options.B: Treat it as possible trench foot: get him out of the wet, dry and gently warm his feet, and arrange medical advice and better boots and socks
options.C: Let him finish the shift in dry socks, since a symptom that eases by the next morning cannot be a lasting cold or wet injury to the feet
options.D: Advise thicker waterproof boots worn all day and treat it as solved, because keeping feet warm matters more than drying them regularly

explanation: Long exposure of the feet to cold and wet damages nerves and tissue, so he needs prompt dry conditions and medical advice, and the site must remove the cause by fixing footwear and drying arrangements.

why_wrong.A: Numb, chilled tissue is easily damaged by rubbing or fierce heat, so warming must be gentle and followed by medical advice.
why_wrong.C: Tissue and nerve damage can persist or worsen after the pain eases, and the wet conditions causing it would be unchanged.
why_wrong.D: Sealed boots hold sweat and water against the skin, so feet still need regular drying and clean dry socks.

common_mistake: Dismissing numb, swollen, painful feet after long wet shifts as ordinary tiredness that will pass.

stem: While a gang clears an overgrown boundary, a labourer is stung by a wasp, then reports a tight chest, swollen lips and dizziness. He mentioned a known allergy at induction and carries an adrenaline auto-injector. What should his colleagues do?

options.A: Seat him in the cabin with an antihistamine tablet, and call 999 only if the swelling spreads beyond his lips or he worsens within the next hour
options.B: Keep him walking about to stop him fainting, and use the injector only once the ambulance crew arrive and confirm the diagnosis themselves
options.C: Drive him to hospital in a site vehicle with the injector left in his pocket, since a colleague driving would be quicker than an ambulance
options.D: Call 999, help him use the auto-injector, lie him down with legs raised (or sit up if breathless), and use a second dose if no better in five minutes

explanation: These are signs of anaphylaxis, where adrenaline and an immediate 999 call matter most, and a second auto-injector is used if there is no improvement after five minutes.

why_wrong.A: Anaphylaxis can worsen within minutes, and an antihistamine is no substitute for adrenaline and an immediate emergency call.
why_wrong.B: Standing or walking can cause collapse, and adrenaline must be given promptly rather than held back for confirmation.
why_wrong.C: Treatment is delayed and he may deteriorate unattended, so 999 should be called and adrenaline given where he is.

common_mistake: Waiting to see whether swelling and breathing trouble settle instead of calling 999 and giving adrenaline straight away.

stem: Look at the scene. The foreman says the operative is correctly dressed because he wears a hard hat, face shield, gauntlets and the hi-vis the site rules require. What is the most significant problem with what he is wearing?

options.A: Washing the waistcoat regularly makes it acceptable, because laundering restores the flame resistance of the ordinary polyester fabric used in hi-vis
options.B: The ordinary polyester hi-vis waistcoat can melt or ignite under sparks, so he needs flame-resistant hi-vis garments suited to hot work
options.C: His face shield should be swapped for tinted goggles, because a shield lets sparks reach his eyes from below and goggles seal better around them
options.D: The bright yellow-green colour is the problem, because vivid fabric attracts hot sparks while darker material would shed them more safely

explanation: Standard synthetic hi-vis fabric melts and burns when sparks land on it, so garments worn for cutting must be flame resistant while still keeping the wearer conspicuous.

why_wrong.A: Washing does not give ordinary polyester flame-resistant properties, and the material would still melt under sparks.
why_wrong.C: A face shield protects more of the face than goggles, and eye protection is not where the picture shows the gap.
why_wrong.D: Sparks are not drawn to colour, and it is the fibre and its treatment that decide whether fabric ignites or melts.

common_mistake: Assuming that any hi-vis garment that meets the site rule is also suitable for hot work.

stem: On a frosty morning, a gate marshal at a vehicle entrance wears his issued hi-vis waistcoat under a dark padded parka because it is too small to go over it. He says he will unzip the parka if a vehicle approaches. What is the best response?

options.A: Swap the parka for a thin jacket so the waistcoat fits over it, since being cold is a matter of comfort that has no bearing on safety
options.B: Provide hi-vis weather clothing, such as a hi-vis coat or larger outer waistcoat, so the conspicuous layer is outside and he stays warm
options.C: Accept the parka if it is clean and has reflective tape on it, since the waistcoat beneath still meets the standard if unzipped in time
options.D: Let him wear the parka and add a bright chest torch, because a lit torch is a recognised substitute for hi-vis clothing at site gates

explanation: Cold-weather clothing should either carry suitable hi- vis features or be worn under the hi-vis garment, and the employer must supply items that fit and work in the conditions.

why_wrong.A: Cold affects alertness and the employer should provide suitable clothing for the weather as well as for visibility.
why_wrong.C: A garment hidden under a dark coat does not make him visible, and relying on him unzipping in time puts the control on a split-second action.
