why_wrong.D: A torch is not equivalent to conspicuous garments that are visible from all sides and in all light conditions.

common_mistake: Letting workers cover their hi-vis with bulky coats because the issued vest does not fit over them.

stem: A crew will install pipework in a 1.5 m deep concrete pump sump in a basement slab, reached by stepping over its open edge. The supervisor says the Work at Height Regulations only apply above 2 m, so extra care is enough. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Treat it as work at height with no minimum drop: assess the fall risk and provide edge protection or a secure cover and safe access first
options.B: Apply the regulations only to work done from above ground level, since a place below ground level falls outside the legal definition of height
options.C: Issue harnesses clipped to the existing pipework and skip edge protection, because personal fall protection satisfies the duty at any depth
options.D: Accept the supervisor's view, as falls of under two metres count as slips and trips, so normal housekeeping controls are all that is required

explanation: The regulations cover any place, including at or below ground level, from which a person could fall a distance liable to cause injury, so a 1.5 m sump is covered and needs planned protection.

why_wrong.B: The definition expressly includes places at or below ground level, so a sump or pit is covered.
why_wrong.C: Collective measures such as edge protection or covers come before personal protection, and installed pipework is not a tested anchor.
why_wrong.D: There is no two-metre threshold, and the duty applies wherever a fall could cause personal injury.

common_mistake: Assuming that falls only matter above a fixed height such as two metres.

stem: A hired 6 m mobile access tower arrives one brace short. The foreman fetches a similar-looking brace from another maker's tower, saying the clips fit and the length is right. The erectors are PASMA-trained. What should happen?

options.A: Use it, because trained erectors can judge a safe fit, and have the finished tower checked at the next inspection afterwards by a competent person
options.B: Do not use the borrowed brace unless compatibility is independently verified and documented; get the correct part from the hire company
options.C: Use it on the lowest lift only, since stresses on bracing are lowest near the base, which makes mixing parts acceptable at that level of the tower
options.D: Use it with a second brace on the opposite face for extra stiffness, as doubling up compensates for any mismatch in the design of the parts

explanation: Tower components from different manufacturers are normally not compatible even if they appear to fit, so mixing is acceptable only where compatibility has been independently verified and documented.

why_wrong.A: A part fitting physically does not prove it is designed to work with the system, and an inspection cannot verify design compatibility.
why_wrong.C: There is no low-level exception, and a mismatched brace can still alter how the whole tower resists racking.
why_wrong.D: Extra parts do not prove compatibility and can create loads and spacings that the manufacturer never designed for.

common_mistake: Assuming that scaffold components from different makers are interchangeable if they physically fit together.

stem: A housing-site haul road for loaded dumpers is planned to cross a live gas main and a cable duct laid just below the surface. The plan says operators know where the services run, so no works are needed. What is the best control?

options.A: Locate the lines with a cable avoidance tool before each crossing and then allow free travel, since knowing their position prevents damage to them
options.B: Let dumpers cross anywhere along the line when empty, since lightly loaded wheels cannot damage a service buried just below the surface of the road
options.C: Spread a thin layer of loose spoil over the line and mark it with tape, since a little extra cover is enough to carry the passing vehicles
options.D: Limit crossing to one marked point, agree temporary protection such as plates or a raft with the service owners, and keep vehicles off elsewhere

explanation: Vehicle crossings over buried services should be kept to a minimum at marked places with temporary protection agreed with the owners, because shallow services are easily damaged by wheel loads.

why_wrong.A: Locating a service shows where it is but does nothing to protect it from the weight of passing vehicles.
why_wrong.B: An empty dumper is still heavy, shallow services are vulnerable, and crossings should be restricted to protected places.
why_wrong.C: Loose spoil gives no controlled load spreading and tape only marks the position without protecting the service.

common_mistake: Thinking that knowing where a buried service lies is the same as protecting it from vehicle loads.

stem: A forklift driver must carry a pallet of kerbs down a short gradient to a lower yard. To see ahead he plans to drive down forwards with the load pointing downhill, then turn on the slope to line up at the bottom. What should the supervisor require?

options.A: Face the forks uphill for the descent, then turn on the slope to line up with the yard, since the gradient is only a short one
options.B: Drive down forwards with the mast tilted fully forward to hold the kerbs on the pallet, because keeping the load in view matters most
options.C: Allow forwards travel down the slope at walking pace, since a low speed removes the stability risk from the load being carried facing downhill
options.D: Reverse down with the forks facing uphill, slowly and with a signaller for view, forks low but clear of the ground, and turn only on level ground

explanation: With a load, the forks should face uphill on a gradient to keep the load stable, travel should be slow with the forks lowered but clear of the ground, and turning on a slope risks overturning.

why_wrong.A: Turning on a slope risks overturning however short the gradient, so the turn must be made on level ground.
why_wrong.B: Tilting forward on a descent lets the load slide off and moves the centre of gravity towards the front wheels.
why_wrong.C: Slow speed does not cure a load carried facing downhill, which can still slide or tip the truck forward.

common_mistake: Putting a clear view ahead before the load's position on a gradient.

stem: A fit-out finishes with 40 unopened, undamaged plasterboard sheets and a heap of clean offcuts. The manager wants the cheapest disposal, with everything going into the general waste skip. Applying the waste hierarchy, what should happen?

options.A: Put everything in the general skip, since the hierarchy only requires that a registered carrier removes the waste and not that it is sorted first
options.B: Return or reuse the unopened sheets first, and send clean offcuts to a plasterboard recycler, kept dry and apart from other waste
options.C: Send the offcuts for energy recovery as the next best option after reuse, since burning board recovers more value than recycling it does
options.D: Tip the offcuts into the timber skip, since both are non- hazardous and the recycling contractor will sort them out later on

explanation: The waste hierarchy puts prevention and reuse before recycling, and plasterboard must be segregated so it can be recycled and kept out of landfill with biodegradable waste.

why_wrong.A: The hierarchy requires reasonable steps to prevent, reuse and recycle waste before it is disposed of.
why_wrong.C: Recycling ranks above energy recovery in the hierarchy, and plasterboard is not suitable for burning.
why_wrong.D: Gypsum contaminates timber recycling, and plasterboard must be kept apart from biodegradable waste.

common_mistake: Treating the cheapest skip as the compliant option because a licensed carrier collects it.

stem: A sub-contractor is hired for a two-day job fitting glazed roof panels. Its owner, a fitter with thirty years' experience but no assessment training, writes the risk assessment alone without speaking to his two operatives, saying a short job needs little. What is the best view?

options.A: The principal contractor's generic site assessment can stand in for it, since the two operatives will be working under that company's control on site
options.B: A brief assessment is acceptable for jobs of under three days, provided the owner signs it and tells the operatives about the controls on the first morning
options.C: The assessor needs knowledge of the work plus an understanding of risk assessment, and should talk to the people doing the job, however short
options.D: Thirty years of practical experience makes him competent to assess it alone, because nobody understands the hazards of glazing better than the fitter himself

explanation: Competence means enough training, knowledge and experience for the task in hand, and assessments must reflect how the work is really done, so involving the operatives matters on a short job as much as a long one.

why_wrong.A: A generic site document cannot cover the specific hazards of the sub-contractor's own task, so the employer must still assess its own work.
why_wrong.B: The duty to assess does not depend on how long a job lasts, and a briefing after the event does not replace gathering their input beforehand.
why_wrong.D: Task experience does not by itself give the skill to identify hazards systematically, rank risks and record controls, and it ignores what the operatives can add.

common_mistake: Assuming that years of practical experience, or the shortness of a job, can stand in for assessment skills and input from the people doing the work.

stem: A plumber must braze copper pipes in a roof void lined with timber joists and loose fibre insulation, directly above a stock of packaging. A press-fit joint system is available and suits the installation. Which approach best follows the principles for controlling fire risk from hot work?

options.A: Braze as planned with a damp cloth laid over the insulation and an extinguisher on the ladder, since a wet cloth makes the timber and fibre non-combustible
options.B: Soak the joists with a water spray before brazing and let the plumber leave as soon as the torch is out, since wet timber cannot smoulder later
options.C: Use press-fit joints to avoid the flame, and if hot work proves unavoidable, use a permit, shield the timber and insulation, and check the void afterwards
options.D: Braze each joint using the smallest torch flame, with no permit needed because a brief flame under ten minutes cannot ignite roof timbers or insulation

explanation: The best control is to remove the ignition source by using a cold method, and only where that is impossible should hot work go ahead under a permit with shielding and a check after the work.

why_wrong.A: A damp cloth soon dries and does not make the fuel non- combustible, and relying on an extinguisher ignores the option of avoiding the flame altogether.
why_wrong.B: Wet surfaces dry quickly and insulation can smoulder unseen, so leaving at once without any check afterwards risks a delayed fire.
why_wrong.D: Small or brief flames still ignite dry timber and fibre, and no time threshold removes the need to control hot work properly.

common_mistake: Jumping straight to permits and extinguishers without first asking whether the hot work can be avoided with a cold method.

stem: Joiners machine large quantities of urea-formaldehyde bonded MDF in a small workshop cabin. The supervisor plans FFP3 masks for everyone and a window fan. A buyer points out that a no-added-formaldehyde board is available at slightly higher cost. What is the best approach?

options.A: Keep the cheaper board and open the window wider, since formaldehyde is released from MDF only when the boards are heated or wet, not when cut
options.B: Specify the no-added-formaldehyde board where suitable and connect the machines to local exhaust ventilation, keeping masks as the last line of protection
options.C: Keep the cheaper board and rely on the FFP3 masks, since a tight-fitting respirator removes dust and vapour exposure for every worker in the cabin
options.D: Switch to the alternative board and cut it by hand indoors, since hand tools produce no harmful dust and so need no extraction

explanation: Substituting a less hazardous material and capturing dust at source come before respirators in the control hierarchy, and MDF dust from machining remains harmful whichever binder is used.

why_wrong.A: Machining MDF releases dust carrying formaldehyde, so general airflow from a window is not a proper control.
why_wrong.C: Respirators are the last resort, depend on fit and a clean-shaven face, and do not remove the need to substitute or extract at source.
why_wrong.D: Hand cutting and sanding still create wood dust that can harm the lungs, so extraction is still needed.

common_mistake: Treating respirators and open windows as the main control and overlooking cheaper-to-fix options at the source.

stem: A joiner with a long-term shoulder condition tells his supervisor that sustained overhead drilling is painful. The supervisor proposes moving him to the gatehouse permanently, saying anyone with that condition should avoid all manual tasks. What is the best approach?

options.A: Ask him to sign a waiver accepting the pain as a personal risk, then leave his tasks unchanged because he chose to carry on working
options.B: Move him to the gatehouse as proposed, since a blanket restriction for the condition is the safest option and avoids any need to assess him as an individual
options.C: Discuss the specific tasks with him, check the assessment covers him, and try adjustments such as a lighter tool, a platform or task rotation
options.D: Keep him on full duties unless he produces a medical certificate, since the employer has no duty to alter tasks until sickness absence has been recorded

explanation: Disabilities affect people differently, so employers should talk to the worker, assess the real tasks and make reasonable adjustments rather than apply blanket restrictions.

why_wrong.A: Employer duties under health and safety and equality law cannot be signed away by the worker.
why_wrong.B: Blanket restrictions based on assumptions can be unnecessary and discriminatory, because symptoms and abilities vary between individuals.
why_wrong.D: The duty to consider adjustments arises once the employer knows of the problem, and does not wait for a certificate or absence.

common_mistake: Assuming that everyone with the same condition needs the same restriction, instead of asking the individual what the real task demands.

stem: Roofers will strip and re-slate a house from a scaffold whose working platform sits 1.2 m below the eaves. It has top rails at 950 mm, intermediate rails and toe boards. The foreman says the rails and toe boards meet the standard. What is the main flaw?

options.A: The roofers should wear harnesses clipped to the roofing battens, which will give the missing protection without any change to the scaffold
options.B: None, because rails at 950 mm with a toe board and intermediate rails are all the standard asks, and platform height relative to the eaves is a matter of convenience
options.C: Debris netting should be fitted over the gap between the scaffold and the eaves, because netting will catch anyone sliding off the lower roof slope
options.D: The platform is too far below the eaves for the rails to stop someone sliding down the slope, so scaffolders should raise it close to the eaves

explanation: Eaves guidance expects the platform to be within about 300 mm of the eaves, and no more than 450 mm in some cases, otherwise rails sit too low to catch a roofer who slips.

why_wrong.A: Loose battens and slates are unreliable anchors, and this swaps a collective measure for a weaker personal one.
why_wrong.B: The rails only work if the platform height relates properly to the eaves, which here leaves the roof edge above the protection.
why_wrong.C: Debris netting is meant for catching small falling items and is not designed or tested to stop a falling person.

common_mistake: Checking rail heights and toe boards in isolation without asking where the platform sits relative to the roof edge.

stem: Look at the scene. The painter says he is only on the third step with the spreader bar locked and the floor is clean and level. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The stepladder is too short for the ceiling height, so he should swap to a longer leaning ladder and tie it securely at the top
options.B: The ladder legs are splayed too narrowly on the floor, so a wider stance or a stabilising brace is needed before anyone uses it again
options.C: He is working from the top platform of the stepladder, which should be used only as a handhold, so he ought to stand lower to be stable
options.D: The ladder stands where a door can swing into it and people are passing, with no barrier, door lock-off or lookout protecting the working area

explanation: A ladder in a doorway or traffic route can be struck by an opening door or a passing load, so the area should be guarded or the door secured before work starts.

why_wrong.A: The task is light work within reach from the third step, and swapping to a leaning ladder would not address the door and passers-by.
why_wrong.B: The spreader bar is locked and the floor is level, so stability of the ladder itself is not the weakness shown.
why_wrong.C: He is on the third step, not the top platform, so this does not describe the picture.

common_mistake: Checking only the ladder and the person on it, and forgetting doors, traffic and other people around the work area.

stem: Pipelayers dig a 3.5 m deep square pit in firm clay for a new manhole. They plan to dig to full depth, then climb down to fit struts and sheets from inside because the sides look stable. The pit was inspected on Monday. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Fit supports only to the lower half of the pit, since falling soil from above a depth of 2 m is unlikely to injure a person standing below
options.B: Fit support as the pit deepens, or place a system from the surface, so nobody enters unsupported ground, with inspection at each shift start
options.C: Dig to full depth and then fit supports from inside, because the Monday inspection covers the whole week while the clay remains dry
options.D: Climb down once the clay feels sound, since firm clay stands unsupported for as long as it has not been disturbed by vibration or weather

explanation: No ground can be relied on to stand unsupported, so support must go in before people enter, and a competent person must inspect at the start of each shift and after any event.

why_wrong.A: Collapse from any height can bury or crush a worker, so there is no safe depth for leaving the sides partly unsupported.
why_wrong.C: Inspection is required at the start of each working shift and after events affecting stability, not once a week.
why_wrong.D: No ground can be relied on to stand unsupported in all circumstances, so appearance and feel do not make entry safe.

common_mistake: Judging an excavation safe by how firm the ground looks rather than by what supports it and when it was last inspected.

stem: A dry underground attenuation tank, 4 m deep with a single 600 mm access, is to be inspected. The supervisor holds a gas detector at arm's length inside the opening, gets normal readings and declares the space clear for entry. What is wrong with this check?

options.A: Nothing is wrong, because a reading at the opening shows the air throughout the tank, which mixes evenly once the cover has been lifted
options.B: The reading must be repeated by a second person at the opening, since a different operator gives a more reliable result from the same air
options.C: Gases can layer, so readings are needed at several depths, ideally with a long probe from outside before entry, and monitoring should continue during the work
options.D: The reading is valid, but he should also smell the air at the foot of the ladder, since the absence of any smell shows there is no toxic gas

explanation: Heavier and lighter gases collect at different levels, so a reading at the opening may not represent the air where people will work, and conditions can change during the task.

why_wrong.A: Air in a deep enclosed space does not necessarily mix, and gas pockets can persist at the bottom or the roof.
why_wrong.B: Repeating the same flawed sampling point does not fix it, because the problem is where the sample is taken, not who takes it.
why_wrong.D: Many dangerous gases are odourless, and some deaden the sense of smell, so smell is not a safe test.

common_mistake: Trusting a single reading taken at the opening as proof that the whole space is safe to breathe.

stem: A contractor clears small broken asbestos cement fragments from a garage roof. He puts them in one black bin bag, tapes it shut, writes nothing on it and leaves it by the gate for the next general skip. What is wrong?

options.A: A single heavy-duty bag is enough if it is taped shut, because sealing prevents fibres escaping and labels are only needed at the disposal site
options.B: The waste should be double wrapped, typically a red inner bag with asbestos warning labels in a clear outer bag, and stored securely until sent to a licensed site
options.C: Double-bag the fragments in clear polythene and place them in the general rubble skip, since fully wrapped waste no longer counts as hazardous
options.D: Mark the bag "asbestos" in pen and leave it at the gate, since a marked bag will be collected by the council as ordinary household waste

explanation: Asbestos waste must be double wrapped and labelled so that fibres stay contained and handlers know what it is, then kept secure and sent only to a licensed disposal site.

why_wrong.A: A single bag can split and unlabelled waste can be handled unknowingly, so double wrapping and labelling are needed from the start.
why_wrong.C: Wrapping does not change the hazardous nature of asbestos waste, which must not be mixed with general waste.
why_wrong.D: Asbestos waste is not accepted as household rubbish and needs proper packaging and a licensed disposal route.

common_mistake: Believing that a taped bag or a quick pen mark is enough packaging for asbestos waste.

stem: A site beside a river keeps forty lidded 20-litre cans of diesel and petrol for pumps on grass 6 m from the bank, under a tarpaulin with a spill kit beside them. The foreman says lids and a kit are enough. What is the best response?

options.A: Stand the cans on pallets above likely flood level, as raising them off the ground stops any spilt fuel from reaching the water below
options.B: Leave them where they are, since lidded containers cannot leak and a spill kit within reach satisfies the guidance on storing fuel close to water
options.C: Keep the cans in place but add a silt fence between the store and the bank, which will filter out any fuel leaving the area
options.D: Move the store at least 10 m from the river onto an impermeable surface in trays or a bund that holds a spill, locked and labelled

explanation: Fuel stores should be sited at least 10 m from watercourses on a sealed surface with secondary containment, because a spill kit only helps after fuel has already escaped.

why_wrong.A: Height off the ground does not contain a spill, and fuel running off pallets would still flow across grass towards the river.
why_wrong.B: Lids do not stop leaks from damage or knocks, and a spill kit is a response measure that does not provide containment or distance.
why_wrong.C: A silt fence traps soil particles, not oil or fuel, so it gives no real protection against a fuel spill.

common_mistake: Relying on a spill kit and lids as the main protection instead of distance and containment.

stem: A site manager says the Health and Safety at Work Act is the only real law, that regulations such as the Work at Height Regulations are just HSE opinion, and that HSE guidance leaflets are binding on everyone. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Regulations and guidance carry the same legal force as the Act itself, so any departure from the wording of an HSE leaflet is a criminal offence in its own right
options.B: Regulations bind only employers with five or more staff, and guidance becomes law once the employer has been handed a copy of the relevant leaflet by an HSE inspector
options.C: Only the Act creates offences, regulations are enforced through civil claims alone, and guidance must be followed to the letter on every single job to avoid prosecution
options.D: Regulations are made under the Act and breaching them is an offence, whereas HSE guidance is optional and a different method that meets the law is allowed

explanation: Regulations have full legal force under section 33 of the Act, whereas HSE guidance is advice that normally demonstrates compliance but may be replaced by an alternative that still meets the legal duty.

why_wrong.A: Guidance is not compulsory, so departing from it is not itself an offence if the law is still met.
why_wrong.B: Regulations apply regardless of headcount, and handing over guidance does not turn it into law.
why_wrong.C: Contravening health and safety regulations is itself a criminal offence, and guidance can be replaced by an equivalent method.

common_mistake: Assuming that only the Act counts as law, or that every HSE leaflet is a legal command.

stem: A shopping centre owner lets a lift contractor's engineers reach a rooftop motor room across a roof with an unguarded edge, which the owner knows about. He says the engineers are the contractor's employees, so their safety is not his concern. What is the position?

options.A: As the person controlling the premises he owes duties for safe access and plant so far as reasonably practicable, and must share risk information
options.B: A signed contract passing responsibility for the work to the lift firm ends the owner's duty for the access route, even where the edge protection is missing altogether
options.C: The duty rests with the contractor as the engineers' employer, and the owner only has to warn them verbally about the roof edge if they happen to ask about it
options.D: Premises duties protect only people the owner employs, so a roof used by outside contractors falls outside his responsibility whatever he knows about the unguarded edge

explanation: Section 4 of the Act covers non-employees using non- domestic premises as a place of work, extends to anyone with any control of them, and is supported by the duty to cooperate and coordinate with other employers.

why_wrong.B: A contract cannot remove a statutory duty tied to the owner's control of the access and premises.
why_wrong.C: The owner's own duty arises from his control of the premises and cannot be reduced to answering questions.
why_wrong.D: The premises duty is specifically owed to people who are not the controller's employees.

common_mistake: Believing that only the employer of a worker has legal duties towards that worker's safety.

stem: A contractor will core-drill 150 mm holes through a first-floor slab for new ducts above a working office. The risk assessment names only the drill operator as at risk and gives 'wear PPE' as the control. Which improvement is most important?

options.A: Name the staff below as exposed, scan the slab for reinforcement and services, and cordon off the area underneath before any drilling begins
options.B: Keep PPE as the main control but add a second operative to watch the drill, since the office staff are outside the contractor's work area
options.C: Add only a dust and slurry control, because falling cores and hidden cables in the slab are matters for the rig manufacturer rather than for the assessment
options.D: Ask the office manager to tell staff to avoid their desks, because the occupier's own rules cover anyone who is not employed by the drilling contractor

explanation: A suitable assessment considers everyone who could be harmed, including people below, and uses physical controls such as scanning and exclusion zones ahead of PPE.

why_wrong.B: A second watcher does nothing to protect people below, who remain unassessed.
why_wrong.C: Dropped cores and drilling into hidden services are foreseeable hazards that the assessment must cover.
why_wrong.D: The contractor must plan and control the risk it creates and cannot hand it to the occupier.

common_mistake: Listing only the people doing the work when the assessment should cover everyone the work could harm.

stem: Floor finishers power-float a ground-floor slab in a closed-up building using a petrol-engined float, with doors shut to slow the drying. By mid-afternoon two have headaches, nausea and drowsiness, which they blame on a long day. What is the best response?

options.A: Swap to a half-mask with organic vapour cartridges, as these remove the exhaust gases from the air the finishers are breathing
options.B: Suspect carbon monoxide from the engine, get them into fresh air for medical advice, and switch to electric tools or extract the exhaust outdoors
options.C: Open one door a little and resume when the symptoms ease, since a single opening dilutes the exhaust enough for the float to keep running
options.D: Treat it as heat and tiredness, so allow water and rest breaks and carry on with the petrol float once the finishers put on disposable dust masks

explanation: Carbon monoxide gives flu-like symptoms, cannot be seen or smelt, and is best prevented by avoiding petrol equipment indoors unless ventilation has been properly assessed.

why_wrong.A: Vapour cartridges do not remove carbon monoxide, so the exposure would continue.
why_wrong.C: Ventilation must be assessed and is rarely adequate indoors, and a single opening gives no assurance.
why_wrong.D: Dust masks do nothing to stop carbon monoxide, and the symptoms point to exhaust gas.

common_mistake: Putting headaches and drowsiness down to tiredness instead of suspecting exhaust fumes from petrol equipment.

stem: A 'Danger: hot work' sign has hung on a stair door for a week since the welding ended, while a new floor opening on the same landing has only a 'Warning: floor opening' sign propped against it. The supervisor says the two signs cover both hazards. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both signs should stay, because an extra sign does no harm and the opening sign meets the duty provided it is large and placed where it can be easily seen
options.B: Both signs should be swapped for red and white tape, which is a recognised legal alternative to safety signs and is much quicker to renew on a busy landing
options.C: The hot work sign should go because it now misleads people, and the opening needs a cover or guardrail, as signs do not replace physical controls
options.D: The hot work sign should go, but a sign alone is enough for the opening because only a few trades are using that landing this week

explanation: A sign must be removed when the situation ceases to exist, and signs warn only of significant risk that remains after other controls have been applied.

why_wrong.A: A sign for a finished hazard misleads people, and a sign cannot stand in for a cover or guardrail.
why_wrong.B: Tape is not a substitute for a physical barrier or for a compliant safety sign.
why_wrong.D: The number of people exposed does not remove the need to guard a fall hazard.

common_mistake: Treating a safety sign as a control in its own right rather than a warning of risk that remains after other controls.

stem: Two fitters want to clip their harness lanyards to one anchor plate bolted to a steel purlin. The plate is marked for a single user. The supervisor says a fall by both at once is unlikely, so sharing is fine. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Sharing is acceptable because the chance of both falling together is small, and the energy absorbers on the lanyards would share the load between the two users
options.B: Sharing is fine provided both fitters keep their lanyards short, because a short lanyard cuts the fall distance and so halves the force on the plate
options.C: Each anchor must be strong enough for the loads expected, so a one-user anchor suits one person unless a competent person confirms more users
options.D: The marking is guidance for the installer only, and workers may clip on once the plate has been bolted to a structural steel member

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations require every anchor and its connection to withstand foreseeable loads, and the marked user number reflects what the anchor was designed and tested to carry.

why_wrong.A: Likelihood does not change the rated capacity, and absorbers do not reduce the load on the anchor to a shareable level.
why_wrong.B: Shortening the lanyard does not turn a one-user anchor into a two-user anchor.
why_wrong.D: The marking tells users the number of people the anchor was designed for, and being fixed to steel does not override it.

common_mistake: Judging an anchor by how solid it looks instead of by what it is rated and marked to carry.

stem: A newly laid 150 mm water main is to be pressure tested with compressed air to save water. The gang plans to stand beside the pipe ends while the test runs. A senior engineer objects. What is the main reason for the objection?

options.A: Air tests take longer than water tests, so the gang would be exposed to the pipe for more of the day than necessary
options.B: Air cannot find leaks as well as water, so the main would need re-testing, and that is mainly a cost issue
options.C: Compressed air is a flammable gas, so the test needs a hot work permit and a fire watch for the duration of the test
options.D: Air stores far more energy than water, so a failure can throw parts violently; hydraulic testing is safer or exclusion zones are needed

explanation: Compressed air is compressible and stores energy that is released suddenly in a failure, so water testing is preferred or people must be kept clear with restrained ends.

why_wrong.A: The duration is not the main hazard; the stored energy is.
why_wrong.B: The objection concerns safety, not test accuracy.
why_wrong.C: Compressed air is not flammable and no hot work permit applies.

common_mistake: Treating a compressed air test as equal in safety to a water test.

stem: Look at the scene. The driver holds a valid operator card and is travelling at walking pace. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The driver should sound the horn continuously, because an audible warning makes a shared route safe when the load hides the way ahead
options.B: The heaped skip blocks the driver's forward view while a pedestrian walks unsegregated on the same route directly ahead of the machine
options.C: The skip is loaded above its rim, so spilled brick and soil on the route is the main concern at walking pace, and the pedestrian is a lesser one
options.D: The pedestrian needs gloves and eye protection, because personal protective equipment is what protects people who walk near dumpers moving slowly

explanation: Loads must not obstruct the driver's view, and vehicles and pedestrians should be kept apart, because a driver who cannot see ahead cannot avoid someone in the path.

why_wrong.A: A horn does not restore the driver's view, and a pedestrian carrying a long timber with his head down may not react.
why_wrong.C: Spillage matters, but the loss of forward view with a person in the path is the dominant hazard.
why_wrong.D: PPE does not prevent being struck by a vehicle whose driver cannot see ahead.

common_mistake: Judging a vehicle task safe because the driver is licensed and slow, without checking what he can actually see.

stem: A mobile crane lifts a 6 m precast beam. As it rises, a steelfixer with no slinger training loops the tag line round his wrist to stop the spin and stands under the swing path. Which statement is correct?

options.A: He should be stopped; a trained slinger-signaller should steer the load with tag lines held clear of the body, from outside its path
options.B: Wrapping gives better grip, so it is acceptable provided he wears gloves and a second person stands beside him to share the pull on the line
options.C: Tag lines should not be used because they bring people near the load, so the operator should steady the beam by slewing against the spin
options.D: His method is acceptable if the line is kept short, since a short line gives the closest control of a rotating beam while it is being lifted

explanation: Lifting is controlled by trained people, tag lines are a normal way of controlling rotation, and operatives must stay clear of the load and its tag lines because wrapped lines can drag people up.

why_wrong.B: Gloves and a second person do not remove the risk of being dragged off the ground.
why_wrong.C: Tag lines are a standard control, and slewing against a spin can make the load swing more.
why_wrong.D: Wrapping a line round the body is dangerous at any length, and he is also untrained and standing in the swing path.

common_mistake: Thinking that a hand or a wrapped line is a fine way to steady a suspended load if the person is strong enough.

stem: After wet-cutting a floor slab inside a building, a contractor collects the grey slurry in buckets and wants to tip it down a site toilet, reasoning that it is only water and cement dust and the sewage works will cope. What is the correct view?

options.A: It can be spread thinly on the access road to bind the dust, since the cement sets hard and nothing then reaches any drain or watercourse
options.B: It can go down the building's rainwater downpipe, because that pipe is separate from the sewage system and therefore carries no sewage at all
options.C: The foul drain is the right place for the liquid once it has been diluted about ten times with tap water, and only the solids need to go in a skip
options.D: Contaminated wash water needs the water company's permission to enter the foul sewer, so collect and settle it and dispose of the solids as waste

explanation: Businesses need the water company's consent to discharge contaminated water to foul sewer, and settled solids are waste that must be consigned lawfully.

why_wrong.A: Slurry on a road is washed into drains by rain and is still an unpermitted disposal.
why_wrong.B: Rainwater pipes usually lead to surface water or a watercourse, where alkaline slurry causes pollution.
why_wrong.C: Dilution does not replace the need for consent, and cement slurry remains a polluting discharge.

common_mistake: Assuming cement slurry is harmless because it is only water, sand and cement, and that any drain will do.

stem: A joiner sees a basement ceiling prop buckle and a crack open above his head. He leaves the area and refuses to return until it is checked. The engineer later finds the load was not critical, and the contractor docks his pay and issues a warning. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: He is protected if the danger proves real, because the law judges his belief by what the engineer later found rather than by what he saw at the time
options.B: The employer may deduct pay because work stopped, since the right to leave dangerous work belongs to appointed safety representatives acting for the whole site
options.C: He is protected if his belief in serious, imminent danger was reasonable, even though the engineer found otherwise, so the deduction and warning may be unlawful
options.D: He should have obtained a supervisor's permission first, because leaving a work area without authority is a breach of contract that no statutory protection can override

explanation: Employment law protects a worker who leaves or refuses to return to a place of work in circumstances they reasonably believed to be serious and imminent danger, and the test is the reasonableness of that belief, not what is found afterwards.

why_wrong.A: The test is whether his belief was reasonable when he formed it, so a later finding that the load was not critical does not remove protection.
why_wrong.B: The protection applies to individual workers, not just to representatives, and is not removed by a general loss of working time.
why_wrong.D: The protection exists precisely so that a worker need not wait for authority before moving away from reasonably perceived serious danger.

common_mistake: Assuming a worker who walks away from a danger is only safe from discipline if the danger is later proved to have been real.

stem: Over six weeks a site log records seven near-hits, five involving pedestrians stepping into a dumper route through the same gap in the fencing beside the welfare cabins. The manager plans to speak to each driver and file the log. What is the best use of this information?

options.A: Treat the five as a pattern pointing to one shared cause, review the assessment and layout at that gap, then brief every contractor
options.B: Reassess the route for each dumper driver separately, since individual behaviour is the likely common cause and group changes should wait for an injury
options.C: Brief the drivers involved on awareness and revisit the assessment if an actual injury occurs, since near-hits without harm carry no weight in reviewing risk
options.D: Add a warning sign at the gap and close the log entries, because a sign is the cheapest control and the pattern shows pedestrians ignored the rules

explanation: Repeated near-hits at one location suggest the existing controls may no longer be valid, which calls for a review of the assessment and layout and for sharing the outcome with everyone affected.

why_wrong.B: Five events at one location point to a system or layout cause, not to five individual lapses.
why_wrong.C: A review is triggered when there is reason to suspect an assessment is no longer valid, which repeated near-hits supply without waiting for harm.
why_wrong.D: A sign is a weak control that ranks below physical separation, and blaming pedestrians ignores the shared cause.

common_mistake: Treating each near-hit as a separate event to be dealt with person by person instead of looking for the pattern across the log.

stem: Operatives repair a quay wall beside a tidal river, working from a pontoon with no lifebuoy on site. A labourer slips into the water, surfaces and shouts. A colleague wants to dive in after him. What is the best planning and response?

options.A: Wait for the labourer to swim to the bank by himself, since he has surfaced, and call 999 only if he goes under again
options.B: Fetch a rope from the van and tie it to the colleague so he can wade in from the quay edge and drag the labourer out
options.C: Let the colleague dive in at once, because the quickest rescue is a swimmer, and cold water is dangerous only after several minutes
options.D: Provide throwable rescue equipment and a rescue plan beforehand, then throw a lifebuoy and call 999, without anyone entering the water

explanation: Water rescue kit and a plan should be in place before work starts; throwing a line or buoy and calling for help avoids a second casualty from cold water shock.

why_wrong.A: He may be affected by cold water, so help and rescue equipment are needed straight away.
why_wrong.B: Sending a person into the water on a rope is dangerous without training and equipment.
why_wrong.C: Cold water shock can overcome a rescuer within seconds, so entering the water risks a second casualty.

common_mistake: Planning to rescue a person from water by entering it, rather than by throwing equipment and calling for help.

stem: Air sampling shows a floor sealer applicator's exposure to a xylene-based solvent is well below its workplace exposure limit, which carries an 'Sk' notation. He works in thin disposable gloves with solvent-splashed forearms, and the supervisor says no further control is needed. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The limit already includes an allowance for skin uptake, so wearing any glove satisfies the duty without a check that the material resists the solvent
options.B: Air results below the limit show the whole dose is controlled, so skin controls are optional extras that matter unless a rash appears
options.C: The Sk notation warns that skin absorption can add to the dose, so air results cannot show adequate control and skin contact must be prevented too
options.D: Skin exposure counts if the product is labelled corrosive, so the Sk notation is a labelling point for the supplier rather than a duty for the employer

explanation: A skin notation means the substance can be absorbed through the skin enough to matter, so a good air result does not prove control and skin exposure must be assessed and controlled separately.

why_wrong.A: Limits cover inhaled air only, and gloves must be chosen for resistance to the specific solvent, not just worn.
why_wrong.B: Absorption through intact skin can raise the body's dose with no rash, which is exactly what the notation warns about.
why_wrong.D: The notation concerns systemic absorption by any route, and it informs the employer's own COSHH assessment.

common_mistake: Treating a below-limit air reading as proof that a solvent is under control when it can also pass through the skin.

stem: A crew repairing a foul sewer cleans up with the van's alcohol gel before lunch. One man vomited and had diarrhoea overnight, but feels better and wants to return the next morning, twelve hours after his last symptoms. What is the best action?

options.A: Allow his return on lighter duties away from the sewer, because the infection spreads through sewage contact and keeping him from the sewer protects colleagues
options.B: Keep him off site until he has been symptom-free for 48 hours, and provide soap, running water and a clean eating area rather than relying on gel
options.C: Allow his return, as twelve symptom-free hours is enough once he uses the alcohol gel, since gel kills the viruses behind sewage-related stomach bugs
options.D: Keep him off site for 48 hours but accept alcohol gel as the crew's handwashing method, as gel is quicker and copes with visible dirt on the hands

explanation: Stomach bugs spread easily by the faecal-oral route and alcohol gel does not kill norovirus, so exclusion for two days after symptoms stop and proper soap-and-water washing both matter.

why_wrong.A: He can still spread infection through shared surfaces, tools, food and the cabin, regardless of where he works.
why_wrong.C: Gel does not kill norovirus and twelve hours is too short, as people stay infectious after symptoms stop.
why_wrong.D: Gel is ineffective on visibly soiled hands and against norovirus, so it cannot replace soap and running water.

common_mistake: Assuming hand gel and a few symptom- free hours are enough protection against stomach bugs in sewer work.

stem: A roofer's harness webbing is caked with cement slurry and bitumen smears. Overnight he scrubs it with a strong solvent cleaner and bleach, dries it on a cabin heater and plans to use it again. His colleague says it looks cleaner than ever. What is the main concern?

options.A: Solvents, bleach and direct heat can weaken webbing and stitching without showing, so it should be cleaned per the maker's instructions and checked before use
options.B: The harness must go to a competent person for a formal thorough examination each time it is washed, because cleaning resets its examination interval
options.C: The risk comes from the heater, since bleach and solvents rinse out of polyester completely, so air drying indoors would have made the harness fit for use
options.D: The harness is now in better condition, because strong cleaning removes contamination that hides damage and heat drying prevents mildew in the fabric

explanation: Harness fibres are degraded by harsh chemicals and heat in ways the eye cannot detect, so manufacturer cleaning and drying instructions must be followed and the harness inspected before it is used.

why_wrong.B: Thorough examination follows a set interval or specific events and is separate from the user's pre-use check, and cleaning does not restart it.
why_wrong.C: Bleach and solvents can also degrade the fibres, and any harness cleaned against the maker's instructions needs inspection before use.
why_wrong.D: Appearance is no guide to strength, and the harsh chemicals and heat may have caused the very damage that cannot be seen.

common_mistake: Judging a harness by how clean it looks instead of by how it was cleaned and then checked.

stem: Look at the scene. The operative says his visor, ear defenders and safety boots mean he has all the protection a petrol brushcutter needs. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: His ear defenders are clipped to a hard hat and will not seal against his head, so he needs foam earplugs worn instead for brushcutter noise
options.B: His hi-vis vest could snag in the cutting head, so it should be removed while he works with the machine beside the fence
options.C: His lower legs are bare, so thrown stones or the cutting head could injure them; he needs protective trousers or leg guards
options.D: His mesh visor is the wrong type for flying stones, so he needs sealed chemical goggles worn in place of it for the whole task

explanation: A brushcutter throws stones and debris at ground level and the cutting head can strike the legs, so legs need protective trousers or guards in addition to visor, hearing and foot protection.

why_wrong.A: Hat-mounted defenders suit this task, and replacing them with earplugs would not address the visible gap in protection.
why_wrong.B: A close- fitting hi-vis vest is not the main hazard, and removing it would reduce visibility to plant working nearby.
why_wrong.D: A mesh visor is the usual face protection for brushcutting, and goggles would not give the same coverage against debris.

common_mistake: Assuming that protecting the head, ears and feet means the whole body is covered when a machine throws debris at leg height.

stem: A concrete slab is propped from below by falsework. The slab has been cast for five days and the programme is slipping. The foreman wants the props struck today because the concrete has gone hard to the touch. What is needed before striking?

options.A: The temporary works coordinator must confirm the concrete strength and the striking sequence in writing, and only authorised people do it
options.B: Nothing more, because hardness to the touch shows the slab is strong enough, and the foreman may order the props out
options.C: Removal of every prop at once to avoid uneven loads, with the gang standing clear of the slab edge as a precaution
options.D: A count of five days, because five days after pouring is a fixed legal minimum before any falsework can be removed

explanation: Falsework should be struck only when the designer's criteria are met and the temporary works coordinator has permitted it, since concrete that feels hard may not carry its load.

why_wrong.B: Hardness to the touch does not prove the concrete has gained design strength.
why_wrong.C: Striking all together without a planned sequence can overload the slab and cause collapse.
why_wrong.D: No fixed number of days applies; it depends on strength and design.

common_mistake: Judging concrete to be ready for striking by touch or by the number of days since casting.

stem: A 110 V transformer in the compound feeds a 3 kW mixer motor through several long, thin reels 90 m away. The motor hums, starts slowly and the cable feels warm. The operator suggests fitting an RCD to cure it. What explains the fault, and what is the sensible fix?

options.A: An RCD limits overload current as well as earth leakage, so fitting one at the transformer would stop the motor drawing excess current in the cable
options.B: Warm thin cable shows the supply is under-rated, so switching the mixer to a 230 V socket on the same reels would halve the current and clear the fault
options.C: Voltage drops along long, thin cable at high current, so the motor overheats; move the transformer near the work and use heavier cable
options.D: Joining another reel in series will lower the resistance of the circuit, because more copper carries the current and gives the motor a stronger supply

explanation: Resistance rises with cable length and falls with conductor size, and at 110 V the current for a given power is higher, so the voltage drop starves the motor and heats the cable.

why_wrong.A: An RCD detects earth leakage, not overload or voltage drop, and does not cure the underlying problem.
why_wrong.B: Moving a hand-held or site tool to 230 V removes the reduced-voltage protection that site supplies rely on.
why_wrong.D: Extra length adds resistance, which increases the voltage drop and makes the problem worse.

common_mistake: Assuming a long lead delivers the same voltage at the tool as at the supply, and that an RCD protects against every electrical fault.

stem: A mobile crane will lift a 3.4 t precast unit from a lorry at 8 m radius and set it at 13 m. The chart shows capacity before deducting 0.4 t of slings and hook block: 4.5 t at 8 m and 3.6 t at 13 m. The operator says the unit weighs less than both. Is the lift acceptable?

options.A: No, the unit plus 0.4 t of accessories is 3.8 t, above the 3.6 t chart value at the largest radius, so it must be re-planned
options.B: No, though it becomes acceptable if the operator travels the load slowly, since low speed reduces the dynamic load that the chart assumes
options.C: Yes, because the lift starts at 8 m where the chart allows 4.5 t, and capacity needs checking where the load is first raised
options.D: Yes, because the unit weighs less than the chart value at both the pick-up and set-down radii, and the slings are covered by the crane's safety margin

explanation: Capacity falls as radius increases, and the whole gross load including slings and hook block must be checked against the chart at the greatest radius reached anywhere along the lift.

why_wrong.B: Slow movement does not change the chart capacity at a given radius and cannot make an overloaded lift acceptable.
why_wrong.C: The largest radius on the path, here the set-down point, governs the lift, not the start.
why_wrong.D: Accessories count towards the load and the chart's safety margin is not available to cover them.

common_mistake: Comparing only the weight of the item with the chart figure at the pick-up point and forgetting accessories and the set-down radius. PRACTICE TEST 16

stem: A contractor recognises a union whose appointed safety representatives cover its labourers, but its ten directly employed joiners are non-members. Before moving a refurbishment to night shifts, the manager plans to consult the union representatives only. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Union recognition means the appointed representatives speak for the whole workforce, so consulting them alone satisfies the duty towards the non-member joiners as well
options.B: Union representatives are consulted for their members, and the joiners must be consulted, directly or via elected representatives, before the decision
options.C: Consultation with the joiners is only required if they ask for it in writing, because without an elected representative there is no right to be consulted
options.D: The joiners are informed of the night-shift decision at a toolbox talk once it has been agreed with the union, which is sufficient as notification under the law

explanation: Where some employees are not covered by union- appointed representatives, the employer must consult them under the 1996 Regulations, so that both groups are heard before the change is made.

why_wrong.A: Union-appointed representatives only represent the employees they cover, so the joiners remain a separate group to consult.
why_wrong.C: The duty to consult rests on the employer and does not depend on employees requesting it or electing anyone.
why_wrong.D: Telling people after a decision is made is information, not consultation, which must happen in good time beforehand.

common_mistake: Assuming that having recognised union representatives means the whole workforce has been consulted.

stem: A groundworks firm will drive piles for a retaining wall beside a live electrified railway, using a rig taller than its distance from the boundary fence. The risk assessment covers only its own operatives and members of the public. What is the most important gap?

options.A: The railway is the infrastructure owner's responsibility, so the firm only needs to assess hazards on its own side of the boundary and keep its workers away from the fence
options.B: Risks to the railway, such as the rig toppling or items dropping onto the line, are unassessed, and the railway owner's asset protection team must be engaged
options.C: Piling can safely proceed if it is timed between scheduled trains, since the line is only at risk while a train is actually passing the site
options.D: The boundary fence is a sufficient barrier against anything falling or toppling, so only noise and vibration to railway neighbours remain to be assessed

explanation: A risk assessment must cover everyone affected by the work, including train crews and passengers, and the infrastructure owner must agree measures where plant could foul the line.

why_wrong.A: The firm's duty extends to anyone affected by its work, including the railway and its users beyond the boundary.
why_wrong.C: A rig or object foul of the line is hazardous at any time, and train timetables change, so timing alone is not a control.
why_wrong.D: A fence does not stop a rig or dropped materials reaching the line, so it is not an adequate control for that risk.

common_mistake: Assessing only the people on your own site and treating a neighbouring railway as someone else's problem.

stem: A scaffolder falls from a mobile tower onto concrete and is unresponsive but breathing, with snoring sounds, and a first-aider suspects a neck injury. A colleague says nobody should touch his head until paramedics arrive. After 999 is called, what should the first-aider do?

options.A: Hold the head and neck in line and open the airway with a jaw thrust, using the recovery position only if the airway cannot be kept clear
options.B: Leave him exactly as found with the head untouched until the ambulance crew arrive, because any movement could worsen a possible injury to the spine
options.C: Tilt the head fully back and lift the chin firmly to clear the tongue, since this is the quickest way to open the airway of any unresponsive casualty
options.D: Roll him onto his side straight away with the help of a bystander, because the recovery position is required for every unresponsive breathing casualty

explanation: Keeping the airway open takes priority, and a jaw thrust does so with least neck movement; the recovery position is a last resort when the airway cannot be maintained.

why_wrong.B: Snoring signals a partly blocked airway, and an obstructed airway is more immediately life-threatening than a suspected spinal injury.
why_wrong.C: Tilting the neck back is avoided with a suspected spinal injury, where a jaw thrust is the preferred technique.
why_wrong.D: Rolling is reserved for when the airway cannot be kept open by other means, as it risks moving the spine unnecessarily.

common_mistake: Freezing in the belief that a possible spinal injury means nothing can be done about a blocked airway.

stem: A fabrication yard keeps acetylene, oxygen and LPG cylinders in a fenced compound by the gate. Its fire plan puts the assembly point at the gate and tells staff to cool nearby cylinders with hoses in a fire. How should the plan change?

options.A: Move all the cylinders into the main workshop overnight and in an emergency, so that the compound is empty and no risk is left at the gate
options.B: Keep the assembly point at the gate and form a trained cooling team in protective clothing, so that the cylinders stay cold until the fire service arrives
options.C: Move the assembly point well clear, forbid staff from approaching the cylinders, and have a named person give the fire service the cylinder types and positions
options.D: Leave the layout alone but display a sign at the gate showing cylinder contents, so that fire crews know the hazard when they arrive at the site

explanation: Cylinders can burst or explode when heated, so people must be kept away and responders need to know what is stored and where.

why_wrong.A: Storing cylinders inside a workshop increases the fire and explosion risk to people, and it does not remove the need for a plan.
why_wrong.B: Staff should never approach heated cylinders, as they may fail without warning and cooling is a task for the fire service.
why_wrong.D: A sign does not move people out of the danger zone and does not replace a person briefing the crew on the quantities and positions.

common_mistake: Thinking that staff cooling heated cylinders with a hose is a brave and sensible first response.

stem: A joiner sprays solvent-based lacquer on doors in a portable cross-draught booth. He stands beyond the doors, between them and the filter wall, and the filter-blockage gauge reads in the red. He says the booth makes his position and the gauge irrelevant. What is correct?

options.A: His position makes no difference because the extraction is strong enough to catch all mist, and the gauge is only relevant to the annual service contractor
options.B: Only the position needs correcting, as the gauge reading shows how much dust has collected and the filters can be changed at the end of the shift
options.C: He should stand on the intake side so air carries mist away from his face, and the blocked filters must be replaced before spraying resumes
options.D: He may continue provided he sprays in short bursts, since brief exposures with a running fan keep the vapour concentration below the exposure limit

explanation: A booth only controls exposure while air flows past the work away from the operator, so position and filter condition are both essential.

why_wrong.A: Standing downstream puts his breathing zone in the contaminated airflow, and a blocked filter reduces airflow when it matters.
why_wrong.B: A blocked filter cuts the airflow that carries mist and vapour away, so continuing to spray with it is itself a failure.
why_wrong.D: Short bursts do not compensate for reduced airflow, and nothing here shows that the concentration has been measured.

common_mistake: Believing a spray booth protects the operator wherever he stands and whatever state the filters are in.

stem: A canopied air compressor stands in the corner of a concrete stairwell with its canopy doors propped open for cooling. Two plasterers work 3 m away. Which approach best reduces their noise exposure?

options.A: Close the canopy doors, put the compressor outside or in an open area, and use a longer hose so it sits further from the plasterers
options.B: Move the compressor closer to the plasterers to shorten the hose, as a shorter air line reduces pressure losses and so makes the machine quieter
options.C: Leave the layout as it is because the stairwell walls enclose the noise, so the sound level cannot rise beyond that of the canopy alone
options.D: Keep the doors open for cooling and issue ear defenders to both plasterers, which brings their exposure down to a safe level without moving any equipment

explanation: Enclosures only attenuate noise when closed, corners and hard walls reflect it, and levels fall with distance from the source, so ear protection is the last control.

why_wrong.B: A shorter hose does not make the compressor quieter and bringing it nearer increases exposure.
why_wrong.C: Hard enclosed walls reflect sound and raise levels, which is the opposite of containing the noise.
why_wrong.D: Hearing protection is the last resort, and relying on it ignores the cheap controls that reduce noise at the source and on its path.

common_mistake: Propping open a noise enclosure for convenience and relying on ear defenders to make up the difference.

stem: After handover, bricklayers prop the self-closing gate at each scaffold ladder opening with a brick, so labourers can pass bricks up by hand. The foreman says the handover record shows the gates fitted. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The gate is the scaffolder's responsibility, and users need take no action beyond reporting to the scaffolder at the next weekly inspection
options.B: Gates only need to be closed at the end of the shift, because the handover record covers their use as long as someone stays at each opening
options.C: Propping is acceptable for light loads, since a brick holds the gate in a position where operatives can still see the opening and avoid stepping into it
options.D: A propped gate gives no protection at the opening, so gates must close after each use and materials be moved by hoist or another method

explanation: A fitted gate protects against a fall through the ladder opening only when it is closed, so the handover record does not excuse defeating it.

why_wrong.A: Everyone using the scaffold must keep protection in place and may not alter it, and defects need prompt reporting rather than waiting.
why_wrong.B: The opening is a fall hazard whenever people work nearby, so the gate must close after every passage, not just overnight.
why_wrong.C: Whether or not the opening is visible, an open gate leaves a gap that someone can fall through.

common_mistake: Treating a paper handover record as proof that protection will still be working once other trades are using the scaffold.

stem: Look at the scene. The site supervisor says the ladder is secure because the man is using both hands and it has been set at a proper angle. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The ladder top rests against plastic guttering, which cannot carry its load, so a stand-off or another form of support is needed
options.B: The man should be wearing a full-body harness clipped to the ladder rungs, since a fall from 3 m could cause serious injury without fall arrest
options.C: The base needs a second person footing it, because a ladder on paving is stable only if someone is standing on the bottom rung at all times
options.D: The ladder is set too shallow for safe use, so the base should be moved closer to the wall to reduce the chance of the ladder sliding outwards

explanation: Guttering is not a suitable support, as it may deform or crack and let the ladder slip, so a stand-off frame or a different access method is needed.

why_wrong.B: Harnesses are not normally clipped to ladder rungs, which are not designed as an anchor point.
why_wrong.C: The base is on firm level paving with a stabiliser bar, so the fault in the picture is at the top.
why_wrong.D: The ladder is shown at a correct angle of about one in four, so the angle is not the problem.

common_mistake: Checking the angle and the footing of a ladder but never looking at what the top is resting against.

stem: Two crews pull a new low-voltage cable through an underground duct from a drum at one pit to a winch at another, 80 m away. The winch operator cannot see the drum and relies on shouted signals, and a fitter plans to guide the cable by hand at the duct mouth. What best reduces injury risk?

options.A: Replace the pulling rope with a heavier one to prevent it snapping, so that the crew can safely stand beside the pit while the cable is moving
options.B: Use shouted signals but have the winch run at its slowest speed throughout, because slow pulling reduces the tension and so removes the need for communication
options.C: Provide reliable two-way radio contact with a stop signal, fit a guide at the duct mouth, and keep hands and bodies clear of the cable and rope under tension
options.D: Let the fitter steady the cable at the duct mouth wearing thick gloves, since gloves protect the hands from friction and from being drawn into the duct

explanation: Cable and rope under tension can crush hands at the duct mouth and snap back, so a guide, clear communication and exclusion from the danger zone are needed.

why_wrong.A: A heavier rope still stores energy and can recoil, and people should stay out of the danger zone whatever the rope size.
why_wrong.B: Slow speed does not remove the hazard, and shouted signals over a long distance and machinery noise are unreliable.
why_wrong.D: Gloves do not prevent a hand being pulled in or crushed, so the hands must be kept away from the mouth altogether.

common_mistake: Trusting gloves and a loud voice to manage the hazards of pulling a cable under tension.

stem: A lorry-mounted loader crane keeps stopping as the driver extends the boom to place a pallet of blocks over a hoarding, and its load-moment limiter alarm sounds. He holds the override key to finish, saying the delivery note weight is within the crane's maximum rating. What is correct?

options.A: Overriding is acceptable because the pallet weighs less than the stated maximum capacity, and the limiter is only an advisory warning for newer drivers
options.B: Overriding is acceptable if a banksman watches the lorry while he places the load, and signals to stop when the vehicle begins to lift or tilt
options.C: Overriding is acceptable once every stabiliser is fully extended and pinned, because the lorry then cannot tip however far the boom is extended
options.D: He should not override it, because capacity falls as outreach grows; the lorry should be moved nearer, the load split, or a larger crane used

explanation: The maximum rating applies only at short outreach, and the limiter warns that the overturning moment is exceeded, so the lift needs re-planning rather than defeating the safety device.

why_wrong.A: The limiter works on load multiplied by outreach, so a load under the maximum rating can still exceed capacity at that reach.
why_wrong.B: A tipping lorry gives little warning, so watching for movement is no substitute for the limiter that prevents the overload.
why_wrong.C: Fully set stabilisers do not make the rated capacity at long outreach unlimited, and overriding defeats the protection against overload.

common_mistake: Comparing the load only with the crane's maximum rating and ignoring how far it is being reached out.

stem: An inspector finds a hired-in concrete pump being run with its boom hose clamp visibly worn, and fears a hose could whip loose. The site manager says no notice can be served because no regulation is named and only the employer can receive one. What is correct?

options.A: The inspector may only serve an Improvement Notice with a compliance period, since the pump is hired and the hire company holds the legal duty
options.B: A notice needs a proven breach of a named regulation and must go to the employer, so the inspector can only give verbal advice until one is found
options.C: A Prohibition Notice can be served only after an injury has happened, because the inspector must show the risk has already caused serious harm
options.D: A Prohibition Notice goes to whoever controls the activity if the inspector sees a risk of serious personal injury, with no breach needed

explanation: The test for a Prohibition Notice is the inspector's opinion of a risk of serious personal injury, and it goes to the person in control of the activity, which may be an operator rather than the employer.

why_wrong.A: An Improvement Notice needs a contravention and gives time to comply, whereas a serious risk can be stopped at once whoever owns the equipment.
why_wrong.B: Both halves are wrong, because a breach is not a precondition and the notice goes to whoever controls the activity.
why_wrong.C: The power exists to stop a risk before harm occurs, so no injury is required.

common_mistake: Assuming an inspector needs a named legal breach, or must deal only with the employer, before stopping a dangerous activity.

stem: Six operatives grind concrete floors under a COSHH assessment that requires annual lung function tests. One worker's results show a clear drop since last year, though he feels fine. The manager proposes keeping his job as it is and retesting him alone next year. What should happen?

options.A: Move him to lighter duties and leave the controls alone, because a drop in one person suggests personal susceptibility and not a workplace problem
options.B: Refer him to occupational health, and review the dust controls and the other workers' exposure, as the result may show failing controls
options.C: Wait for him to report symptoms before acting, since lung test results mean nothing until he coughs or becomes breathless at work
options.D: Issue him a tighter-fitting mask and retest next year, because respiratory protection is accepted as the answer to any adverse lung result

explanation: Health surveillance results must feed back into the risk assessment, because one worker's decline can signal inadequate controls that put everyone doing the same work at risk.

why_wrong.A: Removing one person without checking the controls leaves the others exposed to the same dust.
why_wrong.C: Surveillance exists to find early changes before symptoms show, so waiting defeats its purpose.
why_wrong.D: PPE is the last resort, and an adverse result should prompt a review of the whole control strategy and not just a change of mask.

common_mistake: Treating an adverse health check as one person's problem instead of evidence about how well the controls work for everyone.

stem: A telehandler's lead-acid battery is topped up by a fitter. Electrolyte splashes his forearm through a soaked sleeve, and he feels only mild tingling. He wants to finish the job and wash later. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Remove the wet sleeve while flooding the skin with running water for twenty minutes, then get medical advice and give the product details
options.B: Wipe the skin with a dry cloth, finish the repair and wash at the break, because mild tingling shows the splash was too weak to cause burns
options.C: Dab bicarbonate paste on the area to neutralise the acid, then rinse briefly, because neutralising is quicker and gentler than water alone
options.D: Rinse for about a minute under the cabin tap, cover the area with a plaster and carry on, because the rest is left to heal by itself

explanation: Acid keeps burning while it stays in contact, so prolonged flushing with removal of contaminated clothing is needed even when pain is slight, and the chemical details help treatment.

why_wrong.B: Wiping spreads the acid, and a chemical burn can be serious before it hurts.
why_wrong.C: Neutralising generates heat and is slow, whereas copious water dilutes and removes the acid safely.
why_wrong.D: A minute of rinsing is far too short to remove the chemical, and covering it traps residue against the skin.

common_mistake: Judging a chemical splash by how much it hurts rather than by what it is and how long it stayed on the skin.

stem: Look at the operative breaking out the slab. The hearing protection is the right type for this noise. Which statement best identifies the main problem with how it is being worn?

options.A: The ear defenders should be worn loosely so the operator can still hear instructions from the second worker standing nearby with the barrow
options.B: The thick woollen hat between the cushions and his head stops them sealing, so the protection is much lower than the rating suggests
options.C: The defenders should not be worn with a hard hat at all, because the headband pushes the helmet shell forward and loosens its fit
options.D: Defenders are too heavy for a breaker operator, and foam earplugs would meet the same duty while keeping his head warm and comfortable

explanation: Ear defender cushions must seal directly against the skin, and bulky material in the way leaves gaps that can cut the attenuation sharply.

why_wrong.A: Loose cups give less protection, and communication needs are met by other arrangements, not by reducing attenuation.
why_wrong.C: Headband defenders and helmets are routinely worn together, and helmet- mounted types exist for the purpose.
why_wrong.D: Weight is not the fault shown, and swapping type does not fix the issue of poor fit.

common_mistake: Believing any ear defender works as rated no matter what is worn underneath it.

stem: Strip-out workers wear white disposable Type 5/6 coveralls to clear dusty ceiling voids. Later the same crew use angle grinders to cut brackets, throwing sparks onto their sleeves. The supervisor says the coveralls cover them fully and are already the right protection. What is the best view?

options.A: Standard disposable coveralls resist dust but can melt or ignite from sparks, so the grinding needs flame-resistant garments
options.B: The coveralls suit both jobs, because the Type 5 marking proves protection against any hazard where the whole body is covered by the suit
options.C: Reusable cotton overalls are always weaker than disposable suits, so the crew should wear a second disposable suit over the first for the grinding
options.D: The sleeves can be taped shut at the cuffs, since a taped seal stops sparks entering and removes any need for flame- resistant clothing

explanation: Coverall type marks the particle and splash category, not the flame performance, so a task adding sparks needs a flame-resistant garment chosen for that hazard.

why_wrong.B: A Type 5 marking covers airborne particles only, and says nothing about sparks.
why_wrong.C: Doubling a suit that can melt adds fuel and does not make it flame-resistant.
why_wrong.D: Tape does not stop the outer fabric melting or burning, and it can make the injury worse.

common_mistake: Assuming one type of protective suit covers every hazard in a mixed task because it covers the whole body.

stem: A supplier's trained fixers are to clamp a lightweight temporary edge system around a new roof of 22 degrees pitch and 7 m eaves height. The kit offered is rated Class A under EN 13374. The site manager says fixer training means the system is suitable. What is the best view?

options.A: Class A is acceptable on any roof once the fixers are trained, because the class only matters for roofs steeper than forty-five degrees
options.B: Class A suits slopes up to 10 degrees, so a Class B system rated for slopes under 30 degrees is needed, whatever the training
options.C: A Class C system is needed, since any roof over fifteen degrees counts as a steep slope and requires the highest class available
options.D: Class A is fine if a harness is added for the roofers, since personal protection replaces the need for the edge system to match the pitch

explanation: EN 13374 classes reflect roof pitch, and Class A is designed only for surfaces up to 10 degrees, so the equipment must match the slope and not rely on installer skill alone.

why_wrong.A: The class limit begins at 10 degrees, and training cannot make a system stop someone sliding.
why_wrong.C: Class C is for steeper pitches of 30 to 45 degrees, so 22 degrees falls under Class B.
why_wrong.D: Collective edge protection must itself suit the slope, and a harness does not make an unsuitable system acceptable.

common_mistake: Treating installer training or a certificate as proof that a system suits the specific roof it is fitted to.

stem: A site store has a loading bay 1.2 m above the yard, fitted with a hydraulic dock leveller. Once a trailer leaves, the roller door stays open and the leveller is left lowered. A forklift also loads a docked trailer that has no restraint. What is the best set of controls?

options.A: Keep the door open so the forklift driver can see the yard, and paint a yellow line at the bay edge to mark where the fall begins
