options.B: Rely on the driver's handbrake while loading, and tell staff to keep clear of the edge since 1.2 m is too low to need any protection
options.C: Restrain docked trailers with chocks or a restraint device, and close the door or barrier the open edge with the leveller stowed
options.D: Leave the leveller lowered when idle so it fills the gap, and station a banksman at the bay while loading to watch for movement

explanation: A trailer can creep away during loading, and the open bay edge is a fall risk whatever its height, so both need controlling by restraint and edge protection.

why_wrong.A: A painted line warns but does not stop a person or truck from going over the edge.
why_wrong.B: A handbrake alone does not prevent creep, and the Work at Height Regulations apply to any height where a fall could cause injury.
why_wrong.D: A lowered leveller does not close off the drop at its sides, and a banksman cannot hold a trailer or guard the open edge.

common_mistake: Thinking a fall of about a metre does not need edge protection because it is less than two metres.

stem: A loaded dumper is bogged to its axles in soft clay. The foreman wants to pull it out with a chain from an excavator, looped round the dumper's front axle, and tells two labourers to guide the chain from beside the dumper. What is the best approach?

options.A: Use designated recovery points with rated tackle, pull in line slowly without jerking, and keep everyone clear of the pulling line
options.B: Loop the chain round the axle but have the labourers stand behind a plant-mounted guard while the excavator takes up the slack with a sharp tug to free it
options.C: Let the labourers stay close to the dumper to watch the chain, since they can warn the driver sooner if the chain begins to slip or the tackle shifts
options.D: Empty the dumper first, then pull from any strong part of the frame using an old chain, since the lighter load removes the need for special care

explanation: Recovery loads can be high and a failed link or chain can recoil, so rated gear on designated points and an exclusion zone along the line protect people.

why_wrong.B: A sharp tug increases shock loading, and axles and unrated chain are not designed as recovery points.
why_wrong.C: People near a loaded chain are in the recoil path, and signalling should come from a safe distance outside the line.
why_wrong.D: A lighter load does not make unrated tackle or an unsuitable fixing point safe.

common_mistake: Treating recovery of stuck plant as a quick improvised job where any chain and any strong-looking part will do.

stem: A trench excavator has a tilt rotator and a bucket. A groundworker with a level staff stands beside the bucket as the cab is stationary, thinking the machine is not slewing. The operator then rotates and tilts the bucket in place. What principle best explains the risk?

options.A: The risk is limited to the tail swing of the cab, so the standard fence around the rear counterweight is enough to protect the groundworker
options.B: The risk is only present when the bucket is loaded, so a groundworker may stand beside an empty bucket if he wears a hard hat
options.C: The tool can swing and tilt without the machine moving, so the exclusion zone must cover the tool's full reach, and entry needs the operator's agreement
options.D: A groundworker is safe beside a bucket whenever the operator can see him through the cab window and has been told where he is

explanation: A tilt rotator moves the attachment independently of the body, so a stationary cab is no sign of safety and people must stay outside the tool's reach until the operator has grounded it.

why_wrong.A: The danger here is from the attachment, which moves well beyond the tail swing area.
why_wrong.B: An empty bucket on a rotating tool can still strike or crush, and a hard hat is no defence against it.
why_wrong.D: Visibility does not remove the risk, because rapid unexpected tool movement can still strike a person who is within reach.

common_mistake: Judging safe distance by whether the machine body is moving rather than by where the attachment can reach.

stem: Conversion work on an old farm involves emptying a slurry pit into open skips that sit in the yard for days in warm weather. Neighbours complain of a strong smell, and the contractor says it is only a natural odour and not a legal issue. What is the right response?

options.A: Wait until the council issues an abatement notice before doing anything, since the law only starts to apply once a notice has been served on the site
options.B: Treat it as a possible statutory nuisance, and use practicable controls such as covered skips and prompt removal, and record them
options.C: Ask neighbours to sign a note accepting the smell for the project length, since their agreement removes the legal risk of the nuisance
options.D: Continue as before because smells are only a legal matter if they harm health, and a farm job is expected to smell of slurry in summer

explanation: Smells from trade or business premises can be a statutory nuisance, and showing best practicable means were used is the recognised defence, so prompt controls and records both matter.

why_wrong.A: The duty to avoid the nuisance exists beforehand, and acting early prevents a notice and enforcement.
why_wrong.C: Informal consent does not stop a nuisance being established or the council acting on later complaints.
why_wrong.D: A statutory nuisance can arise from interference with comfort and enjoyment, not only from proven harm.

common_mistake: Assuming a nuisance smell only matters if it can be proven to harm health.

stem: A crane lift of a 1.2 tonne air-handling unit onto a roof has a risk assessment giving a numeric wind limit from the crane manual. It has no plan for what happens if the limit is passed with the load in the air. What is the best improvement?

options.A: Have a competent person add a stop-and-land procedure with a cleared set-down point and a named person with authority to halt the lift
options.B: Brief only the crane operator on abandoning the lift, since sharing the plan with the slinger and signaller would create conflicting instructions
options.C: Leave the numeric limit as the only control, because an experienced operator can decide where to land the load if conditions worsen once it is airborne
options.D: Start the lift only when the forecast shows no wind at all, which removes the need to plan for stopping part-way through the operation

explanation: Regulation 8 of LOLER requires lifting operations to be properly planned by a competent person, so the plan must cover abandoning the lift safely, not just the conditions for starting it.

why_wrong.B: Everyone involved in the lift must know the stop criteria and the landing area, or the plan cannot be followed.
why_wrong.C: Improvising a landing mid-lift is the opposite of proper planning and leaves the crew without a rehearsed response.
why_wrong.D: Forecasts are unreliable and local gusts at roof height can differ, so conditions can still change during the lift.

common_mistake: Assuming a risk assessment is complete once it sets a start condition, without planning how to stop the operation safely part-way.

stem: A groundworker is pulled, coughing and shivering, from a flooded 1.5 m deep chamber after slipping in. He is breathing normally and talking, says he swallowed water but feels fine, and wants to carry on working. What is the correct action?

options.A: Get him into dry clothes and keep him warm and watched, and arrange hospital assessment because inhaled water can cause delayed breathing problems
options.B: Give him a hot sweet drink and a hot shower to rewarm him quickly, then reassess him next morning if symptoms have not settled
options.C: Press firmly on his abdomen to force swallowed water out, then send him home if he is alert and talking normally afterwards
options.D: Let him rest in the warm cabin for an hour and return to work if the cough stops, since coughing shows his airway has cleared the water by itself

explanation: Water in the lungs can cause problems hours later even when a casualty looks well, so medical assessment is advised after any near-drowning while he is kept warm and monitored.

why_wrong.B: Rapid rewarming alone ignores the lung risk and delays medical assessment until a deterioration may already have begun.
why_wrong.C: Abdominal pressure is not recommended, risks vomiting and inhalation, and does not remove the need for medical assessment.
why_wrong.D: A settled cough does not show the lungs are undamaged, and delayed breathing difficulty can follow.

common_mistake: Judging a rescued casualty by how well they look and talk, rather than by what they may have inhaled.

stem: On a sunny day a labourer brushes coal-tar creosote onto post ends in a T-shirt and fabric gloves. By evening his forearms are red and sore. A colleague says it is ordinary sunburn that moisturiser will fix. Which response is correct?

options.A: Creosote is harmful only if swallowed or inhaled, so the redness is plain sunburn needing after-sun cream and a sun hat for the next shift ahead
options.B: Creosote on skin can heighten sunlight sensitivity and cause burns, so he should wash it off, report it and use sleeves and chemical-resistant gloves
options.C: The only risk is vapour, so a dust mask and working in the shade would remove the hazard, with no need to change the way he handles it
options.D: Thicker fabric gloves would keep the product off his skin, and the redness is a normal reaction to sun that does not need to be reported

explanation: Skin contact with creosote can increase sensitivity to light and cause burns and irritation, so exposure must be controlled at the skin and the incident reported for review.

why_wrong.A: Skin is a significant route of exposure for creosote and sunlight can worsen the damage.
why_wrong.C: A dust mask does not stop vapour or skin contact, so neither route is controlled by shade and a paper mask.
why_wrong.D: Fabric absorbs creosote and holds it against the skin, and the injury should still be reported and investigated.

common_mistake: Putting skin reactions down to sunburn or weather instead of asking what substance was on the skin.

stem: A new joiner has existing hearing loss shown in a pre- employment test. His average daily noise exposure at the machines is 82 dB(A), below the upper action value. The employer says hearing surveillance applies only above 85 dB(A). What is the correct position?

options.A: He should be included, since existing hearing loss puts him at risk even below the upper value, and early tests give a baseline
options.B: Surveillance can wait until he reports hearing difficulty, since testing is triggered by symptoms and not by exposure level or individual susceptibility
options.C: He must be moved off all noisy work immediately, as a person with hearing loss cannot lawfully be exposed to any noise at work
options.D: Surveillance is optional below 85 dB(A), but ear protectors must then be compulsory for him, which removes the exposure risk and any need for testing

explanation: Hearing surveillance covers workers likely to be regularly exposed above the upper action value and those at risk for other reasons, such as existing hearing loss.

why_wrong.B: Surveillance exists to detect damage early, before the worker notices symptoms.
why_wrong.C: There is no ban on such work; the duty is to control the risk and monitor his hearing.
why_wrong.D: Hearing protection does not remove the need for surveillance for a worker already at risk.

common_mistake: Treating the upper action value as the only trigger for hearing checks, ignoring workers who are more vulnerable.

stem: A fitter must use a braced mobile tower on a gentle concrete ramp between two warehouse bays. The crew apply all four castor brakes and say stabilisers are unnecessary because the wheels are locked. What is the main flaw?

options.A: A ramp is acceptable if the tower is half-height and cross- braced, since the height-to-base ratio is the only measure of stability on any surface
options.B: Stabilisers should be left off on a ramp because they lift the castors clear and leave the brakes carrying less of the tower's weight
options.C: Locked castors do not stop tipping on a slope; check the maker's gradient limits, use adjustable legs on base plates and fit the specified stabilisers
options.D: Locked castors prevent movement in every direction, so on a ramp the only extra check needed is that the platform boards are secured to the frame

explanation: Brakes only stop rolling, whereas stability on a slope depends on the manufacturer's gradient limits, levelling and stabilisers, and base plates are safer than castors on a slope.

why_wrong.A: Stability also depends on the slope, the ground and the manufacturer's instructions, not height alone.
why_wrong.B: Stabilisers are fitted as the manufacturer's schedule requires and help to prevent the tower overturning.
why_wrong.D: Brakes cannot prevent overturning, which is the main danger on a slope.

common_mistake: Believing that locking the castor brakes makes a mobile tower safe on any surface.

stem: Look at the scene. The slinger says the work is quick and the containers are an everyday sight, so no special precautions are needed. Which statement best describes the hazard?

options.A: The task is brief and routine, so the main risk is the swinging hook, which can be managed by the ground worker watching the crane and warning him
options.B: The ladder is the only fault, and a second person footing it is sufficient, since a person holding the base removes the need for edge protection
options.C: A fall of about 5 m from an unprotected edge is possible, and the ladder gives no handhold at the top, so a safer way of hooking on is needed
options.D: A hard hat and hi-vis vest are adequate for roof access this low, because height rules apply only when the work is above two metres

explanation: Working at the open edge of a high roof with an unsecured ladder creates a serious fall risk, and the work should be avoided or done from a proper platform with edge protection.

why_wrong.A: Duration and familiarity do not remove the fall risk from an unprotected edge.
why_wrong.B: Footing a ladder does not fix a missing handhold at the top, and the open roof edge is still unprotected.
why_wrong.D: There is no minimum height in the Work at Height Regulations, and a 5 m fall is serious in any case.

common_mistake: Treating familiar, short tasks as low risk although the person is standing at an unprotected edge.

stem: A mobile crane will set out loads on a plot where bare overhead lines run along the far boundary. The operator plans to keep an eye on the jib as it slews, and nobody has yet contacted the line owner. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Regard the lines as the owner's concern because they sit outside the working area, and rely on the crane's rubber tyres to protect the driver
options.B: Consult the line owner on safe clearance, then fit restraints or barriers so the jib cannot reach it, since contact is not needed for a flashover
options.C: Keep the jib about 3 m clear by eye, a distance that suits lines of any voltage, with the signaller watching the boom tip and shouting if it drifts
options.D: Treat the lines as dead if no humming or buzzing is heard, and slew freely while the load stays beneath them and the operator stays seated

explanation: HSE guidance says to consult the line owner, treat lines as live, and use physical restraints and barriers because close approach alone can cause arcing.

why_wrong.A: Plant can reach lines beyond the working area, and tyres do not protect against arcing or a step potential.
why_wrong.C: Judging distance by eye is unreliable, and safe clearance depends on the line owner's advice.
why_wrong.D: Silence does not prove a line is dead; all lines are assumed live unless the owner proves otherwise.

common_mistake: Relying on operator skill and watching by eye instead of physical controls that stop the jib reaching the lines.

stem: Hand-digging a footpath trench, an operator exposes yellow plastic warning tape 450 mm down. He says yellow means gas, so any pipe is just below it and he can bring in the mini-excavator and take the bucket down to the tape. What is wrong?

options.A: Tape only warns that a service lies somewhere below, so colour is not proof of type, and digging should stay by hand until it is confirmed
options.B: The problem is only that he removed the tape, so the proper step is to re-lay it above the service and continue digging mechanically
options.C: Yellow tape reliably identifies gas and sits directly above the pipe, so the bucket can go down to the tape and only then switch to hand tools
options.D: The tape means the area is safe to dig to the tape depth, because services below it are always protected by a concrete or plastic cover

explanation: Warning tape shows that a service is present beneath but not its exact depth or position, and colours cannot be relied upon, so safe digging practice continues with hand tools and confirmation.

why_wrong.B: Re-laying tape does nothing to locate the service, and mechanical digging near it risks a strike.
why_wrong.C: Colour is not a reliable identifier, and a bucket at tape level may already be too close to the service.
why_wrong.D: Tape is a warning of presence, not a protective barrier, and nothing guarantees a cover over the service.

common_mistake: Reading the colour of a warning tape as a full description of what is beneath it and where.

stem: On a sloping site, runoff reaches a road gully protected by a silt-filter mat. The foreman adds a silt fence with its fabric simply laid on the ground across the flow path and checks it weekly. Which improvement is best?

options.A: Let silt build up against the fence, since a deeper layer filters finer particles and a weekly check is enough whatever the weather
options.B: Place the fence directly across the swale where runoff concentrates, because the biggest flow needs the biggest barrier to hold the sediment back
options.C: Trench in the fabric foot, run the fence along the contour, inspect after heavy rain and clear silt, and limit soil washing off at source
options.D: Swap the mat for a finer-weave fabric so no silt can pass, which makes extra measures upstream of the gully unnecessary on a sloping site

explanation: Silt fences work when the fabric is trenched in and set along the contour, and they need inspection after rain, with measures that limit soil washing off at source.

why_wrong.A: Excess silt reduces capacity and causes overtopping, and checks are needed after rain.
why_wrong.B: Fences are not suited to concentrated, continuous flow and are overwhelmed or undercut.
why_wrong.D: Finer filters clog quickly and cannot replace controlling soil loss at source.

common_mistake: Assuming a drain mat or silt fence will cope with any sediment, instead of keeping soil out of runoff at source.

stem: A mechanic puts engine-oil-soaked rags and used oil filters in a lidded drum marked "oily waste". The manager books the registered skip firm to collect it, with no consignment note because the quantity is small. What is the correct position?

options.A: The rags can go in general waste once wrung out, because only free-flowing liquid oil makes waste hazardous, not material soaked in it
options.B: Oily rags and filters are hazardous waste, so a consignment note is completed and kept in the register for three years at the premises
options.C: The note can be skipped because the drum is lidded and labelled, since proper storage already shows that the duty of care has been met
options.D: A waste transfer note is enough because the carrier is registered, as consignment notes apply only to hazardous waste that is exported abroad

explanation: Hazardous waste leaving site needs a consignment note, and the producer must keep the register of notes for three years at the premises that produced or stored the waste.

why_wrong.A: Oil-soaked material remains contaminated and hazardous even without free liquid.
why_wrong.C: Storage and labelling do not replace the required paperwork when the waste is collected.
why_wrong.D: Consignment notes apply to hazardous waste moved within the country, not just exports.

common_mistake: Thinking a registered carrier or a small quantity removes the need for hazardous waste paperwork.

stem: A school appoints one electrical contractor, working alone, to rewire a classroom block over six weeks. The contractor says no construction phase plan is needed because there is no principal contractor and the job is small. Which statement is correct?

options.A: No plan is needed, because the duty sits only with a principal contractor, who is appointed when several contractors work on the same project
options.B: As the only contractor, it must draw up a construction phase plan before work starts, kept proportionate to the size and risks of the job
options.C: The school's designer must write the plan, because without a principal contractor the contractor simply follows the designer's arrangements
options.D: A plan is needed only if the project is notifiable to HSE, so the contractor should first check the thresholds for sending an F10

explanation: Under CDM 2015 a construction phase plan is needed for every project, and where there is a single contractor that contractor is the one who must prepare it before the construction phase begins.

why_wrong.A: A plan is required on every project, and a sole contractor takes on the drawing-up duty itself.
why_wrong.C: Designers supply pre-construction information, but the plan for the work itself comes from the contractor or principal contractor.
why_wrong.D: The plan duty does not depend on notification thresholds, which only decide whether HSE must be told.

common_mistake: Assuming that a small job with one firm on it is too minor to need a written plan before work begins.

stem: A notifiable office refurbishment will start on Monday. The client asked her principal designer to send the F10 to HSE, but it was never sent and nobody noticed. Which statement about responsibility is most accurate?

options.A: The duty to notify stays with the client even though a colleague was asked to send it, and notice was due before the construction phase began
options.B: The principal designer alone is responsible, because once the client delegated the task the legal duty to notify transferred to the person who agreed
options.C: The principal contractor is responsible, because it controls the construction site and so inherits the client's notification duty once it is appointed
options.D: Nobody is yet in breach, because notice is only required once the project has actually run for thirty working days on site

explanation: CDM 2015 places the duty to notify HSE on the client; the client may ask someone else to submit it, but doing so does not pass the legal duty on.

why_wrong.B: Delegating the task does not transfer the client's legal duty to the person who accepted it.
why_wrong.C: The principal contractor has no automatic duty to notify; that duty belongs to the client.
why_wrong.D: Notice must be given as soon as practicable before the construction phase begins, not after thirty days of work.

common_mistake: Believing that asking someone else to send the F10 also hands them the client's legal responsibility for it.

stem: A permit to work for maintenance on a roof-mounted extract fan is valid from 07:00 to 15:00. At 14:30 the engineer says the job needs another two hours, and the isolation is still in place. What should happen?

options.A: The engineer can carry on to finish, since the isolation is unchanged, and then note the overrun on his own copy when he hands the permit back
options.B: The engineer can extend it himself by writing a later time on his copy, because as the holder he best knows how long the task will take
options.C: Work can continue until 17:00 because a permit stays valid until the task it describes is complete, whatever times are written on it
options.D: Work should stop at expiry unless the issuing authorised person re-checks the area and signs an extension with a new expiry time

explanation: A permit is time-limited, and it can only be extended by the person who issued it after confirming the area is still safe and that everyone working under it knows the details.

why_wrong.A: An expired permit gives no authority to work, and noting the overrun afterwards does not replace the issuer's check.
why_wrong.B: Only the authorised person who issued the permit may extend it, not the person holding it.
why_wrong.C: A permit is a time-limited document, and the stated expiry time is part of the control.

common_mistake: Treating the end time on a permit as a rough guide that the holder can stretch when a job runs late.

stem: A flooring crew dry-grinds old rubber-backed floor covering in an occupied school corridor. The foreman says rubber is not labelled hazardous and no data sheet applies, so no COSHH assessment is needed. What is the most accurate response?

options.A: An assessment is needed only after air monitoring shows the dust is above a limit, so grinding should start and be measured on day one
options.B: An assessment is needed only where the supplier's data sheet classes the product as hazardous, so the missing label means the task is outside COSHH
options.C: The task is covered, but a disposable mask is enough because rubber dust is non-toxic, so extraction is for silica or wood dust only
options.D: COSHH covers dust created by the work itself, so the task needs assessing and the dust controlling at source, for example with on-tool extraction

explanation: COSHH applies to hazardous dust generated by work activity even where the material carries no label, and controls at source come before reliance on masks.

why_wrong.A: The assessment must come before exposure, not after monitoring has shown a problem.
why_wrong.B: Dust produced by grinding is covered whether or not the original product was labelled.
why_wrong.C: Rubber dust can harm lungs and skin, and masks are the last control, not the first.

common_mistake: Assuming that a material without a hazard label cannot create a COSHH problem when it is cut, sanded or ground.

stem: A hired gas cylinder arrives with its paint faded and a label peeling off. A fitter says he knows an acetylene cylinder by its maroon colour and starts to connect it to a regulator. What is the correct view?

options.A: Ask a colleague what he thinks it is and connect it if they agree, since two opinions are as good as a label
options.B: Use the colour, since cylinder colours are fixed by law so that any gas can be identified safely from the paint alone
options.C: Identify the contents from the supplier's label or marking, not the colour, and return the cylinder if it cannot be identified
options.D: Connect it and check for a smell of the gas, since each gas has a distinct smell which would show the contents

explanation: Cylinder colours vary and fade, so contents must be confirmed from the label or marking; an unidentified cylinder should be returned to the supplier.

why_wrong.A: Opinions are no substitute for the supplier's label.
why_wrong.B: Colour is not a reliable identifier and cannot replace the label.
why_wrong.D: Smelling for a gas is dangerous and not a reliable method.

common_mistake: Trusting the paint colour of a cylinder when the label is missing.

stem: A birdcage scaffold inside a heated church hall carries a plastering platform over the whole floor. No wind or rain reaches it, and ten days have passed since its first inspection. The manager says weekly inspections are unnecessary indoors. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Inspection is needed only before first use and after alterations, because weather is what causes the deterioration that the weekly rule addresses
options.B: The scaffolder's handover check is enough, with the plasterers glancing at the platform each morning and no written report being needed
options.C: Inspection is required, but monthly is enough indoors, since loading and exposure are lower than on an external facade scaffold
options.D: Inspection at intervals not exceeding seven days still applies indoors, as well as after any alteration or event affecting stability, with a written report

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations require scaffold inspection by a competent person before use, at intervals of up to seven days and after events that may affect stability, wherever it stands.

why_wrong.A: The seven-day inspection applies to scaffolds generally and is not limited to those exposed to weather.
why_wrong.B: Informal user glances do not replace a recorded inspection by a competent person.
why_wrong.C: The maximum interval is seven days and is not extended for indoor scaffolds.

common_mistake: Thinking that a scaffold sheltered from the weather can go without its regular recorded inspections.

stem: A ground-investigation team has traced a live electricity cable with a locator and will expose it in a hand-dug trial hole before drilling. A labourer plans to dig straight down on the traced line, scanning once more at the end. What is the best correction?

options.A: Dig straight down but only with insulated tools, because a located cable is a known hazard and the insulated handles give the protection
options.B: Drive a steel probe down vertically along the traced line to find the depth first, then hand-dig directly above the contact point
options.C: Break the top 300 mm with a hydraulic breaker for speed and hand-dig below that, since cables are rarely laid shallower than that
options.D: Dig alongside the line with insulated hand tools, repeat the locator checks as the hole deepens, and finish exposing the cable horizontally

explanation: HSE advises excavating alongside a service rather than above it, using insulated hand tools, scanning repeatedly during the work and exposing the service finally by horizontal digging.

why_wrong.A: Digging directly on top of the cable is what risks striking it, and insulated handles do not make a strike safe.
why_wrong.B: Driving a steel probe into the line risks piercing a live cable and does not remove the need to dig alongside.
why_wrong.C: Cable depth varies and cannot be assumed, so mechanical breaking over a live service risks a strike.

common_mistake: Believing that once a cable has been traced the only remaining job is to dig down on it until it appears.

stem: Look at the scene at the crushing area. The loader driver says he is fully trained and the crusher has its own emergency stop. What is the most serious problem?

options.A: The stockpile behind the crusher is too tall, because large heaps are the main cause of fatal injuries around mobile crushing plant
options.B: The loading shovel is working too close to the crusher, because machines this size need a clear zone of at least 12 metres between them
options.C: A labourer clears spillage beside the moving belt and drum while the plant runs, with no guard and out of the loader driver's view
options.D: Dust at the discharge point is the main hazard, because it will cause serious lung disease within a day if no respirator is worn

explanation: Clearing material next to running, unguarded conveyor parts risks entanglement, and standing where the loader driver cannot see him adds a risk of being struck.

why_wrong.A: The stockpile is a secondary concern compared with a person working at unguarded moving machinery.
why_wrong.B: The loader's distance is not the key hazard, and no such fixed separation figure applies.
why_wrong.D: Dust is a real health risk but it is managed by suppression and does not match the immediate danger of the moving parts.

common_mistake: Letting someone clean or clear material near running plant on the strength of an emergency stop being nearby.

stem: A site manager hires a mobile crane and driver from a plant firm on a plain crane-hire basis for one lift of precast units. He says the hire firm's driver owns the lift and its planning. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The operator is responsible for planning, because he is the crane expert, and the hirer's duties finish once the hire charge is agreed
options.B: A planner is needed only where the load exceeds half the crane's capacity, with smaller lifts being planned by the operator on the day
options.C: On crane hire the hirer takes control, so it must appoint a competent appointed person to plan the lift, with the operator working to their direction
options.D: Responsibility moves automatically to the hire firm because it supplies both crane and driver, so the hirer need only give an address

explanation: Under a crane-hire arrangement responsibility for planning and controlling the lift rests with the hirer's appointed person, whereas a contract lift passes it to the crane firm.

why_wrong.A: The hirer cannot hand the planning duty to the operator under hire terms, since a separate appointed person takes control.
why_wrong.B: Every lifting operation must be properly planned by a competent person, whatever the load's proportion of capacity.
why_wrong.D: Only a contract lift transfers planning to the crane firm, and plain hire leaves it with the hirer.

common_mistake: Assuming that hiring a crane with a driver also hires in someone else's responsibility for the lift.

stem: A 6 m stockpile of crushed concrete is planned beside the boundary of a housing estate, with a loading shovel working it from 7 am. The manager will spray water only after residents complain. What is the best approach?

options.A: Put up a plain site fence on the boundary, since a solid barrier stops windblown dust and shovel noise from reaching the houses
options.B: Site it well away from homes and as low as practicable, keep it damp and sheeted when idle, and limit drop heights and hours
options.C: Rely on the crew wearing FFP3 masks, since the main legal duty concerns workers' health and not neighbours' amenity
options.D: Spraying on complaint is adequate, because nuisance only arises once residents report it and waiting keeps water use and costs down

explanation: Dust and noise are best prevented at source through siting, height, damping and covering, rather than dealt with after neighbours have been affected.

why_wrong.A: A fence cannot stop fine dust and noise travelling, and does not replace control at source.
why_wrong.C: Masks protect only the wearer, and the contractor also has duties to limit dust and noise affecting neighbours.
why_wrong.D: Controls must be in place before the problem arises, and a complaint shows harm has already occurred.

common_mistake: Waiting for a complaint before controlling dust and noise that the layout of the site could have prevented.

stem: A carpenter passing through a corridor used by several trades sees the cover missing from a temporary lighting junction box, with conductors exposed. He wraps tape round it and says nothing, as he is not an electrician. Which statement best describes his duties?

options.A: He should keep others clear and promptly tell his supervisor or the site electrician, so a competent person repairs it; his own taping is not a proper fix
options.B: He should raise it at the next weekly safety meeting, because the duty to inform is met by mentioning the hazard through the normal scheduled channel on site
options.C: He has no duty to act, because reporting electrical faults is for the electrical contractor and other trades only need to report equipment they own
options.D: He has done enough by taping the box, because employees must take reasonable care and a quick fix removes the immediate danger without bothering anyone

explanation: Employees must report serious dangers and shortcomings in protection to their employer and take reasonable care of others, and electrical repairs belong to someone competent to make them.

why_wrong.B: An exposed live conductor is a serious and immediate danger that must be reported promptly, not held for a meeting.
why_wrong.C: The duty to report and to care for others applies to any danger he encounters at work, whoever owns the equipment.
why_wrong.D: Tape is not a competent repair, and the shortcoming still has to be reported so the circuit is checked.

common_mistake: Assuming that a hazard in someone else's trade is not your business to report, or that a quick personal fix discharges your duty.

stem: After adding every practicable control, a rope-lowering task for heavy glazing still leaves a high residual risk of a dropped load. The gang leader says the controls are listed, so work can begin and the remaining risk is just the job. What is the best view?

options.A: Proceed once the gang signs the assessment to show they understand the remaining risk and accept it as part of the job
options.B: A high residual risk is not acceptable as it stands, so stop, escalate and redesign the method before work starts
options.C: Proceed because all practicable controls are listed, and the remaining risk belongs to the people carrying out the task
options.D: Proceed but only in dry weather, since weather is the main factor in whether a heavy glazing load can be dropped

explanation: Listing controls does not make a risk acceptable. If a high risk remains, the method should be redesigned, for example with mechanical handling, and the decision referred to someone with authority.

why_wrong.A: A signature does not reduce the risk, and workers cannot accept a hazard that the employer must control.
why_wrong.C: A high risk that remains is not accepted just because controls are listed, and it cannot be passed to the workers.
why_wrong.D: Weather is one factor, but the method still leaves a high risk of dropping the load.

common_mistake: Treating a task as ready to start once controls are listed, even when a high risk remains.

stem: At the end of a cold day a manager leaves a thermostatic electric fan heater running in the empty drying room. Cardboard boxes of fixings are stacked against its grille. He says the tip-over switch and thermal cut-out make this safe. What is the best response?

options.A: Plug it into a timer socket so it runs for a limited period, because shorter running time reduces the fire load and the cardboard can then stay put
options.B: Fit a wire guard over the grille and leave it running, because a guard stops the boxes touching the element so the stack can stay exactly where it is
options.C: Move the boxes back about 100 mm and leave it running overnight, since the cut-outs make unattended use acceptable once nothing is touching the grille
options.D: Switch it off when the room is unattended and keep combustibles well clear, because built-in cut-outs are a backup and do not justify stacking stock against it

explanation: Safety devices can fail, and unattended heating with combustible materials touching it is a clear ignition and fire- spread risk that is controlled by separation and switching off.

why_wrong.A: A timer still leaves the heater running unattended next to combustibles during the period it is on.
why_wrong.B: A guard does not stop radiated heat or airflow blockage igniting cardboard stored right beside the heater.
why_wrong.C: A token gap is not adequate separation, and leaving a heater running unattended still relies on devices that can fail.

common_mistake: Trusting a heater's built-in safety cut-outs instead of keeping combustibles away and switching it off when nobody is there.

stem: Floor layers spend six hours a day kneeling and bending to lay vinyl tiles in a long corridor. After two weeks several have sore knees and lower backs. The foreman suggests they simply take longer breaks and buy their own knee pads. What is the best response?

options.A: Redesign the task to cut awkward postures, using long- handled tools and rotation, with knee protection supplied and complaints reviewed
options.B: Leave it to the workers, as longer breaks and self-bought pads are enough, because kneeling is a normal part of floor laying
options.C: Move the same people to the same task on alternate days only, because the pain comes from tiredness and not from the posture
options.D: Issue back supports for everyone, since a support belt removes the strain and so the working method needs no change

explanation: Posture and repetitive kneeling are manual handling and ergonomic risks to be reduced by changing the task and equipment, with protection provided by the employer and early symptoms acted on.

why_wrong.B: The employer must reduce the risk and provide equipment, not rely on workers to buy their own.
why_wrong.C: The posture is the cause and alternating days does not change the way the work is done.
why_wrong.D: Back supports do not remove the risk and are not a substitute for improving the method.

common_mistake: Relying on breaks and personal protection to cope with kneeling and bending instead of changing how the work is done.

stem: Eight operatives work twelve-hour night shifts resurfacing a city road. The site cabin has a kettle and a cold tap, and the manager says welfare is covered, so the crew can bring their own food. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Welfare duties relax at night because fewer people are on site, so a kettle and a cold tap are enough until the day shift returns in the morning
options.B: Arranging takeaway deliveries to the gate meets the duty, because the employer has then ensured that meals can be eaten on site each night
options.C: The night crew need a rest area with food preparation and eating facilities, a way to boil water, seating and winter heating, as any day shift does
options.D: The kettle satisfies the rule, since only boiling water is required and preparing food is a private matter for each worker on their own time

explanation: Welfare duties apply on every shift, and a rest area should let workers prepare and eat food and boil water, with enough seating and heating.

why_wrong.A: Welfare duties do not reduce after dark, and night workers often have fewer alternatives.
why_wrong.B: Deliveries do not provide the preparation, seating and heating facilities that a suitable rest area needs.
why_wrong.D: A rest area must also let workers prepare and eat food, not merely boil water.

common_mistake: Thinking welfare is a day-shift requirement that can be scaled back for night work.

stem: Pipelayers lever 400 kg concrete pipe sections into a trench, all wearing S3 steel-toecap boots. One has his instep crushed when a pipe rolls onto his foot, though his toes are unhurt. What should the manager do next?

options.A: Issue boots with a higher-rated steel toecap, because the instep injury shows the toecaps in use were not strong enough for the load
options.B: Retrain the injured pipelayer in foot placement, as the boots met the standard and the fault lay with the way he positioned himself
options.C: Switch to higher-ankle boots with extra support, because a taller upper protects the instep against a rolling load better than low boots do
options.D: Review the task assessment and issue boots marked M for metatarsal protection as well as a toecap, and review the pipe- handling method too

explanation: A toecap protects only the toes, so a crushing risk to the top of the foot calls for a metatarsal guard, and the handling method should still be improved.

why_wrong.A: A stronger toecap still leaves the instep uncovered, so the risk remains.
why_wrong.B: Blaming the worker ignores the foreseeable risk to the instep that the PPE selection did not cover.
why_wrong.C: Ankle height gives support, not crush protection over the top of the foot.

common_mistake: Assuming that any safety boot with a toecap protects the whole foot from heavy rolling or dropped loads.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the labourer is correctly equipped for working next to the roller. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: He is not wearing a dust mask while raking, so respiratory protection is the largest gap in his equipment for the task shown
options.B: His work gloves are too light for the task, so thick leather gauntlets are the single greatest gap in his protection on this kind of job done by hand
options.C: His safety glasses give too little side protection for raking stone, so a full-face visor is the main gap in his equipment for this job
options.D: He wears wireless earbuds instead of ear defenders; they give no rated hearing protection and mask the sounds of plant warning of danger

explanation: Earbuds are not hearing protection, so the noise exposure is uncontrolled, and listening through them also reduces his awareness of plant moving nearby.

why_wrong.A: The stone is damp, so little dust is produced and the mask is not the main problem.
why_wrong.B: Close-fitting leather-palmed gloves suit raking stone, and gauntlets would reduce his dexterity.
why_wrong.C: The glasses shown have side shields, which suit raking damp stone.

common_mistake: Counting any device in or on the ears as hearing protection, and forgetting that it blocks warning sounds from plant.

stem: A trained operator in a boom MEWP basket 10 m up slumps over the controls, unconscious but breathing. The machine is working, the basket is clear of structures, and a trained colleague is at the base. What should happen first?

options.A: Climb the boom or a ladder wearing a harness to reach him, because direct contact is the quickest way to start first aid and check his breathing
options.B: A trained ground person uses the ground controls to lower the platform under the rescue plan with care, then gives first aid and calls 999
options.C: Call 999 and wait for the fire service, because only emergency crews should bring a platform down when the operator is incapacitated and could be hurt by it
options.D: Raise a second MEWP or a telehandler cradle to the basket and transfer him across, so the first machine stays undisturbed

explanation: Ground controls are provided for emergency descent as part of a rescue plan, and a trained person should bring the casualty down quickly while controlling the movement.

why_wrong.A: Climbing a boom puts a second person at risk, and the ground controls give a quicker, safer rescue.
why_wrong.C: A casualty cannot wait at height, and the plan should enable trained site staff to lower the platform.
why_wrong.D: A transfer between machines at height is hazardous and slow compared with lowering the first machine.

common_mistake: Improvising a rescue at height, or waiting for outside help, instead of using the ground controls named in the rescue plan.

stem: A fitter must drill and fix brackets in a damp plant room 60 m from the nearest 110 V outlet, with other trades walking through. Which choice of drill is best?

options.A: A battery drill with no further controls, as removing the lead eliminates the main hazards of the job, so dust and noise need no assessment
options.B: A 230 V drill through a portable RCD, as a fast-acting trip means mains voltage can be used safely in damp areas without other precautions
options.C: A 110 V drill on two 30 m extension leads joined mid-run, since reduced voltage makes damp conditions and a trailing cable acceptable
options.D: A battery SDS drill, as it removes the trailing lead and shock source, though dust extraction and eye protection are still needed

explanation: Battery tools remove the supply cable, and so the shock and trip hazards, though dust, noise and vibration from the task still need their own controls.

why_wrong.A: Battery power removes only the electrical hazards, and drilling still creates dust, noise and vibration.
why_wrong.B: An RCD is a last line of defence, and mains voltage is not appropriate where safer options exist.
why_wrong.C: Reduced voltage lowers the shock risk but leaves a long trailing cable, vulnerable joints and trip hazards for the passing trades.

common_mistake: Assuming that a battery tool makes a task low-risk and needs no further assessment of the other hazards.

stem: After a hot three-hour haul to site, a flatbed driver finds one rear tyre reading 0.4 bar above the cold figure on the vehicle plate, with a bulge in its sidewall. A colleague says to bleed it to the plate figure and carry on unloading. What is correct?

options.A: Log the bulge in the defect report but drive on site slowly, because a lower speed reduces the stress on the tyre until the delivery has been finished
options.B: Leave it as it is, since the bulge is minor and extra pressure is safer than too little, so it need only be reported at the end of the working day
options.C: Bleed it down to the plate figure now, because a reading above the cold figure means overinflation, and the bulge is cosmetic once the pressure is corrected
options.D: Do not bleed the hot tyre, as the rise is normal, but the bulge shows internal damage, so take the vehicle out of use until a competent fitter replaces it

explanation: Tyre pressure rises with heat and should be set when cold, while a sidewall bulge indicates structural failure that makes the tyre unsafe to use.

why_wrong.A: Slow speed does not remove the burst risk, and a defect of this kind needs the tyre taken out of use.
why_wrong.B: A bulge means damaged internal cords, and delaying the report allows continued use of a tyre liable to burst.
why_wrong.C: Releasing air from a hot tyre leaves it underinflated when cold, and a bulge is not cosmetic.

common_mistake: Treating a high hot-tyre reading as a fault to bleed, while treating a sidewall bulge as something that can wait. PRACTICE TEST 17

stem: A principal contractor's site rules ban work under suspended loads and require permits for hot work, but they are shown only on the gate noticeboard. A subcontractor's crew start work without being told, saying their own firm's rules are good enough. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Induction must cover the rules before work starts, and contractors must follow the principal contractor's directions and relevant plan as well as their own rules
options.B: The rules bind only the principal contractor's directly employed staff, because subcontractors' workers are covered by their own employer's duties and procedures on site
options.C: A noticeboard at the gate is enough notice, because workers are expected to read the displayed site rules for themselves before they begin any work
options.D: Each contractor may follow its own rules where they are broadly similar, because only the client can require compliance with another firm's site rules

explanation: The principal contractor must ensure a suitable site induction is provided under CDM 2015 regulation 13, and on multi-contractor projects each contractor must comply with its directions and the relevant parts of the construction phase plan under regulation 15.

why_wrong.B: The principal contractor coordinates everyone on the project, and subcontractors' workers must follow its site rules as well as their employer's.
why_wrong.C: A displayed notice is not a suitable site induction, so the principal contractor has not met its duty to ensure one is provided.
why_wrong.D: Regulation 15 requires contractors to comply with the principal contractor's directions, so similarity to their own rules is no defence.

common_mistake: Assuming that a rule displayed on a board or followed in the contractor's own firm counts as the induction and compliance the principal contractor must secure.

stem: A contractor will take the only passenger lift serving a hospital's day-surgery floor out of service for ten days of modernisation. Its risk assessment covers only the lift engineers' entrapment and fall risks. Which omission is most significant?

options.A: Patient risks matter only if the contractor works inside a clinical room, so a lift shaft and machine room are outside the assessment's scope
options.B: The assessment should be repeated only after the lift is back in service, once patients can be seen using the new equipment safely again
options.C: Nothing is missing, because the hospital assesses risks to its own patients and the contractor assesses only the risks to its own operatives at work
options.D: People affected by the closure, such as bed moves and urgent patient access, are not assessed or agreed with hospital managers

explanation: Employers must assess risks to others affected by their work, and co-ordinate with the premises controller, so the loss of the lift for patients and staff must be considered and planned.

why_wrong.A: The risk comes from loss of the lift route for patients, not from where the engineers physically work.
why_wrong.B: Assessment must come before the work starts so controls can be planned, not after the changes have been made.
why_wrong.C: A contractor's duty extends to non- employees affected by its work, and the closure is a risk the contractor creates.

common_mistake: Limiting the assessment to the contractor's own operatives and forgetting people elsewhere in the building who are affected by the work.

stem: In a depot charging bay, three electric forklifts with lead-acid batteries are on overnight charge. The roller door is shut for security, and a fitter is about to unclip a charger lead from a battery. Which action best reduces the fire and explosion risk?

options.A: Keep the bay ventilated so hydrogen cannot collect, and switch each charger off before disconnecting its leads
options.B: Keep the door shut to hold the heat in, and place a dry- powder extinguisher beside the chargers to fight any flash fire quickly
options.C: Disconnect the leads while the charger is running to stop the gas at once, and wear antistatic clothing so that no spark can occur
options.D: Charge with the battery compartment covers closed to contain any gas, and top up the electrolyte only after charging has finished

explanation: Charging releases hydrogen, which is explosive in air, so ventilation prevents a build-up and isolating the charger first avoids a spark at the terminals.

why_wrong.B: An extinguisher responds to a fire but does nothing to stop the hydrogen building up in a closed bay.
why_wrong.C: Breaking a live charging connection creates the very spark that can ignite hydrogen around the battery.
why_wrong.D: Covers should be open during charging so gas can disperse, and trapped hydrogen under a closed lid raises the explosion risk.

common_mistake: Treating a battery bay as a place where heat is the only fire danger and forgetting that charging gives off explosive hydrogen.

stem: Fire breaks out in a site store holding paints, thinners and resin drums, 15 m from a surface-water drain that leads to a stream. Everyone is out and the fire service is called. What should the site manager do before crews start firefighting?

options.A: Open the nearest drain covers so firewater leaves the compound quickly and does not flood the cabins or the road outside it
options.B: Tell the crews what chemicals are stored and where drains run, so they can block them and contain the contaminated firewater
options.C: Start diverting the run-off by hand into the foul sewer, because the sewage works can treat any liquid that enters it
options.D: Wait until the fire is out before mentioning the drains, since pollution is dealt with only after the emergency is over

explanation: Firewater from a chemical fire is potentially polluting, so the fire service needs the information to choose its tactics and to block drains and contain run-off.

why_wrong.A: Opening drains sends contaminated firewater straight to the stream, when drains should be blocked and the water contained.
why_wrong.C: Discharge to the foul sewer needs the water company's permission and cannot be treated as a quick fix for contaminated firewater.
why_wrong.D: Containment must be in place while the water is being used, because most of the polluting run-off is produced during firefighting.

common_mistake: Thinking that firefighting water is harmless and that pollution is a clean-up task for afterwards.

stem: Two workers dry-sand plasterboard joint filler throughout a 40- room refurbishment over three weeks. The supervisor says gypsum is not silica, so it is only nuisance dust and masks are optional. Which approach best follows the control hierarchy?

options.A: Issue disposable dust masks to both workers, because protecting each person is the quickest way to deal with the dust problem
options.B: Agree that no controls are needed as gypsum is not silica, and open the windows while the dry sanding of filler continues
options.C: Avoid sanding where the finish allows, otherwise use on- tool extraction, and add suitable RPE only if assessment shows exposure remains
options.D: Limit each worker to short bursts of sanding and rotate them hourly, so that nobody exceeds the eight-hour exposure limit

explanation: Dust must be controlled under COSHH at source first, so avoiding sanding or using on-tool extraction comes before respiratory protection, which is the last line of defence.

why_wrong.A: Masks only protect the wearer and sit at the bottom of the hierarchy, leaving dust in the air for everyone else.
why_wrong.B: Gypsum dust has its own exposure limits and breathing it in at high levels is harmful, so open windows are not a substitute for assessment.
why_wrong.D: Rotating people shares the dust exposure rather than reducing it, and short bursts still produce high peak concentrations.

common_mistake: Assuming dust is harmless unless it contains silica, and reaching for a mask before controlling the dust at source.

stem: Two labourers push a hand pallet truck carrying 900 kg of tile adhesive up a ramp to a basement store, about 25 m, leaning hard into the handle. They say the wheels do the work, so no assessment is needed. What is the best response?

options.A: Add a third person pulling from the front of the truck, so the effort is shared and nobody has to lean on the handle
options.B: Reduce the pallet to what two people can start moving, then swap the pair over every ten minutes to avoid fatigue
options.C: Accept the task, because wheeled equipment carries the weight and only the effort needed to start the load moving really counts
options.D: The slope and distance need a detailed assessment, and a powered truck or a level route should replace hard pushing

explanation: Slopes, long distances and leaning to generate force take a push-pull task beyond the low-risk filter, so it should be assessed and the force removed with powered aids or a better route.

why_wrong.A: Pulling a loaded truck up a ramp introduces new risks, including being struck if the load runs back.
why_wrong.B: Swapping workers only spreads the strain around, while the awkward force and slope remain unchanged.
why_wrong.C: Wheels reduce friction but the slope still demands large sustained force, and leaning to apply it signals significant risk.

common_mistake: Believing that putting a load on wheels removes the need to assess the push-pull force and the route.

stem: On a facade lift, 38 mm boards project about 350 mm beyond the last transom, and across one bay the boards sag underfoot because the transoms are far apart. The scaffolder says the boards are tied, so they are safe. What is the best response?

options.A: Paint the overhang as a warning and limit the bay to one person at a time, since such light use will not overstress the boards
options.B: Accept the overhang as tying prevents any tipping, and lay a second layer of boards over the sagging bay to stiffen it up
options.C: Cut the overhang to no more than four times board thickness and support the boards on transoms at each end and between
options.D: Fit a toe board along the overhang and keep people out of the sagging bay until the next scheduled inspection of the lift is done

explanation: HSE guidance says boards must be properly supported and not overhang excessively, with four times the board thickness as the example, and a sagging span shows inadequate intermediate support.

why_wrong.A: A warning and fewer users leave the defect in place, and a board can still tip or break under a single person.
why_wrong.B: Tying does not make a long overhang safe, and doubling boards across a poorly supported span only adds load.
why_wrong.D: A toe board does not support the board end, and leaving a known defect in use is not an acceptable control.

common_mistake: Judging a platform safe because it feels firm or is tied, without checking that every board is properly supported along its length.

stem: Look at the scene. The roofer says he is safe because the parapet wall is solid brick and he is only leaning on it for a few minutes. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The scraper is too long for one person, so a colleague should hold it while he works from the same position at the wall
options.B: The parapet is too low to act as edge protection, so he could topple over it, and proper guardrails or a restraint system are needed
options.C: The roof deck is wet and slippery, so he should wear boots with a better sole before working near the roof edge
options.D: The brick wall might crumble under his weight, so he should stand further back and use a longer scraper to reach the gutter

explanation: A parapet below guardrail height does not stop a person leaning or overbalancing over it, so edge protection to the required height, or a restraint system, is needed.

why_wrong.A: Sharing the tool does not prevent a fall over the low wall.
why_wrong.C: The deck is dry, and better soles do not deal with a low edge.
why_wrong.D: The main risk is falling over a low wall, not the wall crumbling.

common_mistake: Assuming any solid parapet wall counts as edge protection, whatever its height.

stem: A groundworker digging a 1.2 m trench for a new water service uncovers a dark grey pipe crossing the trench. It is on no drawing. A colleague says it looks old and disused, so they can cut it out with an angle grinder. What is the best response?

options.A: Stop work there, treat the pipe as live, have the owner identify and isolate it, and support it while exposed
options.B: Cut a small slot in the pipe first, since a little leakage will show whether it carries anything under pressure
options.C: Backfill around it and carry on past, since a pipe missing from the drawings cannot belong to a service that is in use
options.D: Tap the pipe with a hammer and cut it if it sounds hollow, since an empty-sounding pipe cannot hold anything dangerous

explanation: Unidentified services must be treated as live until disconnected and proven safe at the point of work, and exposed services may need supporting while the owner is contacted.

why_wrong.B: Cutting an unidentified pipe is itself the hazard and could release gas or pressurised liquid or damage a cable duct.
why_wrong.C: Drawings are often incomplete, so a pipe being unrecorded is no evidence that it is abandoned.
why_wrong.D: Sound does not show what a pipe contains, and a hollow-sounding pipe could still carry gas, water or fuel.

common_mistake: Assuming that an unmarked pipe or one missing from the plans is disused and therefore safe to cut.

stem: At a materials loading bay, delivery drivers park, then walk across the unloading area to sign in at the cabin while a telehandler works and a lorry reverses. The manager proposes hi- vis for drivers and a wave from the operator. Which control best fits the hierarchy?

options.A: Provide a barrier-protected walkway and a driver waiting area clear of the working zone, so that nobody has to cross it
options.B: Sound horns more often and slow the vehicles in the bay to walking pace, so that a driver can step clear in time
options.C: Brief each driver on the dangers at the gate, since an informed pedestrian can then judge the gaps in the traffic safely
options.D: Rely on hi-vis and a wave from the telehandler operator, as a visible driver can cross when the operator stops

explanation: Physically separating pedestrians from vehicles removes the conflict, and this ranks above reliance on visibility or signals from operators.

why_wrong.B: Reduced speed lowers the risk a little but still leaves pedestrians and vehicles sharing the same space.
why_wrong.C: Information alone is a weak control and cannot be relied on to prevent people entering the working zone.
why_wrong.D: This depends on one operator's attention and a signal, and visibility does not prevent someone being struck in a blind spot.

common_mistake: Relying on hi-vis, signals and briefings to manage pedestrians who could instead be kept physically apart from vehicles.

stem: On his third day, a new labourer tells the site manager that edge protection is missing on a roof. The site has no safety representative. He is dismissed the next morning, and the employer says he has under two years' service, so no claim is possible. What is the correct position?

options.A: The employer may dismiss freely in the first month, because protection for raising concerns starts only after a formal probation period ends
options.B: If raising the concern was the reason, the dismissal is automatically unfair and needs no minimum service, so he can claim at an employment tribunal
options.C: The HSE can serve a notice ordering his reinstatement, because victimisation for a safety complaint is dealt with by enforcement officers
options.D: He needs two years' service for any unfair dismissal claim, so his only remedy is to report the missing edge protection to the HSE

explanation: Dismissal for reasonably raising a health and safety concern, where no safety representative exists, is automatically unfair under the Employment Rights Act, and the two-year qualifying period does not apply to it.

why_wrong.A: The protection applies from the first day of employment and does not depend on any probation period.
why_wrong.C: The HSE enforces safety standards but cannot order reinstatement, which is a matter for an employment tribunal.
why_wrong.D: Health and safety dismissals are exempt from the two-year qualifying period, so a tribunal claim is open to him from day one.

common_mistake: Assuming that a short-serving worker has no employment protection when he raises a safety concern.

stem: On a frosty 7 am start, a gang begins hand-laying heavy kerbs straight away in thin clothing. By mid-morning two workers report stiff, aching backs, and the manager points out that lifting technique training was given. Which response best addresses the risk?

options.A: Issue back support belts to every worker, because supports let stiff muscles take heavy loads safely when the temperature is low
options.B: Let workers set their own pace and start later, since cold mainly affects people who already have a history of back trouble
options.C: Reassess the task including the cold, provide lifting aids, rotate the gang, and allow a gentle warm-up and layered clothing that does not restrict movement
options.D: Repeat the lifting technique training and keep the same gang on kerbs all day, since good technique removes the extra strain that cold causes

explanation: Cold is an environmental factor that raises manual handling risk, so the assessment should be revisited and the load, task and conditions improved rather than relying on technique alone.

why_wrong.A: Back belts are not proven to prevent injury and can give false confidence while the load and cold conditions remain unchanged.
why_wrong.B: Cold affects all workers, and leaving it to individuals does not reduce the load or the exposure for the gang.
why_wrong.D: Training alone does not remove the load or the effect of cold on muscles, and it ranks below changing the task.

common_mistake: Treating manual handling risk as a matter of technique and ignoring the weather and the working conditions.

stem: A contractor tells a drainage crew working in live sewers that anyone wanting hepatitis A vaccination must book a GP appointment and pay for it, and that workers who decline will be treated as having accepted the risk. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Vaccination is compulsory for sewer work, so workers who decline can be removed from the task, because it is the main control for the infection
options.B: After risk assessment the employer should offer the vaccine at its own cost, workers may decline, and other controls stay in place for all
options.C: The employer need only pay for vaccines once a worker has been ill, because immunisation is treated as a personal health matter until then
options.D: Offering vaccination is needed only for hepatitis B, because hepatitis A spreads through food and has no recognised link with work in sewers

explanation: Vaccination is offered, not forced, and paid for by the employer as a supplement to other controls, which must protect all workers whether or not they accept it.

why_wrong.A: Immunisation is offered rather than imposed, and it supplements other controls instead of being the main one.
why_wrong.C: Where the risk assessment calls for vaccination, the employer must provide it at its cost before any illness occurs.
why_wrong.D: Hepatitis A is caught from raw sewage on hands, clothing or splashes, so sewer workers are at recognised risk.

common_mistake: Believing that a worker who declines a vaccine has taken over the employer's duty to control the infection risk.

stem: Look at the scene. The labourer wears a helmet, hi-vis, gloves and boots, and says all of it is in good order. What is the most significant problem, and the correct action?

options.A: The lamp's battery pack hangs from the back of the helmet, so he should move it to his belt and keep using the same helmet
options.B: The helmet colour does not match his role as a labourer, so he should swap to the colour for labourers, as colour shows the level of protection
options.C: The lamp is bright enough to dazzle colleagues, so he should fit a dimmer one, as holes only matter after the helmet takes a heavy impact
options.D: The helmet shell has been drilled for a lamp bracket, which weakens it; replace it with a helmet whose maker supplies approved lamp fittings

explanation: Drilling or bolting through a helmet shell can crack it and reduce its impact protection, so a damaged or modified helmet must be replaced by one with manufacturer-approved accessories.

why_wrong.A: Moving the battery leaves the drilled and cracked shell in use, which is the actual weakness.
why_wrong.B: Helmet colours identify roles by site convention only and do not indicate protection, and the shell damage is the real problem.
why_wrong.C: A hole weakens the shell before any impact, so a dimmer lamp does not fix the damaged helmet.

common_mistake: Assuming a helmet can be adapted or drilled to suit the job as long as it still looks like a helmet.

stem: A plasterer passed a face fit test on one make of valved FFP3 disposable mask. The site buys a cheaper unvalved FFP3 from another maker, and the supervisor says his test still counts because both are FFP3 and he is clean-shaven. What is correct?

options.A: The test carries over to any FFP3 mask, since the standard class sets the same filter performance and fit is judged by that class
options.B: A pass covers only the make, model and size tested, so he needs a new fit test on the unvalved mask before relying on it
options.C: The unvalved mask will fit at least as well as a valved one, so a seal check at each use is enough without a further test
options.D: The test carries over while he stays clean-shaven and checks the seal, since facial hair matters more than which mask is used

explanation: Fit testing matches a person to a specific facepiece, so a change of make or model requires a repeat test, whatever the filter class or valve type.

why_wrong.A: The class describes filter performance only, while face seal depends on the shape of each particular make and model.
why_wrong.C: A pre- use seal check does not replace a fit test on the new model, since the valve does not decide how the mask seals.
why_wrong.D: Being clean-shaven is needed in addition to a fit test, not as a substitute for one on the new model.

common_mistake: Treating the FFP3 rating as proof that any FFP3 mask will seal on a worker who has passed a test on one.

stem: Maintenance staff must reseal the glazing bars on top of a lantern light standing 1.5 m proud of a flat roof 10 m up. The roof has a solid deck and edge protection round its perimeter. A technician proposes leaning a ladder against the lantern frame. Which approach best controls the risk?

options.A: Lean the ladder on the frame, tie it to the glazing bars and have a colleague foot it, since the perimeter edge protection covers the roof
options.B: Lay a crawling board across the lantern top to spread his weight, since the board prevents any fall through the glazing
options.C: Use a small guarded platform, such as a low access tower, on the solid deck, with nothing resting on the lantern glazing or frame
options.D: Anchor his harness to the lantern frame and work from the ladder, because the harness would arrest a fall from the lantern

explanation: A guarded platform on the solid deck gives collective protection, and the lantern glazing and frame are not designed to carry a ladder or a person.

why_wrong.A: A ladder tied to glazing bars relies on a component not designed to take the load, and perimeter protection does not stop a fall through the lantern.
why_wrong.B: A board placed over glazing is unsupported and unguarded, so a slip or a break could still drop him through.
why_wrong.D: The frame is not an adequate anchor point, and a harness anchored to it could fail or fall with him.

common_mistake: Using the nearest roof structure as a ladder rest or anchor when it was never designed to take a person's weight.

stem: Scaffolders stripping a scaffold beside a public footway stack 6.4 m tubes and loose couplers on the top lift to lower later. The tube ends project beyond the guardrail over the footway, and the stack sits at the access ladder. Which change best controls the risk?

options.A: Keep tubes inside the guardrail line, lash them in bundles and bag the fittings, then lower them as stripping goes on, not stockpile them
options.B: Pile the tubes at the ladder access, because it keeps them away from the edge and makes them quickest to lower at the end of the shift
options.C: Leave the stack as it is but cone off the footway beneath it, since the toe boards stop any tube or coupler from falling off the lift edge
options.D: Push the stack back until the ends clear the guardrail, and leave the couplers loose on the boards where they are within easy reach

explanation: Keeping materials to a small, secured quantity inside the guardrails, clear of the access and the public, limits both the dropped-object and the trip hazard.

why_wrong.B: A stack at the access blocks the way on and off the lift and creates a trip hazard in the escape route.
why_wrong.C: Toe boards do not hold projecting tubes or loose couplers, and cones do not stop an object hitting someone who walks past.
why_wrong.D: Loose couplers still roll or get kicked over the edge, and the stack still blocks the access ladder.

common_mistake: Stockpiling stripped scaffold materials on a lift as if the platform were a store.

stem: A fitter must clear a jammed rock from a tracked crusher's jaw. He stops the engine, locks the isolator with his padlock, removes the key and reaches in. A colleague says the isolation is complete. What important step is missing?

options.A: Fit a second padlock owned by the supervisor, because two locks on the isolator remove the risk from any stored hydraulic pressure
options.B: Prove the isolation by trying to start the machine, then release residual hydraulic pressure and secure the jammed rock first
options.C: Nothing, because a locked isolator with the key held by the fitter guarantees that the jaw and the rock have no movement left in them
options.D: Ask the operator to stay at the controls so he can stop the jaw if it moves, since locked isolators can still fail in service

explanation: Isolation must be proved effective and any stored energy, such as hydraulic pressure or a rock held by gravity, must be released or blocked before anyone puts a hand in.

why_wrong.A: Extra locks do not release stored pressure, which needs a deliberate procedure after the energy source is isolated.
why_wrong.C: A lock stops the energy supply but does not remove energy already stored in the system or held by the jammed rock.
why_wrong.D: Relying on a person at the controls is a weaker control than proving isolation, and a person at the controls could start the machine.

common_mistake: Believing that once a machine is locked off it holds no energy and is safe to reach into.

stem: A telehandler's forks are replaced with a jib and hook to place steel beams. The driver, whose view of the hook is blocked by the boom, relies on the fork load chart in the cab and checks the load indicator is switched on. What is the main concern?

options.A: None if the beam is within the fork chart, because the machine rating governs whichever attachment is fitted and the indicator adjusts automatically
options.B: The indicator should be switched off with a jib fitted, because it gives readings for forks only, and he should rely on his own judgment
options.C: The beam should be lifted on the forks instead, because a hook may only be used on a crane and never on a telehandler
options.D: The chart and indicator setting must match the jib attachment, and a signaller should guide him because his view of the load is restricted

explanation: Each attachment has its own rated capacity and indicator configuration, and a restricted view of the load needs a trained signaller to guide the lift.

why_wrong.A: A jib changes the load geometry and capacity, so the fork chart and a fork-set indicator would give wrong limits.
why_wrong.B: Disabling the safety system removes the warning of overload, and the correct step is to set it for the attachment.
why_wrong.C: A suitable jib and hook can be used on a telehandler when the attachment, chart and lifting arrangements are correct.

common_mistake: Assuming the load chart for the forks applies to every attachment that can be fitted to the same machine.

stem: A fit-out crew washes emulsion-paint brushes and a small cement mixer at an outside tap near the site gate. The grey water runs toward a surface-water gully. Which arrangement best controls pollution?

options.A: Pour the washings onto bare ground away from the gully so they soak in, since soil filters out the cement and the paint
options.B: Wash in the cabin sink so it reaches the foul sewer, since any foul drain accepts site washings without needing permission from anyone
options.C: Let it flow to the gully, as emulsion is water-based and the tap water dilutes the cement enough to cause no harm to a watercourse
options.D: Provide a contained washing area away from drains, with the water collected and removed by a registered carrier or sent to foul sewer with consent

explanation: Surface-water drains discharge to the environment, so contaminated washings must be contained and either removed by a registered carrier or discharged to the foul sewer with the water company's consent.

why_wrong.A: Alkaline cement and paint washings can pollute soil and groundwater, and soil does not filter them out safely.
why_wrong.B: Discharging contaminated site washings to foul sewer needs the water company's consent, and sinks are not designed for cement.
why_wrong.C: Paint and cement washings are polluting even when diluted, and a surface-water gully leads directly to a watercourse.
