common_mistake: Thinking water-based paint and cement washings are harmless once they have been diluted with tap water.

stem: A 23-year-old with an NVQ and good references is promoted to supervise a crew forming an opening in a load-bearing wall using needles and props. His experience is in decorating teams. The manager says his qualification proves competence. How should his competence for this task be judged?

options.A: Replace him with the longest-serving worker available, since years in the industry reliably show the ability to supervise temporary support work on any structure
options.B: Assess his knowledge, skills, experience and attitude against this specific task, then limit his role or add supervised mentoring until he proves it
options.C: Accept the qualification and references as proof of competence, because a recognised award already covers every task within the wider trade and its related duties
options.D: Let him run the job from the method statement, because a competent supervisor will ask for help whenever he reaches the limit of his knowledge and skill

explanation: Competence is the combination of training, skills, experience and knowledge for the particular task, so it must be tested against the work and not assumed from age, grade or a general qualification.

why_wrong.A: Length of service alone is not evidence of the specific skills, knowledge and attitude this task needs, so it is no better a test than age.
why_wrong.C: A general award does not show experience of temporary support to structural openings, which is a different and higher-risk task.
why_wrong.D: Relying on a person to recognise his own gaps is unsafe, as the employer must check capability before allocating a high-risk task.

common_mistake: Assuming that a card, a qualification or a number of years in the trade proves someone can safely supervise a task they have never done.

stem: A pipe rolls onto a labourer's forearm, crushing it and tearing a deep wound. Blood is pumping out and soaks through two pressure dressings within minutes. The first aider has a commercial tourniquet in the kit. What should he do?

options.A: Keep adding dressings and raise the arm, because a tourniquet risks the limb and should be left until a paramedic arrives to decide on it
options.B: Peel off the soaked dressings to inspect the wound, then re-dress it and press with a fresh pad before deciding on any other step
options.C: Apply the tourniquet but loosen it every ten minutes to restore circulation, which stops the limb from dying while help is on its way to the site
options.D: Call 999, fit the tourniquet above the wound and tighten until the bleeding stops, note the time, and leave it on for the ambulance crew

explanation: Life-threatening limb bleeding that dressings cannot control needs a tourniquet applied above the wound, and it must stay tightened and be timed so the ambulance crew know when it went on.

why_wrong.A: Waiting while blood continues to pump risks death within minutes, and a tourniquet is the accepted step when pressure fails.
why_wrong.B: Removing dressings disturbs clots and wastes time, and pressure has already failed to control this bleed.
why_wrong.C: Loosening the tourniquet restarts the bleeding and it should be left in place for medical staff to remove.

common_mistake: Treating a tourniquet as a last resort that must be loosened periodically, when for a life-threatening limb bleed it is left tight and timed.

stem: Fitters in a small plant room bond insulation using a hot-melt adhesive applicator. To speed the flow, one sets the heater to maximum, and a sharp vapour begins irritating their throats. Which response best applies the COSHH approach?

options.A: Treat throat irritation as the warning sign and stop only if it continues for several days, because the vapour is a nuisance rather than a hazard to health
options.B: Set the applicator to the safety data sheet temperature, provide extraction or fresh air, and keep the hot adhesive off bare skin to avoid fume and burns
options.C: Rotate the fitters every hour at maximum temperature, which keeps individual exposure low enough without altering the equipment settings or the ventilation
options.D: Issue dust masks and carry on at maximum heat, since a mask removes irritant vapours as well as particles and heat only affects how fast the glue flows

explanation: Overheating raises vapour release, so controlling the source temperature and ventilating the work area comes before any personal protection, and hot adhesive also needs burn protection.

why_wrong.A: Irritation is already a sign of harmful exposure, and waiting for it to worsen is not a control.
why_wrong.C: Rotation shares the exposure without reducing it, and it ignores the simple step of lowering the temperature at source.
why_wrong.D: A simple dust mask does not filter vapours, and it leaves the cause of the extra fume uncontrolled.

common_mistake: Reaching for a mask or a rota before checking whether the process itself is generating more vapour than the data sheet intends.

stem: Roofers cutting lead flashing clean their hands with alcohol gel and eat lunch beside the lead stack, as the welfare cabin is a short walk away. One says lead is only a problem when it is heated. What is the best response?

options.A: Wear gloves while eating and wash at home after the shift, because dust left on the skin during the working day cannot be swallowed by mistake
options.B: Move the lunch spot only on cutting days, since cold sheet and loose offcuts leave nothing on the hands that could be harmful if swallowed
options.C: Accept the gel as a substitute for washing, since it clears contamination from skin quickly provided lunch is eaten upwind of the work area
options.D: Wash hands and face with soap and water in the welfare cabin before eating, drinking or smoking, and keep food away from the work area

explanation: Swallowing lead dust from hands, food and cigarettes is a main route into the body, so washing with soap and water and eating away from the work area breaks that route.

why_wrong.A: Gloves carry the dust to food and mouth, and delaying washing until home extends the time the lead stays on the skin.
why_wrong.B: Handling the sheet and offcuts transfers lead dust to the hands whether or not it is being cut, so the hygiene rule applies throughout the work.
why_wrong.C: Gel is designed to kill germs and does not remove metal dust, and being upwind does not stop dust on hands reaching the mouth.

common_mistake: Believing a quick wipe or gel is enough, when only proper washing before eating, drinking or smoking removes lead dust from skin.

stem: Free-standing counterweighted guardrails are to be placed around a flat roof's perimeter before roofers start. The installers plan to walk right up to the open edge, and use whatever bricks are to hand as ballast. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Stack extra bricks at each base to compensate for any roof slope, because added weight can make up for the system not being set out as the designer intended
options.B: Use the guardrail as an anchor for the installers' harness lanyards, since a complete guardrail is rated to hold the load of a falling person
options.C: Fit them quickly at the open edge without protection, since the guardrail is the control, and add more bricks later if the wind rises
options.D: Install to the designer's instructions with the specified ballast and set-back, using trained fitters working from a protected position until it is stable

explanation: A counterweighted system only resists a fall when it is assembled and ballasted as designed, and the people installing it are themselves working at height so need protection while doing so.

why_wrong.A: Ballast figures depend on the design, the roof surface and slope, and random weight does not make up for a layout the system was never tested for.
why_wrong.B: Free-standing guardrails are not designed as anchor points, and a fall load could tip the whole line over the edge.
why_wrong.C: The installers are exposed to the open edge before any guardrail is in place, and untested ballast may fail under load.

common_mistake: Treating a free-standing guardrail as safe because it is heavy, without checking it was ballasted and installed as designed for that roof.

stem: Look at the wall-pour platform. The foreman says the guardrails are in place and the crew are experienced. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The top guardrail is below the required height and nobody is wearing a harness, so a fall over the outer edge is most likely
options.B: The access ladder is tied at the wrong angle and cannot be climbed safely, so users are likely to fall while reaching the platform
options.C: A board is missing, leaving an open gap in the platform, and the edge has no toe board, so people or tools could fall through or off
options.D: The formwork has too few ties and will burst under the pressure of concrete, which would drop the platform and the whole crew

explanation: A working platform must be fully boarded without gaps and have toe boards, so a missing board and absent toe board are the faults most likely to cause a fall of a person or material.

why_wrong.A: The top rail is at the correct height with a mid rail, and harnesses are not the primary control where guardrails are provided.
why_wrong.B: The ladder is tied and set at a suitable angle, so it is not the main failing in the picture.
why_wrong.D: Tie spacing cannot be judged from the picture and it is not the visible fault in the platform itself.

common_mistake: Judging a platform safe from its top rail alone, without checking every board, gap and toe board along its length.

stem: A 2.2 m deep, 12 m long drainage trench is to be dug in firm clay using hydraulic props and sheets. To save time, the gang plan to dig the whole length to full depth, then climb in to fit the supports. Which sequence is correct?

options.A: Dig the full length first because firm clay stands up while props are fitted, with a lookout at one end to shout out if the sides begin to move
options.B: Fit supports after the first operative climbs down, so the person installing them can judge exactly where each prop and sheet is needed
options.C: Dig in short lengths but fit support only if cracks appear, since clay gives visible signs before it moves and so can be watched by the gang
options.D: Excavate and support in stages, fitting supports from the top or a protected position, and let nobody enter a length until it is supported and inspected

explanation: Support has to go in as the digging progresses so that no one works in an unsupported length, because even firm clay can collapse without warning.

why_wrong.A: A lookout cannot give enough warning of a sudden collapse, and unsupported depth is exactly what exposes the fitters.
why_wrong.B: Entering an unsupported excavation to fit support puts the fitter at the greatest risk before any protection exists.
why_wrong.C: Clay can fail suddenly with little warning, so waiting for cracks leaves the workers exposed when it happens.

common_mistake: Assuming firm-looking ground can be left unsupported for a short time while the support is fitted by hand.

stem: A hired floating-earth generator powers a mixer and a cutting saw, both Class I tools, on a paved yard. The foreman wants to fit a link between the generator's neutral and earth terminals so it will behave like the mains. What is the best course?

options.A: Drive an earth rod beside the generator and bond it to both tool bodies, which gives any fault current a clear path back to the source of supply
options.B: Leave the generator's connections as supplied, follow the hire firm's instructions, and run one Class I tool at a time or use Class II tools
options.C: Fit the link, since linking neutral to earth is how every supply is earthed, and the saw and mixer will then be safe to run together on it
options.D: Leave the generator as supplied but run both tools together, because the circuit RCD makes sure that any fault is cut off at once and safely

explanation: A floating-earth generator relies on its designed arrangement, so hirers must not change its connections, and limiting the load to one Class I item or to Class II tools keeps a fault from putting dangerous voltages on other equipment.

why_wrong.A: Linking tool bodies to a rod does not create a return path to the source on this type of supply and may add hazards.
why_wrong.C: Altering the internal connections can defeat the protection the generator was designed to give and is not for the hirer to do.
why_wrong.D: An RCD helps but does not make it acceptable to run two Class I items at once on a floating-earth set.

common_mistake: Thinking every temporary supply must be earthed like the mains, when a floating-earth generator relies on its designed arrangement left unaltered.

stem: A housing site has a swale designed to take surface water along its boundary. The manager wants to use the swale footprint as a haul route and silt-settling channel now, then tidy it up before handover. Which approach protects its function?

options.A: Leave it open for use but sweep the silt out at handover, as removal at the end restores the original condition of the whole swale
options.B: Fence the swale off from traffic and stockpiles, route runoff through separate silt controls, and finish the swale late in the programme
options.C: Lay a geotextile and thin stone layer for the haul route, and plant the swale early so the roots stabilise it before the vehicles pass
options.D: Use the footprint as a haul route and settlement channel, since a swale is made to carry dirty water and the grass will recover afterwards

explanation: Compaction and silt reduce infiltration and storage, so keeping vehicles and muddy runoff out and building the final form near the end of the works protects the design performance.

why_wrong.A: Sweeping cannot reverse compaction of the underlying soil, and silt that has washed in can clog infiltration.
why_wrong.C: Plant roots and a thin layer cannot stop compaction by heavy plant, and the surface is still silted by runoff.
why_wrong.D: Traffic compacts the ground and silt clogs the surface, which can permanently reduce how well the swale drains.

common_mistake: Viewing a drainage feature as a convenient place to put dirty water or traffic while the rest of the site is built.

stem: At a plant yard wash-down area, the oil separator's high-level alarm sounds. The yard supervisor suggests flushing it through with hot water and a degreaser so the oil is pushed out into the surface-water drain. What is the correct action?

options.A: Carry on using the wash area and check it again at the next six-monthly inspection, since the alarm only warns that oil is near its limit
options.B: Skim the oil off the top with a bucket and tip it into the site's general waste skip, then reuse the separator without refilling it with water
options.C: Stop using the wash area, have a registered waste carrier empty it and refill it with clean water, and log the work and hazardous waste paperwork
options.D: Flush it with hot water and degreaser to disperse the oil to the drain, since detergent breaks the oil down so it does little harm to the watercourse

explanation: An alarm shows oil or silt has reached its limit, so the separator must be emptied by a registered carrier, with oily waste treated as hazardous, and refilled with clean water before reuse.

why_wrong.A: The alarm means the separator should be emptied right away, as continued use will pass oil through into the drain.
why_wrong.B: Oily waste is hazardous and does not belong in a general skip, and the separator must be refilled with clean water to work.
why_wrong.D: Detergents emulsify oil and stop the separator working, and the oil would reach the surface- water drain and pollute the watercourse.

common_mistake: Treating a separator alarm as a routine reminder, when oil that is not removed properly goes straight to the drain.

stem: Midway through a build, the client says the principal designer should have supervised the contractors daily after a worker was hurt fixing cladding. The principal contractor had never told the designer about a changed fixing detail. Which statement best describes the principal designer's role during construction?

options.A: It includes supervising contractors' work on site every day, because the appointment lasts for the whole project and carries overall authority over site health and safety
options.B: It ends once the construction phase plan is accepted, because design decisions and site control then pass entirely to the principal contractor and the contractors
options.C: It is to liaise with the principal contractor and share information, including on design changes, while the principal contractor manages the site work
options.D: It requires approving each contractor's method statement before the task starts, because the principal designer signs off how every activity is to be carried out

explanation: Under CDM 2015 the principal designer must liaise with the principal contractor throughout the appointment and assess the effect of design changes, but planning, managing and monitoring site work is the principal contractor's duty.

why_wrong.A: The principal designer has no duty to supervise site work, which belongs to the principal contractor and each employer.
why_wrong.B: The appointment continues into construction, and changes to the design still need the principal designer's input.
why_wrong.D: Approving how site tasks are carried out is not a principal designer duty; contractors and the principal contractor manage that.

common_mistake: Assuming the principal designer is the site safety supervisor, when the role is design coordination and liaison with the principal contractor.

stem: Before a client audit, a site manager writes the last three weeks of fire-alarm tests into the log, although nobody carried them out. Nothing has happened, and he says no harm is done. Which statement about his position is most accurate?

options.A: Knowingly making a false entry in a required record is itself an offence under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act, and he can be prosecuted personally
options.B: Only the company can be prosecuted, because he acted as its employee, so he faces at most internal discipline from his employer for the false log
options.C: It is only a paperwork breach, which matters if the alarm later fails and someone is hurt, because enforcement action needs actual harm to follow from it
options.D: It is acceptable if the missed tests are carried out in the following week, because the log then ends up accurate and nothing misleading remains

explanation: Section 33 of the Act makes it an offence intentionally to make a false entry in a required record, so no injury is needed and the individual as well as the company can be prosecuted.

why_wrong.B: Individuals who intentionally make false entries can be prosecuted personally.
why_wrong.C: False entries are offences in their own right and do not depend on any injury.
why_wrong.D: Recording tests that were not done when written is still false, and later testing does not undo the offence.

common_mistake: Treating a tidied-up record as harmless paperwork when no one was hurt.

stem: A day crew rated removing a plant-room boiler as medium risk, then leave at 18:00 with the pipework half cut and drained. The night crew, three instead of six, are told the job is assessed, so carry on. Which approach best manages the risk at changeover?

options.A: Keep the medium rating, because the task and method are unchanged and the day supervisor has already approved the assessment for the night crew to use
options.B: Pass on the day crew's method statement alone, because it describes every step and the incoming crew can work out what is already done from it
options.C: Lower the rating, because fewer people are exposed overnight with the building empty and so the likelihood of anyone being harmed is reduced
options.D: Re-rate the task against its partly finished state and smaller crew, with a face-to-face handover of what is isolated, drained or cut

explanation: A risk assessment must be reviewed when circumstances change, and a half-completed task with a different crew is not the situation the day rating covered.

why_wrong.A: The state of the work and the crew size have changed, so the original rating no longer fits.
why_wrong.B: A written method describes the plan, not the actual condition of a half-finished job.
why_wrong.C: Fewer people does not offset unknown isolation status, fatigue and thinner supervision, which raise the likelihood.

common_mistake: Assuming a risk rating stays valid across a shift change because the task has the same name.

stem: An installer sprays aerosol adhesive onto wall panels in a windowless 6 m2 lobby with the door shut and a gas boiler with a pilot flame in the cupboard. He plans a P2 dust mask, short bursts and a fan blowing into the corridor. What is the best action?

options.A: Replace the P2 dust mask with a P3 filter mask, which is the highest standard of protection and so suits fine mist from spray products
options.B: Keep the aerosol but fit an organic-vapour filter and run the fan, because the correct filter handles the health risk and the airflow takes out the fire risk
options.C: Switch to a roller-applied water-based adhesive, which removes both the flammable propellant vapour and the inhalation hazard at source
options.D: Spray in short bursts with the door propped open, because propellant gas disperses quickly in the corridor and does not build up in the lobby

explanation: Substitution removes the hazard itself, whereas the aerosol keeps a flammable vapour cloud near an ignition source and a vapour that a dust mask does not filter.

why_wrong.A: Particle filters do not stop solvent or propellant vapour, and respirators do not deal with ignition.
why_wrong.B: A filter does nothing about flammable vapour, and a pilot flame remains an ignition source in a small room.
why_wrong.D: Vapour can still pool near the boiler, and relying on dispersal is not a reliable control.

common_mistake: Picking a mask for a vapour problem without asking whether a safer product removes the hazard and the fire risk.

stem: A fabricator wearing vented goggles to grind weld spatter is about to pour a 5-litre container of acid descaler into a bucket. He says the goggles stopped sparks so they will stop splashes. Which action is correct?

options.A: Wear the face shield alone, because a full-face visor covers more of the face than goggles and so stops splashes arriving from all directions
options.B: Wear safety spectacles with side shields, because they meet the impact standard and block liquid coming from the front and from both sides
options.C: Carry on with the vented goggles, because impact-rated lenses resist liquid as well as particles and the lens strength matters more than the venting
options.D: Swap to indirectly vented or sealed goggles suitable for liquids, with a face shield over them for pouring, keeping the vented pair for grinding

explanation: Direct-vent goggles let liquid through their vents, so splash work needs goggles that seal against liquid, and a face shield adds cover for pouring.

why_wrong.A: A visor leaves gaps under and around it, and is a secondary protector used over eyewear.
why_wrong.B: Spectacles do not seal against the face, so liquid can run or splash behind the lenses.
why_wrong.C: Strong lenses do not help when liquid can enter through the direct vents at the side.

common_mistake: Assuming eyewear that stops flying particles will also keep liquid out.

stem: Debris has built up in the pit under a material hoist, whose platform is parked at third-floor level. A labourer plans to climb in and shovel it out, saying the hoist is switched off and the gate is shut. What should happen first?

options.A: Finish the clean-out quickly with the platform parked, because the pit is entered for only a few minutes and the brake is holding the load
options.B: Station a colleague at the control with a radio, so he can stop the platform at once if it starts to move while the pit is being cleared
options.C: Isolate and lock off the hoist, then mechanically support the raised platform so it cannot descend, before anyone enters the pit
options.D: Switch off at the hoist control and close the landing gate, because an unpowered platform stays where it was left and cannot fall on someone

explanation: Entry beneath a raised platform needs power isolation and a positive mechanical support, because brakes, controls and switches can fail.

why_wrong.A: A short exposure does not make it safe to stand beneath a platform held only by its brake.
why_wrong.B: A person at the controls cannot stop a mechanical failure, and a radio call is too slow to prevent a fall.
why_wrong.D: Isolation alone relies on the rope and brake holding, and a failure would drop the platform onto the labourer.

common_mistake: Trusting a switched-off control or a brake to hold a raised platform while someone is underneath it.

stem: A fitter must hang cable tray in a plant room with 2.4 m headroom, where bare live busbars run across the ceiling. He plans a fibreglass stepladder, saying fibreglass does not conduct, and a colleague will warn him if his head gets close. What is the correct view?

options.A: Neither measure is adequate; work within reach should wait until the busbars are made dead or physically barriered so nobody can come into contact
options.B: The fibreglass ladder makes the job acceptable, provided he uses plastic-handled tools and takes care not to touch the busbars with his hands
options.C: The spotter is a sufficient control if he is competent, because a verbal warning gives the fitter time to move away before any contact
options.D: A shorter stepladder solves the problem, because keeping his head below 2 m leaves a clear gap to the busbars at 2.4 m

explanation: Under the Electricity at Work Regulations live conductors that could cause injury must be made dead or guarded, and a fibreglass ladder or spotter does not prevent contact or arcing.

why_wrong.B: Fibreglass does not guarantee safety, because dirt, damp and conductive tools or tray can still bring him into contact or arcing range.
why_wrong.C: A warning cannot stop a slip or a long tray length touching live parts, so it is not a barrier.
why_wrong.D: Tools, tray and raised arms reach well above the head, so the busbars remain within reach.

common_mistake: Relying on an insulating ladder or a lookout instead of making the live parts dead or inaccessible.

stem: Look at the scene. The operator is trained and the cab is fully enclosed. Which is the most serious problem?

options.A: A second worker is holding a shovel near the fence, so tools are being used within the work area during breaking
options.B: The breaker is working on a slab rather than from a stable base, which risks the excavator rocking and hitting the cab
options.C: Dust is hanging in the air and the hose is unused, which alone makes the operation unacceptable until suppression is running
options.D: A labourer stands within reach of flying fragments and the moving machine, with no exclusion zone set up

explanation: People on foot inside the working radius of a breaking excavator risk being struck by fragments or the arm, so the area must be cleared and marked off while the breaker works.

why_wrong.A: He is well back from the machine, so his position is not the main danger.
why_wrong.B: Breaking a slab from the ground is normal practice and is not the greatest danger shown.
why_wrong.C: Dust control matters, but it is a lesser problem than a person standing inside the strike zone.

common_mistake: Believing an enclosed cab and a trained operator make it safe for others to stand close to a working machine.

stem: A mini-dumper operator tops up from a bowser with the engine idling to save restart time, wedges the nozzle trigger open and walks off for a delivery ticket. Diesel overflows onto the hot exhaust. What should have been done?

options.A: Fill slowly with the engine running and with the exhaust covered by a wet cloth, since cooling the manifold removes any ignition risk
options.B: Stop the engine and let hot parts cool before filling, and stay at the nozzle throughout so the flow can be stopped at once
options.C: Keep the engine idling and use the wedge only while a spill kit stands beside the machine, since a kit contains any overflow before it can ignite
options.D: Fill the tank to the brim before shutting down, since a full tank leaves no air space for vapour and so cannot burn

explanation: Fuel spilled on hot surfaces can ignite, and an unattended wedged nozzle removes the chance to stop an overflow.

why_wrong.A: A damp cloth gives no dependable protection and the running engine and unattended nozzle remain.
why_wrong.C: A spill kit does not stop fuel contacting hot parts, and leaving the nozzle unattended still causes overfill.
why_wrong.D: A full tank cannot take thermal expansion, increases spillage, and does not remove the ignition source.

common_mistake: Refuelling a running or hot machine and leaving the nozzle held open to save a few minutes.

stem: A contractor works nights beside a hedgerow and housing. Two tower floodlights are aimed horizontally to light the work, and light floods bedroom windows and the hedge where bats and birds feed. Residents complain. What is the best response?

options.A: Leave the lights as they are because night work needs strong lighting, and tell residents to close their curtains if they object
options.B: Aim lights downward, shield and lower them, use only the lighting needed and switch off when not working, keeping spill off the hedge
options.C: Keep the lights on all night so that the hedge and the work area stay lit, which is said to deter bats and birds from nesting
options.D: Raise the lights higher on the towers to reach more of the site, since a wider beam spreads the light thinner over homes

explanation: Light can be a nuisance to neighbours and harm wildlife, so lights should be directed to the work area, shielded, kept as low as practicable and switched off when not needed.

why_wrong.A: Spill light can be reduced without making the work unsafe.
why_wrong.C: Continuous light can disturb wildlife and increases the nuisance.
why_wrong.D: Higher lights usually spill more widely over neighbours and wildlife.

common_mistake: Aiming floodlights outward at the site boundary and treating the neighbours' complaints as unavoidable.

stem: A principal contractor launches a phone-app system for reporting hazards and consults only its direct employees, because 14 of the 40 labourers are agency staff who, it assumes, can raise concerns through their agency. What is the best course before launch?

options.A: Leave the agency labourers out, since consultation is limited to elected safety representatives, and show the app to them during their arrival induction
options.B: Consult the direct employees now and the agency labourers after launch, because a few weeks of use shows which problems really affect them
options.C: Include the agency labourers in the consultation, with the agency cooperating, so those who must use the system can say whether it works for them
options.D: Brief the agency's account manager by email, since the agency holds the whole duty to consult its workers and the site only has to host them

explanation: Workers affected by a new arrangement should be consulted before it starts, and the hirer and agency must cooperate, so agency staff directed on site cannot simply be left to their agency.

why_wrong.A: Consultation is not confined to elected representatives, and an induction briefing informs people rather than seeking their views.
why_wrong.B: Consultation is meant to shape the arrangement beforehand, not to collect comments once it is already running.
why_wrong.D: The hirer controls the work and the arrangement, and the hirer and agency must work together rather than pass the duty across.

common_mistake: Assuming that people supplied through an agency are the agency's concern when the site is changing how they work.

stem: A supplier's competent team finishes erecting a hired tower crane at 11 am. The contractor's assessment records 'competent crew, low risk', and the manager wants lifting to start at noon with the erectors choosing the operator. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Wait for the independent thorough examination, and check operator, slinger and lift plan for this site, since skill in erecting is not skill in using
options.B: Begin with light loads while the operator tests the controls, since that proves the crane and a written examination is needed only at the yearly interval
options.C: Start at noon, because the people who built the crane are best placed to judge it safe, and their own commissioning checks serve as the examination
options.D: Obtain the examination report, then start, because the erectors' competence also covers choosing the operator and the lifts, so no site checks follow

explanation: Equipment assembled on site needs a thorough examination after assembly and before use, and the users must separately confirm operating competence and a lift plan for their own site.

why_wrong.B: A trial lift is not an examination, and assembly at a new location triggers one before first use regardless of the yearly cycle.
why_wrong.C: The thorough examination must be done by a sufficiently independent competent person, not by the erecting team checking their own work.
why_wrong.D: Competence to erect does not show that an operator or lift plan is suitable for this site's loads, routes and signalling.

common_mistake: Treating the competence of the erecting team as proof that the crane is examined and its users are ready.

stem: A plumbed emergency eyewash in a chemical store has not been run since installation six weeks ago. A test run gives rust- brown, cloudy water for several seconds before clearing. The foreman signs the tag, saying it clearly works. What is the best response?

options.A: Treat it as not ready: run it regularly as the maker directs to clear stagnant water, check flow and temperature, and keep records
options.B: Arrange an annual engineer service only, because frequent running wastes water and wears the valve, and a yearly check shows whether it works
options.C: Accept the tag, because water that clears shows the pipework is clean, so flushing is needed only after a unit has actually been used
options.D: Swap it for a sterile saline bottle and stop running the unit, since stagnant water is only a risk to drinking supplies and not to eyes

explanation: Standing water breeds contamination and corrosion debris that would be flushed into a casualty's eyes, so plumbed units need regular activation, flow checks and records.

why_wrong.B: A yearly check leaves the water stagnating for months, so the unit could be unfit exactly when it is needed.
why_wrong.C: Clearing after several seconds proves contamination was present, and a casualty cannot wait for the water to run clean.
why_wrong.D: Contaminated water in the eyes is a serious hazard, and a single small bottle cannot give the sustained flushing of a plumbed unit.

common_mistake: Signing off an eyewash because water comes out, without asking what condition the water is in.

stem: A floor layer scrapes old adhesive from a screed using a short- handled hand scraper, kneeling with the wrist cocked upward for hours, and now has forearm pain. The supervisor offers wrist supports. Which change best controls the cause?

options.A: Issue elasticated wrist supports to every floor layer, because limiting wrist movement removes the strain while the same short scraper is used
options.B: Provide a long-handled scraper used standing so the wrist stays straight and the body supplies the force, and mix the task with other work
options.C: Rotate a colleague onto the scraper each hour, so total exposure is shared between two people although the short tool and kneeling remain
options.D: Supply thick padded gloves, to cushion the handle and spread pressure over the palm, which relieves the strain on the wrist joint

explanation: Tools should let the wrist stay straight and use a power grip, and removing the kneeling, bent-wrist posture tackles the cause rather than the symptom.

why_wrong.A: Supports mask the symptoms and leave the awkward posture and sustained force that cause the injury unchanged.
why_wrong.C: Sharing the exposure reduces each person's dose but still puts two people in the same harmful posture.
why_wrong.D: Bulky gloves reduce grip and often increase the force needed, and they do nothing to correct wrist angle.

common_mistake: Fixing the worker's wrist with a support instead of fixing the tool and posture that bend it.

stem: Two workers clear silt from a warm, humid 1.2 m culvert in planned three-hour entries. The supervisor lets them carry water bottles to sip at the work face and eat lunch inside to save time. What is the best approach?

options.A: Plan shorter entries with rest, drinks and food in a clean area outside, since heat builds up inside and silt on hands can be swallowed
options.B: Have them drink well before entering and after leaving only, because sipping inside would raise toilet needs and distract from the task
options.C: Keep three-hour entries and allow both inside, because time saved by not leaving means less total exposure and fewer awkward re-entries
options.D: Allow bottles but ban food inside, because water helps cooling at the work face and the contamination risk comes only from eating a meal

explanation: Time in a hot, humid confined space may need limiting, and fluids and food should be taken in a clean place so that contaminated hands do not carry material to the mouth.

why_wrong.B: Fluid loss during hot work is real, and the answer is planned breaks outside rather than none during a three-hour entry.
why_wrong.C: Long entries in humid heat risk heat stress, and avoiding breaks does not reduce the harm of staying in the space.
why_wrong.D: Contaminated hands handling a bottle spout carry silt to the mouth just as they would with food.

common_mistake: Judging that a drink at the workface is a kindness when it is actually a route for contamination.

stem: Operatives repair a canal bank, working within a metre of deep water. Foam-filled lifejackets are kept in the van. The supervisor says nobody has fallen in so far and that the jackets can stay stowed until someone does. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Wear them only on days with a visible current, because still water poses little risk of drowning to workers on the bank
options.B: Make them optional for confident swimmers, as a good swimmer can reach the bank unaided after falling in cold water
options.C: Assess the risk of falling in, then provide lifejackets that fit and are worn, checked before use, with a rescue plan
options.D: Keep them in the van and fetch them if someone falls in, since stowed equipment is quicker to use than clothing worn all day

explanation: Where there is a risk of drowning the right buoyancy aid must be worn, fitted and inspected, and backed by a rescue plan, because wearing it after a fall is too late.

why_wrong.A: Still water can be as dangerous because of cold shock and deep water.
why_wrong.B: Cold water shock can overcome even strong swimmers within seconds.
why_wrong.D: A person in cold water cannot wait for equipment to be fetched.

common_mistake: Storing lifejackets near the water but not requiring them to be worn.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative's PPE is fine, since he has glasses, a dust mask and gloves. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The bucket sits on the floor, and bending to mix creates a manual handling hazard that outweighs any hazard from the spinning paddle
options.B: His nitrile-coated gloves should be leather gauntlets for mixing, because thicker gloves are always the safer choice around powered tools
options.C: His FFP2 dust mask is inadequate for tile adhesive, which needs an air-fed hood, so respiratory protection is the most serious failing
options.D: Something hanging from his neck could be caught by the rotating paddle and pull him in, so it should be removed or be a breakaway type

explanation: Loose items near rotating tools can be snagged and drag the wearer into the machine, so neck cords should be removed or of a quick-release design.

why_wrong.A: Posture is a real concern, but a snagging risk can cause severe injury within a moment.
why_wrong.B: Thick or loose gloves near rotating parts add an entanglement risk, and the gloves shown are not the main failing.
why_wrong.C: An FFP2 or FFP3 mask is the usual protection against cement-based dust, and it does not match the immediate danger of entanglement.

common_mistake: Checking the PPE list and missing the loose item near the moving part.

stem: Forecast gusts will exceed those assumed in the design of an 18 m scaffold fully clad in sheeting. A labourer suggests slitting the sheets with a knife to let the wind through. Which action is correct?

options.A: Do not cut them; ask the scaffold designer or contractor to advise on removing sheeting in a controlled way before the wind, then inspect afterwards
options.B: Leave the cladding as it is, because ties designed for sheeting cope with any forecast gust, and an inspection after the wind is unnecessary
options.C: Slit every bay at mid-height, since the cut area cuts the load and the ties designed for sheets will then be well oversized for the wind
options.D: Let the bricklayers pull the sheets off from the lifts in the morning wind, since less sheeting means less load and they can refix it later

explanation: Sheeting adds wind load that the design and ties must resist, so changes are for a competent scaffolder working to the design, and the scaffold is inspected after severe weather.

why_wrong.B: A design has a limiting wind speed, and storm conditions beyond it require action and an inspection afterwards.
why_wrong.C: Random slits tear further in the wind, flap loose, and do not give a load reduction that anyone has designed or checked.
why_wrong.D: Removing sheets in high wind is hazardous, and the task needs a competent scaffold team with a plan rather than general operatives.

common_mistake: Improvising a change to sheeting on a scaffold instead of going back to its design and its scaffolders.

stem: The foreman logs that a 30 mA RCD on the board feeding the welfare cabins passes its test button every morning and says nothing more is needed. An electrician disagrees. What is the best position?

options.A: Stop pressing the button and rely on instrument tests, since repeated button use wears out the device and shortens its working life
options.B: Test with an instrument only after a trip incident, because a daily pass shows the RCD would trip at the rated residual current
options.C: Keep the daily check, but the button proves only the mechanism, so a competent person must also instrument-test trip current and time
options.D: The daily button check is the only test required on sites, and instrument testing applies to domestic installations rather than construction supplies

explanation: The test button confirms the mechanism operates but does not show that it trips at the rated current within the required time, which needs an instrument test.

why_wrong.A: Daily user checks are recommended, and pressing the button does not damage a sound device.
why_wrong.B: A pass only shows the mechanism works, and waiting for an incident means a slow or failing device stays in service.
why_wrong.D: Construction supplies are not exempt, and daily checks are in addition to periodic testing rather than a substitute.

common_mistake: Treating a pressed test button as proof that the RCD protects at its rated current and speed.

stem: A contractor resurfaces half of a busy supermarket car park while the rest stays open. A dumper must cross open parking aisles to the works. The manager plans cones, a 5 mph limit and a banksman waving it through. What is the best approach?

options.A: Provide a fenced haul route with controlled crossings and trained marshals, with plant movements timed away from peak customer hours
options.B: Rely on high-visibility vests for the dumper driver and banksman, since being seen by shoppers is the main way to avoid collisions
options.C: Run the dumper at the busiest time with two banksmen, since a busier car park makes drivers slower and shoppers more watchful
options.D: Keep the plan, adding a flashing beacon and a sign at each aisle, because the speed limit and banksman already control the main risk

explanation: Vehicles and pedestrians should be separated where practicable, and the public, including children, will not obey cones or signs the way trained workers do.

why_wrong.B: Being visible helps, but it does not stop shoppers, children and cars crossing the dumper's route.
why_wrong.C: Peak customer traffic raises the chance of conflict, and more banksmen do not remove the shared route.
why_wrong.D: Warnings and a speed limit leave the public and plant sharing the same ground, which is a weak control.

common_mistake: Expecting members of the public to follow cones and a wave from a banksman. PRACTICE TEST 18

stem: A cold-store operator hires an electrical firm to pull cables through plant rooms containing ammonia refrigeration pipework. The operator says the contractor's own employer must brief its people, so nothing needs passing on. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The operator must give the contractor's employer comprehensible information on the risks its work poses to those workers and its controls, and co-ordinate with it
options.B: The operator must supply risk details only if the contractor asks in writing, because the duty is triggered by a request rather than by the work itself
options.C: The operator may leave out hazards visible on a walk round, because information is required only for risks that the contractor could not discover itself
options.D: Only the contractor's own employer owes a duty here, since information follows the contract of employment, so the operator need only provide site access and a plan

explanation: Under the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations, a host employer must give outside employers comprehensible risk information and work with them, so the contractor can brief its own people properly.

why_wrong.B: The duty applies automatically; it does not depend on the contractor asking for the information.
why_wrong.C: The duty is to give relevant risk and control information regardless of whether a visit might reveal some hazards.
why_wrong.D: The host employer has its own duty to give the contractor's employer risk information about its undertaking.

common_mistake: Assuming that a contractor's own employer carries the whole duty to inform, so the host of the premises has nothing to pass on.

stem: A subcontractor's method statement for unloading steel uses the main car park as the lay-down area, yet the construction phase plan shows that car park as the pedestrian route for all trades. The principal contractor stamps it 'received' and says checking content is the subcontractor's job. What should have happened?

options.A: A signed declaration from the subcontractor that it has read the construction phase plan is enough, so the clash can be left to the workforce
options.B: Approving it is correct, because the subcontractor is the competent specialist and carries sole responsibility for the safety of its own working method on this site
options.C: Review it against the construction phase plan and other trades' work, have the clash resolved before work starts, and re- check it whenever the plan changes
options.D: It should be passed to the client for sign-off, because the client holds the duty to manage how the contractors share the site space

explanation: A principal contractor must plan, manage and co- ordinate the construction phase, so it has to check that each method statement fits the plan and other work on site.

why_wrong.A: A declaration does not resolve a conflict between the method and the pedestrian route in the plan.
why_wrong.B: Specialist competence does not remove the principal contractor's duty to co-ordinate work and keep the plan consistent.
why_wrong.D: Day-to-day co-ordination of contractors' methods is a principal contractor duty, not something to hand to the client.

common_mistake: Treating the logging of a subcontractor's method statement as a review, when nobody has checked it against the plan or neighbouring work.

stem: On a refurbishment, a labourer unblocking a drain gets caustic drain-cleaner in one eye. There is no eyewash bottle, only a tap, and the first aider is next to him. What is the best action?

options.A: Rinse until the stinging stops, then let him resume light duties and review the eye at the end of shift once the pain has eased off
options.B: Hold the eye shut and wait for the paramedics, since running water may carry the product into the other eye and make the injury a lot worse
options.C: Rinse for about a minute, cover the eye with a pad and drive him to hospital, because caustic products need specialist neutralising treatment, not water
options.D: Irrigate under running tap water for at least ten minutes, affected eye lowest, while 999 is called, and send the product label with him to hospital

explanation: Prolonged irrigation dilutes and removes the chemical, and the product details help hospital staff treat the injury.

why_wrong.A: Pain relief does not mean the chemical has gone, and a caustic splash always needs hospital assessment.
why_wrong.B: Waiting wastes the critical early minutes; the head can be tilted so water runs away from the good eye.
why_wrong.C: Water is the correct first aid and must continue for several minutes, not be cut short for a car journey.

common_mistake: Stopping irrigation as soon as the pain eases, rather than flushing for the full time and sending the product details with the casualty.

stem: A materials hoist loaded with blocks drops a few centimetres, then judders to a halt between floors. The operator presses the emergency stop. A labourer offers to free the brake by hand with a bar to lower the load. What should happen next?

options.A: Keep everyone clear beneath, isolate and lock off the supply, and leave recovery and brake examination to a competent person following the maker's procedure
options.B: Release the brake gradually by hand, because the emergency stop has already made the machine safe for anyone to work on, including the labourers
options.C: Reset the emergency stop and run the platform down slowly under power, since the motor gives a more controlled descent than any manual brake release can give
options.D: Unload the blocks by hand from the landing gate to remove the load, then restart the hoist and report the fault to the supervisor at the end of the shift

explanation: A failing hoist can drop its load, so people must be kept clear, the energy source locked off, and only a competent person should recover it and decide on repair.

why_wrong.B: An emergency stop is not isolation, and a manual brake release by untrained staff can let the load fall.
why_wrong.C: Restarting a hoist with a suspected brake or drive fault risks an uncontrolled drop.
why_wrong.D: Working beneath or beside a failing hoist is dangerous, and the fault must be examined before any restart.

common_mistake: Believing that pressing the emergency stop makes a faulty machine safe, so anyone can then free it without isolation.

stem: Joiners fixing fibre-cement cladding boards cut about eighty a day with a circular saw on trestles in a ground-floor room with the windows shut. Other trades are working in adjacent rooms. Which change controls the dust best?

options.A: Carry on cutting indoors but issue FFP3 masks to the saw operators, since a good mask fully protects the one person who is doing the cutting
options.B: Change to a fine-toothed wood blade, because it produces larger chips that fall quickly and so leaves less harmful airborne dust behind
options.C: Open the windows and run a fan to push the dust outside, which dilutes the airborne dust below the level that matters to health
options.D: Cut at a dedicated outdoor station, using shears or a saw with H or M class on-tool extraction, keep others clear, and treat RPE as the back-up

explanation: Cement-based boards can release harmful respirable dust, which is best controlled at source and away from other people, with RPE only as a back-up.

why_wrong.A: Relying on RPE alone leaves the dust in the building and exposes other trades.
why_wrong.B: Blade choice does not remove fine respirable dust, and the hazardous fraction stays airborne.
why_wrong.C: Dilution ventilation does not capture dust at source and can carry it into neighbouring rooms.

common_mistake: Handing masks to the cutter and treating that as the dust control, while the dust still spreads to everyone nearby.

stem: Two labourers must get twenty 25 kg bags of render up to a first-floor scaffold lift. One proposes carrying a bag on his shoulder up the access ladder, saying he lifts 25 kg at ground level all day. What is the best approach?

options.A: Avoid carrying bags up a ladder; raise them on a pallet by hoist or telehandler, and use lighter bags where hand-handling cannot be avoided
options.B: Let two people climb together, one behind the other, so that the bag load is shared and each carries less than the full 25 kg
options.C: Allow it if he keeps one hand on the stile and takes regular breaks, since 25 kg is within the ground-level guideline for a fit adult man at ground level
options.D: Provide a back support belt and tie the ladder at the top, which reduces both the lifting strain and the risk of the ladder moving

explanation: The handling hierarchy says to avoid hazardous handling first, and climbing a ladder with a load removes the secure grip needed for safe climbing.

why_wrong.B: Two people on one ladder is unsafe and the bag cannot be shared between them.
why_wrong.C: A ground-level handling guideline does not make it safe to carry a bag on a ladder, where hand grip is vital.
why_wrong.D: Back belts are not a proven control, and securing the ladder does not remove the load from the climber.

common_mistake: Judging a load only against the weight limit for lifting at ground level, and ignoring the loss of grip and balance on a ladder.

stem: A temporary roof of corrugated sheeting spans a tall scaffold over a re-roofing job. Overnight 15 cm of wet snow settles on it and the sheets are sagging. The supervisor wants two harnessed labourers to walk on the sheets and shovel it off. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Let the sun clear it and restrict work to areas under sheets that sag visibly, since unsagged areas are plainly carrying the load
options.B: Carry on working beneath it, since the weekly scaffold inspection was done only three days ago and so is still in date for use
options.C: Send the harnessed labourers up at once, because removing the load quickly is the safest way to relieve the roof and harnesses control the fall risk
options.D: Keep people off and from beneath it, have the temporary works designer assess it, clear the snow by an approved method, and inspect before reuse

explanation: Snow is an exceptional event that can overload the structure, so it needs assessment, a safe removal method that avoids walking on the sheeting, and inspection before work resumes.

why_wrong.A: Unseen overload and damage can exist in unsagged areas, so the whole structure needs assessment.
why_wrong.B: Exceptional weather requires an inspection in its own right, whatever stage the routine cycle has reached.
why_wrong.C: Sagging sheeting is fragile and may collapse under their weight, so a harness does not make walking on it acceptable.

common_mistake: Assuming a routine inspection date covers a structure after heavy snow, wind or other weather has loaded it.

stem: Look at the bricklayer on the scaffold lift. The scaffold has been inspected and tagged. What should the supervisor do before any more brickwork is laid?

options.A: Ask him to clip a lanyard to the top guardrail while he stands on the blocks, since this arrests any fall from the stack
options.B: Have him come down off the stacked blocks and re-site materials, so he works from the platform and the rails give proper edge protection
options.C: Accept the set-up, because guardrails and toe boards are fitted and the current inspection tag shows the protection is built into the scaffold
options.D: Have a colleague steady the blocks while he works, since the guardrails stop him falling over the edge of the platform

explanation: Standing on loose blocks raises his body above the guardrail height and on an unstable base, so the rails no longer protect him from falling.

why_wrong.A: A guardrail is not a suitable anchor point, and a fall from the stack could still be over the rail.
why_wrong.C: Inspection covers the scaffold itself, not how workers then use it or raise themselves above its protection.
why_wrong.D: Holding loose blocks is not a stable base, and his raised position makes the guardrail ineffective.

common_mistake: Judging scaffold safety from the fitted rails and the inspection tag, without checking how workers stand and use the platform.

stem: In light rain, a roofer on a pitched slate roof uses a 230 V mains circular saw on a long lead from a 30 mA RCD in the cabin. The lead lies across wet slates. The foreman says the RCD makes it safe. What is the best control?

options.A: Use battery-powered tools so there is no mains lead on the wet roof, because a shock could cause a fall and the RCD is only a back-up
options.B: Keep the mains saw but swap to a sealed, heavy-duty outdoor extension lead, which resists rain well enough for the cable to lie on wet slates
options.C: Run a 110 V supply instead and let the cable lie on the wet slates, since reduced voltage makes contact with water harmless
options.D: Keep the mains saw but have the roofer wear rubber- soled boots and insulated gloves and press the RCD test button each morning

explanation: Removing mains voltage from a wet roof is the better control, since even a non-fatal shock may cause a fall and an RCD only limits the duration of a shock.

why_wrong.B: A sturdier lead is still a mains supply lying in water on a roof, so the shock and fall risks remain.
why_wrong.C: Reduced voltage lessens the risk but does not make wet cable joints and damaged cable safe.
why_wrong.D: Clothing is a weak control and a daily test only proves the RCD trips, not that the wet equipment is safe.

common_mistake: Treating an RCD as permission to use mains tools in wet conditions, instead of removing the mains hazard first.

stem: In a busy warehouse, an office door opens straight onto a main forklift aisle. Contractors fitting lights cross that aisle to reach the welfare room while counterbalance trucks run past. Which is the best control?

options.A: Cut truck speed to walking pace across the whole warehouse, which gives drivers time to stop without changing the aisle layout
options.B: Fit barriers guiding people to a marked crossing with clear sightlines set back from the door, with trucks required to stop and give way
options.C: Fit blue spot lights on each truck and sound horns at the door, so walkers get early notice without any layout change
options.D: Paint yellow lines on the floor and require hi-vis for contractors, since marked routes and conspicuous clothing let drivers see and avoid walkers

explanation: Physical separation and a defined, controlled crossing remove the chance of people stepping straight into a truck's path.

why_wrong.A: Slower trucks reduce harm but still meet pedestrians at a blind door, and speed limits alone are a weak control.
why_wrong.C: Warning devices depend on people noticing them and do not separate pedestrians from traffic.
why_wrong.D: Markings and clothing rely on behaviour and do not stop a person stepping out into a truck's path.

common_mistake: Relying on painted lines, hi-vis and warnings to keep people and trucks apart, when physical separation is what removes the risk.

stem: A safety representative inspects a loading bay and writes to the site manager about a missing edge barrier and a damaged floodlight cable. The manager replies that this is only opinion, that he will act if an inspector agrees, and that the representative will be liable if anyone is hurt meanwhile. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The manager keeps his own duty to assess the reported hazards and act in proportion to the risk, and the representative carries no personal liability for them
options.B: The manager may wait for an inspector to agree, because a representative's report has no legal weight until an enforcing authority has confirmed it in writing first
options.C: The representative is now responsible for the hazards he listed, because putting a problem in writing transfers the duty to deal with it to him
options.D: The manager need only act once the representative has served an improvement notice, because reports are not enforceable until formal notice is given

explanation: The employer's general duties apply once he knows of a hazard, and the regulations state that a representative's functions do not impose any duty on him personally.

why_wrong.B: An employer's duty arises from the hazard itself and does not depend on an inspector confirming a representative's report.
why_wrong.C: Reporting a hazard never moves the employer's duty onto the representative, who has no duty under these regulations.
why_wrong.D: Safety representatives cannot serve notices, which only inspectors can issue, and the employer's duty exists without one.

common_mistake: Assuming a hazard becomes someone else's problem, or can wait for an inspector, once a representative has reported it.

stem: Two labourers drive to a rural job with a can of petrol for a breaker standing in the van cabin behind the seats. After an hour both have headaches and nausea. The driver says petrol only matters if something ignites it. What is the best response?

options.A: Stop and ventilate, since the vapour is a health and fire hazard, then carry petrol only in a closed approved container kept out of the cabin
options.B: Accept the symptoms as brief and harmless, and simply ban smoking in the van, since only an ignition source needs controlling on the journey
options.C: Open the windows and leave the can where it is, since fresh air clears the vapour and a capped can cannot give off anything harmful to the crew
options.D: Seal the can inside a plastic bag in the cabin and wear dust masks while driving, so the vapour is kept in and kept out of the lungs of the crew

explanation: Petrol vapour causes headache and nausea when breathed and ignites easily, so fuel must be in a suitable sealed container kept away from the people in the vehicle.

why_wrong.B: Breathing petrol vapour is itself harmful, so controlling ignition sources alone ignores the health effect already shown.
why_wrong.C: A can left in the cabin keeps releasing vapour and remains a fire risk, and fresh air only masks the problem.
why_wrong.D: A bag is not a safe fuel container and dust masks give no protection against vapour.

common_mistake: Treating fuel as dangerous only when a flame is present, and ignoring what its vapour does to people in a closed space.

stem: Annual occupational health checks on twelve painters who spray coatings find early work-related chest symptoms in two of them. The manager asks the nurse for each man's medical details so he can decide who keeps spraying. Which course reflects HSE guidance?

options.A: Move the two affected men to other work and leave the controls as they are, since the other ten painters have shown no symptoms at all
options.B: Treat the findings as a private medical matter and take no action until a painter makes a formal complaint about his work or his health
options.C: Act on the nurse's fitness advice for the two men, and review controls for all similarly exposed painters using grouped, anonymous feedback
options.D: Insist on each man's full medical details, because the employer pays for the checks and needs the information to make its decision on who sprays

explanation: Surveillance is only complete when its results are acted on, which means protecting affected workers and reviewing the risk assessment for the whole group without disclosing confidential medical detail.

why_wrong.A: Symptoms in two men signal that controls may be failing, so the assessment and controls must be reviewed for everyone exposed.
why_wrong.B: Work-related ill health found by surveillance must be acted on without waiting for any complaint.
why_wrong.D: The employer needs fitness- for-task advice rather than confidential clinical detail, which stays with the health professional.

common_mistake: Filing surveillance results as a personal medical matter instead of using them to check that the controls work for everyone.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative is fine because he has been issued with every item of PPE this task needs. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: His hard hat needs a chin strap, because any hard hat worn while leaning over a rotating tool will slip off during the work
options.B: His work gloves should be replaced by thin disposable ones, since thick gloves cause the operator to lose grip on the grinder handle
options.C: His ear defenders are unsuitable, because grinding steel produces only low-frequency noise that earmuffs cannot reduce for the wearer at all
options.D: His eye protection is not over his eyes, so it gives no defence against flying wire and sparks, and work should stop until it is worn

explanation: PPE only protects when worn in the right place at the point of exposure, and workers must use it as instructed while supervisors enforce that.

why_wrong.A: A hard hat is not at risk of falling off while working at chest height, and the strap is not the issue seen here.
why_wrong.B: Gloves suited to handling steel are appropriate, and the visible fault is where the eye protection sits.
why_wrong.C: Earmuffs reduce grinding noise perfectly well, so they are not the main failing in the picture.

common_mistake: Believing that being issued with PPE is enough, when it protects only if it is worn correctly at the moment of exposure.

stem: Joiners lay chipboard flooring on a new first floor with screw tips and grit on the deck, kneeling for hours. The supervisor buys thin foam garden pads on tight straps, saying any padding counts as knee protection. What is the best response?

options.A: Choose EN 14404 knee protection with puncture resistance suited to screw tips, that stays put when kneeling and has straps that spare circulation
options.B: Keep the pads but tighten the straps further, so they cannot slip down while the joiners crawl across the deck all shift long
options.C: Choose the thickest foam available, since cushioning matters most and puncture resistance is unimportant when the pads are well padded up
options.D: Treat knee pads as comfort items that joiners buy themselves, because the employer has no duty over their choice or their suitability

explanation: Knee protection must suit the actual hazard, and the standard covers puncture resistance, staying in position and straps that do not impair blood flow in the leg.

why_wrong.B: Over-tight straps can restrict circulation in the leg, and thin foam still does not resist punctures.
why_wrong.C: Thick foam can still be pierced by screw tips, so cushioning alone does not match the hazard.
why_wrong.D: Suitable knee protection is PPE, so the employer must ensure it is appropriate for the risk assessed.

common_mistake: Assuming any padding will do for kneeling work without checking it against the actual hazard on the floor.

stem: An electrician on a handrailed step platform needs to fix a cable tray about a metre beyond its side rail. He suggests leaning out over the rail with one foot braced on the lower bar to reach it. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Tie the platform to the cable tray as he works, so the structure steadies the platform against the force of his leaning out
options.B: Keep his body within the handrails and reposition the platform so the work is in easy reach, or use a tower or MEWP if moving it constantly
options.C: Lean out over the rail but keep both feet on the platform floor, because the handrail will arrest any slip while he stretches to reach
options.D: Lay a scaffold board across the rails to extend the platform, since the rails then give edge protection over the whole distance he needs

explanation: Handrails only protect a person who stays inside them, and leaning out raises the risk of falling or tipping the platform, so the platform should be moved or a better access system used.

why_wrong.A: A cable tray is not designed as an anchorage and could be pulled off, dropping both the tray and the electrician.
why_wrong.C: A rail is not designed to take a leaning body and over-reaching can topple the platform or tip him over it.
why_wrong.D: A board laid on the rails is an unsupported, unstable extension that defeats the platform's own protection.

common_mistake: Over-reaching beyond the handrails because moving the platform feels slower than a quick stretch.

stem: A mobile crane will lift a 3 m glass pane on a vacuum lifter to a sixth-floor balcony. The pump has stopped and the gauge shows the required vacuum. The glazier wants to hoist at once to limit the time the pane is suspended. What is the correct step?

options.A: Hoist at once, since a gauge showing the correct reading when the pump stops proves the grip will hold throughout the whole lift up
options.B: Have a colleague steady the lower edge by hand during the lift, so any slip of the pads can be caught before the pane falls away
options.C: Raise the pane a short way and hold it while watching the gauge to confirm the vacuum is stable, keeping everyone clear of its route
options.D: Skip the test lift because a pre-use check was made at the start of the week, and the lifter has not been changed or moved since then

explanation: A short test lift shows the grip is holding before the pane goes up the building, and nobody should be beneath a suspended load that could fall.

why_wrong.A: A reading at the start does not prove the grip is stable once the weight comes on the pads.
why_wrong.B: A person cannot catch a falling pane and would be directly beneath it if the grip failed.
why_wrong.D: A pre-use check must be carried out before each use, so an earlier check does not cover this lift.

common_mistake: Trusting the vacuum gauge reading alone instead of proving the grip with a short test lift before going up.

stem: A mini-excavator with a short rear overhang digs along a site hoarding. The supervisor says that as a reduced tail swing machine its only danger is behind the counterweight, so a labourer may stand beside the cab to clear spoil while it slews. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The solid hoarding acts as the barrier, so no further exclusion zone is needed as long as the operator sounds the horn before slewing
options.B: Reduced tail swing removes the crushing risk, so a labourer is safe anywhere in front of the cab provided he wears hi-vis clothing and a helmet
options.C: Standing near the cab is safe because the operator can see the labourer, so only the rear of the machine needs to be cordoned off with fencing or tape
options.D: Barrier off the full area the machine and boom can sweep, since slewing can trap people against structures, and allow entry only once the operator stops

explanation: Reduced tail swing lessens but does not remove the slewing hazard, so an exclusion zone around the whole working area, controlled by the operator, is needed.

why_wrong.A: A hoarding next to the machine creates a trapping point, and a horn is no substitute for keeping people out.
why_wrong.B: Hi-vis clothing does not stop a boom or body sweeping into a person, and the crush hazard remains.
why_wrong.C: Being visible does not prevent contact during a slew, and the boom and body still sweep the area beside the cab.

common_mistake: Believing that a compact or reduced tail swing machine has no real danger zone around it.

stem: A skip lorry driver arrives to collect a skip on a busy street. Bricks and rubble stand above the rim, and the labourer offers to throw a sheet over them from the ground. What should the driver do?

options.A: Decline to lift it until the contents are reduced below the rim, then cover them from ground level so nothing falls onto the road
options.B: Lift it and drive slowly, since low speed on a public road means loose pieces cannot be thrown off the vehicle as it moves
options.C: Climb onto the skip rim and spread the sheet by hand, which keeps the load tidy and is quick to do before leaving the street
options.D: Accept the load because a sheet pulled over the high rubble will hold it in place, and any pieces that fall become the producer's concern later

explanation: An overfilled skip cannot be secured safely, and the load must be positioned and secured so it causes neither danger nor nuisance on the road.

why_wrong.B: Slow speed does not stop rubble sliding or falling off when the vehicle brakes, corners or hits bumps.
why_wrong.C: Climbing on the rim risks a fall from height and still leaves rubble standing above the sides.
why_wrong.D: A sheet cannot hold material standing above the rim, and the driver remains responsible for the load on the road.

common_mistake: Letting an overfilled skip go because a sheet over the top looks like a fix.

stem: A ready-mix wagon's chute leaks and leaves grey slurry across 15 m of a public road, running towards a surface-water gully while traffic passes. What is the best response?

options.A: Sweep it away as soon as it dries without barriers or cones, since a thin film on the road is a nuisance and nothing more
options.B: Leave the slurry to set hard on the road and break it out later, because traffic will cause no harm to drains or other road users passing here
options.C: Cover the gully, contain the slurry with sand or absorbent, shovel it up for disposal as waste, and work inside coned-off traffic control
options.D: Flush it along the gutter with water from the wagon tank, since heavy dilution makes cement slurry harmless to the drainage system there on the road

explanation: Cement slurry is highly alkaline and harms watercourses, so it must be kept out of drains and collected as waste while people clearing it are protected from traffic.

why_wrong.A: Sweeping without controls exposes the sweepers to traffic and creates dust, and does nothing to stop slurry reaching the gully.
why_wrong.B: Wet slurry can run into the gully and a setting film on the road is a hazard to vehicles in the meantime.
why_wrong.D: Hosing slurry towards a gully puts alkaline cement water into the drain, which dilution does not make harmless.

common_mistake: Assuming cement slurry is just stone and sand that can be washed into the nearest drain.

stem: A pipeline contractor works beside a quarry that blasts on two unannounced afternoons a week. The risk assessment rates blasting 'remote' because it is only occasional, and nobody has contacted the quarry. What is the best way to cover this intermittent hazard?

options.A: Cover the hazard with PPE by issuing hard hats and safety glasses to the whole crew, since protective equipment can be worn all week whenever blasts occur
options.B: Agree blast times and signals with the quarry, then plan exclusion and shelter for those periods in the site plan and brief everyone
options.C: Ask the quarry to warn the site only when a blast is unusually large, because routine blasts are already covered by the quarry's own risk assessment
options.D: Keep the rating as remote, since a hazard present for a few hours each week exposes workers for a small share of their time and so adds little risk

explanation: Employers sharing a workplace or boundary must co- operate and co-ordinate under the Management Regulations, and a severe hazard with a predictable timing can be planned around rather than ignored.

why_wrong.A: PPE is the last line of defence and cannot stop flyrock or blast overpressure, whereas timing and distance can be controlled.
why_wrong.C: The quarry's assessment does not cover the contractor's workers, and the two employers must co-ordinate for every blast, not just large ones.
why_wrong.D: Brief exposure does not reduce severity, and flyrock or overpressure can kill, so low frequency alone does not justify a low rating.

common_mistake: Judging a hazard by how often it occurs rather than by how severe it is and whether its timing can be known and planned around.

stem: A site joinery shop's dust extractor hopper is full of fine sawdust, with fine dust coating beams and a grinder working nearby. A joiner says sawdust only burns when it is lit with a flame, so there is no explosion risk. What is the correct view?

options.A: Dust explodes only in factories handling flour or coal, so a small joinery shop need not worry about sparks near its dust
options.B: The risk comes only from an open flame, so banning smoking and naked lights is enough while the grinder keeps working
options.C: Fine dust suspended in air can explode if ignited, so clean regularly, control ignition sources such as grinder sparks and empty the hopper
options.D: A full hopper is safer than an empty one because the dust is packed tight, and compacted dust cannot catch fire

explanation: Fine combustible dust can burn very fast when dispersed in air and ignited by a spark, so housekeeping, ignition control and emptying collectors are needed.

why_wrong.A: Wood dust is also combustible and can explode when dispersed and ignited.
why_wrong.B: Sparks from grinders and other sources can ignite dust cloud as well.
why_wrong.D: A full hopper holds fuel and can still smoulder or burn.

common_mistake: Assuming dust is only a health problem and cannot cause fires or explosions.

stem: A fabricator will weld stainless steel brackets inside a 12 m shipping container with the doors open at one end. He plans a pedestal fan blowing from the doorway past him and a paper dust mask. The assessment says the doors give good ventilation. What is the best control?

options.A: Swap the paper mask for a disposable FFP2 with an exhalation valve and weld in short bursts, because shorter arc time keeps the exposure below the limit
options.B: Capture the fume at source with on-torch or portable extraction discharged outside, and add a powered or air-fed respirator for the exposure it cannot remove
options.C: Place a second fan at the far end to push fresh air through the container, since a through-draught dilutes the fume enough to make respiratory protection unnecessary
options.D: Rely on the open doors and natural airflow, because a container with a large opening gives enough air changes to disperse the fume safely

explanation: HSE says capturing welding fume at source is the most effective control, with suitable RPE added where extraction alone cannot control exposure, and stainless fume carries added chromium risk.
