why_wrong.A: A particulate filter does not remove welding gases, a disposable mask has not been face-fit tested for him, and short bursts do not remove the need for source control.
why_wrong.C: Fans only move the plume around, often past his face, and dilution does not replace capture at source for a carcinogenic fume.
why_wrong.D: HSE states that natural ventilation through open doors is not sufficient to disperse welding fume, and a long metal box traps it near the welder.

common_mistake: Treating an open door or a fan as a ventilation control, when it only moves fume past the welder instead of capturing it.

stem: Operatives fitting a kitchen are confronted by the homeowner, who swears, blocks the doorway and threatens to 'sort them out' over a delay. They leave unhurt, and the supervisor calls it part of dealing with the public. What is the best employer response?

options.A: Send the customer a firm letter and carry on with the same arrangements, since the fault lies with one person rather than with how the job is set up
options.B: Treat it as reportable only if someone is injured, since threats without physical contact fall outside what an employer is responsible for at work
options.C: Record the incident, review the job's risk assessment with the crew for changes such as agreed contact routes and pairing up, and offer support to those affected
options.D: Leave it to the contract terms, since a customer's conduct is a commercial matter and the firm can recover lost time through the final invoice

explanation: HSE defines work-related violence to include abuse and threats from the public, so employers should assess it, record incidents and learn from them, and support affected workers.

why_wrong.A: Blaming the individual leaves the crew exposed to a repeat, as the employer must review controls such as contact arrangements and working in pairs.
why_wrong.B: Verbal abuse and threats count as work-related violence, and internal reporting should not depend on an injury.
why_wrong.D: The employer's duty to protect staff from risks arising at work extends to people other than employees, so it cannot be left as a commercial issue.

common_mistake: Dismissing threats and abuse from the public as part of the job unless someone is physically hurt.

stem: A scaffold stair tower serves six lifts. Plasterers carry 20 kg tubs of adhesive up it, one hand on the rail, and prop each landing gate open with a tub to get past. The supervisor says stairs are safer than ladders. Which response is best?

options.A: Replace the gates with a single strip of tape across each landing, which is quicker to move for loads and still warns people of the edge
options.B: Keep the gates shut and move heavy or bulky loads by hoist or another mechanical route, so a hand is always free to hold the handrail
options.C: Accept the stairs as the main control, since the treads and handrails are designed for carrying and extra measures for materials add little protection
options.D: Allow open gates while one person is on the stair at a time, because the chance of a fall through a landing opening depends on how crowded it is

explanation: A gate is the edge protection at a landing and must be closed, and stairs only reduce risk if users keep a hand free rather than carrying awkward loads.

why_wrong.A: Tape warns but cannot stop a person falling, so it is not edge protection.
why_wrong.C: Stairs do not make carrying 20 kg tubs safe, because a loaded worker cannot hold the rail or see the treads.
why_wrong.D: One person can fall through an open landing just as easily, and the gate exists to prevent exactly that.

common_mistake: Assuming a stair tower is so safe that carrying loads and defeating the gates is acceptable.

stem: Look at the scene. The foreman says the bracket is a five- minute job on a solid roof, with the ladder tied and a colleague footing it. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The ladder is unsecured and too short, so it could slip sideways or leave him without a handhold when stepping on and off the roof
options.B: He lacks hi-vis clothing and a fastened chin strap, so inadequate PPE is the main fault and would otherwise make this short roof task acceptable
options.C: The ladder needs a second person to foot it, which is the one missing measure that would make a short task on a solid roof acceptable here
options.D: A fall of about three metres is possible from an unprotected edge of a roof not built for access, and the job could be done from a platform on the ground

explanation: A cabin roof is not designed as a work platform, and with no edge protection or fall arrest the fall risk remains, so work should be avoided at height or done from a suitable platform.

why_wrong.A: The picture shows the ladder tied at the top with its stiles projecting above the edge, so access is not the main fault.
why_wrong.B: He is wearing hi-vis and a fastened chin strap, and PPE does not replace edge protection or avoiding work at height.
why_wrong.C: A colleague is already footing the ladder, and footing does nothing about the unprotected roof edge.

common_mistake: Treating a short job on any flat surface as safe, without asking whether it could be done without going up there.

stem: Hand-dug trial holes were cleared at the design positions of a bored-pile job. The engineer then moves eight positions 1.5 m to avoid a clash, and the rig operator says the earlier scan and holes already cover the area. What must happen before drilling the moved positions?

options.A: Proceed on the earlier clearance, since 1.5 m is within normal scanner accuracy and a competent person already declared the whole area clear
options.B: Have the rig operator countersign the earlier permit for the new points, since the same rig, crew and method statement apply to the moved positions
options.C: Drill the new positions at reduced torque and watch the spoil, since a buried service usually announces itself with obvious resistance before it is damaged
options.D: Review the service drawings and scan again at the revised positions, then dig fresh hand-dug inspection holes there, as checks apply to exact points

explanation: Safe digging checks are position-specific, so when a drilling point moves, the plans, scan and inspection holes must be redone for the new point before the auger enters the ground.

why_wrong.A: A clearance covers the points actually checked, and a service could lie in the strip that was not dug or scanned.
why_wrong.B: A signature on an old permit does not show the new points are free of services, which needs fresh checks.
why_wrong.C: Spotting a strike afterwards is not prevention, and an auger can sever a cable or pipe with little warning.

common_mistake: Assuming earlier all-clear checks travel with the job when the dig or drill points have moved.

stem: A 400 V armoured cable feeding a dewatering pump crosses a site road where portable traffic lights control 26-tonne lorries. The electrician lays it flat and covers it with a light plastic ramp. The foreman says the armour and the lights make it safe. What is the best arrangement?

options.A: Leave it flat but have the electrician inspect it each shift, because armour with a daily visual check will find any damage before it can cause harm
options.B: Take it overhead on posts, clear of the tallest vehicles and marked, or run it in a duct below the road surface, so vehicles cannot crush or snag it
options.C: Keep the surface route and add a second light plastic ramp with hazard tape either side, since doubling the cover halves the chance of a lorry damaging the cable
options.D: Feed the pump at 110 V through a transformer at the road edge and keep the surface route, since the lower voltage removes the need for cable protection

explanation: Electricity at Work Regulation 6 requires equipment to be protected from foreseeable mechanical damage, which is best achieved by keeping the cable out of vehicle paths altogether.

why_wrong.A: An inspection finds damage after it happens, whereas the regulation requires protection to prevent damage, and crush damage can be hidden.
why_wrong.C: Light ramps are not rated for 26-tonne wheel loads, so adding another does not give protection that is suitable.
why_wrong.D: A crushed cable at any voltage can still cause danger and fail, so reduced voltage does not remove the need to protect it.

common_mistake: Relying on armour or traffic control instead of keeping the cable out of the path of vehicles.

stem: While digging a drainage run in made ground, an operator sees fragments of grey, fibrous cement sheet in the spoil. The foreman wants to carry on and tip the spoil on the stockpile for reuse as fill. What should happen first?

options.A: Send a sample to a laboratory and continue digging meanwhile, since the operator is in an enclosed cab and the result will come back within days
options.B: Stop work, keep people away from the area and treat the material as asbestos until a competent person has identified it and assessed the risk
options.C: Pick out the visible fragments by hand, double-bag them and keep digging, because the soil is clean once the large pieces have been removed
options.D: Carry on with the spoil lightly wetted and move it to the stockpile, since cement-bound asbestos releases too few fibres to need any change of method

explanation: HSE advice is to stop work immediately and treat suspect material as asbestos until it is confirmed otherwise, then assess whether the work needs a licensed contractor.

why_wrong.A: Work must stop until the material is identified, because others on the ground and the stockpile are exposed in the meantime.
why_wrong.C: Small fragments and fibres remain in the soil, and untrained hand-picking exposes the worker.
why_wrong.D: Broken asbestos cement can release fibres, and moving and stockpiling the spoil would spread the contamination.

common_mistake: Carrying on until a laboratory result arrives, instead of stopping and treating suspect material as asbestos until proved otherwise.

stem: Overnight, someone dumps about forty used car tyres inside the site gate. The manager wants the area tidy before a client visit, by tipping them into the general waste skip due for collection tomorrow. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Photograph and log the dumping, report it to the local authority, and have a registered waste carrier remove the tyres under a transfer note describing them
options.B: Accept a passing man with a van who offers to take them away for cash, provided he promises to dispose of them properly elsewhere
options.C: Stack them at the back of the site until completion, since one later removal costs less and dumped items are not the site's responsibility
options.D: Tip them into the skip as planned, since waste left on the site becomes site waste and a general skip carrier will accept any mixed load

explanation: Waste on the site must be described accurately, passed only to a registered carrier with a transfer note under the duty of care, and a general skip does not describe or cover tyres.

why_wrong.B: An unregistered carrier with no transfer note leaves the site liable if the tyres are dumped elsewhere.
why_wrong.C: The occupier remains responsible for waste on the land, and a stack of tyres is a fire hazard.
why_wrong.D: The skip's waste description would not include tyres, so this misdescribes the load and breaks the duty of care.

common_mistake: Assuming waste dumped by someone else stops being the site's problem, or can be hidden in the next skip.

stem: A retail chain hires a small contractor for a ten-day store refit. The contract says the contractor arranges welfare, but he arrives with no cabin and assumes he can use the staff toilets. The chain says welfare is now entirely his matter. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Welfare is the contractor's duty alone once it is written into the contract, so the client only has to allow access to its staff toilets if he asks
options.B: The client must make arrangements that ensure suitable welfare is provided for the workers, and should confirm this before work starts and keep it under review
options.C: The client's duty ends when a contractor is appointed, because welfare then becomes part of that contractor's own risk assessment and the client plays no further role
options.D: The client duty applies only to projects notifiable to HSE, so a ten-day refit with a few workers falls outside the welfare requirement entirely

explanation: Under CDM 2015 regulation 4 the client's arrangements must ensure the Schedule 2 welfare facilities are provided, and must be maintained and reviewed, so a contract clause does not remove that duty.

why_wrong.A: The client keeps its own duty to ensure welfare is provided and cannot pass it away by contract wording.
why_wrong.C: The arrangements must be maintained and reviewed throughout the project, not discharged at appointment.
why_wrong.D: Client duties under CDM apply to commercial projects whether or not they are notifiable.

common_mistake: Assuming a contract clause passing welfare to the contractor means the client no longer has to check it is actually provided.

stem: An HSE inspector sees a dumper with failed brakes nearly crush a worker. By her next visit the owner has had the brakes repaired and says she can do nothing more, as no notice was served. In England, which statement is correct?

options.A: She must first serve an improvement notice and can prosecute only if that notice is ignored, because a case brought without a notice would not be valid
options.B: Once the defect is remedied the inspector may only give advice and guidance, because both notices and prosecution require a breach that is still continuing at the time
options.C: Only a magistrates' court can decide whether a case is brought, and HSE must obtain its formal permission before any prosecution can begin
options.D: Prosecution is a separate option needing no prior notice, so HSE can still decide under its enforcement policy to prosecute the earlier breach despite the repair

explanation: Notices deal with ongoing or likely contraventions, but a past breach can be prosecuted, and HSE decides whether to do so by applying its enforcement policy to the evidence and public interest.

why_wrong.A: A prior notice is not a precondition for prosecution.
why_wrong.B: Prosecution can relate to a breach that has since been put right.
why_wrong.C: HSE decides whether to bring a prosecution; the court decides the verdict and sentence.

common_mistake: Believing a fault that has been fixed after the inspector's visit wipes the slate clean and removes any chance of prosecution.

stem: In March, a risk assessment for resurfacing a seafront car park assumed a quiet site with gated access. The job slips to late July, when holiday crowds, a weekend market and heavy summer traffic use the same approach, and there is no fallback if deliveries are refused entry. What is the best response?

options.A: Re-brief the operatives verbally on the summer crowds and leave the written document unchanged, because rewriting it would delay the start and add more paperwork
options.B: Update only the public-interface controls with extra barriers and signs, since a plan for refused deliveries is a commercial matter rather than a safety one
options.C: Review and update the assessment for summer conditions, including the public and traffic interface, and add a contingency for blocked deliveries
options.D: Keep the March assessment as it stands because it was suitable and sufficient when written, and let the supervisor judge the crowds and deliveries on the day

explanation: A significant change in the conditions the assessment relates to requires a review, and the revised document should cover the new interface and a fallback for the access plan failing.

why_wrong.A: A verbal briefing does not replace a reviewed and recorded assessment of the changed risks.
why_wrong.B: Access failure affects traffic, storage and pedestrian routes, so a contingency belongs in the safety planning.
why_wrong.D: A significant change in circumstances means the assessment must be reviewed, not left to improvised judgement.

common_mistake: Treating a risk assessment as a one-off document that stays valid after the season, access or public presence has changed.

stem: A decorator must move twelve 25-litre drums of masonry sealer, about 27 kg each, from a van up two flights of stairs to a flat. The back-belt-wearing carriers propose one drum per trip with rests. What is the best approach?

options.A: Hold a briefing on bending the knees and keeping a straight back, as technique training is the main control for repeated stair carrying
options.B: Keep the back belts for everyone carrying, as they take the compressive load off the spine and so permit the heavier drums to be carried
options.C: Allow one drum per trip with a rest between, since the carried weight is then within a capable adult's strength and no assessment is needed
options.D: Cut the handling at source by ordering smaller containers or floor delivery, then assess whatever carrying remains and reduce it further

explanation: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations require avoiding hazardous handling where reasonably practicable, then assessing and reducing the risk of any that remains.

why_wrong.A: Training supports but does not replace avoiding and reducing the load.
why_wrong.B: Back belts are not an accepted control for heavy handling and do not remove the risk.
why_wrong.C: Repeated carrying of heavy loads on stairs still needs avoidance and assessment, whatever one person can manage.

common_mistake: Relying on lifting technique, rests or support belts instead of first asking whether the load can be avoided or made smaller.

stem: At dusk a groundworker walks an unlit private access track carrying a dark rucksack that covers the rear reflective bands of his vest. His supervisor says the fluorescent colour makes him visible in any light. What is the best view?

options.A: The fluorescent background is what shows up best in low light, so the reflective bands are optional and covering them with a rucksack matters little
options.B: Reflective bands glow by themselves in the dark, so covering part of them only reduces the visible area slightly and the vest still works well
options.C: Fluorescence works mainly in daylight and reflective bands only when light such as headlights falls on them, so keep them clear and light the track
options.D: Retro-reflective material is a requirement mainly on public roads, so on a private site track the bands need not be kept visible to drivers

explanation: Retro-reflective material returns light to its source and needs a light source and a clear surface, so it works only if uncovered and if lighting or vehicle lamps reach it.

why_wrong.A: Fluorescence depends on daylight and gives little benefit as light fades; the bands carry the night-time effect.
why_wrong.B: Reflective material is not self-lit and only returns light that falls on it.
why_wrong.D: The risk from site vehicles exists on private tracks too, so the bands must remain visible there.

common_mistake: Assuming a hi-vis vest makes the wearer visible in any light, however it is worn and wherever it is used.

stem: On a concrete frame, a gang fixes slab reinforcement beside the lift core while another gang, on a platform on the core wall 3 m higher, strikes and passes formwork. Nothing separates the two gangs. What is the best control?

options.A: Issue the slab gang with impact-rated hard hats and let both gangs carry on as planned, because head protection is the standard control for overhead work
options.B: Fit a debris net at slab level beneath the core platform and let the formwork gang work as before, as the net will catch anything dropped
options.C: Stop objects falling with toe boards and secured materials on the platform, and bar people from the area below where a fall remains possible
options.D: Have a banksman shout when formwork is being moved overhead, as a verbal warning gives the slab gang time to step clear of the area

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations require steps to prevent objects falling first, then steps to prevent anyone being struck where that is not reasonably practicable.

why_wrong.A: PPE is a last resort and does not replace preventing falls or keeping people clear.
why_wrong.B: A net at slab level would sit where the other gang works and cannot take the place of preventing falls or exclusion.
why_wrong.D: A shouted warning is unreliable and does not prevent objects falling or people being struck.

common_mistake: Treating hard hats or warning shouts as the answer to work going on above people instead of preventing falls and separating the gangs.

stem: A civil contractor applies a head-office annual test rule to all portable electrical equipment, including 110 V grinders and drills used on a muddy site, where the last test found many failures. A manager says an annual interval is a legal requirement. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Because 110 V tools carry little shock risk, they are exempt from formal inspection, so only the 230 V items need any scheduled checks on site
options.B: The legal minimum is an annual test for all work equipment, and a rising failure rate only makes a six-monthly test advisable as good practice
options.C: The interval is set by the tool maker and cannot be altered by the employer, so the annual rule applies only if the maker's manual states it
options.D: The law sets no fixed interval; equipment must be maintained to prevent danger, so frequency should follow risk and be cut where faults are found

explanation: The Electricity at Work Regulations require maintenance to prevent danger without a set interval, so the frequency of checks and tests should reflect the equipment, environment, use and fault history.

why_wrong.A: Reduced voltage lowers the risk but the tools still need maintenance, particularly in harsh conditions.
why_wrong.B: No legal minimum interval exists, and a high failure rate is itself a reason to increase frequency.
why_wrong.C: The dutyholder sets the frequency based on risk and need not be limited to a maker's figure.

common_mistake: Believing there is a single legal test interval for portable tools instead of setting frequency by risk and fault history.

stem: Look at the scene. A concrete pour is under way. Which statement best identifies the most significant problem?

options.A: The boom is working too close to the operatives' heads, so the main hazard is wet concrete dripping into unprotected eyes, which goggles alone would solve
options.B: The operatives stand on reinforcement mesh, so the main hazard is tripping, which boards would fix since the pump operator controls any hose movement
options.C: The operatives are stretching the end hose out horizontally to reach the pour, so air or a blockage could whip it and throw them; the pump should be moved
options.D: The pump lorry is parked too far back, so the main hazard is the pump operator losing sight of the pour, solved by a second operator on a radio

explanation: The end hose should hang near vertical and be guided, never pulled out horizontally, because pressure surges can make it whip violently and strike or throw the handlers.

why_wrong.A: Splash is a real but lesser risk than hose whip with the line stretched out.
why_wrong.B: Boards are present and the hose end moves with pressure surges that the pump operator cannot fully control.
why_wrong.D: Moving the pump closer is part of the fix, but the hazard shown is the stretched hose, not visibility.

common_mistake: Focusing on splash or tripping while overlooking the risk of the delivery hose whipping when it is held out and stretched.

stem: A mobile crane lifts a plant unit into a courtyard where the operator cannot see the landing point. The signaller plans to direct the lift by mobile phone on speaker, saying everyone has signal. Which arrangement is best?

options.A: Use a dedicated crane radio, with one voice giving commands, test the link each shift, and have the operator stop if communication is lost
options.B: Keep the phone but add a second person shouting and waving to the operator as a backup, so two signalling methods run at the same time during the whole lift
options.C: Keep the open call but allow the operator to carry on with the last command until the call reconnects, so the load is not left hanging
options.D: Use a chain of two relayed hand signals instead and allow the operator to guess at the intended landing point if one signal is missed

explanation: HSE guidance on crane radio use says commands come from one person, the link is checked each shift, and the operator stops the operation if communication breaks down.

why_wrong.B: Two people signalling gives conflicting instructions; commands should come from one person only.
why_wrong.C: Continuing blind after a lost link is the very risk, and the operator should stop.
why_wrong.D: Relayed signals are slow and unreliable, and guessing a movement is unacceptable in a lift.

common_mistake: Treating a personal phone as equal to a dedicated, tested crane radio and carrying on moving when the link drops.

stem: After heavy use, a site welfare unit's foul holding tank overflows at 6 am before the contractor's scheduled emptying. The sewage spreads across the yard towards a surface-water gully that drains to a brook. What is the best first response?

options.A: Close the unit, block the gully and contain the flow, have a registered waste carrier empty it, and tell the Environment Agency if any reached the drain
options.B: Hose the area down at once so the diluted liquid soaks away before it shows, since less visible pollution means less risk to the nearby brook
options.C: Cordon the area and close the unit, then wait for the scheduled emptying visit, since a spill not yet in a watercourse needs no containment
options.D: Pump the overflow into the nearest foul sewer manhole with an available pump, as sewage belongs in the public sewer network and so is properly dealt with there

explanation: Stopping the source and keeping sewage out of surface-water drains limits harm, and sewage must be removed by a registered carrier, with any reach of a watercourse reported to the regulator.

why_wrong.B: Washing spreads sewage and can push it into the drain, causing the pollution it should prevent.
why_wrong.C: Containment is needed now to stop it reaching the gully, and waiting for the routine visit leaves the risk open.
why_wrong.D: Discharging to a public sewer needs the sewerage undertaker's consent and does not deal with contamination on the ground.

common_mistake: Assuming a spill is only a problem once it has visibly reached a watercourse, rather than containing it before it reaches a drain.

stem: At 06:15 in winter darkness, a haulier's own employee is told to unload plasterboard in an unlit site bay littered with offcuts. The site manager says the haulier alone must protect its driver, because site duties cover only the site's own workforce. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The site's duty is met by giving the driver a hi-vis vest and a verbal warning about the bay, since a visitor is taken to accept the conditions he finds there
options.B: The site's duty begins only once the driver has signed the site rules, so with no signature yet the manager has taken on no responsibility for him at all
options.C: Both owe duties: the site must run its work so the driver is not put at risk, including a lit, clear bay, alongside the haulier's own duty to him
options.D: Only the haulier is responsible, because it employs the driver and the site's legal duties stretch solely to people on its own payroll or on its direct contracts

explanation: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act requires an employer to conduct its undertaking so that people not in its employment are not exposed to risk, and this sits alongside the haulier's separate duty to its own employee.

why_wrong.A: A warning does not remove a hazard that the site can reasonably control, and visitors do not accept risk by arriving.
why_wrong.B: The duty arises from the site's activities exposing him to risk, not from any paperwork he has or has not signed.
why_wrong.D: Duties to people affected by the undertaking do not depend on who employs them, so the site cannot hand the whole duty to the haulier.

common_mistake: Assuming that a visiting driver's safety belongs entirely to his own employer because he is not on the site's payroll.

stem: A cladding subcontractor hands the principal contractor's manager its RAMS at 07:00, the planned start time. Knowing the firm is experienced, the manager proposes letting the crew begin prep work while he reads the documents at lunch. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Allow the prep work if the foreman signs to accept personal liability for anything the RAMS later turn out to have missed on this particular cladding job
options.B: Hold the hazardous work until the RAMS are checked against the construction phase plan and site conditions; the subcontractor still owns its method
options.C: Let the work start and approve the RAMS afterwards, which then transfers responsibility for the method from the subcontractor to the principal contractor
options.D: Let the crew start because the review is only a paperwork check, and the subcontractor's own duty to work safely will cover any gap left in the method it chose

explanation: The principal contractor must plan, manage, monitor and coordinate the construction phase, which means reviewing a subcontractor's method before it starts, while the subcontractor stays responsible for its own work.

why_wrong.A: A signature cannot transfer or remove the principal contractor's coordination duty, and it does nothing to prevent the hazard.
why_wrong.C: Approval does not transfer responsibility for the method, and approving after the work has started defeats the purpose of review.
why_wrong.D: Reviewing before work begins is part of coordination, and a subcontractor's own duty does not replace the principal contractor's.

common_mistake: Treating the principal contractor's review of subcontractor RAMS as a formality that can follow the start of work.

stem: At a monthly walk-round, a supervisor finds a portable water extinguisher with a missing safety pin, a pressure gauge in the red and a service sticker two years old. A worker says it still looks fine and nobody has needed it. What should happen?

options.A: Keep it in use until the next annual service is due, since the gauge reading only matters when an extinguisher is discharged
options.B: Move it to a quieter area where it is less likely to be needed, and rely on the extinguishers in the busier parts
options.C: Leave it in place because it has never been used, and replace the pin and sticker so that it looks serviced on inspection
options.D: Take it out of use, replace it with a serviced extinguisher, and check all others for condition and service dates

explanation: An extinguisher with a missing pin, a low gauge and an out-of-date service cannot be relied on, so it must be replaced and others checked to keep fire-fighting equipment effective.

why_wrong.A: A gauge in the red shows it may not work when needed.
why_wrong.B: A faulty extinguisher left on site may be used in an emergency and fail.
why_wrong.C: Altering the appearance does not restore its working condition.

common_mistake: Leaving a visibly faulty extinguisher on the wall because it has never been needed.

stem: Two steel fitters cut plate with an oxy-fuel torch in a poorly ventilated bay off a plant room. A grinder works 3 m away, outside the cutter's area. The supervisor plans to issue an FFP3 mask to the cutter only and let the room fan run. What is the better plan?

options.A: Time-limit the cutting to short bursts and have both workers wear an FFP3 mask, because rotation and masks together make extraction unnecessary
options.B: Fit the cutter with an FFP3 mask and leave the grinder where he is, since fume exposure affects only the person actually making the cut with the torch
options.C: Capture the fume at the cutting point with local extraction vented outside, which also protects the grinder, and keep respirators for what remains
options.D: Run the fan across the bay to dilute the fume, which is enough control so long as the doors stay open and the cutter wears suitable eye protection

explanation: Extraction at source controls fume for everyone nearby, and respiratory protective equipment is the last line for residual exposure, rather than the main control.

why_wrong.A: Limiting time and issuing masks controls neither the fume at source nor the exposure of anyone without a fitted mask.
why_wrong.B: Fume spreads through the bay and affects others nearby, and a mask for one person leaves the source uncontrolled.
why_wrong.D: General ventilation spreads fume rather than capturing it, and in a poorly ventilated bay it exposes everyone to it.

common_mistake: Reaching for a mask or a fan first, rather than capturing welding and cutting fume at the source.

stem: An experienced pipefitter returns from three weeks off to a boiler house that is very hot in summer. The foreman puts him on a full shift straight away, saying he has done the job for years and the law sets no maximum workplace temperature. Which view is correct?

options.A: A full shift is fine because a worker who has acclimatised once stays acclimatised for good, so only brand-new starters ever need a gradual build-up in the heat
options.B: Build his time in the heat up over days with water and cooling breaks, as a long absence cuts tolerance and the employer must still assess the risk
options.C: He should work the full shift but in lighter clothes, since the temperature in a boiler house is a matter of comfort and not a matter of safety or health
options.D: A full shift is fine as long as he drinks when he feels thirsty, since the missing legal maximum temperature means the employer has no duty to manage the heat

explanation: Heat tolerance is reduced after a break, so gradual reintroduction is needed, and the lack of a legal maximum temperature does not remove the duty to assess and control the risk.

why_wrong.A: Tolerance fades after a prolonged absence, so returning workers need a gradual build-up as well.
why_wrong.C: Clothing alone does not manage the strain of working in great heat, which is a health risk and not merely comfort.
why_wrong.D: Thirst lags behind fluid loss, and the general duty to assess and control risk still applies without a legal maximum.

common_mistake: Assuming that experience, or the lack of a legal maximum temperature, makes a gradual build-up unnecessary after a long absence.

stem: Three roofers of very different builds pass one fall-arrest harness between them on a gable roof. The foreman adjusted its straps to fit himself at the start of the shift and says a pre-use inspection each time is enough. What is the correct approach?

options.A: A universal-size harness fits all builds once the buckles are fastened, so inspecting the webbing and the lanyard is all the fit checking that is needed
options.B: Issue a correctly sized harness to each worker where practicable, and have each wearer adjust it snugly, with the back attachment between the shoulder blades
options.C: Sharing is acceptable if each wearer tightens only the chest strap to take up any slack, as the leg and shoulder straps seldom differ much between workers
options.D: Set the harness once for the largest wearer and take up the rest with the lanyard, since a looser fit protects the smaller men as well as a snug one does

explanation: PPE must fit the wearer correctly after adjustment within its designed range, and a harness set for someone else may leave slack or sit wrongly, so it needs adjusting by every wearer each time.

why_wrong.A: No single size fits all builds, and fastened buckles do not show that the harness is correctly adjusted to the wearer.
why_wrong.C: Leg and shoulder straps differ greatly between builds, and a loose harness can shift and fail to hold the wearer properly in a fall.
why_wrong.D: A lanyard cannot take up slack in the harness, and a loose harness can ride up, let the wearer slip or hurt him in a fall.

common_mistake: Treating a harness as one-size-fits-all so that only its condition, and not its fit on the wearer, gets checked.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the blaster's air-fed helmet is the best respiratory protection available and fits him well. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The helmet should be swapped for an FFP3 disposable mask, since grit blasting dust is too fine for any hood to filter reliably in the open air
options.B: The helmet needs a face-fit test before use, because air- fed blasting helmets seal to the skin of the face in the same way that disposable masks do
options.C: The breathing air may be contaminated at source, as the compressor intake sits where engine exhaust drifts over it, so siting and air quality must be fixed
options.D: The air hose is too long for blasting, because a hose that loops back across the ground will always starve the helmet of enough air to breathe

explanation: An air-fed helmet is only as good as the air supplied to it, and the intake must be sited in clean air away from exhaust, with supplied air meeting the breathing air standard.

why_wrong.A: A disposable mask gives far lower protection than a clean-air-fed helmet for heavy dust, so it would worsen the protection.
why_wrong.B: Loose- fitting air-fed helmets rely on the airflow rather than a face seal, and the real problem is the quality of the air supplied.
why_wrong.D: Hose length matters within the manufacturer's limits, but the scene's main problem is contaminated supply, not a looped hose.

common_mistake: Judging air-fed protection by the helmet's fit and rating, without checking where the air comes from.

stem: Before raising a mast climbing work platform loaded with cladding panels, the operator sees the ground-level base is marked only with caution tape and the load is about 10% over the displayed rating. The foreman says the masts have a large safety margin. What is the correct view?

options.A: Remove the excess load and fence the base with a physical barrier; the rated load must not be exceeded, and tape cannot stop people walking beneath
options.B: The load is acceptable, since the rating includes a built-in margin, but the base needs a barrier because anyone standing under the platform risks being struck by falling items
options.C: Both are acceptable for one lift because the platform will stay at working height for only a few minutes before it comes back down again to be unloaded
options.D: The base is acceptable if a banksman stands at the tape, but the load must be cut to the rating, since the platform and mast are designed around that weight

explanation: Rated load must never be exceeded whatever margin is built in, and access beneath a mast climbing work platform should be prevented by proper fencing, since tape or rope is not an acceptable barrier.

why_wrong.B: The displayed rating is a limit, not a starting point for a margin, and exceeding it can overload the platform and mast.
why_wrong.C: Duration does not alter the load limit or the need for a barrier, as an overload or fall of materials can happen at any time.
why_wrong.D: A person at the tape is not a physical barrier, and tape cannot stop others entering beneath the platform.

common_mistake: Assuming a built-in safety margin allows a platform to be loaded past its rating, or that tape counts as a barrier.

stem: In an occupied shop, a fitter asks the owner if he can plug a 110 V site transformer feeding his tools, plus a 2 kW heater, into a wall socket. The owner shrugs and says to go ahead. The fitter's leads are all PAT tested. What should the fitter do?

options.A: Check the socket works and the plug is fused at 13 A, then use it, since any domestic socket is built to carry two appliances at full load
options.B: Connect it only for short bursts, since an overloaded socket circuit trips its breaker well before any cable could overheat or catch fire
options.C: Go ahead, since the owner has agreed and his own PAT- tested leads and plug fuses will protect against any overload on the shop's existing wiring and its socket circuit
options.D: Have the shop's responsible person confirm the circuit's rating and protection, and a competent electrician approve the temporary supply, before connecting

explanation: The shop's wiring was not installed for site loads, so its capacity and protection must be known and approved by a competent person, as a casual consent does not make the circuit suitable.

why_wrong.A: Sockets share a circuit with other loads, so a working socket says nothing about the circuit's capacity or protection.
why_wrong.B: Protective devices on an unknown circuit cannot be assumed to trip in time, and short bursts still carry the risk.
why_wrong.C: Plug fuses and tested leads protect the equipment, not the shop's fixed wiring, whose rating and protection are unknown.

common_mistake: Treating a client's casual permission to use a wall socket as proof that the circuit is suitable for site equipment.

stem: A tracked dumper is being driven up the ramps onto a low- loader. Halfway up it drifts toward the ramp edge and the driver turns the steering sharply to correct it, while the banksman stands beside the ramp to guide him. What is the correct response?

options.A: Carry on up to the bed, where there is more room to straighten the machine, because stopping halfway risks it rolling back down the ramps
options.B: Have the banksman step onto the ramp and push the drifting track edge across by hand, as that will line the machine up quite safely
options.C: Keep climbing and correct gently with the steering, since slow progress means the tracks will pull the whole dumper back towards the centre of the narrow ramps
options.D: Stop and reverse straight back down, re-align square to the ramps with the banksman clear of its path, then drive up again in one straight run

explanation: Plant should not be steered while on ramps, so a drifting machine should be backed off and re-aligned, with the banksman positioned where he is seen and outside any fall or tip zone.

why_wrong.A: Continuing leaves the drift uncorrected on a narrow ramp, and a braked machine can be reversed safely.
why_wrong.B: Anyone on or beside a moving ramp load risks being crushed or struck if the machine slips.
why_wrong.C: Steering on ramps risks one track slipping off the edge, and slow speed does not make that correction safe.

common_mistake: Steering mid-ramp to fix a bad approach instead of backing off and re-aligning before the climb. PRACTICE TEST 19

stem: A firm's dumper driver ignores the marked pedestrian route and cuts across it, injuring a self-employed electrician working for another contractor. He was trained and had a written rule, but supervisors had seen him do it before and said nothing. Which statement on legal responsibility is most accurate?

options.A: The electrician's own employer carries the responsibility, as it should have kept him out of areas where another firm's vehicles are operating
options.B: The firm is cleared once it proves the rule existed, because liability ends the moment an individual deliberately disobeys a clear instruction
options.C: The firm can be prosecuted for exposing others to risk, as tolerated rule-breaking shows weak supervision, and the driver can be prosecuted too
options.D: Only the driver is answerable, because the firm trained him and issued a written rule, and its duties cover its own employees rather than outsiders

explanation: Employers must conduct their work so that non- employees are not exposed to risk, and ignored breaches show supervision failed, while employees also carry personal duties for their own acts.

why_wrong.A: Another employer's duties do not remove the dumper firm's separate duty to control its vehicles and the people it supervises.
why_wrong.B: Deliberate disobedience does not end the employer's duty, particularly where managers knew of the behaviour and did nothing.
why_wrong.D: The employer's duty extends to other people affected by its undertaking, and a written rule that is not enforced does not discharge it.

common_mistake: Assuming that a written rule and past training transfer all legal blame to the individual who breaks the rule.

stem: A manager plans the hazard walk-round for a three-week refurbishment. He will tour the empty rooms alone on Sunday with the drawings and a checklist, then brief the gang on Monday. Which change would most improve how well hazards are identified?

options.A: Walk the areas with operatives who will do the work and ask how each task will really be done, including cleaning and maintenance
options.B: Delay the walk-round until the gang has started, so hazards are recorded as they appear and the findings reflect real working conditions
options.C: Limit the walk to supervisors and the safety adviser for independence, then ask operatives to sign the findings during the Monday briefing
options.D: Rely on the checklist and past accident-book entries, because operatives' views are subjective and a consistent method gives more reliable results

explanation: The people doing the work know the shortcuts, awkward access and non-routine tasks, so involving them finds hazards that drawings and checklists miss.

why_wrong.B: Hazards must be identified and controlled before exposure begins, not discovered once people are already working.
why_wrong.C: Signing a finished list is not involvement, and it leaves out the first-hand knowledge that would improve the assessment.
why_wrong.D: Checklists and past accidents only reveal known or recorded hazards, and they ignore the practical knowledge of the workers.

common_mistake: Treating a hazard walk-round as a desk or checklist exercise for managers rather than a conversation with the people who do the work.

stem: A scaffolder lands badly after stepping off a 1 m platform. His lower leg is bent at an odd angle and swelling, he is conscious, in severe pain and cannot stand. There is no ongoing danger and an ambulance is 25 minutes away. What should the first aider do?

options.A: Gently straighten the leg to its normal line, then tie it firmly to a spare scaffold board so the bone stays in place before the ambulance arrives
options.B: Help him stand with support to check whether the leg takes any weight, since a genuine fracture would not allow him to stand at all
options.C: Lift him into a van and drive him to hospital at once, because this is quicker than waiting for the ambulance and avoids the cold
options.D: Keep him still and support the leg in the position found with hands or padding, keep him warm and reassured, and stay with him until help arrives

explanation: Supporting the limb where it lies limits movement and further damage, and a serious injury needs paramedic care rather than improvised realignment or transport.

why_wrong.A: Trying to realign a deformed limb can damage nerves and vessels and should be left to trained clinicians.
why_wrong.B: Weight-bearing tests can worsen the break, and some fractures still let casualties put weight on the leg for a moment.
why_wrong.C: Moving him unsupported risks more injury, and a casualty in severe pain with a deformity needs ambulance care and a call for help.

common_mistake: Assuming that straightening, testing or moving a suspected fracture is helpful first aid rather than something that can cause further harm.

stem: A contractor will fit out level 4 of a multi-tenant office building that has zoned fire alarms and a phased evacuation strategy run by the building's management. The foreman assumes his usual 'everyone out to the yard' routine applies. What should happen before work starts?

options.A: The tenants' fire wardens will direct the crew on the day, so the contractor as a temporary occupier has no need to learn the strategy in advance
options.B: Get the evacuation strategy, alarm zones and signals from the building's responsible person, co-ordinate with them and brief the crew
options.C: The crew should telephone the building manager for instructions every time any alarm sounds, and stay put until a reply confirms what to do
options.D: Nothing special is needed, because the contractor's own evacuation routine takes precedence over the building's arrangements for the duration of the works

explanation: Where responsible persons share premises, even temporarily, they must co-operate and co-ordinate, so the crew must know what each signal means in this building.

why_wrong.A: Contractors have their own duty to co-operate and must brief their people in advance, as wardens may not be present or notice them.
why_wrong.C: Waiting on a phone call during an alarm wastes time and replaces a planned strategy with improvisation.
why_wrong.D: A contractor cannot override a building's fire strategy, and two conflicting routines could send people the wrong way.

common_mistake: Assuming that a contractor's own site fire routine automatically replaces the evacuation arrangements of the building where the work takes place.

stem: A kerbing gang will use petrol disc cutters for three weeks. The hire firm offers the standard model, or a quieter model of similar output for a small extra cost. The manager prefers the standard cutter and plans to issue ear defenders, calling this equally compliant. Which view is correct?

options.A: The choice should be made on hire price alone, since suppliers' noise data are unreliable and exposure can only be judged from site measurements
options.B: The two choices are equally compliant, because a high enough rated pair of ear defenders removes any difference in exposure between the models
options.C: Noise should be cut at source first, including choosing the quietest suitable equipment, with hearing protection covering only the exposure that remains
options.D: The quieter model matters only if the standard model is proven to exceed the upper exposure action value, since lower levels carry no duty to reduce noise

explanation: The noise regulations require risk to be eliminated or reduced at source as far as reasonably practicable, which includes choosing equipment that emits least noise, with hearing protection as a later measure.

why_wrong.A: Suppliers must give noise emission data and it should guide equipment choice before work begins, not be dismissed.
why_wrong.B: Hearing protection is not a substitute for reducing noise at source, and attenuation in real use is less than the rating suggests.
why_wrong.D: The duty to reduce noise risk as far as reasonably practicable applies below the upper action value too.

common_mistake: Treating hearing protection as the main noise control instead of first choosing quieter equipment and methods.

stem: Two joiners must move 18 mm plywood sheets, 2440 by 1220 mm and about 40 kg each, from a van along a corridor and through two narrow doorways into a room. Which approach is best?

options.A: Make each carry quickly without stopping, since a shorter time under load lowers the strain, and ask the pair to swap ends after each doorway
options.B: Use a sheet trolley or carry each sheet on edge, with one person calling every move, after checking the route width, door swing and floor
options.C: Let the stronger joiner lead, walking backwards, and take most of the weight while the other steers the trailing end through the doorways
options.D: Carry each sheet flat above head height to clear the door frames, since the weight is then shared equally and no one needs to turn the sheet

explanation: Handling assessment covers the task, load, individual and environment, and a planned route with an aid and clear co- ordination reduces strain and the chance of a drop or trapped fingers.

why_wrong.A: Rushing reduces control and ignores route checks, and changing ends mid-carry adds awkward handling.
why_wrong.C: Walking backwards risks tripping, and unequal weight-sharing overloads one person and leaves the other poorly placed to react.
why_wrong.D: Lifting a bulky sheet overhead blocks vision, strains the shoulders and back, and makes control through doorways harder.

common_mistake: Assuming that two people carrying a sheet automatically halves the risk without planning the route and agreeing how to move.

stem: A facade scaffold stands beside a street used by schoolchildren, and the site will be shut for two days. A ladder runs from the ground to the first lift, and loose boards and a bundle of tubes lie on the bottom lift. What is the best arrangement before leaving?

options.A: Lash the bottom of the ladder with rope and fix a 'Keep off' sign at its base, since lashing and signage together will deter children from climbing
options.B: Leave everything in place, because a green tag showing a recent inspection means the scaffold is secure against misuse and needs no further steps
options.C: Remove the bottom ladder to a locked store or fit a padlocked guard, and clear loose boards and tubes from the lower lifts into secured storage
options.D: Raise the ladder and leave it on the first lift platform, so reaching it from the pavement would need a jump and most children would not attempt it

explanation: Taking away or guarding the access ladder stops unauthorised climbing, and clearing loose items removes things that could be moved or pulled down onto people.

why_wrong.A: Rope lashing is easily undone and signs alone are unlikely to deter children, so neither makes the rungs unusable.
why_wrong.B: An inspection tag shows structural checks, not protection against unauthorised access or loose materials.
why_wrong.D: A ladder left on the first lift can still be reached or pulled down, so it should be removed or locked away rather than just moved.

common_mistake: Assuming that an inspected, tagged scaffold is secure out of hours when ladders and loose materials remain accessible.

stem: Look at the fixer working beside the overhead steel beam. Which feature of his fall-arrest set-up is the most serious weakness?

options.A: He is using a restraint lanyard with no energy absorber, so the force on his body in a fall would be too high for the anchor
options.B: The lanyard is looped round the beam with its connector hooked back onto itself, loading it over an edge in a way it was not designed for
options.C: The anchor beam is far above his harness, so a fall would be much longer than the lanyard's rated distance and strike the platform
options.D: The harness straps are twisted and loose at the legs, so the harness could not hold him upright if a fall were arrested

explanation: Wrapping a lanyard round steel and connecting it back to itself can damage or overload the webbing at a sharp edge and may not hold as designed, so a suitable anchor connector is needed.

why_wrong.A: The lanyard has a visible energy absorber pack, so the problem lies in how it is connected, not in its type.
why_wrong.C: The beam is about head height, so there is little slack and the fall distance is short, not excessive.
why_wrong.D: The harness is shown correctly fitted with snug, untwisted straps, so this is not the weakness.

common_mistake: Judging a fall-arrest set-up by whether a harness and lanyard are worn rather than by how the lanyard is actually connected to the anchor.

stem: A distant thunderstorm is forecast to reach a site where a crew is working with tall metal scaffold and a crane. The foreman says lightning only strikes the tallest object, so everyone else can keep working. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Monitor the forecast, agree stop-work and shelter triggers, lower or secure the crane and move people away from tall metal structures
options.B: Carry on as normal since only the tallest object is at risk, and ask the crane operator to stay at the controls for the duration
options.C: Keep working until the first thunder is heard, then shelter under the scaffold, since a metal frame conducts a strike safely to earth
options.D: Pause work only when rain starts falling, because lightning occurs only in heavy rain and not in distant storms

explanation: Lightning is a hazard to people near tall metal structures and cranes, so conditions are monitored, work is stopped by agreed triggers, plant is made safe and people go to proper shelter.

why_wrong.B: Strikes affect people on the ground nearby, and the operator should not stay exposed in a crane.
why_wrong.C: Sheltering under metal scaffolding exposes people to a strike and to current in the ground.
why_wrong.D: Lightning can strike miles ahead of the rain, so waiting for rain is too late.

common_mistake: Waiting for rain or thunder overhead before stopping work near tall metal structures and cranes.

stem: A crowded yard is full of parked skips and pallet stacks. A visiting lorry driver must reverse into a tight bay. The yard marshal, who has never worked with him, plans to walk backwards ahead of the lorry using his own gestures to keep it centred. Which approach is best?

options.A: Walk ahead of the lorry, backwards, in its path so the driver keeps a clear view of the signals, and use whatever gestures come naturally
options.B: Brief the driver verbally, then stand at the rear of the bay behind the load to guide it in and raise a hand to stop it if needed
options.C: Let the driver reverse on mirrors alone, with a single horn blast before each short move and the marshal watching only for pedestrians
options.D: Agree standard signals with the driver first, stand in a safe, visible position clear of the vehicle's path, and have him stop if sight is lost

explanation: A signaller must use an agreed signalling system, stay visible to the driver and out of the vehicle's path, and the driver must stop immediately if he loses sight of the signaller.

why_wrong.A: Standing in a reversing vehicle's path is dangerous, and unagreed gestures can be misread by a driver who has not met the marshal.
why_wrong.B: Standing between the lorry and a fixed obstruction creates a crush risk, and a raised hand may not be seen in time.
why_wrong.C: Mirrors and a horn do not replace guidance in a tight space, and without agreed signals the driver has no direction.

common_mistake: Assuming that a marshal's own gestures are enough for a driver who has not agreed the signals beforehand.

stem: A firm with 40 staff holds a signed health and safety policy statement from 2019, filed in the director's office. Since then it has bought a tower crane, taken on agency labour and started work beside a railway. An inspector asks whether the statement still meets the law. Which view is correct?

options.A: It must be rewritten every twelve months by law and each new version sent to the HSE for approval before it takes effect
options.B: It stays valid until the HSE asks for any changes to be made, because the law only requires the statement to be prepared, signed and filed once
options.C: It must be revised as often as is appropriate to reflect such changes, and the revised statement brought to the notice of all employees
options.D: Only the arrangements section needs updating, and existing employees need not be shown it again after they have read the original

explanation: Section 2(3) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires the written policy to be revised as often as may be appropriate and any revision to be brought to the notice of all employees.

why_wrong.A: The Act sets no fixed interval and does not require HSE approval, only revision whenever it is appropriate.
why_wrong.B: The Act places a continuing duty on the employer to revise the statement as often as appropriate, without waiting for the regulator.
why_wrong.D: Any revision of the statement, not just the original, must be brought to the notice of all employees.

common_mistake: Treating the safety policy as a document signed once and filed, rather than one that must change when the business and its risks change.

stem: A labourer has worked 12-hour days for three weeks on a completion push, under a signed opt-out from the 48-hour average limit. Today he yawns, misjudges a step and says he fears dozing off on the long drive home. The supervisor says the opt- out settles the matter. What is the right response?

options.A: Let him go home after a strong coffee and with an open window, since the opt-out shows he accepted the long hours and the journey is his own concern
options.B: The opt-out only waives the average weekly limit, so the employer must still manage fatigue by relieving him and setting and recording limits on hours
options.C: Move him to lighter tasks for the rest of the shift, since fatigue is a hazard only while a person is actually working on site
options.D: Reduce his hours only after he formally withdraws the opt-out in writing, because without that notice the employer cannot change his shifts

explanation: Compliance with working time rules alone does not manage fatigue, and the duty to control the risk applies regardless of a worker's willingness to work long hours.

why_wrong.A: A voluntary opt-out does not remove the employer's duty, and caffeine only masks drowsiness without removing the underlying fatigue.
why_wrong.C: Fatigue impairs judgement and reaction time in any task, and tired workers also face risk on their way home.
why_wrong.D: The employer can and must act on fatigue risk at any time, and no withdrawal notice is needed for it to do so.

common_mistake: Assuming that a signed opt-out or willingness to do overtime means the employer has no further duty to control the effects of long hours.

stem: After a burst pipe, a refurbishment crew must strip black- mould-covered plasterboard from a bedroom. They plan to scrape it off, dry-sweep the debris, then spray bleach over the studs. One labourer already has a chesty cough. Which plan best controls the respiratory risk?

options.A: Scrape and sweep as planned, then spray bleach on every surface, because bleach kills the spores and so removes the respiratory hazard
options.B: Let the crew work in basic dust masks with a window open, because mould is natural and the coughing worker will simply adapt
options.C: Stop the leak, remove wet board with dust suppressed and bag it, use fit-tested respiratory protection, and get health advice for the cough
options.D: Remove the boards but leave the leak until the end of the job, since the water source does not affect the mould exposure

explanation: Cutting off the moisture source, limiting disturbance of spores, using suitable RPE and checking on an already symptomatic worker together tackle both the cause and the exposure.

why_wrong.A: Dry scraping and sweeping throw spores into the air, and dead spores can still trigger allergic and asthmatic reactions.
why_wrong.B: A basic mask may not suit the exposure, and sensitised or symptomatic workers should not be expected to just adapt.
why_wrong.D: An active leak keeps the area damp and allows mould to regrow, so the moisture source must be dealt with first.

common_mistake: Believing that killing mould with bleach makes it safe to disturb, when the spores and dust are what people breathe in.

stem: Look at the scene. The foreman says the operative is well protected because he wears a hard hat, ear defenders, a respirator and a full face visor. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The respirator is unnecessary because the water feed on the cutter already removes all of the silica dust, so it only restricts breathing
options.B: The hard hat should be swapped for a bump cap, since the work is done kneeling at ground level where nothing can fall on him
options.C: A clear face visor is secondary protection and does not seal around the eyes, so impact-rated glasses or goggles should be worn underneath
options.D: A clear visor is the wrong type for this task, and a mesh visor would give better protection against flying fragments from the cutter

explanation: A face visor shields the face but leaves gaps, so fragments can reach the eyes, and it is intended to be used over primary eye protection.

why_wrong.A: Water suppression reduces dust but does not remove it all, so suitable respiratory protection is still needed for this task.
why_wrong.B: Plant and traffic operate alongside, and a bump cap gives no protection against falling or moving objects.
why_wrong.D: Mesh visors are meant for brushcutters and similar work and are no substitute for a solid visor with eye protection under it.

common_mistake: Counting the number of items of PPE worn instead of checking that each one gives the level of protection the hazard needs.

stem: On a wet road-widening job, a labourer works beside reversing plant in a dark green waterproof jacket, with the hood up over his hard hat. His hi-vis vest is back in the van. He says the hood keeps him dry. Which approach best deals with the wet- weather clothing?

options.A: Supply waterproofs that are high-visibility, with a hood that fits under or around the helmet without limiting side vision or muffling alarms
options.B: Keep the dark jacket and hood, and add a banksman to warn him of moving plant, so awareness becomes the banksman's job
options.C: Replace the jacket with a hi-vis vest over a thick hooded sweatshirt, since a fluorescent colour is all that matters for safety near plant
options.D: Allow the dark jacket and hood, adding a reflective strip across the hood, since reflective material makes up for lost vision and hearing

explanation: Wet-weather clothing has to keep the wearer visible to drivers and still allow him to see and hear plant, so conspicuity and the hood design both matter.

why_wrong.B: A banksman cannot replace the worker's own ability to see and hear, and a dark garment still leaves him hard for drivers to spot.
why_wrong.C: A hooded sweatshirt does not keep out rain and the hood still limits side vision and hearing, so the problem remains.
why_wrong.D: A reflective strip may help drivers see him but does nothing to restore the vision and hearing he loses with the hood up.

common_mistake: Judging wet-weather clothing only on whether it keeps the wearer dry, ignoring its effect on being seen and on hearing plant.

stem: A roofer repointing a gable verge on a 35-degree house roof, with eaves edge protection already fitted, hooks a home-made roof ladder over the ridge capping and slides it down the slope. The capping is old and loosely bedded. What is the main problem with this set-up?

options.A: The ladder should stop short of the ridge, so that its weight is kept off the capping and the ladder lies only on the slates
options.B: The roof ladder is not needed at all, as eaves edge protection alone gives enough protection for work on a sloping roof surface
options.C: Ridge capping can break away, so it needs a properly designed ridge hook on the opposite slope or another secure fixing
options.D: The ladder should instead be tied at its foot to the eaves gutter bracket, since the gutter fixing is the strongest point on the roof

explanation: HSE roof work guidance says the top anchorage should not depend on the ridge capping, and should instead use a purpose-made ridge hook or other secure means.

why_wrong.A: A roof ladder that is not anchored at the top can slide down the roof, and a ladder that simply rests on slates is not secure.
why_wrong.B: On most sloping roofs a roof ladder or crawling board is needed in addition to edge protection, so that nobody works directly on the slates.
why_wrong.D: Domestic gutters are not strong enough to support a roof ladder and must not be relied on as a footing or fixing.

common_mistake: Assuming that anything solid-looking at the ridge, such as the capping, is a safe anchor for a roof ladder.

stem: A fitter finishes ceiling work in one bay of a warehouse and wants to shift a braced mobile tower 12 m to the next. Nobody is on the platform, but a drill, a tub of fixings and a roll of cable are left on it. A labourer will push on the top guardrail. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Clear the platform and push from the base, since the route can be checked when the tower arrives and the brakes applied once it stops
options.B: Push from the base but leave the heavy items on the lowest deck, since a low load will not affect how the tower behaves
options.C: Clear the platform, push from the base, check the route for holes and overhead obstructions, then re-apply all brakes at the new position
options.D: Leave the items on the platform, as the toe boards will hold them in place, and push at the top rail where steering is easiest

explanation: Loose items raise the centre of gravity and can fall, pushing at height can tip the tower, and an unchecked route can hide hazards, so each step is needed.

why_wrong.A: Floor holes, level changes and overhead services must be checked before the tower moves, not after it has reached them.
why_wrong.B: Equipment should be removed from every level before a tower is moved, because any load can shift or fall as the tower moves.
why_wrong.D: Loose items can shift or fall and pushing high up makes the tower easier to overturn, whatever the toe boards do.

common_mistake: Treating a tower move as a quick shuffle, when the load left aboard, the pushing point and the route all affect stability.

stem: A subcontractor sends a driver holding a full HGV licence but no site plant experience to drive a forward-tip dumper on a housing site. The subcontractor says the licence proves he can drive anything on wheels. What should the principal contractor require?

options.A: Nothing further, because a licence covers all driving and a dumper that stays within the site boundary needs no other check
options.B: Evidence he has been trained and assessed as competent on this type of dumper, with familiarisation and authorisation before he drives alone
options.C: A short ride-along with a labourer, since heavy-vehicle experience carries straight over to rough-terrain, forward-tip site dumpers
options.D: A written declaration from the subcontractor that he is competent, since competence of its own driver is solely its responsibility

explanation: Drivers need to be trained, competent and authorised for the specific dumper, and a road licence says nothing about site plant competence.

why_wrong.A: Lawful driving on roads is not evidence of the training and competence needed for site dumpers, which have their own hazards.
why_wrong.C: Dumpers handle very differently from road lorries, so a brief ride- along does not replace assessed training and familiarisation.
why_wrong.D: The principal contractor still has to be satisfied about competence on its site, and a bare declaration is no evidence.

common_mistake: Treating a driving licence as proof of competence to operate site plant.

stem: A 13-tonne excavator lowers drain pipes into a trench. The operator cannot see the trench bottom, so a groundworker gives informal waves and thumbs-up, while another labourer sometimes shouts. Which arrangement is best?

options.A: Allow any worker to signal, since the operator can judge which signals are sensible from experience and then keep moving at a slow pace
options.B: Let the groundworker signal from the trench because he sees the pipe best, and have the operator carry on slowly if the signal is lost
options.C: Rely on shouted instructions over the engine noise, with gestures as a backup because they leave the signaller's hands free
options.D: Appoint one trained signaller using agreed standard signals in clear view, and have the operator stop if a signal is unclear or lost

explanation: A single known signaller using standard signals removes confusion, and a rule to stop on any doubt stops the machine moving blind.

why_wrong.A: Competing signals from different people cause confusion, and judging signals by experience is no substitute for a clear system.
why_wrong.B: Operators must stop when the signaller cannot be seen or understood, because carrying on blind is how people are hit.
why_wrong.C: Shouted words are easily lost under engine noise, so they are unreliable as the main method.

common_mistake: Assuming that informal gestures between two people who know each other are as safe as an agreed signal system.

stem: A contractor will demolish a concrete garage block 15 m from a care home with frail residents, using a hydraulic breaker. The manager says working in daytime hours and wearing ear defenders is enough. Which plan best applies best practicable means?

options.A: Agree sensitive times with the care manager, use a quieter method such as a crusher where possible, and site plant and screens to shield the home
options.B: Start work and deal with any complaints as they arise, since the home can only object once a measured noise level has been exceeded
options.C: Keep to daytime hours and give the workers ear defenders, since protecting the operators is what controls the noise reaching the nearby home
options.D: Send a leaflet about the dates to the home and use the breaker throughout the job, as advance warning removes the need for any other noise controls

explanation: Best practicable means looks at the noise source, working methods and control measures, and liaison with the neighbour helps plan the noisiest work for the least sensitive times.

why_wrong.B: Waiting for complaints is reactive, and neighbours should be consulted and noise controlled before the work begins.
why_wrong.C: Ear defenders protect only the wearer and do nothing to reduce the noise reaching the residents.
why_wrong.D: Warning residents is helpful but does not reduce noise, and best practicable means requires controls at source as well.

common_mistake: Thinking that daytime working hours and PPE for the workforce are enough to protect neighbours from construction noise.

stem: A supplier will deliver 40 kg rolls of roofing membrane and tins of solvent-based adhesive to a cramped city site on Thursday. The manager intends to decide where to unload once the lorry arrives. Which approach best controls the risks?

options.A: Order the smallest practical quantity and keep both materials together in the cabin, because limiting volume removes the need for a planned drop zone or store
options.B: Leave the assessment to the haulier, since the driver is responsible for the load until it is on the ground, and keep site staff away until then
options.C: Brief the driver on arrival and unload at the nearest kerb, because the delivery note shows what is on board and a single drop needs no earlier assessment or planning
options.D: Assess beforehand using the supplier's weights and safety data sheet, then plan the unloading method, a pedestrian-free drop zone and a separate adhesive store

explanation: Risks from materials are controlled by assessing the delivery before it arrives, using the supplier's hazard information to plan unloading, segregation and storage rather than improvising at the kerb.

why_wrong.A: Reducing the quantity helps but does not remove the manual handling or the fire risk, and flammable adhesive should not be kept with other materials in a cabin.
why_wrong.B: The site controls its own premises and must plan access, ground, storage and people, so it cannot hand this assessment to the haulier.
why_wrong.C: A delivery note is not hazard information, and deciding on the spot leaves no time to arrange safe unloading or storage.

common_mistake: Assuming that deliveries can be sorted out when they turn up, rather than assessing the materials before they are ordered or arrive.

stem: A fire in a half-built timber-frame block is put out, and the fire and rescue service hands the area back. Short of programme time, the manager wants trades back in at 7 am. What should be done before anyone is allowed back in?

options.A: Keep it closed until a competent person has checked the structure and temporary works and the fire risk assessment and alarms are reviewed
options.B: Re-admit workers once the area has been cleaned and dried, because soot and water are the remaining hazards and a structural check can follow later
options.C: Allow trades back on any floor the fire did not reach, since only the burnt area is unsafe and the fire service has already cleared the whole building
options.D: Restart when the insurer's loss adjuster has photographed the damage and approved a restart, because the insurer would otherwise refuse the claim

explanation: A fire can weaken frames, props and floors and put out of action detectors and escape routes, so re-occupation needs a competent structural check and a revised fire risk assessment.

why_wrong.B: Hidden structural weakening is the main danger and must be checked before people return, not after.
why_wrong.C: Handing back the area ends firefighting but does not confirm the structure is sound, and smoke, water and damaged fire systems affect floors beyond the burnt area.
why_wrong.D: An insurer's approval is about cover and says nothing about whether the structure and fire precautions are safe.

common_mistake: Believing that once the fire is out and the brigade has left, the area is safe to re-occupy.

stem: While stripping out an old boiler house, a fitter breaks a mercury thermostat switch and silver beads roll into floor cracks. The room is small and warm. What is the best immediate response?

options.A: Brush the beads into a dustpan, wipe the floor with a damp cloth and put everything in the general skip, since mercury is a heavy liquid that does not spread as vapour
options.B: Vacuum the beads with the site's industrial dust vacuum, because its filter will trap them and stop them settling deeper into the floor cracks
options.C: Flush the beads down the floor drain with plenty of water, then carry on stripping out while wearing a dust mask, as dilution makes mercury harmless
options.D: Clear and ventilate the room, keep the heating off, and have a trained person collect the beads with a mercury spill kit for disposal as hazardous waste

explanation: Mercury gives off toxic vapour, especially when warm, so people should be removed, the room ventilated, and the beads collected by a trained person with the right kit rather than swept or vacuumed.

why_wrong.A: Mercury does evaporate to a toxic vapour, and sweeping breaks beads into smaller ones that run into cracks.
why_wrong.B: An ordinary vacuum does not capture mercury and its warm exhaust can spread the vapour around the room.
why_wrong.C: Washing mercury into drains pollutes the environment, and a dust mask gives no protection against mercury vapour.

common_mistake: Treating a mercury spill like any other liquid spill that can be swept, mopped or hoovered away.

stem: A site has three women on it, but their toilet has no bin and items are being flushed, blocking the unit. A labourer who cleans the cabins is told to bag whatever he finds and put it in the general skip. Which arrangement is best?

options.A: Fit a lidded sanitary bin in the women's toilet, plan regular emptying by a licensed waste contractor, and give the cleaner gloves and handwashing
options.B: Supply a bin, treat the contents as clinical waste for specialist incineration, and restrict all emptying to trained first- aiders on site
options.C: Tell everyone to flush the items and have the cleaner clear blockages by hand as part of routine cleaning, since a bin only attracts complaints and odour
