options.D: Supply a bin but let the cleaner empty it into the general skip each Friday, since the contents are ordinary rubbish needing no handling controls

explanation: Sanitary waste disposal must be provided where women work, and a planned, hygienic emptying arrangement by a licensed carrier protects the cleaner and the drainage.

why_wrong.B: Sanitary waste does not normally need to be treated as clinical waste, and tying emptying to first-aiders is impractical.
why_wrong.C: Flushing blocks the unit and exposes the cleaner to sewage, so the bin is a required control.
why_wrong.D: Waste needs hygienic collection through a licensed carrier and the cleaner needs gloves and washing facilities.

common_mistake: Assuming a toilet cabin is adequate welfare without a way for women to dispose of sanitary waste hygienically.

stem: A tower crane lands pallets on a cantilevered loading platform through a gate on an upper floor. The plate reads 1,000 kg, but two 600 kg pallets are due together and the gate is to be left open between lifts. Which change best controls the risk?

options.A: Land the pallets singly but leave the gate open for the whole shift, since respecting the weight limit is the main control the platform needs
options.B: Land one pallet at a time within the plate limit, open the gate only to receive it, and close it again once the load is unhooked and moved clear of the edge
options.C: Keep the gate open all shift but hang a rope across the gap, since people will see the rope and each pallet is below the stated limit
options.D: Land both pallets together if the slinger clips a harness to the building, because personal protection allows the gate to stay open and the load plate to be exceeded

explanation: The platform's rated load must not be exceeded and the edge should be protected whenever no load is being received, so loads are handled singly and the gate is opened only when needed.

why_wrong.A: Respecting the load limit does not protect people from the open edge between lifts, so the gate must be closed whenever it is not in use.
why_wrong.C: A rope is not edge protection and cannot stop a person or a load from falling out of the opening.
why_wrong.D: A harness does not make an overloaded platform safe and collective edge protection should not be removed for convenience.

common_mistake: Treating the edge gate on a loading platform as an obstruction to be left open rather than as part of the edge protection.

stem: Look at the plasterer working on stilts in the picture. Which condition in the scene is most likely to cause him to fall?

options.A: The absence of a harness anchor, because anyone working on stilts must be fall-arrested whenever the stilts are raised above knee height
options.B: The height setting of the stilts, since adjustable stilts above ankle height are prohibited under the Work at Height Regulations
options.C: The wet plaster on the wall ahead of him, which will make him lean away from the surface and lose his footing on the stilts
options.D: A trailing cable and loose offcuts lying on the floor across his walking route, which can catch a stilt and throw him off balance

explanation: Stilts raise the user and make him far more sensitive to trip hazards, so the floor must be kept clear of cables, offcuts and debris before he moves around.

why_wrong.A: No rule requires a harness for stilts, and the real danger is losing balance on the floor because of obstructions.
why_wrong.B: The regulations do not ban stilts at any set height, and the key control is a clear, even floor for the user.
why_wrong.C: Wet plaster does not make him lean away, whereas obstructions on the floor are a direct cause of falls.

common_mistake: Assuming that stilts are safe because the user is not far off the ground, and ignoring trip hazards on the floor.

stem: A 1.5 m deep trench for a water pipe runs 2 m from a mature oak in clay, where a service plan shows a gas main nearby. Thick roots cross the line. Which approach best controls the risks?

options.A: Dig mechanically along the line to full depth then hand- clean, since a mature tree's root mat binds the clay and makes side support unnecessary at 1.5 m
options.B: Hand-dig only the top 500 mm then switch to the excavator, as roots and buried services both lie within that depth in clay
options.C: Cut every root that crosses the line flush with the trench wall to give a clean face, then support the sides and rely on the service plan for the gas main
options.D: Hand-dig or vacuum-excavate to expose services and roots, support the sides as roots cannot be relied on to hold soil, and take advice before cutting large roots

explanation: Services and roots are exposed safely by hand or vacuum methods, the trench sides need proper support whatever the roots seem to do, and large structural roots should not be cut without specialist advice.

why_wrong.A: Roots do not reliably hold trench sides and mechanical digging risks hitting the gas main, while clay can still collapse suddenly.
why_wrong.B: Services and structural roots can be deeper than 500 mm, so excavating mechanically beyond that depth risks striking them.
why_wrong.C: Cutting large roots can destabilise the tree and ground, and a plan alone does not locate the main accurately.

common_mistake: Believing that a mass of tree roots is holding the soil together and that a trench beside a tree can be left unsupported.

stem: A trial hole exposes an 11 kV cable. The network plan marks it 'disconnected', and one section ends in a bottle-shaped pot end. The foreman says a sealed end proves it is disused and wants to cut it with a hacksaw. What should happen?

options.A: Cut it with insulated tools and rubber gloves since the plan says disconnected, because the plan is the owner's record and the gloves protect against 11 kV
options.B: Ask the owner to say by phone that it is dead, then have a competent electrician cut it, because verbal assurance from the owner is enough
options.C: Treat it as live and keep clear until the owner confirms disconnection in writing and proves it dead at the point of work, supervising any cutting
options.D: Check the cable's outer sheath with a voltage detector, and if there is no reading treat it as dead, because an 11 kV cable gives a clear signal when live

explanation: Cables must be assumed live until disconnected and proven safe at the point of work, and pot-ended cables must not be treated as abandoned, so the owner confirms and supervises.

why_wrong.A: A plan can be out of date, and hand tools and gloves give no dependable protection against the arc from an 11 kV cable.
why_wrong.B: Confirmation must be in writing and the cable must be proven dead at the point of work, so a call is not enough.
why_wrong.D: A detector on the outside of a sheathed cable cannot prove an HV cable dead, so this gives false reassurance.

common_mistake: Taking a plan note or a sealed pot end as proof that a buried cable is dead.

stem: A trench on a former fuel depot fills with groundwater showing a rainbow sheen and a diesel smell. The contractor plans to pump it through a silt bag to a nearby stream under the Environment Agency's temporary dewatering position for clean water. What is the best course?

options.A: Stop pumping, contain the water, and arrange testing and treatment or disposal under a bespoke permit or water company consent, as the allowance excludes contamination
options.B: Dilute it by running clean mains water into the trench while pumping, so the sheen disappears before the water reaches the stream and nothing shows
options.C: Continue through the silt bag and add a second settlement tank in series, as settling removes the hydrocarbons and leaves the discharge compliant with the rules
options.D: Pump it to the nearest foul sewer manhole, since sewage works treat contaminants anyway and no consent is needed for temporary flows

explanation: The temporary dewatering position covers uncontaminated water only, so contaminated groundwater must be contained and discharged or removed with the proper permit or consent.

why_wrong.B: Dilution does not remove the contamination and the discharge would still be unpermitted pollution of the stream.
why_wrong.C: Silt bags and settlement remove solids, not dissolved or emulsified hydrocarbons, and the discharge still lacks a permit.
why_wrong.D: Discharge to a sewer needs the sewerage company's consent, and fuel contamination can damage the sewer and its treatment.

common_mistake: Assuming that any water pumped out of a trench can go to a stream or drain once it has passed through a silt bag.

stem: A fencing gang receives 25-litre drums of solvent-based wood preservative for three weeks of work. The compound has a lockable steel container, a surface-water gully, and a cabin with an LPG heater. Where should the drums be kept overnight?

options.A: In the locked container on a bund tray with lids closed and a spill kit beside it, away from heater and gully, taking out only the day's quantity
options.B: On hardstanding away from the gully with the lids loosened to vent vapour, since outdoor air disperses fumes and a loose lid prevents pressure build-up
options.C: Beside the cabin under a tarpaulin on pallets, because raised drums cannot leak into the gully and the cabin heater stops the liquid thickening
options.D: Stacked on the container floor with an LPG heater run overnight to prevent freezing, since the lockable door is the one control that really matters

explanation: Storing flammable, polluting liquids secure, contained and away from ignition sources and drains limits both the fire risk and pollution from any spill, and small working quantities reduce exposure.

why_wrong.B: Loosened lids allow spills and rain contamination, and an unsecured, unbunded stack is open to tampering and pollution.
why_wrong.C: A tarpaulin gives no containment or security, and storing flammable liquid beside a cabin heater creates a fire risk.
why_wrong.D: Heating a store holding flammable vapour is an ignition risk, and a lock alone does not contain any spill.

common_mistake: Thinking a container's lock or a distance from the drain is enough to store flammable chemicals safely.

stem: After a fatal fall, an HSE inspector formally requires a site supervisor to answer questions about the work and sign a declaration of truth. A coroner has opened an inquest, and the supervisor says he will stay silent until it ends in case his answers are used against him. What is the correct position?

options.A: He must answer, but anything he says can then be used against him in a prosecution, so he is right to insist on a solicitor first
options.B: He may decline questions about his own actions, because the right to silence covers employees while only the employer must account for the work
options.C: He may wait until the inquest ends, because coroner proceedings take priority over inspector questioning and early statements could prejudice the verdict
options.D: He must answer and sign; answers given under that requirement cannot be used as evidence against him, and he may have a person he nominates present

explanation: Inspectors can require answers under section 20 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act, and section 20(7) bars those answers being used in evidence against the person who gave them.

why_wrong.A: Section 20(7) prevents answers given under the requirement being used in evidence against him.
why_wrong.B: The requirement applies to any person the inspector believes can give relevant information, employee or not.
why_wrong.C: An inquest does not suspend or outrank the inspector's statutory powers to require answers.

common_mistake: Assuming that talking to an inspector is optional or that an inquest lets people hold back until it is over.

stem: Roofers leave a stripped roof under loosely tied sheeting overnight. A storm tears it off and rain ruins stock in the neighbouring shop. The HSE takes no action, and the contractor's manager says that without enforcement there is no liability. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The claim succeeds automatically without proof of fault, because damage caused by building work attracts strict liability for the contractor
options.B: The owner can sue in negligence for foreseeable loss whatever the HSE does, though breaching the Act's duties itself gives no civil claim
options.C: No claim is possible, because the duties of a contractor under the Act protect only employees and workers on site, not neighbouring businesses
options.D: The shop owner can claim only if the HSE prosecutes, because proof of a breach of the Act is what gives a neighbour the right to compensation

explanation: Civil liability rests on the common-law duty of care, and section 47 of the Act says its duties do not confer a right of action, so the claim does not depend on HSE enforcement.

why_wrong.A: Negligence still requires a breach of the duty of care that caused foreseeable loss, so fault must be shown.
why_wrong.C: The Act also protects non-employees affected by the work, and the common-law duty of care extends to neighbours.
why_wrong.D: Section 47 removes any civil right of action for breach of the Act's general duties, and civil claims do not need a prosecution.

common_mistake: Believing that no enforcement action means no liability, or that civil claims depend on the HSE.

stem: A team will inspect a 1.5 m surface-water culvert, entering through a shaft. The assessment covers atmosphere and escape, assuming dry weather. Heavy rain is forecast over the catchment 8 km upstream, though the site itself is dry today. What must the assessment address?

options.A: The foreseeable surge from upstream rainfall, with a forecast check before entry, a clear stop-work trigger and a prompt exit route for everyone below
options.B: Nothing further, since the site is dry today and any later flooding would be an emergency matter for the rescue team to deal with once it happens
options.C: Review the assessment only if rain actually falls at the site itself, since weather upstream lies outside the employer's control and knowledge
options.D: Issue waders and buoyancy aids to everyone below, which would make an upstream surge survivable without any need to alter the working plan

explanation: A suitable and sufficient assessment must cover foreseeable hazards that arise from conditions away from the site, and prevent exposure rather than rely on rescue.

why_wrong.B: A foreseeable flood hazard must be assessed and prevented in advance, not left to emergency response.
why_wrong.C: Foreseeable conditions elsewhere in the catchment are part of the hazard and cannot be ignored for being off site.
why_wrong.D: PPE is the last line of control and does not make a fast-moving surge in a tunnel survivable.

common_mistake: Judging tunnel and culvert conditions from the weather at the entrance rather than from the whole catchment.

stem: A crew fixes a bridge parapet in minus 2 degrees C air with a strong wind, wearing several layers soaked with sweat from heavy lifting. The supervisor judges conditions by the thermometer. One man's ears feel numb and look waxy white. Which approach controls the risk best?

options.A: Plan by wind chill, not air temperature, with windbreaks, warm-up breaks, dry spare layers and covered skin, as numb white patches signal freezing
options.B: Provide hot drinks and sweet food at the start of the shift, which keeps the body warm enough to prevent cold injury to exposed skin
options.C: Rely on the thermometer, since minus 2 degrees is only mildly cold, and let each worker add or remove layers until he feels personally comfortable
options.D: Issue extra-thick insulated clothing and leave workers to set their own pace, since insulation alone prevents cold injury whatever the wind or sweat

explanation: Wind makes exposed skin colder than the thermometer suggests, and damp insulation loses its value, so planning must cover shelter, breaks and dry clothing.

why_wrong.B: Drinks help but cannot protect exposed skin from freezing in strong wind.
why_wrong.C: Air temperature ignores wind chill and the numb, white ears show that individual comfort is not a safe guide.
why_wrong.D: Sweat-soaked insulation loses effect, and clothing alone does not replace shelter and warm-up breaks.

common_mistake: Reading the thermometer as the true cold exposure and forgetting wind chill and sweat-damp clothing.

stem: On a winter day at 1 degree C, a crew places concrete in an outdoor slab. The store holds fleece-lined cold-rated gloves and thin chemical-resistant nitrile gloves, and a worker says either pair alone will do. Which glove choice best deals with both hazards?

options.A: Leather gloves worn over thin nitrile, since the leather's thickness blocks the mix and also keeps the hands warm during the task
options.B: The thin nitrile gloves alone, since a chemical-proof material makes insulation unnecessary and keeps the hands dry throughout the pour
options.C: Waterproof chemical-resistant gauntlets over a thermal liner, replaced as soon as wet mix gets inside the cuff or the glove is torn
options.D: The fleece-lined cold-rated gloves alone, since their cold rating also gives protection against the alkaline wet mix during placing

explanation: Wet cement needs a waterproof, chemical-resistant barrier, while the cold needs insulation underneath, and mix trapped inside a cuff keeps alkali against the skin.

why_wrong.A: Leather absorbs wet cement and holds alkali against the glove beneath, so it is a poor barrier.
why_wrong.B: Thin nitrile gives no insulation, so cold hands lose grip and dexterity and risk cold injury.
why_wrong.D: Cold rating is not chemical protection, and fleece soaks up wet cement and holds it against the skin.

common_mistake: Picking one glove for the most obvious hazard and forgetting that cold and wet cement need different protection.

stem: In a lane closure, a boom MEWP operator is to hang a 6 m by 1 m vinyl event banner from a lamp bracket. Wind is well below the machine's plated limit, and the banner weighs little. The operator says the plated limit and safe working load are both satisfied. What is the correct view?

options.A: The lane closure deals with the real risk, since traffic is the hazard and wind limits matter only for machines working near buildings
options.B: A large banner adds sail area, so it can overturn the machine below plated wind speed; seek maker approval or use another method
options.C: The plated wind limit holds whatever is being carried, so working below it with the lane closed and the load within its limits is acceptable
options.D: Only the weight of the banner matters, since the safe working load is the figure that governs stability, while wind affects only heavy loads

explanation: Wind ratings are based on a set surface area, and a banner acts as a sail that adds wind load far beyond what its weight suggests.

why_wrong.A: Wind limits apply to every MEWP use, and traffic management does not address overturning.
why_wrong.C: The rating depends on the exposed area allowed for, which a large banner exceeds.
why_wrong.D: A light but wide sheet can create big wind forces, so weight alone does not govern stability.

common_mistake: Treating the plated wind speed as a fixed limit and forgetting that sheets and banners add sail area.

stem: A cable locator traces a line and shows 1.3 m depth. The drawings show nothing in the area. The operative plans to machine-dig to 1.0 m, then hand dig, saying the reading leaves a safe 300 mm margin. What is the main flaw?

options.A: Depth readings go wrong only on plastic pipes, so for a traced metallic line the figure can be trusted when a signal generator was used
options.B: A second scan from the opposite direction giving the same depth would confirm the figure, so the digging plan could then go ahead
options.C: The depth shown is only a guide and the service may lie shallower, so hand-dug trial holes should confirm its position and depth first
options.D: The 300 mm margin is too small, and a margin of 600 mm would make machine digging acceptable on the strength of the reading

explanation: Locator depth indications can be wrong, especially where other buried metal re-radiates signals, so services are positively identified by hand-dug trial holes.

why_wrong.A: Plastic pipes are not detected at all, and readings on traced metallic lines can still be distorted.
why_wrong.B: A repeated reading only repeats the same limitation and is not positive identification.
why_wrong.D: No margin makes a depth reading reliable, because the service must be physically exposed and confirmed.

common_mistake: Taking the locator's depth display as a measured fact rather than an estimate.

stem: Look at the scene. The driver says it is a short trip across level, firm ground and everyone is wearing the right PPE. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The dumper has no flashing beacon, so one must be fitted before it is driven among pedestrians and other site traffic
options.B: Two workers are riding in the skip, not a passenger position, so they should walk or use a vehicle with proper seats
options.C: The driver's seat belt is unfastened, so the dumper must stay stationary until it is worn properly before any movement across the site
options.D: The skip is raised while the machine travels, which makes it unstable on sloping ground and means it must be lowered first

explanation: Dumper skips are not designed to carry people, and riders risk being thrown out or crushed whatever PPE they wear or how short the journey is.

why_wrong.A: The beacon is lit in the picture, so this is not the hazard.
why_wrong.C: The picture shows the driver's belt fastened, so this is not the problem.
why_wrong.D: The skip is fully lowered in the picture, so this is not the hazard.

common_mistake: Letting people ride on plant because the trip is short and they are wearing PPE.

stem: A firm tows a weighed 2,400 kg compressor on an overrun- braked trailer behind a pickup whose handbook gives a maximum braked towing mass of 2,000 kg. The driver's licence covers the combination. The foreman says that is enough. What is the correct view?

options.A: The vehicle's own towing limit is a separate ceiling that licence and trailer brakes do not raise, so a more capable tow vehicle is needed
options.B: Draining the compressor's fuel and air receiver for the journey would bring the combination within the limit and so make the trip acceptable
options.C: The trailer's overrun brakes make up for the excess mass, so this pickup can pull it provided the driver keeps to a low speed throughout
options.D: The licence entitlement is the only limit that counts, since handbook figures are only advice and a competent driver can manage the extra weight

explanation: Driver entitlement, the trailer's braking and the tow vehicle's rated limit are separate checks, and the combination must pass every one of them.

why_wrong.B: Fuel and air are far less than the 400 kg excess, and the trailer is already weighed at 2,400 kg.
why_wrong.C: Brakes help stopping but do not raise the tow vehicle's rated limit, and low speed does not cure overloading.
why_wrong.D: The manufacturer's towing limit is a firm rating covering the vehicle's braking, hitch and stability.

common_mistake: Treating a valid driving licence as proof that any combination of vehicle and trailer is acceptable.

stem: To warm a cabin, a foreman feeds offcuts of pressure-treated fence posts into its wood-burning stove, saying wood is wood and the stove heats well. A neighbour smells a sharp smoke from the flue. What is the correct view?

options.A: It is acceptable in an enclosed stove, since high burning temperatures destroy the preservative and leave treated wood as harmless as clean timber
options.B: It is acceptable because the offcuts come from the site's own work, and waste burned where it is produced is exempt from controls
options.C: It is acceptable if the stove is an approved smoke-control model, since only the chimney smoke matters and not what the appliance burns
options.D: Treated timber is waste, and burning it releases preservative metals and toxic fumes, so it should be kept apart and sent for licensed disposal

explanation: Preservative-treated wood is not clean fuel; burning releases its chemicals into the smoke, and it should be segregated as waste and removed by a registered carrier.

why_wrong.A: Metal-based preservatives are not destroyed by burning and pass into the smoke and ash.
why_wrong.B: No blanket exemption applies, because burning waste is controlled wherever it was produced.
why_wrong.C: Appliance approval applies to the fuels it is designed for, and treated waste timber is not one of them.

common_mistake: Treating offcuts of treated wood as free fuel rather than as waste needing proper disposal.

stem: On a 30-person refurbishment the principal contractor employs one first aider and keeps the main first-aid room. A four- man plastering subcontractor and a self-employed electrician both assume this covers them, and nothing has been agreed. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Each employer must appoint its own qualified first aider whatever is agreed, because the law forbids relying on another firm's first-aid room or personnel on a shared site
options.B: Sharing cover is sensible, but each firm stays responsible for its own people, so agree it in writing, and the electrician still needs his own first-aid kit
options.C: The subcontractor must provide cover for its four plasterers, but the self-employed electrician has no duty and can rely on the principal contractor's first aider if he is hurt
options.D: Because the principal contractor controls the site, its first aider and room cover every trade, so the subcontractor and electrician carry no first-aid duty of their own once signed in

explanation: Joint first-aid arrangements are encouraged, but each employer keeps its own legal duty and a self-employed person must have equipment to treat himself, so the shared arrangement should be confirmed in writing.

why_wrong.A: Sharing first-aid provision by agreement is permitted and often sensible, so a ban on relying on another firm is wrong.
why_wrong.C: Self- employed workers must provide their own adequate first-aid equipment and cannot assume another firm's arrangements cover them.
why_wrong.D: Duties under the First-Aid Regulations stay with each employer and each self-employed person, and are not transferred by signing in.

common_mistake: Assuming that working on someone else's site means their first-aid arrangements automatically cover your own people without checking or agreeing it.

stem: A permit to work covers replacing the motor on duty pump A in a plant room, with its isolations listed. Once the motor is out, the fitter spots a leaking seal on neighbouring pump B and wants to strip it too, saying the same area and permit apply. What should happen?

options.A: Strip pump B once the fitter has personally closed its isolation valves and drained it, as his competence makes a further permit unnecessary for such a closely related task
options.B: Carry on, because the permit covers the plant room and the same crew, provided the fitter first notes pump B's seal fault on his daily task sheet for the supervisor
options.C: Telephone the client's maintenance manager for a verbal go-ahead and begin, then have the permit amended at the end of the shift to record the extra work
options.D: Stop the extra work, make the area safe and tell the permit issuer, who must check pump B's isolation and hazards and revalidate or reissue the permit first

explanation: A change in the nature or scope of the work means work stops until the issuing authority has assessed it and revalidated or issued a permit, because the existing isolations were not set up for pump B.

why_wrong.A: Competence does not replace the permit system, and the issuer has not verified isolation or checked interactions with pump A.
why_wrong.B: A permit covers the specific work and isolations it lists, not a whole room, so recording the fault does not authorise new work.
why_wrong.C: Work must not start on an informal approval; the permit has to be revalidated or reissued before the new work, not after it.

common_mistake: Treating a permit as general approval for a location and crew, so that a related job nearby can be added without going back to the issuer.

stem: A wheelchair-using inspector must check completed work on the third floor of a new building served by one passenger lift and two stairs. The visit cannot be moved downstairs. Which arrangement for a fire alarm is best?

options.A: Have two fit site operatives carry her down the stairs in her chair, since the descent is only three floors and they can do it quickly
options.B: Use the passenger lift when the alarm sounds, as it is the only accessible route and her escort can ride down with her to ground level and the assembly point
options.C: Leave her in the stair refuge with an instruction to wait for the fire service, while her escort leaves with the others and reports to the assembly point
options.D: Agree a plan beforehand: a trained escort, a route to a stair refuge with two-way communication, and a way to tell the person in charge where she is

explanation: Advance planning with the person, a trained escort, a refuge with communication and passing her location to the person in charge, who informs the fire service, is the approach recommended in fire safety guidance.

why_wrong.A: Carrying down is only acceptable with a risk assessment and proper training, and untrained lifting risks injury to her and to them.
why_wrong.B: Ordinary lifts are taken over by the fire service and must not be used in a fire unless designed as evacuation lifts.
why_wrong.C: A person should not be left alone in a refuge to wait for the fire service, and the plan must not depend on rescue arriving.

common_mistake: Thinking that the standard alarm and assembly point cover everyone, and that colleagues can improvise a carry-down when the alarm sounds.

stem: Roofers set up a bitumen boiler on a flat roof 3 m from a plant-room air intake serving the occupied offices below. Fumes are drifting into the building. The foreman proposes handing out disposable dust masks. What is the best response?

options.A: Move the boiler well away from and downwind of the intake, agree with building management to close or shut it down during heating, and keep the temperature as low as workable
options.B: Raise the boiler temperature so the bitumen is used quickly and the fumes pass sooner, which cuts the time that the office occupants are exposed to them
options.C: Fit a taller flue to the boiler alone, because dispersing the fumes higher removes the risk to the offices without needing to move equipment or contact the building's managers
options.D: Issue the masks to the roofers and ask the office staff to keep windows shut, since the fumes are a short-term nuisance and not a health hazard to the occupants

explanation: Fumes are best controlled at source by siting, downwind positioning and the lowest workable temperature, with building management protecting occupants, who masks for the roofers would not protect.

why_wrong.B: Higher temperatures increase fume emission and fire and burn risk, so they worsen exposure rather than reducing it.
why_wrong.C: Raising the discharge does not guarantee fumes stay clear of intakes, and the building's occupants and managers still need to be involved.
why_wrong.D: Fume from heated bitumen is an irritant hazard, and paper dust masks give poor protection while doing nothing for people in the building.

common_mistake: Reaching for respirators or masks for the workers first, instead of moving the source and protecting other people who share the building.

stem: A scaffolder tells his supervisor he has had two panic attacks on the upper lifts, with shaking and dizziness. The supervisor says height is part of the trade and he should toughen up. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Let him carry on at height because he is trained and holds a card, and ask a colleague to stay nearby in case he has another attack while he works on the lifts
options.B: Treat it as a capability issue: talk to him, seek occupational health advice, and give him low-level work while the risk assessment is reviewed
options.C: Remove him from the gang and the site, since anyone who has a panic attack at height is unfit for any scaffolding role and must be dismissed
options.D: Leave the decision to him, because his health is private and the employer has no duty to consider it when deciding who works on the upper lifts

explanation: Employers must take account of employees' capabilities as regards health and safety when allocating tasks, so a worker reporting panic at height needs support, advice and interim safe work.

why_wrong.A: Training does not remove the risk of a panic attack at height, and a colleague nearby cannot prevent a fall.
why_wrong.C: Fitness depends on assessment and advice, not a blanket judgement, and low-level work may remain suitable.
why_wrong.D: Regulation 13 requires employers to consider capabilities when entrusting tasks, so the employer cannot ignore health information it has been given.

common_mistake: Treating anxiety or panic at height as a matter of toughness instead of a health and safety capability issue that the employer must assess.

stem: A groundworker with a valid CSCS card and a yellow Class 3 hi- vis jacket is told to walk the lineside of a live railway to collect a drum near the fence. His foreman says that is all the competence and PPE needed. What is the correct view?

options.A: Orange hi-vis is the extra item required, because the colour marks him as a track worker and removes the need for separate track competence on short tasks
options.B: A lookout watching for trains is enough on its own, since a trained lookout can make up for lacking track competence and a non-rail hi-vis jacket
options.C: The CSCS card shows general construction competence and the yellow Class 3 jacket meets the visibility standard, so both are accepted for a short lineside task
options.D: Lineside work needs rail-specific track safety competence, such as a Sentinel Personal Track Safety card, and orange rail hi- vis, under controlled access

explanation: Network Rail lineside access requires track-specific competence and orange hi-vis, which is not interchangeable with a general construction card and a yellow jacket.

why_wrong.A: Colour alone does not give competence; the worker must also be trained and registered for track safety.
why_wrong.B: A lookout is one control within a track safety system and does not substitute for competence or the correct clothing.
why_wrong.C: General construction credentials do not cover track hazards such as trains and traction power, and orange is used to identify track workers.

common_mistake: Believing a CSCS card and any Class 3 hi- vis jacket are enough for every construction environment, including the railway.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the carpenter is wearing every item of PPE listed in the drilling task assessment. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: His eye protection is inadequate for bench drilling, so a full-face visor must replace the safety glasses even though the glasses have side shields
options.B: The gloves and loose cuffs near the rotating bit can be caught and drag his hand in, so they should be taken off or secured despite being PPE
options.C: A dust mask is missing, so respiratory protection is the main gap because drilling any timber creates dust above the workplace exposure limit
options.D: The chuck guard is in place but should be removed so he can see the cutting point, since the clamped workpiece and gloves protect his hands

explanation: Gloves and loose sleeves near a rotating spindle can wind onto the bit and drag the hand in, so the PPE itself creates an entanglement hazard that outweighs any protection from handling.

why_wrong.A: Side-shielded safety glasses are suitable for drilling timber, and a visor would not address the entanglement risk.
why_wrong.C: A few drilled holes produce little dust, and respiratory protection would not remove the more serious risk of entanglement.
why_wrong.D: Guards must stay in place, and gloves do not protect hands from rotating parts, which is the very hazard they add.

common_mistake: Assuming that more PPE is always safer, when gloves and loose cuffs near rotating machinery can themselves pull the hand in.

stem: An electrician on guarded podium steps lifts out a ceiling tile and wants to put his head and shoulders into the void to trace a cable, resting a knee on the ceiling grid. Nobody has seen an asbestos survey for the void. What is the correct response?

options.A: Keep off the grid and out of the void; first confirm asbestos information for it, then inspect from within the podium's guardrails using a torch and camera
options.B: Swap the podium for a stepladder, which lets him climb higher and see further into the void without needing to rest any weight on the ceiling
options.C: Proceed, since the podium's guardrails make the platform safe, provided he keeps most of his weight on the platform and touches the grid only lightly with his knee
options.D: Ask a second person to hold the grid steady while he leans in, because shared support makes the grid adequate for the load of one knee

explanation: A suspended ceiling grid is not designed to carry a person, leaning out of the guarded platform defeats its protection, and the void must be checked for asbestos information before it is disturbed.

why_wrong.B: A stepladder is less suitable for a long task, still leaves the void entry and asbestos question unresolved, and adds a fall risk.
why_wrong.C: Guardrails protect only while he stays inside them, and a ceiling grid is not designed to support any body weight.
why_wrong.D: A colleague holding the grid cannot make it a safe working platform, and the asbestos question is ignored.

common_mistake: Assuming a guarded podium makes any posture safe, including leaning or kneeling beyond its rails into a ceiling void.

stem: An electrician isolates the lighting circuit for a staircase in an occupied office and locks off the breaker, keeping the key. He starts to replace a failed fitting while staff are still using the now- dark stairwell. What has he missed?

options.A: Nothing, because once the circuit is locked off and he holds the key the electrical risk is controlled, and the stairwell lighting is the building manager's problem alone
options.B: A warning notice at the breaker and another at the foot of the stair should replace the lock, because notices tell staff and the key can stay in the cabinet
options.C: He should have warned the occupants beforehand and arranged temporary lighting or closed the stair, and he still needs to prove the fitting dead at the point of work
options.D: He should tell staff to use the lift instead and rely on the wall switch being off as proof that the fitting is dead, rather than testing it

explanation: Safe isolation requires notifying those affected by the loss of supply and controlling the new hazard it creates, while locking off and then proving the fitting dead before touching conductors.

why_wrong.A: Isolation creates a new hazard for occupants that the person isolating must warn about and help control, beyond the electrical lock-off.
why_wrong.B: Notices are easily missed and are not a substitute for keeping the isolation under the control of the person working.
why_wrong.D: A wall switch off does not prove the fitting is dead, and sending people to a lift does not address safe lighting for the stair.

common_mistake: Thinking safe isolation is only about protecting the electrician, and forgetting the people who lose lighting or other services when the circuit goes off.

stem: A chain-lift skip lorry driver arrives for a large skip filled level with its sides with broken concrete and brick. It looks too heavy, but the contractor insists it is not overfilled and wants it gone quickly. What should the driver do?

options.A: Lift it, because material level with the sides is not overfilled and the customer who hired the skip carries the legal responsibility for the weight of its contents
options.B: Lift it a short distance to test it, then lower it and decide, since the vehicle's behaviour will show whether the chain lift is overloaded
options.C: Decline to lift it if he judges it over the vehicle's weight limit, and ask for material to be removed, since a level skip of dense waste can be too heavy
options.D: Net the load, drive carefully on minor roads to the tip, and let the weighbridge show whether it was overweight, since the tip will check it later

explanation: Weight, not volume, decides whether a skip can be lifted and carried, so a driver should check the load is not overweight and refuse to lift it when the pick-up seems unsafe.

why_wrong.A: The driver and operator must not lift or carry an overweight load, whoever filled the skip and however level it looks.
why_wrong.B: A trial lift loads the chains and vehicle beyond their limits and risks failure with people close by.
why_wrong.D: Driving an overweight vehicle is unlawful and unsafe, and a weighbridge check afterwards does not make the lift or journey safe.

common_mistake: Judging whether a skip can be lifted by how full it looks instead of how heavy the contents are. PRACTICE TEST 20

stem: A firm replaces its disc cutters with new battery saws that have a different guard and kickback behaviour. The manager says experienced operators need no retraining and offers an optional toolbox talk on Saturday morning, unpaid. What does the law require?

options.A: Training may be held outside working hours if operators agree in writing, since a signed agreement passes the time and cost of it to the worker
options.B: Training is a legal requirement only on recruitment, so experienced staff may join a voluntary session outside their normal hours if they choose to
options.C: Experience on cutters is presumed to cover any similar tool, so handing out the manufacturer's written instructions is enough to meet the employer's duty
options.D: Operators must be trained on the new saws' risks before they use them, repeated where appropriate, and the training must take place during working hours

explanation: The Management Regulations require health and safety training when new work equipment is introduced, adapted to the changed risks, repeated where appropriate and delivered during working hours.

why_wrong.A: The duty to train in working hours stays with the employer and an operator's agreement cannot move it on.
why_wrong.B: Training is also required when new equipment brings new or changed risks, and it cannot be left to voluntary unpaid attendance.
why_wrong.C: Experience on the old discs does not cover the new guard and kickback, and leaflets alone are not training.

common_mistake: Assuming that experienced workers do not need retraining when the equipment they use changes.

stem: To take operatives away from a noisy, dusty breaking-out task, a firm swaps hand breakers for a remote-controlled demolition machine. The assessor marks the job low risk because nobody now stands at the work face. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A new assessment is needed only for the noise and dust, since the machine's electronic controls mean its movement hazards are already covered by the manufacturer
options.B: The original assessment still stands, because moving people away from the work face removes the hazard and a fresh one is needed only if someone is hurt
options.C: The change needs reassessing before work starts, as it brings new hazards such as the operator's view, the machine's reach and flying debris
options.D: Reassessment is required but can wait until the machine has run for a week, as observed working conditions give a more reliable picture than predictions

explanation: Substituting equipment removes some exposure but creates new hazards, so the assessment must be reviewed before the work starts, with an exclusion zone and a trained operator.

why_wrong.A: The manufacturer's design does not address the site-specific reach, debris and visibility hazards, which the employer must assess.
why_wrong.B: A change of method alters the hazards, and waiting for an injury before reassessing defeats the purpose of assessment.
why_wrong.D: The assessment must be suitable and sufficient before the work begins, not after exposure has already happened.

common_mistake: Assuming that a control which removes people from one hazard has removed every hazard from the task.

stem: A groundworker who uses breakers and vibrating plates every day gives his employer a doctor's letter diagnosing hand-arm vibration syndrome. The manager says RIDDOR covers only accident injuries and files the letter. What is the correct position?

options.A: The worker must report it to the HSE himself, since a diagnosis letter is his own medical information and the employer has no part in reporting it
options.B: RIDDOR covers only sudden injuries, so a gradual condition belongs in the health record and becomes reportable only if he later loses more than seven days
options.C: The employer must report the disease to the HSE, because it is reportable where the work regularly involves vibrating tools and a doctor has diagnosed it
options.D: Reporting is required only if the doctor ties the condition in writing to one named incident, because years of general tool use cannot be linked to work

explanation: RIDDOR lists hand-arm vibration syndrome as a reportable disease when a doctor diagnoses it in someone whose work regularly involves vibrating tools, whether or not any time is lost.

why_wrong.A: Once an employee gives a written diagnosis, the employer has the duty to make the report.
why_wrong.B: RIDDOR also lists specified work-related diseases, and reporting does not depend on lost working days.
why_wrong.D: The disease is reportable from regular use of vibrating tools and needs no single named incident.

common_mistake: Thinking that RIDDOR reporting applies only to sudden accidents and not to diagnosed work-related diseases.

stem: A bracket falls 5 m and strikes a labourer on his helmet. He says he is fine and goes back to work. An hour later he vomits and seems confused and drowsy. What should the supervisor do, and why?

options.A: Send him home in a colleague's car with advice to see a doctor if symptoms last until the next morning, to save waiting
options.B: Call 999, keep him still and watched, and record the accident, as a delayed head injury can turn life-threatening
options.C: Give him a sweet drink and a painkiller, then move him back to light duties where the supervisor can see him
options.D: Let him rest in the welfare cabin for the afternoon, because he walked away unaided and the helmet absorbed the impact safely

explanation: Drowsiness and vomiting after a blow to the head can signal bleeding or swelling in the skull, so he needs emergency medical help and constant observation, and the accident must be recorded.

why_wrong.A: Delaying help and moving him unobserved risks collapse on the way; this needs emergency care now.
why_wrong.C: Light duties do not treat a possible head injury, and giving medication is not an acceptable first-aid response here.
why_wrong.D: Walking away does not exclude serious brain injury, and symptoms like these need urgent medical assessment.

common_mistake: Judging a head injury by whether the person can walk and talk straight afterwards.

stem: Four labourers will barrow wet concrete 60 m along a rutted, sloping plank route to a footing, about 200 loads in a day. The foreman says barrows are cheap and the lads are fit. Which approach best follows the manual handling regulations?

options.A: Pick the four strongest workers after assessing their fitness, since individual capability is the main factor and the route and load matter much less
options.B: Allow a rest break each hour and rotate the barrow users, since a task is acceptable under the regulations when the time spent on it is limited
options.C: Avoid the manual movement if reasonably practicable with a dumper or pump, otherwise assess the task and route and reduce the load, distance and slope
options.D: Issue back support belts and lifting technique training, as these two measures keep a barrow task within the regulations without altering the route

explanation: The regulations require avoiding hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable, then assessing and reducing the remaining risk, including task, load and ground conditions.

why_wrong.A: The individual is only one factor, and the task, load and working environment must also be assessed and improved.
why_wrong.B: Rotation shortens each person's exposure but leaves the avoidable hazard and the poor route unchanged.
why_wrong.D: Belts are not a proven control and training does not replace avoiding or redesigning the handling operation.

common_mistake: Relying on fit workers, rotation or technique training instead of first asking whether the load can be moved mechanically.

stem: Groundworkers wash oily hands and scrub concrete off tools using diesel from the site bowser, and one rinses his boots with petrol before lunch in a cabin where a heater is running. Which statement best identifies the problems?

options.A: Fuels strip skin oils and can cause dermatitis, and petrol vapour near a heater can ignite, so provide a skin cleanser and a safer tool-cleaning method
options.B: Wearing disposable gloves removes the hazard, so fuel can remain the cleaning method provided the cabin heater is switched off while it is used
options.C: Washing with fuel is acceptable if followed by soap and water, since the main risk is swallowing it, which hand washing before lunch controls
options.D: Diesel is harmless to skin because it is oily, but petrol vapour is a fire risk, so petrol should be banned and diesel allowed for cleaning

explanation: Fuels are unsuitable cleaning agents because they harm skin and give off flammable vapour, so the substitute should be a proper cleanser and a safer method of cleaning tools.

why_wrong.B: Thin gloves can be permeated by fuel, and the better control is to stop using fuel for cleaning at all.
why_wrong.C: Skin damage and absorption happen during contact, so washing afterwards does not undo them and the vapour fire risk remains.
why_wrong.D: Diesel also strips skin oils and irritates the skin, so neither fuel is suitable for washing hands or tools.

common_mistake: Treating fuels as handy cleaning products when they damage skin and give off flammable vapour.

stem: An electrician must fit a rain cowl on the flat roof of a 1.8 m high electrical kiosk, standing on the roof beside an open edge above a paved yard. The supervisor says the Work at Height Regulations apply only above 2 m, so a stepladder and care will do. What is the best response?

options.A: There is no minimum height, so avoid the roof work if possible, for example with a long-handled tool, or use a guarded platform before personal protection
options.B: Work under 2 m falls under the general duty only, so a risk assessment is enough and the electrician may choose equipment by his own judgement
options.C: The 2 m figure applies, but a harness and short lanyard should be used because personal protection is the accepted standard at any height near an edge
options.D: The regulations apply, but only where the surface below is hard, so the paved yard makes it a controlled task needing a colleague to foot the ladder

explanation: The regulations apply wherever a fall could cause injury, and the hierarchy is to avoid the work, then prevent falls with collective protection, before relying on personal equipment.

why_wrong.B: The regulations apply at any height and require the hierarchy to be followed, which personal judgement alone does not do.
why_wrong.C: No height threshold exists, and a harness ranks below avoidance and collective measures and cannot work with so little fall clearance.
why_wrong.D: The rules apply whenever a fall could cause injury, and footing a ladder does not stop a fall from the roof edge.

common_mistake: Believing that work below 2 m is exempt from the Work at Height Regulations.

stem: Look at the scene. The decorator says the set-up is wide and steady and that he will be up there for only an hour. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: The stepladders are the wrong height for the room, so taller ones fitted with a locked spreader would give the board a more secure rest
options.B: The board is too thick for the span, so a thinner one would flex less and share the load more evenly between the two stepladders beneath it
options.C: He is not wearing a harness, which is the main protection needed on any raised platform, and a lanyard clipped to a stepladder would solve it
options.D: Stepladders are not designed to carry a board as a working platform, so the board can slip or twist and the legs can spread under sideways load

explanation: A stepladder is a means of access, not a support for a platform, so bridging two with a board gives an unstable and unsuitable work surface that is a common cause of falls.

why_wrong.A: No height of stepladder is designed to carry a board, so taller ones would only increase the fall height.
why_wrong.B: Board thickness is not the flaw, because ladders are not designed to support a platform of any thickness.
why_wrong.C: A stepladder is not a suitable anchor for fall arrest, and the unsuitable platform itself is the fault to correct.

common_mistake: Improvising a working platform from ladders and a board because it looks wide and steady for a short job.

stem: Aggregate has bridged in the outlet of a 4 m deep storage hopper at a batching plant. A fitter proposes climbing in through the top hatch on a rope to break the arch with a bar while the feed is stopped and a colleague watches. What is the best advice?

options.A: Treat it as a confined space and do not enter, as the arch can collapse and engulf him, but clear it from outside with rodding or a vibrator
options.B: It is not a confined space because the top hatch is open to the air, so a work-at-height assessment and a gas test cover the hazards
options.C: Entering is acceptable because the feed is stopped, provided he wears a harness and the watcher can haul him out if the material moves
options.D: Entry is acceptable under a permit once the hopper is half emptied, because a lower material level removes the engulfment risk for the fitter

explanation: Free-flowing solids that can engulf a person are a specified risk, and entry should be avoided by doing the work from outside whenever that is possible.

why_wrong.B: Engulfment by loose material is a specified risk whether or not the space is open, and a gas test does not deal with it.
why_wrong.C: A rope cannot pull a person out of collapsing material quickly enough, and entry must be avoided if the work can be done from outside.
why_wrong.D: Partly emptying does not stop a remaining arch collapsing, and a permit does not replace the duty to avoid entry.

common_mistake: Assuming a confined space needs a bad atmosphere, and ignoring engulfment by loose material.

stem: A dumper driver regularly takes calls from the office while driving between the stockpile and the compound, using a hands- free earpiece. The foreman says that is fine because both hands stay on the controls. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A ban is unnecessary since the dumper has a camera and alarm, and these aids will warn pedestrians even when his attention is on the call
options.B: Hands-free calls are acceptable on private ground, since phone restrictions apply only on public roads and each driver can judge when it is safe to talk
options.C: Only handheld use needs controlling, so hands-free calls can continue if the driver slows to walking pace and keeps each call under two minutes
options.D: Calls distract plant drivers even hands-free, so the assessment should ban phone use while plant moves and give a safe way to pass urgent messages

explanation: The risk comes from divided attention rather than hand position, so the employer should stop calls while plant moves and provide safe alternatives such as stopping points or radios.

why_wrong.A: Aids support an alert driver but cannot replace one, and they do not warn of every hazard.
why_wrong.B: The employer's health and safety duties apply on site, and distraction is a mental load that a driver cannot reliably judge for himself.
why_wrong.C: Lower speed and shorter calls reduce but do not remove the loss of attention, so the moving-plant risk remains.

common_mistake: Believing that hands-free calling is safe because the driver's hands stay on the controls.

stem: A labourer lifts two sections of pedestrian barrier away from a deep excavation so he can wheel a barrow through, then leaves them down. Nobody is hurt. The manager says no offence arose because there was no injury. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: It is an offence only if he was warned in writing not to move the barrier, because intent cannot be shown without a signed instruction from his supervisor
options.B: Reckless or intentional interference with a safety provision is an offence under HSWA section 8 even without injury, and the manager should ask why the route was blocked
options.C: Only the employer can be prosecuted, because workers have no personal legal duty over barriers and are covered entirely by the employer's general duty to provide safe arrangements
options.D: The labourer commits an offence only if someone is later hurt, because section 8 depends on actual harm, so the manager should log a near miss and take no further action

explanation: Section 8 makes deliberate or reckless interference with anything provided for safety an offence for any person, with no need for harm, and a sound employer also fixes the access problem that prompted it.

why_wrong.A: Section 8 covers intentional or reckless acts, and no written warning is needed to establish that.
why_wrong.C: Workers carry personal duties under the Act, including not interfering with safety provisions, in addition to the employer's duties.
why_wrong.D: Section 8 is breached by the interference itself, so the absence of injury does not remove the offence.

common_mistake: Assuming that moving a safety barrier is only a problem once somebody has been injured by its absence.

stem: A rotating laser level, marked Class 3R, is set on a tripod in a corridor where other trades walk, with its beam sweeping at head height. The operator says it is only a weak red line. What is the best way to control the eye risk?

options.A: Set the beam well above or below head height or screen it, warn other trades, and switch it off when unattended, since the blink reflex is no dependable defence
options.B: Keep the laser running all day for stability and put one warning sign at each end of the corridor, since a sign alone gives passers-by complete protection
options.C: Issue ordinary impact-rated safety glasses to everyone using the corridor, because standard eyewear filters laser light of this power and so removes any need to move the beam
options.D: Leave the beam at head height and rely on the blink reflex, since visible red light of this class always makes anyone look away before any harm occurs

explanation: Removing the beam from eye level and limiting its use controls the hazard at source, whereas the aversion reflex cannot be relied on to prevent a harmful direct exposure.

why_wrong.B: A sign only warns and does not remove the beam from eye level, so it cannot be the sole control.
why_wrong.C: Impact eyewear is not designed to filter laser wavelengths, so it gives a false sense of protection.
why_wrong.D: The blink reflex is not guaranteed, particularly if someone stares or views the beam through optical aids.

common_mistake: Assuming a low-power visible laser is harmless because it looks dim and people will blink away from it.

stem: A specialist firm will radiograph pipe welds in a plant room on Friday evening. The site manager says the radiographer will look after everything, so other trades need not be told. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Let other trades pass through while the work continues, as radiation harms only those who stand directly in front of the equipment while an exposure is under way
options.B: Give the contractor advance written notice and agree access control, so trades are told of the controlled area and kept out until the source is confirmed secured
options.C: Let other trades carry on behind the plant room wall, since any wall absorbs the radiation and access control is needed only inside the room where the work happens
options.D: Tell only the night security guard, since the radiographer's lead apron also protects any other worker who happens to wander into the area during a short exposure

explanation: Radiography contractors need advance notice and liaison on restricting access to their controlled area, so everyone else on site is excluded while the source is exposed.

why_wrong.A: Scattered radiation can affect people outside the direct beam, so the controlled area has to be kept clear.
why_wrong.C: Shielding and distance must be assessed by the contractor, and a wall cannot simply be assumed to make the area outside safe.
why_wrong.D: A lead apron worn by someone else gives other workers no protection, and access must be physically controlled.

common_mistake: Leaving a specialist contractor to manage their own hazard without telling the other trades who share the site.

stem: Look at the scene. The foreman says the painter is fully protected because he wears a respirator, goggles, coveralls and gloves. What is the most significant problem, and what should be done?

options.A: His gloves are the wrong type, and thick chemical- resistant gauntlets would stop paint penetrating at spray pressure, so he could then clean the tip safely while it is live
options.B: His coveralls are inadequate, since liquid-tight Type 3 suits are needed for paint contact with skin, and that is the main route of harm from airless spraying
options.C: His respirator is inadequate, because airless spraying of any coating requires an air-fed hood, and that is the main hazard to put right before any other change
options.D: He is wiping the tip of a gun still under pressure, and gloves cannot stop paint injecting through skin, so release the pressure and lock the trigger first

explanation: Airless paint leaves the nozzle at a pressure that can inject through skin and glove alike, so the only safe controls are depressurising, locking the trigger and fitting a tip guard.

why_wrong.A: No glove withstands high-pressure injection, so changing glove type does not make wiping a live tip safe.
why_wrong.B: The serious danger is injection at the nozzle, which a different suit would not prevent.
why_wrong.C: Respiratory protection depends on the coating's assessment, and it is not the most urgent danger shown in the picture.

common_mistake: Believing that wearing gloves makes it safe to touch the tip of a pressurised spray gun.

stem: A fixer handling sharp-edged metal studs finds a split across the palm of his issued gloves. The stores are closed. His supervisor suggests wrapping tape round the split and carrying on until morning. What is the correct response?

options.A: Stop using them and report the defect at once, because the employer must keep PPE in good repair and replace it, and tape cannot restore protection
options.B: Carry on at his own risk, because once PPE is issued the wearer alone decides whether it is still good enough and the employer has no further duty
options.C: Carry on with the taped gloves, because tape restores the cut resistance of the palm and the repair only needs reporting at the next weekly PPE check
options.D: Buy a pair from a shop and wear them, because the employer's duty to replace PPE ends once the original pair has been used for a full shift

explanation: Workers must report loss or obvious defects immediately, and the employer must keep PPE in efficient working order and good repair, which includes prompt replacement.

why_wrong.B: The employer must maintain and replace PPE, so the risk cannot simply be passed to the wearer.
why_wrong.C: Tape does not restore tested cut resistance, and a defect must be reported immediately and not saved for a later check.
why_wrong.D: The employer's duty to maintain and replace PPE continues, and a worker should not be left to source equipment.

common_mistake: Patching damaged PPE with tape and carrying on rather than reporting it and swapping it for a sound replacement.

stem: A scaffolder's competent person inspects a facade scaffold each week and hangs a fresh tag, but keeps the written reports at the scaffolder's yard. The principal contractor holds no copies. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Reports are needed only for a monthly check, since the weekly inspections need nothing more than a verbal confirmation to the principal contractor on the day concerned
options.B: For a platform with a possible fall of 2 m or more, the report must reach the person it was done for within 24 hours and stay on site until work ends
options.C: The tag is the legal record of the inspection, so a separate written report is optional provided the tag carries the date, the inspector's initials and the lift covered
options.D: The reports may stay at the scaffolder's yard indefinitely, because only the firm that carried out the inspection has any duty to hold the records of its own checks

explanation: The inspection report must be given to the person on whose behalf the inspection was carried out within 24 hours and kept at the site until the construction work is finished.

why_wrong.A: Each required inspection must be recorded and reported, and a verbal confirmation does not meet that duty.
why_wrong.C: A tag is only evidence of a recent inspection, and the written report is still required.
why_wrong.D: The report goes to the person who obtained the inspection, who must keep it on site until the work ends.

common_mistake: Treating a scaffold tag as a substitute for the written inspection report that has to be on site.

stem: A steel fixer works 7 m up a portal-frame column, held by a waist belt and an adjustable positioning lanyard looped round the column so both hands are free to bolt. Nothing else is fitted. The supervisor says a taut lanyard means he cannot fall. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A second positioning lanyard looped round the same column counts as the required back-up, since it would give him identical protection should the first lanyard slip
options.B: The belt and lanyard are enough alone, because a taut lanyard stops any fall and a back-up is needed only for rope work carried out above ten metres high
options.C: A work positioning system may be used only with a suitable back-up that prevents or arrests a fall, such as a separate fall-arrest line to a harness
options.D: Replacing the belt with a full-body harness allows the lanyard to serve as the only system, since a harness spreads load and removes the need for a back-up

explanation: Schedule 5 of the Work at Height Regulations allows work positioning only with a suitable back-up, because a positioning line can slacken or fail and the user may fall.

why_wrong.A: A second line of the same kind on the same anchorage does not arrest a fall if the positioning method fails.
why_wrong.B: A back-up is required whatever the height, and the ten-metre threshold is invented.
why_wrong.D: A harness improves body support but the positioning system still needs its own separate back-up.

common_mistake: Assuming that a tight positioning line, by itself, makes a separate fall-arrest back-up unnecessary.

stem: A concrete pump's placing hose blocks during a slab pour. The operator wants to knock off a coupling clamp to clear the plug quickly, while the hose-end man stays at the discharge to keep the pour going. What is the safest course?

options.A: Knock off the clamp straight away but stand to one side of the coupling, because any pressure escapes only in a straight line along the hose itself
options.B: Stop pumping and release pressure as the maker requires, keep everyone clear of the hose line, and open the coupling only when pressure is confirmed off
options.C: Keep the hose-end man at the discharge holding the hose firmly, because a hose held tightly by hand cannot whip when the clamp is finally released
options.D: Strike the blocked section with a lump hammer while pumping continues slowly, so the pour is not delayed while the plug is shaken loose from outside

explanation: A blocked line can hold stored pressure that throws out the plug or whips the hose, so pressure must be released and people kept clear before any coupling is opened.

why_wrong.A: Released pressure can eject the plug and whip the hose unpredictably, so standing to one side is not a control.
why_wrong.C: A person cannot restrain a pressurised hose, and holding it places him in the danger zone.
why_wrong.D: Continuing to pump into a blockage increases stored pressure and puts workers beside the likely failure point.

common_mistake: Opening a blocked pump line quickly to save the pour without first making sure the stored pressure is gone.

stem: Overnight, a steel road plate was laid over a trench across a street used by buses and delivery lorries. By morning it has shifted a few centimetres, leaving a gap at one edge. The supervisor wants to cone the gap and leave it for the day. What should happen?

options.A: Allow only cars and vans across until the end of the shift, since lighter vehicles cannot move a plate and a small gap is a minor fault
options.B: Leave it in place and cone the gap, since a plate that has carried traffic overnight has proved it is strong enough for the rest of the day
options.C: Lay a second plate over the first to cover the gap, because doubling the steel thickness removes any need to secure either plate against movement later
options.D: Stop vehicles using it, then re-fix the plate secured against movement and ramped at the edges, and confirm it is rated for the heaviest traffic expected

explanation: A plate over a live trench must be rated for the traffic and secured so it cannot move, because coning a gap does not stop heavy vehicles shifting or dislodging it.

why_wrong.A: Light vehicles can still catch a loose plate or edge, and the plate must be properly secured before any traffic uses it.
why_wrong.B: Surviving traffic overnight proves nothing about its rating, and a plate that has already moved is a clear failure of its securing.
why_wrong.C: Stacking plates does not stop movement and can create a trip and a sliding hazard between the layers.

common_mistake: Treating cones as the fix for a loose road plate instead of securing it and confirming it is rated for the traffic.

stem: A site has stripped 400 kg of old copper cable. A man in a van offers cash on the spot, saying he is in the scrap trade and will take it with no paperwork because it has resale value. Which approach correctly follows waste and scrap rules?

options.A: Hand it over without paperwork, because material with a resale value counts as a product rather than as waste, so no transfer records are needed at all
options.B: Hand it only to a registered waste carrier with the right dealer or collector licence, keep written transfer records, and take payment by cheque or transfer
options.C: Accept the cash after noting his van registration, because that note satisfies the duty of care for waste and cash payment is allowed for small loads
options.D: Sell it for cash if the value is under a set limit, since the waste and payment rules apply only to larger loads of scrap metal from site

explanation: Scrap metal is still waste, so the duty of care applies to its carrier and paperwork, and scrap metal dealers may not pay cash.

why_wrong.A: Scrap sent for recycling is waste in the hands of the site, so the duty of care and records still apply.
why_wrong.C: Cash payment for scrap is prohibited whatever the amount, and a note of the van does not prove he is authorised.
why_wrong.D: The cash ban and duty of care apply to scrap loads of any size, so no size limit permits this sale.

common_mistake: Treating valuable scrap as a product to sell for cash to whoever turns up, instead of waste that must go to an authorised carrier.

stem: Plasterers must carry 20 kg tubs of adhesive up to a second- floor flat. The assessment specifies a sack trolley, but the stair doorway is too narrow, so the gang carries tubs by hand. The manager wants to discipline them. What is the best response?

options.A: Discipline the gang for ignoring the written control, because a documented assessment sets the standard that workers must follow as written
options.B: Let the gang choose how to carry the tubs, since experienced workers' judgement can replace a control that does not suit the building
options.C: Review the assessment with the gang, adopt a control that suits the real layout such as a hoist, then brief everyone
options.D: Keep the trolley requirement and repeat it at the next briefing, because the assessment is sound and only compliance has failed

explanation: A control that cannot be used in practice is a flaw in the assessment, so it must be reviewed with the people doing the work and replaced by one that is workable.

why_wrong.A: Discipline leaves an unworkable control in place and ignores the employer's duty to review an assessment that is no longer valid.
why_wrong.B: Leaving the method to individual judgement removes the planned control and leaves the heavy carry unassessed.
why_wrong.D: Repeating an impossible instruction does not remove the manual handling risk or make the control achievable.

common_mistake: Blaming workers for bypassing a control without asking whether the control was ever practical on that site.

stem: A fitter wipes a hydraulic hose on a tracked excavator with his gloved hand and feels a sting. There is a tiny pinhole in his fingertip, with little pain and no bleeding. He wants to finish the shift. What should happen?

options.A: Clean and plaster the puncture, then watch it for a day, as a small painless wound with no bleeding is unlikely to be deep
options.B: Squeeze the finger to push the oil back out and wash it with soap, because removing the fluid quickly stops it spreading
options.C: He should go to hospital urgently and tell staff it may be a high-pressure injection, as deep damage can hide beneath a small mark
options.D: Record it in the accident book and see his GP if swelling appears, since hospital treatment is for wounds that bleed or hurt badly

explanation: Fluid forced under the skin by a pinhole leak can destroy deep tissue while the surface looks trivial, so it needs urgent specialist treatment.

why_wrong.A: The small, painless appearance is typical of an injection injury, and delay can lead to amputation.
why_wrong.B: Squeezing can drive the fluid further into the tissue, and washing does not remove what is already under the skin.
why_wrong.D: Waiting for swelling or pain wastes the critical early hours, and the severity of the injury does not match its look.

common_mistake: Judging an injury by how small and painless it looks rather than by what was under pressure.

stem: A supplier delivers sealed, unlabelled crates of ducting fittings to a first-floor job. Their weights vary widely and some are heavier at one end. Two fitters must carry them up a stair, and the manager says to tell them to lift carefully. What is best?

options.A: Set a single weight limit for one person on every crate, because a fixed figure removes any need to know each load's weight
options.B: Tell them to tilt each crate to feel its weight before lifting, since judging the load on the day replaces a formal assessment
options.C: Issue back support belts for the job, as supports reduce the strain enough to let unmarked crates be carried by hand
options.D: Weigh each crate and mark its weight and heavy end, assess the carry, and use a hoist or team lift for heavy ones

explanation: Where a load could cause injury, the employer should avoid or assess the handling and give information on its weight and heaviest side so the method can be matched to it.

why_wrong.A: The law sets no safe weight, and a single figure ignores the stair route, awkward shape and uneven balance of each crate.
why_wrong.B: Testing by feel exposes the person to the risk and does not give the information needed to plan the carry.
why_wrong.C: Back belts are not proven to prevent injury and are no substitute for avoiding, assessing and reducing the handling risk.

common_mistake: Assuming that telling people to lift carefully, or issuing a support belt, counts as a manual handling control.

stem: A slinger-signaller with Type 1 diabetes, who skipped breakfast, becomes sweaty, shaky and muddled by mid-morning. A colleague says he must be drunk and should be left to sleep it off. What is the right action?

options.A: Keep him signalling but pair him with a second signaller, because he is conscious and his colleague can cover any errors he makes
options.B: Give no sugar until a breath test rules out alcohol, since sweet drinks could mask the real cause of his confusion
options.C: Take him off the lifting task, give a fast-acting sugary drink if he is conscious, and keep him supervised until he recovers
options.D: Let him rest in the cabin for an hour with nothing to eat or drink, because the confusion will pass once he is calm

explanation: Confusion, sweating and shaking in a person with diabetes suggests low blood sugar, which needs quick sugar and removal from safety-critical work until fully recovered.

why_wrong.A: A person with impaired judgement must not carry out safety-critical lifting duties, even with a second person alongside.
why_wrong.B: Delaying treatment while testing for alcohol risks worsening low blood sugar, and the symptoms point to a hypo first.
why_wrong.D: Rest alone does not raise blood sugar, so his condition can deteriorate towards unconsciousness.

common_mistake: Assuming that confusion and unsteadiness at work must come from alcohol rather than a treatable medical condition.

stem: A six-storey facade scaffold runs along a busy public pavement while bricklayers work on its upper lifts. The planner proposes only a hanging debris net and cones along the kerb. Which arrangement best protects pedestrians below?

options.A: Barriers set one metre out from the scaffold base, because falling objects drop straight down and cannot travel beyond that line
options.B: Debris netting on the outer face, plus a banksman who stops pedestrians whenever a bricklayer shouts that material is moving
options.C: A thin plywood canopy at first-floor level, since any overhead cover is enough once netting has been fitted above it
options.D: A lit, covered walkway with a deck strong enough to stop falling objects, plus brick guards and toe boards on the working lifts

explanation: Overhead protection that can arrest falling objects, combined with edge protection at source, protects the public where netting and cones cannot.

why_wrong.A: Objects bounce, roll and are carried by wind, and a barrier does not protect against anything that falls.
