why_wrong.B: Netting does not stop heavy items, and a shouted warning gives too little time for pedestrians to react.
why_wrong.C: A canopy that is not designed for impact loads can fail or shatter and drop its own debris onto the walkway.

common_mistake: Relying on nets, cones or warnings to protect the public when a falling object needs a physical barrier overhead.

stem: Look at the scene. The roofer says the ladder is tied, set at a safe angle and standing on firm paving. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: Nobody is footing the base of the ladder, so it could slip sideways while he climbs towards the roof edge
options.B: The ladder stands on paving without a purpose-made stabiliser, so its feet could skid outwards under his weight
options.C: He is not clipped to the ladder with a harness, which is mandatory for every ladder climb to a flat roof
options.D: The ladder stiles stop level with the roof edge, so he has no handhold while stepping across onto the roof

explanation: A ladder used to reach another level should extend at least 1 m above the landing point so that the climber keeps a secure handhold when stepping on or off.

why_wrong.A: A ladder that is tied at the top does not also need footing, which is only a last-resort way of securing it.
why_wrong.B: Firm, level paving with a correctly angled, tied ladder gives a stable base, and the real fault is at the top of the ladder.
why_wrong.C: Harnesses are not a requirement for climbing a secured ladder, and a lanyard clipped to a ladder gives no real fall protection.

common_mistake: Checking the angle, base and tie of a ladder but forgetting that the top must extend above the landing for a handhold.

stem: Digging a drainage trench in a former wartime dock area, an excavator bucket uncovers a rusty, finned metal cylinder about a metre long. The operator wants to lift it out and set it aside until the engineer arrives. What is correct?

options.A: Tap it with a spade to hear whether it rings hollow, since an empty casing is harmless scrap that can go in a skip
options.B: Photograph it, keep digging at the far end of the site, and ask the client to arrange a survey by the end of the week
options.C: Stop work, leave it untouched, move everyone well back and alert the police, treating it as live until experts say otherwise
options.D: Lift it carefully clear of the trench and cordon off the pile, because a slow, smooth lift is safer than leaving it beside an unstable trench wall

explanation: Suspected unexploded ordnance can be unstable after decades underground, so it must not be moved or disturbed and the area must be cleared pending specialist disposal.

why_wrong.A: Striking an unknown item is dangerous, and it is impossible to tell from outside whether it is empty or fused.
why_wrong.B: Carrying on work and waiting days leaves people near a possible explosive, when the area should be cleared at once.
why_wrong.D: Lifting or moving a suspect item can set it off, and the bucket and trench wall should not be disturbed further.

common_mistake: Treating a rusty old object as scrap or as someone else's problem instead of as possibly live ordnance.

stem: While trenching, an excavator bucket cuts into an unmarked buried cable, with a flash and bang. The operator is unhurt in the cab, and the cable may still be live. A banksman shouts for him to climb out. What is the best action?

options.A: Reverse the bucket out of the cable at once to free it, then lower the bucket and check the damage on foot
options.B: Stay in the cab, keep the machine still, warn others to keep clear and call the network operator at once
options.C: Climb down quickly and run to the banksman, so that he can check for burns while the machine stays where it stopped
options.D: Wait a few minutes to see if the flash dies away, then cover the cable with soil and carry on with the trench

explanation: A damaged live cable can energise the machine and the ground nearby, so the operator stays inside, others are kept well away and the supplier is called to make the cable dead.

why_wrong.A: Moving the machine could drag or tear the cable further and increase the danger to everyone close by.
why_wrong.C: Stepping from an energised machine to the ground can cause a fatal shock and the area is not safe.
why_wrong.D: A cable that has flashed is a continuing danger and burying it hides it from the supplier.

common_mistake: Assuming the danger is over once the bang and flash have stopped.

stem: A strip-out crew will remove ten split air-conditioning units from an office. The foreman plans to cut the copper pipework with a disc cutter to save time, then scrap the units, saying the gas inside will soon disperse. What is correct?

options.A: A suitably certified engineer must recover the refrigerant before removal, since releasing it harms the climate and cutting charged pipework is hazardous
options.B: Remove the units as they are and let the carrier deal with the gas later, since a signed transfer note passes on all responsibility
options.C: Cut the pipes outdoors in the open air, because the gas then disperses harmlessly and release in the open is permitted
options.D: Cap each pipe after cutting and send the units for scrap, since the small amount of gas in each unit falls below any legal limit

explanation: Refrigerant gases are strong greenhouse gases that must not be deliberately vented, and recovering them before pipes are cut also avoids a pressurised release.

why_wrong.B: A transfer note does not remove the producer's duty, and the gas must be recovered by qualified people before disposal.
why_wrong.C: Deliberately releasing these gases is prohibited wherever it happens, and it also harms the atmosphere.
why_wrong.D: There is no small-quantity exemption for deliberate venting, and cutting the pipe has already released the charge.

common_mistake: Assuming that gas inside scrap equipment is harmless and will simply blow away.

stem: A contractor will pressure-wash flaking old paint, possibly lead-based, and algae from a brick facade beside a road. The run- off would flow along the kerb to a surface-water drain, and the foreman suggests a gully sock to catch the solids. What is better?

options.A: Keep the gully sock and add a spill kit beside the drain, since a sock removes dissolved paint residues as well as solids
options.B: Add a biodegradable detergent to the wash water, because water treated with it is safe for the surface-water drain
options.C: Wash only on dry, warm days so the run-off evaporates, because the water will dry before it can reach the gully
options.D: Collect the run-off with bunds and a vacuum, settle or filter it, and dispose of it with the sewerage undertaker's consent or as waste

explanation: Surface-water drains lead to watercourses, so contaminated wash water must be contained and disposed of through a route with consent rather than allowed into them.

why_wrong.A: A sock catches only coarse solids and does nothing to dissolved or very fine pollutants such as lead compounds.
why_wrong.B: Detergent adds pollution, and it does not make water containing paint residues acceptable for a surface-water drain.
why_wrong.C: Run-off from pressure washing flows freely and is not removed by evaporation, so the paint residues still reach the drain.

common_mistake: Treating a gully sock or a spill kit as enough to let contaminated wash water run into a surface-water drain.

stem: A labourer notices that the barrier line separating his work bay from the plant route has been dragged aside by delivery drivers for two days. He tells nobody, reasoning that supervisors walk the site daily and reporting is their job. Which statement about his legal position is most accurate?

options.A: He has done enough by mentioning it informally to a workmate, because that shows reasonable care and passes responsibility up the chain of command
options.B: His reporting duty covers only injuries and near misses, so a moved barrier remains a management matter until someone has actually been hurt or nearly struck
options.C: Only supervisors and managers carry a duty to monitor protection arrangements, so a worker with no safety role cannot be in breach by staying quiet
options.D: He must tell his employer or a nominated person about a shortcoming in the protection arrangements affecting his work, so staying silent is itself a breach

explanation: Regulation 14 of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations requires employees to report serious danger and any shortcoming in the employer's protection arrangements that affects their work.

why_wrong.A: The report must reach the employer or a person nominated to receive such reports, not simply a colleague.
why_wrong.B: The duty extends to shortcomings in protection arrangements, not just to harm that has already occurred.
why_wrong.C: Employees have their own statutory duty to report, whatever their job title.

common_mistake: Assuming that because supervisors walk the site, spotting a failed control is their job alone and not the worker's duty to report.

stem: A joiner who has heated a two-part epoxy adhesive daily for months gives his employer a doctor's written diagnosis of occupational asthma. The manager calls it a private medical matter, does not report it, and changes nothing for the five other joiners. What is the correct response?

options.A: Wait until the HSE confirms the cause of the illness, because a doctor's written diagnosis alone cannot show that his work was responsible for it
options.B: Report it under RIDDOR as a diagnosed disease, then review the COSHH controls and consider health surveillance for colleagues with the same exposure
options.C: No report is needed unless he is off work for more than seven days, because a reportable occupational disease follows the same threshold as a workplace injury
options.D: Log it in the accident book only, because RIDDOR disease reports are made by the treating doctor and the employer has no part in the reporting process

explanation: Occupational asthma from regular exposure to a known respiratory sensitiser is reportable on a doctor's written diagnosis, and the COSHH duty to review controls protects the others exposed.

why_wrong.A: A written diagnosis from a doctor is exactly what triggers the report; the HSE does not need to confirm causation first.
why_wrong.C: Reportable diseases are triggered by the written diagnosis and the type of exposure, not by days lost.
why_wrong.D: The employer is the responsible person who must report a diagnosed reportable disease.

common_mistake: Treating a diagnosed work-related illness as a private health matter instead of a trigger to report and to review the controls for everyone exposed.

stem: A risk assessment for lining a tank records 84 dB(A) from a nearby compressor, controlled by ear defenders, and separately rates a toluene-based coating as low risk because vapour levels are modest. The assessor treats the two hazards independently. What should the assessment have considered?

options.A: Nothing further, because each hazard has its own limit and meeting both separately guarantees that their combined effect on hearing is also acceptable to the employer
options.B: The ear defenders, which remove the extra risk entirely because attenuating the noise cancels any added hearing effect of the vapour that is being inhaled
options.C: Whether the two interact, since solvents such as toluene can add to noise-induced hearing damage, so the combined effect may need tighter controls or earlier checks
options.D: Only the noise, because solvent vapour harms the lungs and skin and has no bearing on hearing, so any interaction belongs in the COSHH file and nowhere else

explanation: The Control of Noise at Work Regulations require the assessment to consider, so far as practicable, any interaction between noise and ototoxic substances used at work.

why_wrong.A: Separate compliance does not rule out additive harm, which the assessment must consider.
why_wrong.B: Defenders do nothing about the solvent absorbed by breathing, so the interaction is not removed.
why_wrong.D: Some solvents are ototoxic and can damage hearing, so they are relevant to the noise assessment.

common_mistake: Assessing each hazard in isolation and assuming that their effects on the body never combine.

stem: In a closed basement, a crew uses a petrol-driven disc cutter, with a fan blowing air across the doorway. One worker develops a headache and feels dizzy, and a colleague says it is just the dust. What is the correct view?

options.A: Rotate the crew every thirty minutes to limit individual exposure and keep the cutter running to finish the job on time
options.B: Open a second doorway and carry on, since the symptoms show the worker is unfit and the others have no sign of any effect
options.C: Treat it as dust irritation and fit tighter dust masks, as masks also filter engine fumes and will protect the whole crew
options.D: Suspect carbon monoxide, stop work, move everyone into fresh air, then switch to a battery or electric tool

explanation: Petrol engines give off odourless carbon monoxide, which builds up in enclosed spaces, so work stops, people move to fresh air and a non-combustion tool replaces the cutter.

why_wrong.A: Rotation keeps people exposed to a gas that is dangerous at low levels and has no safe exposure routine.
why_wrong.B: Symptoms in one person are a warning for all and the cause must be removed first.
why_wrong.C: A dust mask does not filter carbon monoxide gas.

common_mistake: Blaming headaches in enclosed spaces on dust when engine exhaust is in use.

stem: A worker grinding a concrete floor wears a battery-powered respirator with a loose-fitting hood. Twenty minutes in, its low- airflow alarm sounds. A colleague says the fan means he can carry on until the shift ends. What is the correct action?

options.A: Keep working but use shorter grinding passes, because the alarm shows only reduced filter efficiency and less time at the floor lowers the dose he receives
options.B: Carry on while the hood still feels inflated, because the fan keeps positive pressure inside and any leakage then flows outwards rather than inwards
options.C: Leave the dusty area at once and check the battery, filter and hose, because the alarm means airflow has dropped below the safe minimum
options.D: Silence the alarm and continue, since a warning that clears after a few seconds only reflects a brief dip in battery voltage and not a loss of airflow

explanation: A low-airflow alarm shows the hood is no longer delivering its designed protection, so work stops until the cause is found and corrected.

why_wrong.A: Shorter passes do not restore protection and the wearer still breathes unfiltered dust through the hood.
why_wrong.B: Pressure felt by the wearer is not reliable evidence of the minimum airflow the hood needs.
why_wrong.D: Dismissing the alarm ignores a warning that protection may have fallen, whatever the cause.

common_mistake: Assuming that powered respiratory equipment keeps protecting the wearer after its airflow warning has sounded.

stem: Scaffolders erecting a facade scaffold clip double lanyards to ledgers as they work and fit each lift's guardrails only after its boards are laid. The supervisor says the harnesses make this acceptable. What does the work at height hierarchy require them to consider first?

options.A: A suspension rescue plan on its own, because planning for rescue is what the regulations treat as the effective control for people working at an open edge
options.B: Collective protection that goes up before the people, such as advance guardrails or temporary platforms, with harnesses only where that is impossible
options.C: Nothing more, because trained scaffolders with double lanyards are safer than guardrails, which crews tend to knock or interfere with while they are erecting
options.D: A stricter inspection regime, since regular checks by a competent person are the main legal safeguard for the erectors while the scaffold is being built

explanation: The Work at Height Regulations give collective protection priority over personal protection wherever it is reasonably practicable.

why_wrong.A: A rescue plan is needed with harnesses, but it responds to a fall rather than preventing one.
why_wrong.C: Personal systems rely on the worker's behaviour and rank below collective measures.
why_wrong.D: Inspection of the finished scaffold does not protect erectors from falling while they build it.

common_mistake: Treating a harness as the default protection when erecting scaffolds instead of fitting collective measures ahead of the person.

stem: Mains power fails at an occupied shop where fitters are working. To restore lighting, a labourer plugs a portable generator into a wall socket using a lead with a plug at each end, leaving the main switch on. Which statement correctly describes the danger and the proper arrangement?

options.A: It is safe once the main switch is turned off, because the building is then cut off from the supply and the generator behaves like any other source of power
options.B: The lead can leave live pins exposed and back-feed the supply, so fixed wiring may be connected only through a changeover switch fitted by a competent electrician
options.C: It is acceptable if the generator is rated below the socket circuit's fuse, because the circuit then cannot be overloaded and the lead is just another extension
options.D: The only risk is damage to the generator from mains voltage, since the socket's RCD already protects everyone else working on the premises from any shock

explanation: Connecting a generator to fixed wiring by a plug-in lead can energise exposed pins and back-feed the supply, so a competent electrician must install an interlocked changeover arrangement.

why_wrong.A: Switching off does not remove the exposed pins, lack of earthing arrangements or the risk of the supply being restored.
why_wrong.C: Rating does not remove the exposed live pins or the back-feed to the supply.
why_wrong.D: The main danger is to people, and an RCD does not prevent live pins or back-feed.

common_mistake: Treating a generator as just another socket outlet that can be plugged into fixed wiring with a home-made lead.

stem: Look at the scene. The driver says it is only a two-minute run to the stockpile and the track is level and dry. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: People ride on a machine built only for the driver, so a bump or braking could throw them off or under the wheels
options.B: The skip should be raised slightly while travelling, so that the driver has a clearer view of the track surface ahead of him
options.C: The pallet of kerbs on the verge is too close to the track, so vibration from the passing dumper could bring the whole stack down
options.D: No banksman is walking ahead of the machine, so the driver cannot be guided along what is a straight and otherwise clear stretch of track

explanation: Site dumpers are not built to carry passengers, and anyone riding on the skip is at risk of falling and being run over or crushed.

why_wrong.B: Travelling with the skip raised reduces stability and is not good practice; it is also not what makes this scene dangerous.
why_wrong.C: The stack is neat, set back from the track and not the most significant hazard in the picture.
why_wrong.D: A banksman is not the key issue on a clear, level track; the bigger fault is people on the machine.

common_mistake: Assuming a short journey on firm, level ground makes it acceptable to let colleagues ride on plant not built for passengers.

stem: Two mobile cranes will share a lift of a 14-tonne steel truss. Each operator has checked that his own crane's chart covers the whole load, so the foreman proposes that each follows his own signaller and works at his own pace. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A tandem lift is a complex lift needing a written plan from a competent person, with load shares for both cranes and coordinated control
options.B: The foreman's approach is fine, since each crane could carry the full load alone, so the lift stays safe even if one crane takes all the weight
options.C: The two operators can agree signals by radio between themselves, as a trained pair does not need a formal plan or coordinated control of the lift
options.D: A written plan is needed only if the cranes are different makes, because matched cranes share a load equally whatever the rigging or lift speed

explanation: The HSE treats multi-crane lifts as complex, requiring a written plan from someone with specific competence because load sharing changes as the lift proceeds.

why_wrong.B: Capacity of each crane alone does not control how the load shifts between them as they lift and slew.
why_wrong.C: Complex lifts need a written plan and suitable supervision rather than informal agreement between operators.
why_wrong.D: Equal sharing cannot be assumed, even with identical cranes, so every tandem lift needs planning.

common_mistake: Assuming that two competent operators with adequate cranes can safely share a load without a specific plan.

stem: In June, a manager must clear rough grass and scrub from a 0.4 ha plot where a walkover finds slow-worms beneath old roofing felt. He plans to strip it with a bulldozer in one pass, saying slow-worms are common and so unprotected. Which approach best fits the law and good practice?

options.A: Proceed with one pass, because common species are protected only from sale and keeping, not from being harmed by lawful development works
options.B: Hand-pick the animals from under the felt before machines start, then scrape immediately, which removes any risk of an offence on the rest of the plot
options.C: Clear it in midwinter instead, since hibernating reptiles lie deep and are unaffected by surface scraping, so the works would not harm any of them
options.D: Take advice from a qualified ecologist and clear in stages in the active season, with refuges removed, so animals move out before machines arrive

explanation: Native reptiles are protected from intentional killing and injury under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, and phased clearance in the active season reduces harm.

why_wrong.A: Intentional killing or injuring is itself an offence, and being common gives no exemption.
why_wrong.B: Picking up a few visible animals does not clear the rest of the site, and handling may itself need a licence.
why_wrong.C: Hibernating reptiles are vulnerable to being crushed or exposed, so winter clearance is not safer.

common_mistake: Thinking that a species being common means it has no legal protection when works kill or injure it.

stem: A drainage firm's three gangs work on a different customer's site each week and never visit the yard office, where the HSE health and safety law poster hangs. The owner says displaying it there meets the legal duty. What is the correct position?

options.A: A spoken summary of the main duties at the start of each new job is a lawful substitute, as no particular format is required
options.B: A poster no gang ever sees does not count, so each employee should be given the approved leaflet or pocket card
options.C: The duty passes to each customer whose site the gangs visit, because the occupier must inform everyone working on its premises
options.D: A poster in the yard office is enough, because the duty is owed to the company as a whole and not to each employee on its books

explanation: Employers must either display the approved poster where employees can read it or give each employee the approved leaflet, and a poster in a yard nobody visits achieves neither.

why_wrong.A: The regulations specify the approved poster or leaflet, so a verbal summary does not satisfy them.
why_wrong.C: The employer's duty to inform its own employees is not transferred to the occupier of the premises they visit.
why_wrong.D: The information duty is owed to every employee, so it must actually reach them wherever they work.

common_mistake: Assuming a poster on the wall of a base office informs employees who spend their working week on other people's sites.

stem: A contractor strips ceilings in a corridor beside an occupied hospital ward. The risk assessment covers only the operatives' own dust exposure, with FFP3 masks as the control. Several patients on the ward are immunosuppressed. What is the most important omission?

options.A: Nothing is missing, because masks protect those doing the work and the hospital alone is responsible for its patients' safety
options.B: The ward windows should be kept shut during the work, since closing them removes the need for any further dust control measures
options.C: Patients are not considered, so dust must be contained at source with sealed barriers and extraction before it can reach the ward
options.D: A higher-rated mask should be issued to the operatives, since better personal protection also prevents spores leaving the work area

explanation: Employers must assess risks to non-employees affected by their work, and for vulnerable patients this means containing dust at source rather than relying on masks worn by the workers.

why_wrong.A: The contractor owes a duty to others affected by its work, and masks do nothing to stop dust spreading.
why_wrong.B: Dust travels through doors, corridors and ventilation, so shut windows alone do not stop it reaching patients.
why_wrong.D: Masks protect only the wearer, while dust on clothing and in the air still spreads from the work area.

common_mistake: Writing the assessment around the workers' own exposure and forgetting vulnerable people nearby who can be harmed by the same dust.

stem: A joiner grips a mains drill with a cracked casing, shaking and unable to let go. A colleague reaches him first. What should the colleague do, and what should happen once the joiner is free and says he feels better?

options.A: Isolate or unplug at the supply without touching him, then get him checked medically, as shock can upset the heartbeat
options.B: Cut the drill's cable with the nearest side cutters to end the contact, then watch him on site for an hour before deciding on a medical check
options.C: Pull him clear by his clothing to break contact at once, then let him resume work if he feels well and looks perfectly normal again
options.D: Keep everyone back until an electrician arrives to isolate the supply, then leave it to the joiner whether he sees a doctor

explanation: Touching a casualty still in contact with the supply risks a second victim, and electric shock can cause heart rhythm problems that are not obvious at first.

why_wrong.B: Cutting a live cable is itself dangerous, and observation on site is no substitute for a medical check.
why_wrong.C: Touching him while he is live endangers the rescuer, and feeling well does not exclude delayed heart effects.
why_wrong.D: Leaving him in contact while waiting is dangerous, and the decision to seek care should not rest with the casualty.

common_mistake: Rushing to grab a shock victim before the supply is off, then assuming no treatment is needed because the casualty looks fine.

stem: A concreter kneels for an hour in wet concrete and wet cement has gone inside his boots. He feels no pain and wants to finish the pour first. By afternoon his knees are red and sore. What is the correct view?

options.A: Cement only harms skin when it is dry and dusty, so let the concrete dry on his knees and brush it off in the evening
options.B: Wet cement is alkaline and can burn without early pain, so wash with clean water, remove wet clothing, get medical advice
options.C: Rinse his knees with a little solvent from the site store to cut the cement, because water would make the burn spread
options.D: Mild redness from cement is normal for the trade, so apply barrier cream after work and keep using the same boots tomorrow

explanation: Cement burns can develop painlessly over hours, so affected skin is washed thoroughly, soaked clothing and boots are removed, and medical advice is sought, with proper waterproof PPE used in future.

why_wrong.A: Wet cement is the main cause of burns, and leaving it on the skin makes injury worse.
why_wrong.C: Solvents irritate skin further and do nothing helpful; copious clean water is the standard treatment.
why_wrong.D: Redness may be a chemical burn, and barrier cream does not treat it or make wet boots safe.

common_mistake: Waiting for pain before treating skin that has been in contact with wet cement.

stem: A supervisor notices a normally reliable plumber has become withdrawn, makes errors and has worked long hours on a tight deadline for weeks. A colleague says it is his own business and he should toughen up. What is the best approach?

options.A: Record a warning for his errors, because a formal process will motivate him to improve quality before the deadline
options.B: Move him to a lighter task without discussing it and tell the gang the reason so that they can keep an eye on him
options.C: Talk to him privately, treat work stress as a risk to assess, adjust workload and hours, and point him to support
options.D: Leave him alone since stress is a personal matter outside the employer's duties, and step in only if he asks for help

explanation: Employers must assess and manage work-related stress like other health risks, which means a private conversation, changes to workload and hours, and access to support.

why_wrong.A: Discipline adds pressure and ignores the likely cause of the errors.
why_wrong.B: Telling colleagues breaches his privacy and acting without talking to him may not tackle the cause.
why_wrong.D: Work-related stress is a health risk that the employer must manage.

common_mistake: Treating signs of work-related stress as a personal weakness rather than a hazard to manage.

stem: A cleaner is given thin disposable gloves to wipe parts with a solvent, and finds they go soft and tacky within minutes. The supervisor says any glove is fine if the worker changes it when it looks damaged. What is the best response?

options.A: Carry on with the same gloves but double them up, since two thin layers always give the same protection as one thick glove
options.B: Keep to the thin gloves and wash hands afterwards with a hand cleaner, since the gloves are only there for general hygiene
options.C: Use the heaviest leather gloves in the store, because thick material resists any liquid and keeps the hands dry and safe
options.D: Pick gloves from the solvent's safety data sheet by breakthrough time, and replace them before that time has passed

explanation: Solvents can pass through some glove materials without visible damage, so gloves are chosen for the substance using safety data and breakthrough times and replaced on schedule.

why_wrong.A: Doubling gloves of the wrong material still lets the solvent through to the skin.
why_wrong.B: Washing afterwards does not stop skin absorbing the solvent while the work is going on.
why_wrong.C: Leather absorbs solvents and holds them against the skin, so thickness is not the right test.

common_mistake: Judging chemical glove protection by how thick or intact the glove looks.

stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the fitter is properly protected because he wears cut-resistant gloves and safety boots. What is the most significant problem?

options.A: A fixed blade is drawn towards his body, so a retractable knife and cut-away technique should come before gloves
options.B: A longer blade should be fitted so the sheet is sliced in one pass, because shorter exposure time makes the task much safer
options.C: Kneeling on the floor is the problem, so he should cut the sheet on a bench, since posture is the main factor in knife injuries
options.D: The gloves are too thin for blade work, so a heavier leather pair should be issued since hand protection is the main control for knives

explanation: PPE is the last line of defence, and the safer tool and cutting method remove the hazard of the blade travelling towards the body and the guiding hand.

why_wrong.B: A longer exposed blade increases the injury potential and does not change the direction of cut or the guiding hand position.
why_wrong.C: Posture matters for strain, but the exposed blade drawn towards the body is the main cause of knife injury here.
why_wrong.D: Heavier gloves would still be PPE, which ranks below changing the tool and technique, and they would reduce his grip and feel.

common_mistake: Assuming that gloves and boots make unsafe cutting practice acceptable.

stem: A steel erector must cross a 12 m run of beams to reach a connection, clipping and unclipping one single lanyard at each bracket as he moves. He says he is clipped on most of the time. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Each change leaves him unconnected for a moment, so he needs continuous protection such as a twin-tail lanyard or a running line
options.B: Moving unclipped is allowed for experienced steel erectors, as they are competent to judge when a slip is unlikely
options.C: A longer single lanyard solves it, by letting him reach the next bracket before he unclips from the one he is leaving
options.D: Being attached most of the time is acceptable, because a fall is only likely during the few seconds he spends crossing between brackets

explanation: A fall can happen at any moment, so a system that keeps at least one connection attached throughout movement is required rather than one that leaves gaps.

why_wrong.B: Competence does not remove the need for continuous protection, since falls are caused by unexpected slips and trips.
why_wrong.C: A longer lanyard increases the fall distance and still does not give him a second connection at the point of transfer.
why_wrong.D: A fall is possible at any moment, and the unprotected seconds are exactly when it can happen.

common_mistake: Accepting short gaps in connection while moving between anchors because the unprotected time seems brief.

stem: A supported 2 m trench was inspected at 07:00. At 10:30 a block of soil slumps from one wall into the trench without hurting anyone. The foreman says the morning inspection is valid for the whole shift, so work can resume once the soil is cleared. What is correct?

options.A: The 07:00 inspection covers the shift, so work can restart once the fallen soil is shovelled out and the gang checks the supports
options.B: Any trained operative may confirm it is safe again, because a competent person is needed only if supports have been removed
options.C: The fall is an event that may affect stability, so a competent person must inspect again and be satisfied before anyone re-enters
options.D: A further inspection is needed at the start of the next shift, since the rules tie checks to shift starts and not to events

explanation: Excavations must be inspected at the start of each shift and after any event likely to affect strength or stability, including a fall of earth, before work continues.

why_wrong.A: An earth fall is a trigger for a fresh inspection, so the morning inspection does not cover it.
why_wrong.B: The inspection must be done by a competent person, whatever the condition of the supports.
why_wrong.D: Inspection is also required after events affecting stability, not only at the start of each shift.

common_mistake: Treating the start-of-shift inspection as covering everything that happens until the end of the shift.

stem: A fitter must change a wheel on an articulated dumper. He jacks the front axle clear of the ground and works beneath it on level ground with the engine off. He says the jack and the stopped engine make it safe. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A jack can slip or fail, so the axle needs rated stands or blocks, and the articulation lock must be fitted to stop folding
options.B: A jack plus the stopped engine is enough on level ground, so nothing more is needed under a raised axle while he works there
options.C: The articulation lock matters only when travelling on slopes, so fitting it for maintenance on level ground is unnecessary extra work
options.D: Chocks on the other wheels replace stands, because a chocked machine cannot move whatever happens to the jack at the raised end of it

explanation: Raised plant must be supported by suitably rated stands or blocks rather than a jack alone, and the articulation lock prevents the machine pivoting while someone is working under it.

why_wrong.B: A jack alone is not a safe support to work beneath, and level ground does not prevent it failing or slipping.
why_wrong.C: The lock is also a maintenance safeguard, preventing the frame from pivoting while someone works near the joint or beneath.
why_wrong.D: Chocks stop rolling but do nothing if the jack fails and the raised axle drops onto the person below.

common_mistake: Trusting a jack and a stopped engine to hold a raised machine while working beneath it.
